title: A consumer declares its project facts in one tracked file
description:
## What

The foundation every other child depends on. Introduce `<consumer>/.claude/cerebro-project.conf` and
one reader for it, in the shape cerebro-#58 §1 specifies.

**Tracked, not under `.cerebro/`.** `.cerebro/models.conf` is a personal preference and rightly
ignored; how a project installs itself, what its gate is called and where its source lives are facts
every clone needs. A file under the gitignored `.cerebro/` vanishes on a fresh clone and every new
machine silently skips the step, surfacing much later as a confusing failure inside somebody's
worktree.

## The format is already proven

`key value`, one per line, `#` to end of line is a comment — exactly `models.conf`, whose 17-line
bash-3.2 `config_lookup` in `scripts/launch:94-140` already parses it and already resolves
most-specific-first. Reuse that, do not invent a second mechanism.

## The reader

A `scripts/project-conf <key> [default]` sibling to `scripts/consumer-root`. `consumer-root` is the
established seam — 12 scripts already ask it rather than deriving a root — and this belongs next to
it, resolved the same way. It must answer for a missing file and a missing key without failing, so
an unconfigured consumer degrades rather than aborts.

## Keys this epic will need

Named here so the file is designed once rather than grown by accident:

    project_name        Atlantis HUD
    bead_prefix         ah            # or probe: bd config get issue_prefix
    default_branch      main          # or probe: git symbolic-ref refs/remotes/origin/HEAD
    app_paths           ^(packages|crates|apps)/
    audience_noun       player        # default: user
    install             pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
    prewarm             pnpm --filter @atlantis/browser-core build:wasm
    reclaim_dirs        target node_modules
    retro_dir           docs/retrospectives
    mockup_dir          docs/ui
    release_cmd         pnpm run release

## Detect, never guess

Absent keys fall back to detection where detection is safe — `pnpm-lock.yaml` -> `pnpm install
--frozen-lockfile`, `package-lock.json` -> `npm ci`, `yarn.lock` -> `yarn install --immutable`,
otherwise nothing. **No prewarm is ever inferred**: nothing could guess `build:wasm`, and a wrong
guess costs minutes per worktree. Whichever branch is taken is printed, so a skipped step is visible
rather than a mystery.

Note `bead_prefix` and the forge slug need not be configured at all — the consumer's
`.beads/config.yaml` already holds `issue_prefix` and `github.repository`, readable with
`bd config get`. Prefer the probe to a duplicated key wherever bd already knows the answer.

## Tests

Against the fabricated consumer the bash suite already builds: a configured key wins; a missing key
falls back; a missing file is not an error; comments and blank lines are ignored; a value containing
spaces survives.

Upstream: https://github.com/rmstdope/cerebro/issues/58 §1
design:
## Context

**The foundation of the ah-qled epic: six of its children depend on this bead** (`.2`, `.3`, `.4`,
`.6`, `.7`, `.8`), so it is the one that must be right.

Cerebro is meant to be mountable at `.claude/cerebro` by any repository, but it was extracted from
atlantis-hud and still carries it — `.claude/cerebro/CLAUDE.md:11-14` says so outright. This bead
introduces **`<consumer>/.claude/cerebro-project.conf`** and one reader for it, in the shape
`rmstdope/cerebro#58 §1` specifies.

**Tracked, not under `.cerebro/`.** `.cerebro/models.conf` is a personal preference and rightly
git-ignored; how a project installs itself, what its gate is called and where its source lives are
facts **every clone needs**. A file under the ignored `.cerebro/` vanishes on a fresh clone, so every
new machine silently skips the step and it surfaces much later as a confusing failure inside
somebody's worktree.

Cerebro change, so **two PRs** — and this one has a second half in the consumer, see *Increments*.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### 1. The format is already proven — reuse it, but not verbatim

`key value`, one per line, `#` to end of line — exactly `models.conf`, whose bash-3.2
`config_lookup` (`scripts/launch:100-121`) already parses that shape.

**But `config_lookup` cannot be reused as written, and this is the trap in the bead.** It does:

```bash
read -r k m e <<<"$line"      # three columns: key, model, effort
```

so `install pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` would yield `m=pnpm`, `e=install --frozen-lockfile`.
`models.conf` genuinely has three columns; **this file has two — a key and a value that runs to the
end of the line.** The reader must be:

```bash
read -r k rest <<<"$line"     # key, then everything else as one value
```

That is precisely the bead's own test *"a value containing spaces survives"*, and it is the one way
to get this wrong while believing you reused the proven code.

**Keep everything else about `config_lookup`**, especially the comment-stripping, whose reasoning
carries over word for word:

```bash
line="${line%%#*}"
```

Everything from a `#` on is a comment **wherever it starts**, so `default_branch main # for now`
does not read `# for now` as part of the branch name. **The cost is that a value can never contain
`#`** — state that in the file's header rather than leaving it to be discovered.

### 2. The reader — `scripts/project-conf`

A sibling of `scripts/consumer-root`, which is **the established seam**: twelve scripts already ask
it for a root rather than deriving one, and this belongs next to it and resolves the same way.

```
scripts/project-conf <key> [default]
```

- Reads `$(consumer-root --shared)/.claude/cerebro-project.conf`. **`--shared`**, matching how
  `launch` reads `models.conf` and how `agent-state` resolves its state directory — the fleet's
  configuration is one answer for the checkout, not per-worktree.
- Prints the value, or `default` when the key is absent, or nothing when neither exists.
- **Never fails.** A missing file, a missing key and an unreadable file all exit `0` with the
  default. An unconfigured consumer must degrade, not abort — this reader will be called from
  scripts that already run under `set -euo pipefail`, where a non-zero exit would take the caller
  down with it.

### 3. Detect, never guess

Where a key is absent, detection is allowed **only when it is safe**:

| Probe | Answer |
|---|---|
| `pnpm-lock.yaml` | `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` |
| `package-lock.json` | `npm ci` |
| `yarn.lock` | `yarn install --immutable` |
| none of those | nothing |

**No `prewarm` is ever inferred.** Nothing could guess `pnpm --filter @atlantis/browser-core
build:wasm`, and a wrong guess costs minutes per worktree. Absent means absent.

**Whichever branch was taken is printed to stderr**, in the manner `launch` already prints its
`models.conf` hit (`:135`) — *"a session on an unexpected model is otherwise a mystery three days
later"*. The same is true of a skipped install.

### 4. Prefer a probe to a duplicated key

`bead_prefix` and the forge slug **need not be configured at all**: the consumer's
`.beads/config.yaml` already holds `issue_prefix` and `github.repository`, readable with
`bd config get`. **A key that duplicates something `bd` already knows is a second source of truth
that will drift.** Where `bd` knows the answer, ask `bd`.

### 5. The keys, designed once

Named now so the file is designed rather than grown by accident. **This bead adds the file and the
reader; it changes no caller** — each key is consumed by a later child.

```
project_name   Atlantis HUD
default_branch main                 # or probe: git symbolic-ref refs/remotes/origin/HEAD
app_paths      ^(packages|crates|apps)/
audience_noun  player                # default: user
install        pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
prewarm        pnpm --filter @atlantis/browser-core build:wasm
reclaim_dirs   target node_modules
retro_dir      docs/retrospectives
mockup_dir     docs/ui
release_cmd    pnpm run release
```

### 6. The consumer's own file — in the second PR

`atlantis-hud` gets `.claude/cerebro-project.conf` with the values above, **tracked**, in the same PR
that bumps the submodule pin. Nothing reads it yet; it is there so the children that follow have
something true to read, and so the tracked-not-ignored decision is exercised immediately.

## Increments

**In `.claude/cerebro` (PR one):**

1. **A key is read.**
   RED: `tests/project-conf.sh` against the fabricated consumer the suite already builds —
   a configured key wins.
   GREEN: the reader.
2. **The awkward lines.**
   RED: **`a value containing spaces survives`**; a comment after a value is stripped; a whole-line
   comment is ignored; a blank line is ignored; a key with no value yields the default.
   GREEN: `read -r k rest` and the `%%#*` strip.
3. **An unconfigured consumer degrades.**
   RED: a missing key returns the default; **a missing file is not an error** (exit 0); an
   unreadable file is not an error.
   GREEN: the guards.
4. **Detection, and only where it is safe.**
   RED: `pnpm-lock.yaml` yields the pnpm install; `package-lock.json` yields `npm ci`; no lockfile
   yields nothing; **`prewarm` is never inferred**.
   GREEN: the probes.
5. **The branch taken is said out loud.**
   RED: the chosen source appears on **stderr**, never stdout — a caller substituting the value must
   not get the explanation in it.
   GREEN: the message.

**In `atlantis-hud` (PR two):** the tracked `.claude/cerebro-project.conf`, and the submodule pin
bump. **PR one merges first.**

## The test plan

| Test | Where | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| a configured key wins | `tests/project-conf.sh` | the reader |
| **a value containing spaces survives** | same | the `read -r k rest` trap |
| a trailing comment is stripped from a value | same | `%%#*` |
| a whole-line comment and a blank line are ignored | same | the format |
| a missing key returns the default | same | degradation |
| **a missing file is not an error** | same | exit 0 under `set -e` callers |
| an unreadable file is not an error | same | same |
| `install` is detected from each lockfile | same | safe detection |
| **`prewarm` is never inferred** | same | the explicit rule |
| **the explanation goes to stderr, not stdout** | same | substitutability |
| every existing test | `tests/*.sh` | **unchanged — no caller changes in this bead** |

**Suites:** cerebro's CI runs `for t in tests/*.sh`, so a new file needs no registration.

## User-facing decisions

**None, and none to ask for.** Nothing here reaches a player: it is a config file and a bash reader
in the fleet harness. The decisions this bead contained were settled upstream in
`rmstdope/cerebro#58 §1` and restated in the bead — the tracked location, the `key value` format, and
the key list.

**Decided here** (architecture): `read -r k rest` rather than `config_lookup`'s three-column read;
`consumer-root --shared` for consistency with `models.conf` and `agent-state`; exit 0 on every
absence; the explanation on stderr; and shipping atlantis-hud's own conf file in the second PR so the
tracked decision is exercised at once.

## Out of scope

- **Every other child of ah-qled.** This bead adds the file and the reader and **changes no caller** —
  `.2` through `.11` each consume a key. If a script other than the new one appears in the diff,
  scope has slipped.
- **`models.conf`**, which stays exactly as it is: personal, ignored, three columns.
- **Removing the hardcoded `origin/main`** (`.3`) and the rest of the audit.
- **Adding keys nobody consumes yet** beyond the list above.

## Validation

In `.claude/cerebro`:

```bash
bash tests/project-conf.sh
for t in tests/*.sh; do bash "$t" || echo "FAILED: $t"; done
```

Then by hand, from the consumer root:

1. `scripts/project-conf project_name` → `Atlantis HUD`.
2. **`scripts/project-conf install`** → `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, **whole**. If it comes back
   as `pnpm`, the three-column read was reused and the bead is wrong.
3. `scripts/project-conf nonexistent_key fallback` → `fallback`, exit `0`.
4. **Move the conf file aside and repeat**: still exit `0`, still the fallback, nothing on stdout.
   Then put it back.
5. `scripts/project-conf install 2>/dev/null` — the value alone, with the explanation suppressed.
   Confirm the explanation was on **stderr**.
6. `scripts/project-conf prewarm` in a consumer with no such key → **nothing**, never a guess.
7. Confirm the file is **tracked**: `git status` after a fresh clone shows it present, and
   `git check-ignore .claude/cerebro-project.conf` says nothing.
8. Confirm **no existing script behaves differently** — nothing consumes the file yet.

## Known traps

- **`config_lookup` reads three columns; this file has two.** `read -r k m e` splits
  `install pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` into a model and an effort. Use `read -r k rest`. This is
  the single way to reuse the proven code and still be wrong, and the bead's own test for it is
  *"a value containing spaces survives"*.
- **Exit 0 on every absence.** Callers run under `set -euo pipefail`; a non-zero exit for "no such
  key" takes the caller down instead of falling back.
- **A value cannot contain `#`.** The comment strip is `%%#*` and runs wherever the `#` appears —
  correct, deliberate, and worth stating in the header rather than discovering.
- **Never infer `prewarm`.** Nothing could guess `build:wasm`, and a wrong guess costs minutes per
  worktree.
- **The explanation goes to stderr.** A caller doing `x="$(project-conf install)"` must get the value
  and nothing else.
- **Do not add a `bead_prefix` key.** `bd config get issue_prefix` already knows, and a duplicate is a
  second source of truth that will drift.
- **Tracked, not under `.cerebro/`.** Putting it beside `models.conf` makes it vanish on a fresh
  clone — the exact failure this bead exists to prevent.
- **Change no caller.** Six children depend on this one; a caller changed here is a conflict with
  whichever child owns it.
- **Two PRs, cerebro first.**
acceptance_criteria:
- `<consumer>/.claude/cerebro-project.conf` exists as a TRACKED file (not under the gitignored .cerebro/), in `key value` format with `#` to end of line and blank lines ignored.
- `scripts/project-conf <key> [default]` reads it via `consumer-root --shared` and prints the value, or the default when the key is absent, or nothing when neither exists.
- A value runs to the end of the line: `scripts/project-conf install` returns `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` WHOLE. The reader uses `read -r k rest`, NOT config_lookup's three-column `read -r k m e`.
- The reader NEVER fails: a missing file, a missing key and an unreadable file all exit 0 with the default, because callers run under `set -euo pipefail`.
- `install` is detected from a lockfile when unconfigured (pnpm-lock.yaml, package-lock.json, yarn.lock, else nothing). `prewarm` is NEVER inferred.
- Whichever branch was taken is printed to STDERR, never stdout, so a caller substituting the value gets the value alone.
- No `bead_prefix` key is added - `bd config get issue_prefix` already knows, and a duplicate would drift.
- The header states that a value cannot contain `#`.
- NO existing caller changes in this bead. Six children of ah-qled consume the keys; if any script other than the new one appears in the diff, scope has slipped.
- atlantis-hud gets its own tracked .claude/cerebro-project.conf in the second PR, alongside the submodule pin bump, after the cerebro PR merges.
- cerebro's test suite passes, including a new tests/project-conf.sh.
close_reason: Delivered in PR #515 (consumer half) and rmstdope/cerebro#67 (the reader)

title: Cerebro runs in a project that is not atlantis-hud
description:
## Why

Cerebro is meant to be mountable at `.claude/cerebro` by any repository, but it was extracted from
atlantis-hud and still carries it. `.claude/cerebro/CLAUDE.md:11-14` says so outright: "they were
extracted from `atlantis-hud` and still name it throughout".

The upstream audit is **rmstdope/cerebro#58** (2026-08-18), and its structure is adopted here: a
consumer-owned project file, then the agent instructions, then the prose. Its decision that the file
must be **tracked** — `<consumer>/.claude/cerebro-project.conf`, not under the gitignored `.cerebro/`
— is adopted too: how a project installs itself is a fact every clone needs.

## What this epic adds to that issue

A full re-audit at `e1e64dd` (2026-08-21, five commits past the audit) found the issue's §1
understates the executable coupling. It says `scripts/prepare-worktree` is "the only part that
breaks another consumer". It is not:

- **`origin/main` is hardcoded 15 times across 5 scripts.** `scripts/launch-preflight:64` refuses to
  start *any* agent unless the branch is literally `main`, then runs `git merge --ff-only` on the
  consumer's tree. On a `master`/`trunk` consumer the fetch fails, `$target` goes empty and the whole
  staleness guard is silently skipped — ah-puoj's guarantee stops holding with nothing said.
- **`scripts/prune-worktrees.sh:115` deletes `$tree/target` by name.** Cargo's build dir, in a
  destructive sweep. A Node consumer's `node_modules/` is never reclaimed; a consumer with a source
  directory called `target/` loses it.
- **The sweeps encode atlantis-hud's git conventions** — `sweep-claims.sh:96` detects delivery by the
  commit scope `($id):`, `:97` excludes the literal `docs($id): mockup`, `sweep-stalled.sh:86`
  assumes branches start `<id>-`.
- **The roster is not overridable** (`scripts/roster:39-59`), and `scripts/agent-state:108` *rejects*
  an unknown phase with exit 2, so a consumer-added role cannot report state at all.
- **`emacs/cerebro.el` is not project-neutral either** — `bd` is a bare literal in 7 argv positions
  including `bd dolt push`; the label vocabulary and a 60-minute stalled threshold are `defconst`;
  the mount point `.claude/cerebro` is hardcoded twice. 18 `defconst` against 5 `defcustom`.
- **`source_dirs` has seven copies, not four** — `^(packages|crates|apps)/` and its prose form in
  `architect.md` (x2), `planner.md`, `reviewer.md`, `verifier.md` (x2), `user-feedback.md`,
  `release-notes/SKILL.md` and `CLAUDE.md:144`.
- **Cerebro's CI never mounts it as a consumer's submodule**, which is why none of the above was
  caught.

## Definition of done

The issue's, unchanged: a fresh consumer repository with no JavaScript in it can mount cerebro, run
`sync-symlinks.sh`, start every role from the fleet view, and have an implementer take a bead to a
merged PR without any agent running a command the project does not have. Made enforceable by the CI
child below, so it cannot rot again.

## What must not be stripped

The bead lifecycle and label handover; claim/heartbeat/lease discipline; P4-as-unranked; the
planner/implementer split; the eight mandatory plan headings; interview-don't-ask and
mockups-before-decisions; TDD; one bead per session; wait-by-blocking-not-by-ending-a-turn; the
state-file contract; the four-eye principle and one-review-per-bead; closed-is-not-terminal; the
retrospective discipline; the X-Men roster branding. That set is cerebro's product. Every coupling
below is removable without touching any of it.

Filed by Forge, commissioned investigation of 2026-08-21, cerebro at e1e64dd.
close_reason: All children closed; last was ah-qled.10, whose last child ah-qled.10.5 was delivered in PR #548

title: The F8 problem walk silently jumps back to the first problem whenever validation re-runs
description:
## The cost being paid

`the walk buttons step to the next problem and back, and wrap at the end`
(`tests/smoke/shortcuts.spec.ts:458`) fails in CI on diffs that cannot reach it, passes locally
every time, and goes green on a re-run. Three implementers have now paid a cycle each to work that
out from scratch, and the fix the first two agreed on is already in the file and did not hold.

The failure is always the same: `expect(unitPane).toHaveText(first)` times out at 15s having
resolved the locator ~34 times to the *previous* unit's text. `toHaveText` is a whole-pane exact
match, so the assertion has no barrier of its own — it waits for a pane to become byte-identical to
a string captured earlier, with nothing on screen that means "the walk has landed".

The important new fact is that the diagnosed remedy is already applied. ah-dlao and ah-f9q9 both
concluded the spec must wait on the header's `problems-chip` before clicking. `git blame` shows
that wait at `shortcuts.spec.ts:469`, added by ah-dlao itself on 2026-08-19 — and ah-3pr9 hit the
same failure on 2026-08-21 anyway, on both the first attempt and Playwright's retry. So the
validation debounce is not the whole cause, and the next implementer to meet this will re-run it a
fourth time.

## Evidence

- 0a0484d `feat(ah-dlao): walk a turn's problems by mouse as well as by key (#463)` —
  `docs/retrospectives/ah-dlao.md` §"Smoke tests raced the debounced validation and moved nothing":
  **three smoke runs, about 20 minutes, spent looking for a wiring fault that was not there.**
- 23d3404 `ci(ah-f9q9): run the PR browser jobs in the Playwright image (#465)` —
  `docs/retrospectives/ah-f9q9.md` §"The walk-buttons smoke spec failed in CI and passed eleven
  times out of eleven locally": **two CI cycles and one local spec run, about 20 minutes.**
- a003d41 `fix(ah-3pr9): draw fleets as ships and count vessels (#501)` —
  `docs/retrospectives/ah-3pr9.md` §"The walk-buttons smoke spec failed in CI again on a diff that
  cannot reach it": **one CI cycle plus a local wasm build and smoke run, about 15 minutes.** That
  retrospective ends "it has now cost three separate implementers a cycle each, which is the
  argument for doing it rather than re-running it a fourth time. That is a bead for the navigator
  to rank."
- Verified at 440b51f: `git blame -L 466,472 tests/smoke/shortcuts.spec.ts` attributes the
  `problems-chip` wait to 0a0484d (2026-08-19), two days before ah-3pr9's failure.

## Where

- `tests/smoke/shortcuts.spec.ts:458` — the spec
- `packages/shared/src/workspace/UnitPanel.tsx`, and whatever the walk buttons dispatch into — the
  barrier the spec needs has to be something the application actually renders

## What a refactoring would change

Give the walk a completion signal the test can wait on instead of comparing whole-pane text: a
testid carrying the current stop's identity (the unit id, or an index into the problem list), so
each step asserts `toHaveAttribute` on a single value that changes exactly once per click. That
removes both the 15s whole-text poll and the dependency on how much unrelated prose the unit pane
happens to render. If the pane text must stay the assertion, the alternative is an explicit
"walk settled" marker rather than a second timing heuristic — the first one is already in the file
and did not work.

Filed by Forge, daily sweep of 2026-08-21, range cec1dd0..440b51f.
design: ## Context `tests/smoke/shortcuts.spec.ts:458` — *"the walk buttons step to the next problem and back, and wrap at the end"* — has failed in CI on three separate beads, on diffs that cannot reach it, and passed locally every time. Forge filed this bead after the third (`ah-dlao`, `ah-f9q9`, `ah-3pr9`; about 55 minutes of implementer time between them). Its own summary is that the spec needs a barrier to wait on, and that the remedy the first two agreed on — waiting for the `problems-chip` before clicking, added by `ah-dlao` at `shortcuts.spec.ts:469` — is already in the file and did not hold. **Reading the application found why, and it is not a test problem.** Two facts, both in `AppShell.tsx`: 1. **The walk's position is a `useRef`.** `lastDiagnostic` (`AppShell.tsx:757`, read and written by `walkProblems`) is a ref, so **nothing renders from it**. There is no element anywhere whose content or attributes change when the walk moves. That is why the spec has to compare whole-pane text — there is nothing else to look at — and `toHaveText` against a string captured earlier has no barrier of its own, so it simply polls for fifteen seconds and gives up. 2. **Every re-validation silently resets the walk to the start.** ```ts // A fresh validation is a fresh walk: the old stop indexes a list that no longer exists. useEffect(() => { lastDiagnostic.current = null; }, [validated]); ``` Validation is debounced and re-runs while the player is still stepping. When one lands between two clicks, the walk goes back to problem 1 and neither the player nor the test is told. **Fact 2 is what defeated `ah-dlao`'s fix.** Waiting on the `problems-chip` proves the *first* validation landed; it does nothing about a *later* one arriving mid-walk. And it explains the CI-only signature exactly: CI is slower, so a debounce is far likelier to land between two clicks there than on a developer's machine. There is a **third, independent defect in the spec** worth fixing while here: `await expect(unitPane).not.toHaveText(first)` assumes two consecutive stops are in *different units*. `diagnosticTargets` walks problems in document order, so two problems in one unit are adjacent stops and the pane text is identical between them — that assertion then times out by design, whatever the timing. So the fix is not a testid bolted on for a test. It is to make the walk's position **real state that the application renders**, which fixes the flake, removes the invisible reset, and — the navigator's decision — tells the player where they are in a walk that wraps and therefore has no end to bump into. ## Files to change and what to reuse **`packages/shared/src/diagnosticNav.ts`** — two new pure functions and a type. This is where `diagnosticTargets` and `stepDiagnostic` already live, and the new logic belongs beside them: it is the same question (where does the walk stand) asked across two validations instead of one step. **`packages/shared/src/diagnosticNav.test.ts`** — the new functions' tests, following the shape already there. **`packages/shared/src/workspace/AppShell.tsx`** — `lastDiagnostic` becomes React state, the reset effect becomes a resume effect, and the position is passed down to `OrdersPanel`. Lines 739–772 are the whole of it. **`packages/shared/src/workspace/OrdersPanel.tsx`** — `WalkProblems` (line 194) gains the counter; `OrdersPanelProps` gains one prop beside `onWalkProblems` (line 61). **`packages/shared/src/workspace/OrdersPanel.test.tsx`** — already asserts the walk buttons' testids (lines 36, 51). Extend it. **`tests/smoke/shortcuts.spec.ts:458`** — the spec rewritten against the new barrier. Reuse, and do not re-implement: - `diagnosticTargets(text, diagnostics)` — unchanged. It already returns stops **in document order**, sorting by the block's `firstLine` plus the block-relative line, then by column. The new key function must produce keys consistent with that same ordering, so read the sort comparator at `diagnosticNav.ts:58-71` and derive from it rather than inventing a second notion of order. - `findUnitBlocks(text)` (`ordersDocument.ts`) — how the sort turns a block-relative line back into an absolute one. - `stepDiagnostic(count, last, direction)` — **unchanged.** Its contract (wrap at both ends; from `null`, start at the end matching the direction) is exactly what the resume rule below leans on. ## Increments ### 1 — `diagnosticNav.ts`: a comparable position for a stop ```ts /** Where a stop sits in the whole document, for comparing stops across two validations. */ export type StopKey = { line: number; column: number }; /** Each target's document position, in the order `diagnosticTargets` returned them. */ export function stopKeys(text: string, targets: readonly DiagnosticTarget[]): StopKey[]; ``` `line` is the block's `firstLine` plus the target's block-relative `problem.lineStart`; `column` is `problem.columnStart ?? 0`. **This is the same arithmetic the sort comparator already does** — factor it into a small local helper and have both the comparator and `stopKeys` call it, so the two can never drift. That shared helper is the point of this increment; two copies of it is the defect this whole bead is an instance of. Tests: keys come back in non-decreasing order for any input `diagnosticTargets` produced; two problems in one unit get distinct keys differing in `line` or `column`; a document with two blocks gives the second block's problems strictly larger `line`s than the first's. ### 2 — `diagnosticNav.ts`: the resume rule ```ts /** Where the walk stands after the problem list was rebuilt. */ export type Resume = { /** The stop the walk is on, as `stepDiagnostic`'s `last`. */ index: number | null; /** Whether `index` is a problem the player is actually standing on, or only a place to resume from. */ standing: boolean; }; export function resumeWalk(keys: readonly StopKey[], remembered: StopKey | null): Resume; ``` The rule, exactly — this is the navigator's **K1**, "the next one down the document": 1. `remembered === null` → `{ index: null, standing: false }`. 2. A key **equal** to `remembered` (both fields) → `{ index: thatIndex, standing: true }`. The problem survived; the player is still on it, and the next step goes to the one after it. 3. Otherwise, the first index whose key is **greater than** `remembered` (compare `line`, then `column`) — call it `after`: - `after > 0` → `{ index: after - 1, standing: false }`. Standing one *before* it is what makes the next `stepDiagnostic(count, index, 1)` land **on** `after`, which is K1's promise: the problem that would have come next anyway. - `after === 0` → `{ index: null, standing: false }`, because `stepDiagnostic` from `null` in direction 1 already gives 0. 4. Nothing greater than `remembered` → `{ index: null, standing: false }`. The walk wraps, so the next step goes round to the top. **`standing: false` is why the counter blanks after you fix the problem you were on**, and that is correct rather than a compromise: you are not on a problem any more, and the navigator chose (**N1**) that no position means no counter. The place to resume from is still remembered; it is simply not shown. Tests, one per branch, plus: - The exact-match branch beats the "first greater" branch when both could apply. - A remembered key that is now the **last** problem still returns `standing: true`. - An empty `keys` array returns `{ index: null, standing: false }` for any `remembered`. - Composed with `stepDiagnostic`: with keys for 7 problems, remembering #3, deleting #3, then `stepDiagnostic(6, resume.index, 1)` returns the index of what was #4. **Write this one first** — it is the bead's actual promise, and it is the assertion that catches an off-by-one in branch 3. ### 3 — `AppShell.tsx`: the position becomes state `lastDiagnostic` stops being a ref: ```ts const [walkStop, setWalkStop] = useState({ index: null, standing: false }); /** The document position of the stop the walk is on, kept across re-validations. */ const walkKey = useRef(null); ``` The keys for the current validation, beside `problemTargets` (line 733): ```ts const problemKeys = useMemo(() => stopKeys(validated.text, problemTargets), [validated, problemTargets]); ``` The reset effect at line 739 **becomes a resume effect** — same position in the file, same dependency: ```ts // A fresh validation rebuilds the list, so the old index means nothing - but the player's place in // the turn does. Resume by document position: the same problem if it survived, otherwise the first // one at or after where they stood (ah-9ess). Resetting to the top was the old behaviour; it moved // the walk under the player without telling them, and it is what three CI failures were actually // about. useEffect(() => { setWalkStop(resumeWalk(problemKeys, walkKey.current)); }, [problemKeys]); ``` **Key on `problemKeys`, not on `validated`.** `problemKeys` is memoised from `validated`, so it moves whenever `validated` does — but keying on the derived value is what makes the effect's dependency the thing it actually reads. `walkProblems` (line 757) keeps its shape and updates both: ```ts const walkProblems = useCallback( (direction: 1 | -1) => { const step = stepDiagnostic(problemTargets.length, walkStop.index, direction); if (step === null) return; setWalkStop({ index: step, standing: true }); walkKey.current = problemKeys[step] ?? null; const target = problemTargets[step]; // ... unchanged from here: selectProblem, or goToUnit + setPendingProblem }, [problemTargets, problemKeys, walkStop.index, unit, goToUnit] ); ``` **`walkKey` stays a ref on purpose.** Nothing renders from it, and putting it in state would make the resume effect depend on a value it also writes. Pass down beside `onWalkProblems` (line 3259): ```tsx walkPosition={ walkStop.standing && walkStop.index !== null ? { at: walkStop.index + 1, of: problemTargets.length } : null } ``` `null` covers every state the navigator's **N1** says shows nothing: before the first step, with no problems at all, and after fixing the problem you were standing on. ### 4 — `OrdersPanel.tsx`: the counter `OrdersPanelProps` gains, beside `onWalkProblems`: ```ts /** Where the F8 walk stands, one-based, or null when it is not on a problem. */ walkPosition?: { at: number; of: number } | null; ``` and `WalkProblems` renders it between the two buttons: ```tsx {walkPosition ? ( {walkPosition.at}/{walkPosition.of} ) : null} ``` Two things about that, both load-bearing: - **`hidden … sm:inline` is the navigator's W2** — below the breakpoint the counter is not shown and the arrows remain. **But the element is still in the DOM, carrying `data-position`.** That is the whole trick that makes W2 free: Playwright's `toHaveAttribute` does not require visibility, so the test's barrier exists at every width even though the counter is only drawn above `sm`. Rendering nothing at all below the breakpoint would put the flake back at narrow viewports, which is the one cost the navigator was told W2 carried — and this removes it. - **Tokens, not hex** (`text-brass`, `bg-brass/15`). `theme.test.ts` enforces it. `OrdersPanel` passes `walkPosition` into `` at line 139. ### 5 — The spec, rewritten `tests/smoke/shortcuts.spec.ts:458`. The walk now has a signal, so **every assertion becomes an attribute assertion** and the whole-pane text comparisons go: ```ts const position = page.getByTestId("walk-position"); await next.click(); await expect(position).toHaveAttribute("data-position", /^1\/\d+$/); await next.click(); await expect(position).toHaveAttribute("data-position", /^2\/\d+$/); await prev.click(); await expect(position).toHaveAttribute("data-position", /^1\/\d+$/); ``` and the wrap becomes: read the total out of the attribute once, click `next` that many times, and assert the position is back to `1/`. **No loop with a break condition and no `textContent()` comparison anywhere.** - Keep the `problems-chip` wait at line 469. It is still needed — the walk has nothing to step until the first validation has landed — it was simply never sufficient on its own. - **Drop the `unitPane` `toHaveText`/`not.toHaveText` assertions entirely.** They are the third defect described in *Context*: two problems in one unit make them fail by design. - Keep one `toContainText(/\(\d+\)/)` on the unit pane after the first click, so the test still proves the walk actually *moved the view* rather than only a counter. Also add a test the old spec could not express: **the walk keeps its place across a re-validation.** Step twice, type a character into the orders editor, wait for the chip to settle, and assert the position is still `2/…` rather than blank or `1/…`. This is the regression that the whole bead is about, and without it increments 2 and 3 are unproven end to end. ### 6 — Component tests In `OrdersPanel.test.tsx`, with `renderToStaticMarkup`: - With `walkPosition={{ at: 3, of: 7 }}`, the markup contains `data-position="3/7"` and the text `3/7`. - With `walkPosition={null}`, `data-testid="walk-position"` does not appear at all — the navigator's N1, pinned. - The two buttons keep their existing testids and are still never disabled (the existing assertions at lines 36 and 51 must still pass unchanged). ## The test plan Unit tests are `vitest`: `diagnosticNav.test.ts` for increments 1 and 2, written first and red. Component tests use `renderToStaticMarkup` from `react-dom/server` — **this repository has neither jsdom nor Testing Library, and this bead must not add either.** The behaviour that matters lives in Playwright (`tests/smoke/shortcuts.spec.ts`). Because the point of the bead is a flaky browser test, **run the smoke suite locally more than once** before opening the PR — `pnpm run test:smoke` twice, and a third time if either run was quick. A single green run is exactly the evidence the previous two attempts had. `pnpm run check:fast` before the PR. No Rust changes. ## User-facing decisions Settled with the navigator on 2026-08-21 over two rounds of mockups (`docs/ui/problem-walk.html`, `docs/ui/problem-walk-edges.html`). **Decided; raise disagreements through the `human` queue rather than choosing differently.** | # | Question | Chosen | |---|---|---| | 1 | Should the walk show where it is? | **Yes — a counter between the arrows**, `‹ 3/7 ›`, in the Orders pane header. The walk wraps, so without it there is no way to know you have seen everything | | 2 | What does a re-validation do to a walk in progress? | **It keeps your place by identity.** Today it silently returns to the start; that is the root cause of three CI failures and something the player feels | | 3 | You fixed the problem you were standing on | **K1 — the next one down the document.** The walk resumes at the first problem at or after where you stood: nothing skipped, nothing repeated | | 4 | Before the first step, and with no problems at all | **N1 — nothing at all.** No counter until the walk has a position, and it goes again if it loses one | | 5 | A narrow window | **W2 — the counter drops out**, the arrows stay, the unit hint stays whole | The counter reads `3/7` — figures and a slash, not "problem 3 of 7". It is `at/of` where `at` is one-based. ## Out of scope - **Any change to which problems the walk visits, or their order.** `diagnosticTargets` is read and reused, never altered. - **Any change to `stepDiagnostic`'s wrapping contract.** The resume rule is built on it as it is. - **Disabling or hiding the walk buttons when there are no problems.** They stay enabled and visible; `OrdersPanel.tsx:188-193` explains why, and a test already pins it. - **The debounce on validation.** Making it faster or slower is not the fix and would only move the race. - **The other smoke specs in `shortcuts.spec.ts`.** Only the walk-buttons test at line 458 is rewritten. - **A keyboard shortcut for "first problem" or "last problem"**, or any new control. - **Fixing the disk-floor or apt-install costs** that Forge filed alongside this (`ah-90gu`, `ah-j6j7`). Separate beads. ## Validation 1. `pnpm run check:fast` passes. 2. `pnpm run test:smoke` passes **twice in a row**. See *The test plan* — one green run is not evidence here. 3. Pressing F8 three times shows `1/n`, `2/n`, `3/n` in the Orders pane header. 4. Standing on problem 3 of 7, typing a character elsewhere in the orders and letting validation settle, the counter still reads `3/7` (or `3/n` if the count changed) — **not** blank and **not** `1/n`. 5. Fixing the problem you are standing on blanks the counter, and the next F8 lands on the problem that immediately followed it — not on the top of the list, and not skipping one. 6. With no problems at all, the arrows are present, enabled, and there is no counter. 7. Narrowing the window below the `sm` breakpoint hides the counter, keeps both arrows usable, and leaves the `— unit NNNN` hint whole. `data-position` is still on the element in the DOM. 8. Shift-F8 walks backwards and the counter counts down, wrapping from `1/n` to `n/n`. ## Known traps - **The reset effect is the bug, not a safety net.** It is easy to read `lastDiagnostic.current = null` as prudent — the comment above it argues for it — and leave it in "just in case" beside the new resume. Leaving it in reinstates the exact defect. It is *replaced*. - **Branch 3 of `resumeWalk` is an off-by-one waiting to happen.** Standing on `after - 1` is what makes the *next* step land on `after`. Standing on `after` would skip it. The composed test in increment 2 is the guard; write it before the function. - **The counter must stay in the DOM below the `sm` breakpoint.** `hidden sm:inline` hides it visually and keeps `data-position` readable. Replacing it with a conditional render "because that is cleaner" puts the flake back at narrow viewports. - **`walkKey` must stay a ref.** In state, the resume effect would depend on a value it writes. - **Do not add a testid whose only reader is the test.** The navigator chose a visible counter partly for this reason: the barrier the test waits on is the thing the player reads, so it cannot rot unnoticed. If a later change makes the counter wrong, the test fails — which is the point. - **Two problems can share a unit.** This is why the old spec's `not.toHaveText(first)` was wrong, and it is worth checking the fixture actually exercises it once the spec is rewritten. - **`stopKeys` and the sort comparator must share their arithmetic.** Two copies of "block `firstLine` plus block-relative line" is precisely the kind of duplication that produced this bead; `diagnosticNav.ts`'s own module comment for `walk.rs` in the Rust tree makes the same argument. - **CI is where this reproduces and local runs are where it does not.** If the rewritten spec passes locally, that is not yet evidence. It is evidence when it passes twice locally *and* in CI. - **Disk space.** Eleven of this repository's retrospectives name `scripts/diskPreflight.ts` refusing to start a bead below its 8 GB floor, and it can trip again mid-`check:fast`, where it surfaces as a failing *tooling* test that reads like a defect in the diff. Safe offline reclaims: `~/.cargo/registry/src`, `target/debug/incremental`, `~/Library/Caches/Mozilla.sccache`.

title: Monster habitats and gateways are drawn as anonymous buildings on the map
description:
`hexView.ts`'s `classify()` decides what mark every map theme draws for a structure by matching its kind against sets of **bare words** - `LAIR_KINDS` is `lair, cave, ruin, ruins, barrow, crypt, tomb, pit`, `SHAFT_KINDS` is just `shaft`. Real reports qualify most of these, so the match fails and the structure falls through to `building`.

PR #487 fixes the *shape* of this - it strips the report's trailing clause (`Lair, closed to player units` -> `lair`) before the sets are consulted, which is right and should be assumed done here. What it does not fix is that the word left over is often still not one of the listed ones.

# What is actually missed

Measured across every distinct structure kind in `tests/fixtures/reports/*.rep` (66 of them), after #487's comma split. Of the ten habitats a report marks `closed to player units`, three classify and **seven do not**:

| Kind, as the report sends it | After #487 |
| --- | --- |
| `Lair, closed to player units` | lair |
| `Ruin, closed to player units` | lair |
| `Crypt, closed to player units` | lair |
| `Ice Cave, closed to player units` | **building** |
| `Demon Pit, closed to player units` | **building** |
| `Whirlpool, closed to player units` | **building** |
| `Bog, closed to player units` | **building** |
| `Empowered Altar, closed to player units` | **building** |
| `Giant's Castle, closed to player units` | **building** |
| `Magician's Tower, closed to player units` | **building** |

`Ice Cave` and `Demon Pit` are the sharp ones: `cave` and `pit` are both already in `LAIR_KINDS`, and the qualifier alone is what defeats the match.

# The shaft question, which is the more interesting half

**No fixture contains a `Shaft` structure at all.** The only line carrying the word is `+ Central Mine Shaft [10] : Mine`, whose kind is `Mine`. The structure that actually reports itself as leading somewhere is:

```
+ Gateway [1] : Gateway, contains an inner location.
```

`SHAFT_KINDS` does not contain `gateway`, so it draws as a building. Since a shaft is described in `hexView.ts` as "the only non-magical way between the surface and the underworld" and is said to anchor inter-level route planning, whether a Gateway earns that same mark is a real question rather than a lookup-table omission - a gateway is the *magical* way between levels, so it may deserve a mark of its own, or none, rather than the shaft's. **Decide it with the navigator; do not just add `gateway` to the set.**

It is also worth establishing whether a bare `Shaft` kind is something a report ever sends, or whether `SHAFT_KINDS` has only ever matched a structure that does not exist. If it is the latter, no theme has ever drawn a shaft mark, and the sets should say so rather than implying coverage.

# Approach

Whatever shape the fix takes, the thing to avoid is a longer list of literal strings that the next unseen kind defeats in the same way. Options worth weighing: matching the report's own `closed to player units` marker (which is what actually means *unenterable monster habitat*, the thing `LAIR_KINDS` is documented as identifying) rather than enumerating names; or matching the last word of the kind against the existing sets so `Ice Cave` and `Demon Pit` resolve through `cave` and `pit`. The first is closer to what the data means; the second is smaller. The implementer decides, but should say which and why.

**Test against real strings, not invented ones.** The coverage gap that hid the original bug was tests written from bare synthetic words. `tests/fixtures/reports/*.rep` is the source of truth for what a kind looks like; take the cases from there.

# Not in scope

The `Fleet, 6 Airships` ship-classification regression introduced by PR #487 - raised on that PR and to be fixed there.
design:
## Context

`classify()` (`packages/shared/src/workspace/mapThemes/hexView.ts:207-222`) decides what mark every
map theme draws for a structure by matching its kind against sets of **bare words**. Real reports
*qualify* most kinds, so the match fails and the structure falls through to `building`.

**Measured across every distinct structure kind in `tests/fixtures/reports/*.rep` — 100 of them.**
Of the ten habitats a report marks `closed to player units`, after PR #487's comma split, three
classify and **seven do not**:

| Kind, as the report sends it | seen | After #487 |
|---|---|---|
| `Lair, closed to player units` | 5 | lair |
| `Crypt, closed to player units` | 4 | lair |
| `Ruin, closed to player units` | 2 | lair |
| `Whirlpool, closed to player units` | 4 | **building** |
| `Ice Cave, closed to player units` | 1 | **building** |
| `Demon Pit, closed to player units` | 1 | **building** |
| `Bog, closed to player units` | 1 | **building** |
| `Empowered Altar, closed to player units` | 1 | **building** |
| `Giant's Castle, closed to player units` | 1 | **building** |
| `Magician's Tower, closed to player units` | 1 | **building** |

`Ice Cave` and `Demon Pit` are the sharp ones: `cave` and `pit` are **already** in `LAIR_KINDS`, and
the qualifier alone defeats the match.

**One finding stronger than the bead's**, which explains how this survived: **every lair-word kind in
every fixture carries a qualifier.** There is no bare `Lair` or `Cave` anywhere. So before #487,
`LAIR_KINDS` matched *nothing at all* on real data — the lair mark has never once been drawn from a
real report, and no test caught it because the tests were written from synthetic bare words.

**PR #487 is still OPEN** and touches these exact two files. It strips the trailing clause, which
this bead **assumes done**. See *Known traps*.

Branch from `origin/main`; line numbers are that tree.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### 1. Classify on the report's own marker — `hexView.ts`

The navigator chose **matching `closed to player units`** over enumerating more names. It is what
actually means *unenterable monster habitat* — which is exactly what `LAIR_KINDS` is documented as
identifying (`:66-68`) — and it catches all ten, including kinds nobody has seen.

**A last-word match was measured and rejected**: `Ice Cave`→`cave` and `Demon Pit`→`pit` resolve, but
Whirlpool, Bog, Giant's Castle, Empowered Altar and Magician's Tower still fall through. **It fixes 2
of the 7.**

**`classify()` must see the kind *before* the clause is stripped.** #487 strips it ahead of the sets;
the marker lives in that clause, so the unstripped kind has to reach this decision. Whether that is a
second parameter or classifying before stripping is the implementer's call — but **if the marker has
already been discarded by the time `classify()` runs, this bead cannot work**, and that is the first
thing to check.

Keep `LAIR_KINDS` as well, as the fallback for a genuinely bare `Lair`: nothing in the fixtures sends
one, but the marker is the report's phrasing and another ruleset may differ. Two rules, marker first.

### 2. A Gateway lights the reserved `gate` — `hexView.ts:107-112`

`hexView.ts` already carries this:

```
/** Reserved. Every theme's layout keeps a slot for a battle and for a gate; both turn true when
    the parser learns to read them, and no layout changes when they do. */
battle: boolean;
gate: boolean;
```

**28 Gateways in the fixtures** — the most common qualified kind there is — all reporting
`Gateway, contains an inner location`, and all currently drawn as anonymous buildings. The parser can
read them today, so `gate` becomes true for a hex holding one.

Consequently `gate` **joins `BadgeName` and the badge list** (`:126-156`). That list deliberately
excludes it today because *"a control that does nothing is worse than no control"* (`:122-124`) —
that reason expires with this bead, and **the comment must be updated rather than left contradicting
the code.** `battle` stays reserved and stays out.

Each theme draws the slot it already reserved. **No layout moves** — that is what the reservation was
for.

### 3. `Shaft` is real — and it is the fixtures that are short, not the code

**Corrected by the navigator, 2026-08-21.** I had established that no fixture contains a `Shaft`, and
concluded `SHAFT_KINDS` had never matched anything. True of the committed fixtures; **false of the
game.** `report-neworigins-v7-95-55.rep` contains:

```
+ Shaft [1] : Shaft, contains an inner location.
```

So `SHAFT_KINDS = {"shaft"}` is **correct** and matches as soon as #487 strips the clause. **Do not
remove it, and do not add `gateway` to it.**

**That turn is to be added as a fixture** (`tests/fixtures/reports/`, matching the existing
`neworigins-3.0.0-g7-f95-t<turn>.rep` naming — this is game 7, faction 95, turn 55), so a shaft is
exercised by real data for the first time.

**It also kills the marker-based approach for this half.** `contains an inner location` is carried by
**both** `Shaft` and `Gateway`, so it means *leads to an inner location* and **cannot tell them
apart.** The shaft/gate split keys on the **kind word**; only the lair rule uses a marker.

### 4. 🔴 The new fixture carries a real password — redact it before committing

**`report-neworigins-v7-95-55.rep`'s `#atlantis` line carries the faction's real password, and
`rmstdope/atlantis-hud` is a PUBLIC repository.**

Every committed fixture has it replaced with the literal `"<password>"` — verified on t70, t71, t72
and t74. **The new fixture must be redacted identically before it is added**, in the same commit that
adds it, never as a follow-up.

CLAUDE.md's rule is that the faction password must never reach the screen, a log, an error message or
storage. **Committing it to a public repository is the worst version of that**, and it is
irreversible in the sense that matters: a force-push does not un-publish a secret.

## Increments

1. **A qualified habitat is a lair.**
   RED: `hexView.test.ts` — the seven failing strings **taken verbatim from the fixtures**, asserting
   `lair`. Plus the three that already worked, unchanged.
   GREEN: the marker rule.
2. **A Gateway is a gate.**
   RED: `Gateway, contains an inner location` sets `gate`; a hex without one leaves it false.
   GREEN: `gate` in the tally and the view.
3. **The badge exists.**
   RED: `gate` is in `BADGES`; switching it off clears the mark.
   GREEN: the badge entry, and the corrected `:122-124` comment.
4. **A real shaft is covered.**

5. **Every theme draws its reserved slot.**

| `Gateway, contains an inner location` sets `gate` | same | §2 |

| ship, road and settlement classification | same | **unchanged** |

**Every string in these tests must come from `tests/fixtures/reports/*.rep`.** Synthetic bare words
are what hid this bug for the whole life of the feature; a test written from an invented kind proves
nothing about what a report sends.

**Suites:** `pnpm run check:fast`.

## User-facing decisions

Interviewed with the navigator on 2026-08-21 over `.cerebro/scratch/ah-lcyn-map-marks.html`, which
carries the corrections and is committed to `docs/ui/`.

**Q1 — what a Gateway draws.** Chosen: **light the reserved `gate` mark.** The slot already exists in
every theme's layout for exactly this, and a gateway is the *magical* way between levels, genuinely
distinct from a shaft. Accepted cost: a badge and each theme drawing its slot. Rejected: **giving it
the shaft mark** (`hexView.ts:60-62` says a shaft is *"the only non-magical way between the surface
and the underworld"*, which would stop being true, and the reserved slot would go unused for the one
thing it was reserved for) and **leaving it a building** (28 of them, invisible to a player scanning
for a way off the level).

**Q2 — the lair rule.** Chosen: **match `closed to player units`**, accepting that Giant's Castle,
Magician's Tower and Empowered Altar draw as lairs. Correct by the data's own meaning, and an unseen
kind can never silently fall through. Accepted cost: "lair" is an odd word for a Magician's Tower if
the mark is ever labelled. Rejected: **a building look plus a hostile badge** (a new mark to design
and two ways of saying the same thing) and **last-word matching** (measured: fixes 2 of 7).

**Q3 — `SHAFT_KINDS`.** The navigator **corrected the premise**: a real report does contain
`Shaft, contains an inner location`, so the set is right and **the fixtures are what is missing.**
That turn is added as a fixture.

**Not asked** (architecture): keeping `LAIR_KINDS` as a fallback beside the marker; and that the
shaft/gate split keys on the kind word, which the correction forced.

## Out of scope

- **PR #487 itself**, including the `Fleet, 6 Airships` ship-classification regression raised on it —
  to be fixed there.
- **The `battle` field**, which stays reserved and out of the badge list.
- **Route planning, or anything that consumes `gate`.** This bead makes the mark appear.
- **Redesigning any theme's marks.** Each draws the slot it already reserved.
- **The other 90 structure kinds.** Ships, roads and settlements are unchanged.

## Validation

grep -c '"<password>"' tests/fixtures/reports/neworigins-3.0.0-g7-f95-t55.rep   # must be 1
grep -c 'tinto' tests/fixtures/reports/*.rep                                    # must be 0 everywhere

1. Load **g3-f42-t82** and confirm the **Ice Cave**, **Demon Pit**, **Giant's Castle** and

2. Load **turn-71** and confirm its two **Whirlpools** draw as lairs. This is the case the navigator

6. Load the **new t55 fixture** and confirm the **Shaft** draws a **shaft** mark, distinct from the

7. Switch the **Gate** badge off: the mark goes, nothing else moves. Switch **Lairs** off: the

## Known traps

- **Check which fixture holds the case before validating against it.** The turn-71 report contains
  no Ice Cave and no Demon Pit, only Whirlpools. ah-o0d3's plan named turn-71 for a Lair/Ruin/Crypt it
  does not contain, and the verification went sideways as a result (ah-pw0d). The table above is
  measured; use it.

- **🔴 The new fixture carries a real faction password and the repository is public.** Redact it to
  `"<password>"` in the same commit that adds it, exactly as t70/t71/t72/t74 do. A secret pushed to a
  public repo is not undone by rewriting history.
- **PR #487 is still open and touches both of these files.** This bead assumes its comma split.
  **Rebase on it once it merges rather than reimplementing the split** — two implementations of the
  same strip is how the sets end up consulted with two different strings.
- **`contains an inner location` does NOT identify a Gateway.** A `Shaft` carries it too. Keying the
  gate on that marker classifies every shaft as a gate — and the fixtures alone would never show it,
  which is precisely how this bead's own first draft was wrong.
- **`classify()` needs the kind before the clause is stripped.** The lair marker lives in the clause
  #487 removes. Check this first; if the marker is gone by then, nothing else in the bead works.
- **Do not add `gateway` to `SHAFT_KINDS`.** The navigator chose the reserved `gate` field, and a
  shaft is documented as the *non-magical* way between levels.
- **Do not lengthen the word lists.** A longer list of literals defeated by the next unseen kind is
  the bug, not the fix.
- **Test from real strings.** The original bug survived because the tests used bare synthetic words.
  Take every case from `tests/fixtures/reports/*.rep`.
- **Update the comment at `hexView.ts:122-124`.** It explains why `gate` is *not* a badge; that
  reason expires here, and a comment contradicting the code is what ah-pgc7 exists about.

title: Interactive roles sleep inside their own session, so none of them can be stopped cleanly
description:
The interactive roles schedule themselves. agents/user-feedback.md:86-91:

  for i in $(seq 5); do sleep 60; echo "Moira idle, ${i}/5 of this half"; done

Ten minutes, in two five-minute halves, because a single ten-minute silent Bash
call is rejected outright. plan-bead/SKILL.md:326 says the same thing again in
its own words. Every interactive role carries a "Sleeping without dying" section
that exists only to work around the tool.

WHAT THAT COSTS

  - Opaque. An agent blocked inside sleep is indistinguishable from one that
    has hung. The fleet view sees `idle` and cannot tell which.
  - Unstoppable. A stop flag cannot land cleanly on a session that is mid-sleep;
    the flag is read between beads, and a sleeping role is not between anything.
  - Unreliable. An instruction to loop is an instruction, and agents forget.
    scripts/agent-asking exists as a PreToolUse hook for exactly this reason
    (agent-asking:9-15) -- state-writing was an instruction, agents forgot, so
    it was made mechanical. Cadence is the same class of problem.
  - Rigid. Changing a role's cadence means editing prose and restarting the
    session. In elisp it is a defcustom.

THE INVERSION. The monitor owns cadence; the agent still owns policy. The fleet
view decides WHEN a role resumes; the role's own skill still decides WHAT to do
on waking -- Xavier still checks its buffer and refills below half, Moira still
walks the issues oldest first. This removes the timer from the roles, not their
judgement, and it deletes the "Sleeping without dying" prose from all of them at
once.

DESIGN THIS AGAINST THE LOG, NOT AGAINST A GUESS. This bead is deliberately
ordered behind ah-hiib.1 and ah-hiib.2 so the intervals come from measured idle
frequency and duration. The ten minutes in the prose today has never been
