title: A claimed bead whose implementer has stopped working is invisible to every sweep
description:
An agent state machine that supervises three of its four states.

cerebro--supervise-action (emacs/cerebro.el:775-783) has arms for done, idle and
asking. `working` falls through to (_ nil): there is no elapsed-time bound on it
anywhere in cerebro.

Worse, the claims sweep actively protects a stalled bead. cerebro--claim-finding
(cerebro.el:947) returns nil for any assignee in live-names BEFORE it looks at
lease_age_min, and "live" means the pid exists (cerebro--session-alive-p), never
that anything is happening. An implementer that ends its turn waiting is
therefore indistinguishable from one deep in a build, indefinitely, with an
expired lease.

So: asking has a 900-second watchdog. The state that means "I am blocked and
said so" is supervised; the state that means "I am blocked and did not" is not.

WHY THIS IS WORTH DOING. Measured over the 72 hours to 2026-08-20:

  - Four beads sat more than two hours between being claimed and their first
    commit: ah-rpnb (9h43m), ah-5jkt.1 (4h07m), ah-v09e (3h16m), ah-5jkt.2
    (2h16m). Nothing noticed any of them.
  - Those four held 21.7 hours of claim. All 36 beads that ran cleanly in the
    same window took 23.3 hours between them. A parked bead is nearly as
    expensive as the entire working fleet.
  - ah-rpnb was claimed at 06:15Z, made its first commit at 15:58Z, and went
    from first commit to merged in ten minutes.

THE SIGNAL. Not raw elapsed time -- a legitimate bead can sit 40 minutes in CI.
Time since the last commit on the bead's own branch, from the claim onward.
That quantity does not exist today: sweep-claims.sh computes commit_age_min
against origin/main only, and only once on_main is true, i.e. only after the
work has already landed.

THE THRESHOLD IS EMPIRICAL. Every one of the 36 clean beads made its first
commit 6 to 36 minutes after being claimed. The four parked ones sat 2.3h or
more. Sixty minutes separates them with zero false positives across the window.

HONEST LIMIT. This does not answer the question the implementer was stuck on.
It releases the claim so the session can take other work, which converts into
throughput only when the queue has something in it.
design:
## Context

Cerebro's agent state machine supervises three of its four states. `cerebro--supervise-action`
(`emacs/cerebro.el:773-783`) has arms for `done`, `idle` and `asking`; **`working` falls through to
`(_ nil)`**, and no elapsed-time bound on it exists anywhere.

Worse, the claims sweep actively protects a stalled bead. `cerebro--claim-finding` (`:947`) returns
nil for any assignee in `live-names` **before** it looks at `lease_age_min`, and "live" means only
that the pid exists (`cerebro--session-alive-p`). An implementer that ended its turn waiting is
therefore indistinguishable from one deep in a build, indefinitely.

So `asking` — "I am blocked and said so" — has a 900-second watchdog, and `working` — "I am blocked
and did not" — has nothing.

**What it costs**, measured over the 72 hours to 2026-08-20:

- Four beads sat more than two hours between claim and first commit: **ah-rpnb 9h43m**, ah-5jkt.1
  4h07m, ah-v09e 3h16m, ah-5jkt.2 2h16m. Nothing noticed any of them.
- Those four held **21.7 hours of claim**; all 36 beads that ran cleanly took 23.3 hours between
  them. A parked bead is nearly as expensive as the entire working fleet.
- ah-rpnb was claimed at 06:15Z, first-committed at 15:58Z, and went from first commit to merged in
  **ten minutes**.

**The threshold is empirical.** Every one of the 36 clean beads made its first commit **6 to 36
minutes** after being claimed; the four parked ones sat 2.3h or more. **Sixty minutes separates them
with zero false positives** across the window.

**This is a cerebro change, not an atlantis-hud one.** `.claude/cerebro` is a submodule of its own
repository (`rmstdope/cerebro`) with its own `main`, CI and tests, so it takes **two pull requests** —
see *Increments*.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### 1. The signal does not exist yet — a new `scripts/sweep-stalled.sh`

`sweep-claims.sh` computes `commit_age_min` against `origin/main` **and only when `on_main` is
true** — i.e. only after the work has already landed. The quantity this bead needs is the opposite:
progress on a branch that has *not* landed.

A new script, modelled on `sweep-claims.sh` line for line — same `--json` argument, same
`consumer-root --shared`, same `iso_to_epoch` helper, same **strictly read-only** contract, and the
same header explaining why read-only is what makes the guarantee checkable.

One object per `in_progress` bead:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `id`, `assignee`, `title` | as `sweep-claims.sh` |
| `branch` | the bead's branch, or null if no worktree holds one |
| `progress_age_min` | minutes since the last sign of progress |
| `progress_source` | `"commit"` or `"claim"` — which of the two the age came from |

**Finding the branch.** Implementers build in `.cerebro/worktrees/`, on a branch named for the bead
(`ah-t65-load-multiple-reports`). Enumerate them from the shared checkout:

```bash
git -C "$repo_root" worktree list --porcelain
```

and match a branch whose name begins **`<id>-`**. The trailing hyphen is load-bearing, exactly as the
colon is in `sweep-claims.sh:95`: without it, `ah-t65-` would also match a branch for `ah-t65.1`.

**Measuring progress.** On the branch's worktree:

```bash
git -C "$worktree" log origin/main..HEAD -1 --format=%ct
```

`origin/main..HEAD`, **not** bare `HEAD`: a freshly created branch points at the commit it forked
from, whose timestamp is main's and may be hours old. That would report every new claim as stalled
within the hour — the single most likely way to build this wrong.

**When there is no commit yet** — no worktree, or the branch has none — fall back to the claim, which
is what "from the claim onward" means. `bd` carries it as **`started_at`** on the bead
(`2026-08-20T16:59:20Z` on ah-yk6b). `progress_source` records which was used, so the label can say
so and a reader is never left guessing.

### 2. The decision is pure — `cerebro--stalled-finding`, beside `cerebro--claim-finding`

```elisp
(defconst cerebro--stalled-minutes 60
  "Minutes without a commit past which a claim is offered as stalled.

Empirical, not chosen (ah-4xm4): across the 72 hours to 2026-08-20 every
one of the 36 beads that ran cleanly made its first commit 6 to 36 minutes
after being claimed, and the four that parked sat 2.3 hours or more. Sixty
separates them with no false positive in that window - and it is well clear
of a long CI wait, which is the legitimate reason a working bead is quiet.")

(defun cerebro--stalled-finding (candidate live-states now)
  "Pure. What the stalled sweep should offer for CANDIDATE, or nil.

CANDIDATE is one parsed object from `sweep-stalled.sh --json'. LIVE-STATES
is an alist of (NAME . STATE-SYMBOL) for sessions whose pid is alive. NOW is
unused, taken for symmetry with `cerebro--claim-finding'.

Returns nil or (unclaim ID). Nil covers four cases: nobody live holds it
\(a dead claim is the claims sweep's, not this one's); the session is
`asking', so it is blocked and has said so and `cerebro--supervise-action'
already nudges it; there is no age to judge; or the age is inside the
threshold - which includes every bead sitting in CI."
  (ignore now)
  (let-alist candidate
    (let ((state (cdr (assoc .assignee live-states))))
      (cond
       ((null (assoc .assignee live-states)) nil)
       ((eq state 'asking) nil)
       ((null .progress_age_min) nil)
       ((> .progress_age_min cerebro--stalled-minutes) (list 'unclaim .id))
       (t nil)))))
```

**`(assoc ... )` for the membership test, not `state` being non-nil**: a live session whose state
file is unreadable has a nil state and must still count as live, or an unparsable file would turn
into a finding against a working implementer.

### 3. Four shapes, not three

- **`cerebro--finding-command` (`:972-987`)** gains one arm:
  ```elisp
  (`(unclaim ,id) (list "bd" "unclaim" id))
  ```
  `bd unclaim` and not `bd reclaim --older-than`: reclaim is for a claim whose session is *gone*,
  and its window would refuse a bead whose lease is still being heartbeated. This finding is
  specifically about a session that is **alive and not moving**.
- **`cerebro-test/finding-command-covers-only-the-three-shapes` (`cerebro-test.el:2352`) must be
  renamed as well as extended** — "three shapes" is in its name *and* in its `should-error` clause.
  `…-covers-only-the-known-shapes`, with the `unclaim` case added.
- **`cerebro--sweep-label` (`:508-521`)** gains an arm. Say which measurement it is, because the two
  mean different things to a reader:
  ```elisp
  (`(unclaim ,id)
   (format "unclaim %s — %s stalled, no %s for %sm" id .assignee
           (if (equal .progress_source "commit") "commit" "start")
           .progress_age_min))
  ```

### 4. Wiring the third sweep — `cerebro--findings-from` and `cerebro--request-sweeps`

`cerebro--findings-from` (`:642-657`) takes a third list and appends a third `delq nil` block,
passing `live-states` where the claims block passes `live-names`. Both are derived from the same
`cerebro--gather-states` read; **gather once and derive both**, rather than walking the state files
twice.

`cerebro--request-sweeps` (`:659-682`) is **hand-nested two callbacks deep already**, and a third
would nest it three. Replace the nest with a small list-driven sequencer over
`("sweep-claims.sh" "sweep-epics.sh" "sweep-stalled.sh")` that collects parsed output in order and
calls back with all three, keeping the existing contract exactly: **nil if any script fails or
prints something that is not JSON**, and `busy` if a sweep is already out. The three scripts are
identical in shape, which is what makes the sequencer a simplification rather than an abstraction
for its own sake.

### 5. The prose spec — `agents/orchestrator.md`

The existing sweeps record their guard rationale there, and this one carries a caveat that must be
written down: **unclaiming does not answer the question the implementer was stuck on.** It releases
the claim so the bead can be taken by another session, which converts into throughput only when the
queue has something in it. Say so, next to the other three.

### 6. Nothing in `cerebro--supervise-action`

**Deliberately unchanged.** The bead's description diagnoses the gap through that function, so the
obvious move is to add a `working` arm — but the navigator chose **a Sweeps finding over an
automatic nudge** (recorded in the bead's design, 2026-08-20): the decision goes where the other
three sweeps already live, and nothing acts unattended. An arm there would act on the fleet poll,
without confirmation, which is the design that was rejected.

## Increments

Two repositories, and the order matters.

**In `.claude/cerebro` (PR one, against `rmstdope/cerebro`):**

1. **The signal exists.**
   RED: `tests/sweep-stalled.sh` over a fabricated consumer — a bead with a recent commit, one with
   an old commit, one whose branch has no commit at all, one with no worktree.
   GREEN: `scripts/sweep-stalled.sh`.
2. **The decision is made, and refuses four ways.**
   RED: four ERT tests, one per nil case, plus the positive.
   GREEN: `cerebro--stalled-minutes` and `cerebro--stalled-finding`.
3. **It can be acted on.**
   RED: extend and **rename** the shapes test; a label test.
   GREEN: the `unclaim` arms in `cerebro--finding-command` and `cerebro--sweep-label`.
4. **It reaches the panel.**
   RED: a `cerebro--findings-from` test with all three lists.
   GREEN: the third block, and the list-driven `cerebro--request-sweeps`.
5. **It is written down.** `agents/orchestrator.md`.

**In `atlantis-hud` (PR two):** bump the submodule pin to the merged cerebro commit. Nothing else.
**PR one must be merged first** — a pin to an unmerged commit is a pin to something that may be
rebased away.

## The test plan

| Test | Where | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| `a bead whose branch committed recently is not stalled` | `tests/sweep-stalled.sh` | the happy case |
| **`a branch with no commit measures from the claim`** | same | the `started_at` fallback |
| **`a fresh branch is not stalled by main's commit date`** | same | `origin/main..HEAD` — the likeliest bug |
| `a bead with no worktree reports a null branch` | same | the missing-worktree case |
| `the script writes nothing` | same | the read-only contract, as the other sweeps have |
| `no finding when no live session holds it` | ERT | the claims sweep's job, not this one's |
| `no finding when the session is asking` | ERT | already nudged |
| `no finding inside the threshold` | ERT | a bead in CI |
| `no finding without an age` | ERT | null safety |
| **`a live working session past the threshold is offered`** | ERT | the bead |
| `…-covers-only-the-known-shapes` (was `…-three-shapes`) | ERT | **renamed**, four shapes |
| `the stalled label names which measurement it used` | ERT | commit vs start |
| `findings-from returns all three sweeps' findings` | ERT | the wiring |
| the existing sweep tests | ERT | **unchanged** — claims and epics behaviour must not move |

**Suites:** cerebro's CI runs `for t in tests/*.sh`, so a new file there is picked up with no
registration. Run the ERT suite as `emacs/` already documents.

## User-facing decisions

**None to make.** The one interface decision this bead had — a Sweeps finding the navigator confirms
with `x`, rather than an automatic vterm nudge — **was already taken by the navigator on 2026-08-20**
and is recorded in the bead's own design field. It is not reopened here.

Nothing else in this bead is visible to a player: it is entirely fleet tooling, seen only in the
Emacs fleet view by the navigator.

**Not asked** (architecture, decided here): `bd unclaim` rather than `bd reclaim`; the 60-minute
constant, which is empirical; the list-driven sequencer replacing the callback nest; `progress_source`
existing at all; and matching the branch on `<id>-`.

## Out of scope

- **`cerebro--supervise-action`.** Its `working` fall-through stays; see §6.
- **Answering the question the implementer was stuck on.** This releases a claim; it does not
  unblock anybody, and `agents/orchestrator.md` must say so.
- **Nudging, messaging or killing the stalled session.** Rejected by the navigator in favour of the
  sweep.
- **ah-hiib.3** ("Every role carries its own sleep loop"), which this bead blocks but does not touch.
- **Changing the claims or epics sweeps.** They keep their exact behaviour; only their plumbing gains
  a sibling.

## Validation

In `.claude/cerebro`:

```bash
for t in tests/*.sh; do bash "$t" || echo "FAILED: $t"; done
emacs -Q --batch -l emacs/cerebro.el -l emacs/cerebro-test.el -f ert-run-tests-batch-and-exit
```

Then by hand, which is the only way to see the finding actually appear:

1. `scripts/sweep-stalled.sh --json` with **nothing claimed**: prints `[]`, exits zero.
2. Claim a bead, make no commit, and run it again: one object, `progress_source` **`"claim"`**, a
   small `progress_age_min`. **No finding yet** — it is inside the threshold.
3. Confirm the script **wrote nothing**: `git status` clean, the bead unchanged.
4. Open the fleet view with a genuinely stalled claim (or a temporarily lowered
   `cerebro--stalled-minutes`) and confirm **one Sweeps line** appears naming the bead and the
   assignee, and that `x` prompts with the exact `bd unclaim` command before running it.
5. Confirm a bead **sitting in CI for 40 minutes raises nothing** — the case the threshold exists to
   tolerate.
6. Confirm an implementer showing **`asking`** raises nothing, however long it has waited: that is
   `cerebro--supervise-action`'s nudge, and two mechanisms firing on one session is noise.
7. Confirm the **claims and epics sweeps still produce their own findings** unchanged, which is what
   proves the sequencer rewrite kept the contract.

## Known traps

- **`origin/main..HEAD`, never bare `HEAD`.** A new branch points at the commit it forked from, whose
  timestamp is main's. Using `HEAD` reports a just-claimed bead as an hour stale the moment main
  happens to be an hour old — the single most likely way to build this wrong, and it fails *toward*
  false positives against working implementers.
- **The branch match needs its trailing hyphen.** `<id>-` and not `<id>`, or `ah-t65` matches
  `ah-t65.1`'s branch. `sweep-claims.sh:95` documents the same trap for its commit grep.
- **Do not add a `working` arm to `cerebro--supervise-action`.** The description points there; the
  navigator's recorded decision points at the sweeps. An arm there acts unattended.
- **The three-shapes test encodes "three" in its name and its `should-error`.** Renaming it is part
  of the change, not tidying.
- **A live session with an unreadable state file must count as live.** Test membership with `assoc`,
  not by the state being non-nil, or a corrupt file becomes a finding against a working implementer.
- **`bd unclaim`, not `bd reclaim --older-than`.** Reclaim's window is about a *gone* session and
  would refuse this bead, whose session is alive.
- **This sweep must not overlap the claims sweep.** No live session holding the bead means it is the
  claims sweep's case, and returning a finding here as well would offer the navigator two lines for
  one bead.
- **The script must stay read-only**, like its two siblings, and its header should say so for the
  same reason theirs do: it is what makes "only a confirmed path can mutate" checkable at a glance.
- **Two PRs, cerebro first.** Bumping the submodule to an unmerged commit pins something that may be
  rebased away.
acceptance_criteria:
- A bead that is in_progress, held by a live session, and whose branch has had no commit for longer than the threshold raises a line in the Sweeps section of the bead panel.
- The line is confirmed with x like every other finding; cerebro never acts on its own here. The command is `bd unclaim <id>`.
- Guards are pure functions with one ERT test each, in the manner of cerebro--claim-finding and cerebro--epic-finding:
  - no finding below the threshold (a bead sitting in CI raises nothing)
  - no finding when a commit landed inside the window
  - no finding when the agent state is asking (cerebro--supervise-action already nudges it)
  - no finding when no live session holds the bead (that is the claims sweep's case)
- The detecting script is read-only and prints a JSON array, matching the contract sweep-claims.sh and sweep-epics.sh already keep.
- Progress is measured as the last commit on the bead's own branch reachable from origin/main..HEAD, falling back to the bead's started_at when the branch has no commit yet; which of the two was used is reported and shown in the label.
- cerebro--supervise-action is NOT given a `working` arm - the navigator chose a confirmed Sweeps finding over an automatic nudge.
- The claims and epics sweeps keep their exact behaviour.
- cerebro's shell tests and ERT suite pass; the submodule pin is bumped in a second PR after the cerebro PR merges.

title: A palette search silently hides most matches, so the structure you wanted is unreachable
description:
Found during verification of ah-wkwk (2026-08-20, origin/main 0eb1e7d). That bead passed - structure rows and building rows are distinguishable, ids and kinds resolve, ordering is right - and this is the follow-up filed alongside the pass.

## What the player sees

The navigator's words: "When I type mine, I get a number of 'Miners' units. So many that the structure cannot be seen. It seems the palette only shows the first n matches. It needs to show all so that I can scroll."

Typing `mine` matches every unit named "Miners" as well as the Mines on the map. The units fill the list and the structure rows - the whole point of ah-wkwk - are cut off below the fold, with nothing on screen to say anything was dropped. The player concludes the palette cannot find their Mine.

## The cause

`packages/shared/src/workspace/CommandPalette.tsx:6`:

    const SHOWN_LIMIT = 12;

passed to `filterPalette`, which ends (`commandPalette.ts:147`):

    return limit === undefined ? kept : kept.slice(0, limit);

A hard truncation to twelve rows, with no scroll and no indication that more matched. The cap is not new to ah-wkwk; what ah-wkwk changed is how easily it bites, because structures now compete for those twelve places against units that were already there. A faction with many similarly-named units will always crowd out the newer row types.

Note also that `kept` is sorted by fit alone, with no interleaving by entry type, so there is no guarantee that any structure appears in the first twelve however good its match.

## Shape of a fix

The navigator asked for all matches, scrollable. Worth settling at planning:

- **Scroll the full list** - simplest and what was asked for. Needs a max height on the list and the arrow-key highlight to scroll its row into view, which the palette does not do today (`paletteKeyReduce` moves an index; nothing calls `scrollIntoView`).
- **Whether to keep any cap at all** as a backstop for a very large faction, and if so whether to say "and N more" rather than truncating silently. The current silence is the part that reads as a bug.
- **Whether type should influence order** as well as fit - e.g. guaranteeing at least one row per matching type before filling the rest by fit - so a single overwhelming type cannot hide the others. This is the deeper version of the complaint and may be worth more than raw scrolling.

Keep ah-wkwk's decided ordering intact: with an empty query, units first, then structures, then the dictionary.

## Acceptance

Typing a term that matches many units and at least one structure shows the structure, either because every match is reachable by scrolling or because the ordering guarantees it a place. Nothing is dropped without the player being told.
design:
## Context

Your words at verification of ah-wkwk (which passed): *"When I type mine, I get a number of 'Miners'
units. So many that the structure cannot be seen. It seems the palette only shows the first n
matches. It needs to show all so that I can scroll."*

The cap is `SHOWN_LIMIT = 12` (`workspace/CommandPalette.tsx:6`), applied by `filterPalette` as a
bare `kept.slice(0, limit)` (`commandPalette.ts:147`). There is no scroll container and nothing on
screen says anything was dropped, so a truncated list is indistinguishable from a complete one.

**Measured against the committed turn-71 report** (831 palette entries), which is what makes this a
P1 rather than a tidy-up:

| Query | Matches | Dropped in silence |
|---|---|---|
| `m` | 202 | **190** |
| `mi` | 75 | **63** |
| `min` | 31 | **19** |
| `mine` | 20 | **8** |

Two findings decide the design:

1. **The cap bites hardest while you are still typing** — every keystroke on the way to the word you
   wanted.
2. **The five Mine structures survive by one row.** On this report they land at positions 7–12. One
   more unit named "Miner-something" and every structure falls off, silently. So raising the number
   does not fix it; the ordering has to stop one kind from taking every place.

A third measurement drove the fuzzy-match decision: across eight sample queries, **35% of all
matches are subsequence matches** — letters in order with gaps, which is how `mine` matches
`MAGICIAN'S TOWER`. They sort last, so they are what gets dropped, but they are also what inflates
`mine` from 7 real matches to 20.

Branch from `origin/main`; every line number here is that tree.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### 1. The filter: no cap, fuzzy suppression, one seat per kind — `commandPalette.ts:130-148`

`filterPalette` **loses its `limit` parameter entirely.** Nothing will call it, and a capping
parameter left in place is an invitation to reintroduce the defect. Delete the parameter, not just
its use.

The pipeline becomes, in this order:

```ts
/**
 * The entries a query leaves standing, best fit first, reading order among equals.
 *
 * Three rules, all of them ah-yk6b, and all of them about one kind of thing not being able to
 * hide another:
 *
 *  1. **No cap.** Every match is returned; the list scrolls (`CommandPalette`). It used to slice
 *     to 12 with nothing on screen to say so, which is how five Mine structures could sit below
 *     the fold behind units named "Miners".
 *  2. **Subsequence matches are a fallback, not a result.** If anything matched as prefix, word
 *     start or substring, only those are returned - `mine` should not offer "Magician's Tower"
 *     while a Mine is standing on the map. When a subsequence match is all there is, it is kept,
 *     which is the half-remembered-name rescue the rule exists for.
 *  3. **Every matching kind gets a seat at the top.** The best of each kind leads, in fit order,
 *     then everything else in fit order. A single overwhelming kind can therefore never crowd the
 *     others off the first screenful, which was the complaint even before scrolling.
 *
 * An empty query is untouched by all three: it is the whole list, in the order
 * `buildPaletteEntries` built it.
 */
export function filterPalette(entries: readonly PaletteEntry[], query: string): PaletteEntry[] {
  const needle = query.trim().toLowerCase();
  if (needle === "") {
    return [...entries];
  }

  const scored = entries
    .map((entry) => ({ entry, fit: score(entry.label, needle) }))
    .filter((s): s is { entry: PaletteEntry; fit: number } => s.fit !== null);

  // Rule 2. `some` before `filter`, so an all-subsequence result survives intact.
  const strong = scored.some((s) => s.fit < SUBSEQUENCE)
    ? scored.filter((s) => s.fit < SUBSEQUENCE)
    : scored;

  // Stable, so entries of equal fit keep `buildPaletteEntries`' reading order.
  const byFit = [...strong].sort((a, b) => a.fit - b.fit).map((s) => s.entry);

  // Rule 3. Walking an already fit-sorted list and taking the first of each kind yields the
  // representatives *in fit order* for free - so the best match overall is still the first row.
  const seen = new Set<PaletteEntryKind>();
  const leading: PaletteEntry[] = [];
  const rest: PaletteEntry[] = [];
  for (const entry of byFit) {
    if (seen.has(entry.kind)) {
      rest.push(entry);
    } else {
      seen.add(entry.kind);
      leading.push(entry);
    }
  }
  return [...leading, ...rest];
}
```

`SUBSEQUENCE` is a named constant for `3`, beside `score`, so the two agree by construction. **Update
`score`'s own doc comment** (`:104-107`) to say that 3 is now a fallback tier rather than merely the
worst tier.

**With one matching kind, `leading` is one entry and the output is exactly today's order** — which
is why most existing tests do not move.

### 2. The keyboard: clamp, and paginate — `commandPalette.ts:151-172`

`paletteKeyReduce` stops wrapping and learns a page. `count` alone cannot size a page, so the state
gains `pageSize`:

```ts
/**
 * Where an arrow key moves the highlight, or null for any other key - which stays with the input,
 * where typing belongs.
 *
 * It clamps at the ends rather than wrapping (ah-yk6b). Wrapping was harmless on a list capped at
 * twelve; on an uncapped one, holding Down would cycle past what you wanted forever, and a single
 * Up from the top would teleport you 200 rows. `Home` and `End` still make that jump on purpose.
 */
export function paletteKeyReduce(
  state: { index: number; count: number; pageSize: number },
  key: string
): number | null {
  if (state.count === 0) {
    return null;
  }
  const last = state.count - 1;
  const clamp = (at: number) => Math.max(0, Math.min(last, at));
  switch (key) {
    case "ArrowDown":
      return clamp(state.index + 1);
    case "ArrowUp":
      return clamp(state.index - 1);
    case "PageDown":
      return clamp(state.index + state.pageSize);
    case "PageUp":
      return clamp(state.index - state.pageSize);
    case "Home":
      return 0;
    case "End":
      return last;
    default:
      return null;
  }
}
```

**`clamp` must return the same index rather than null at the ends.** Returning null would let the
key fall through to the input, and `event.preventDefault()` would not run — so Down on the last row
would move the text caret. The caller only cares that a number came back.

### 3. The list scrolls, and follows the highlight — `workspace/CommandPalette.tsx`

- **Delete `SHOWN_LIMIT`** (`:6`) and its comment, and drop the third argument at `:25`.
- The `<ul>` (`:100`) becomes the scroll container: add **`max-h-[70vh] overflow-y-auto`**. The
  dialog opens at `pt-[15vh]`, so 15 + 70 leaves a margin at the bottom on any window — the list
  grows to use a tall screen and simply scrolls on a short one, and **the dialog can never run past
  the bottom edge**, which a fixed row count does not guarantee.
- **Scroll the highlighted row into view.** A ref per row, or one ref on the list plus a query by
  index; on `active` changing, `scrollIntoView({ block: "nearest" })`. `"nearest"` matters: it
  scrolls only when the row is actually out of view, so arrowing within the visible rows does not
  jog the list.
- **Do not scroll on pointer hover.** `onPointerEnter` sets the index (`:109`), and scrolling in
  response would move the row out from under the pointer, which fires another `pointerenter`. Guard
  the effect so it runs for keyboard-driven changes only — the simplest honest version is a ref flag
  set by `onKeyDown` and cleared by `onPointerEnter`.
- `pageSize` for the reducer: the number of rows that fit, from the list's `clientHeight` over a row
  height. **A fixed sensible number is acceptable** if measuring proves fiddly — say so in a comment
  rather than leaving a magic number unexplained.

### 4. Nothing else

`buildPaletteEntries`, its ordering, the row design, the kind column and `structureLabel` are all
ah-wkwk's and untouched.

## Increments

1. **Nothing is dropped in silence.**
   RED: `returns every match, with no cap` — build more than twelve matching entries and assert the
   full length. Also delete `caps the list when asked to` (`:143-145`), which pins the parameter
   being removed.
   GREEN: drop the `limit` parameter and the `slice`; drop `SHOWN_LIMIT` and its argument.

2. **Fuzzy matches stop crowding out real ones.**
   RED: `drops subsequence matches when better ones exist` and — **unchanged, and it must stay
   passing** — `keeps subsequence matches, for the half-remembered name` (`:131-137`).
   GREEN: rule 2.
   **This increment breaks `ranks prefix above word-start above scattered letters` (`:108-129`)**;
   see *Known traps*. Fix it here, in this increment, deliberately.

3. **One kind cannot take every seat.**
   RED: `gives every matching kind a place at the top`, and `still puts the best match first`.
   GREEN: rule 3.

4. **The keyboard suits a long list.**
   RED: rewrite `moves the highlight down and up with wrap-around` as
   `clamps the highlight at both ends`; add `moves a page at a time`.
   GREEN: the reducer.

5. **The list scrolls and the highlight stays visible.**
   RED: smoke — `arrowing down a long list keeps the highlight on screen`.
   GREEN: `max-h-[70vh] overflow-y-auto` and `scrollIntoView`.

## The test plan

| Test | Where | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| **`returns every match, with no cap`** | `commandPalette.test.ts` | the bead |
| `caps the list when asked to` (`:143`) | same | **deleted** — the parameter is gone |
| **`drops subsequence matches when better ones exist`** | same | rule 2 |
| `keeps subsequence matches, for the half-remembered name` (`:131`) | same | **unchanged, must still pass** — proof the rescue survives |
| `ranks prefix above word-start above scattered letters` (`:108`) | same | **must be rewritten** — see traps |
| **`gives every matching kind a place at the top`** | same | rule 3 |
| **`still puts the best match first`** | same | P, the chosen representative order |
| `shows everything, in reading order, for an empty query` (`:139`) | same | **unchanged** — the empty query bypasses all three rules |
| `tells a structure and a building type apart when both match "mine"` (`:66`) | same | unchanged, and stronger under rule 3 |
| `finds a unit by its number` (`:102`) | same | unchanged — `13401` matches as substring, so rule 2 does not touch it |
| **`clamps the highlight at both ends`** (was the wrap test, `:153`) | same | N |
| **`moves a page at a time`** | same | PageUp/PageDown |
| `jumps to the ends on Home and End` (`:159`) | same | unchanged |
| `stays put with nothing to highlight` (`:169`) | same | unchanged |
| **`arrowing down a long list keeps the highlight on screen`** | `tests/smoke/shortcuts.spec.ts` | the scroll container and `scrollIntoView` |
| `the palette goes to a structure's hex…` (`:69`) | same | unchanged |

**Suites:** `pnpm run check:fast`, plus the smoke suite for increment 5. **There is no jsdom in this
repository** — the vitest suites assert `renderToStaticMarkup` output only — so `scrollIntoView`,
the scroll container and the hover guard **cannot be unit-tested and belong in Playwright**. Do not
add a DOM environment to test them.

## User-facing decisions

Interviewed with the navigator on 2026-08-20 over two rounds, using
`.cerebro/scratch/ah-yk6b-palette-matches.html` and `.cerebro/scratch/ah-yk6b-palette-details.html`.

**Q1 — what replaces the hard cap.** Chosen: **A, every match, scrollable.** No cap at all; the list
gets a max height and scrolls. Literally what was asked for, and nothing is ever hidden. Accepted
cost: typing `m` yields a 202-row scroller. Rejected: a generous backstop at ~50 with an "and N more"
footer (still a cap, and 50 has no principle behind it), and keeping 12 with a footer count (does not
solve it — the structure is still unreachable when it is 13th).

**Q2 — should the kind of thing affect the order.** Chosen: **E, every matching kind gets one place
first** — best of each kind, then the rest by fit. It fixes the complaint on the first screenful
rather than resting on the player's willingness to scroll. Accepted cost: the second row is no longer
the second-best match. Rejected: fit alone (today's rule), and grouping under headings (headings cost
rows in a list whose problem is rows, and would reopen ah-wkwk's row design by making the kind column
redundant).

**Q3 — the subsequence matches.** Chosen: **H, drop them when real matches exist.** `mine` goes from
20 matches to 7, every one a thing the player might have meant, and the half-remembered-name rescue
still fires when nothing better matched. Accepted cost: a genuine subsequence match is hidden
whenever any weak substring match exists.

**Q4 — how tall the list is.** Chosen: **L, as tall as the window allows** — a max height in `vh`.
Uses a big screen properly and cannot overflow a shrunk window. Accepted cost: the dialog changes
size as you type. Rejected: a fixed twelve rows (ignores window height, and twelve rows plus the
input can run past the bottom of a short window) and eight rows (fewer than today, so *more*
scrolling — an odd outcome for a bead about hidden things).

**Q5 — the arrow wrap.** Chosen: **N, clamp at both ends.** Holding Down settles on the last row
instead of cycling; `Home`/`End` still make the jump. Accepted cost: changed behaviour on lists that
were never long enough for it to matter.

**Q6 — PageUp and PageDown.** Chosen: **yes, a screenful at a time.** Cheap, since the reducer
already turns a key into an index.

**Q7 — the order of E's representatives.** Chosen: **P, by fit.** The best match overall is still the
first row, so Enter on a well-aimed query does what it always did, and the rule stays one idea.
Rejected: ah-wkwk's fixed kind order, which reads the same every time but can put a perfect
dictionary match below a weaker structure match.

**Not asked** (architecture, decided here): removing the `limit` parameter rather than leaving it
unused; `pageSize` joining the reducer's state; `block: "nearest"`; and the pointer-hover guard.

## Out of scope

- **`buildPaletteEntries`, the empty-query order, the row design and the kind column** — all
  ah-wkwk's, and deliberately untouched. An empty query must return exactly what it returns today.
- **Changing `score` itself.** The four tiers stay as they are; rule 2 only decides when tier 3 is
  shown.
- **Grouping headings, and a "N more" footer** — both considered and rejected above.
- **`aria-activedescendant`.** The listbox keeps its current `role="option"` buttons with
  `aria-selected`; making the scroll container accessible is `scrollIntoView`, not a rewrite of the
  ARIA model.
- **Searching by anything other than the label.** Ids and tags are already in labels.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
pnpm exec playwright test --project=web
```

Then by hand, with the turn-71 report loaded — this is the report the numbers above come from:

1. Open the palette and type **`mine`**. Every Mine structure must be reachable, and **at least one
   structure must be visible without scrolling.** This is the acceptance.
2. Type **`m`** alone. All 202 matches are there and the list scrolls; confirm the dialog **does not
   run off the bottom of the window**.
3. **Shrink the window to something short** and repeat. The list must get shorter and scroll, never
   overflow.
4. Hold **Down** to the bottom: the highlight stops on the last row and stays there. Hold **Up**: it
   stops on the first. Neither wraps, and **the text caret in the input never moves**.
5. **PageDown/PageUp** move a screenful; **Home/End** jump to the ends. In every case the highlighted
   row is on screen after the key.
6. **Move the mouse over the list.** The highlight follows the pointer and **the list does not scroll
   under it** — no jitter, no runaway.
7. Type **`svneight`**: "Seven of Eight" is still found. The half-remembered-name rescue must survive.
8. Type **`zzzz`**: "nothing matches", unchanged.
9. Type nothing at all: units first, then places, then structures, then the dictionary — ah-wkwk's
   order, undisturbed.

## Known traps

- **`ranks prefix above word-start above scattered letters` (`commandPalette.test.ts:108-129`) will
  fail, and it is right to.** It asserts that "Seven of Eight" is *present* as a scattered match for
  `st` and `set` — but `STUDY` is a prefix and `Open settings` a word start, so rule 2 now drops it.
  `expect(scattered).not.toBe(-1)` is the line that goes red. **Rewrite it, do not delete it**: keep
  the prefix-beats-word-start half, and move the scattered-letters half to a query where nothing
  matches better. Deleting the test would lose the ranking coverage entirely.
- **`keeps subsequence matches` (`:131-137`) must keep passing untouched.** `svneight` matches
  nothing as a substring, so subsequence is all there is and rule 2 keeps it. If this test needs
  changing, rule 2 has been written as an unconditional filter rather than a fallback — which
  deletes the fuzzy finder.
- **`some` before `filter`.** Deciding whether strong matches exist must be a separate pass over the
  scored list. Filtering first and testing the result is the same bug in a different shape.
- **The empty query must bypass all three rules.** `filterPalette(entries, "")` returns the list as
  built; rule 3 applied to it would reorder the whole palette and break ah-wkwk's decided ordering
  and its test at `:139`.
- **Clamping returns the index, never null.** Null falls through to the input and `preventDefault`
  never runs, so Down on the last row moves the text caret instead of doing nothing.
- **Do not scroll on pointer hover.** `onPointerEnter` sets the index; scrolling in response moves
  the row out from under the pointer, which fires `pointerenter` again. That loop is a scrolling
  list that will not stand still.
- **`block: "nearest"`, not `"center"`.** Centring scrolls on every arrow press even when the row is
  already comfortably in view.
- **Delete the `limit` parameter, do not merely stop passing it.** An unused capping parameter is how
  this comes back.
- **There is no jsdom here.** The scroll container, `scrollIntoView` and the hover guard are smoke
  tests. Adding a DOM environment to unit-test them is a much larger change than this bead.
- **`max-h-[70vh]` pairs with the dialog's `pt-[15vh]`.** Changing one without the other is how the
  dialog ends up taller than the window.

- Typing a term that matches many units and at least one structure shows a structure WITHOUT scrolling - every matching kind gets a seat at the top, best of each kind first, in fit order.
- The best-matching entry overall is still the first row, so Enter on a well-aimed query is unchanged.
- Subsequence matches are a fallback: if anything matched as prefix, word start or substring, only those are shown. "mine" no longer offers "Magician's Tower".
- A query with only subsequence matches still finds them - "svneight" still finds "Seven of Eight".
- The list's max height is in vh, so the dialog never runs past the bottom of the window, and shrinks with it.
- Arrow keys clamp at both ends instead of wrapping, and never let the keypress reach the text input.
- PageUp and PageDown move a screenful; Home and End still jump to the ends.

title: Drop line lands mid-column when a table column is dragged rightwards
description:
Found during verification of ah-1owr.3 (2026-08-20, origin/main c6fc980). That bead passed - the chip tracks the pointer from the first pixel, Escape cancels, the keyboard path and persistence all behave - and this is the follow-up filed alongside the pass.

## What the player sees

The navigator's words: "When I drag columns to the left everything is fine, but when I drag them to the right, the yellow markers for where it will land is not in the right places (should be at the start of another column)."

Dragging a column **leftwards**, the drop line sits exactly on a column boundary. Dragging the same column **rightwards**, the line sits somewhere inside a column instead of at its edge - so the one thing ah-1owr.3 exists to provide, seeing where the column will land, is wrong in one of the two directions.

## The cause, exactly

`dropBoundaryX` (packages/shared/src/unitTable.ts:498) walks the **prospective** order and sums widths until it meets the dragged column:

    let x = 0;
    for (const column of prospective) {
      if (column === dragged) break;
      x += widthPxOf(column);
    }

That is the left edge of the dragged column **in the order it will have after the drop**. But the table on screen has deliberately not reordered yet - `reorderFeedback.ts` says so in its own header, and reordering under the pointer was the rejected option A. So the line is drawn in prospective coordinates over a table still laid out in the starting order.

Dragging **left**, those two coincide: every column that will precede the dragged one already precedes it on screen, so the sum is the same in both layouts.

Dragging **right**, they do not. The columns that will precede the dragged one include ones that currently sit *after* it, and the dragged column itself still occupies its old slot to the left of them. The visual boundary is therefore further right by exactly **the dragged column's own width**.

Worked from the existing test's own numbers (`unitTable.test.ts:582`), with own=24 and every other column 100, order `own, unitId, name, faction`:

- drag `name` one place right -> prospective `own, unitId, faction, name` -> `dropBoundaryX` = 24+100+100 = **224**
- but on screen the layout is still `own, unitId, name, faction`, and the right edge of `faction` - where the line belongs - is 24+100+100+100 = **324**
- the difference is 100, exactly `widthPxOf("name")`

## Why the tests did not catch it

`unitTable.test.ts:585` asserts precisely the 224 above. The test pins the prospective-layout arithmetic and never asks whether that coordinate lands on a boundary of the layout actually on screen, so it passes while the line is visibly wrong. `reorderFeedback.ts`'s header remarks that "The arithmetic was never the defect - showing its answer was"; the arithmetic is in fact correct for a table that has already reordered, and the table deliberately has not.

## Shape of a fix

Compute the boundary in the **starting** order rather than the prospective one - or equivalently, add `widthPxOf(dragged)` when the column's prospective index is greater than its starting index. The second is a smaller change; the first is harder to get subtly wrong later, and worth weighing at planning.

Whichever is chosen, the regression test must be expressed against the **displayed** layout, not the prospective one, or it will pin the same mistake again. A test that drags right and asserts the line falls on a boundary of the starting order would have failed today.

## Acceptance

Dragging a column in either direction, the drop line sits on a boundary between two columns of the table as it is currently drawn, and the column lands where the line said. A regression test covers the rightward drag specifically.

## Context

column **rightwards**, it sits somewhere inside a column. The navigator: *"when I drag them to the
right, the yellow markers for where it will land is not in the right places (should be at the start
of another column)."*

So the one thing `ah-1owr.3` exists to provide — seeing where the column will land — is wrong in one
of the two directions. That bead passed verification; this is the follow-up filed alongside the pass.

**Psylocke diagnosed it exactly, and the diagnosis holds.** `dropBoundaryX`
(`packages/shared/src/unitTable.ts:498-513`) sums widths over the **prospective** order:

```ts
  let x = 0;
  for (const column of prospective) {
    if (column === dragged) break;
    x += widthPxOf(column);
  }
```

That is the left edge of the dragged column *in the order it will have after the drop*. But the table
on screen **deliberately has not reordered yet** — `reorderFeedback.ts`'s own header says reordering
under the pointer *"was the rejected option A"*. So the line is drawn in prospective coordinates over
a table still laid out in the starting order.

- **Dragging left**, the two coincide: every column that will precede the dragged one already
  precedes it on screen.
- **Dragging right**, they do not: the columns that will precede it include ones that currently sit
  *after* it, while the dragged column still occupies its old slot to their left. The visual boundary
  is further right by exactly the dragged column's own width.

**Two things made this survive review**, and both are worth naming:

1. **The doc comment asserts the opposite.** *"Stated that way it is correct in both directions
   without an off-by-one."* It is a claim, it is wrong, and it is exactly the sort of confident
   comment a reader trusts.
2. **The existing test asserts the defect.** `unitTable.test.ts:591`:
   `expect(dropBoundaryX(right, "name", widthPxOf)).toBe(224)` — 224 is the wrong number. With
   `own` 24 and the rest 100 in order `own, unitId, name, faction`, dragging `name` one place right
   should put the line at the right edge of `faction`, **324**. The test has been pinning the bug.

Branch from `origin/main`; every line number here is that tree.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### 1. The boundary is a position in the *current* layout — `unitTable.ts:492-513`

The function cannot be fixed as it stands: **it is not given the current order**, only the
prospective one, and the answer depends on both. It gains a parameter.

```ts
/**
 * The x offset, from the table's left edge, of the boundary the dragged column will land on -
 * measured in the layout the player is actually looking at.
 *
 * That distinction is the whole of ah-gfzu. The table deliberately does not reorder until the drop
 * (`reorderFeedback.ts`, the rejected option A), so a boundary computed in the prospective order is
 * drawn over a table laid out in the starting one. Dragging left the two coincide; dragging right
 * they differ by exactly the dragged column's own width, and the line landed mid-column.
 *
 * So: find the last column that will precede the dragged one, and measure to its right edge *in the
 * current order* - which is where the gap the player is aiming at actually is. Nothing precedes it,
 * and the answer is 0.
 */
export function dropBoundaryX(
  current: ColumnOrder,
  prospective: ColumnOrder,
  dragged: UnitColumn,
  widthPxOf: (column: UnitColumn) => number
): number {
  const before = new Set<UnitColumn>();
  for (const column of prospective) {
    if (column === dragged) break;
    before.add(column);
  }
  if (before.size === 0) {
    return 0;
  }

  // Walk the *current* order, accumulating every width up to and including the last column that
  // will end up before the dragged one. The dragged column's own width counts when it still sits
  // within that span on screen - which is precisely the rightward case.
  let x = 0;
  let boundary = 0;
  for (const column of current) {
    x += widthPxOf(column);
    if (before.has(column)) {
      boundary = x;
    }
  }
  return boundary;
}
```

**Worked against the existing fixture** (`own` 24, others 100, order `own, unitId, name, faction`):

| gesture | prospective | expected line | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| no move | `own, unitId, name, faction` | **124** | left edge of `name`, unchanged |
| `name` one right | `own, unitId, faction, name` | **324** | right edge of `faction` on screen |
| `name` one left | `own, name, unitId, faction` | **24** | right edge of `own` |
| `name` to the far left | `name, own, unitId, faction` | **0** | nothing precedes it |

Only the second differs from today, and it is the bug.

### 2. The caller already has what it needs — `workspace/ColumnReorderHandle.tsx:89`

`startOrder` is in scope (`:81`), so the change is one argument:

```tsx
      feedback.showAt(
        dropBoundaryX(startOrder, prospective, column, widthPxOf),
        moveEvent.clientX - tableLeft
      );
```

**`startOrder` is right and `prospective` is not** — the table is laid out in `startOrder` for the
whole gesture, which is the premise of the whole fix.

### 3. Nothing else

`dragColumnOrder`, `reorderFeedback.ts`, the chip, Escape, the keyboard path and persistence are all
untouched. `ah-1owr.3` passed verification on every one of them.

## Increments

1. **The test stops asserting the bug.**
   RED: change `unitTable.test.ts:591` from `toBe(224)` to **`toBe(324)`**, and add the far-left case
   expecting `0`. It fails — against the current implementation, which is the point.
   **Do this first and on its own.** The existing test is the reason this shipped, and watching it go
   red is the proof that it is now pinning the right thing.
2. **The boundary is measured where the player is looking.**
   RED: the above.
   GREEN: the new signature and body, and the call site.
3. **The other three cases did not move.**
   RED: none — the check. The no-move, one-left and far-left cases keep their existing numbers.
   GREEN: nothing. **If any of them moved, the rightward fix broke the leftward case**, which is the
   one way this change can do damage.

## The test plan

| Test | Where | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| **`… lands at the right edge of the column it passed`** (was `toBe(224)`) | `unitTable.test.ts:582` | 324 — the defect, now asserted correctly |
| `no move puts the line at the column's own left edge` | same | 124, unchanged |
| `dragged one place left` | same | 24, unchanged |
| **`dragged to the far left sits at zero`** | same | 0, the empty-`before` branch |
| the 500-step fuzz at `:565-579` | same | unchanged — it exercises `dragColumnOrder`, not this |
| `ColumnReorderHandle`'s existing tests | its own file | unchanged |

**Suites:** `pnpm run check:fast`. The smoke suite is worth running for `ah-1owr.3`'s reorder
coverage, but the arithmetic is pure and belongs in the unit test.

## User-facing decisions

**None to make.** The correct behaviour is fixed by the navigator's own description of the defect —
*"should be at the start of another column"* — and by the existing design decision that the table does
not reorder until the drop. There is nothing to choose, so there is **no mockup**: a picture of a line
in the right place is the bug report.

The wording, the colour and the chip were all settled by `ah-1owr.3` and are unchanged.

## Out of scope

- **Reordering the table under the pointer**, which would make prospective coordinates correct and is
  `ah-1owr.3`'s explicitly rejected option A.
- **`dragColumnOrder`.** The order it computes is right; only the line's position was wrong. The
  bead's own words: *"the arithmetic was never the defect - showing its answer was."*
- **The chip, Escape, the keyboard path and persistence**, all verified.
- **Column widths and resizing** — `ah-1owr.2`.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
```

Then by hand, which is how this was found and is the only way to be sure:

1. Open the units table and **drag a column to the right**, slowly, past one neighbour. The drop line
   must sit **on a column boundary** — the start of the next column, or the table's right edge — and
   never inside a column.
2. **Drag the same column left.** Still on a boundary; this is the case that already worked and must
   keep working.
3. **Drag past several columns in each direction**, watching the line step from boundary to boundary.
4. **Drag a column to the far left**, so nothing precedes it: the line sits at the table's left edge,
   not one column in.
5. Release and confirm the column lands **exactly where the line said it would.** That correspondence
   is the feature; a line in a plausible-looking place that lies is no better than the bug.
6. Escape mid-drag still cancels, and the order is unchanged.

## Known traps

- **The existing test asserts the wrong number.** Change it before the implementation and watch it
  fail. A "fix" made with the old assertion in place would either be reverted to satisfy it or would
  silently keep the bug.
- **The doc comment claims correctness in both directions.** It is wrong and it is why this was
  believed. Replace it — do not leave a confident comment describing behaviour the code no longer has.
- **`startOrder`, not `prospective`, is the current layout.** Passing `prospective` for both
  arguments reproduces the bug exactly, and every leftward test still passes.
- **The dragged column's own width counts when it lies within the span.** That is not an off-by-one to
  be tidied away; it is the physical fact that the column is still on screen in its old slot.
- **The leftward case must not move.** It works today, and increment 3 exists because the obvious
  fixes to the rightward case tend to break it.
- **Do not reorder the table during the drag.** It would make the old arithmetic correct and is the
  option `ah-1owr.3` rejected on purpose.
acceptance_criteria:
- Dragging a column rightwards puts the drop line on a column boundary - the start of the next column or the table's right edge - never inside a column.
- Dragging leftwards is unchanged: the line still sits on a boundary, as it already did.
- Dragging a column to the far left, so nothing precedes it, puts the line at the table's left edge (0), not one column in.
- The column lands exactly where the line said it would, in both directions.
- `dropBoundaryX` measures in the order on screen, not the prospective one: with `own` 24 and the rest 100 in order `own, unitId, name, faction`, dragging `name` one place right gives 324.
- The existing test's `toBe(224)` - which asserts the defect - is corrected to `toBe(324)` rather than deleted, and is watched failing before the fix.
- The doc comment claiming the function is "correct in both directions without an off-by-one" is replaced; it is why the defect was believed.
- The table still does not reorder under the pointer.
- `pnpm run check:fast` passes.

title: The dictionary says a structure needs mages when it means it shelters them
description:
Found during verification of ah-5jkt.1 (2026-08-20, origin/main c6fc980). That bead passed; this is a follow-up filed alongside the pass.

## What the player sees

In the game-data dictionary, a building entry labels its `mages` number **"Mages needed"**. The navigator: 'one entry states "Mages needed". That should be "Mages sheltered".'

`packages/shared/src/workspace/GameDataDialog.tsx:345`:

    <Field label="Mages needed">{detail.mages}</Field>

## Why it is wrong, not merely awkward

The number is a **capacity**, not a requirement. It is how many mages the structure houses, which is what the existing magic-study warning reads it for - ah-3cj4.1's own validation exercises "half of this month's study of ... is wasted outside a building that houses mages", and a Fort silences that warning by sheltering mages rather than by demanding them.

So the current label states the opposite of what the field means. A player reading `Mages needed: 0` on an ordinary structure would reasonably conclude no mages may be housed there, when 0 means exactly that no mage is sheltered - and on a structure that does shelter mages, they would read a build prerequisite that does not exist. It is a small string, but it makes the number actively misleading rather than merely unhelpful.

## Shape of a fix

Change the label to **"Mages sheltered"**, which is the navigator's own wording. One string, one line.

Worth a moment at planning: whether the field should be **omitted entirely when the value is 0** rather than shown as a zero, since almost every structure shelters none and the row is noise on all of them. That is a separate judgement from the wording and should not hold up the correction.

## Acceptance

The building detail labels the mages number "Mages sheltered". No other field's wording changes.
design:
## Context

The game-data dictionary labels a structure's mage capacity **"Mages needed"**, which states the
opposite of what the number means.

`packages/shared/src/workspace/GameDataDialog.tsx:345`:

```tsx
          <Field label="Mages needed">{detail.mages}</Field>
```

**It is a capacity, not a requirement** — how many mages the structure houses, which is exactly what
the magic-study warning reads it for. A Fort silences *"half of this month's study of … is wasted
outside a building that houses mages"* by **sheltering** mages, not by demanding them. So
`Mages needed: 0` tells a reader a build prerequisite exists where there is none, and on a structure
that does shelter mages it invents a requirement.

Found by Psylocke verifying `ah-5jkt.1`, which passed; filed alongside the pass.

**Two facts measured from `config/public/ruleset.json` on main**, which decide the second half:

- **58 buildings**, and only **8 shelter any mages** — so about fifty entries print `0`.
- A `LAIR` carries `{"mages": 0}` and nothing else: no cost, no materials, no size, no build skill.
  **Its entire fields list is that one misleading zero**, and 22 of the 58 are like that.

Every other field in this dialog is already conditional (`detail.size === null ? null : …`,
`:339-344`). This one alone renders unconditionally.

Branch from `origin/main`; every line number here is that tree.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### One line, in `workspace/GameDataDialog.tsx:345`

```tsx
          {/* A capacity, not a prerequisite: how many mages the structure houses, which is what
              the magic-study warning reads it for. It used to say "Mages needed", which invented a
              requirement (ah-q3o1). Omitted at zero like every other field here - about fifty of
              the fifty-eight buildings shelter none, and after ah-3cj4.1 a zero is a fact rather
              than missing data, so silence means "none" rather than "unknown". */}
          {detail.mages === 0 ? null : <Field label="Mages sheltered">{detail.mages}</Field>}
```

**"Mages sheltered" is the navigator's own wording**, given to Psylocke at verification.

**Nothing else changes.** No data, no scraping, no Rust, no other field. `detail.mages` keeps its
type and its meaning; only the label and the condition move.

## Increments

1. **The label tells the truth, and a zero says nothing.**
   RED: `GameDataDialog`'s render tests — `a structure that shelters mages says so`
   (a Fort: contains `Mages sheltered` and `1`) and **`a structure that shelters none says nothing`**
   (a Lair: contains neither `Mages` nor the old `Mages needed`).
   GREEN: the line above.

## The test plan

| Test | Where | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| `a structure that shelters mages says so` | `GameDataDialog.test.tsx` | the new label, on a Fort |
| **`a structure that shelters none says nothing`** | same | the omission, on a Lair |
| `the old label is gone` | same | asserting `Mages needed` appears nowhere |
| the existing building-entry tests | same | unchanged |

**Suites:** `pnpm run check:fast`. No Rust, no browser suite — this is one conditional in one
component, and the rendering tests already run without a browser.

## User-facing decisions

Interviewed with the navigator on 2026-08-20 over
`.cerebro/scratch/ah-q3o1-building-entry.html`, which draws both this and `ah-rpnb` on real entries.
The chosen mockup is committed to `docs/ui/ah-q3o1-building-entry.html`.

**Q1 — the wording.** Settled before this bead reached planning: the navigator gave Psylocke
**"Mages sheltered"** at verification, and it is used verbatim.

**Q2 — whether a zero earns a row.** Chosen: **omit it at zero.** The row then appears only where it
says something — 8 of 58 entries — and it matches every other field in the dialog, all of which are
already conditional. Accepted cost: a lair's entry becomes description-only, which is honest but
looks empty, and *"does this shelter mages?"* is answered by silence, which a reader has to learn to
read. Rejected: **always showing it**, which answers definitely on every entry — after `ah-3cj4.1` a
zero really is a fact rather than missing data — at the cost of a `0` row on about fifty entries.

## Out of scope

- **`ah-rpnb`**, the missing build skill, which is the same dialog and the same mockup but a
  different bead.
- **The `mages` value itself, and how it is scraped.** `ah-3cj4.1` settled that silence in the page
  means zero; nothing here revisits it.
- **The other fields' labels.** Only this one states something untrue.
- **The magic-study warning**, which reads the same number and is correct.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
```

Then by eye, in the running app:

1. Open the dictionary on the **Buildings** tab and find a **Fort**. It reads
   **`Mages sheltered  1`**.
2. Find a **Tower** — the trap `ah-a2k.3` recorded, which is named in the rules table and seats
   **zero**. The row must be **absent**, not `0`.
3. Find a **Lair**. Its entry is now description-only, with no fields at all. Satisfy yourself that
   reads as "nothing more is known" rather than as a broken page — that is the one thing this change
   could get wrong.
4. Search the dictionary for `Mages needed` and confirm it appears nowhere.

## Known traps

- **It is a capacity, not a requirement**, and the label is the whole bug. Anything that reads like a
  prerequisite — "needs", "requires", "must have" — reintroduces it.
- **A Tower seats zero mages**, which `ah-a2k.3` recorded as the obvious assumption being wrong. With
  the row omitted at zero, a Tower shows nothing here — correct, and worth checking by eye because it
  is the entry a reader is most likely to go looking at.
- **Do not make the field nullable.** `detail.mages` is a number and stays one; the condition belongs
  in the render, beside the other conditional fields.
- **A lair's entry becomes description-only.** That is intended. If it reads as broken rather than as
  empty, say so — it is the accepted cost of Q2 and the navigator should hear it.
acceptance_criteria: GameDataDialog's building detail labels the mages number 'Mages sheltered' rather than 'Mages needed', and omits the field entirely when the value is zero - matching every other field in that detail, all of which are already conditional. A Fort shows 'Mages sheltered 1'; a Tower, which seats none, shows no such row; a Lair, which carries only mages:0, shows no fields at all and reads as an entry with nothing more known rather than a broken page. The string 'Mages needed' appears nowhere in the codebase. detail.mages keeps its type and meaning - the condition lives in the render, not in the data - and no ruleset, scraper or Rust change is made.

title: A building entry never says what skill builds it
description:
Found during verification of ah-5jkt.1 (2026-08-20, origin/main c6fc980). That bead passed; this is a follow-up filed alongside the pass.

## What the player sees

Open the game-data dictionary on the Buildings tab and read any building entry. It shows the description, cost, materials, size and the mages number - but never says **what skill, and at what level, a unit needs in order to build it**. The navigator's words: "when I look at a building, I cannot see what skill and level that is needed to build them."

That is the first question a player asks of a building they have not built before, and it is the one thing the entry does not answer.

## The data is already there

ah-bwly.1 scraped exactly this and committed it. Every buildable structure in config/public/ruleset.json carries `buildSkill` and `buildLevel` beside the fields the dialog already shows:

    TOWER: buildLevel, buildSkill, cost, description, mages, materials, size
    FORT:  buildLevel, buildSkill, cost, description, mages, materials, size

`git grep buildSkill packages/shared/src` finds nothing - the dialog simply never reads them. So this is a display gap, not a data gap, and no scraping or parsing work is needed.

## Shape of a fix

Render the pair in GameDataDialog's building detail, beside cost and materials. Worth deciding at planning:

- the wording and form - `Building requires: Building 3` reads oddly given the skill is itself named "Building"; something like `Built with Building 3` may read better;
- whether the skill name is a **clickable cross-reference** into the Skills tab, as `produces`, `requires` and the derived `producedBy` already are (ah-5jkt.1's decision was that cross-references are clickable, so consistency argues yes);
- what an entry with no `buildSkill` shows - NONE and the roads have no build requirement, and the field should presumably be omitted rather than shown empty.

## Acceptance

A building entry in the dictionary names the skill and level needed to build it, taken from the committed ruleset. A structure with no build requirement does not show an empty field.
