title: The ruleset scraper can misread the page and its own tests stay green
description:
## The cost being paid

`packages/ruleset/src/data.ts` is a hand-rolled regex parser over a scraped HTML page whose grammar
is asserted in prose. The package's own suite cannot catch a misread of that grammar, because
`committed.test.ts` asserts that `config/public/ruleset.json` equals what the scraper produces from
the committed fixture — which is true by construction whenever the parser is wrong and the JSON was
regenerated from it. Its own doc comment names what it catches: "A hand edit, or a scraper change
nobody regenerated after." A *wrong* scraper change that *was* regenerated passes.

Two consecutive beads on this module each shipped a wrong `config/public/ruleset.json`, and neither
was caught by the package. One was caught by two unrelated Rust tests, the other by a human reviewer.

## Evidence

- docs/retrospectives/ah-9js.md §"The plan's parser rule and the plan's expected result disagreed, and only the Rust suite said so" (commit a262d59, PR #401): "Implemented literally, the rule produces 58 entries... **Nothing in the TypeScript suite objected — the parser tests I wrote from the plan all passed.** Two pre-existing Rust tests... failed." Cost: "About twenty minutes: one wrong implementation, **one regeneration of `config/public/ruleset.json`**, one round of test edits."
- docs/retrospectives/ah-6qp.md §"The plan measured the page's grammar and got it wrong, and I coded the measurement rather than the page" (commit 72c6cb8, PR #412): the `" and "` split "silently dropped the middle requirement" of two three-requirement sentences. "The Copilot review found it... and pointed out that **the regenerated `config/public/ruleset.json` was wrong too**." And: "**My own check while building reproduced the same number the same way, which read as confirmation rather than as the same mistake twice.**" Cost: one review round and one extra CI cycle, roughly 20 minutes.
- ah-6qp's own Seen before names ah-3ej as "same file, previous bead" and the same shape.
- The construct that cost ah-6qp is still live one function away: `packages/ruleset/src/data.ts` `readCastCost` splits a cast-cost list on `" and "`, the exact grammar assumption the requirement parser was rewritten to remove.

## Where

- `packages/ruleset/src/data.ts` — ~673 lines, roughly 20 regex grammar claims about the page.
- `packages/ruleset/src/committed.test.ts` — the tautological check described above.
- `packages/ruleset/src/data.test.ts` — parser tests written from the same assumption as the parser.
- `tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-data.html`, `config/public/ruleset.json`.

## What a refactoring would change

The seam is a check that reads the *fixture page* rather than the parser's assumptions. For each
field the scraper claims to read, count the page's own marker phrase — "This skill requires", "via
magic at a cost of", "provides defense to the first" — and assert the parsed catalogue carries
exactly that many entries, none of them empty. That turns "my grammar is right" from prose into a
test that fails the moment the page carries a form the parser does not understand, and it fails
whether or not the JSON was regenerated. Then finish the separator removal ah-6qp started, so every
list parse reads self-delimiting `[TAG] n` pairs out of the sentence and `readCastCost`'s `" and "`
split goes with the rest.

Note for triage: both sightings were the same implementer and both retrospectives blamed the plan
rather than the code, so a reviewer could read this as a planning-discipline cost. The counter is
that the artifact shipped wrong twice and the package's own suite was green both times.

asserted in prose, and the package's own suite cannot catch a misread of that grammar.
`committed.test.ts` asserts that `config/public/ruleset.json` equals what the scraper produces from the
committed fixture — which is **true by construction whenever the parser is wrong and the JSON was regenerated
from it.** Its own doc comment names what it catches: *"A hand edit, or a scraper change nobody regenerated
after."* A wrong scraper change that *was* regenerated passes.

Two consecutive beads on this module each shipped a wrong `config/public/ruleset.json` and neither was caught
by the package: `ah-9js` (caught by two unrelated Rust tests) and `ah-6qp` (caught by a Copilot reviewer). The
parent bead carries the retrospective citations.

**What planning established, by measuring the fixture rather than reasoning about it.** These figures are the
plan's foundation and the implementer should reproduce them before changing anything:

| Field | Marker the page states | Occurrences | Catalogue entries carrying it |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cost` | `This skill costs <n> silver per month of study` | 95 | 95 |
| `requires` | `This skill requires … to begin to study.` | 66 | 66 |
| cast costs | `via magic at a cost of …` | 23 | **24** |
| `produces` | `may PRODUCE …` | 31 | **13** |

Two of those disagree, and **neither disagreement is a defect** — which is precisely why the naive check Forge
sketched must not be built as sketched:

- **Cast costs, 23 vs 24.** `readCastCost` has a *second* marker, `the attempt costs <n> silver`, which
  contributes a `SILV` input. It occurs once. 23 + 1 = 24.
- **Produces, 31 vs 13.** `may PRODUCE` appears in several of a skill's level paragraphs, and `produces`
  merges per skill. Thirty-one occurrences across thirteen skills.

So the check must compare **per-skill sets**, not raw counts, and must know that one field can be stated by
more than one marker.

**One further trap, and it cost an hour of planning to find.** The page line-wraps its sentences:

```
This skill
  requires force [FORC] 1, pattern [PATT] 1 and spirit [SPIR] 1 to
  begin to study.
```

A marker count taken over the raw HTML gives 49 for a phrase that occurs 66 times. **Whitespace must be
collapsed before any marker is counted**, exactly as the parser does. Any check written without that is
measuring nothing and will "fail" from the first run.

**The second half of the bead**, and its state today: `readCastCost` still splits its cost list on `" and "`
(`data.ts:417`) — the exact grammar assumption `ah-6qp` rewrote the requirement parser to remove. Measured
over the committed page, **zero cast-cost clauses contain a comma**, so it is not broken; it is one page change
away from repeating `ah-6qp` verbatim. That is worth removing while the evidence is fresh, and the new check is
what would catch it if it ever did break.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### New — `packages/ruleset/src/pageGrammar.test.ts`

The whole point of the bead: a check that reads the **fixture page** rather than the parser's assumptions.
A new file rather than an addition to `committed.test.ts`, because that file is about the committed artifact
agreeing with the scraper, and this one is about the scraper agreeing with the page. Two different claims.

The shape, for each field:

```ts
const FLAT = read("tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-data.html")
  .replace(/<[^>]+>/gu, " ")
  .replace(/\s+/gu, " ");
```

Then, per field, derive **the set of skill tags the page says should carry it** by walking the page's own
entries and testing each entry's text for the marker, and assert it equals the set of tags the catalogue
carries it for. Splitting the page into entries uses the same opening the parser does — `SKILL_OPENING`
(`data.ts:335`) — which must be **exported** for the test to use, so the test and the parser cannot drift on
what an entry even is.

Four assertions, one per field, each stated as a set comparison:

- `cost`: tags whose entry states `This skill costs \d+ silver per month of study` === tags with `cost !== null`.
- `requires`: tags whose entry states `This skill requires .+? to begin to study\.` === tags with a non-empty
  `requires`.
- cast: tags whose entry states `via magic at a cost of [^.]+\.` **or** `the attempt costs \d+ silver` ===
  tags with a non-empty `cast.costs`.
- `produces`: tags whose entry states `may PRODUCE [^.]*\.` === tags with a non-empty `produces`.

**And, for each, that no parsed entry is empty**: no `requires` entry with a blank tag or a zero level, no
`produces` entry with a blank tag, no cast input with a blank tag. A grammar misread that swallows a clause
shows up as a missing entry, not a missing skill, so the set check alone would not see it —
`ah-6qp`'s defect *was exactly that*: the middle requirement of a three-requirement sentence was dropped and
the skill still had requirements.

**One more assertion that would have caught `ah-6qp` directly:** the page has two three-requirement sentences.
Assert that the catalogue carries **two skills with exactly three requirements**, and name them. That is a
single line, and it is the regression test the module never had.

Write the marker regexes in this file **independently of `data.ts`** — do not import them. A check that shares
its patterns with the thing it checks is the tautology this bead exists to remove. Say so in the file's doc
comment, since it will otherwise read as duplication somebody should tidy away.

### Changed — `packages/ruleset/src/data.ts`

- **Export `SKILL_OPENING`** so the test can split entries the same way. Nothing else needs exporting; the
  markers are deliberately re-stated in the test.
- **Remove the `" and "` split in `readCastCost`** (line 417). Read self-delimiting `[TAG] n` pairs out of the
  clause with a global regex, as `readRequirements` now does with `REQUIREMENT_CLAUSE` (`data.ts:351`):
  ```ts
  const CAST_INPUT = /(?:(\d+) )?[a-z][a-z ]*\[([A-Z0-9]{2,6})\]/giu;
  ```
  and iterate `costMatch[1].matchAll(CAST_INPUT)`. That handles `a and b`, `a, b and c`, and any separator the
  page adopts next, because it never looks at the separator at all.
  **Keep the error path.** Today an unparseable part throws `RulesetScrapeError` naming the skill and the
  clause, which is good behaviour and must survive: if the clause contains no `[TAG]` pair at all, throw the
  same error with the same message shape. Silence there would be a scraper that reads nothing and says nothing.
- `ATTEMPT_COST` and `TRANSMUTE` are untouched.

### Changed — `packages/ruleset/src/data.test.ts`

The existing cast-cost tests were written from the `" and "` assumption. Keep them — they must still pass —
and add the cases the new implementation makes meaningful: a two-item clause separated by `,` and `and`, and a
three-item clause. Neither occurs on today's page, which is the point: the parser should be right about
grammars the page does not currently use, since that is how both previous defects arrived.

### Not changed — `packages/ruleset/src/committed.test.ts`

It stays exactly as it is. It catches a real thing (a hand edit, or a regeneration nobody did) and the new file
catches the thing it cannot. Its two independent assertions — the twenty-six mundane skills and the
mage-seating buildings — are earlier instances of exactly the discipline this bead generalises, and are
evidence the approach works.

### Where state lives

Nothing stateful. The parser is pure and the tests read files.

## Increments

Each opens with the named failing test.

1. **The page can be split the way the parser splits it.** `pageGrammar.test.ts` →
   `"reads the same ninety-six skill entries out of the page that the parser does"`. Export `SKILL_OPENING`,
   split `FLAT`, assert the entry count and that the tag set equals `Object.keys(ruleset.skills)`. **Do this
   first**: every later assertion stands on it, and if the split is wrong every one of them is meaningless.
2. **Cost.** → `"every skill the page prices is priced in the catalogue, and no other"`. Expect 95.
3. **Requirements.** → `"every skill the page gives requirements has them, and none is empty"`. Expect 66, and
   assert no requirement has a blank tag or a level below 1.
4. **The three-requirement case.** → `"the two skills the page gives three requirements carry all three"`.
   This is `ah-6qp`'s defect as a test.
5. **Cast costs, both markers.** → `"a skill's casting cost is read from either phrase the page uses"`.
   Expect 24 from the union of the two markers.
6. **Production.** → `"every skill the page says may PRODUCE something produces it"`. Expect 13 skills from 31
   occurrences — assert the *set*, and let the comment say why the two numbers differ.
7. **The separator goes.** `data.test.ts` → `"reads a casting cost list however it is punctuated"`. Then
   rewrite `readCastCost`.

Increments 1-6 must all pass **before** increment 7 changes any parser code — that is what makes the check a
check rather than something shaped to fit whatever the parser already does.

## The test plan

Vitest, in `packages/ruleset`, co-located as `<module>.test.ts` — the package's existing convention.

| File | Pins |
|---|---|
| `packages/ruleset/src/pageGrammar.test.ts` (new) | increments 1-6 |
| `packages/ruleset/src/data.test.ts` | increment 7, added to the existing 68 tests |

**Every existing test in the package must still pass, untouched.** 102 tests across five files pass today
(verified during planning). This bead adds checks and removes one grammar assumption; it changes no output.
`config/public/ruleset.json` must be **byte-identical** afterwards — if regenerating it produces a diff, the
`readCastCost` rewrite changed behaviour on the current page and something is wrong.

**Suites to run:** `pnpm run check:fast`. The browser suites are irrelevant — nothing here renders.

## User-facing decisions

**None.** No player can see any of this: it is a scraper, its tests, and a generated data file whose contents
do not change. The one thing a player would eventually see is a *wrong* ruleset, which is what the bead exists
to prevent.

## Out of scope

- **Rewriting the parser to something other than regexes.** The bead asks for a check that reads the page and
  for one grammar assumption to go. A parser-combinator or HTML-structure rewrite of `data.ts` is a much larger
  bead and this one does not authorise it.
- **Widening what the scraper captures.** Descriptions, non-fortification buildings, terrain and races are
  `ah-3cj4` and its children. This bead changes no output at all.
- **The rules-page parser**, `packages/ruleset/src/rules.ts`. The two shipped defects were both in `data.ts`,
  and the same treatment for `rules.ts` would be a separate bead with its own evidence.
- **Changing `committed.test.ts`.** It is not the problem; it is merely not sufficient.
- **The `MAGIC_WORDS` heuristic** (`data.ts:389`), which classifies magic from prose. It is a known
  approximation with its own long doc comment and its own assertion in `committed.test.ts`; leave it.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm --filter @atlantis/ruleset run test
pnpm run check:fast
```

Both green, with 102 existing tests still passing and the new file's assertions among them.

Then the check that the bead is actually worth anything — **make the parser wrong on purpose and watch it
fail**:

1. In `readRequirements`, change `REQUIREMENT_CLAUSE`'s global flag to non-global so only the first requirement
   of each sentence is read. `pageGrammar.test.ts` increment 4 must fail. Revert.
2. In `readCastCost`, delete the `ATTEMPT_COST` branch. Increment 5 must fail. Revert.
3. Regenerate `config/public/ruleset.json` while one of those is broken:
   ```bash
   pnpm --filter @atlantis/ruleset scrape -- \
     --rules tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-rules.html --data tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-data.html
   ```
   `committed.test.ts` now **passes** — the tautology, demonstrated — and `pageGrammar.test.ts` still fails.
   That contrast is the bead's whole claim, and seeing it once is worth more than any amount of prose about it.
   Revert both.

None of this needs a person to look at a screen; it needs the implementer to run three deliberate breakages and
confirm the new file catches what the old one cannot.

## Known traps

- **Collapse whitespace before counting anything.** The page line-wraps sentences mid-phrase
  (`This skill\n  requires force [FORC] 1 …`). Counted over raw HTML, a phrase that occurs 66 times reads as
  49. This cost an hour during planning and will cost the same again if it is not done first.
- **Do not import the parser's regexes into the check.** Sharing patterns between the parser and the thing that
  verifies it rebuilds the tautology in a new file. Re-state them, and say why in a comment so nobody tidies
  the "duplication" away later.
- **Marker count ≠ skill count.** `may PRODUCE` occurs 31 times across 13 skills, because a skill has a
  paragraph per level and `produces` merges. Compare sets of tags, never raw totals.
- **A field can have two markers.** Cast costs come from `via magic at a cost of …` *and* from
  `the attempt costs <n> silver`. 23 + 1 = 24. A check on one marker alone reports a false failure on the
  first run, which is how a new check gets deleted rather than fixed.
- **`readCastCost`'s `" and "` split is latent, not broken.** Zero clauses on the current page contain a
  comma, so removing it must change no output. If regenerating `ruleset.json` produces a diff, the rewrite is
  wrong — the byte-identical file is the proof it was a safe change.
- **Keep `readCastCost`'s `RulesetScrapeError`.** A clause it cannot read must still throw, naming the skill
  and the clause. A rewrite that quietly returns an empty list turns a loud failure into a silent one, which is
  a worse version of the bug being fixed.
- **`SKILL_OPENING` bounds the name at 40 characters and excludes `.`, `:`, `[`, `]`.** If the test's split
  finds a different number of entries than the parser, that regex — not the page — is where to look.
- **Work in a worktree under `.cerebro/worktrees/`**, never the main checkout, per `CLAUDE.md`.

title: CI browser jobs have no time limit, so one stall holds a runner for an hour
description:
## The cost being paid

Five browser jobs per PR run install Playwright's system libraries with apt at run time, and not one
of them carries a `timeout-minutes`. When that step stalls — a known, repeated failure — a runner is
held for 25 to 55 minutes instead of failing fast, and the fleet queues behind it. Four beads in five
days, four different implementers, one step name, roughly 3.5 hours of wall-clock.

The repository has already made the opposite choice once, deliberately, and written down why:
`ci.yml`'s `native` job carries `timeout-minutes: 30` with the comment "The largest hang surface in
the workflow ... so unlike its siblings this job carries its own ceiling." In ah-k6i.5 `native` hung
on this same class of step and was bounded at 30; its unbounded siblings went 40 and 55. That
inconsistency is the repository's, whatever the cause of the stall is.

The browser cache buys nothing against this: on a cache hit the workflow still runs
`playwright install-deps chromium`, so 100% of runs hit apt. The workflow's own comment admits it —
"the system libraries it links against do not [cache], so those are installed either way."

Secondary, and a cost in itself: three agents read the same recovery path three different ways.
ah-bn6.1 concluded a cancelled run cannot be re-run and paid a push; ah-mjy explicitly corrects it
("Reading that retrospective and pushing instead would have cost a full second CI cycle"); ah-vw63
hit a third outcome again.

## Evidence

- docs/retrospectives/ah-k6i.5.md §"Three CI jobs sat 'in_progress' for 20+ minutes, stuck on an apt-get step" (2026-08-15) — `smoke (web,1,2)`, `smoke (web,2,2)`, `native`; 21+ min; ~20 min, one cycle.
- docs/retrospectives/ah-bn6.1.md §"A cancelled CI run cannot be re-run, so the recovery from a hung job is a push" (2026-08-17) — `smoke (web,2,2)`, ~40 min stall; rerun refused, recovery was a push; ~45 min, one cycle wasted.
- docs/retrospectives/ah-mjy.md §"The `pwa` job hung 25 minutes in 'Install Playwright system dependencies' and was cancelled" (2026-08-18) — 25m42s; after rerun the job passed in **47 seconds**; ~30 min, one cycle. Its Prevent by: "A step timeout on the Playwright install ... would turn a 25-minute stall into a two-minute failure."
- docs/retrospectives/ah-vw63.md §"Two smoke shards hung an hour in 'Install Playwright system dependencies', and the re-run then sat queued for another hour" (2026-08-19) — 55 min; ~2 hours. Its Prevent by: "four sightings and no fix ... caching that layer, pinning the browser image, or adding a step `timeout-minutes` ... it is no longer a fluke."

## Where

- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` — the `smoke` job, matrix `project: [web, desktop-shell] x shardIndex: [1,2]` = 4 jobs, no `timeout-minutes`. Steps "Install Playwright Chromium" (`playwright install --with-deps chromium`) on cache miss and "Install Playwright system dependencies" (`playwright install-deps chromium`) on cache hit — both run apt.
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` — the `pwa` job, no `timeout-minutes`, the identical pair of steps. Five apt installs per PR run.
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` — the `native` job: `timeout-minutes: 30`, the only ceiling in the whole file. `git grep -n 'timeout-minutes' -- .github/` returns exactly one line.
- `.github/workflows/release.yml` — the same cache + install + install-deps trio a third time.

## What a refactoring would change

Give `smoke` and `pwa` the job-level ceiling `native` already has, so an hour of held runner becomes a
minutes-long failure that is retryable inside a review window. Collapse the three copies of the
cache/install/install-deps trio into one composite action under `.github/actions/`, so the ceiling and
any image change are made once instead of three times. The larger move, if the navigator wants the
exposure gone rather than bounded, is to run the browser jobs in the official
`mcr.microsoft.com/playwright` container matching the pinned `@playwright/test` version, which bakes
the libraries in and deletes both install steps. Not a retry rule — `implement-bead` already has one,
and three agents derived three incompatible recoveries from it.

Note for triage: the stall itself is GitHub-Actions infrastructure nobody here can fix, and ah-vw63
attributes roughly half its two hours to an unrelated repo-wide queue stall. What is repo-owned is
where apt runs, how many times, and whether anything bounds it.

design:
## Context

Five browser jobs per PR run install Playwright's system libraries with apt at run time, and **not one
of them carries a `timeout-minutes`**. When that step stalls — four sightings in five days — a runner
is held for 25 to 55 minutes instead of failing fast, and the whole fleet queues behind it. Forge
measured roughly **3.5 hours of wall-clock** across four beads and four different implementers.

`git grep -n 'timeout-minutes' -- .github/` returns **exactly one line**, and the repository has
already made the opposite choice there deliberately (`ci.yml:453-455`):

```yaml
    # The largest hang surface in the workflow - xvfb, a native webview and a fixed port - so
    # unlike its siblings this job carries its own ceiling.
    timeout-minutes: 30
```

In `ah-k6i.5` the `native` job hung on this same class of step and was bounded at 30; its unbounded
siblings went 40 and 55. **The inconsistency is the repository's**, whatever the cause of the stall
is — and the cause is GitHub Actions infrastructure nobody here can fix. What is repo-owned is where
apt runs, how many times, and whether anything bounds it.

**The cache buys nothing against this.** On a cache *hit* the workflow still runs
`playwright install-deps chromium` (`ci.yml:332-334`, `:398-400`), so **100% of runs hit apt** — the
workflow's own comment says so: *"The browser itself caches; the system libraries it links against do
not, so those are installed either way."*

**How long these jobs actually take**, measured from the last eight `ci.yml` runs on 2026-08-19 —
this is what makes a ceiling a number rather than a guess:

| job | successful runs sampled | average | longest |
|---|---|---|---|
| `smoke (desktop-shell, 1, 2)` | 3 | 2.3 min | **4 min** |
| `smoke (web, 1, 2)` | 3 | 2.0 min | 3 min |
| `smoke (desktop-shell, 2, 2)` | 2 | 1.5 min | 3 min |
| `smoke (web, 2, 2)` | 3 | 1.3 min | 2 min |
| `pwa` | 2 | under 1 min | under 1 min |
| `native` | 2 | 1.0 min | 1 min |

So `native`'s 30 is generous by a factor of thirty, and a ceiling of **15 minutes** on the browser
jobs is nearly four times the longest real run while turning a 55-minute stall into a 15-minute
failure that is retryable inside a review window.

Branch from `origin/main`; every line number here is that tree.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

Two workflow files and one new composite action. **No application code, no tests, no
`package.json`.**

### 1. The ceiling — `.github/workflows/ci.yml`

`timeout-minutes: 15` on the `smoke` job (`:280`) and the `pwa` job (`:360`), each with the comment
that makes it survive the next reader:

```yaml
  smoke:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: [changes, wasm]
    if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
    # Four minutes is the longest this job has taken when it works (measured over eight runs,
    # 2026-08-19). The ceiling is for the failure mode, not the work: `playwright install-deps`
    # runs apt on every run, cache hit or miss, and has stalled 25-55 minutes four times in five
    # days (ah-3c80). Unbounded, one stall holds a runner for an hour and the fleet queues behind
    # it; bounded, it is a fast failure anyone can re-run.
    timeout-minutes: 15
```

`pwa` gets the same value and a one-line version of the same comment pointing at `smoke`'s.

**`native`'s 30 is not changed.** Its comment explains a different hang surface — xvfb, a native
webview and a fixed port — and this bead has no evidence about it. Say so rather than tidying it.

### 2. One copy of the trio — `.github/actions/playwright-browser/action.yml`

The cache/install/install-deps trio appears **three times**: `ci.yml`'s `smoke` (`:319-334`),
`ci.yml`'s `pwa` (`:387-400`), and `release.yml`. A composite action so the next change to it — the
container in `ah-f9q9`, a pinned image, a different cache key — is made once:

```yaml
name: Playwright browser
description: >
  Chromium and the system libraries it links against, cached where cacheable.
  One copy of a trio that was written out three times; see ah-3c80.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - name: Cache the Playwright browser
      id: playwright-cache
      uses: actions/cache@v4
      with:
        path: ~/.cache/ms-playwright
        key: playwright-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('pnpm-lock.yaml') }}

    # The browser itself caches; the system libraries it links against do not, so those are
    # installed either way - which is why every run reaches apt, and why the callers carry a
    # `timeout-minutes` (ah-3c80).
    - name: Install Playwright Chromium
      if: steps.playwright-cache.outputs.cache-hit != 'true'
      shell: bash
      run: pnpm exec playwright install --with-deps chromium

    - name: Install Playwright system dependencies
      if: steps.playwright-cache.outputs.cache-hit == 'true'
      shell: bash
      run: pnpm exec playwright install-deps chromium
```

Two things that will bite if they are skimmed:

- **A composite step needs `shell: bash` on every `run`.** Omitting it is a workflow-parse error, not
  a runtime one, so it fails the whole file rather than the step.
- **The `if: needs.changes.outputs.code == 'true'` guards do not move into the action.** A composite
  action has no access to `needs`. Keep the guard on the `uses:` step in each caller —
  `- uses: ./.github/actions/playwright-browser` with `if: needs.changes.outputs.code == 'true'` —
  which is where it already is in spirit.

`release.yml`'s copy (`:307-318`) is replaced the same way — and **it has no `changes` guard at
all**, verified, so its `uses:` step carries no `if:`. Copying `ci.yml`'s condition into it would
reference a `needs.changes` that does not exist there.

**`release.yml`'s job gets the ceiling too**, which goes slightly beyond what Forge proposed and is
the planner's call: it runs the identical apt step with the identical exposure, and a release that
hangs for an hour is worse than a PR that does, not better. Same value, same comment, pointing at
`smoke`'s.

### 3. The container, filed rather than built

Running the browser jobs in `mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v<pinned>` bakes the libraries in and
deletes both install steps — removing the exposure rather than bounding it. That is
**`ah-f9q9`**, filed alongside this bead: it changes the environment every browser test runs
in, which is not a thing to land while five beads are in flight, and the image tag must be kept in
step with the pinned `@playwright/test` version, which is a maintenance rule this bead should not
invent in passing.

## Increments

1. **The ceiling.**
   RED: not expressible as a test — CI configuration has no local suite. The check is
   `git grep -c 'timeout-minutes' -- .github/`, which must go from **1 to 4**.
   GREEN: `timeout-minutes: 15` on `smoke`, `pwa` and `release.yml`'s browser job, with their
   comments.
   **Push this on its own and let CI run before going further.** It is the whole value of the bead,
   it is two lines, and it must not be held up behind a refactor that could go wrong.

2. **One copy of the trio.**
   RED: `git grep -c 'playwright install-deps' -- .github/` is **3** and must become **1**.
   GREEN: the composite action, and all three call sites replaced.

3. **It still works.**
   RED: none — this is the check, and it can only be made on CI. The `smoke` and `pwa` jobs must run
   green **on both a cache hit and a cache miss**: the two install steps are mutually exclusive on
   `cache-hit`, so a single green run exercises only one of them. Force a miss by touching
   `pnpm-lock.yaml`'s hash — or simply confirm the first run after merge (a new key) and a later one
   (a hit) both pass, and say which was which in the PR.

## The test plan

**There is no local suite for this bead.** `pnpm run check:fast` must still pass, and it is
unaffected — nothing outside `.github/` changes.

What stands in for tests:

| Check | How |
|---|---|
| the ceiling exists everywhere it should | `git grep -n 'timeout-minutes' -- .github/` returns four lines: `smoke`, `pwa`, `native`, and `release.yml`'s browser job |
| the trio exists once | `git grep -c 'playwright install-deps' -- .github/` is 1 |
| the workflow still parses | the PR's own CI run — a composite-action mistake fails the whole file, loudly and immediately |
| the browser jobs still pass | `smoke (web, 1, 2)`, `smoke (web, 2, 2)`, `smoke (desktop-shell, 1, 2)`, `smoke (desktop-shell, 2, 2)` and `pwa` green on the PR |
| **both cache paths work** | one run on a cache miss and one on a hit, named in the PR body |
| the ceiling is not too tight | the observed maximum is 4 minutes against a ceiling of 15; if any job times out on this PR, the number is wrong and the evidence above is stale |

**Do not add a workflow-linting dependency** (`actionlint`, `yamllint`) to prove increment 2. It is a
new tool in the gate for a three-line refactor, and CI itself is the check.

## User-facing decisions

Nothing here reaches a player. Two decisions were still the navigator's, on 2026-08-19, and there is
no mockup — CI configuration has no interface to draw.

**Q1 — how far to go.** Chosen: **bound now, unify the three copies, and file the container.**
Rejected: **bound only** (smallest change, merges in minutes, but leaves three copies so the next
change to the trio is made three times again) and **going straight to the container** (deletes the
exposure rather than bounding it, but changes the environment every browser test runs in, which is a
large thing to land with five beads in flight).

**Q2 — the recovery guidance.** The bead's secondary finding is that three agents derived three
incompatible recoveries from a hung job — `ah-bn6.1` concluded a cancelled run cannot be re-run and
paid a push, `ah-mjy` explicitly corrected that, `ah-vw63` hit a third outcome. Fixing it means
editing the `implement-bead` skill, which is a change to the workflow itself and so the navigator's.
Chosen: **leave the documentation alone** — a bounded job fails in fifteen minutes and is retried like
any other failure, so the question largely stops arising. Rejected: a sentence in `implement-bead`
(the bead argues a retry rule is the wrong shape) and filing it separately.

**Decided here, not asked, because tooling and CI are the planner's:** the value 15 (measured, four
times the longest real run); leaving `native`'s 30 alone; **extending the ceiling to `release.yml`'s
browser job**, which Forge did not propose but which carries the identical exposure; the composite
action's name and location; and not adding a workflow linter.

## Out of scope

- **The Playwright container**, `ah-f9q9`, filed alongside this bead and blocked on it. It is the fix that
  removes the exposure; this one bounds it.
- **`native`'s existing `timeout-minutes: 30`.** A different hang surface with its own comment, and
  this bead has no evidence about it.
- **The stall itself**, which is GitHub Actions infrastructure. `ah-vw63` attributes roughly half its
  two hours to an unrelated repo-wide queue stall — nothing here can fix that either.
- **A retry rule.** `implement-bead` already has one, and the bead is explicit that three agents
  derived three incompatible recoveries *from* it. Adding a fourth statement is not the fix.
- **The `changes` gating**, the cache key, and which jobs run on which paths. Untouched.
- **Caching the apt layer.** Considered by Forge and not proposed: the container supersedes it.

## Validation

There is nothing to run locally that exercises this. The validation is the PR's own CI run, read
deliberately rather than glanced at:

1. `git grep -n 'timeout-minutes' -- .github/` → four lines.
2. `git grep -c 'playwright install-deps' -- .github/` → one.
3. `pnpm run check:fast` → green, and unchanged; nothing outside `.github/` moved.
4. On the PR: all four `smoke` shards and `pwa` green. **Read their durations** — they should be
   within a minute or two of the table in *Context*. A job that now takes materially longer means the
   composite action changed what runs, not merely where it is written.
5. **Confirm both cache paths.** The first run after the action is added takes whichever path the
   existing key gives; a later run takes the other. Name in the PR body which run was a hit and which
   a miss, so the reviewer does not have to infer it.
6. Check the workflow parses at all — a composite action missing `shell: bash` fails the file, and
   the failure names YAML rather than the step.

## Known traps

- **`shell: bash` is required on every `run` in a composite action.** Its absence is a parse error
  that fails the whole workflow file, and the message points at YAML rather than at the missing key.
- **A composite action cannot see `needs`.** The `if: needs.changes.outputs.code == 'true'` guards
  must stay on the `uses:` step in each caller. Moving them inside silently runs apt on every job,
  including the ones the `changes` filter exists to skip — which would make this bead *worse* than
  the problem it fixes.
- **The two install steps are mutually exclusive on `cache-hit`**, so one green run proves only one
  of them. This is why increment 3 asks for both.
- **`release.yml` has the trio at `:307-318` and no `changes` guard at all** — verified, not
  assumed. Copying `ci.yml`'s `if:` into it references a `needs.changes` that does not exist there,
  which is a parse-time failure on the release workflow, found at release time.
- **The ceiling is a failure bound, not a budget.** Fifteen minutes against a four-minute job is
  deliberate slack for a cold cache and a slow runner. Tightening it toward the observed maximum
  turns an infrastructure hiccup into a red PR, which is the failure this bead is trying to stop
  costing people time.
- **`git grep -n 'timeout-minutes'` returning one line is the measurement that started this.** If it
  returns more than three when you are done, something else grew a ceiling and that was not this
  bead's doing — find out what.
acceptance_criteria: The smoke job, the pwa job and release.yml's browser job each carry timeout-minutes: 15, so git grep -n 'timeout-minutes' -- .github/ returns four lines rather than one, each with a comment saying the ceiling is for the failure mode and naming the measured four-minute maximum. native's existing 30 is unchanged. The cache/install/install-deps trio exists once, as a composite action under .github/actions/, used by all three call sites, so git grep -c 'playwright install-deps' -- .github/ returns 1; every run step in it carries shell: bash, and the needs.changes guards stay on the callers' uses: steps because a composite action cannot see needs - release.yml's call site carries no guard, having none today. All four smoke shards and pwa pass on the PR, on a cache hit and on a cache miss, with the PR body naming which run was which, and their durations remain within a minute or two of the measured baseline. No application code, no test file and no package.json changes, and no workflow linter is added to the gate.

title: A full disk fails the code gate and silently skips fmt and clippy
description:
## The cost being paid

`check:fast` is an `&&` chain: `lint && typecheck && test && check:generated && cargo fmt --check &&
cargo clippy`. The machine's disk state is enforced as a vitest case (`scripts/diskPreflight.test.ts`
shells out to the preflight and fails under an 8 GB floor) inside `test`, three steps before `cargo
fmt --check` and `cargo clippy`. So an environmental refusal fails the code gate, is
indistinguishable at a glance from a real failure, and silently skips exactly the two checks that are
seconds each and need no headroom.

That has already put a defect through to CI, and it has already degraded the four-eye gate: two beads
opened PRs on a knowingly red local gate with a paragraph in the PR body explaining it.

Twelve retrospectives in this sweep's range name the disk floor, ~133 minutes; ah-vkut counts itself
the fifteenth in the corpus. In eight of the twelve nothing in the repository could reclaim anything,
and `prune-worktrees.sh` freed space in zero of the twelve.

**Scope note for triage:** this is *not* a request for a shared `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`. The per-worktree
build tree is a settled, already-litigated decision — `.cargo/config.toml` records that a shared tree
would serialise every implementer's Rust build behind cargo's file lock, and ah-gdp exists because
earlier retrospectives blamed a shared tree that was never real. The disk scarcity is mostly the
navigator's machine, not the fleet's (ah-vkut measured the fleet's own build trees at 2.2 GB against
191 GiB used). What is filable here is the *gate coupling*, which is entirely the repository's.

## Evidence

- docs/retrospectives/ah-j0e.md §"An unformatted review fix reached CI, because the local gate could no longer be run at all" — `check:fast` exited 1 on `diskPreflight.test.ts` alone at 7.5 GB; read as environmental and pushed; CI's `rust` job then failed on `cargo fmt --check`. **Two CI cycles, ~20 minutes.** Its own Why names the mechanism: "The tooling suite runs before cargo, so the disk floor masks fmt and clippy specifically." Its Seen before lists seven prior files and adds: "none of which names what it hides downstream of it."
- docs/retrospectives/ah-quw.md and ah-58n.1.md — both record a PR opened on a red local gate with a paragraph explaining it; the gate degraded to "CI is the real gate".
- docs/retrospectives/ah-vkut.md — blocked before a line was read; a navigator round-trip, who chose "proceed anyway"; "had they been asleep — a bead handed back for a reason that has nothing to do with the bead."
- docs/retrospectives/ah-kdgc.md — a navigator interruption before work began, and the preflight's advice line was actively misleading: it printed "2.2 GB sits in 2 build trees" when those trees were 24 MB and 342 MB.
- docs/retrospectives/ah-1znc.md — ~25 min across two stalls, blocking both the start and the gate.
- Also in range: ah-do8.2, ah-do8.3, ah-l2i.1, ah-l2i.2, ah-l2i.3, ah-vfq — each 5-15 min.
- The repository already learned this lesson one level down: `scripts/runSuites.ts`'s header explains it is exhaustive rather than short-circuiting precisely so "a broken leg can no longer hide whether the others ran" (ah-vek). That reasoning was never applied to `check:fast`'s own `&&` chain.

## Where

- `package.json` — the `check:fast` script's `&&` chain, and `test:tooling`.
- `scripts/runSuites.ts` — already exhaustive; the precedent.
- `scripts/diskPreflight.ts` — `FREE_SPACE_FLOOR_GB = 8`, a flat constant; the direct-invocation block exits non-zero.
- `scripts/diskPreflight.test.ts` §"the preflight as a command" — `execFileSync` throws on the non-zero exit, which is what makes machine state a red unit test.

## What a refactoring would change

Take the disk question out of the vitest suite: keep `diskPreflight.test.ts` for the pure functions
(`hasHeadroom`, `describeSpace`, `describeReclaimable`) and move "does this disk have room" to a
first-line step of `check:fast` that reports separately from the code verdict. Make `check:fast`
exhaustive the way `runSuites.ts` already is, so fmt and clippy run even when an earlier leg fails —
that alone removes ah-j0e's defect class. Have the opening preflight and the gate read one floor, not
two (ah-quw, ah-58n.1 and ah-l2i.2 all lost time to a 5 GB vs 8 GB skew), and let the refusal name
reclaims that actually exist rather than pointing at a sweep that freed nothing in twelve for twelve.

Filed by Forge, daily sweep of 2026-08-19, range a19f579..cec1dd0.
design:
## Context

`check:fast` is an `&&` chain:

```
lint && typecheck && test && check:generated && cargo fmt --check && cargo clippy
```

and the machine's **disk state is enforced as a vitest case inside `test`** — three steps before
`cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy`. `scripts/diskPreflight.test.ts:139-146` shells out to the
preflight with `execFileSync`, which throws on its non-zero exit:

```ts
describe("the preflight as a command", () => {
  it("says what it found, and succeeds while this disk has room", () => {
    const said = execFileSync(TSX, [SCRIPT], { encoding: "utf8", timeout: 20_000 });
```

So an **environmental** refusal fails the **code** gate, is indistinguishable at a glance from a real
failure, and **silently skips exactly the two checks that are seconds each and need no headroom**.

That has already put a defect through to CI and has already degraded the four-eye gate:

- `ah-j0e` — `check:fast` exited 1 on `diskPreflight.test.ts` alone at 7.5 GB; read as environmental
  and pushed; CI's `rust` job then failed on `cargo fmt --check`. **Two CI cycles, ~20 minutes.**
- `ah-quw` and `ah-58n.1` — **PRs opened on a knowingly red local gate**, each with a paragraph in the
  PR body explaining it. The gate degraded to "CI is the real gate".
- `ah-vkut` — blocked before a line was read; a navigator round-trip. *"Had they been asleep — a bead
  handed back for a reason that has nothing to do with the bead."*
- Twelve retrospectives in Forge's range name the disk floor, ~133 minutes.

**The repository already learned this one level down.** `scripts/runSuites.ts`'s header says it is
exhaustive rather than short-circuiting precisely so *"a broken leg can no longer hide whether the
others ran"* — after an agent read a tooling failure as unrelated and silently skipped the entire
576-test Rust suite. **That reasoning was never applied to `check:fast`'s own chain.**

### Two things in the bead's proposal that do not survive checking

**There is no second floor to unify.** Forge cites a 5 GB vs 8 GB skew. `git grep` finds exactly one
constant, `FREE_SPACE_FLOOR_GB = 8` (`scripts/diskPreflight.ts:35`), and exactly one importer. Reading
`ah-l2i.1` explains it: *"8.1 GB free, reported against a 5 GB floor **in the main checkout** … below
the 8 GB floor **the worktree's copy of the script** enforces."* Those were two *versions* of one
file, not two constants — a stale main checkout, which is **`ah-puoj`**. Nothing to unify here, and a
bead that "unified" them would be papering over that.

**The reclaim advice is wrong in a way this plan will not claim to fix.** `ah-kdgc` records the
preflight printing *"2.2 GB sits in 2 build trees"* when those trees were 24 MB and 342 MB.
`describeReclaimable` (`:82-94`) sums what it is handed correctly, so the fault is upstream in
`findBuildTrees`/`duGb` (`:135-146`) — and **nobody has diagnosed it.** This plan makes the mismatch
*visible* rather than pretending to fix it; see §4.

Branch from `origin/main`; every line number here is that tree.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### 1. The gate becomes exhaustive — `scripts/runGate.ts` (new) and `package.json:21`

Follow `scripts/runSuites.ts` exactly — it is the precedent, it already solves this, and it is 60
lines. Its shape: a `readonly Suite[]` of `{ name, command, args }`, run **sequentially** with
`spawnSync`, every one of them, then a pure reporter that prints each result and decides the exit
code.

```ts
/**
 * Runs every leg of the fast gate, and reports on every one of them.
 *
 * `lint && typecheck && test && check:generated && cargo fmt --check && cargo clippy` used to be an
 * `&&` chain, so anything failing early meant fmt and clippy never ran - and the disk-space
 * preflight, enforced as a vitest case inside `test`, is an *environmental* refusal that skipped
 * them every time the machine was full (ah-tn2z). ah-j0e is the defect that reached CI that way.
 *
 * Sequential rather than parallel, so cargo and vitest do not contend for the machine and the
 * output stays readable; exhaustive rather than short-circuiting, so a broken leg can no longer
 * hide whether the others ran - the same trade `runSuites.ts` makes, for the same reason.
 */
const LEGS: readonly Leg[] = [
  { name: "lint", command: "pnpm", args: ["run", "lint"] },
  { name: "typecheck", command: "pnpm", args: ["run", "typecheck"] },
  { name: "test", command: "pnpm", args: ["run", "test"] },
  { name: "generated", command: "pnpm", args: ["run", "check:generated"] },
  { name: "fmt", command: "cargo", args: ["fmt", "--check"] },
  { name: "clippy", command: "cargo", args: ["clippy", "--workspace", "--all-targets", "--", "-D", "warnings"] }
];
```

`"check:fast": "tsx scripts/runGate.ts"`. The exit code is non-zero if **any** leg failed — the gate
is not weakened, only made honest about what it ran.

**Reuse `runSuites.ts`'s reporter shape rather than inventing one.** If its printing helper can be
exported and shared, do that; if that means reshaping `runSuites.ts`, keep the change to extraction
and leave its behaviour alone — its own tests must stay green untouched.

### 2. The disk stops being a code verdict — `scripts/diskPreflight.test.ts:139-146`

The case exists for a good reason its own comment gives: the script *"was importable but not
runnable"* before the direct-invocation block. Keep that, drop the machine dependence — assert the
output, tolerate either exit:

```ts
  it("says what it found, whether or not this disk has room", () => {
    // Deliberately indifferent to the exit code: this asserts the script *runs and reports*, which
    // is a property of the code. Whether the machine happens to have 8 GB free is not, and
    // asserting it here made a full disk fail the code gate and skip fmt and clippy (ah-tn2z).
    const said = runPreflight();

    expect(said).toMatch(/GB free/u);
    expect(said).toContain(String(FREE_SPACE_FLOOR_GB));
  });
```

where `runPreflight()` wraps `execFileSync` and returns stdout on either path — on a non-zero exit
`execFileSync` throws an error carrying `stdout`, so catch it and read that rather than re-running.

The pure-function cases (`hasHeadroom`, `describeSpace`, `describeReclaimable`) are **unchanged**: they
take a number and return a string, and are exactly the right thing to unit-test.

### 3. The disk is reported, first, and does not fail the gate

A first leg in `runGate.ts` that runs the preflight for its **message**, prints it, and does **not**
contribute to the exit code:

```ts
// Reported, never fatal. A full disk is a fact about the machine, not a verdict on the code, and
// the whole of ah-tn2z is that conflating them skipped fmt and clippy exactly when somebody was
// most likely to push anyway. It goes first so it is read before the output that matters.
```

So a full disk now reads: *"disk: 7.5 GB free, below the 8 GB floor needed to build."* at the top,
then every leg's result, then a verdict about the code. The cargo legs may well fail on a genuinely
full disk — that is fine and honest; what must not happen is their being **skipped in silence**.

### 4. The reclaim advice names what it found — `scripts/diskPreflight.ts:82-94`

`describeReclaimable` returns one total. `ah-kdgc` saw that total disagree with reality by two orders
of magnitude, and the cause is undiagnosed. Make the disagreement self-evident by naming each tree:

```
2.2 GB sits in 2 build trees: .cerebro/worktrees/ah-x/target (1.9 GB), target (0.3 GB);
.claude/cerebro/scripts/prune-worktrees.sh reclaims what is safe.
```

**This is not a claim to have fixed the measurement.** It makes a wrong measurement visible at the
moment it is printed, instead of a bare total nobody can check. If the implementer *does* find the
cause in `findBuildTrees`/`duGb` while here — measure a known tree with `du -sh` and compare — **file
it rather than fixing it in passing**; it is a different defect and deserves its own evidence.

## Increments

1. **The gate runs everything.**
   RED: `scripts/runGate.test.ts` — over the pure reporter, mirroring `runSuites`'s own tests:
   `reports every leg, including ones after a failure`, `exits non-zero when any leg failed`,
   `exits zero when all passed`.
   GREEN: `runGate.ts` and the `package.json` change.

2. **A full disk no longer fails the code gate.**
   RED: `diskPreflight.test.ts` — `says what it found, whether or not this disk has room`. To see it
   fail for the right reason, temporarily set `FREE_SPACE_FLOOR_GB` absurdly high (say 10_000) so the
   script exits 1: the **old** case fails, the **new** one passes. Restore the constant.
   GREEN: `runPreflight()`'s catch.

3. **The disk is reported and not fatal.**
   RED: with the floor temporarily at 10_000, `pnpm run check:fast` must still run fmt and clippy and
   must report them — the exact failure `ah-j0e` describes, reproduced deliberately. Restore.
   GREEN: the first leg in `runGate.ts`.

4. **The advice can be checked.**
   RED: `describeReclaimable names each tree and its size`, over a hand-built list.
   GREEN: the message change.

## The test plan

| Test | Where | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| `reports every leg, including ones after a failure` | `scripts/runGate.test.ts` | exhaustiveness — the whole bead |
| `exits non-zero when any leg failed` | same | the gate is not weakened |
| `exits zero when all passed` | same | the ordinary case |
| **`says what it found, whether or not this disk has room`** | `diskPreflight.test.ts` | the machine is no longer a code verdict |
| the pure cases (`hasHeadroom`, `describeSpace`) | same | unchanged |
| `describeReclaimable names each tree and its size` | same | the advice is checkable |
| `runSuites`'s own tests | `scripts/runSuites.test.ts` | **unchanged** if its reporter was extracted |

**Suites:** `pnpm run check:fast` — which is the thing being changed, so run it before and after and
compare the output, not just the exit code. `cargo test --workspace` is unaffected but is one of the
legs, so it runs anyway.

**The reproduction is the acceptance**, and it is cheap: set the floor to 10_000, run the gate, and
confirm fmt and clippy still ran. That is `ah-j0e` in one command.

## User-facing decisions

**None reach a player.** The navigator is the user of `check:fast`, and what changes for them is the
output shape — every leg reported rather than a chain stopping at the first failure, with the disk
line first and advisory. No mockup: the artefact is terminal output, and it is quoted in §3.

**Decided by the planner, as tooling**, and recorded because each declines something Forge offered:

- **Not a shared `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`.** Forge's own scope note rules it out — `.cargo/config.toml`
  records that a shared tree would serialise every implementer's Rust build behind cargo's file lock,
  and `ah-gdp` exists because earlier retrospectives blamed a shared tree that was never real.
- **Not a floor unification**, because there is only one floor. The 5-versus-8 was a stale checkout,
  which is `ah-puoj`.
- **Not a fix for the reclaim measurement**, which nobody has diagnosed. §4 makes it visible instead.
- **The gate keeps failing when code is wrong.** Exhaustive means "runs everything and then decides",
  never "reports and exits 0".

## Out of scope

- **A shared cargo target directory**, ruled out above.
- **Lowering, raising or removing `FREE_SPACE_FLOOR_GB`.** Whether 8 is the right number is a
  separate question; this bead is about where the answer is enforced.
- **`prune-worktrees.sh` freeing nothing in twelve for twelve.** A real observation of Forge's, and a
  different bead — this one only stops the preflight *pointing at* it as though it were an answer.
- **The undiagnosed `findBuildTrees`/`duGb` mismatch**, to be filed if found.
- **`pnpm run check`** (the full gate). The same `&&` chain problem applies, but its browser legs are
  minutes each and the ordering trade is different; if the implementer wants to convert it too, that
  is a follow-up with its own reasoning, not a freebie.
- **The stale-checkout cause of the floor confusion**, which is `ah-puoj`.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast          # before and after; compare the output, not just the exit code
```

Then the deliberate reproduction, which is the point of the bead:

1. Set `FREE_SPACE_FLOOR_GB = 10_000` in `scripts/diskPreflight.ts`.
2. `pnpm run check:fast`. It must:
   - print the disk line **first**, saying the machine is below the floor;
   - **still run `fmt` and `clippy`**, and report their results;
   - not fail *because of* the disk — the exit code reflects the code legs only.
   Before this bead, the same experiment skips fmt and clippy entirely. That contrast is the
   acceptance.
3. Restore the constant. Confirm `git diff` shows it back at 8 — this is the one step most likely to
   be forgotten, and shipping a 10_000 floor would be a memorable way to fail.
4. Break something cheap and real — a stray space that `cargo fmt --check` will object to — and
   confirm the gate reports lint, typecheck, test and generated as having run, then fmt as failed,
   then clippy's result too. Revert.
5. `git diff --stat`: `package.json`, `scripts/runGate.ts`, `scripts/runGate.test.ts`,
   `scripts/diskPreflight.ts`, `scripts/diskPreflight.test.ts`, and `scripts/runSuites.ts` only if
   its reporter was extracted.

## Known traps

- **Exhaustive is not lenient.** The gate must still exit non-zero when any leg fails. The failure
  this bead fixes is *skipping*, not *reporting*, and a `runGate.ts` that always exits 0 would be far
  worse than the `&&` chain.
- **`execFileSync` throws on a non-zero exit, and the error carries `stdout`.** Read it from the
  thrown error rather than re-running the script — re-running doubles a `du` walk that is already the
  slow part.
- **Restore `FREE_SPACE_FLOOR_GB` after the reproduction.** It is edited twice during this bead and
  is exactly the sort of thing that reaches a PR.
- **`runSuites.ts` has its own tests, and they must not change.** If its reporter is extracted for
  reuse, that is a pure refactor; behaviour changes there belong to a different bead.
- **`test` is one leg and it contains the whole vitest and cargo test run.** Keeping it as one leg is
  deliberate — `runSuites.ts` already reports inside it — so do not flatten its suites into
  `runGate.ts` and end up with two reporters disagreeing.
- **The disk leg must run first and print first.** Its whole value is being read *before* the output
  that matters; buried at the end it is the same silent condition under a different name.
- **Do not "fix" the reclaim measurement on the way past.** It is undiagnosed, and a plausible-looking
  fix to a number nobody has measured is how it got wrong in the first place.
acceptance_criteria: check:fast runs every leg and reports on every one of them, following scripts/runSuites.ts's precedent: lint, typecheck, test, check:generated, cargo fmt --check and cargo clippy all run even when an earlier leg fails, and the gate still exits non-zero if any of them failed. The machine's free space is reported as a first, advisory line and never contributes to the exit code, so a full disk no longer masks fmt and clippy - proven by setting FREE_SPACE_FLOOR_GB absurdly high, running the gate, and seeing fmt and clippy still run and report, which is ah-j0e reproduced in one command. diskPreflight.test.ts's command case asserts that the script runs and reports whatever the disk holds, reading stdout from the thrown error on a non-zero exit rather than requiring this machine to have room; its pure cases are unchanged. describeReclaimable names each build tree and its size rather than only a total, so a measurement as wrong as ah-kdgc's is visible where it is printed - without claiming to fix that undiagnosed measurement. runSuites.ts's own tests pass unchanged. No shared CARGO_TARGET_DIR, no change to the value of the floor, and FREE_SPACE_FLOOR_GB is back at 8 in the diff.

title: A map-centring smoke test fails on changes that never touch the map
description:
## The cost being paid

`tests/smoke/shortcuts.spec.ts`'s "right-click centres the view on a hex" asserts exact string
equality on a browser transform derived from a layout measurement the spec never waits for. Six
beads, six implementers, all on diffs touching no map code, have each paid a reproduce-and-re-run
cycle for it — roughly 86 minutes of named CI and local wall-clock in two days — and it has taken

design:
## Context

`tests/smoke/shortcuts.spec.ts`'s *"right-click centres the view on a hex, without selecting it"*
asserts **exact string equality** on a browser transform derived from a layout measurement the spec
never waits for. Six beads, six implementers, all on diffs touching no map code, have each paid a
reproduce-and-re-run cycle — roughly **86 minutes** of named CI and local wall-clock in two days — and
it has taken down main's own runs on **three documentation-only merges** (#428, #427, #424).

It has never been fixed, only re-run: `git log -L 245,299:tests/smoke/shortcuts.spec.ts` returns
exactly two commits, the test's creation and an unrelated refactor. No stabilisation commit exists.
Two retrospectives escalate it as work no implementer can file from inside a planned bead.

**The cause is not flakiness in the usual sense — it is a race the test sets up itself**, and it is
worth being precise because the fix follows from it:

- The spec's first gesture is `page.mouse.click(open.x, open.y, { button: "right" })` (`:277`), and
  **nothing before it waits for `data-map-insets`**.
- `gameSetup.ts:86-107`'s `visibleStrip` exists precisely because that attribute *"is absent until
  the first measurement lands"* — and it is first called at `:294`, **after** that click.
- `MapCanvas.tsx:566` centres with `centreOn(..., insets ?? NO_INSETS)`. Before the strip is
  measured, the map centres against the **whole canvas**; after it lands, against the **strip**.
- So the first right-click and the second measure against different rectangles, and the final
  assertions compare their transforms as exact strings. `ah-l2i.2` recorded the delta: expected
  `translate(945.09,-103.11)`, got `translate(945.09,-102.57)` — **0.54 px in y**.
- `MapCanvas.tsx:287-292` writes the transform synchronously via `setAttribute`/`toFixed(2)`; there is
  no animation. **The variable is the measured strip, not time**, which is why waiting longer has
  never helped.

**And the property the test is trying to prove already has a pure, deterministic seam.**
`mapViewport.ts` exports `centreOn`, `coordinateAt` and `transformString` (`:89`, `:154`, `:256-271`)
as pure functions of coordinate, viewport, width, height and insets, and `mapViewport.test.ts:258-289`
already tests centring against insets with `toBeCloseTo`. It has no idempotence case — which is
exactly what the last ten lines of the spec are trying to establish in a browser.

So this is **a test written in the wrong place**, not a test that needs a browser.

Branch from `origin/main`; every line number here is that tree.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

Two test files. **No production code** — see *Out of scope* for the one production change that was
considered and deliberately declined.

### 1. The idempotence claim moves to the pure seam — `mapViewport.test.ts`

Into the existing `describe` that already holds the insets cases (`:258-289`), beside
`counts a hex hidden behind a pane as off screen, and centres it clear of one`:

```ts
  it("centring on the hex already in the middle of the visible strip changes nothing", () => {
    // What `shortcuts.spec.ts` used to try to prove in a browser by right-clicking twice and
    // comparing transform strings - which raced the strip measurement and cost six beads a
    // re-run each (ah-d00t). Here it is exact and deterministic: no runner, no layout, no timing.
    const insets = { left: 300, right: 330, top: 48, bottom: 520 };
    const centred = centreOn(at(7, 53), ORIGIN, 1000, 800, insets);

    // The hex now in the middle of the visible strip, asked for again. `coordinateAt` takes the
    // pointer position in canvas pixels, the viewport and the level (mapViewport.ts:154-158).
    const middle = coordinateAt(
      insets.left + (1000 - insets.left - insets.right) / 2,
      insets.top + (800 - insets.top - insets.bottom) / 2,
      centred,
      1
    );
    const again = centreOn(middle, centred, 1000, 800, insets);

    expect(again.tx).toBeCloseTo(centred.tx);
    expect(again.ty).toBeCloseTo(centred.ty);
    expect(again.step).toBe(centred.step);
  });
```

`coordinateAt` is `(pointerX, pointerY, viewport, level)` — four positional arguments, verified at
`mapViewport.ts:154-158`, not an options object. The `level` is `1`, matching `at(7, 53)`'s, which
the existing cases in this file already use. The claim is: *centre, read back the hex now in the
middle, centre again, and land in the same place.*

**`toBeCloseTo`, not `toBe`.** Hex centres are irrational (`ROW_PITCH = HEX_RADIUS * √3 / 2`,
`:27`), so the round trip is exact only up to floating point. Demanding exact equality here would
reproduce the original sin at a lower level.

### 2. The spec keeps only what needs a browser — `tests/smoke/shortcuts.spec.ts:244-299`

**Delete the last block** (`:290-299`), which is both the exact-string comparison and the only reason
the spec calls `visibleCentre` at all:

```ts
  // Right-clicking the middle of the visible strip a second time is now a no-op: ...
  const centred = await mapTransform(page);
  const centre = await visibleCentre(page);
  await page.mouse.click(centre.x, centre.y, { button: "right" });
  await expect.poll(() => mapTransform(page)).toBe(centred);
  await page.mouse.click(centre.x, centre.y, { button: "right" });
  await expect.poll(() => mapTransform(page)).toBe(centred);
```

Removing it takes the race with it: the measurement was only needed to compute `centre`.

**Everything above it stays, and is the part that genuinely needs a browser** — that a real
right-click reaches the handler, that `preventDefault()` was called (the `__contextMenuPrevented`
witness at `:262-274`, whose comment explains why it is a bubble-phase listener), that the map moved
at all, and that the selection ring survives. Its one transform assertion is already the right shape:

```ts
  await expect.poll(() => mapTransform(page)).not.toBe(before);
```

— **changed, never equals-this-string.** Leave it exactly so, and add a line to the test's own
comment saying that the idempotence claim now lives in `mapViewport.test.ts`, so the next reader does
not restore it here.

If `visibleCentre` becomes unused in this file, drop the import; **do not delete the helper** from
`gameSetup.ts`, which other specs use.

## Increments

1. **The claim exists at the pure seam.**
   RED: the new `mapViewport.test.ts` case, written before anything is deleted. It must pass at once
   — the property is true of the pure functions. **If it fails, stop**: either the round trip is not
   idempotent (a real bug this bead has just found, and a much more interesting one) or
   `coordinateAt` was called wrongly. Do not weaken the assertion to make it pass.
2. **The browser stops asserting it.**
   RED: none. Delete `:290-299` and, if now unused, the `visibleCentre` import.
   GREEN: `pnpm exec playwright test tests/smoke/shortcuts.spec.ts` green — and run it **several
   times**, because the point is that it stops failing intermittently.
3. **It is still testing the gesture.**
   RED: temporarily break `preventDefault()` in the context-menu handler and confirm the spec fails;
   revert. Then temporarily make the right-click not recentre and confirm the `not.toBe(before)`
   assertion fails; revert. **Both must fail**, or the remaining spec asserts nothing.

## The test plan

| Test | Where | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| **`centring on the hex already in the middle of the visible strip changes nothing`** | `mapViewport.test.ts` | the idempotence property, exactly and without a browser |
| the existing insets cases (`:258-289`) | `mapViewport.test.ts` | unchanged |
| `right-click centres the view on a hex, without selecting it` | `shortcuts.spec.ts` | the gesture reaches the handler, `preventDefault` fires, the map moves, the ring survives — and **no exact transform string** |

**Suites:** `pnpm run check:fast` covers the unit test. The smoke suite must be run for this bead —
`pnpm exec playwright test tests/smoke/shortcuts.spec.ts` — and run **repeatedly**, since "it stopped
being flaky" is the acceptance and a single green run does not show it.

**A grep is part of the acceptance:** `grep -n 'toBe(centred)' tests/smoke/` must return nothing, and
no smoke spec should compare a `transform` attribute with `toBe(` against a literal. That is the
class of assertion this bead exists to remove.

## User-facing decisions

**None.** Nothing here reaches a player; no production code changes; there is no interface, so no
mockup. The bead is a test moved from a place that cannot decide it to one that can.

**One decision was the planner's and is recorded because it is the tempting alternative:** Forge
offers, as an option, dropping the `insets ?? NO_INSETS` fallback at `MapCanvas.tsx:566` so that a
recentre before the strip is known is not silently computed against a different rectangle. **This
plan declines it.** That fallback is what makes an early right-click do *something* rather than
nothing, and removing it changes what a player sees when they gesture before layout settles — a
user-facing behaviour change, which is the navigator's and not a thing to smuggle into a test-quality
bead. The test racing its own measurement is the test's bug, and deleting the racing assertion fixes
it without touching behaviour. If the navigator wants that fallback reconsidered, it is a bead.

## Out of scope

- **`MapCanvas.tsx`'s `insets ?? NO_INSETS` fallback**, declined above. No production file changes.
- **Awaiting `visibleStrip` before the first right-click.** Forge's other suggestion, and unnecessary
  once the block that needed the measurement is gone: the surviving assertion is *"changed"*, which
  is true against either rectangle.
- **`tests/smoke/workspace.spec.ts:1430-1446`** — *"a folded panel shrinks to its title bar"*, which
  `ah-l2i.3` suggests may be the same class. Possibly; not established, and not measured. If it is,
  it deserves its own evidence rather than riding along.
- **The wider "smoke tests pin workspace geometry from many angles" problem**, which is `ah-csni`.
- **`gameSetup.ts`'s `visibleStrip` / `visibleCentre` helpers**, which other specs use and which are
  not at fault — they poll correctly; they were simply called too late.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
pnpm exec playwright test tests/smoke/shortcuts.spec.ts
grep -rn "toBe(centred)" tests/smoke/          # must return nothing
```

Then, and this is the part that actually proves the bead:

1. **Run the spec ten times in a row.** `for i in $(seq 10); do pnpm exec playwright test
   tests/smoke/shortcuts.spec.ts || break; done`. Ten greens is not proof, but one red is
   disproof, and the failure has been frequent enough that ten runs is a meaningful sample.
2. **Run it with the map deliberately slow to measure**, if that can be arranged — throttling CPU in
   the Playwright config, or a wider viewport — since the failure is a race with the strip
   measurement and widening the window is the honest way to hunt it.
3. **Break the handler and watch the spec fail.** Remove `preventDefault()` from the context-menu
   handler: the spec must go red on the `__contextMenuPrevented` assertion. Revert. A test that
   cannot fail is worse than the flake it replaced.
4. Confirm `git diff --stat` shows **two test files and nothing else**.

## Known traps

- **The variable is the strip, not time.** The transform is written synchronously with no animation
  (`MapCanvas.tsx:287-292`), so adding waits, retries or `expect.poll` timeouts has never helped and
  will not now. Anything that looks like "wait a bit longer" is the wrong fix.
- **`toBeCloseTo`, not `toBe`, at the pure seam.** `ROW_PITCH` is `HEX_RADIUS * √3 / 2`; the round
  trip through a coordinate is exact only up to floating point. Demanding exact equality reproduces
  the original mistake one layer down.
- **If the new pure test fails, that is a finding, not an obstacle.** It would mean centring is
  genuinely not idempotent — which is what the browser test was intermittently telling everyone, and
  which nobody has checked. Do not relax the assertion to get to green.
- **Do not delete `visibleCentre`/`visibleStrip`** from `gameSetup.ts`; other specs use them. Only
  the import in this spec, and only if it becomes unused.
- **Keep the `__contextMenuPrevented` witness and its comment.** It is subtle — a bubble-phase
  listener specifically so it reads `defaultPrevented` *after* React has had its chance — and it is
  the one thing here that genuinely needs a browser.
- **Six beads have "fixed" this by re-running.** The bead is not done when the suite is green once;
  it is done when the exact-string assertion is gone. The grep is the check.

What remains in the browser is only what needs one - that a real right-click reaches the handler, that preventDefault fired via the __contextMenuPrevented witness, that the map moved at all via not.toBe(before), and that the selection ring survives - with a comment saying where the idempotence claim now lives so it is not restored.
