heading, and they are the reason this is confusing.

## For the planner to settle with the navigator

This is a user-facing design and the shape is the navigator's to choose. Worth putting in front of
them as a mockup rather than described: grouping under hex headings, severity glyphs or colour, the
unit named on each line, indentation, or some combination.

Two things worth their attention while choosing:

- **The counts must still read.** The header shows a problem count and a zero count is the good
  outcome; whatever grouping arrives must not make "how many" harder to see.
- **Colour alone is not enough** to separate a hex from a problem, and the panes' type is small.

## Validation

A turn with problems across several hexes, some belonging to units and some to hexes alone: a reader
can tell locations from problems without reading the words. The same design in the region panel does
not repeat what the panel already says. Clicking a problem that has a line still reaches it in the
editor.
design:
## Context The problems list mixes two kinds of line — the hex a problem is in, and the problem itself — and reads as one undifferentiated run. The worst case is a diagnostic that belongs to a hex and to no unit ("Nobody is guarding this hex."): `ProblemsPanel.tsx:80-82` and `RegionPanel.tsx:251-253` both render the unit column as `{finding.unitId === null ? null : }`, so such a row starts hard against the left edge with no id — exactly the shape of the brass hex heading above it. That is the confusion this bead removes. It appears in two places and one design serves both: the header dropdown (`ProblemsPanel`, whole turn, grouped by hex) and the region panel's *Problems* section (`RegionPanel`, one hex). The navigator additionally asked that the new severity mark reach the two *other* lists that draw the same amber/red rule — the per-unit list under the orders editor (`OrdersPanel`) and the orders-import summary dialog — so all four agree. **When this lands**, a player scanning the dropdown sees a bordered card per hex with a brass header strip, and inside it one row per problem, each led by ⚠ or ✕. A problem belonging to the hex says `hex` where a unit id would be. Nothing about counts, ordering, keyboard, the chip, the F8 walk or the region *Problems* toggle changes. Mockup, committed and merged (PR #407): `docs/ui/problem-lists.html`. Nothing blocks this bead. ## Files to change, and what to reuse ### New shared pieces — `packages/shared/src/workspace/primitives.tsx` This file already holds `POPOVER_BODY_MAX_H` (`:13`), `Section` (`:16`), `Row` (`:44`), `Field` (`:54`), `Absent` (`:64`) and `StaleBanner` (`:69`), and is already imported by `ProblemsPanel` (`ProblemsPanel.tsx:2`) and `RegionPanel`. Add three exports there. The severity ternary `problem.severity === "error" ? "text-danger" : "text-warn"` is currently duplicated verbatim in four files (`ProblemsPanel.tsx:83`, `RegionPanel.tsx:254`, `OrdersPanel.tsx:205`, `OrdersImportSummaryDialog.tsx:89`); after this bead there is one copy, inside `SeverityMark`. ```tsx import type { OrderDiagnosticSeverity } from "@atlantis/core-client"; /** * The box a hex's problems sit in. * * Whole literal, never assembled from pieces: Tailwind scans source text for class names. */ export const PROBLEM_CARD = "overflow-hidden rounded border border-edge bg-panel"; /** * How a diagnostic's severity reads: a glyph and a colour, never colour alone. * * The glyph is decorative and hidden; the word beside it is what a screen reader announces. */ export function SeverityMark({ severity }: { severity: OrderDiagnosticSeverity }): ReactNode; /** * Whose problem it is: a unit id, or `hex` for a diagnostic that belongs to the hex and to no unit. */ export function ProblemWho({ unitId }: { unitId: string | null }): ReactNode; ``` `SeverityMark` renders exactly: ```tsx <> {severity === "error" ? "✕" : "⚠"} {severity === "error" ? "error" : "warning"} ``` `sr-only` is `position:absolute`, so the second span costs no layout inside the flex row. It is the established pattern here — `AppHeader.tsx:373-380` uses `sr-only` for the same reason and `AppHeader.test.tsx:209` asserts on it. `ProblemWho` renders exactly: ```tsx unitId === null ? ( <> hex the whole hex ) : ( unit {unitId} ) ``` `text-pane-sm` is the 11px rem token from `theme.css:117` (bead ah-46p.1). **Never write a pixel size**: `theme.test.ts` has `it("sets no pane type in absolute pixels")`, which walks the sources for `text-[…px]` and fails the build. ### `packages/shared/src/workspace/ProblemsPanel.tsx` Signature, props and the wiring in `AppShell.tsx:2494-2502` are unchanged — this is a markup change inside the existing component. Keep `total`, the header sentence, the footer sentence, `POPOVER_BODY_MAX_H`, and every `data-testid` (`problems-panel`, `problem-hex-`, `problem-entry`) and `data-code`. The outer `
    ` gains `space-y-2` and drops the per-`li` `border-t border-edge-soft py-1 first:border-t-0`, which the card border replaces. Each hex `
  • ` carries `PROBLEM_CARD`. The existing hex `
acceptance_criteria: In both the header problems dropdown and a region's problem list, a reader can distinguish a hex from a problem at a glance without reading the text. The problem count remains easy to read. A problem that has a source line is still clickable through to the editor, and one belonging only to a hex is presented as such.

title: The events list is grouped by the unit each event is about
description:
The events list is one flat run of lines in report order. A turn's events are mostly per-unit — the
sample turn reads:

    Taxers (8047): Gives 50 silver [SILV] to Lookout (12159).
    Woodsmen (9431): Gives 20 wood [WOOD] to Smiths (11933).
    Unit (5476): Gives 80 silver [SILV] to Unit (7223).
    Taxers (8909): Gives 50 silver [SILV] to Unit (12160).
    Taxers (8909): Gives 100 silver [SILV] to Carpenters (12881).

so following one unit through a turn means reading the whole list and remembering. The same unit
appears repeatedly, scattered.

**The request:** group events by unit number. Anything with no discernible unit goes under
**General**.

## The shape is regular

Events carry `Name (id): message`, and the id in the leading position is the unit the event is about.
Not every line has one — the same turn opens with `Times reward of 200 silver.`, which belongs to the
faction and to no unit.

Note the id also appears *inside* messages — `Gives 50 silver [SILV] to Lookout (12159)` names a
second unit. Grouping must key on the leading unit only, or every gift files itself under both parties
and the receiving unit's group fills with events it did not cause.

## For the planned to settle with the navigator

- **Group heading.** The number alone, or the name and number — names are more use to a reader and
  change between turns, and the same number can carry different names.
- **Order of the groups**, and of General: unit order as first seen, numeric, or by how much
  happened. General first or last.
- **Collapsed or open** by default, given a busy turn has many units and a group of one line is
  common.
- Whether an event naming a second unit should be findable from that unit's group too, which is
  useful and is the thing the warning above says not to do naively.

## Validation

A turn whose events name several units repeatedly: each unit's events appear once, under that unit,
in report order. A faction-level line appears under General. An event mentioning a second unit is
filed under the acting unit only, unless the navigator decided otherwise.
design:
## Context

The events list is one flat run of lines in report order, so following one unit through a turn means
reading the whole list and remembering. The sample turn has `Taxers (8047)` appearing three times,
scattered between other units' lines.

After this bead the events are **grouped by the unit that caused them**, with a **General** group for
the lines that name no unit (`Times reward of 200 silver.`).

**The trap the bead warns about is already avoided.** An event names a second unit inside its message
— `Gives 50 silver [SILV] to Lookout (12159)` — and grouping on any bracketed id would file every
gift under both parties. `splitTurnMessage` (`packages/shared/src/turnMessages.ts:63`) already reads
**only** the leading `Name (id): ` prefix, and its `UNIT_PREFIX` comment explains why the colon is
what makes that safe. So `TurnMessage.unitId` is exactly the grouping key, and no new parsing is
needed.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### `packages/shared/src/turnMessages.ts` — the grouping, as a pure function

Beside `splitTurnMessages` (line 87), in the same module and for the reason its header gives — "Pure,
and tested beside itself, because the repository has no jsdom and a component could not be tested at
all":

```ts
/** One unit's events, or the faction-level ones. */
export type TurnMessageGroup = {
  /** The unit these belong to, or `null` for the General group. */
  unitId: string | null;
  /**
   * The unit's name as its first line printed it, or `null` for General.
   *
   * From the first line rather than the last: a report can print two names for one id within a
   * turn, and the first is the one the reader met.
   */
  unitName: string | null;
  /** In report order, always - the order within a group is never rearranged. */
  messages: TurnMessage[];
};

/**
 * The messages grouped by the unit that caused them.
 *
 * General first when it has anything, then each unit in the order the report first mentioned it, so
 * the list still walks the turn the way the report tells it and no group moves between turns for a
 * reason the reader cannot see (navigator, 2026-08-17). An empty input is an empty list, and a
 * General group is omitted entirely rather than shown empty.
 */
export function groupTurnMessages(messages: readonly TurnMessage[]): TurnMessageGroup[];
```

A `Map<string | null, TurnMessageGroup>` keyed by `unitId` preserves insertion order for the units;
General is spliced to the front at the end. Nothing is sorted.

### `packages/shared/src/workspace/TurnMessagesPanel.tsx`

The `<ul>` body (line 70) renders groups instead of rows **for the events tab**. The errors tab keeps
today's flat list — see *Out of scope*.

Each group is a `<li>` carrying `data-testid={`turn-messages-group-${unitId ?? "general"}`}`, with:

- **A heading**: `Name (id)`, and for General the literal word `General`. The id half is the existing
  `Unit` control (line 154, `data-testid={`turn-messages-unit-${unitId}`}`) — **moved from the row to
  the heading**, unchanged, so the way back to the map is still there and still gated on
  `knownUnitIds`. That control already renders exactly `${message.unitName} (${unitId})`, which is the
  heading the navigator chose, so it is reused whole rather than reimplemented.
- **A count**, right-aligned and dimmed, of the group's messages. Every variant the navigator saw
  carried one.
- **The rows**, each keeping its `verb` (line 84) and its `text` (line 88) and **losing its unit**,
  which is now the heading it sits under. Indented, as the mockup shows.

All groups are rendered open: there is no collapse control and no per-group state.

### Nothing else

- **No change to `splitTurnMessage`, `UNIT_PREFIX` or `VERB_PREFIX`.** The key already exists.
- **No change to `describeTurnMessages`** or the header chip's counts — the same messages, arranged
  differently.
- **No change to `onSelectUnit`, `knownUnitIds`** or the panel's props.

## Increments

1. **The grouping.** RED: the six `groupTurnMessages` tests below. GREEN: the function.
2. **The panel shows it.** RED: the three `TurnMessagesPanel.test.tsx` tests. GREEN: the body's
   render.

## The test plan

| Test | File | What it pins |
|---|---|---|
| `groups a unit's events together, in report order` | `turnMessages.test.ts` | `Taxers (8047)`'s three lines in one group, in the order the report printed them |
| `puts the faction's own lines under General` | same | `unitId === null` → the General group |
| `puts General first, and the units in the order the report met them` | same | The navigator's O1, as an assertion on the group order |
| `omits General entirely when every line names a unit` | same | No empty group |
| `does not file an event under a unit it merely mentions` | same | **The bead's own trap**: `Taxers (8047): Gives 50 silver [SILV] to Lookout (12159).` appears once, under 8047, and `12159` has no group at all |
| `names a group from the first line that named the unit` | same | Two lines, two names, one id → the first name |
| `shows one group per unit, headed by name and number` | `TurnMessagesPanel.test.tsx` | The heading text and the `turn-messages-group-*` testids |
| `the group heading is the way back to the map` | same | `turn-messages-unit-8047` is in the heading, calls `onSelectUnit`, and a unit outside `knownUnitIds` is dimmed rather than clickable — the existing rule, in its new place |
| `every group is open` | same | Every message is in the markup with no control to press |
| (existing) the errors tab's tests | same | Unchanged: errors are still a flat list |

Suites: `pnpm -r run test`. No Rust, no browser suite — the panel is static markup and this package's
tests render it with `renderToStaticMarkup`.

## User-facing decisions

All four the navigator's, 2026-08-17, against
`file:///Users/henrikku/repos/atlantis-hud/docs/ui/ah-7rd-events-grouping.html` (mockup in the
scratchpad; commit it with the work if it is worth keeping).

1. **The heading is name and number** — `Taxers (8047)` — matching how the rest of the workspace
   writes a unit. *Rejected: the number alone* — narrow and stable across a rename, but it reads as a
   list of numbers and the name is the half a player remembers.
2. **General first, then the units in report order.** Nothing is sorted, so nothing moves between
   turns for a reason the reader cannot see. *Rejected: units by number with General last* — a unit
   would sit in the same place every turn, but the order would say nothing about what happened and
   General would end up past everything. *Rejected: busiest unit first* — every group moves between
   turns.
3. **Every group is open.** Grouping alone does the work and nothing hides behind a click.
   *Rejected: all collapsed* — the turn would fit on one screen as a contents page, at a click per
   reading and a one-line group hidden behind a control. *Rejected: collapsing only on busy turns* —
   the panel would behave differently on two turns for a reason the reader is never told.
4. **One event, one group.** An event belongs to the unit that caused it and is not repeated under a
   unit it merely mentions. *Rejected: showing it under both, marked as received* — it would fill a
   unit's group with things it did not do and make the counts meaningless. *Rejected for now: making
   the mentioned unit clickable in the line* — a smaller, separate idea the navigator did not ask for
   here.

## Out of scope

- **The errors tab.** The bead, the mockup and every answer are about the events list; errors stay a
  flat list with their `verb` column. They would group by the same key and it is an obvious follow-up
  — file one rather than widening this bead, and note that errors are few (three against eleven in
  the sample turn) so the flat list is not costing much.
- **Making a mentioned unit clickable inside a message.** Decision 4's third option, explicitly not
  taken here.
- **Sorting, filtering or searching the list.**
- **`splitTurnMessage`'s parsing**, including the `Cpt Stanley (13423) is caught attempting to steal`
  shape its comment records — a line that names a unit mid-sentence has no leading prefix, so it lands
  in General, which is right.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
```

Then in the application: load a turn with a busy events list, open the events chip, and read it. Each
unit appears once, with its lines beneath it in report order; `Times reward of 200 silver.` is under
**General** at the top; a gift appears only under the unit that gave it; and clicking a group heading
still takes you to that unit on the map.

## Known traps

- **Group on `TurnMessage.unitId` and nothing else.** Any attempt to find ids in `text` re-creates the
  exact defect the bead was filed about, and it will look like an improvement while doing it.
- **The `Unit` control is gated on `knownUnitIds`** (line 149): a unit the loaded turn does not
  describe is shown dimmed and is not clickable. That rule moves to the heading with the control —
  do not reimplement the heading and lose it.
- **A message with no unit and no verb currently renders no header row at all** (line 81's comment:
  "three hundred rows of placeholder say nothing three hundred times"). Under General that is still
  right — the group heading says what the whole group is, and the rows are just text.
- **Do not sort the groups.** Insertion order out of a `Map` is the report's order, which is the whole
  of decision 2; a `.sort()` anywhere in this function is the bug.
- **`renderToStaticMarkup` cannot see a store's non-default state** — the trap ah-3i3 gave the
  repository a helper for (`packages/shared/src/testing/storeState.ts`). This panel takes everything
  through props, so it does not arise here; do not reach for the helper out of habit.
acceptance_criteria: Events are grouped by the unit they concern, with each unit's events together and in report order. Events with no discernible unit appear under a General group. An event that mentions another unit in its text is not duplicated into that unit's group unless the navigator asked for that.

title: The game list offers Reset beside Delete, in one confirmation
description:
Second child of ah-58n. The control, the words and the wiring.

Pressing the game list's X opens one panel offering Delete, Reset and Cancel. The navigator designed it against three mockups on 2026-08-17; every string, the focus behaviour, the failure behaviour and the saved map view are settled and recorded in ah-58n's design field.

Depends on ah-58n.1 for the operation.
design:
## Context Second and last child of the epic ah-58n. **Read the epic's `design` field first** — it carries the navigator's seven decisions, the rejected alternatives, and the three mockups merged by PR #390. ah-58n.1 gives both platforms a `resetGame(gameId, now)` that empties a game and keeps its id, name and ruleset. Nothing calls it. This bead is the control, the words and the wiring — and it is where every decision the navigator took gets implemented. The shape, in one line: **the game list's `✕` opens one panel offering Delete, Reset and Cancel.** No new control appears on the row. ## Files to change, and what to reuse ### `packages/shared/src/workspace/mapViewportStorage.ts` The saved map view is the only per-game state outside the game's own data, and a reset clears it — otherwise the emptied game reopens on a hex it no longer knows about (epic decision 6). ```ts /** Forgets one game's saved view. Called when a game is emptied (ah-58n). */ export function forgetMapView(gameId: string): void { try { optionalStorage()?.removeItem(viewportStorageKey(gameId)); } catch { // Remembering a view is a convenience and forgetting one must never crash the application - // the same trade every other function in this module makes. } } ``` `ViewportStorage` (line 17) is `Pick` and must gain `"removeItem"`. Check the test doubles in `mapViewportStorage.test.ts` — a hand-written storage stub will not satisfy the widened type until it grows the method, and that failure is increment 1's RED. ### `packages/shared/src/gameActions.ts` One function, modelled on `deleteGame` (line 138) — same parameters, same discard-first reasoning: ```ts export type ResetGameOutcome = { /** The emptied game, ready to open. */ opened: OpenedGame; games: GameManifest[]; /** Whether the game that was emptied is the one on screen. */ wasOpenGame: boolean; }; /** * Empties `gameId` and keeps it: same id, name and ruleset, nothing else (ah-58n). * * The open draft is discarded first when the game being emptied is the open one, for exactly * `deleteGame`'s reason: the database its orders would be written to is about to be replaced, and a * flush on the way out would write into a game that no longer holds it. * * The saved map view goes with the rest. It lives in localStorage rather than in the game, so the * core cannot reach it and this is the only place it can be cleared. */ export async function resetGame( client: GameClient, gameId: string, openGameId: string | null, now: string, discardOpenDraft: () => void ): Promise { const wasOpenGame = openGameId === gameId; if (wasOpenGame) { discardOpenDraft(); } const opened = await client.resetGame(gameId, now); forgetMapView(gameId); return { opened, games: await client.listGames(), wasOpenGame }; } ``` `GameClient` (line 26) is a `Pick` union of method names — add `"resetGame"` to it. ### `packages/shared/src/workspace/GamePicker.tsx` **Extract the confirmation into a component in the same file.** It needs `useEscapeToDismiss` (`./dismissLayer:12`) and a focus ref, and a hook cannot be called from inside the `sorted.map` callback that renders the rows. A small `` beside `GameForm` is where both belong. ```tsx function RemoveGameConfirm({ gameName, busy, failure, onDelete, onReset, onCancel }: { gameName: string; busy: boolean; /** What went wrong last time one of the two was pressed, or null. */ failure: string | null; onDelete: () => void; onReset: () => void; onCancel: () => void; }) ``` Its markup keeps the row's existing wrapper exactly — `data-testid={`game-delete-confirm-${gameId}`}` and `className="mt-1 rounded border border-danger/40 p-1.5"` — see *Known traps* for why the testid does not change. Inside it, **the navigator's copy, verbatim** (P3, from `docs/ui/ah-58n-combined-panel.html`): ```tsx

Delete “{gameName}”, or empty it and keep the game?

Either way its turns, orders, remembered map and notes are erased. Reset keeps the name and ruleset.

Export it first if you might want it back.

``` then the buttons, in this order, with the existing classes: ```tsx ``` `Reset` is amber (`border-warn`/`text-warn`), `Delete` stays danger-red — the mockup's treatment, and `GameForm`'s import prompt already uses `border-brass` the same way for a middle option. **When `failure` is set, the panel shows that instead of the three paragraphs** (mockup, bottom right): ```tsx

{failure}

… ``` where **Try again** repeats whichever action failed. Hold that in the picker's state alongside the message — `{ gameId, action: "delete" | "reset", message: string }` — rather than guessing from the text. The row itself changes in exactly one place, the `✕` button's accessible name (line ~391): ```tsx aria-label={`remove ${game.metadata.gameName}`} ``` `confirmingDeleteOf` (line 52) is renamed `confirmingRemovalOf`; the `✕`'s `onClick` still sets it, and Cancel still clears it. **Escape closes the panel and returns focus to the `✕`** (epic decision 5), which is what the ref on that button is for; `useEscapeToDismiss` handles the key and the layering so a nested prompt is not closed twice. ### `packages/shared/src/workspace/AppShell.tsx` `resetGame`, beside `deleteGame` (line 1587) and shaped like it: ```tsx const resetGame = useCallback( (gameId: string) => runGameAction(async () => { const result = await resetGameAction( client, gameId, game?.manifest.metadata.gameId ?? null, new Date().toISOString(), () => writer.discard() ); setGames(result.games); // Only when it was the open one: emptying some other game must not move the player. if (result.wasOpenGame) { enterGame(result.opened); } closePopover("games"); }), [client, enterGame, game, runGameAction, writer] ); ``` `enterGame` on the fresh `OpenedGame` is what empties the workspace — the same call `deleteGame` makes when it falls back to another game — so no state is cleared by hand here. Wire it through as `onReset={(gameId) => void resetGame(gameId)}` beside `onDelete` (line 2434), and give `GamePicker` the matching prop. **The failure path**: `runGameAction` today reports into the picker's error line. Both Delete and Reset now report inside the panel instead (the navigator's second answer, 2026-08-17), so these two handlers catch their own failure and hand the message to the picker's panel state rather than letting it reach the shared error slot. Read `runGameAction` before writing this — if it swallows the error, the catch belongs inside the callback passed to it. ## Increments 1. **Forgetting a view.** RED: `forgets one game's saved view` in `mapViewportStorage.test.ts`, plus the stubs that must grow `removeItem`. GREEN: `forgetMapView` and the widened `ViewportStorage`. 2. **The action.** RED: the four `resetGame` tests in `gameActions.test.ts`. GREEN: `resetGame` and `GameClient` gaining `"resetGame"`. 3. **The panel.** RED: the `GamePicker` tests below — the new copy, the three buttons, the `✕`'s new label. GREEN: `RemoveGameConfirm` and the row change. 4. **The failure and the keyboard.** RED: the failure and Escape tests. GREEN: the failure state, the `autoFocus` on Cancel, and `useEscapeToDismiss`. 5. **The shell.** RED: none available (`AppShell` has no unit test — no DOM in this package). GREEN: the `resetGame` callback and the prop. Proved by the smoke test below. ## The test plan | Test | File | What it pins | |---|---|---| | `forgets one game's saved view` | `mapViewportStorage.test.ts` | The key is removed, and only that game's | | `tolerates storage that will not let it forget` | same | A throwing `removeItem` does not propagate | | `empties the game and refreshes the list` | `gameActions.test.ts` | `client.resetGame` called with the id and the stamp; `listGames` re-read | | `discards the open draft when the game being emptied is the open one` | same | `discardOpenDraft` called, and `wasOpenGame` true | | `leaves another game's draft alone` | same | Not called; `wasOpenGame` false | | `forgets the emptied game's saved view` | same | `forgetMapView`'s key gone after the call | | `offers Delete, Reset and Cancel in one panel` | the `GamePicker` test file | The three buttons, and that no `↺` or `Reset` control exists on the row itself | | `says what is lost and what is kept` | same | The two sentences and the export line, quoted exactly | | `the remove control is named for the panel it opens` | same | `aria-label="remove "` | | `a failed reset keeps the panel open and offers Try again` | same | The red message and the two buttons; the three paragraphs are gone | | `a failed delete reports in the same place` | same | The navigator's second answer | | `Escape closes the panel and cancels nothing else` | same | Panel gone, no call to either handler | | `Cancel has focus when the panel opens` | same | `autoFocus` on the safe button | | (existing) `the delete confirmation wraps inside the picker rather than running off it` | `tests/smoke/games.spec.ts:129` | **The panel is now three paragraphs, not one** — this test measures the first `p`'s overflow and must stay green | | (existing) `deleting a game asks first, then falls back to the one that is left` | `tests/smoke/games.spec.ts:151` | Still passes: the copy still contains "erased" and the button is still `Delete` | | `resetting a game keeps it in the list and empties it` | `tests/smoke/games.spec.ts` (new) | Create a game, import a report, reset, and see the game still listed with no report loaded | Suites: `pnpm -r run test` **and** `pnpm run test:smoke` — the shell wiring has no unit test, so the smoke suite is the only thing that proves the button reaches the core. ## User-facing decisions Every one is the navigator's, taken 2026-08-17 against three mockups merged by PR #390, and recorded with its rejected alternatives in the epic ah-58n's `design` field. Quoted here because this is the bead that writes them: - `file:///Users/henrikku/repos/atlantis-hud/docs/ui/ah-58n-reset-control.html` — **C**: no control on the row; `✕` opens one panel. *Rejected: a `↺` icon beside `✕`, with and without a gap; the word "Reset" on every row.* - `file:///Users/henrikku/repos/atlantis-hud/docs/ui/ah-58n-combined-panel.html` — **P3** for the prose, **Reset** for the middle button's label, panel-stays-open for a failure, focus on Cancel with Escape closing. *Rejected: P1 and P2; "Empty it" and "Keep the game"; reporting the failure in the picker's error line.* - `file:///Users/henrikku/repos/atlantis-hud/docs/ui/ah-58n-reset-wording.html` — **B2** for the third line: mention Export, do not offer it. *Rejected: saying nothing; an "Export first" button.* **The strings, exactly as they ship:** | Where | Text | |---|---| | Panel, line 1 | `Delete “{name}”, or empty it and keep the game?` | | Panel, line 2 | `Either way its turns, orders, remembered map and notes are erased. Reset keeps the name and ruleset.` | | Panel, line 3 (dim) | `Export it first if you might want it back.` | | Buttons | `Delete` · `Reset` · `Cancel` | | Failure | `“{name}” could not be reset: {reason}` / `“{name}” could not be deleted: {reason}` | | Failure buttons | `Try again` · `Cancel` | | The `✕` | `aria-label="remove {name}"` | Curly quotes `“ ”` in the panel, matching the delete copy this replaces. Two further answers, given 2026-08-17 in this bead's own round: - **The `✕` is named `remove `.** *Rejected: "delete or reset "* (wordy on every row); *rejected: leaving it "delete "* (announces one outcome, then offers two). - **A failed Delete now reports in the panel too**, exactly as a failed Reset does. *Rejected: leaving delete's failure in the picker's error line* — one panel reporting two failures in two places depending on which button was pressed. ## Out of scope - **The reset operation itself** — ah-58n.1, which this depends on. - **Any change to what Delete does.** Only where its *failure* is reported changes. - **The import prompt, the rename field, the export button** and everything else in the picker. - **Orphaned `atlantis-hud-viewport-*` keys from past deletes.** This bead clears the key for the game it resets and nothing else. - **Making `deleteGame` clear the saved map view too.** Defensible, out of scope, and a bead of its own if it is wanted. ## Validation ```bash pnpm run check:fast pnpm run test:smoke # required: the shell wiring has no unit test ``` The human check, and the epic's own acceptance: reset a game with several imported turns, orders, a remembered map and some hex notes. It stays in the list under its own name and ruleset; opening it looks exactly like a game just created; the other games are untouched; cancelling changes nothing. Then press Escape on an open panel and confirm focus lands back on the `✕`. ## Known traps - **Keep the `game-delete-confirm-${gameId}` testid**, even though the panel is no longer only about deleting. `tests/smoke/games.spec.ts:141` matches `/^game-delete-confirm-/u` and measures the first `p`'s overflow; renaming it turns a mechanical change into a red smoke run. Rename it in a later tidy-up if it grates. - **That overflow test measures a paragraph, and there are now three.** The picker's header sets `whitespace-nowrap`, which inherits, and the confirmation is the one piece of prose in there — every new paragraph needs the same wrapping treatment as the existing one, or the test fails on whichever `p` it happens to pick first. - **Three smoke selectors say `name: "delete "`** — `games.spec.ts:136`, `:161`, `:174`. They break the moment the aria-label changes, and that is the intended RED for increment 3, not a surprise. Update all three. - **A hook cannot be called inside the `sorted.map` callback.** That is why the panel becomes a component; trying to call `useEscapeToDismiss` where the panel is rendered today breaks the rules of hooks and React will say so at runtime, not at compile time. - **`enterGame(result.opened)` is what empties the workspace.** Do not clear `parsed`, `rawReport`, the orders document or the memory by hand — `deleteGame`'s fallback path already proves that call does it, and a hand-written clear is how one piece gets forgotten. - **Discard the draft before resetting the open game**, exactly as `deleteGame` does, or the writer flushes into a database that has just been replaced. - **`GameClient` is a `Pick`** (`gameActions.ts:26`); a method used but not listed there fails the typecheck at the call site rather than at the import, which reads confusingly.

title: A game can be emptied and kept, on both platforms
description:
First child of ah-58n. The operation only - no control, no confirmation, nothing on screen.

reset_game(games_root, game_id, now) on the desktop and resetGame(gameId, now) on the web return a game to the state it would be in if it had been deleted and created again, keeping its id, name and ruleset. Everything the game holds goes: turns, order drafts, remembered sightings, merged reports and hex notes, and the manifest's reportSources and activeFactionId.

ah-58n.2 adds the control and the confirmation the navigator designed.
design:
## Context

First child of the epic ah-58n. **Read the epic's `design` field first** — it carries the navigator's
seven decisions and the three merged mockups. **None of them apply to this bead**: it adds the
operation and nothing a player can see or reach. ah-58n.2 adds the control, the words and the wiring.

A reset returns a game to the state it would be in if it had been deleted and created again, keeping
its **id**, **name** and **ruleset**. Everything else in the game goes: imported turns, order drafts,
remembered sightings, merged reports and hex notes — all of which live in the game's own database and
nowhere else (`delete_game`'s comment, `crates/core-persistence/src/lib.rs:438`, re-checked while
planning: hex notes arrived after that comment was written and are in the same database) — plus the
manifest's `reportSources` and `activeFactionId`.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

**Reset is delete-then-create on both platforms.** Neither side gets a new way to erase things; both
compose the two operations they already have, which is what keeps "reset" and "deleted and recreated"
the same thing by construction rather than by a comment saying so.

### `crates/core-persistence/src/lib.rs`

```rust
/// Empties a game and keeps it: same id, same name, same ruleset, nothing else.
///
/// Composed of `delete_game` and `create_game` rather than written afresh, so a reset game and a
/// newly created one are the same thing by construction. `created_at` and `last_opened_at` are both
/// `now` - the game the player is left with was made at this moment, whatever the one it replaced
/// was made at - and `report_sources` and `active_faction_id` are cleared with everything else: an
/// emptied game has imported nothing, so it is nobody's faction (ah-do8.1).
///
/// # Errors
///
/// Returns an error when no game exists under this id, when its manifest cannot be read, or when
/// the directory cannot be replaced.
pub fn reset_game(
    games_root: &Path,
    game_id: &str,
    now: &str,
) -> Result<OpenedGame, PersistenceError>
```

The body, and the one part that is not obvious:

1. Read the manifest through `load_game_manifest` and `ensure_supported_manifest_version`, exactly as
   `set_game_name` (line 364) does, and refuse with `GameNotFound` when the game file is absent.
2. Build the replacement:

```rust
    let fresh = GameManifest {
        manifest_version: atlantis_hud_core::backup::CURRENT_MANIFEST_VERSION,
        metadata: GameMetadata {
            game_id: manifest.metadata.game_id.clone(),
            game_name: manifest.metadata.game_name.clone(),
            ruleset_id: manifest.metadata.ruleset_id.clone(),
            active_faction_id: None,
        },
        report_sources: Vec::new(),
        created_at: now.to_string(),
        last_opened_at: now.to_string(),
    };
```

   Written field by field on purpose, **not** as `GameManifest { report_sources: Vec::new(), ..manifest }`:
   a struct-update expression carries every future field through a reset silently, and the next field
   added to a manifest is exactly the one that should not survive.

3. **Move the old directory aside, create, then remove it.** Not delete-then-create: a failure
   between the two would leave the player with no game at all, while the panel ah-58n.2 builds says
   "could not be reset" and offers **Try again** — a retry against a game that is already gone.

```rust
    let home = game_home(games_root, game_id);
    let aside = home.with_extension("resetting");
    // A leftover from a reset that died between these two renames. Removing it is safe: it is only
    // ever the *old* copy, and it exists only while a reset is in flight.
    if aside.exists() {
        fs::remove_dir_all(&aside)?;
    }
    fs::rename(&home, &aside)?;
    match create_game(games_root, &fresh) {
        Ok(opened) => {
            fs::remove_dir_all(&aside)?;
            Ok(opened)
        }
        Err(error) => {
            // Put it back rather than leaving the player with nothing. If this second rename also
            // fails there is nothing further to try, and the original error is the one worth
            // reporting.
            let _ = fs::rename(&aside, &home);
            Err(error)
        }
    }
```

`game_home` is line ~ (the private helper `set_game_name` and `delete_game` both use); read it before
writing, and use `with_extension` rather than composing a sibling path by hand.

### `crates/core-tauri/src/lib.rs`

One command, modelled on `command_set_game_name` (line 1115) and returning what `command_create_game`
returns:

```rust
pub fn command_reset_game(
    games_root: &str,
    game_id: &str,
    now: &str,
) -> Result<OpenedGameDto, String>
```

### `apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/main.rs`

A games-root wrapper beside `set_game_name` (line 116), plus the `use` list (line 5) and the
`generate_handler![…]` list (line 139) — the same three edits every games-root command needs.

### `packages/core-client/src/index.ts` and `tauriCommands.ts`

- `CoreAdapter` (line 480) gains, beside `deleteGame` (line 485):

```ts
  /** Empties a game and keeps it: same id, name and ruleset, nothing else. Resolves the fresh game. */
  resetGame(gameId: string, now: string): Promise<OpenedGame>;
```

- `tauriCommands.ts:28` gains `resetGame: ["reset_game", "game_id", "now"],` beside `deleteGame`.
- `packages/core-client/src/index.test.ts`'s adapter stub gains
  `resetGame: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(openedGame)` — use whatever opened-game value that file
  already builds for `createGame`.

### `packages/browser-core/src/webCoreAdapter.ts`

The web has no directory to rename, so it composes its two existing store operations in the order
that cannot lose the game — **the registry row is rewritten first, and the game's own database is
dropped second**:

```ts
    async resetGame(gameId: string, now: string) {
      const game = await store.getGame(gameId);
      if (!game) {
        throw new Error(`no game with id ${gameId}`);
      }

      const previous = game.manifest as GameManifest;
      const manifest: GameManifest = {
        manifestVersion: previous.manifestVersion,
        metadata: {
          gameId: previous.metadata.gameId,
          gameName: previous.metadata.gameName,
          rulesetId: previous.metadata.rulesetId
        },
        reportSources: [],
        createdAt: now,
        lastOpenedAt: now
      };
      // The registry row first: a failure after this leaves an empty game, which is what was asked
      // for; a failure the other way round would leave a full game the picker no longer lists.
      await store.putGame({ ...game, manifest });
      await store.dropGameData(game.databasePath);

      return { ...game, manifest, gameFilePath: game.databasePath };
    },
```

`activeFactionId` is simply absent from the rebuilt metadata, which is how the optional field says
"none" (ah-do8.1).

### `packages/browser-core/src/webStore.ts`

`deleteGame` (line 348) already closes the handle and deletes the per-game database, but it deletes
the registry row too. Extract the half a reset needs, and have `deleteGame` call it so there is one
copy of the handle-closing dance and its comment:

```ts
  /** Drops one game's own IndexedDB database, leaving the registry row alone. */
  dropGameData(databasePath: string): Promise<void>;
```

declared on the store interface beside `deleteGame` (line 114). Move the existing body's second half
into it verbatim — including the comment about closing the handle first, which is the part that took
someone a while to learn.

### `tests/native/sweep.ts`

One row, and **the position matters**: the file's header says `create_game` runs first "to mint the
database every scoped command needs" and `delete_game` last "to leave nothing behind" (lines 15 and
48). `reset_game` empties the game, so it must come **after** every scoped command that needs the
seeded turn and **immediately before** `delete_game` (line 264):

```ts
  { command: "reset_game", args: () => ({ game_id: GAME_ID, now: ISO }) },
```

## Increments

1. **The desktop operation.** RED: the four `reset_game` tests below. GREEN: `reset_game`.
2. **The command surface.** RED: `resetting_a_game_returns_the_fresh_game` in
   `crates/core-tauri/src/lib.rs`. GREEN: `command_reset_game`.
3. **The transport.** RED: add the `TAURI_COMMANDS` row — `scripts/tauriCommands.test.ts` goes red
   naming `main.rs` and the sweep. GREEN: the wrapper, its two list entries, the sweep row, the
   `CoreAdapter` method and the `index.test.ts` stub.
4. **The web operation.** RED: the three `webCoreAdapter.test.ts` tests below. GREEN:
   `store.dropGameData`, `deleteGame` refactored onto it, and the adapter method.

## The test plan

| Test | File | What it pins |
|---|---|---|
| `a_reset_game_keeps_its_id_name_and_ruleset` | `crates/core-persistence/src/lib.rs` | The manifest after a reset, read back off disk |
| `a_reset_game_holds_no_turns_orders_notes_or_sightings` | same | Seed a turn, a draft, a sighting, a merged report and a hex note; after the reset every one of the five reads empty |
| `a_reset_game_forgets_which_faction_was_yours` | same | `active_faction_id` is `None` after `set_active_faction` and a reset (ah-do8.1) |
| `resetting_a_game_that_does_not_exist_is_an_error` | same | `PersistenceError::GameNotFound`, like `set_game_ruleset`'s error test (line 1770) |
| `a_reset_leaves_other_games_alone` | same | Two games, one reset; the other's turn is still there |
| `resetting_a_game_returns_the_fresh_game` | `crates/core-tauri/src/lib.rs` | The DTO carries the same id and name and an empty `report_sources` |
| `empties a game and keeps it in the list` | `packages/browser-core/src/webCoreAdapter.test.ts` | `listGames` still names it; `loadLatestImportedTurn` is `null`; `listHexNotes` is empty |
| `keeps the name and ruleset and forgets the faction` | same | The manifest the reset resolves, and the one a later `openGame` reads back |
| `a reset game is not another game's business` | same | Two games in the registry, one reset |
| (existing) every `deleteGame` test | same | Unchanged: the refactor onto `dropGameData` changed nothing |

Suites: `cargo test --workspace`, `pnpm -r run test`, `pnpm run test:tooling` — all three are
`pnpm test`. Then `pnpm run check:fast`.

## User-facing decisions

**None in this bead.** It adds a client method and two commands; no control, no wording, nothing on
screen. Every decision the navigator took is recorded in the epic ah-58n's `design` field and is
implemented by ah-58n.2 — including the one that looks like it might belong here: **clearing the
saved map view** (`atlantis-hud-viewport-<gameId>`) is the shell's, because that key lives in
`localStorage`, which the core cannot reach.

## Out of scope

- **The control, the confirmation panel and every string** — ah-58n.2.
- **Clearing the saved map view** — ah-58n.2, as above.
- **Reopening the game, or emptying the workspace when the reset game is the open one** — ah-58n.2.
- **Undo, and any backup taken automatically.** The epic settled that: the confirmation mentions
  Export and does not perform one.
- **Orphaned `atlantis-hud-viewport-*` keys from past deletes.** A separate tidy-up.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
```

Nothing for a person to look at: with no caller, this bead changes nothing visible. Psylocke can mark
it as needing no verification pass, and verify the epic through ah-58n.2.

## Known traps

- **Do not write `GameManifest { ..manifest }`.** The whole point of the reset is that most fields do
  *not* survive it, and a struct-update expression makes every future field survive silently. The
  same applies to the TypeScript object literal — build it field by field, do not spread `previous`.
- **`activeFactionId` must be cleared** (`crates/core/src/backup.rs`, added by ah-do8.1 and merged
  today). A stale faction on an emptied game decides which turn it reopens on the moment a report is
  imported.
- **Rename aside, do not delete first.** ah-58n.2's panel offers **Try again** on failure, which is a
  promise that the game is still there. Delete-then-create breaks that promise in exactly the case
  the button exists for.
- **The web order is the opposite of the desktop's** — registry row first, game database second — and
  for the same reason: whichever step fails, the player is never left with a game the picker cannot
  see. Say so in the comment; a later reader will otherwise "make the two consistent".
- **`webStore.deleteGame` closes its IndexedDB handle before deleting the database**, because an open
  connection blocks the delete and a silent wait would leave the turns behind. That comment moves
  into `dropGameData` with the code; do not leave it behind.
- **`tests/native/sweep.ts` is ordered**, and `reset_game` empties the game. Put it immediately before
  `delete_game`, or every scoped command after it runs against an empty game and the sweep's own
  seeding becomes a lie.
- **`create_game` refuses when the game file already exists.** That is why the old directory is
  renamed aside rather than left in place.

title: Interface size grows the boxes as well as the text
description:
Found while verifying ah-46p (Psylocke, 2026-08-17, origin/main 0ed5814). The navigator passed the epic - the setting works, the panes follow it, the map correctly does not - and raised this alongside the pass.

## What the reader sees

Settings > Global > Interface size at 200%. The Settings dialog's own text grows, but the dialog does not, so nearly every settings row wraps onto two or three lines and the panel becomes hard to read. The navigator reports the same of the dropdowns. The higher the setting, the worse it is, which is backwards: the setting exists for a reader who cannot read the panes, and at the stop that reader most needs it the layout is at its worst.

## Cause

packages/shared/src/theme.css:117-119 applies --ui-scale to exactly three tokens:

    --text-pane-sm: calc(0.6875rem * var(--ui-scale, 1));
    --text-pane:    calc(0.75rem   * var(--ui-scale, 1));
    --text-pane-lg: calc(0.8125rem * var(--ui-scale, 1));

settingsStore.ts:195-200 stamps --ui-scale on the document element and nothing else. So the type scales and every other length does not: the root font-size is untouched, which means every rem width, padding and gap in the app still resolves against 16px. SettingsDialog.tsx:88 is w-[26rem] - a width that looks like it should follow the reader's text and does not, because only the font tokens were put on the multiplier.

This is the half of ah-46p.1 that stopped at type. The epic's own validation says 'the panes' text grows and stays laid out - nothing clipped, nothing overlapping'; at 200% that does not hold.

## For planning to settle

Two shapes, and the choice is the bead:

- Scale the root font-size (html { font-size: calc(1rem * var(--ui-scale)) }) and let every rem in the app follow. One line, and containers, padding and gaps all move together. The risk is reach: anything deliberately left off the scale, and anything in rem that should stay put, moves too - the map sets its own sizes and must be checked to be genuinely unaffected.
- Give the containers scaled tokens of their own, as the type has. Narrower and safer, but it is a list of sites rather than one line, and the next fixed width added will have the same bug again.

Whichever is chosen, 200% is the stop to check, and the Settings dialog is the worst case to check it on.
design:
## Context

Found by Psylocke while verifying ah-46p (2026-08-17). The navigator passed the epic — the setting
works, the panes follow it, the map correctly does not — and raised this alongside the pass.

At **Settings › Global › Interface size 200%** the Settings dialog's text grows but the dialog does
not, so nearly every settings row wraps onto two or three lines and the panel becomes hard to read.
The navigator reports the same of the dropdowns. The higher the setting the worse it is, which is
backwards: the setting exists for a reader who cannot read the panes, and at the stop that reader
most needs it, the layout is at its worst.

The cause is exact. `packages/shared/src/theme.css:117-119` puts the multiplier on three tokens and
nothing else:

```css
  --text-pane-sm: calc(0.6875rem * var(--ui-scale, 1));   /* 11px at a 16px root, at 100% */
  --text-pane: calc(0.75rem * var(--ui-scale, 1));        /* 12px */
  --text-pane-lg: calc(0.8125rem * var(--ui-scale, 1));   /* 13px */
```

`settingsStore.ts:194-200` stamps `--ui-scale` on the document element and nothing else. So the type
scales and no other length does: the root font size is untouched, every `rem` width, padding and gap
still resolves against the browser's 16px, and `SettingsDialog.tsx:79`'s panel is a fixed `w-[26rem]`
that looks like it should follow the reader's text and does not.

After this bead **one multiplier, at the root, and every `rem` in the application follows it** — type,
widths, padding, gaps — while the map, which uses no `rem` at all, stays exactly where the epic put
it.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

**Read `origin/main`, not a stale working tree.** This bead lands on top of ah-46p.2 (e0075a7) and
twenty other commits from today; the line numbers below are `ec82563`.

### `packages/shared/src/theme.css` — the whole of the fix, in two rules

**1. The three tokens lose their multiplier** and go back to plain `rem` (lines 117–119), with the
comment above them (114–116) rewritten to say where the multiplier moved:

```css
  /* The panes' type scale. Three steps, in rem so both the reader's own font-size preference and
     the Interface size setting reach them - the root font size carries the multiplier for every
     rem in the application, type and boxes alike (ah-ziv), so a token that multiplied by
     `--ui-scale` here would scale twice. The map sets its own sizes in SVG user units and is on
     neither scale. */
  --text-pane-sm: 0.6875rem;   /* 11px at a 16px root, at 100% */
  --text-pane: 0.75rem;        /* 12px */
  --text-pane-lg: 0.8125rem;   /* 13px */
```

**2. The root carries it instead**, beside the `--ui-scale: 1` default already at line 307:

```css
:root {
  --pane-transparency: 90;
  --ui-scale: 1;

  /* Interface size, applied once. Every rem in the application resolves against this, so a
     reader who doubles it gets boxes, padding and gaps twice the size as well as type - which is
     what "Interface size" says on the tin, and what ah-ziv was filed about.
     `1rem` in the root element's own font-size is the *initial* root size (the browser's, and so
     the reader's own preference) rather than the computed one, so this is not circular however
     much it looks it - CSS Values 4, §5.1.1. */
  font-size: calc(1rem * var(--ui-scale));
}
```

**3. One rule keeps a scaled dialog on screen** — the navigator's O1. It goes on `[role="dialog"]`
rather than on nine components, so the next dialog added cannot forget it. All nine of the
application's dialogs already carry that role (`BattlesDialog`, `ChangesDialog`, `CommandPalette`,
`ImportSummaryDialog`, `MapExportDialog`, `OrdersImportSummaryDialog`, `SettingsDialog`,
`ShortcutHelp`, `ViewerFactionPrompt` — checked, one each):

```css
/* A dialog declares the width its content wants (`w-[64rem]` for Battles), and at 200% that is
   twice the pixels - past the edge of a laptop window, taking the Close button with it. The
   viewport is the last word: cap, and let the contents scroll (ah-ziv, navigator's choice O1).
   On the role rather than on nine components, so a tenth dialog inherits it. */
[role="dialog"] {
  max-width: 95vw;
  max-height: 90vh;
  overflow: auto;
}
```

### `packages/shared/src/settingsStore.ts`

**No change.** It already stamps `--ui-scale` on the document element (line 199), which is now read by
one more rule. Update only the doc comment on `applyInterfaceSize` (line 194), which says "the
multiplier the pane type scale is expressed against" — it is now the multiplier every `rem` is
expressed against.

### Nothing else

No component changes at all. The ten fixed `rem` widths (`w-[64rem]` Battles, `w-[48rem]` Changes,
`w-[34rem]` ShortcutHelp, `w-[30rem]` ×3, `w-[28rem]` ×2, `w-[26rem]` ×2) are left exactly as they
are: they scale by themselves once the root does, and the cap above keeps them on screen.

## Increments

1. **The root carries the scale.** RED: rewrite the two `theme.test.ts` assertions named below —
   the existing one demands each token contain `var(--ui-scale)`, which is precisely what must stop
   being true. GREEN: the two `theme.css` rules.
2. **A dialog never leaves the window.** RED: the `[role="dialog"]` test below. GREEN: the third rule.
3. **Proof at 200%.** RED: extend `tests/smoke/settings.spec.ts`'s existing walk (line 259). GREEN:
   nothing — if this needs code, increments 1 and 2 are wrong.

## The test plan

| Test | File | What it pins |
|---|---|---|
| (rewritten) `declares the pane type scale as rem tokens in the theme block` | `packages/shared/src/theme.test.ts:136` | Still three `rem` tokens, still not `px` — but the loop demanding `var(--ui-scale)` on each (lines 156–161) is **inverted**: none of them may carry it now, or the scale applies twice |
| `applies the interface size once, at the root` | same | `:root` declares `font-size: calc(1rem * var(--ui-scale))`. The one place the multiplier lives |
| (existing) `declares --ui-scale with a default of 1, outside the @theme block` | `theme.test.ts:164` | Unchanged and must stay green: the app renders correctly before the store has stamped anything |
| `keeps a dialog inside the window` | `theme.test.ts` | A `[role="dialog"]` rule with `max-width`, `max-height` and `overflow` |
| (existing) `the panes grow when the interface size does` | `tests/smoke/settings.spec.ts:259` | Unchanged and must stay green — including its assertion that the **map ruler does not grow** (`fontSize={10}` in `MapCanvas.tsx:1242`, SVG user units, on no scale) |
| `the settings dialog grows with the interface size` | `tests/smoke/settings.spec.ts` (new, in the same walk) | At 200%: the dialog panel's width is measurably larger than at 100%, **and** its bounding box is inside the viewport. Both halves — the first is the bug, the second is O1 |

Suites: `pnpm -r run test` **and** `pnpm run test:smoke`. The smoke suite is not optional here: this
is a layout bead, and `theme.test.ts` reads the stylesheet as text — it cannot tell you that anything
actually renders.

## User-facing decisions

Two, taken by the navigator on 2026-08-17 against
`file:///Users/henrikku/repos/atlantis-hud/docs/ui/ah-ziv-scale-overflow.html` (mockup in the
scratchpad; commit it with the work if it is worth keeping):

1. **A dialog that no longer fits is capped at the window and scrolls inside it** (O1) — max width
   ~95% of the viewport, max height 90%, contents scrolling. The accepted cost, stated in the mockup:
   at 200% the two widest tables (Battles, Changes) have less room than their authors assumed and
   will wrap or gain a horizontal scrollbar. *Rejected: O3, scale everything and let it overflow* —
   the dialog runs off the edge taking its Close button with it, for the reader least able to go
   looking for it. *Rejected: O2, dialogs keep fixed pixel widths* — today's bug with extra steps.
2. **The multiplier moves to the root and comes off the three type tokens**, replacing ah-46p.2's
   approach rather than extending it. *Rejected: keeping the token multipliers and adding scaled
   container tokens* — narrower and safer, but a list of sites rather than one rule, and the next
   fixed width added has the bug again.

No new control, no new wording, nothing added to the Settings dialog. What changes is that the
existing setting reaches everything it looked like it already reached.

## Out of scope

- **The map.** It must not scale, and it does not: `MapCanvas` sizes its text in SVG user units
  (`fontSize={10}`, line 1242) and uses no `rem`. The existing smoke assertion that the ruler stays
  put is the guard; do not "fix" it.
- **Adding more stops to Interface size**, or changing the 100–200 range.
- **Full-page zoom.** The setting exists precisely because browser zoom scales the map too, and that
  unhelpful trade is ah-46p's whole reason.
- **Re-tuning any dialog's declared width.** They keep the widths they have; the cap handles the
  extremes.
- **Popovers and the header.** They are not `role="dialog"`, are anchored rather than centred, and
  are already fluid.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
pnpm run test:smoke
```

Then the check only a person can make, which is the bead's own acceptance and what Psylocke will
repeat: set Interface size to 200%, open **Settings › Global**, and read it. No row wraps onto two
lines, the dropdowns are usable, and the dialog is fully on screen. Then open **Battles** on a turn
that has one — it is capped at the window, and its table scrolls rather than disappearing off the
right-hand edge. Then look at the map: unchanged.

## Known traps

- **`font-size: calc(1rem * var(--ui-scale))` on `:root` is not circular**, however much it reads
  like it. In the root element's own `font-size`, `rem` resolves against the *initial* root font size
  — the browser's, and so the reader's own preference — not against the computed value. Writing
  `16px` instead would work and would silently throw away the reader's preference, which is the thing
  ah-46p existed to respect.
- **The three type tokens must lose their multiplier in the same commit that adds the root rule.**
  Either alone is wrong and only one of them is obviously wrong: leaving them multiplied renders type
  at 400% for a 200% setting, which looks like a plausible new bug rather than a half-finished change.
- **`theme.test.ts:156-161` currently asserts the opposite of what will be true.** Rewriting it is
  increment 1's RED, not collateral damage — and rewrite it to assert the tokens are *free* of
  `var(--ui-scale)`, so a well-meaning revert cannot pass.
- **Tailwind's spacing scale is in `rem`** (`p-2` is `0.5rem`), which is why no component needs
  touching — and also why the change reaches further than the ten declared widths. That is the point;
  check a pane and a popover at 200%, not only the dialogs.
- **`--ui-scale` must stay declared outside the `@theme` block** (`theme.css:307`, and
  `theme.test.ts:164` pins it): `@theme` is Tailwind's utility-generating namespace, and
  `--pane-transparency` is the precedent.
- **The map ruler test is the canary.** `tests/smoke/settings.spec.ts` reads the ruler's computed
  font size specifically because it is meant not to move. If it moves after this bead, something in
  the map has picked up a `rem` and the epic's promise is broken.

title: Reset a game from the game list, keeping its name and ruleset
description:
A game can be deleted and it can be created. There is no way to empty one and keep it — so a player
who wants to start the same game over deletes it, then recreates it, and retypes the name and picks
the ruleset again.

**The request:** a reset control beside the `✕` in the game list. After confirmation, it returns the
game to the state it would be in if it had been deleted and created again.

## What that means concretely

Deletion is well defined and the comment on `delete_game` says why:

> The whole directory goes, which is what makes the deletion complete: a game's turns, orders and
> remembered map live nowhere else, so there is nothing left behind to leak into the next game that
> happens to reuse an id.

So a reset is: everything in the game's directory except a freshly-made manifest carrying the same
name and ruleset. The manifest's `reportSources` empties, and imported turns, orders, the remembered
map and manual hex notes go with the rest.

That "live nowhere else" is what makes this safe to specify — and worth re-checking rather than
trusting, since notes arrived after that comment was written.

## The control

The `✕` is a button that sets `confirmingDeleteOf`, and a confirmation panel appears inline beneath
the row, danger-bordered, with copy that names what will be lost: *"Delete 'X'? Its turns, orders and
remembered map are erased."* A reset should follow that pattern exactly rather than invent a second
one — same inline confirmation, same danger styling, its own wording.

## For the planner to settle with the navigator

- **The symbol, and how it reads next to `✕`.** Two destructive controls side by side on every row
  is a misclick risk, and reset is the one that looks less final while being nearly as destructive.
- **Does the game keep its id?** Keeping it is simpler and keeps the game in place in the list;
  a new one is closer to "deleted and recreated" literally. Anything holding a game id across a reset
  — the last-opened pointer, per-game settings — decides this.
- **Do per-game settings reset?** They are not in the game's directory, so "remove all game data"
  does not obviously reach them. A player resetting a game probably wants their preferences kept, but
  that is a guess worth confirming.
- **Offer a backup first?** Export exists, and reset is unrecoverable. Whether the confirmation
  mentions it, offers it, or does it automatically is a judgement about how much friction a
  deliberate destructive act deserves.

## Validation

Reset a game with several imported turns, orders, a remembered map and some hex notes: the game
remains in the list under its own name and ruleset, and opening it looks exactly like a game just
created — no turns, no orders, nothing remembered. The other games are untouched. Cancelling the
confirmation changes nothing.
design:
## Context

An epic: split into ah-58n.1 (the operation) and ah-58n.2 (the control and the words), in that order.
This field records the navigator's decisions so neither child re-opens them.

A game can be deleted and it can be created. There is no way to empty one and keep it — so a player
starting the same game over deletes it, recreates it, and retypes the name and picks the ruleset
again.

A reset is: everything in the game's directory except a freshly-made manifest carrying the same id,
name and ruleset. `delete_game`'s own comment is why that is well defined —

> The whole directory goes, which is what makes the deletion complete: a game's turns, orders and
> remembered map live nowhere else, so there is nothing left behind to leak into the next game that
> happens to reuse an id.

— and that was re-checked while planning rather than trusted: hex notes (which arrived after that
comment was written) are in the game's own database and go with it. **One thing does live outside**:
the saved map view, in `localStorage` under `atlantis-hud-viewport-<gameId>`
(`packages/shared/src/workspace/mapViewportStorage.ts:25`), which a delete does not clear today
either.

## The interview (navigator, 2026-08-17)

Three mockups, merged by PR #390:

- `docs/ui/ah-58n-reset-control.html` — where the control lives.
- `docs/ui/ah-58n-reset-wording.html` — the confirmation copy, while the panel was still reset-only.
- `docs/ui/ah-58n-combined-panel.html` — the panel as it will ship.

**1. No new control on the row.** Pressing the existing `✕` opens one panel offering both outcomes
(variant **C**). *Rejected: a `↺` icon beside `✕`* — flush (**A**) or with a fourteen-pixel gap
(**A2**); two destructive controls a character apart, and `↺` looks less final than it is.
*Rejected: the word "Reset" on every row* (**B**) — clearest, but it eats four more characters of the
game name at the pane's minimum width.

The cost the navigator accepted with C, and it is stated in the mockup: a player looking for "start
this over" does not find it until they press `✕`.

**2. The panel's prose is P3**, whose first line is the actual choice:

> Delete “X”, or empty it and keep the game?
>
> Either way its turns, orders, remembered map and notes are erased. Reset keeps the name and
> ruleset.
>
> Export it first if you might want it back.

*Rejected: P1*, which keeps today's delete sentence untouched and adds a line about the difference —
safest, but its first line is not the decision. *Rejected: P2*, shortest, but it states rather than
asks.

The third line is decision **B2** from the second mockup: mention the export, do not offer it.
*Rejected: B1*, saying nothing (as delete does today); *rejected: B3*, an "Export first" button —
three buttons where there were two, and a save-then-return flow to design and to fail.

**3. The buttons are `Delete` / `Reset` / `Cancel`.** *Rejected: "Empty it"* (reads oddly beside
Delete, which is also a verb about the contents); *rejected: "Keep the game"* (names what survives,
but reads as the safe option beside Delete, and it is not safe — it erases everything in the game).

**4. A failure keeps the panel open**, showing `“X” could not be reset: <reason>` in red with
**Try again** and **Cancel**. *Rejected: the picker's own error line with the panel closing* (where a
failed create reports; the retry would mean finding the row and pressing `✕` again);
*rejected: both.*

**5. Focus opens on Cancel, and Escape closes the panel** and returns focus to the `✕` that opened it.
*Rejected: matching today's delete panel exactly*, which has no focus handling and ignores Escape —
inconsistent with every dialog in the application. *Rejected: Escape only.*

**6. The game keeps its id, and its saved map view is cleared.** Keeping the id keeps the game in
place in the list and keeps it open if it was the open one; clearing the view is what stops a reset
game reopening on a hex it no longer knows about. *Rejected: keeping the view* (the selected hex
would not exist); *rejected: a brand new id* — literally "deleted and recreated", but the game moves
in the list, closes if it was open, and orphans the old `localStorage` key exactly as a delete
orphans one today.

**7. Per-game settings.** The saved map view is the only per-game state outside the game's own data,
so decision 6 answers this completely. Global settings (theme, warning toggles, pane sizes) are not
per-game and are untouched.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

Per child.

## Increments

ah-58n.1, then ah-58n.2.

## The test plan

Per child.

## User-facing decisions

The seven above, with their rejected alternatives. ah-58n.2 implements all of them; ah-58n.1 has no
user-facing surface at all.

## Out of scope

- **Undo.** Reset is unrecoverable by design; the export line is the whole of the safety net.
- **Resetting several games at once**, and any bulk action in the picker.
- **Clearing the orphaned `atlantis-hud-viewport-<gameId>` keys that deletes have already left
  behind.** A real tidy-up and a bead of its own; this epic clears the key for the game it resets and
  nothing else.

## Validation

The epic's own: reset a game with several imported turns, orders, a remembered map and some hex
notes. It stays in the list under its own name and ruleset; opening it looks exactly like a game just
created; the other games are untouched; cancelling changes nothing.

## Known traps

Per child. The family's one: **`GameMetadata.activeFactionId` (ah-do8.1, merged today) must be
cleared by a reset.** An emptied game has no faction, and a stale one would decide which turn the
game reopens on the moment a report is imported.
acceptance_criteria: The game list offers a reset control beside the delete control, which after an explicit confirmation returns that game to the state of a freshly created one - same name and ruleset, no turns, orders, remembered map or notes. Other games are unaffected, and cancelling the confirmation changes nothing.
close_reason: All children closed; last was ah-58n.2, delivered in PR #394

title: A sailing fleet arrives with its hull, and so does everyone aboard
description: preview_orders_for_remembered_report clears an arriving unit's structure_id outright, commented 'a walker cannot take a building with it; whether a ship sails along is a question for a later issue'. This is that later issue: a sailing fleet demonstrably takes its hull, and so does everyone aboard it, so the destination hex's 'in' column should read the fleet rather than a dash. Depends on ah-l2i.2, which is what puts the passengers in the destination hex at all.
design:
## Context

Third and last child of the epic ah-l2i. **ah-l2i.1's `design` field carries the navigator's
decisions for the family; ah-l2i.2 builds the machinery this bead switches on.** Read both.

`preview_orders_for_remembered_report` clears an arriving unit's `structure_id` outright
(`crates/core/src/orders/effects.rs:151`), with the comment:

> A walker cannot take a building with it; whether a ship sails along is a question for a later
> issue, so the safe answer is to arrive outside.

This is that later issue. A sailing fleet demonstrably takes its hull, and so does everyone aboard,
so the destination hex's `in` column should read the fleet rather than `—`. The navigator settled it
against `docs/ui/ah-l2i-passenger-markers.html` (decision 6 in ah-l2i.1's plan): *"the fleet arrives
with its hull, so `in` reads the ship in the destination hex"*, and chose to do it rather than defer
it, in a child of its own, because it means deciding which structures travel and today the clear is
unconditional.

**This is a small bead — one conditional and its tests.** No TypeScript at all: the `in` column
renders `[${unit.structureId}]` and nothing else (`UnitTableDock.tsx:573`), with no lookup into the
destination region's structures, so a hull that is not in that region's report still renders
correctly. That is the whole reason this is cheap, and it is worth checking is still true before
starting.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### `crates/core/src/orders/effects.rs` — one conditional

ah-l2i.2 leaves a map of the fleets that are leaving:

```rust
/// (region, structure) of every fleet leaving this month, and where it ends up.
let mut sailing: BTreeMap<(String, String), Option<String>> = BTreeMap::new();
```

A unit keeps its hull on arrival exactly when the structure it stands in is one of those — which is
true for the unit that wrote the `SAIL` and for every passenger ah-l2i.2 carries, in one condition and
without asking which of the two it is:

```rust
            let mut arrived = entry.unit.clone();
            arrived.region_id.clone_from(&destination);
            // A walker cannot take a building with it. A ship can, and does: the hull is what is
            // moving, so the unit is still standing in it when it gets there - the one that wrote
            // the SAIL and every passenger alike (ah-l2i.3).
            let sails_along = entry
                .unit
                .structure_id
                .as_deref()
                .is_some_and(|id| sailing.contains_key(&(entry.unit.region_id.clone(), id.to_string())));
            if !sails_along {
                arrived.structure_id = None;
            }
```

in place of the unconditional `arrived.structure_id = None;` at line 151. Replace the comment as
shown — the old one says this is a question for later, and it is now answered.

Note it reads `entry.unit.region_id`, the **origin**, because that is how `sailing` is keyed; by this
point `arrived.region_id` has already been overwritten with the destination, so keying off `arrived`
silently matches nothing and the bead does nothing at all.

`structure_id` is read after the orders have been applied, so a unit that wrote `ENTER 329` and then
sailed is aboard by the time this runs, and a unit that wrote `LEAVE` is not. Both fall out of the
condition without a special case.

### Nothing else

- **No TypeScript.** As above.
- **No new field, no wire change.** `ReportUnit.structure_id` already crosses and is already
  rendered.
- **No change to the `changes` list.** `changes` is computed from the working entry against the
  report before the arrival copy is made (line 115), so keeping the hull adds no `structureId` change
  entry and removes none.

## Increments

One, because it is one conditional.

RED: `a_sailing_fleet_arrives_with_its_hull` and `everyone_aboard_arrives_still_aboard` in
`crates/core/src/orders/effects.rs`'s test module. GREEN: the conditional above.

## The test plan

| Test | What it pins |
|---|---|
| `a_sailing_fleet_arrives_with_its_hull` | The unit that wrote `SAIL`: its arriving row's `structure_id` is the fleet's, not `None` |
| `everyone_aboard_arrives_still_aboard` | A passenger carried by ah-l2i.2: same hull on its arriving row |
| `the_arriving_row_carries_the_other_changes_but_not_the_structure` | **Existing** (`effects.rs:1237`), and it must stay green **unchanged**: `unit 900` walks (`ENTER 4`, `MOVE SE`), so it still arrives outside. This is the test that says the conditional is a condition and not a deletion |
| `a_walker_leaving_a_fort_arrives_outside_it` | The same rule stated positively for a unit standing in a non-fleet structure that is not going anywhere |
| `a_unit_that_left_the_ship_before_moving_arrives_outside` | `LEAVE` then `MOVE`: `structure_id` is `None` before this runs, so nothing is carried |

Suites: `cargo test --workspace`, inside `pnpm run check:fast`.

## User-facing decisions

**One, already taken** — decision 6 in ah-l2i.1's `design`, chosen by the navigator against
`file:///Users/henrikku/repos/atlantis-hud/docs/ui/ah-l2i-passenger-markers.html`:

> The destination hex's `in` column reads the fleet rather than `—`.

*Rejected: keeping the present unconditional clear* (the map and the preview would go on disagreeing
about where the ship is); *rejected: doing it inside ah-l2i.2* (the navigator chose a child of its
own, since it means deciding which structures travel).

Nothing new is introduced by this bead: no string, no colour, no column. A cell that read `—` reads
`[329]`.

## Out of scope

- **Any structure other than a fleet.** A Fort does not travel, and the condition is written in terms
  of "the structure this unit is standing in is itself leaving", which no building ever is.
- **The `aboard <name> [<id>]` marker** — ah-l2i.2's, and it stays on the departing row only.
- **Rendering the hull's name in the `in` column.** It shows `[<id>]` today, by convention, and the
  navigator's W3 decision was explicitly about the *marker*, not the column — the mockup's
  correction note says the column "renders `[<structure id>]` and nothing else". Leave it.
- **Whether the fleet can legally sail at all** — `check_sailing`'s question (`ah-j0e`).

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
```

Then in the application: order a fleet with passengers to `SAIL`, and look at the destination hex's
units table — every arriving row's `in` column shows the ship's `[id]`, the same one it showed in the
origin hex, instead of `—`.

## Known traps

- **Key off the origin region, not the arrival.** `arrived.region_id` has already been overwritten by
  the time this runs; using it makes the lookup miss silently and the bead a no-op that still passes
  a carelessly written test.
- **The existing walker test must not be edited.** If
  `the_arriving_row_carries_the_other_changes_but_not_the_structure` needs changing to pass, the
  conditional is wrong — that unit walks.
- **This bead is meaningless without ah-l2i.2**, which creates `sailing` and puts the passengers in
  the destination hex at all. If `sailing` is not there, ah-l2i.2 has not merged; wait rather than
  rebuilding it here.
- **`is_some_and` over `structure_id`, not `unwrap_or_default`.** A unit with no structure must not
  match a `("region", "")` key that some other path might one day insert.

title: Units aboard a sailing fleet preview as travelling with it
description: After ah-l2i.1 a SAIL-ordered unit previews as departing, but the units aboard the fleet - which wrote no order of their own and go where the ship goes - still preview as staying put, so the origin hex keeps 22 men the ship is taking away and the destination shows 6 instead of 28. Preview every own unit aboard a sailing fleet as departing to the fleet's destination, marked in the row as 'aboard <name> [<id>]'. A unit with its own movement order keeps its own destination and gets no marker. Navigator chose this behaviour and its wording against the mockups recorded in ah-l2i.1's design.
design: ## Context Second child of the epic ah-l2i. **ah-l2i.1's `design` field carries the navigator's decisions for the whole family, with the rejected alternatives — read it before this, and re-open none of it.** After ah-l2i.1 a `SAIL`-ordered unit previews as departing. The units aboard the fleet — which wrote no order of their own and go where the ship goes — still preview as `Present`, so the origin hex keeps 22 men the ship is taking away and the destination shows 6 instead of 28. The navigator saw that end state in `docs/ui/ah-l2i-sail-preview.html` and rejected it; it is acceptable only as the intermediate state this split deliberately passes through. When this lands, every own unit aboard a sailing fleet previews as departing to the fleet's destination, and its row says why: `→ ocean (49,33) aboard Wavecrest [329]`. ## Files to change, and what to reuse ### `crates/core/src/orders/effects.rs` — two passes instead of one `preview_orders_for_remembered_report` (line 89) currently decides a unit's status and emits its rows in the same loop over `working.units` (lines 114–183). A passenger's status depends on **another** unit's trace, so the loop splits in two. Nothing about how a status is decided changes; it moves. **Pass 1 — decide, and note which fleets sail.** Keep the whole `let status = if entry.formed { … }` block exactly as it is, but capture the traced mode alongside the arrival, and collect the result rather than emitting it: ```rust /// One unit's verdict, held between the two passes. struct Decided { entry: WorkingUnit, status: UnitPreviewStatus, /// Where the unit ends the month, when the trace could say. arrival: Option, /// Set on the departing row of a unit carried by a fleet: ` []`. aboard: Option, } ``` `trace_move` already answers the question "is this a sail": `TracedPath::mode` (`crates/core/src/movement/trace.rs:36`) is `Some(MovementMode::Sail)` exactly when the unit is aboard a priceable fleet — "the planner's own inference otherwise: aboard a priceable fleet, the mode is Sail" (`trace.rs:58-61`). Read it where the path is already in hand rather than re-deriving anything from the order word.
