design:
## Context

`renderToStaticMarkup` is the only renderer this repository's TypeScript tests have — `@atlantis/shared`
runs `vitest run` with no config, so the environment is Node, there is no `window`, and React takes
its server-render branch. zustand's React binding reads `useSyncExternalStore`'s `getServerSnapshot`
on that branch, which is `getInitialState()` — the state object frozen at module load. So
`useSettingsStore.setState({ … })` before a static render is **invisible to that render**, and a
component can only ever be tested against its store's defaults.

That trap has been rediscovered per test file and solved two different ways:

- a `vi.mock` of the store module replacing the hook with one that reads `getState()` — added in
  `UnitTableDock.test.tsx` (4107920, ah-3cs), copied into `SettingsDialog.test.tsx` (581dabc,
  ah-m9q.2), removed again from `UnitTableDock.test.tsx` (3d44bf1, ah-2r3);
- a test-only seam in a production module — `setHexNotesStateForTest`
  (`packages/shared/src/hexNotesStore.ts:142`, 7ee0aa5, ah-o1t.2), which mutates the very object
  `getInitialState()` returns.

ah-o1t.2's retrospective prices the rediscovery at ~20 minutes and records "Seen before: None found",
although two test files had already worked around it that week. `SettingsDialog.test.tsx:9-10` still
says "see `UnitTableDock.test.tsx` for the same trap" — a file that no longer carries it. Thirty-three
test files under `packages/shared/src` render with `renderToStaticMarkup`; every next component that
reads a store in a non-default state pays this again, in whichever of the two ways its author finds
first.

After this bead there is **one test-only helper** that does it, no production module carries a test
seam, and the next author finds the answer instead of rediscovering it.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### New: `packages/shared/src/testing/storeState.ts`

Test-only. **Nothing in production may import it, and `packages/shared/src/index.ts` must not
re-export it** — that is the whole point of the directory, and the doc comment must say so. There is
no build step here (`@atlantis/shared`'s `main` is `src/index.ts` and the shells bundle it with Vite),
so a module nothing imports is a module nothing ships.

```ts
import type { StoreApi } from "zustand";

/**
 * A zustand store as `create()` returns one: the store API plus the React binding's
 * `getInitialState`, which is what a server render reads.
 */
export type TestableStore<T> = StoreApi<T> & { getInitialState: () => T };

/**
 * Makes a store's state visible to a `renderToStaticMarkup` render.
 *
 * Applies `patch` when given, then mirrors the store's whole current state onto the object
 * `getInitialState()` returns - which is what React's server branch reads through
 * `useSyncExternalStore`'s `getServerSnapshot`, and the reason a plain `setState` before a static
 * render changes nothing. Call it with no patch after driving the store through its own actions.
 *
 * Every store it touches is snapshotted the first time, so `restoreStoresForTest()` puts them back
 * exactly as they were - the mutation outlives a `setState`-only reset and would otherwise leak into
 * the next test in the file.
 */
export function setStoreStateForTest<T>(store: TestableStore<T>, patch?: Partial<T>): void;

/** Undoes every `setStoreStateForTest` this file has made. Call it in `afterEach`. */
export function restoreStoresForTest(): void;
```

Implementation: a module-level `Map<TestableStore<unknown>, { state: unknown; initial: unknown }>`;
on first sight of a store, store `{ ...store.getState() }` and `{ ...store.getInitialState() }`; then
`if (patch) store.setState(patch)` and `Object.assign(store.getInitialState(), store.getState())`.
`restoreStoresForTest` replays each entry — `store.setState(snapshot.state, true)` (replace, and the
snapshot is a whole state object including the actions, so replacing is safe) and
`Object.assign(store.getInitialState(), snapshot.initial)` — then clears the map.

### `packages/shared/src/hexNotesStore.ts`

`setHexNotesStateForTest` (line 142) is **deleted**, doc comment and all. `resetHexNotesStore`
(line 128) stays — three test files call it — but becomes an ordinary reset like its two neighbours
(`resetSettingsStore`, `settingsStore.ts:337`; `resetWorkspaceStore`, `workspaceStore.ts:425`):

```ts
export function resetHexNotesStore(): void {
  useHexNotesStore.setState(DEFAULT_TEST_STATE);
}
```

`DEFAULT_TEST_STATE` (line 125) stays where it is.

### `packages/shared/src/workspace/RegionNotes.test.tsx`

The only caller of the deleted seam. `beforeEach(resetHexNotesStore)` (line 44) stays; add
`afterEach(restoreStoresForTest)`; each of the six `setHexNotesStateForTest({ … })` calls (lines 47,
56, 65, 87, 99) becomes `setStoreStateForTest(useHexNotesStore, { … })` with the same object. The
`draw()` helper and every assertion are untouched.

### `packages/shared/src/workspace/SettingsDialog.test.tsx`

The `vi.mock("../settingsStore", …)` block (lines 6–23) is **deleted**, and with it the dangling
comment pointing at `UnitTableDock.test.tsx`. In its place, one comment naming the helper:

```ts
/**
 * `renderToStaticMarkup` runs with no `window`, so React's server branch reads the store's
 * `getInitialState()` rather than `getState()` - see `../testing/storeState.ts`, which is the one
 * place that trap is explained and worked around.
 */
```

`resetSettingsStore()` calls stay. Line 95 drives the store through its real action and then needs
the render to see it, which is what the no-patch form is for:

```ts
    useSettingsStore.getState().setAdvisoryCheck("not-enough-silver", false);
    setStoreStateForTest(useSettingsStore);
```

and `afterEach(restoreStoresForTest)` is added beside the existing `resetSettingsStore()` calls.
Nothing else in the file changes; if a test that passed under the mock now fails, the mock was
hiding a real difference and that is worth stopping on, not papering over.

## Increments

1. **The helper, proved against a store of its own.**
   RED: `packages/shared/src/testing/storeState.test.tsx` — a store created with zustand's `create`
   inside the test file and a one-line component reading it through the hook, rendered with
   `renderToStaticMarkup`. Assert the render shows the default; that `setStoreStateForTest(store, { … })`
   makes the render show the patch; and that `restoreStoresForTest()` puts the default back, both in
   the render **and** in `store.getState()`. A fourth case for the no-patch form: drive an action,
   then `setStoreStateForTest(store)`, and the render sees it.
   GREEN: `packages/shared/src/testing/storeState.ts`.
2. **The production seam goes.**
   RED: delete `setHexNotesStateForTest`; `RegionNotes.test.tsx` no longer compiles.
   GREEN: convert its six calls to the helper, add `afterEach(restoreStoresForTest)`, and reduce
   `resetHexNotesStore` to a plain `setState`. All five of its tests pass unchanged.
3. **The mock goes.**
   RED: delete the `vi.mock` block from `SettingsDialog.test.tsx`; the test at line 94–95 fails,
   because the render stops seeing the advisory code it just switched off.
   GREEN: `setStoreStateForTest(useSettingsStore)` after the action, `afterEach(restoreStoresForTest)`,
   and the corrected comment.

## The test plan

| Test | File | What it pins |
|---|---|---|
| `a static render shows the store's defaults` | `packages/shared/src/testing/storeState.test.tsx` | The trap itself, so the helper's reason is on file |
| `a patched store is visible to a static render` | same | The patch form |
| `state driven through the store's own actions is visible once mirrored` | same | The no-patch form, which is what `SettingsDialog.test.tsx` needs |
| `restoring puts the store back for the next test` | same | The leak this helper would otherwise create — assert both the render and `getState()` |
| (existing, unchanged assertions) `the region panel's Notes section` × 5 | `packages/shared/src/workspace/RegionNotes.test.tsx` | The conversion changed no behaviour |
| (existing, unchanged assertions) `the Warnings settings tab` | `packages/shared/src/workspace/SettingsDialog.test.tsx` | The mock was replaceable, not load-bearing |
| (existing) `hexNotesStore.test.ts`, `RegionPanel.test.tsx` | unchanged | `resetHexNotesStore` still resets |

Suites: `pnpm -r run test` covers all of it. No Rust, no browser suite — nothing here renders in a
browser or crosses the wasm boundary.

## User-facing decisions

**None.** This bead changes test code and deletes a test-only export from a production module; no
player-visible behaviour, wording or layout is touched. No mockup, and nothing to ask the navigator.

## Out of scope

- **Converting the other thirty-one `renderToStaticMarkup` test files.** They render against defaults
  and work; churning them buys nothing. The helper is there for the next one that needs it.
- **`resetSettingsStore` / `resetWorkspaceStore` / `resetHexNotesStore`.** They stay exported from
  their production modules. They are ordinary state resets, not the trap this bead is about, and
  moving them is a separate argument.
- **A lint rule forbidding production imports of `src/testing/`.** The doc comment says it; if that
  proves not to be enough, that is a bead of its own.
- **`UnitTableDock.test.tsx`**, which already had its mock removed by ah-2r3 and needs nothing.
- **Anything about jsdom.** Switching `@atlantis/shared`'s vitest environment would change how
  thirty-three files render and is not a refactoring.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
```

Plus one thing to look at rather than run — `git grep -n "getInitialState"` should return
`packages/shared/src/testing/storeState.ts` and its test, and nothing else. Anywhere else is the trap
being solved a third time.

Nothing here needs a human: no surface changes.

## Known traps

- **`getInitialState()` returns a live object, and mutating it outlives `setState`.** That is exactly
  why `restoreStoresForTest()` exists and why it must restore `initial` from a snapshot rather than
  from the store's defaults — a store whose reset only calls `setState` (both of the other two do)
  would otherwise carry one test's state into the next.
- **`store.setState(snapshot, true)` replaces the whole state, actions included.** That is safe only
  because the snapshot is a shallow copy of a *whole* state object taken before anything was touched.
  Do not snapshot a partial.
- **`@atlantis/shared` has no vitest config**, so its environment is Node — which is *why* React takes
  the server branch. Do not "fix" this by giving the package a jsdom environment: that is a change to
  how every one of its thirty-three static-render tests behaves, and it is out of scope.
- **The helper's file must be `.tsx`-testable.** `storeState.ts` itself has no JSX, but its test needs
  a component, so the test is `storeState.test.tsx`.
- **Do not export the helper from `packages/shared/src/index.ts`.** It re-exports whole modules with
  `export *` (lines 7, 8, 15), so adding one there would put a test helper on the package's public
  surface, which is how a test seam gets back into production by a different door.

title: The ruleset carries what each skill can produce, read from the game's data page
description:
The scraped ruleset knows an item's tag, name, kind, weight, capacity and movement, and a skill's tag, name, cost and maximum level. It does not know **which skill produces which item**, so nothing in the application can answer 'what could this unit produce here'.

The game's data page states it outright, one sentence per skill level:

- `mining [MINI] 1: ... A unit with this skill may PRODUCE iron [IRON] at a rate of 1 per man-month.`
- `weaponsmith [WEAP] 1: ... may PRODUCE swords [SWOR] from iron [IRON] at a rate of 1 per man-month, crossbows [XBOW] from wood [WOOD] at a rate of 1 per man-month, longbows [LBOW] from wood [WOOD] ...`

So it is scrapeable from `tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-data.html` by the same scraper that already reads each skill's cost and maximum level (`packages/ruleset/src/data.ts`), and it belongs in the ruleset for the same reason those do: it is *game* data, and two servers running different games disagree about it.

Filed while planning ah-bai.2, which needs it to narrow the PRODUCE completion popup to what the unit standing in the hex can actually make. It blocks that bead. Nothing a player can see changes when this lands.

Also unblocks checks nobody can write today: a PRODUCE order for a good the unit has no skill for, and the tradeable-goods half of ah-8om.
design:
## Context

The scraped ruleset knows an item's tag, name, kind, weight, capacity and movement, and a skill's
tag, name, study cost, maximum level and — since `ah-dbb.1` — what casting it consumes. It does not
know **which skill produces which item**, so nothing in the application can answer "what could this
unit produce here".

The game's data page states it outright, once per skill level:

> `mining [MINI] 1: … A unit with this skill may PRODUCE iron [IRON] at a rate of 1 per man-month.`
>
> `weaponsmith [WEAP] 1: … may PRODUCE swords [SWOR] from iron [IRON] at a rate of 1 per man-month,
> crossbows [XBOW] from wood [WOOD] at a rate of 1 per man-month, longbows [LBOW] from wood [WOOD] …`

This bead teaches the scraper to read those sentences and puts the answer in the ruleset, where the
study costs and casting costs already live — it is *game* data, and two servers running different
games disagree about it.

**Nothing a player can see changes.** The field is data no code reads yet. Its first consumer is
`ah-bai.2`, which is blocked on this bead: it narrows the `PRODUCE` completion popup to what the unit
standing in the hex can actually make. It also unblocks checks nobody can write today — a `PRODUCE`
order for a good the unit has no skill for, and the tradeable-goods half of `ah-8om`.

**`ah-dbb.1` is the worked example for all of it** (commit `f421133`, PR #342, merged 2026-08-16): it
added `cast` to the same struct, scraped from the same page, across the same six files. Read that
commit before starting; this bead is its sibling and should look like it.

Branch from `origin/main` (`cd092e6` or later). Every line number below is that tree — `ah-dbb.1`
moved most of them.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### The scraper — `packages/ruleset/src/data.ts`

`parseSkillReference` (`:389`) already walks one paragraph per skill level and folds them by tag:
the name from the lowest level, the cost from whichever level states it, the maximum level from the
highest. Production joins that fold.

```ts
/** One thing a skill can make, and the level at which it can first be made. */
export type Production = { tag: string; level: number };
```

added to `SkillEntry` (`:103-117`), after `cast`:

```ts
  /**
   * What a unit with this skill may PRODUCE, in the order the page lists it, each with the level
   * at which it becomes available. Empty for the great majority of skills, which make nothing.
   */
  produces: Production[];
```

Always written, empty array and all — the same posture as `cast: CastCost | null`, and it keeps the
key off the optional path that `committed.test.ts`'s `toEqual` treats specially.

The reader, modelled directly on `readCastCost` (`:333`) including its loud failure:

```ts
/** The clause a production sentence opens with. Every PRODUCE on the page today is a `may PRODUCE`. */
const PRODUCTION = /may PRODUCE ([^.]*)\./i;
/** What separates one production from the next: `at a rate of 1 per man-month`, `… per 3 man-months`. */
const PRODUCTION_RATE = /at a rate of [^.]*?man-months?/i;
/** The tag in `swords [SWOR]`, `a number of meals [MEAL]`. */
const PRODUCED_TAG = /\[([A-Z0-9]{2,6})\]/;

/**
 * What one level's paragraph says the skill may produce, or `[]` when it says nothing - true of
 * most skills.
 *
 * The whole difficulty is telling a product from its materials: `swords [SWOR] from iron [IRON]`
 * names two items and the skill makes only the first. So the clause is cut into one segment per
 * production - the rate phrase is what ends each - and within a segment everything from the first
 * ` from ` is dropped before the tag is read. A trailing empty segment carries no tag and is
 * skipped; a clause that yields no tag at all is the page having changed shape, and throws.
 */
function readProduction(tag: string, paragraph: string, level: number): Production[] {
  const clause = paragraph.match(PRODUCTION);
  if (!clause) {
    return [];
  }

  const made: Production[] = [];
  for (const segment of clause[1].split(PRODUCTION_RATE)) {
    const found = segment.split(" from ")[0].match(PRODUCED_TAG);
    if (found) {
      made.push({ tag: found[1], level });
    }
  }

  if (made.length === 0) {
    throw new RulesetScrapeError(
      `could not read what skill ${tag} produces from "${clause[0]}"`
    );
  }
  return made;
}

/** Unions production across levels: a tag keeps the lowest level that granted it. */
function mergeProduction(existing: Production[] | undefined, found: Production[]): Production[] {
  const merged = [...(existing ?? [])];
  for (const made of found) {
    if (!merged.some((seen) => seen.tag === made.tag)) {
      merged.push(made);
    }
  }
  return merged;
}
```

and one line in the fold at `:402-410`, beside `cast`:

```ts
      produces: mergeProduction(existing?.produces, readProduction(tag, paragraph, Number.parseInt(level, 10)))
```

Lowest level wins because the page lists a skill's levels in order and the fold walks them that way,
so the first sighting of a tag is the level that granted it. That is the same reasoning
`cost: existing?.cost ?? stated` already relies on, and it is what makes `MINI` come out as iron at
1, mithril at 3, admantium at 5.

`RulesetScrapeError` is already imported (`:121` re-exports it); `readNumber` and `entryParagraphs`
(`:129`) are untouched.

**This algorithm has been run over the committed page, through the same paragraph splitting
`entryParagraphs` does** — 96 skill entries in, no clause that would throw, and this out. It is the
expected answer in full, so the tests below assert against fact rather than guesswork; a different
result means the parser is wrong, not that the expectations are stale.

| Skill | Produces (tag at level) |
|---|---|
| `ARMO` | CARM 1, LARM 1, WSHD 1, PARM 3, ISHD 3, MARM 5, ARNG 5, AARM 5, MSHD 5 |
| `CARP` | WAGO 1, SPIN 1, MWAG 3, CATP 4, STED 4, GLID 5 |
| `COOK` | MEAL 1 |
| `FARM` | GRAI 1, LIVE 1 |
| `FISH` | FISH 1, NET 1, TURT 3 |
| `HEAL` | HPOT 3 |
| `HERB` | HERB 1, LASS 1, BAG 1, MUSH 3 |
| `HORS` | HORS 1, CAME 1, WING 5 |
| `HUNT` | FUR 1, FLOA 3 |
| `LUMB` | WOOD 1, IRWD 3, YEW 5 |
| `MINI` | IRON 1, MITH 3, ADMT 5 |
| `QUAR` | STON 1, ROOT 3 |
| `WEAP` | SWOR 1, XBOW 1, LBOW 1, PICK 1, SPEA 1, AXE 1, HAMM 1, JAVE 1, PIKE 2, MSWO 3, BAXE 3, MXBO 4, DBOW 5, ASWR 5 |

**13 producing skills, 53 pairs**, and the other 83 skills produce nothing.

### The core's reader — `crates/core/src/movement/rules.rs`

Beside `CastInput` (`:269`) and `CastCost` (`:278`):

```rust
/// One thing a skill can make, and the level at which it can first be made.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase", deny_unknown_fields)]
pub struct Production {
    pub tag: String,
    pub level: u32,
}
```

and on `SkillEntry` (`:289-301`), after `cast`:

```rust
    /// What a unit with this skill may PRODUCE, and the level at which each becomes available.
    /// Empty for a skill that makes nothing, and for a ruleset generated before production was
    /// scraped.
    #[serde(default)]
    pub produces: Vec<Production>,
```

`#[serde(default)]` is not optional decoration: `SkillEntry` carries `deny_unknown_fields`
(`:288`), and a stored or served ruleset from an older build has no `produces` key at all. `cast`
carries the same attribute at `:299` for the same reason.

### The committed ruleset — `config/public/ruleset.json`

Regenerated, never hand-edited, with the command `committed.test.ts` names:

```bash
pnpm --filter @atlantis/ruleset scrape -- \
  --rules tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-rules.html \
  --data tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-data.html
```

Against the **committed fixture pages**, not the network: `committed.test.ts` compares the file to
what the scraper makes of those fixtures, so a scrape from the live site would fail the gate even if
it were more current.

`apps/web/dist/ruleset.json` and `apps/desktop/dist/ruleset.json` are build outputs under a
gitignored `dist/`. Leave them alone.

`packages/ruleset/src/build.ts` needs no change: it passes `parseSkillReference`'s output through
whole.

## Increments

1. **A skill's production is read.**
   RED: `packages/ruleset/src/data.test.ts` — `reads what a skill may produce`, on a `mining [MINI] 1`
   paragraph, expecting `[{ tag: "IRON", level: 1 }]`. Does not compile: there is no `produces`.
   GREEN: the `Production` type, `readProduction`, `mergeProduction`, and the fold line.

2. **A material is not a product.**
   RED: `does not mistake what a product is made from for a product`, on the `weaponsmith [WEAP] 1`
   paragraph, expecting `SWOR, XBOW, LBOW, PICK, SPEA, AXE, HAMM, JAVE` and asserting `IRON` and
   `WOOD` are **not** among them.
   GREEN: the ` from ` cut, if increment 1 did not already write it — write the test either way, it
   is the one that stops a weaponsmith being able to mine.

3. **The level each product arrives at.**
   RED: `records the level at which each product becomes available`, on `MINI`'s levels 1, 3 and 5 fed
   in order, expecting `IRON 1, MITH 3, ADMT 5`.
   GREEN: `mergeProduction`'s lowest-level-wins union.

4. **The awkward sentences.**
   RED: `reads a product whose sentence puts the materials in an odd place` — `COOK`'s
   `a number of meals [MEAL] equal to skill level divided by 2, rounded up from any of grain [GRAI],
   livestock [LIVE] and fish [FISH]`, expecting `[{ tag: "MEAL", level: 1 }]` alone — and
   `reads several products in one sentence`, on `FISH`'s `fish [FISH] … and nets [NET] from herb
   [HERB]`, expecting `FISH` then `NET`.
   GREEN: nothing new if the segmentation is right, which is the point of writing them.

5. **A shape change fails loudly.**
   RED: `fails loudly on a production it cannot read`, on a paragraph whose `may PRODUCE` clause names
   no bracketed tag, expecting `RulesetScrapeError`.
   GREEN: the `made.length === 0` throw.

6. **The core reads the field, and the file carries it.**
   RED: `crates/core/tests/movement_ruleset.rs` — `reads_what_a_skill_can_produce` (see *The test
   plan*). It does not compile.
   GREEN: `Production` and the `produces` field in `rules.rs`, **then** regenerate
   `config/public/ruleset.json` with the command above. In that order: regenerating first gives every
   ruleset a key the Rust struct rejects, and `deny_unknown_fields` turns that into every ruleset in
   the workspace failing to load. Run `cargo test --workspace` immediately after regenerating.

7. **An older ruleset still loads.**
   RED: `a_skill_entry_without_a_produces_block_still_loads`, on a hand-written skill JSON with no
   `produces` key, modelled on `a_skill_entry_without_a_cast_block_still_loads` in the same file.
   GREEN: `#[serde(default)]`.

## The test plan

**TypeScript — `packages/ruleset/src/data.test.ts`, run by `pnpm -r run test`.** The five tests named
in the increments, written against paragraph strings in the file's existing style (the `cast` tests
`ah-dbb.1` added, at the end of that file, are the pattern to copy — they feed one paragraph at a
time rather than the whole page). Plus:

| Test | Pins |
|---|---|
| `records no production for a skill that makes nothing` | an `observation [OBSE] 1:` paragraph, which states no production → `produces` is `[]`, not absent. 83 of the 96 skills are like this |
| `keeps the page's order` | `WEAP` level 1 comes back `SWOR, XBOW, LBOW, PICK, SPEA, AXE, HAMM, JAVE` in that order |
| `reads a product made from several materials with quantities` | `catapults [CATP] from 250 wood [WOOD], 30 ironwood [IRWD], 80 furs [FUR] and 3000 silver [SILV]` → `CATP` alone |

**`packages/ruleset/src/build.test.ts`:** one case that the assembled ruleset carries production for a
known skill, in the style of the `cast` case `ah-dbb.1` added.

**`packages/ruleset/src/committed.test.ts`:** unchanged, and it is the gate — it fails until the JSON
is regenerated, with the exact command in its own failure message.

**Rust — `crates/core/tests/movement_ruleset.rs`, run by `cargo test --workspace`.** It reads the
committed ruleset through `common::ruleset()` over `atlantis_hud_fixtures::RULESET_JSON`. Add
`Production` to the `use atlantis_hud_core::movement::rules::{CastInput, ItemKind, MovementMode,
Ruleset, RulesetError}` list at the top of that file:

| Test | Pins |
|---|---|
| `reads_what_a_skill_can_produce` | `MINI` produces `IRON` at 1, `MITH` at 3, `ADMT` at 5; `WEAP` produces `SWOR` at 1 and `ASWR` at 5 |
| `a_product_is_not_confused_with_its_materials` | `WEAP`'s productions contain no `IRON` and no `WOOD` — the same guarantee as the TS test, asserted against the shipped file |
| `the_committed_ruleset_names_every_producing_skill` | exactly 13 skills have a non-empty `produces`, 53 skill-item pairs in total. A count, deliberately: when the fixture page is next updated these numbers move, and that is worth a failing test rather than a silent change |
| `a_skill_entry_without_a_produces_block_still_loads` | a skill JSON with no `produces` key parses, with an empty list |

**Suites:** `pnpm run check:fast` covers all of it — the package suites, `cargo test --workspace`,
typecheck and clippy. No browser suite is involved: nothing renders.

## User-facing decisions

**None.** Nothing a player can see changes when this lands: the field is data no code reads yet, and
its first consumer (`ah-bai.2`) is a separate bead. The decision that produced this bead was made
while planning `ah-bai.2` — the navigator chose a `PRODUCE` popup narrowed to what the unit can
actually make, which needs a fact the ruleset did not carry — and it is recorded in that bead's
design field, not this one.

## Out of scope

- **The materials a production consumes, and its rate.** `from 250 wood [WOOD], 30 ironwood [IRWD],
  80 furs [FUR] and 3000 silver [SILV] at a rate of 1 per 4 man-months` is a second parsing problem
  with its own quantities, and no filed bead needs it. The sentence will still be on the page when
  one does.
- **Any use of the new field.** `ah-bai.2` is the first reader and is blocked on this bead. Do not
  wire it into a popup, a check or a panel here.
- **Structures a skill may BUILD.** The same paragraphs state those too (`may BUILD a Mythic Stables
  from 10 ironwood [IRWD]`), and they are a different question.
- **Inverting the map onto items** (`ItemEntry.producedBy`). The skill side is what a consumer asks
  from, since it starts from a unit's skills; the inverse is derivable and unneeded.
- **The `dist` copies of the ruleset**, which are build outputs.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm --filter @atlantis/ruleset scrape -- \
  --rules tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-rules.html \
  --data tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-data.html
pnpm run check:fast
git diff --stat config/public/ruleset.json      # regenerated, and committed with the code
```

Then read the diff of `config/public/ruleset.json`: every one of the 96 skills gains a `produces`
key, 13 of them non-empty, and nothing else in the file moves. A diff that touches an item, a
movement cost or the `source` block means the scrape was run against something other than the
committed fixture pages.

No human check is needed: nothing renders, and there is nothing to look at in the running app.

## Known traps

- **`SkillEntry` carries `deny_unknown_fields`** (`crates/core/src/movement/rules.rs:288`).
  Regenerating the JSON before the Rust field exists makes *every* ruleset unloadable — movement
  costs, routes, the item catalogue, the lot — and the failures land far from the cause. Add the
  Rust field first, regenerate second, and run `cargo test --workspace` between them.
- **`#[serde(default)]` on the new field is what lets an older ruleset load.** A ruleset served or
  stored by a previous build has no `produces` key, and without the attribute that is a hard parse
  error rather than an empty list. `cast` at `:299` is the precedent.
- **A material is not a product.** The single most likely bug in this bead: a scrape that takes every
  `[TAG]` in the sentence records `WEAP` as producing iron and wood, which tells the next feature
  that a weaponsmith can mine. The ` from ` cut and two tests exist for exactly this.
- **The trailing empty segment is normal.** Splitting on the rate phrase leaves an empty string after
  the last production; it carries no tag and must be skipped, not treated as a failure.
- **Every `PRODUCE` on the committed page is a `may PRODUCE`** — 31 of them, checked. The parser keys
  on that phrase, which is why a clause that matches but yields no tag throws instead of returning
  empty: it means the page changed shape.
- **Regenerate against the committed fixtures, never the live site.** `committed.test.ts` compares
  the file with what the scraper makes of `tests/fixtures/ruleset/*.html`; a fresher scrape from the
  network fails that comparison even when it is more correct. Updating the fixtures is a different
  bead.
- **`pnpm --filter @atlantis/ruleset scrape` writes `config/public/ruleset.json` from the repository
  root** however it is invoked (`cli.ts` resolves relative paths against the root deliberately), so
  run it from anywhere in the worktree but check `git status` afterwards.
- **`ah-dbb.1` (`f421133`) is the same change in miniature.** Six files, ~700 lines, and it is on
  `main` now: `git show f421133` is the fastest way to see where each piece goes.

title: Items and skills complete from the game's catalogue as you type
description:
The second half of ah-bai: where an order takes an item or a skill, offer the game's own catalogue - 171 items and 96 skills in the ruleset this build ships - by their four-letter tag with the name beside them (`SILV  silver`). Tags rather than names because 70 of the item names have a space in them and would need quoting.

Depends on ah-bai.1, which builds the core answer and the second completion source; this widens both.

Unlike ah-bai.1 the vocabulary is a served file rather than compiled in, so this stays silent until a ruleset has loaded, and silent for a ruleset whose catalogue is empty.

Settled with the navigator when ah-bai was planned: where an item class and an item are both valid (`GIVE 4573 ALL `), the two go in one flat list with the classes first (193 entries there once this lands). Still open for its own planning session: whether typing matches the tag only or the name too, and what an accepted entry inserts.
design:
## Context

`ah-bai.1` made the completion popup answer argument positions from the ruleset's *grammar*: the
closed keyword lists, the compass, the 22 item classes. It says nothing where an order takes an item
or a skill, because those are *game* data rather than engine data — 171 items and 96 skills that live
in the served ruleset, not in the binary.

This bead completes the feature, and it does more than list a catalogue: **the hex decides.**
`BUY` offers what this hex has for sale, `SELL` what its market wants, `PRODUCE` what can be produced
here — by the ground or by this unit's own skills — and `GIVE` and everything else offer the whole
catalogue. The report already carries all three lists per hex, with each item's tag, name, price and
amount, so the popup can be exactly as narrow as the truth allows.

The two blockers are both planned and must be built first:

- **`ah-bai.1`** builds the grammar walk, the core command, and the second completion source. This
  bead widens all three; do not rebuild them.
- **`ah-9na`** teaches the ruleset which skill produces which item, at which level. Without it
  `PRODUCE` cannot offer the swords a weaponsmith could make here.

It is one bead rather than two by the navigator's decision: nothing of this ships until it narrows,
so a version where `BUY` offers all 171 items never reaches a player.

Branch from `origin/main` at or after whatever commit carries `ah-bai.1` and `ah-9na`. Read both
beads' design fields first — this plan describes the deltas to what they built, and cites the shapes
they promise rather than code that exists today.

The mockup the navigator chose from is `docs/ui/order-argument-completion.html` (this bead's own
round is recorded under *User-facing decisions* below).

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### The wire type widens: `Vec<String>` → `Vec<OrderCompletion>`

`ah-bai.1` answers with bare words, which cannot carry an item's name or a market price. The new
shape, in the core:

```rust
/// One entry in the orders editor's completion popup.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
pub struct OrderCompletion {
    /// What is written into the line when the entry is accepted, and the first thing the typed
    /// word is matched against. Always the canonical spelling: a keyword, or an item or skill tag.
    pub value: String,
    /// The other thing the typed word may match: an item's or skill's name, so `cross` finds
    /// `XBOW`. Empty for a keyword, which has no second name.
    pub name: String,
    /// What the entry shows beside its value. Empty for a keyword, which is its own explanation.
    pub detail: String,
}
```

`name` is separate from `detail` because they are matched and shown respectively: a market entry
shows `perfume · $204, 63 left` and must not be matched on `204`.

Every layer moves with it — the wasm and Tauri returns, `CoreAdapter.orderArgumentCompletions`, the
`CoreWasmModule` member, the two fakes, and `orderCompletion.ts`'s option building. `ah-bai.1`'s
keyword answers become `{ value: "UNIT", name: "", detail: "" }`, and its tests move with them.

### The core command gains what it needs to know: `crates/core/src/orders/completion.rs` (new)

```rust
/// What may stand where the caret is, from the grammar, the catalogue and the hex.
///
/// `ruleset` and `report` are optional because the answer is useful without either: the grammar's
/// own keywords need neither, a market needs only the report, and only the catalogue needs the
/// ruleset. `unit_id` is whose block is being typed, which is what makes "this hex" and "this
/// unit's skills" answerable; without it the hex-narrowed positions fall back to the catalogue.
#[must_use]
pub fn order_argument_completions(
    line_prefix: &str,
    ruleset: Option<&Ruleset>,
    report: Option<&ParsedReport>,
    unit_id: Option<&str>,
) -> Vec<OrderCompletion>;
```

Parsed types rather than JSON, exactly as `validate_turn` takes them
(`crates/core/src/orders/mod.rs`); the shells hand over JSON and go through the cache, below.

**`grammar.rs` keeps the walk and gives up the public function.** `ah-bai.1` put both there. Split
them: the walk is about the grammar table and belongs beside it; the catalogue and the market are
not. So `grammar.rs` exposes what it already computes internally —

```rust
/// The order the caret is inside, and every argument that may stand at the caret across its forms.
///
/// `None` in the command position, inside a comment or an unclosed quote, or for an order the table
/// does not have. The `Arg`s are de-duplicated in form order, exactly as `ah-bai.1` collected them.
pub(super) fn arguments_at_caret(line_prefix: &str) -> Option<(&'static Order, Vec<&'static Arg>)>;
```

— keeping `next_argument` and `keywords` private and unchanged, and `completion.rs` builds the answer
from it. `order_argument_completions` moves out of `grammar.rs`; the re-exports in
`crates/core/src/orders/mod.rs` and `crates/core/src/lib.rs` point at the new module, and
`mod.rs` gains `pub mod completion;`. `ah-bai.1`'s grammar tests that call
`order_argument_completions(prefix)` move to `completion.rs`'s test module and gain the three new
arguments as `None`; their expectations do not change, which is the point of moving rather than
rewriting them.

The body, per `Arg` the walk returns:

| `Arg` | Answer |
|---|---|
| `Kw`, `OneOf`, `ItemClass`, `MoveStep` | `grammar::keywords`, as `ah-bai.1` built it — `value` only |
| `Arg::Item` | by the order's name, see the table below |
| `Arg::Skill` | every skill in `ruleset.skills`, `value` the tag, `name` and `detail` from `SkillEntry` |
| everything else | nothing, unchanged |

Where a position allows several `Arg`s the answers concatenate in the order the walk returned them,
which puts the 22 item classes before the items at `GIVE 4573 ALL ` — the navigator's Q8.

**What `Arg::Item` answers, by order:**

| Order | Offers | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `BUY` | what the hex sells | `region.for_sale` |
| `SELL` | what the hex wants | `region.wanted` |
| `PRODUCE` | what the ground yields here, then what this unit's skills can make | `region.products`, then `ruleset.skills[..].produces` filtered by the unit's own skill levels |
| every other item position | the whole catalogue | `ruleset.items` |

"Every other item position" is `GIVE`, `TAKE`, `TRANSPORT`, `DISTRIBUTE`, `WITHDRAW`, `SACRIFICE`,
`EXCHANGE`, `STEAL`, `PREPARE`, `ARMOR`, `WEAPON` and `SHOW ITEM` — the whole catalogue, monsters
included, because a captured beast is a thing a unit can hold and hand over. Match on the order's
`name` from the `&'static Order` the walk returned, never on the raw first token.

**Finding the hex.** A unit carries its own region id, so this is two lookups and no search of the
region's unit lists:

```rust
let unit = report?.units().find(|unit| unit.unit_id == unit_id?)?;      // report/mod.rs:53
let region = report?.regions.iter().find(|region| region.region_id == unit.region_id)?;
```

`ParsedReport::units()` is at `crates/core/src/report/mod.rs:51-55`; `ReportUnit::unit_id` and
`ReportUnit::region_id` at `crates/core/src/report/model.rs:126` and `:128`;
`ReportRegion::region_id` at `:199`. There is no existing helper for this and none is worth adding
for one caller — but do write it as one private function in `completion.rs`, because the fallback
rules below all hang off whether it answered.

**What `PRODUCE` offers, exactly.** The hex's `products` (`Vec<ItemAmount>`, `model.rs:212`) first,
then every `Production` (from `ah-9na`) of every skill the unit holds at a level at least the
production's, skipping any tag already listed. The unit's skills are `ReportUnit::skills:
Vec<Skill>` with `Skill { name, tag, level, points }` (`model.rs:111-116`), and a skill the ruleset
does not know is skipped rather than guessed at.

**Ordering.** Alphabetical by tag within each group — market entries, catalogue entries and skills
alike — with `PRODUCE`'s two groups kept in order (ground first, then skills). `ruleset.items` and
`ruleset.skills` are `BTreeMap`s keyed by tag, so their iteration is already alphabetical and free;
the market and product lists come in the report's order and must be sorted.

**The exact wording of `detail`**, agreed with the navigator and not to be improvised:

| Entry | `detail` |
|---|---|
| An item from the catalogue | `silver` — the ruleset's `name` |
| A `BUY` entry | `perfume · $204, 63 left` — `{name} · ${price}, {amount} left` |
| A `SELL` entry | `jewelry · $630, wants 82` — `{name} · ${price}, wants {amount}` |
| A `PRODUCE` entry from the ground | `grain · 57 here` — `{name} · {amount} here` |
| A `PRODUCE` entry from a skill | `sword · weaponsmith` — `{item name} · {skill name}` |
| A skill | `observation · 50 silver` — `{name} · {cost} silver` |
| A skill the page prices nowhere | `annihilation` — the name alone |
| A keyword | empty |

The separator is ` · ` (U+00B7 with a space each side) throughout. A market entry's `name` comes from
the **market line**, not the catalogue: the report writes `hill dwarves`, which is what the player is
looking at in the region panel. Item names elsewhere come from the ruleset.

**Silence and fallback**, which is where most of the care goes:

| Situation | `BUY`/`SELL`/`PRODUCE` | Other item positions | Skills |
|---|---|---|---|
| No report, or no `unit_id`, or the unit is not in the report | the whole catalogue | the whole catalogue | the catalogue |
| A report, and the hex's list is empty | **nothing** | — | — |
| No ruleset | `BUY`/`SELL` still answer from the report; `PRODUCE` offers the ground's products only | nothing | nothing |
| Neither | nothing | nothing | nothing |

The second row is the decision worth remembering: an empty `for_sale` is indistinguishable from a
market the report never printed (`crates/core/src/report/scan.rs:180-184` — the game writes
`For Sale: none`, and an ocean prints no line at all), and the navigator chose to trust it. Most
hexes in the fixture genuinely sell nothing, and a popup that opened anyway would be wrong far more
often than right.

### The shells — the same eight files `ah-bai.1` touched

Three arguments join `line_prefix`, in this order: `ruleset_json`, `raw_report`, `unit_id`. That is
the order `validate_orders` already uses for the first two, and matching it is worth more than any
other arrangement.

1. **`crates/core-wasm/src/lib.rs`** — `order_argument_completions_state` gains
   `ruleset_json: Option<String>, raw_report: Option<String>, unit_id: Option<String>` and resolves
   both through the cache, copying `validate_orders_state`'s block verbatim in shape:

   ```rust
   let (ruleset, report) = atlantis_hud_core::cache::with_global(|cache| {
       let ruleset = ruleset_json.as_deref().and_then(|json| cache.ruleset(json).ok());
       let report = raw_report
           .as_deref()
           .map(|raw| cache.classified_when_possible(raw, ruleset_json.as_deref()));
       (ruleset, report)
   });
   ```

   The cache is the whole reason this is affordable per keystroke: it is the same seventy-kilobyte
   ruleset and the same four-hundred-unit report the validator already keyed, and neither is
   re-parsed. `classified_when_possible` rather than `report`, so the parse is shared with the
   validator's rather than made a second time under a different key.
2. **`crates/core-tauri/src/lib.rs`** — the same, with `Option<&str>` arguments and the same cache
   block (`command_validate_orders` is the twin to copy). The command keeps its name, so
   `scripts/tauriCommands.test.ts`'s `renames.size` stays at whatever `ah-bai.1` left it.
3. **`apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/main.rs`** — unchanged: the command is already registered.
4. **`packages/core-client/src/index.ts`** —
   `orderArgumentCompletions(linePrefix: string, rulesetJson: string | null, rawReport: string | null, unitId: string | null): Promise<OrderCompletion[]>`,
   plus the exported `OrderCompletion` type mirroring the Rust struct.
5. **`packages/core-client/src/tauriCommands.ts`** — the row grows its keys:
   `["order_argument_completions", "line_prefix", "ruleset_json", "raw_report", "unit_id"]`. The
   mapped tuple type holds it to the method's arity, so a missed key is a compile error.
6. **`packages/browser-core/src/webCoreAdapter.ts`** — the `CoreWasmModule` member and the adapter
   method both gain the three parameters, passed straight through.
7. **The two fakes** — `packages/core-client/src/index.test.ts` and
   `packages/browser-core/src/webCoreAdapter.test.ts`, whose stubs return `[]` and need only their
   types to keep up.
8. **`tests/native/sweep.ts`** — the row gains real arguments:
   `{ command: "order_argument_completions", args: () => ({ line_prefix: "BUY 5 ", ruleset_json: RULESET, raw_report: REPORT, unit_id: "18642" }) }`.
   `RULESET` and `REPORT` are already read at the top of that file.

### The completion source — `packages/shared/src/orderCompletion.ts`

`orderArgumentCompletions` keeps its shape and changes how it filters, because tag-or-name matching
is richer than CodeMirror's own:

```ts
export type ArgumentLookup = (linePrefix: string) => Promise<readonly OrderCompletion[]>;
```

- Match a candidate when **either** its `value` **or** its `name` starts with the typed word,
  case-insensitively. `cross` finds `XBOW`; `chain` finds `CARM`; `wood` finds both `WOOD` and
  `WELF`. `suggestOrderCommands` no longer serves — write the predicate here, in one small exported
  function so it can be tested alone.
- The accepted text is always `value`, never `name`: that is what keeps `chain armor` out of the
  file and its quoting problem with it.
- Return `filter: false` on the result and **drop `validFor`**. With `filter: false` CodeMirror
  shows what it is given, in the order it is given (it scores such options `1e9 - index`), so
  `sortText` is unnecessary here and the core's ordering stands exactly. Dropping `validFor` costs a
  core call per keystroke instead of per word, which is what tag-or-name matching requires — the
  call is a cache hit on both shells.
- Each option: `{ label: entry.value, detail: entry.detail || undefined, type: "keyword", apply: \`${entry.value} \` }`.
  `detail` is what CodeMirror renders dimmed after the label. `type` stays `"keyword"`: the navigator
  chose one icon for the whole feature.

`orderCommandCompletions` is untouched — it still filters through CodeMirror and still carries the
`sortText` `ah-bai.1` gave it. The two sources never answer in the same position, so the mixed
scoring cannot interleave them.

### Threading — `AppShell.tsx` only

The lookup closes over what it now needs:

```tsx
const argumentCompletions = useCallback<ArgumentLookup>(
  (linePrefix) =>
    client.orderArgumentCompletions(linePrefix, rulesetText, rawReport, unit?.unitId ?? null),
  [client, rulesetText, rawReport, unit]
);
```

`rulesetText` (`AppShell.tsx:287`) is already the ruleset-or-null the storage layer wants, and
`rawReport` is already threaded to every other core call. `OrdersPanel` and `OrdersEditor` need no
change at all: they pass a callback whose signature has not moved.

## Increments

1. **The wire type widens.**
   RED: `crates/core/src/orders/completion.rs`'s moved test — `name_offers_everything_it_may_rename`
   now expects `OrderCompletion { value: "UNIT", name: "", detail: "" }` and friends.
   GREEN: the `OrderCompletion` struct, the module move, `arguments_at_caret` in `grammar.rs`, and
   every layer of the wire including the two fakes and the TS type. `pnpm run typecheck` names each
   remaining site. No behaviour changes in this increment: the same words come back in the same
   order, wrapped.

2. **Items and skills reach the popup.**
   RED: `completion.rs` — `the_catalogue_answers_where_an_item_may_stand`, on
   `order_argument_completions("GIVE 4573 ALL ", Some(&ruleset), None, None)`, expecting the 22 item
   classes first and then catalogue entries in tag order, `SILV` carrying `name: "silver"`.
   GREEN: the `Arg::Item` and `Arg::Skill` arms for the catalogue case, plus the skill `detail`
   wording and its no-cost variant.

3. **The hex narrows BUY and SELL.**
   RED: `a_purchase_offers_only_what_the_hex_sells`, on the committed fixture report and unit
   `18642` in Inholm, expecting exactly `GEM, HDWA, LEAD, PERF` in tag order, `PERF` carrying
   `detail: "perfume · $204, 63 left"`.
   GREEN: the unit-to-region lookup and the `BUY`/`SELL` arms.

4. **The hex and the unit's skills narrow PRODUCE.**
   RED: `production_offers_what_the_ground_yields`, on fixture unit `18642`, expecting exactly
   `GRAI, IRON, STON` with `detail: "grain · 57 here"` and the like.
   GREEN: the `PRODUCE` arm over `region.products`.
   Then RED: `production_offers_what_the_unit_can_make`, on a hand-built report whose unit holds

   GREEN: the walk over `unit.skills` into `ruleset.skills[..].produces`, filtered by level.

5. **Silence where the hex says nothing, the catalogue where nothing was said.**
   RED: `a_hex_with_no_market_offers_nothing` (a fixture hex whose `For Sale` reads `none`) and

   GREEN: the fallback table above.

6. **Typing a name finds the tag.**
   RED: `packages/shared/src/orderCompletion.test.ts` — `matches an item by its name as well as its

7. **End to end.**

## The test plan

three helpers `semantics.rs`'s own test module already has:
`const RULESET: &str = atlantis_hud_fixtures::RULESET_JSON;` (`semantics.rs:1318`),
`fn ruleset() -> Ruleset` (`:1320`), and `fn report(regions: Vec<ReportRegion>) -> ParsedReport`
(`:1409`) for hand-built reports. The whole committed turn is
`atlantis_hud_fixtures::G7_F95_T71`, parsed with `crate::report::parse_report_full`.

## User-facing decisions

Interviewed with the navigator on 2026-08-16, over
`.cerebro/scratch/ah-bai.2-catalogue.html`, whose chosen state is the mockup committed for the epic
(`docs/ui/order-argument-completion.html`).

**Q1 — which items are offered.** Chosen: **the hex decides** — `BUY` what is for sale, `SELL` what
the market wants, `PRODUCE` what can be produced here, `GIVE` and the rest the whole catalogue,
monsters included. Rejected: the whole catalogue everywhere (171 entries, a lion offered where a lion
cannot be bought); the catalogue minus its 58 monsters; and narrowing by item *kind* per order, which
guesses where the report can simply be read.

**Q2 — how a typed word matches.** Chosen: **tag or name, with the tag inserted** — `cross` finds
`XBOW`, `chain` finds `CARM`. Rejected: matching the tag alone, which is simpler and leaves a player
who knows the word but not the code with no popup. The consequence is accepted deliberately: the
source does its own filtering, so it asks the core once per keystroke rather than once per word.

**Q3 — which half of an entry leads.** Chosen: **the tag, with the name beside it** (`SILV · silver`)
— what you read is what the line will say. Rejected: the name leading with the tag beside it, which
reads like English but no longer resembles the line it writes.

**Q4 — what a skill entry says.** Chosen: **name and monthly cost** (`observation · 50 silver`), the
number that actually decides which skill a unit studies. Rejected: the name alone. The one skill the
data page prices nowhere shows its name alone, by the same decision.

**Q5 — one bead or two.** Chosen: **one bead — nothing ships until it narrows.** Rejected: shipping
the catalogue first and narrowing after, which would have helped days earlier at the price of a
window where `BUY` offered more than the hex sells.

**Q6 — `PRODUCE`, where the hex's product list is not the whole truth.** Chosen: **the hex's products
plus what this unit's skills can make** — the sharpest list in the feature, and the reason `ah-9na`
exists at all, since nothing in the ruleset said which skill produces which item until it did.
Rejected: the hex's products alone (hides every crafted good — a weaponsmith typing `PRODUCE` would
get grain, iron and stone and no swords); and products-first-then-everything, which hides nothing but
is a longer list.

**Q7 — the order market entries sit in.** Chosen: **alphabetical by tag**, predictable and stable
turn to turn so muscle memory works. Rejected: dearest first (puts the thing worth selling on top,
but moves under the player every turn); the report's own order.

**Q8 — what a market entry shows.** Chosen: **name, price and amount** —
`perfume · $204, 63 left`, `jewelry · $630, wants 82`. Rejected: name and price only; name alone.
Accepted cost: the widest popup in the feature, about 40 characters, in a rail that is often 150px.

**Q9 — when the hex cannot answer.** Chosen: **no report → the whole catalogue; an empty list →
silence.** The two are different situations and get different answers: with no report the popup
cannot know, so it offers everything; with a report in hand an empty `For Sale` is the report's own
answer and is respected. Rejected: always falling back (suggests purchases in an ocean hex); always
silent (the popup is dead until a report is imported).

**Q10 — where an item class and an item are both valid** (`GIVE 4573 ALL `). Chosen, when `ah-bai.1`
was planned and honoured here: **one flat list with the classes first**. Rejected: two labelled
sections; holding the catalogue back until two letters are typed.

## Out of scope

- **Narrowing `GIVE` to what the unit actually holds.** Explicitly decided against: `GIVE` offers the
  whole catalogue.
- **Spell arguments.** `CAST FARSIGHT ` still offers nothing — the grammar says `Arg::Skill, Arg::Tail`
  because the arguments depend on the spell, and accept-on-doubt keeps it that way. The spell name
  itself is completed, because that is an `Arg::Skill`.
- **Telling a spell from a mundane skill.** `CAST ` offers all 96 skills, not only the magical ones:
  the ruleset marks none of them as magic, and inferring it from the cost or the name would be a
  guess. `STUDY`, `FORGET`, `COMBAT` and `SHOW SKILL` all get the same full list, which is what the
  grammar says of them too.
- **Warning about an order the popup would not have suggested.** A `BUY` of something the hex does
  not sell stays silent, as `semantics.rs` deliberately leaves it (`ah-d8u` is the bead for that
  check). This bead adds no diagnostic.
- **Quantities.** `BUY 5 ` completes the item, never the number, even though the market line says
  how many are left.
- **Remembered hexes.** A `ParsedReport` holds only this turn's regions; a market seen last turn is
  not offered. `known_map.rs` keeps stale regions, and reaching for them here would offer prices
  that may no longer hold.
- **Matching a plural or an underscored name.** `find_item`'s spelling rules
  (`crates/core/src/movement/rules.rs:255`) resolve `swords` and `chain_armor` when the *checker*
  reads an order; the popup matches a prefix of the tag or of the catalogue name and no more. A
  player typing `swords` is typing a word the popup already offered them a tag for.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
pnpm run test:smoke
```

Then by eye, with the g7/f95/t71 fixture loaded and unit 18642 selected (Inholm, 7,53):

- `BUY 5 ` then <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Space</kbd> lists exactly `GEM`, `HDWA`, `LEAD`, `PERF`, and
  `PERF` reads `perfume · $204, 63 left`.
- `SELL ALL ` lists the nine wanted tags in alphabetical order.
- `PRODUCE ` lists `GRAI`, `IRON`, `STON` with `· 57 here` and the like, followed by anything this
  unit's skills can make.
- `GIVE 4573 ALL ` lists the 22 item classes, then the catalogue.
- `BUY 2 cross` offers `XBOW`; accepting writes `XBOW ` and not `crossbow`.
- `STUDY ` lists skills with their monthly cost.
- Move to a hex whose report says `For Sale: none` and check `BUY 5 ` offers nothing at all.

## Known traps

- **An empty market list means two different things** — "this hex sells nothing" and "the report
  never printed the line" are the same empty `Vec` (`crates/core/src/report/scan.rs:180-184`; an
  ocean prints no market line at all). The navigator chose to trust it, so an empty list is silence
  and only a missing *report* falls back. Do not add a cleverer guess.
- **A market entry's `name` is the report's spelling, plural and all** — `hill dwarves`, not the
  catalogue's `hill dwarf`. It is what the player is reading in the region panel, so it is what the
  popup shows; do not normalise it against the ruleset.
- **`classified_when_possible`, not `report`**, when resolving the report through the cache: the
  validator keys its parse that way, and a second key means a second parse of four hundred units on
  every keystroke.
- **This source now asks the core per keystroke.** That is affordable only because both shells go
  through `cache::with_global`; a change that parses the ruleset or the report per call turns a
  millisecond into the whole cost of the feature.
- **`filter: false` also disables CodeMirror's match highlighting**, and it scores options
  `1e9 - index`, so the order returned is the order shown and `sortText` does nothing. Do not set
  both.
- **`SkillEntry.produces` is `#[serde(default)]`** (`ah-9na`): a ruleset from an older build has no
  production data at all, and `PRODUCE` must degrade to the ground's products rather than panic or
  offer nothing.
- **`scripts/tauriCommands.test.ts` holds `TAURI_COMMANDS`' keys equal to the Rust parameter names**,
  in order. Three new parameters mean three new keys, spelled `ruleset_json`, `raw_report`,
  `unit_id`.
- **`scripts/tauriCommands.test.ts` also holds the wasm exports equal to `CoreWasmModule`'s members
  by name *and arity*.** Widening the wasm function without widening the TypeScript member fails
  there rather than at the call site.
- **`bd show --json` returns an array** if the blockers' plans are read back with `jq`: index `.[0]`.
- **The smoke suite's `ordersText` reads rendered lines**, so do not assert the trailing space
  through the DOM; the unit test on `apply` is where that is pinned (`ah-bai.1`'s trap, still true).

title: Directions and the rules' own keywords complete after the order name
description:
Typing `NAME U` offers nothing today: the completion popup only ever fires in the command position, so every word after the order name is on the player to remember and spell.

This child covers everything the ruleset closes and the binary already carries: the fixed keyword lists (`NAME UNIT|FACTION|OBJECT|CITY`, `GIVE ... ALL`, `DECLARE` attitudes, `OPTION` values, `SPOILS` types, `BUILD HELP|COMPLETE`, `TAKE FROM`, `JOIN`, `DESCRIBE`, `SHOW`), the six directions plus `IN`/`OUT` wherever a move step stands, and the 22 item classes. No ruleset needed for any of it - `crates/core/src/orders/grammar.rs` is compiled in.

The reported case ships here: with the vocabulary loaded, typing `NAME U` in the orders editor offers `UNIT`, and accepting it leaves `NAME UNIT `.

Planned with the navigator on 2026-08-16; the interview and the mockup are in the design field.
design:
## Context

The completion popup in the orders editor answers one position: the first word of a line.
`packages/shared/src/orderCompletion.ts:8` states the limit and its reason — "Only there. Everything
after the command is arguments - directions, item names, quantities - and offering TAX inside a
half-typed direction would be noise." That reasoning holds for open-ended arguments and not for the
ones the ruleset closes: `NAME` takes exactly one of `UNIT|FACTION|OBJECT|CITY`, and typing `NAME U`
offers nothing today.

This bead makes the popup answer the argument positions the ruleset closes, and only those. The
vocabulary already exists as data: `crates/core/src/orders/grammar.rs` models every order's argument
positions (`Arg::OneOf(NAMEABLE)` for `NAME`, `Arg::Kw("ALL")`, `Arg::ItemClass`, `Arg::MoveStep`),
and it is the same table the syntax checker validates against — so the popup cannot offer a word the
checker would then reject. What is missing is a way to ask the core *what may stand where the caret
is*, the way `order_commands()` answers the command position, plus a second CodeMirror completion
source that asks it.

Everything here is compiled in: no ruleset, no report, no game state. `ah-bai.2` widens the same
answer with the ruleset's item and skill catalogue and is blocked on this bead; it will extend
`order_argument_completions` and the same completion source rather than adding a second pair.

When it lands: typing `NAME U` offers `UNIT`; `MOVE ` and every step after it offer
`N NE SE S SW NW IN OUT`; `GIVE 4573 ` offers `UNIT` and `ALL`; `GIVE 4573 ALL ` offers the 22 item
classes. Accepting any completion — including a command, which changes today's behaviour — leaves a
trailing space.

The mockup that decided all of this is `docs/ui/order-argument-completion.html` (PR #344), and the
whole interview is under *User-facing decisions* below.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### The core answer — `crates/core/src/orders/grammar.rs`

The walk goes **in `grammar.rs` itself**, not in a new module, for one reason: it must consume
already-typed tokens by exactly the rules the checker consumes them by, and `match_arg`
(`grammar.rs:545`) is that private function. Calling it is what stops the popup and the checker
drifting apart; re-implementing "how many tokens is a unit reference" beside it is the bug this
bead would otherwise ship. Add to the existing `use super::lexer::{Token, TokenKind};` at
`grammar.rs:14` so `lex_line` is in scope.

The public surface:

```rust
/// What the ruleset allows where the caret is, for the completion popup.
///
/// `line_prefix` is one order line from its first character up to the caret, the caret's own
/// half-typed word included: the position is worked out from the complete words before it, and the
/// half-typed word is what the shell filters the answer by.
///
/// Returns the words in the order they should be offered, and an empty list wherever the rules
/// leave the position open - a unit number, a quantity, a name, anything after CAST - which is most
/// positions and is not a failure. The command position answers empty too: `order_commands` speaks
/// there.
#[must_use]
pub fn order_argument_completions(line_prefix: &str) -> Vec<String>;
```

and two private helpers:

```rust
/// The argument that may stand where the caret is, for one form; `None` when the typed words do not
/// match this form, or when the form is already finished.
fn next_argument(form: &'static [Arg], arguments: &[Token]) -> Option<&'static Arg>;

/// The words one argument allows, in the order they should be offered; empty for an open one.
fn keywords(argument: &Arg) -> Vec<&'static str>;
```

`order_argument_completions` does, in order:

1. `let lexed = lex_line(line_prefix);` — `lex_line` is `crates/core/src/orders/lexer.rs:94`, and it
   already handles the indentation, the `@` repeat prefix, quoting and case-insensitivity. Nothing
   here re-splits a line.
2. `if lexed.comment.is_some() || lexed.unterminated_quote.is_some() { return Vec::new(); }` — past a
   semicolon nothing is an order, and inside an unclosed quote nothing is a word yet. Both fields are
   set by the lexer (`lexer.rs:74` and `lexer.rs:80`) and neither needs a second opinion here.
3. Decide whether the last token is the one being typed: `!line_prefix.ends_with(char::is_whitespace)`.
   If so it is dropped before counting the position — a half-typed word says nothing about which
   position the caret is in. (A prefix ending in a closing quote is treated as still-typing by this
   rule and so drops a complete token; every position that can follow a quoted word is `Arg::Tail`,
   which answers empty either way, so the case is harmless. Say so in a comment rather than adding a
   branch for it.)
4. `split_first` the remaining tokens into command and arguments. No tokens left means the caret is
   in the command position → empty.
5. `find_order(&command.text)` (`grammar.rs:427`) → `None` means an unknown order → empty.
6. For each `form` in `order.forms`, `next_argument(form, arguments)`, and collect `keywords(..)` of
   whatever it returns, **de-duplicated by exact equality, keeping the order first seen** — every
   candidate is an upper-case constant out of the table, so nothing subtler is needed. Form
   order is the rules page's order, which is the ordering the navigator chose (see Q6): `GIVE 4573 `
   answers `["UNIT", "ALL"]`, `UNIT` first because `&[Arg::Unit, Arg::Kw("UNIT")]` is the first form
   listed at `grammar.rs:224`.
7. `.map(str::to_string)` into the `Vec<String>` the wire wants.

`next_argument` walks one form against the typed arguments:

```rust
fn next_argument(form: &'static [Arg], arguments: &[Token]) -> Option<&'static Arg> {
    // `match_arg` collects unrecognised item names for the checker's warnings; nothing here wants
    // them, and with no ruleset it never fills this.
    let mut unknown = Vec::new();
    let mut at = 0;

    for (index, argument) in form.iter().enumerate() {
        match argument {
            // Consumes the whole rest of the line, whatever it is. There is no position after it,
            // and nothing to say about the one it swallows.
            Arg::Tail => return None,
            // `inner` binds as `&&'static Arg` - the field is already a reference and the match is
            // through one - so both uses below dereference it. `Arg` is `Copy`, so that is free.
            Arg::Rest(inner) => {
                debug_assert_eq!(index, form.len() - 1, "Rest is a form's last argument");
                loop {
                    if at == arguments.len() {
                        return Some(*inner);
                    }
                    at = match_arg(*inner, arguments, at, None, &mut unknown).ok()?;
                }
            }
            _ => {
                if at == arguments.len() {
                    return Some(argument);
                }
                at = match_arg(argument, arguments, at, None, &mut unknown).ok()?;
            }
        }
    }

    // Every argument matched and the form has no more positions: `TAX` takes nothing, and
    // `DECLARE 15 ALLY` is finished.
    None
}
```

Two things this buys, both of which a hand-rolled walk would get wrong: `Arg::Unit` consumes one to
four tokens (`17`, `NEW 2`, `FACTION 15 NEW 2` — `forms::unit_token_count`, reached through
`match_arg` at `grammar.rs:577`), so `GIVE FACTION 15 NEW 2 ` lands on the same position as
`GIVE 17 `; and `Arg::Rest` repeats, so a move offers its steps again after each one.

`keywords` maps an argument to its words:

| `Arg` | Offers |
|---|---|
| `Kw(k)` | just `k` |
| `OneOf(list)` | the list, in its declared order |
| `ItemClass` | `ITEM_CLASSES` (`grammar.rs:62`) **sorted alphabetically** — the one ordering exception, see Q9 |
| `MoveStep` | `Direction::ALL` by `abbreviation()`, then `IN`, `OUT` |
| everything else | empty — `Unit`, `Faction`, `Object`, `Number`, `Flag`, `Item`, `Skill`, `Name`, and `Tail`/`Rest` which never reach here |

The move steps are built from `Direction::ALL` and `Direction::abbreviation()`
(`crates/core/src/movement/graph.rs:32` and `:70`) rather than from a literal list, so the offered
spellings cannot drift from `Direction::parse`, which is what `match_arg` checks them with
(`grammar.rs:580`). `Direction::ALL` is already clockwise from north — `N NE SE S SW NW` — which is
the order the navigator chose.

`Arg::Flag` deliberately offers nothing: `0` and `1` are a closed set of two digits nobody needs help
spelling, and the popup only opens on a letter anyway.

### The completion source — `packages/shared/src/orderCompletion.ts`

A second exported source beside `orderCommandCompletions`, and the only place the editor learns
anything about arguments:

```ts
/** How the source reaches the core: one order line up to the caret, answered with what may stand there. */
export type ArgumentLookup = (linePrefix: string) => Promise<readonly string[]>;

/**
 * Completion for an argument position: any word after the command, where the ruleset closes what
 * may stand there.
 *
 * The vocabulary is the core's own - `grammar.rs` answers per position, so this side never learns
 * how an order is shaped and cannot drift from the checker. Quiet in the command position, which
 * the core answers empty and `orderCommandCompletions` owns.
 */
export function orderArgumentCompletions(lookUp: ArgumentLookup): CompletionSource;
```

The body, decided in full:

- `const line = context.state.doc.lineAt(context.pos);` and
  `const before = context.state.sliceDoc(line.from, context.pos);` — exactly as
  `orderCommandCompletions` does at `orderCompletion.ts:17-18`. Only the text left of the caret is
  ever read.
- `const match = /(?:^|\s)([A-Za-z]*)$/.exec(before);` — the word being typed, anchored to a
  whitespace boundary. `return null` when it does not match, which is what keeps the source silent
  on `MOVE 12` and `@`: a partly-typed word that is not letters has no keyword to offer, and
  offering one at the caret would produce `MOVE 12N`.
- Then, before anything is asked of the core:

  ```ts
  // Still in the command position - indentation, an optional repeat prefix, and the word itself is
  // all there is. `orderCommandCompletions` owns that position, and asking the core about it means
  // a round trip per keystroke to be told so.
  const head = before.slice(0, before.length - word.length);
  if (!/\S/.test(head.replace(/^\s*@?\s*/, ""))) {
    return null;
  }
  ```

  The core answers the command position empty as well, and keeps doing so: `ah-bai.2` and any other
  caller must not have to know this rule. This guard is about not making a call to learn it.
- `const word = match[1]; if (word === "" && !context.explicit) { return null; }` — Q2: quiet on an
  empty position unless summoned, the same rule and the same shape as `orderCompletion.ts:27-29`.
- `const offered = await lookUp(before).catch(() => []);` — a failed call is silence, never a thrown
  promise into CodeMirror. The whole `before` goes across, half-typed word included; the core drops
  it when counting the position.
- `const options = suggestOrderCommands(word, offered);` — reuse, from `orderEditor.ts:18`: it
  upper-cases the prefix and keeps what starts with it, which is exactly the rule wanted here. Add a
  line to its doc comment saying it now serves both positions.
- `if (options.length === 0) { return null; }` — Q3: nothing matches, nothing is said.
- The result:

  ```ts
  return {
    from: context.pos - word.length,
    options: options.map((keyword, index) => ({
      label: keyword,
      type: "keyword",
      apply: `${keyword} `,
      sortText: String(index).padStart(2, "0")
    })),
    validFor: /^[A-Za-z]*$/
  };
  ```

  `type: "keyword"` is Q7 — the icon a command already gets, no `detail`. `apply` is Q5's trailing
  space. `sortText` is Q6: CodeMirror breaks equal match scores with
  `(a.sortText || a.label).localeCompare(...)`, so without it every list comes back alphabetical and
  `MOVE` offers `IN, N, NE, NW, OUT, S, SE, SW`. It is a documented field of `Completion`, it is
  consulted **only** on a tie, and it is assigned after filtering so the core's order survives among
  whatever matched. `validFor` mirrors the command source at `orderCompletion.ts:40`, and is what
  keeps this to one core call per word rather than one per keystroke.

`orderCommandCompletions` gains the same trailing space in the same file — `apply: \`${command} \``
on the option at `orderCompletion.ts:38` — and nothing else. Q5's answer was "everywhere", and the
command position is the other half of it. Snippets are untouched: a snippet body is a block of
orders, not a word in a line.
