everything. Assert both sides against the live source:

```ts
const all = Object.values(parameters).flat();
expect(all.filter((p) => p.required).length).toBeGreaterThan(20);
expect(all.filter((p) => !p.required).length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
// and one of each by name, so a rule that inverted would be caught rather than merely counted
expect(parameters["set_game_map"]).toContainEqual({ name: "map_json", required: true });
expect(parameters["order_vocabulary"]).toContainEqual({ name: "ruleset_json", required: false });
```

## The test plan

TypeScript tooling tests only; `pnpm vitest run scripts/tauriCommands.test.ts`, which
`pnpm run check:fast` already runs.

| Test | What it pins |
|---|---|
| `reads_whether_each_parameter_may_be_omitted` | the `Option<…>` rule, on a fixture |
| the existing `commandParameters` tests (`:119`, `:133`, `:148`) | unchanged facts, new shape |
| the lockstep test's new sweep loop | every required parameter is supplied |
| `the_required_and_optional_parameter_sets_are_both_populated` | the loop is not vacuous |

**Increment 3's red step is the acceptance criterion and must actually be performed.** A test added
green proves nothing: the whole bead is the claim that this failure is now caught locally, and the
only evidence for that is having seen it fail. Say in the PR description what the failure message was.

**No Rust and no browser suite is touched**, so `cargo test`, `test:smoke`, `test:pwa` and the
`native` job are unaffected — the `native` job will simply stop being where this class of mistake is
discovered.

## User-facing decisions

None. Nothing here ships to the application: two files under `scripts/`, both of them test tooling.
No message, no setting, no command, no layout. The player cannot observe this bead at all.

## Out of scope

- **Generating the command surface from one declaration.** The bead offers that as its first option
  and "or, at least, extend the existing lockstep test" as its second. The second is chosen
  deliberately: it closes the whole of the cost the bead documents (two CI cycles, ~32 minutes) in two
  tooling files, where generation means a Rust→TypeScript codegen step across `main.rs`,
  `core-tauri`, `core-wasm` and the adapter. That is the same shape as ah-gdfe (P3, the ruleset schema
  mirrored by hand) and belongs with it, as its own bead, if the navigator wants it. **Do not start it
  here.**
- **`expect(renames.size).toBe(28)`** (`:249`). The bead calls the pinned count unnecessary "once the
  list has a single source", but there is no single source after this bead and the count is still the
  only thing catching a command that forgets its `rename_all` attribute. Leave it, and leave its
  comment, which already tells the next reader to update it in the same commit.
- **`TAURI_COMMANDS`, `main.rs`, `core-tauri/src/lib.rs`, `core-wasm` and `webCoreAdapter.ts`.** No
  file outside `scripts/` changes, apart from increment 3's temporary edit to `sweep.ts`, which is
  reverted before the commit.
- **The wasm boundary check** (`:264`). It compares arity, not names, and is a separate gap if it is
  one at all.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm vitest run scripts/tauriCommands.test.ts      # after each increment
pnpm run check:fast                                # before the PR
```

`check:fast` covers lint, typecheck, the tooling suites, `cargo fmt --check` and
`cargo clippy` — and the changed return type is exactly the kind of thing `typecheck` catches at the
two call sites, so a green typecheck is meaningful evidence here rather than a formality.

**The human check is increment 3's red step**, described above: the reviewer should be able to read
in the PR description that `set_game_map.map_json` was deleted, that the suite went red naming it,
and that it was restored. There is nothing to look at in a running app.

## Known traps

- **Do not widen the signature regexes past the closing parenthesis.** `\(([^)]*)\)` is what keeps
  `Result<Option<T>, String>` return types out of the parameter list; `command_load_order_draft`
  (`core-tauri/src/lib.rs:625`) and `command_load_imported_turn` (`:711`) both return one, and both
  take only required parameters.
- **`splitTopLevel` exists because a parameter type contains commas** (`tauriCommands.ts:70`):
  `Option<Vec<String>>` in `command_validate_orders` (`:555`) is the live case. A `.split(",")`
  anywhere in this work is a defect.
- **Split the parameter on its first `:` only.** Splitting on all of them, or using `split(":")[1]`,
  reads the wrong half.
- **`app: tauri::AppHandle` is filtered out already** (`tauriCommands.ts:111`) — it is the shell's own
  parameter and not the frontend's. It must stay filtered, and it must not acquire a `required` entry.
- **A vacuously-true assertion is this repository's known failure mode** (ah-ycuj: true for 758 of
  1,392 units, caught only by a reviewer). Increment 4 exists because of it and is not optional.
- **`packages/shared` has no jsdom** — irrelevant here, since nothing leaves `scripts/`, but named
  because it is the trap most beads in this repository meet.

title: Refactoring: three bracket scanners share a depth model, one is hardened
description:
## The cost being paid

The report parser has four hand-written bracket scanners, each carrying its own copy of the depth model:
`split_top_level`, `next_top_level_field`, `scan_leading_id` and `split_trailing_id`. Hardening one
leaves the others wrong, so every punctuation class a player can put in a name has to be found in the
field again — and each one loses data silently until it is.

Two such defects were fixed 22 hours apart, and the second fix was applied to only one scanner.
ah-lt0o's stray-bracket re-scan (`unmatched_brackets` + `scan_leading_id`) went into `split_leading_id`
alone; `split_top_level` (scan.rs:24) and `next_top_level_field` (scan.rs:164) still use the bare
`depth += 1` counter that ah-lt0o proved wrong, and they are called from eight sites.

## Evidence

- `2bdd7887` fix(ah-w544.1): read a unit or faction named with a comma instead of dropping it (#561),
  2026-08-22 — 4 files, 5 call sites re-pointed.
- `16ffe7b7` fix(ah-lt0o): read a unit whose name contains an unclosed bracket (#571), 2026-08-23.
- Live residue: `crates/core/src/report/scan.rs:24` and `:164` versus the hardened `:97`.
- Callers still on the unhardened path: `report/region.rs:45,203,213`, `report/header.rs:162`,
  `report/unit.rs:201`, `report/battle.rs:340`.

## Where

- `crates/core/src/report/scan.rs`, and its callers in `report/region.rs`, `report/header.rs`,
  `report/unit.rs`, `report/battle.rs`

## What a refactoring would change

One scanner that owns the depth model — including the stray-bracket pre-pass — with the four current
entry points as thin wrappers over it that differ only in what they return. A hardening then lands
once, for every caller, and the next surprising character in a player's name costs one fix rather than
four discoveries.

Filed by Forge, weekly sweep of 2026-08-24, range 440b51fb..origin/main.
design:
## Context

`crates/core/src/report/scan.rs` carries the bracket-depth model three times over, and only one copy
has been hardened.

ah-lt0o (`16ffe7b7`, 2026-08-23) established the rule: **a name may contain a stray bracket —
`Smiley :(` is a real one — and a bare depth counter cannot tell that from a nesting that has not
finished yet**, so the brackets are matched first (`unmatched_brackets`, `:58`) and the strays are
stepped over. That fix went into `scan_leading_id` (`:109`) alone, through `split_leading_id`'s
try-then-retry at `:92`. Two other scanners still carry the bare `depth += 1` counter that ah-lt0o
proved wrong:

- `split_top_level(input, separator) -> Vec<String>` (`:16`), called from `region.rs:45,203,213`,
  `unit.rs:201`, `header.rs:162` and `battle.rs:340`.
- `next_top_level_field(input, separator) -> Option<(&str, &str)>` (`:159`), called from
  `unit.rs:150` and `battle.rs:458`.

**`next_top_level_field` is the one that actually bites today, and the bead does not say so.** It
walks a unit's fields *after* the name has been taken off by the hardened `split_leading_id`
(`unit.rs:127`, then the loop at `:150`) — and the text it walks still contains the **faction's**
name, which `unit.rs:165` only reaches by calling `split_leading_id` on the remainder. So a faction
whose name carries a stray bracket derails the field walk before the hardened scanner is ever
reached, and every flag, race and item on that unit is swallowed into one field. `battle.rs:458` has
the same shape.

**The existing tests already know this, and stop just short of saying it.**
`unit.rs:462`'s `keeps_a_unit_whose_name_contains_an_unclosed_bracket` has three cases. The first two
put the stray bracket in the *unit's* name — handled by the hardened `split_leading_id` — and each
asserts `men == 10`, i.e. that the item field after the faction was read. The third (`:487`) puts it
in the *faction's* name:

```rust
let faction = parse_unit("* Scout (100), Wanderers :( (29), 10 humans [HUMN].", true, "1:7,53", None)
    .expect("unit should parse");
assert_eq!(faction.faction_name.as_deref(), Some("Wanderers :("));
assert_eq!(faction.faction_id.as_deref(), Some("29"));
// and no assertion about `men`, unlike its two siblings
```

That omission is the defect. `next_top_level_field` never sees the comma after `(29)`, so
`10 humans [HUMN]` is swallowed into the same field and the unit's men are lost — and the test
documents the working half while quietly declining to check the broken one.

Concretely, on `main` today:

```
next_top_level_field("Smiley :( (100), Wanderers (29)", ',')
  -> Some(("Smiley :( (100), Wanderers (29)", ""))    // one field; the comma was never seen
  should be Some(("Smiley :( (100)", "Wanderers (29)"))
```

`split_top_level`'s exposure is real but smaller, and the plan should be honest about it: its
callers split region-header fields, market lists, product lists, skill lists and unit-id lists —
game vocabulary rather than player-chosen names. It is hardened here for consistency and because the
next caller may not be so lucky, not because a defect is known to be live through it.

**When this lands there is one depth model in the module, and hardening it again lands everywhere at
once.** That is the whole of the bead: the next surprising character in a player's name costs one
fix rather than four discoveries.

**This bead changes behaviour** — that is its point — but only for input containing an unmatched
bracket. Well-formed input, which is every line of every committed fixture, is unaffected, and the
existing tests are the proof of that.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

`crates/core/src/report/scan.rs` only. **No caller changes**: all three public signatures stay
exactly as they are, so `region.rs`, `unit.rs`, `header.rs` and `battle.rs` are untouched.

### What already exists and must be reused

- `unmatched_brackets(input: &str) -> BTreeSet<usize>` (`:58`) — the stray-bracket detector from
  ah-lt0o. Already private, already tested (`finds_the_brackets_that_never_close`, `:469`). Do not
  write a second one, and do not change it.
- `scan_leading_id(input, ignore: &BTreeSet<usize>)` (`:109`) — the hardened scanner. Its `ignore`
  convention (*a bracket at an ignored index changes no depth and opens no candidate*) is the one
  this bead generalises.
- `split_leading_id` (`:92`) — the try-then-retry wrapper. **Keep its two-phase shape**: it can
  detect its own failure (`None`), so it pays for `unmatched_brackets` only on lines that need it.
  The two splitters cannot do that (see below).

### The design of the code

One private primitive, and the three scanners become readings of it.

```rust
/// One character of the input, with the bracket depth on either side of it.
struct Scanned {
    /// Byte index, as `char_indices` reports it.
    index: usize,
    character: char,
    /// Depth before this character is applied: `(` or `[` here at `before <= 0` opens the top level.
    before: i32,
    /// Depth after it is applied: `)` or `]` here at `after <= 0` closes the top level.
    after: i32,
}

/// Walks `input` once, reporting every character with the bracket depth on either side.
///
/// **The one depth model in this module.** `(`, `[`, `)` and `]` are interchangeable, deliberately:
/// every scanner here must agree about the same string, and ah-lt0o and ah-w544.1 were each a case
/// of two of them disagreeing. A byte index in `ignore` is an ordinary character that changes no
/// depth, which is how a stray bracket inside a player's name is stepped over rather than derailing
/// the scan.
fn scan_depths<'a>(
    input: &'a str,
    ignore: &'a BTreeSet<usize>,
) -> impl Iterator<Item = Scanned> + 'a;

/// The byte index of every top-level `separator` in `input`, with stray brackets stepped over.
///
/// Unlike [`split_leading_id`], a splitter has no failure to detect — every input yields *some*
/// answer — so it cannot try the cheap walk and retry. `unmatched_brackets` is therefore computed
/// on every call: one extra O(n) pass whose `BTreeSet` stays empty for well-formed input, against a
/// function that already allocates a `String` per field.
fn top_level_separators(input: &str, separator: char) -> Vec<usize>;
```

Then:

- **`split_top_level`** slices `input` at those indices, trims each piece, and pushes it; the final
  piece is pushed only when it is not blank after trimming. That last rule is current behaviour
  (`:39-41`) and must be preserved exactly — it is why `"a, b,"` yields two fields and not three.
- **`next_top_level_field`** takes the first index: `Some((input[..i].trim(), input[i + separator.len_utf8()..].trim_start()))`.
  With no index, `Some((input.trim(), ""))` unless the trimmed input is empty, in which case `None`.
  That is `:173-180` unchanged apart from where the index came from.
- **`scan_leading_id`** keeps its own loop body — it asks a different question (*where is the first
  top-level `(digits)` group?*, not *where are the separators?*) — but drives it from
  `scan_depths(input, ignore)` instead of its own `depth` counter, using `before` to decide whether a
  `(` opens a candidate and `after` to decide whether a `)` closes the top level. Its `candidate_open`
  state stays exactly where it is.

**`split_trailing_id` (`:185`) is deliberately left out**, and this is a correction to the bead
rather than an omission. It has no depth model to unify: it anchors at the end of the string with
`rfind('(')` and requires the string to end in `)`. That makes it correct on precisely the inputs a
depth walk gets wrong — `split_trailing_id("Smiley :( (95)")` already returns
`("Smiley :(", "95")` today, because the last `(` is the right one whatever came before it. Rewriting
it onto a left-to-right walk would trade a working strategy for one that then needs the stray pre-pass
to get back to where it started. Increment 4 records that reasoning in its doc comment so the next
sweep does not re-file it.

**Where state lives.** Nowhere new and nothing persistent. `Scanned` is a plain `Copy` struct built
and dropped inside the iterator; `scan_depths` closes over `ignore` and one `i32`. No public type
changes, no new module, no new dependency — the module's opening comment ("deliberately hand written
rather than regex based: the crate has no regex dependency") still holds and must keep holding.

## Increments

Each opens with a failing test in `scan.rs`'s own `mod tests` (`:326`). Run
`cargo test -p atlantis-hud-core report::scan` after each.

**Increment 1 — the primitive, proven against the scanner that is already right.**
No behaviour change, so the failing test is on the primitive itself:
`a_depth_walk_reports_the_depth_on_either_side_of_each_bracket`, asserting that for `"a (b) c"` the
`(` has `before: 0, after: 1` and the `)` has `before: 1, after: 0`, and that with the `(`'s index in
`ignore` both report `before: 0, after: 0`. Then add `Scanned` and `scan_depths`, and rewrite
`scan_leading_id`'s loop to drive from it. Every existing test — `reads_a_leading_identifier_past_commas_in_the_name` (`:346`),
`reads_a_name_containing_an_unclosed_bracket` (`:495`) and
`an_unclosed_bracket_does_not_change_a_line_that_already_read` (`:512`) — must stay green untouched.
If any needs editing, the primitive is wrong.

**Increment 2 — the scanner that bites.**
Failing test: `walks_past_a_field_whose_name_carries_an_unclosed_bracket`.

```rust
assert_eq!(
    next_top_level_field("Smiley :( (100), Wanderers (29)", ','),
    Some(("Smiley :( (100)", "Wanderers (29)"))
);
```

It fails on `main` with `Some(("Smiley :( (100), Wanderers (29)", ""))`. Add `top_level_separators`
and rewrite `next_top_level_field` over it. `walks_top_level_fields_one_at_a_time` (`:363`) must stay
green.

**Increment 3 — the splitter.**
Failing test: `splits_past_an_unclosed_bracket`.

```rust
assert_eq!(
    split_top_level("Smiley :( (100), Wanderers (29)", ','),
    vec!["Smiley :( (100)".to_string(), "Wanderers (29)".to_string()]
);
```

It fails on `main` with a single-element vector. Rewrite `split_top_level` over
`top_level_separators`. `splits_only_at_the_top_level` (`:330`) and
`keeps_a_parenthesised_race_with_its_field` (`:340`) must stay green — the second is the one that
proves a legitimate `(` inside a field is still not a separator.

**Increment 4 — say why the fourth scanner is not here.**
Failing test first, so the claim is checked rather than asserted in prose:
`a_trailing_identifier_survives_an_unclosed_bracket_in_the_name`, asserting
`split_trailing_id("Smiley :( (95)") == Some(("Smiley :(".to_string(), "95".to_string()))`. It should
pass on `main` unchanged — if it does not, `split_trailing_id` is not as robust as this plan claims
and it joins increments 2 and 3 instead of being documented out. Then extend `split_trailing_id`'s doc comment (`:183`) with the reasoning above: it is
right-anchored, which makes it correct on stray brackets without a depth model, and it is
deliberately not a reading of `scan_depths`. Name ah-hlqc in it, so the next Forge sweep reads a
decision rather than a smell.

## The test plan

Rust only. Nothing in `packages/` changes and no browser suite is touched.

New unit tests, all in `crates/core/src/report/scan.rs`'s `mod tests`:

| Test | What it pins |
|---|---|
| `a_depth_walk_reports_the_depth_on_either_side_of_each_bracket` | the primitive, including `ignore` |
| `walks_past_a_field_whose_name_carries_an_unclosed_bracket` | `next_top_level_field` hardened |
| `splits_past_an_unclosed_bracket` | `split_top_level` hardened |
| `a_trailing_identifier_survives_an_unclosed_bracket_in_the_name` | increment 4's claim, as a test rather than a comment. Expected green on `main`. |

**Add one integration-level test, because the unit tests above cannot show the defect that matters.**
In `crates/core/src/report/unit.rs`'s test module, add
`reads_the_items_of_a_unit_whose_faction_is_named_with_an_unclosed_bracket`, using the exact line the
existing test at `:487` already uses:

```rust
let faction = parse_unit("* Scout (100), Wanderers :( (29), 10 humans [HUMN].", true, "1:7,53", None)
    .expect("unit should parse");
assert_eq!(faction.faction_name.as_deref(), Some("Wanderers :("));
assert_eq!(faction.faction_id.as_deref(), Some("29"));
assert_eq!(faction.men, 10);          // this is the line that fails on `main`
```

Write it as a new test rather than by adding the `men` assertion to `keeps_a_unit_whose_name_contains_an_unclosed_bracket`
(`:462`): that test is about names surviving, this one is about the fields after them surviving, and
the two fail for different reasons. This is the test that connects the module-level hardening to
something a player would notice; without it the bead is three unit tests about a helper.

**The regression net is every existing test in `scan.rs` and every report-parsing test in
`report/`.** They are all on well-formed input, so all of them must stay green **without a single
edit**. If one needs changing, the hardening has changed behaviour on well-formed input and is wrong.

## User-facing decisions

None.

The one decision this bead embodies — *a stray bracket in a name is stepped over rather than counted*
— was taken by the navigator for ah-lt0o (`16ffe7b7`, 2026-08-23) and is being applied to two more
call sites, not re-opened. Nothing in the interface changes: no message, no setting, no layout. A
player whose faction name contains `:(` sees their unit parse correctly where it previously did not,
which is the fix and needs no choosing.

## Out of scope

- **`split_trailing_id`'s implementation.** Increment 4 touches its doc comment only; see *Files to
  change* for why it is not a reading of `scan_depths`.
- **`parse_coordinate`, `parse_settlement`, `parse_item_amount`, `parse_skill`** and the other
  `rfind`-based readers in this file. They locate one bracket pair in a known shape and have no
  depth model to unify.
- **Any caller change.** The three public signatures are unchanged on purpose, so this bead's diff
  is one file.
- **Regex.** The module's opening comment rules it out and the crate has no such dependency; adding
  one is a framework decision for the navigator, not part of a refactoring.
- **Other punctuation classes** — quotes, a comma inside a bracketed group, a name ending in `.`.
  Each is a separate finding if it is ever seen; this bead hardens exactly the one ah-lt0o found.

## Validation

```bash
cargo test -p atlantis-hud-core report::scan      # after each increment
cargo test -p atlantis-hud-core report            # the whole parser, before the PR
pnpm run check:fast                               # lint, typecheck, unit, fmt, clippy
```

`cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` runs inside `check:fast` and will object to
an `impl Iterator` returned with a lifetime it cannot infer — if `scan_depths` fights the borrow
checker, take `ignore: &BTreeSet<usize>` and return a `Vec<Scanned>` rather than inventing a
lifetime parameter for the module. One allocation per scan is acceptable and is not worth a
redesign.

**The human check is the fixture corpus**: `cargo test -p atlantis-hud-core` parses every committed
report, and none of those tests may change. There is nothing to look at in a running app — this bead
has no visible surface of its own.

## Known traps

- **`unmatched_brackets` treats `(` and `[` as interchangeable** (`:52`), and so must everything
  built on it. Splitting them into two counters looks like a correctness improvement and is not: it
  would make the scanners disagree about the same string, which is the class of defect ah-w544.1
  (`2bdd7887`) and ah-lt0o (`16ffe7b7`) each fixed once.
- **`split_top_level` drops a blank final field** (`:39-41`), so `"a, b,"` is two fields. Rewriting
  the tail as an unconditional push changes that, and no existing test names it directly.
- **`next_top_level_field` returns `&str` borrowed from `input`**, and `split_top_level` returns
  owned `String`s. That difference is the reason both exist (`:154-155`); do not "unify" them into
  one return type.
- **Byte indices, not character positions.** `unmatched_brackets` and `char_indices` both speak
  bytes, and `input[i + separator.len_utf8()..]` is why the current code uses `len_utf8` rather than
  `+ 1`. A report can carry non-ASCII in a player's name.
- **`split_leading_id` must keep its try-then-retry** (`:92`): it is the one scanner here that can
  detect its own failure, and collapsing it into "always compute the strays" costs an allocation on
  every unit line of every report for no gain.
- **`packages/shared` has no jsdom** — irrelevant here, since nothing leaves `crates/core`, but named
  because it is the trap most beads in this repository meet.

title: Refactoring: one shortfall check answers three ways and never says which
description:
## The cost being paid

`report_shortfalls` emits a silver shortfall through three mutually-suppressing arms with different
anchoring — per unit (`unit_id: Some`), pooled across sharers (`unit_id: None`), and maintenance-pooled
— and the per-unit pass silently defers to the other two by `continue`-ing without emitting. Which arm
fired is invisible from outside, so callers, plans and tests keep assuming the per-unit one.

Three different agents have now written a plan for this module as though a hex were judged unit by
unit. ah-fjty's own retrospective says so in as many words: "That is twice now."

## Evidence

- docs/retrospectives/ah-fjty.md §"The plan specified a per-unit reading of a hex that the check it
  must agree with reads as a pool" — invented claimants worth **$870 of phantom claims against $50 of
  real one**; ~25 minutes, caught by adversarial review before the PR opened.
- docs/retrospectives/ah-1wcw.1.md §"The plan asked for a smoke test its own measurement had already
  ruled out" — ~20 minutes; same rule, opposite direction.
- docs/retrospectives/ah-ycuj.md §"A corpus assertion was vacuously true for 758 of the 1,392 units,
  and only the reviewer caught it" — one review round, one CI cycle, ~40 minutes.
- docs/retrospectives/ah-8l9a.md §"The plan's reconstruction arithmetic was wrong, and only the corpus
  said so" — ~40 minutes, four failing runs.

## Where

- `crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs:2294-2520` (`report_shortfalls`), with its `claims` and
  `pooled_tags` accumulators and the `maintenance_short` block; the silent `continue`s at :2357-2363
  and :2371-2374.

## What a refactoring would change

Make the reading explicit rather than implied by control flow: decide the hex's mode once — per unit,
or pooled because something shares — and have each arm return a named result a caller and a test can
assert on, instead of an emission or a silent deferral. The rule "does this hex pool?" then has one
home to grep for, which is what four plans in a row failed to find.

Filed by Forge, weekly sweep of 2026-08-24, range 440b51fb..origin/main.
design:
## Context

`report_shortfalls` (`crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs:2311`) decides three different things and
tells nobody which one it decided:

1. **Per unit** — the unit's own balance is negative and it gets a named finding on its order line.
2. **Pooled** — at least one unit in the hex carries the `sharing` flag, so the tag is judged as one
   purse across the hex. The per-unit pass `continue`s without emitting (`:2377`), the overdraft is
   added to `claims`, and a *hex-anchored* finding may follow in the second pass (`:2436`).
3. **Deferred to maintenance** — silver, in an unflagged hex whose upkeep it could not pay
   (`:2389`). Again a silent `continue`, into `maintenance_short` and a third message shape.

Which arm fired is invisible from outside: all three produce either a `Finding` or nothing, and
nothing names the reading. So a reader of the module — including every planner who has written
against it — assumes arm 1 and is wrong whenever the hex shares.

That has now cost four beads (ah-fjty, ah-1wcw.1, ah-ycuj, ah-8l9a); ah-fjty's retrospective says
"That is twice now", and ah-fjty invented $870 of phantom claims against $50 of real one. **It cost a
fifth on 2026-08-24**: ah-sdda was filed as a defect in `party_id` because a `GIVE 0 20000 HORS` from
a unit holding one horse appeared unwarned. It was warned — arm 2 fired, because hex (36,4) of
`neworigins-3.0.0-g3-f42-t82.rep` holds three sharing units — and the finding went to the hex rather
than to the line. ah-sdda was closed as correct behaviour after a probe; the bead that should not
have needed writing is this one's evidence.

**When this lands, "does this hex pool this tag?" has exactly one home to grep for, and each of the
three readings is a named value a test can assert on.** Behaviour does not change at all — see
*Validation*, which makes byte-identical messages the acceptance criterion.

A second, smaller confusion is fixed with it. `unpayable_upkeep`'s doc comment (`:2032-2041`) still
says "Read a hex exactly as `report_shortfalls` reads it… The two branches below are those two
readings", but ah-e66j removed the second branch: `unpayable_upkeep` (`:2063`) now reads every unit
on its own balance and nothing else. A comment describing a branch that is not there is the same
defect this bead is about, one level down.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

All of it is `crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs`. No other file changes, and no public API moves —
`report_shortfalls` is private and its only caller is `check_resources`, at `:1408`.

### What already exists and must be reused, not reinvented

- `Ordered::shares(&self) -> bool` (`:1129`) — the `sharing` flag test. The only definition; use it.
- `Ordered::holding(&self, tag: &str) -> i64` (`:1136`) — what the report printed.
- `Ordered::finding(&self, hex, code, message, at: Option<&PlacedIntent>) -> Finding` (`:1158`) —
  the unit-anchored finding, carrying `unit_id`, line and columns.
- `Hex::finding(&self, code, message) -> Finding` (`:1048`) — the hex-anchored one, with
  `unit_id: None` and `line: None`.
- `relieved_balance(ledger, unit_id, tag) -> i64` (`:2022`) — the balance with step 7's silver
  relief applied. Every balance read in this pass goes through it.
- `unpaid_upkeep(ledger, unit_id) -> i64` (`:2556`) and `upkeep_still_drawn(ledger, unit_id) -> i64`
  (`:2542`).
- `counted_item(count, tag, hex, ruleset, plurals) -> String` (`:2626`) — the count/name agreement
  from ah-rsdz. Never format an item count any other way.
- `Ruleset::is_man(&self, tag: &str) -> bool` (`crates/core/src/movement/rules.rs:697`).
- `Ledger::maintenance_pooled: bool` (`:1225`), set at `:2160`.
- `codes::NOT_ENOUGH_SILVER` (`:83`) and `codes::NOT_ENOUGH_ITEMS` (`:84`); `options.emits(code)`.

### The design of the code

Three private items, all in `semantics.rs`, placed immediately above `report_shortfalls`.

**1. The hex's sharing, read once.** This is the one home for the pooling rule.

```rust
/// How one item tag is judged in one hex.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum Reading {
    /// Nothing in the hex shares, or the tag is men - which the engine never pools.
    PerUnit,
    /// Something in the hex carries `sharing`, so the tag is one purse across it.
    Pooled,
}

/// The hex's sharing units, read once, and the rule for whether a tag pools in it.
///
/// The single home of "does this hex pool this tag?". Four plans in a row have assumed a hex is
/// judged unit by unit; this is the thing they should have been able to find.
struct Sharing<'a> {
    /// The units carrying `sharing`, in hex order.
    sharers: Vec<&'a Ordered<'a>>,
}

impl<'a> Sharing<'a> {
    fn read(hex: &'a Hex<'a>) -> Self;

    /// Whether the pool's sum can be trusted at all: one doubted sharer makes it untrustworthy.
    fn pool_trusted(&self, ledger: &Ledger<'_>) -> bool;

    /// `Pooled` only when something shares AND the tag is not men.
    fn reading(&self, tag: &str, ruleset: Option<&Ruleset>) -> Reading;

    /// The pool's balance for one tag: the sharers' `relieved_balance`s, summed.
    fn pool(&self, ledger: &Ledger<'_>, tag: &str) -> i64;
}
```

`reading` carries verbatim the rule now inlined at `:2332-2334`, including its comment: *without a
ruleset every tag pools; with one, men never do (the engine's one exception)*, and the paragraph
about maintenance **not** being pooled here.

**2. What the per-unit pass decided, per (unit, tag).** One variant per arm, so the arm is the
value rather than the control flow.

```rust
/// What the shortfall pass decided about one unit and one item tag.
///
/// Every negative balance produces exactly one of these, so a test can assert *which* reading a
/// hex used rather than inferring it from whether a message appeared.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum Verdict {
    /// Judged on the unit's own balance, and short. Anchored to the unit and its order line.
    UnitShort { unit_id: String, tag: String, short: i64 },
    /// The tag pools in this hex, so this overdraft is a claim against the pool rather than a
    /// finding of its own. A sharer's own overdraft is already inside the pool's sum and claims
    /// nothing (`claims_pool: false`).
    DeferredToPool { unit_id: String, tag: String, short: i64, claims_pool: bool },
    /// Silver, in an unflagged hex, whose whole overdraft is maintenance nothing could pay. The
    /// unit is not named: it may well be one the engine feeds (`ah-e66j`).
    DeferredToMaintenance { unit_id: String, short: i64 },
}
```

**3. The two passes, and the renderer.**

```rust
/// Every verdict this hex reaches, in hex order and then tag order.
///
/// Reaches no decision about messages and emits nothing: `report_shortfalls` renders it. Doubted
/// units produce no verdict at all, here as everywhere else in this module.
fn judge_shortfalls(
    hex: &Hex<'_>,
    ledger: &Ledger<'_>,
    sharing: &Sharing<'_>,
    ruleset: Option<&Ruleset>,
) -> Vec<Verdict>;

/// What a pooled tag owes once its claims are netted against its pool, or `None` when the pool
/// covers them. `held` is what the pool's members and its borrowers hold, for the message.
struct PoolShortfall {
    tag: String,
    short: i64,
    held: i64,
}

/// The pooled tags this hex is short of, from the `DeferredToPool` verdicts.
///
/// Returns nothing at all when the pool is not trusted: one doubted sharer silences every pooled
/// tag, which is the existing `if !pool_trusted { return; }` at `:2433` and must stay that way.
fn pool_shortfalls(
    hex: &Hex<'_>,
    ledger: &Ledger<'_>,
    sharing: &Sharing<'_>,
    verdicts: &[Verdict],
) -> Vec<PoolShortfall>;
```

`report_shortfalls` keeps its present signature exactly and becomes a renderer: build `Sharing`, call
`judge_shortfalls`, render every `UnitShort` through `Ordered::finding`, sum the
`DeferredToMaintenance` shorts into the maintenance message, call `pool_shortfalls` and render each
through `Hex::finding`. The three `format!` strings move unchanged, character for character.

**Neither judge takes `CheckOptions`.** Every `options.emits(code)` test stays exactly where it is
today — in `report_shortfalls`, applied when rendering (`:2394` for the per-unit findings, `:2442`
for the pooled ones, `:2504` for maintenance). Do not push it down into `judge_shortfalls` or
`pool_shortfalls` as a filter: today a disabled code still populates `pooled_tags` and still adds to
`maintenance_short`, because the `emits` check sits *after* the `continue`s that do both. Filtering
earlier would silently change which hexes report a pooled shortfall when a code is disabled, and no
existing test covers that combination.

**`PoolShortfall::held` moves verbatim.** The `held` sum at `:2456-2465` — every unit that either
shares, or is undoubted and has a negative `relieved_balance` for the tag — is deliberate and not
obvious: it is what makes the message's "they can have X and their orders spend X + short"
arithmetic hold. Move the expression unchanged into `pool_shortfalls`; do not simplify it to "the
sharers' holdings".

**Where state lives.** Nowhere new. `Sharing` borrows the hex and holds no balances; `Verdict` and
`PoolShortfall` are owned values built and dropped inside one call. `Ledger` is untouched — this
bead adds no field to it and changes nothing that writes one.

**Ordering is behaviour and must be preserved.** Findings are pushed in this order today and must
stay in it: every per-unit finding, in `hex.units` order and then in ledger-key (tag) order; then the
pooled findings in `pooled_tags` order, which is a `BTreeSet<String>` and so is tag-alphabetical;
then the single maintenance finding. `judge_shortfalls` must therefore walk `hex.units` in order and,
within a unit, the `ledger.balance` range in its existing order (`:2358-2366`); `pool_shortfalls`
must collect its tags into a `BTreeSet<String>` (or sort them) before iterating. `check_resources` does not
re-sort, and `validate_turn` (`orders/mod.rs:75`) sorts only by line — which is `None` for every
pooled and maintenance finding, so their relative order is exactly the order they were pushed in.

**The `continue` at `:2377` hides a fourth case, and it must survive.** When `pooled(tag)` is true
the tag is inserted into `pooled_tags` *whether or not* the unit shares, but only a non-sharer's
overdraft is added to `claims`. That is the `claims_pool: bool` field above: a sharer that is
itself overdrawn still puts its tag on the list to be judged, and contributes no claim, because its
overdraft is already inside the pool's sum. Getting this wrong double-counts every sharer's
overdraft — write the test named in increment 3 before touching it.

## Increments

Each opens with a failing test in the `mod tests` block of `semantics.rs`. Run
`cargo test -p atlantis-hud-core` for each.

**Increment 1 — the pooling rule gets one home.**
Failing test: `a_hex_with_no_sharing_unit_reads_every_tag_per_unit` in `semantics.rs`'s test module.
It builds `Hex::read` over `region(vec![with_item(unit("1"), 1, "horse", "HORS")])`, constructs
`Sharing::read(&hex)`, and asserts `sharing.reading("HORS", None) == Reading::PerUnit`. Add a second,
`a_sharing_hex_pools_goods_but_never_men`, over a region with one `sharing` unit, asserting
`reading("HORS", Some(&ruleset())) == Reading::Pooled` and
`reading("ORC", Some(&ruleset())) == Reading::PerUnit`, plus `reading("ORC", None) == Reading::Pooled`
for the no-ruleset case. Then introduce `Reading`, `Sharing`, `Sharing::read`, `reading`,
`pool_trusted` and `pool`, and replace the `sharers` binding (`:2319`), the `pool_trusted` binding
(`:2323`), the `pooled` closure (`:2332`) and the pool sum (`:2446`) with calls to them.
`report_shortfalls` still contains all the control flow. Every existing test must stay green.

**Increment 2 — the per-unit pass returns verdicts.**
Failing test: `a_hex_that_shares_defers_a_shortfall_to_its_pool`. Same fixture shape as the
`the units in this hex are short 10 swords between them` test at `:4765`, but asserting on
`judge_shortfalls` rather than on messages: exactly one verdict, and it matches
`Verdict::DeferredToPool { claims_pool: true, .. }` for the tag. Add
`a_hex_that_shares_nothing_names_the_unit_itself`, asserting a single `Verdict::UnitShort` with the
unit id and the short. Then introduce `Verdict` and `judge_shortfalls`, move the per-unit loop
(`:2348-2429`) into it, and have `report_shortfalls` fold the returned verdicts into the same three
accumulators it keeps today. Messages unchanged.

**Increment 3 — a sharer's own overdraft claims nothing.**
Failing test: `an_overdrawn_sharer_puts_its_tag_up_for_judgement_and_claims_nothing`. A hex with two
`sharing` units, one of which overdraws a pooled tag: assert the verdict is
`Verdict::DeferredToPool { claims_pool: false, .. }`. Pair it with an assertion on the rendered
output through the existing `check`/`codes` helpers, so the claim is pinned on both sides: build the
hex so the pool is genuinely short, and assert the resulting `Finding`'s `message` equals the exact
string the same input produces on `main` — capture that string by running the test against `main`
first, and paste it in. If the sharer's overdraft were double-counted the `short` in that message
would be too large, which is the whole point of the test.

**Increment 4 — the pooled pass returns shortfalls.**
Failing test: `a_doubted_sharer_silences_every_pooled_tag`, over a hex with a `sharing` unit whose
sums are doubted and a second unit overdrawing a pooled tag: `pool_shortfalls` returns an empty
vector. Then introduce `PoolShortfall` and `pool_shortfalls`, move the loop at `:2436-2493` into it,
and leave `report_shortfalls` rendering the messages.

**Increment 5 — the stale comment.**
No test; this is a doc-comment edit. Rewrite `unpayable_upkeep`'s doc (`:2032-2041`) so it says what
the function does — every unit on its own balance, because step 4 has already done the lending — and
drop "The two branches below are those two readings". Keep the `ah-e66j` and `ah-ycuj` references:
they are why it is written that way. Point the reader at `Sharing::reading` for the pooling rule.

## The test plan

Rust only; nothing in `packages/` changes and no browser suite is touched.

New unit tests, all in the `mod tests` block of `crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs`, using the
existing helpers `region` (`:7231`), `unit` (`:7253`), `with_item` (`:7304`), `check` (`:7404`) and
`codes` (`:7467`):

| Test | What it pins |
|---|---|
| `a_hex_with_no_sharing_unit_reads_every_tag_per_unit` | `Reading::PerUnit` is the default |
| `a_sharing_hex_pools_goods_but_never_men` | the men exception, and the no-ruleset case |
| `a_hex_that_shares_nothing_names_the_unit_itself` | `Verdict::UnitShort` carries the unit |
| `a_hex_that_shares_defers_a_shortfall_to_its_pool` | arm 2 is a named value, not a `continue` |
| `an_overdrawn_sharer_puts_its_tag_up_for_judgement_and_claims_nothing` | `claims_pool: false` |
| `a_doubted_sharer_silences_every_pooled_tag` | `pool_trusted` still gates the whole pass |
| `an_unflagged_hexs_unpayable_upkeep_is_deferred_to_maintenance` | arm 3 is a named value |

**The regression net is the existing message tests, and they must not be edited.** These pin the
exact wording of all three shapes and are what proves the refactoring changed no behaviour:

- `semantics.rs:4765` — `"the units in this hex are short 10 swords between them: they can have 20 …"`
- `semantics.rs:8877` — `"the units in this hex are short $80 between them: …"`
- `semantics.rs:8999` and `:9116` — `"… short $80 of upkeep between them: …"`
- `semantics.rs:9788` — `"the units in this hex are short 10 sword between them: …"` (singular name)
- `the_column_and_the_warning_agree_about_a_taxer_in_a_pillaged_hex` (`:6193`) — the ah-ycuj/ah-abwx
  cross-surface guard.
- The `codes::ALL` fixture sweep at `:12803` — one case per code, asserted equal in length and
  distinct. It fails if a code stops being reachable.

**If any of those needs editing, the refactoring has changed behaviour and is wrong.** That is the
acceptance criterion, not a guideline.

## User-facing decisions

None. This bead changes no message, no code, no ordering and no finding — the whole of its
acceptance is that the player sees byte-identical output. The three `format!` strings move between
functions unedited; the anchoring of each finding (unit-and-line versus hex) is preserved exactly.

The navigator was not asked anything, because there is nothing here they could see.

## Out of scope

- **Changing where a pooled finding is anchored.** ah-sdda asked whether a hex-level
  `not-enough-items` should name the offending unit and mark its order line; the navigator judged the
  present behaviour correct on 2026-08-24 and closed it. Do not "improve" the hex message to name a
  unit — that decision has been taken, the other way.
- **Changing the pooling rule itself** — whether `SHARE` should lend for a discard, whether men
  should pool, whether maintenance should. Each is a rules question for the navigator.
- **`silver::forecast_unit`** and the double-pricing of the month's economy. That is ah-lu0f (P2),
  and it is a different defect in a different pair of functions.
- **`unpayable_upkeep`'s body.** Increment 5 touches its doc comment and nothing else.
- Any change to `Ledger`, `Hex`, `Ordered` or the `Finding` type.

## Validation

```bash
cargo test -p atlantis-hud-core                      # after each increment
pnpm run check:fast                                  # before the PR: lint, typecheck, unit, fmt, clippy
```

`cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` is inside `check:fast` and will object to a
new struct or enum that is never constructed, and to `too_many_arguments` if a helper grows past
seven — `report_shortfalls` already carries `#[allow(clippy::too_many_arguments)]`-worthy shapes
elsewhere in this file (`transfer`, `:1688`), so follow that precedent rather than inventing a
parameter struct.

The browser suites and the `native` job are not run locally; nothing here reaches them.

**The human check is the diff, not a screenshot**: no message string may differ from `main` by a
single character. `git diff origin/main -- crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs | grep '^[-+].*"the units in this hex'`
must show every such line moved and none altered.

## Known traps

- **The corpus agreement test is the real gate** (`the_column_and_the_warning_agree_about_a_taxer_in_a_pillaged_hex`,
  `:6193`, and the reason ah-ycuj exists). Two surfaces read this hex — the Silver column via
  `silver::forecast_unit`, and this warning — and a change that passes this module's own tests while
  moving the warning fails there. If it goes red, the refactoring changed behaviour.
- **`unpayable_upkeep`'s doc comment is already wrong** (`:2032-2041`): it describes two branches,
  and ah-e66j left one. Do not take it as a description of `report_shortfalls`. Increment 5 fixes it.
- **A doubted unit is never judged**, here as everywhere in this module (`:2350`). It produces no
  verdict at all — not a verdict saying "doubted". Adding one would be a fifth reading, and the
  pooled pass would then have to skip it explicitly.
- **`pooled_tags` is a `BTreeSet<String>`**, so pooled findings come out tag-alphabetical. A `Vec`
  or a `HashSet` changes the order the panel shows them in, which the message tests will catch —
  but only for hexes short of two tags at once, which the committed corpus may not contain. Keep the
  `BTreeSet`.
- **`counted_item` (`:2626`) is the only correct way to put a count in front of an item name**
  (ah-rsdz): 84 of the 114 items in the corpus pluralise irregularly and 30 do not pluralise at all.
  The singular case is pinned at `:9788` and the plural at `:4765`.
- **`packages/shared` has no jsdom** — irrelevant here, since nothing in this bead leaves
  `crates/core`, but named because it is the trap most beads in this repository meet.
- The maintenance message says *costs* rather than *spend* on purpose (`ah-1wcw.4`, comment at
  `:2497`): a fee is charged whatever a unit is told to do. Do not "make the three messages
  consistent".

title: Refactoring: the month's economy is priced twice and the two drift
description:
## The cost being paid

The month's silver is computed twice from the same orders by two pieces of code that share nothing
but their inputs: `forecast_unit` (`orders/silver.rs`) produces the Silver column, one entry per own
unit counting that unit alone; the ledger (`orders/semantics.rs`) produces the `not-enough-silver`
finding, a hex-wide balance with sharing pooled. Each has a separate arm per order kind, so every
order must be priced identically in two places by hand.

They drift, and the player sees it. Four `fix` commits landed on 2026-08-23 alone, each one a
divergence between the two surfaces, and two further beads (ah-ycuj, ah-8l9a) were spent building
nothing but a cross-check between them. The code now carries hand-written "Mirrors `forecast_unit`'s
arm exactly - two surfaces reading one order must not price it two ways" comments at
`semantics.rs:1607` and `:1621`, which is the smell stating itself.

## Evidence

- `54dd0824` fix(ah-abwx): a pillaging unit earns in the silver column too (#598)
- `7b6de57e` fix(ah-uwa3): wages pay a unit's upkeep but not its orders (#591) — "the two systems had
  drifted to opposite wrong answers, each with a test pinning its own side and nothing asserting they agreed"
- `57a6c7ff` fix(ah-7cdt): the shortfall check and the hover both know about faction food (#585) —
  found by Psylocke's verification, "two surfaces disagreeing with the Silver column about the same fact"
- `a179b474` fix(ah-bumi): a unit's CLAIM counts toward what it will have at month end (#587)
- `crates/core/tests/silver_agrees_with_the_warning.rs:1-13` — a whole test file whose module doc says
  "The economy is computed twice ... they have already drifted apart once ... nothing compared the two"
- ah-ycuj (PR #602) and ah-8l9a (PR #608) exist only to compare the two surfaces

## Where

- `crates/core/src/orders/silver.rs` (`forecast_unit`)
- `crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs` (`apply`, `ledger_for`, `charge_upkeep`)
- `crates/core/tests/silver_agrees_with_the_warning.rs`

## What a refactoring would change

One pricing function per order kind, consulted by both surfaces, so an order is priced once and the
two readings differ only in how they aggregate — per unit for the column, pooled per hex for the
finding. The reactive extractions already made under pressure (`own_unit_pillages`, `late_income`,
`pool_wants`, `unit_upkeep`) are the beginning of that seam; this would finish it rather than add a
fifth. The corpus cross-check then guards an invariant instead of standing in for a missing one.

title: A verification verdict is acted on after main has moved past it
description:
Found by Xavier on 2026-08-23, after the third instance in one day.

Psylocke verifies a merged bead against a specific commit and records her verdict against it. On a fast day the fleet merges several beads while she is verifying, so by the time the verdict lands a sibling has already delivered the thing she found missing. The verdict is then true of the tree she looked at and false of main.

## The three cases

  ah-t2pn.3   failed at ce9d2817 for having no user-visible warning. Its own plan scoped that
              surface out and gave it to ah-t2pn.4, which was in flight and landed at 0b444332
              carrying exactly the wording the verification called the sharper half. Storm picked
              the bead up as a P0, found nothing to build, and handed it back. Two sessions and a
              planner pass spent on a bead that needed only a second look.

  ah-vocw     filed from the verification of ah-t2pn.2 at 0b444332, asking that defaulted workers
              contend for the wage pool. ah-gjq4 merged after that at 6d023924 and shipped it -
              silver.rs:385 and :632. Closed unbuilt.

  ah-fjty     failed for a warning that never fires. The planner's audit found the shipped code
              matched the plan exactly and named two candidate causes that are correct behaviour
              introduced by ah-e66j and ah-eacd, both of which landed after the bead was planned.

## Why this is not just bad luck

Nothing records WHICH commit a verdict was formed against, in a place a later reader checks. The
notes say it in prose - 'at ce9d2817' - and nothing compares that to main's head before the bead
reaches an implementer. So a stale verdict is indistinguishable from a live one, and the cost lands
on whoever picks it up: an implementer that builds a no-op, or a planner that rewrites a sound plan.

It gets worse as the fleet gets faster, which is the wrong direction.

## What it costs

Three beads in one day. Two implementer pickups that built nothing, one planner audit, and one bead
that sat at P0 across three planner passes while it waited for a second look it did not need.
design:
## Context

Psylocke verifies a merged bead against one specific commit and records her verdict against it. On
a fast day the fleet merges several beads while she is verifying, so by the time the verdict reaches
anybody a sibling may already have delivered the very thing she found missing. The verdict is then
true of the tree she looked at and **false of main**.

Three beads in one day, 2026-08-23:

| Bead | Verdict at | What landed after | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ah-t2pn.3` | `ce9d2817` | `ah-t2pn.4` at `0b444332`, carrying exactly the wording the verification called the sharper half | Storm claimed it as a P0, found nothing to build, handed it back. Two sessions and a planner pass. |
| `ah-vocw` | `0b444332` | `ah-gjq4` at `6d023924`, shipping it (`silver.rs:385`, `:632`) | Closed unbuilt. |
| `ah-fjty` | `dd3f67bd` | `ah-e66j` and `ah-eacd` | A planner audit that found the shipped code matched the plan exactly, and named two candidate causes that are *correct behaviour* introduced after the bead was planned. |

**Nothing records which commit a verdict was formed against in a place a later reader checks.** The
sha exists only in prose — `agents/verifier.md:381-384` writes it into a `--reason` string and an
`--append-notes` line — and nothing compares it to main's head before the bead reaches an
implementer or a planner. So a stale verdict is indistinguishable from a live one, and the cost
lands on whoever picks it up: an implementer that builds a no-op, or a planner that rewrites a sound
plan. **It gets worse as the fleet gets faster**, which is the wrong direction.

This is the third of three beads about the reopen path losing information between roles.
**`ah-kjfm` and `ah-tjaz` are both closed and shipped** (cerebro PRs #98 and #99), and this bead is
built on top of what they landed: `ah-tjaz` introduced the `plan:revise` label and the rule that a
`verification:failed` bead without it is *not* a planner's, and `ah-kjfm` added `sweep-assignees.sh`
plus `cerebro--assignee-finding` — **the exact pair this bead copies.** Read `ah-kjfm`'s design
before writing a line of this one; it is the template, and its invariants are this bead's too.

When this lands: a verdict carries its commit in a field, and a failed bead whose verdict main has
moved past is offered back to Psylocke for a second look rather than to an implementer or a planner.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

**Almost all of this is in the `cerebro` submodule**, not in `atlantis-hud`.
`.claude/agents/*` and `.claude/skills/*` are **symlinks into `.claude/cerebro/`**:

```
.claude/agents/verifier.md      -> ../cerebro/agents/verifier.md
.claude/agents/orchestrator.md  -> ../cerebro/agents/orchestrator.md
.claude/skills/implement-bead   -> ../cerebro/skills/implement-bead
.claude/skills/plan-bead        -> ../cerebro/skills/plan-bead
```

So the work is **a PR in `https://github.com/rmstdope/cerebro.git` (branch `main`), then a
`chore: bump cerebro` pointer commit in `atlantis-hud`** — exactly what `ah-kjfm` and `ah-tjaz` did.
The submodule's own commit subjects use **this project's bead
ids** (`docs(ah-tjaz): … (#99)`), so keep that convention.

**Do not make a worktree of cerebro's own repository for this.** Run `prepare-worktree` for an
ordinary consumer tree (`.cerebro/worktrees/ah-e0kf`) and do the submodule work inside
`<tree>/.claude/cerebro`, which has a private git dir of its own — verified on 2026-08-24:
`.cerebro/worktrees/psylocke/.claude/cerebro/.git` reads

### The invariant, inherited from `sweep-claims.sh`'s header and not negotiable

> *This script never mutates anything — no `bd close`, no `bd reclaim`, no git write of any kind …
> Keeping this script read-only is what makes that guarantee checkable at a glance: the only way to
> reach a `bd close` or `bd reclaim` invocation is through the confirmed path in `cerebro.el`.*

And `cerebro--finding-command` is *"the complete list of destructive commands the fleet view can
run"*. **This sweep obeys both**: the script reads, the finding function is pure, and the write runs
only from `cerebro--finding-command`, on confirmation.

### 1. `agents/verifier.md` — the sha becomes a field

`bd` supports custom metadata, it is exposed in **both** `bd list --json` and `bd show --json`, and
**nothing in the fleet uses it yet** — the namespace is unclaimed. Verified by probe on 2026-08-24:
`bd update <id> --set-metadata k=v` then `bd list --status open --json | jq '.[] | select(.id=="…")
| .metadata'` returns `{"k":"v"}`, and `bd update <id> --unset-metadata k` removes it. **When there
is no metadata the key is absent from the object entirely**, not `{}` or `null` — every reader must
say `.metadata // {}`.

Add one line to each of the three verdict recipes (`verifier.md:359-384`), immediately after the
existing commands and before the `bd dolt push`:

```bash
bd update <id> --set-metadata verified_at=<full sha>
```

**The full 40-character sha, not the short one she speaks and writes into prose.** The sweep runs
`git log <sha>..origin/main` and `git merge-base --is-ancestor`, and a short sha is ambiguous in a
repository this size only rarely — but "rarely" is the wrong guarantee for the one field the whole
mechanism reads. She already has the full sha: `prepare-worktree` prints it (`verifier.md:237-240`).
**Leave every existing prose mention exactly as it is** — the short sha in the `--reason` strings and
in the appended note stays, because a human reads those and this field is for a script.

The three recipes that gain it: `passed` (`:361-364`), `passed with a follow-up` (`:370-373`, which
marks the original passed the same way), and `failed` (`:380-384`). **`not-needed` does not**: she
never looked at a tree for it, so there is no commit a verdict was formed against.

Add, in her *Recording a verdict* prose beside `verifier.md:503`'s existing
*"Never records a verdict without the sha"*: that the field is what the staleness sweep reads, that
it is the full sha, and that a verdict recorded without it is invisible to the sweep rather than
wrong.

**One more line in the `failed` recipe**, and it is what stops the sweep looping: when she records a
new verdict on a bead that already carries `verdict:stale`, that label comes off in the same breath.

```bash
bd update <id> --remove-label verdict:stale     # harmless when it is not there
```

`--remove-label` on an absent label is a no-op, so this is unconditional and needs no test of the
current labels.

### 2. `scripts/sweep-verdicts.sh` — new, read-only

```
.claude/cerebro/scripts/sweep-verdicts.sh --json
```

Model the argument parsing, the `--json` contract and the header comment on `sweep-assignees.sh`,
which is the newest of the family and the closest in shape. Model the git half on
`sweep-claims.sh:72` (`git -C "$repo_root" fetch --quiet origin "$default_branch"`) and
`sweep-claims.sh:115`. Take the branch from `scripts/default-branch` and the repo from
`scripts/consumer-root`, as its siblings do.

**Candidates**: beads with `status=open` carrying `verification:failed` and **not** already carrying
`verdict:stale`.

```bash
bd list --status open --json \
  | jq -r '.[] | select((.labels // []) | index("verification:failed"))
              | select((.labels // []) | index("verdict:stale") | not)'
```

One object per candidate:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `id` | the bead id |
| `title` | for the confirmation prompt |
| `priority` | the integer, so the fleet view can shout for a `0` |
| `verified_at` | `.metadata.verified_at`, or `null` when the bead has none |
| `merges_since` | `git log --oneline <verified_at>..origin/<branch> \| wc -l`, or `null` |

**`merges_since` is `null`, never `0`, in all three unknowable cases**, and the script must not
collapse them into a number:

- `verified_at` is absent — every verdict recorded before this ships is in this state, and so is any
  recorded by a session running an older `verifier.md`. **Unknown is not stale**; the finding
  function returns nil for it.
- `git cat-file -e <sha>^{commit}` fails — the commit is not in this clone at all.
- `git merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> origin/<branch>` exits non-zero — the verdict was formed
  against something that is not on the default branch (a worktree that had drifted, a force-push).
  Counting `<sha>..origin/main` there would give a number that means nothing.

The repository squash-merges every PR (`gh pr merge --squash`), so **one commit on main is one
merged PR** and `git log --oneline <sha>..origin/main | wc -l` is directly the number the line
shows. Do **not** filter out `docs(<id>): mockup` commits: `cerebro-project.conf`'s
`non_delivery_commit_pattern` exists to answer *"did this bead get delivered"*, and this sweep asks
a different question — *"has main moved at all since anybody looked"* — for which a mockup commit
counts like any other. Say so in the script's header, or somebody will "fix" it.

### 3. `emacs/cerebro.el` — the finding, pure

```elisp
(defun cerebro--verdict-finding (candidate)
  "Pure. What the verdict sweep should offer for CANDIDATE, or nil.

CANDIDATE is one parsed object from `sweep-verdicts.sh --json'. Returns nil or
 (recheck ID). Nil covers the two cases the script could not answer: the bead
carries no `verified_at', so no verdict commit is known; or `merges_since' is
nil, meaning the commit is not on the default branch and the distance is not a
number. A known distance below `cerebro-stale-verdict-merges' is also nil."
  (let-alist candidate
    (cond
     ((null .verified_at) nil)
     ((null .merges_since) nil)
     ((< .merges_since cerebro-stale-verdict-merges) nil)
     (t (list 'recheck .id)))))
```

It takes **one argument**, unlike `cerebro--assignee-finding`, because everything it needs is in the
candidate: there is no liveness to consult and no roster to check. Do not take `now` or `roster`
"for symmetry" — the other findings take them because they use them.

```elisp
(defcustom cerebro-stale-verdict-merges 1
  "How many commits must land on the default branch after a failed verdict's own
commit before the sweep offers the bead back for a second look. One, because
anything landing on main since the verdict is enough to make it worth
re-checking: the three cases of 2026-08-23 were 4, 2 and 6 merges behind, and
erring toward a re-verification is much cheaper than erring toward an
implementer building a no-op."
  :type 'integer :group 'cerebro)
```

## User-facing decisions

Interviewed with the navigator on 2026-08-24. Mockup, as chosen and committed:
`docs/ui/ah-e0kf-stale-verdict.html` (PR #642, merged). **The fleet view is the navigator's own
surface**, so the line and the action are theirs.

**What the Sweeps line says.**
Chosen: **the commit, and the count of merges since**, shipping verbatim:

> `recheck ah-t2pn.3 — verdict at ce9d2817, 4 merges since`

It matches the family's shape exactly — verb, id, em dash, reason — and the number is the whole
evidence: how far main has moved since anybody looked. Accepted cost: it says nothing about whether
any of those merges touched this bead's files.

Rejected: *how far behind in time* (`3h behind main`). Time is what a navigator has a feel for, but
a quiet three hours and a busy three hours read identically, and it is merges rather than minutes
that make a verdict stale.

Rejected: *naming what merged since* (`ah-t2pn.4 merged since`). In all three real cases that name
**is** the answer and the navigator could often decide without opening anything — rejected because
it is the longest line in the section and has to truncate and pick one to name when several merged,
which is exactly when the line matters most.

**What pressing the key does.**
Chosen: **send it back to Psylocke.** The key sets a label that takes the bead out of both the
implementer and the planner candidate queries and puts it at the top of her next pass. Nothing is
deleted; the verdict, the notes and the plan stay exactly as written.

Rejected: *show the line and do nothing* — a pure alert, keeping the sweep family perfectly
read-only and adding no vocabulary. Rejected because the failure this bead exists to fix is that
**nobody was looking**, and a line with no key behind it strands the bead just as quietly.

Rejected: *flag it automatically and report after*. Nothing is destroyed — no work is taken off
anyone and the verdict is untouched — but it would make this the one sweep that writes without
confirming, and that invariant is what makes the fleet view's safety checkable at a glance.

**The label's spelling.** Put to the navigator as a correction: `verification:` is a bd **state
dimension**, and `bd set-state` replaces the whole dimension, so a `verification:stale` would either
overwrite the `verification:failed` verdict or leave two labels in one dimension.
Chosen: **`verdict:stale`, a dimension of its own**, set with `bd set-state <id> verdict=stale`. The
verdict survives exactly as recorded, and the two facts — what she found, and whether it still holds
— are separately readable.
Rejected: *`verification:stale`, overwriting the verdict*, which adds no new vocabulary but leaves
the fact that she failed it only in the notes.

**How many merges.**
Chosen: **one** — `cerebro-stale-verdict-merges` defaults to `1`. Anything landing on main since the
verdict is enough to make it worth a second look; erring toward a re-verification is much cheaper
than erring toward an implementer building a no-op. Accepted cost: a failed bead is often flagged
within minutes, before an implementer has reached it — which is the point.
Rejected: *three*, which is quieter but would have missed `ah-vocw` at two merges — one of the three
cases this bead was filed for. Rejected: *two*, which catches all three and lets a lone docs commit
pass, but has no case behind it either way.

**Decided by the planner, and stated so the implementer does not re-open them:**

- **The full 40-character sha in the field, the short one everywhere in prose.** The field is read by
  `git merge-base` and `git log`; the prose is read by a person.
- **`not-needed` records no `verified_at`.** She never looked at a tree for it.
- **A missing `verified_at` yields nil, never a finding.** Unknown is not stale, and every verdict
  recorded before this ships is in that state — a sweep that treated absence as staleness would
  flag the entire history on its first run.
- **Mockup commits count toward `merges_since`.** The question is *has main moved*, not *was this
  bead delivered*, so `non_delivery_commit_pattern` does not apply.
- **Psylocke removes `verdict:stale` whenever she records a new verdict**, unconditionally. Without
  it the sweep re-offers the same bead every cycle after the next merge lands.

## Out of scope

- **Whether a merge touched the files this bead's plan names.** The bead's own open questions weigh
  the precise version against the cheap one; the cheap one is chosen, and it errs toward a second
  look rather than toward building a no-op. Filing the precise version later is reasonable; guessing
  at it here is not.
- **Psylocke re-fetching head immediately before recording a verdict.** It was the fourth option in
  the bead's open questions, and it closes only the narrower window — main moving *while she
  verifies*. `ah-vocw`'s sibling merged **after** the verdict was written, so a re-check at record
  time would not have caught it. Worth having in addition; not a substitute, and not built here.
- **Any change to the other five sweeps**, or to the finding functions they own.
- **Automatically deciding a verdict still holds.** The sweep says *main has moved*; only Psylocke
  and the navigator say *and so the finding no longer applies*.
- **A `verified_at` for beads verified before this ships.** They stay unknown, and are invisible to
  the sweep. Backfilling is not worth a plan.
- **Anything in `atlantis-hud`** beyond the one `chore: bump cerebro` commit.
