ask for more than the faction has.** The engine grants in an order the report does not show, so some
of those claims simply fail and the player finds out from next turn's report.

This bead is the second half of a decision the navigator took on 2026-08-23 while planning
**`ah-bumi`**: *"A, but file a new bead to introduce a warning if the total CLAIM in all hexes
exceeds the unclaimed silver."*

`ah-bumi` settled the column — each claiming unit is capped at the whole purse and no contention is
modelled, exactly as `WORK` and entertaining treat their regional pools. That keeps every unit's
figure independent of every other's, which is what was chosen, **and it means two units can together
read more than the purse holds.** This bead is what catches that, in the same shape as `ah-1wcw.2`,
where an unsellable sale earns nothing and the shipped `not-traded-here` check is what tells the
player why.

Agreed design: `docs/ui/ah-wur4-over-claim.html`.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

**This is a faction-wide check**, so it belongs with `check_faction`
(`crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs:2790-2799`) and not with the per-hex checks. That function
already takes `report` — so `report.header.unclaimed_silver` is to hand — and `ordered`, which has
read every unit's block in the whole document.

`check_faction` runs two checks today, `check_quartermasters` and `check_trade_regions`. **The first
is the model to copy**, and copying it settles most of this bead: it is faction-wide, and it anchors
**one finding per offending unit on that unit's own order line**, built as a `Finding` struct literal
rather than through `Hex::finding`/`Ordered::finding` — those helpers are not available at faction
level. Read `check_quartermasters`'s push (around `:2992-3003`) before writing anything.

### `crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs`

**The code**, appended **last** to `codes::ALL` and its length literal bumped — the array's own doc
comment states that rule, and the generated TypeScript copies the order:

```rust
    pub const CLAIMS_EXCEED_UNCLAIMED: Code = Code("claims-exceed-unclaimed");
```

**The check**, called from `check_faction` beside the other two:

```rust
/// Every unit that claims, when the faction's units claim more between them than it holds.
///
/// Faction-wide rather than per hex: the purse is one pool for the whole report, and a claim in one
/// hex spends what a claim in another cannot. Every claiming unit is named because none of them is
/// more at fault than the others - the message says the total, so a unit reading it is not being
/// blamed for the overrun on its own.
fn check_claims(
    report: &ParsedReport,
    ordered: &OrderedUnits,
    options: &CheckOptions,
    findings: &mut Vec<Finding>,
) {
```

The rule:

```
if the check is disabled            -> return
purse = report.header.unclaimed_silver
if purse is None                    -> return          // see below; this is a decision, not a guard
claims = every (own unit, PlacedIntent) whose intent is Intent::Claim(n), across every region
total  = sum of those n
if total <= purse                   -> return
otherwise                           -> one finding per claiming unit, on its CLAIM line
```

**`purse` being `None` means the check does not fire at all**, and that is a decision rather than
defensive coding: a report that states no unclaimed silver is not evidence of an empty purse, and
warning about a limit nobody stated would be inventing the limit. `ah-bumi` counts a claim as written
in exactly that case, for exactly that reason, so the two agree. **Do not treat `None` as zero**,
which would fire on every claim in any report whose header the parser did not read.

**Only the player's own units.** `report.regions.iter().flat_map(|r| r.units.iter()).filter(|u| u.own)`
— the same shape `check_quartermasters` uses (`:2955-2960`). A foreign unit's claim is not from your
purse and you cannot see it anyway.

**A unit with several `CLAIM` orders contributes all of them to the total, and gets one finding per
claim line.** That falls out of iterating placed intents rather than units, and it is right: each
line is separately editable.

**The message**, verbatim, with both numbers interpolated:

```
your units claim {total} between them and the faction has {purse}
```

A finding's message is a fragment read after the unit's name, lower case and no full stop — the house
style (`has no order that spends the month`, `this hex does not want furs - its market wants ...`).
**"between them" is load-bearing**: the same sentence appears on every claiming unit, and without it
each one reads as though that unit alone over-claimed.

### The two registries a check must join, or it does not run

**`codes::ALL`** (`semantics.rs:112-135`) — appended last, and the `[Code; N]` length literal bumped.

**`every_advisory_code_can_be_silenced`** (`semantics.rs:~6287`) — a `Case` fixture must be added or
the test fails on `cases.len() == codes::ALL.len()`. The fixture needs a report whose header states
unclaimed silver and at least two units claiming more than it between them, since one unit claiming
more than the purse is a different and simpler shape.

### `packages/core-client/src/coreVocabulary.generated.ts`

Regenerated, not hand-edited:

```bash
ATLANTIS_UPDATE_GENERATED=1 cargo test -p atlantis-hud-core --test generated_ts
```

Commit what it writes. `DEFAULT_ADVISORY_CHECKS` (`packages/shared/src/settingsStore.ts:44-46`) picks
the new code up **automatically and on**, because it maps every code to `code !== "hex-unguarded"` —
so **no edit there**, and the navigator's "on by default" needs no code of its own.

### `packages/shared/src/workspace/SettingsDialog.tsx`

One entry in `WARNING_GROUPS`, in the **Resources** group beside `not-enough-silver` and
`not-enough-items` — it is about silver the faction has, not about a market or an order's shape.
Both strings ship verbatim:

```ts
      {
        code: "claims-exceed-unclaimed",
        title: "Claiming more than the faction has",
        description: "CLAIM orders across all your units asking for more unclaimed silver than the faction holds."
      }
```

`SettingsDialog.test.tsx` iterates `ADVISORY_CHECK_CODES` asserting a toggle exists for each, and
holds a hard-coded list of titles — **both need the new entry** or it fails.

### `crates/core/tests/validate_real_orders.rs`

`EXPECTED` gains a row **only if the check fires on the committed turn**. Establish that rather than
assuming: if it fires, add `("claims-exceed-unclaimed", n)` and a bullet in the doc comment saying
what real orders caused it, the way every other row is justified. If it does not fire, add nothing
and say so in the PR.

## Increments

**1. The arithmetic, in isolation.**
Failing test: `a_faction_claiming_more_than_it_holds_is_warned` in `semantics.rs`'s test module — two
units claiming 3000 and 2000 against a stated purse of 4935, asserting two findings under
`codes::CLAIMS_EXCEED_UNCLAIMED`, each carrying the other unit's id on its own line, and the exact
message on both.
Then, each its own test:
`claims_within_the_purse_are_not_warned_about` (3000 + 1000 against 4935 — nothing),
`claims_exactly_matching_the_purse_are_not_warned_about` (the boundary),
`a_report_with_no_stated_purse_is_not_warned_about` (`unclaimed_silver: None`, two big claims,
**no** finding — the decision, not a guard),
`a_foreign_units_claim_does_not_count`,
`a_unit_claiming_twice_is_warned_on_each_line`.

**2. It is registered, and can be silenced.**
Failing test: the existing `every_advisory_code_can_be_silenced` fails the moment the code is added
to `codes::ALL` without a fixture — that failure **is** increment 2's red. Add the `Case`, and the
loop proves both directions for free.

**3. The vocabulary and the toggle.**
Run the regeneration, commit the generated file, add the `WARNING_GROUPS` entry and the title to
`SettingsDialog.test.tsx`'s list. The failing test here is that suite, which already asserts a toggle
per code.

**4. The committed turn.**
Establish whether the check fires on it and make `validate_real_orders.rs` say so either way — a row
plus a justification, or nothing plus a line in the PR.

## The test plan

| Test | Pins |
|---|---|
| `a_faction_claiming_more_than_it_holds_is_warned` | the rule, the anchoring and the verbatim message |
| `claims_within_the_purse_are_not_warned_about` | that it stays quiet on an ordinary turn |
| `claims_exactly_matching_the_purse_are_not_warned_about` | the boundary, which is the likeliest off-by-one |
| `a_report_with_no_stated_purse_is_not_warned_about` | the decision about absence |
| `a_foreign_units_claim_does_not_count` | that it is your purse, not anybody's |
| `a_unit_claiming_twice_is_warned_on_each_line` | per-intent rather than per-unit iteration |
| `every_advisory_code_can_be_silenced` | registration, both directions |
| `SettingsDialog.test.tsx` | the toggle and its title |
| `validate_real_orders.rs` | the committed turn, stated either way |

```bash
cargo test -p atlantis-hud-core
cargo fmt --check
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
pnpm run check:generated
pnpm --filter @atlantis/shared test
pnpm run check:fast
```

**No new smoke spec.** The Problems panel already renders whatever findings arrive and is covered;
this adds a finding, not a surface.

## User-facing decisions

Taken by the navigator on 2026-08-23. Mockup: `docs/ui/ah-wur4-over-claim.html`.

**Every claiming unit is warned, each on its own CLAIM line.** Offered against a single finding
anchored on the first claim in the document. **Every unit chosen.**
*Rejected* because a single finding must anchor on some unit, and picking one by document order
blames a unit no more at fault than the others — which is the thing this fleet has twice refused to
do for a shared pool (`ah-1wcw.1`'s wages, `ah-7cdt`'s food). It would also leave the other claims
unreachable from the Problems panel, which is where a player goes to fix them.
The accepted cost is named: one sentence repeated per claiming unit.

**On by default.** Offered against off. *Rejected* because it fires only when the player has genuinely
asked for more than they have — rare, and always a real mistake rather than a style preference — and
a check about a real mistake that you must first know exists is a poor trade. `hex-unguarded` is the
only check that is off, and it is off because it fires across the whole map on a normal turn.

**The message**, chosen from three and shipping verbatim:
`your units claim {total} between them and the faction has {purse}`
*Rejected*: `your units claim {n} more silver than the faction has` (names the shortfall but hides
how close you were and what the purse holds) and `claims more unclaimed silver than the faction has`
(shortest, but reads as though the named unit is the one over-claiming — the single thing this
message must avoid, since it appears on every claiming unit).

**A report that states no purse does not fire the check.** Offered against treating absence as zero.
*Rejected* because a faction with no stated purse is not evidence of an empty one, and every claim in
a report whose header the parser did not read would warn. `ah-bumi` counts a claim as written in the
same case and for the same reason.

**The Settings entry**, verbatim: title `Claiming more than the faction has`, description
`CLAIM orders across all your units asking for more unclaimed silver than the faction holds.` In the
**Resources** group, beside the two other silver checks.

## Out of scope

- **The Silver column.** `ah-bumi` settled it: capped per unit, no contention, no doubt. **This bead
  changes no figure** — it adds a finding. If your diff touches `silver.rs`, stop.
- **Modelling which claims actually succeed.** The engine grants in an order the report does not
  show; that is why this is a warning about the total rather than an adjustment to any unit's number.
- **`semantics.rs`'s ledger**, which credits `CLAIM` uncapped and drives `not-enough-silver`. Its
  findings are pinned in `EXPECTED`; capping it would move them.
- **Any other faction-wide limit.** Trade regions and quartermasters already have checks; nothing
  else is added here.
- **A hover note in the Silver panel.** The Problems panel carries this; duplicating it in the hover
  would be two voices on one fact.

## Validation

```bash
cargo test -p atlantis-hud-core
cargo fmt --check
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
pnpm run check:generated
pnpm --filter @atlantis/shared test
pnpm run check:fast
```

Acceptance, each checkable by running or looking:

1. Two units claiming 3000 and 2000 against a stated purse of 4935 produce **two** findings, each on
   its own CLAIM line, both reading the verbatim message with 5500 and 4935 in it.
2. The same two claiming 3000 and 1000 produce **none**.
3. Settings → Warnings shows **Claiming more than the faction has** under Resources, **checked**.
4. `git diff` does not touch `crates/core/src/orders/silver.rs`.
5. `validate_real_orders.rs` states the committed turn's answer either way — a justified row, or
   nothing plus a line in the PR.

**Only a human can check** that the repeated message reads acceptably when it appears on several
units at once — Psylocke's pass, and the one cost the navigator knowingly accepted.

## Known traps

- **`codes::ALL` is a fixed-length array** (`[Code; N]`) and the literal must be bumped. Appending
  without it does not compile; appending anywhere but last reorders the generated TypeScript, which
  the array's own doc comment forbids.
- **`every_advisory_code_can_be_silenced` asserts `cases.len() == codes::ALL.len()`.** A new code
  without a fixture fails it — deliberately, so a silenced check cannot go unnoticed. That failure is
  increment 2's red rather than a problem to work around.
- **`DEFAULT_ADVISORY_CHECKS` turns a new code on automatically**, so "on by default" needs no edit —
  but it also means forgetting the `WARNING_GROUPS` entry ships a check nobody can turn **off**, and
  only `SettingsDialog.test.tsx` would catch it.
- **A faction-wide check has no `Hex` or `Ordered`**, so `hex.finding` and `ordered.finding` are not
  available. Build the `Finding` literally, as `check_quartermasters` does, and take `region_id` from
  the unit itself.
- **Iterate placed intents, not units.** A unit with two `CLAIM` lines must contribute both to the
  total and receive a finding on each; iterating units and taking the first claim silently
  under-counts the total, which is the one arithmetic error that makes the check quietly not fire.
- **`ah-dwk6`'s retrospective**: a default-on check with no exemptions broke 26 `semantics` fixtures
  and 9 smoke specs, because `check:fast` runs no browser suite. This check needs a stated purse
  *and* an overrun, so it should fire on almost nothing — but run the Rust suite before believing
  that, and read the `EXPECTED` diff rather than regenerating anything.
- **`corpus_errors` compares against a committed generated table.** Nothing here should change it.

title: The P4 triage filter's not-somebody's-child exclusion never excludes anything
description:
skills/plan-bead/SKILL.md's triage query builds a $children list to drop beads that are somebody's child, so the navigator is asked about parents rather than about children whose ordering the parent already decides. It cannot work as written, for two independent reasons, and both fail SILENTLY as an empty list - so the filter reads as a no-op and every child is presented for triage alongside its parent.

1. It pipes 'bd list --status open --json'. A bd list bead has NO dependencies key at all - only dependency_count. Verified 2026-08-23: 'bd list --status open --json | jq [.[] | select(has("dependencies"))] | length' returns 0.
2. It then selects on .type=="parent-child". The field is .dependency_type. (The same wrong spelling appeared in ah-ywj7's new epic-ownership lookup and was corrected there; docs/decisions.md already records .dependency_type as the right spelling for the blocks query.)

Only 'bd show <id> --json' embeds dependencies, and the entry IS the parent bead embedded whole, so the parent's id is .id and there is no depends_on_id.

Found by an adversarial review during ah-ywj7. NOT fixed there: ah-ywj7's plan puts the triage split explicitly out of scope, and the fix is approach-level rather than a typo - a per-bead 'bd show' is one call per candidate, which may or may not be acceptable in a triage pass over the whole P4 backlog. That trade is a planner's to make.

Scope note: this is a change to the cerebro submodule, not to this application.
acceptance_criteria:
- The triage query demonstrably excludes a bead that is somebody's child, shown by running it against the live database with a known parent/child pair.
- Whatever command shape is chosen, its cost over a full P4 backlog is stated in the skill.
- No other query in the skill still selects on .type for a parent-child edge.
notes:
Xavier 2026-08-23: verified against live data, and the bead is half wrong in a way that makes it much cheaper.

CLAIM 1 IS FALSE. `bd list --status open --json` DOES carry a `dependencies` key, and populates it. Checked just now:

  bd list --status open --json | jq '[.[] | select(has("dependencies"))] | length'   -> 5 of 5
  bd list --status open --json | jq '[.[] | select(.dependencies != null)] | length' -> 1 (ah-7cdt, the only open bead that has any)

`dependencies` is in the key set of every row and is an array wherever `dependency_count > 0`. So no per-bead `bd show` is needed, and the bead's argument for why this is "approach-level rather than a typo" - that a fix would cost one call per candidate - does not hold.

CLAIM 2 IS TRUE, and is the whole bug: the field is `.dependency_type`, not `.type`. The triage query's `$children` list therefore always comes out empty and the filter is a no-op, exactly as reported.

So the fix is ONE field name in the triage query in skills/plan-bead/SKILL.md. Verified working:

  bd list --status open --json | jq -r '[.[] | . as $b | ($b.dependencies // [])[] | select(.dependency_type=="parent-child") | $b.id] as $children | ...'

A SECOND OCCURRENCE, not mentioned in the bead, in the same file: the parent/child priority-drift reconciliation query under "Then: triage the P4 backlog" has the same wrong spelling AND uses `.depends_on_id`, which does not exist - a `bd show` dependency entry embeds the parent bead whole, so the parent's id is `.id`. That query has therefore never been able to report drift either. Xavier reported "no drift" on four consecutive passes on the strength of it; that was a query that could not fail rather than a tree that was clean. Corrected form, verified to run:

  jq -r '(INDEX(.id)) as $by | .[] | . as $c | ($c.dependencies // [])[] | select(.dependency_type=="parent-child") | select($by[.id] != null and $by[.id].priority != $c.priority) | "\($c.id)\t\($by[.id].priority)"'

Both are in skills/plan-bead/SKILL.md and should be fixed together; fixing one leaves the other silently lying.
Xavier 2026-08-23, SECOND NOTE - RETRACTING MY FIRST ONE, AND THE BEAD.

My earlier note on this bead is wrong and must not be acted on. So is the bead. Measured properly this time, against beads that actually have parent-child edges (the open set had none at the moment I first looked, which is what misled me):

  bd list --status closed --json | jq '[.[] | . as $b | ($b.dependencies // [])[]
                                       | select(.type=="parent-child") | $b.id] | length'
    -> 550

  ... the same with select(.dependency_type=="parent-child")
    -> 0

THE TWO COMMANDS RETURN DIFFERENT SHAPES:

  bd list --json   dependency entries have keys: created_at, created_by, depends_on_id,
                   issue_id, metadata, TYPE.  `dependency_type` is null.
  bd show --json   dependency entries have `dependency_type`, and the entry IS the parent bead
                   embedded whole, so the parent's id is `.id` and there is no depends_on_id.

So the triage query in plan-bead, which pipes `bd list` and selects on `.type`, IS CORRECT. So is the priority-drift query, which pipes `bd list` and reads `.depends_on_id`. Neither has ever been a no-op. They only LOOK like no-ops because they run over the P4 backlog, and a child of a split family is created at its parent's priority - so a child is almost never at P4 and almost never in that query's input at all.

Claim 1 of this bead ("a bd list bead has NO dependencies key") is false: the key is present on every row and populated wherever dependency_count > 0. Claim 2 ("the field is .dependency_type") is true of `bd show` and false of `bd list`, which is the command the query actually uses.

MY FIRST NOTE COMPOUNDED THE ERROR by "confirming" claim 2 and proposing .dependency_type as the fix. Applying that would break two working queries. Disregard it entirely.

THERE IS A REAL DEFECT, BUT IT IS NOT HERE. ah-ywj7 merged (cerebro #95) carrying a "three things about that command" list in plan-bead's new family-ownership section which states, as general facts, that `bd list` has no dependencies key and that the field is `dependency_type`. Both are true only of `bd show`, which is what that section uses - but they are written as though they were true of bd generally, and the same passage then tells every planner that "the triage queries earlier in this file do not follow those three rules, and they are known to be wrong rather than an alternative worth copying". That is backwards, and it is now in the skill every planner reads.

Recommend closing this bead as not-a-defect and filing the skill correction instead - the navigator's call.
close_reason: Not a defect. The triage query pipes bd list and selects on .type, which is correct: a bd list dependency entry carries type and depends_on_id, while a bd show entry carries dependency_type and embeds the parent whole. Measured against beads that actually have parent-child edges - bd list with select(.type=="parent-child") finds 550, with select(.dependency_type==...) finds 0. The filter only looks like a no-op because it runs over the P4 backlog and a child is created at its parent's priority, so a child is almost never at P4 and almost never in that query's input. The priority-drift query is correct for the same reason. Both of this bead's claims are true of bd show and false of bd list, which is the command the queries use. The real defect is in plan-bead's newly merged family-ownership section, which states those bd show facts as general and then tells planners the triage queries are wrong; filed separately. Navigator confirmed the close on 2026-08-23.

title: Opening a header popover announces it, and closing puts focus back
description:
Found while planning ah-w544.2, and deliberately left out of it.

Neither ChipPopover panel moves focus when it opens. TurnMessagesPanel.tsx and ProblemsPanel.tsx have no autoFocus, no ref and no .focus() call; popover.tsx's usePopoverDismiss handles Escape and outside pointerdown but nothing else. So a keyboard or screen-reader user who activates a header chip is told a dialog opened (aria-haspopup=dialog, aria-expanded=true) and then has to tab forwards to find it - and tab lands in the panel only because the panel happens to follow the chip in the DOM.

ImportSummaryDialog.tsx:79 already does the right thing with autoFocus on its close button, so the pattern exists in the codebase; the popovers just never adopted it.

ah-w544.2 adds a third chip of exactly this shape and matches the existing behaviour rather than diverging from its neighbour - the navigator chose that on 2026-08-22 explicitly, so this bead is the other half of that decision. Fix all three together (turn messages, order problems, unreadable lines) so they stay identical, and decide once whether focus goes to the panel heading or its close button.

Each has smoke coverage in tests/smoke/workspace.spec.ts already, so the regression net exists.
design:
## Context

Every header popover is a `role="dialog"` carrying an `aria-label` (`popover.tsx:82-89`), and
**none of them moves focus when it opens**. A keyboard or screen-reader user presses a chip, is told
by `aria-haspopup="dialog"` and `aria-expanded="true"` that a dialog opened, and is then left
standing on the chip with nothing saying where that dialog is. It is usable today only because the
panel happens to follow the chip in the DOM, so Tab reaches it next — an accident of markup order,
not a decision.

Closing is the other half: the panel simply unmounts (`ChipPopover`, `popover.tsx:114-121`), so focus
falls to `<body>` and the user tabs from the top of the page.

**The bead's description says three panels. It is eleven**, verified by grepping for `PopoverFrame`:
`BadgeMenu`, `ExportMenu`, `FactionDossierPanel`, `FactionPanel`, `GamePicker`,
`MergedFactionsPanel`, `ProblemsPanel`, `TradePanel`, `TurnMessagesPanel`, `TurnPicker`,
`UnreadableLinesPanel`. That is good news: they share one frame, so this is **one change in one
file** and all eleven inherit it. Fixing only the three named would leave eight behaving differently
from their neighbours, which is the inconsistency the bead exists to remove.

This bead is the other half of a decision the navigator took while planning `ah-w544.2`: that bead
adds a twelfth popover of exactly this shape and **deliberately matches the existing behaviour**
rather than diverging from its neighbour, on the understanding that all of them would be fixed
together here.

The agreed design is `docs/ui/ah-pdly-popover-focus.html`. Open it before starting; it carries both
decisions and the reasons the two rejected focus targets were rejected.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### `packages/shared/src/workspace/popover.tsx` — the whole change

**`PopoverFrame` takes focus when it mounts.** It is already the `role="dialog"` element with the
`aria-label`, so focusing it announces the dialog and its name — which is precisely the thing the
user was told about and could not find. It gains `tabIndex={-1}` (focusable by script, never a Tab
stop of its own) and an effect that focuses it once:

```tsx
const ownRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement | null>(null);

useEffect(() => {
  ownRef.current?.focus({ preventScroll: true });
}, []);
```

`{ preventScroll: true }` is load-bearing: without it the browser scrolls the focused element into
view, and a popover anchored under a header chip can drag the whole workspace. Empty dependency
array, because the frame mounts when the popover opens and unmounts when it closes — there is no
"already open" state to guard against.

**`frameRef` already exists** as an optional prop (`popover.tsx:77-78`, "so a popover that has to
know where it is on screen can measure itself (ah-mwqa)"), and one caller passes it.
`PopoverFrame` must therefore focus **its own** internal ref and keep honouring the caller's:
attach both to the same node with a small callback ref, or keep `ownRef` and call
`frameRef.current = node` alongside. **Do not repurpose `frameRef`** — a caller that does not pass
it would then get no focus at all, which is nine of the eleven.

**`ChipPopover` restores focus when the panel closes.** It already owns `wrapperRef`, which contains
both the chip and the panel, so it is the only place that knows what to go back to:

```tsx
const returnTo = useRef<HTMLElement | null>(null);

useEffect(() => {
  if (open) {
    returnTo.current = document.activeElement as HTMLElement | null;
    return;
  }
  const target = returnTo.current;
  returnTo.current = null;
  // Only take focus back if it is still inside this popover - a press that closed one popover by
  // opening another must not be dragged back here.
  if (target && wrapperRef.current?.contains(document.activeElement)) {
    target.focus({ preventScroll: true });
  }
}, [open]);
```

**That containment test is the whole correctness of the close half**, and it is easy to leave out.
The header's chips dismiss each other — `toggle` sets `openPopover` to the new id — so closing
popover A and opening popover B happen in one render. Without the test, A's restore would yank focus
off B's freshly-focused panel and back onto A's chip, and the user would land somewhere they did not
ask for. With it, A restores only when focus is still somewhere it owns.

`returnTo` is captured on open rather than assumed to be the chip: a popover can be opened by a
keyboard shortcut with focus elsewhere (`AppShell` has cycling chords), and going back to where the
user actually was is the rule that holds in every case.

**Nothing else changes.** `usePopoverDismiss` (`popover.tsx:20-52`) already handles Escape and
outside-`pointerdown`; both call `onDismiss`, which flips `open`, which is what the effect above
watches. So "Escape returns focus to the chip", "the ✕ returns focus to the chip" and "a press
outside returns focus to the chip" all fall out of one effect rather than three code paths.

### The eleven panels — no changes at all

`BadgeMenu`, `ExportMenu`, `FactionDossierPanel`, `FactionPanel`, `GamePicker`,
`MergedFactionsPanel`, `ProblemsPanel`, `TradePanel`, `TurnMessagesPanel`, `TurnPicker`,
`UnreadableLinesPanel`. Every one renders a `PopoverFrame` as its root and inherits both halves. **If
you find yourself editing one of them, stop** — either the change belongs in the frame, or something
about that panel is genuinely different and is worth saying out loud rather than special-casing.

`MapViewControls.tsx` also uses `ChipPopover`; it gets the close-half behaviour for free and must be
checked, not edited.

### What is deliberately not added

**No focus trap, and no `aria-modal`.** These are popovers beside a map, not modal dialogs, and
`popover.tsx:13-16` says so in as many words — "a popover beside the map is not an overlay the player
cannot see through". Trapping Tab inside would make the rest of the header unreachable while a chip
is open, which is worse than today. The panels stay escapable by Tab in both directions.

## Increments

**1. The panel takes focus.**
Failing test: `moves_focus_to_the_panel_when_it_opens` in
`tests/smoke/workspace.spec.ts`. Load a report, click the turn-messages chip, and assert
`page.getByTestId("turn-messages")` is the focused element — `expect(panel).toBeFocused()`.
This is a smoke test and not a unit test, deliberately: `packages/shared` has no jsdom, so
`renderToStaticMarkup` runs no effects and cannot observe a focus call. See *Known traps*.
The unit test that **can** be written goes alongside it in `popover.test.tsx`:
`the_frame_is_focusable_by_script_but_not_by_tab`, asserting the rendered markup carries
`tabindex="-1"`.

**2. Focus comes back to where it started.**
Failing test: `returns_focus_to_the_chip_when_the_panel_closes`, in the same spec. Click the chip,
press `Escape`, assert `page.getByTestId("turn-messages-chip")` is focused. Then
`returns_focus_after_the_close_button` and `returns_focus_after_a_press_outside`.

**3. One popover closing another does not steal focus.**
Failing test: `opening_a_second_popover_leaves_focus_in_the_second`. Open the turn-messages chip,
then click the problems chip, and assert the **problems** panel is focused rather than the
turn-messages chip. This is the containment test from *Files to change*, and it is the one an
implementer will otherwise ship broken — write it before the effect, not after.

**4. Every popover, not just the two with tests.**
Failing test: `every_header_popover_takes_focus_when_it_opens`. A table-driven spec over the chips
reachable from a loaded report — at least the game, turn, faction, merged-factions, export, trade,
problems and turn-messages chips — clicking each and asserting its panel is focused. Skip any that
needs fixture state the spec cannot reach, and **say which in a comment** rather than silently
covering eight of eleven.

## The test plan

| Test | File | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| `the_frame_is_focusable_by_script_but_not_by_tab` | `popover.test.tsx` | `tabindex="-1"` in the markup |
| `moves_focus_to_the_panel_when_it_opens` | `tests/smoke/workspace.spec.ts` | the open half |
| `returns_focus_to_the_chip_when_the_panel_closes` (+ ✕, + outside press) | same | the close half, all three routes |
| `opening_a_second_popover_leaves_focus_in_the_second` | same | the containment test |
| `every_header_popover_takes_focus_when_it_opens` | same | that this is one rule, not two panels' worth |

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
pnpm run test:smoke tests/smoke/workspace.spec.ts --project=web
pnpm run test:smoke tests/smoke/workspace.spec.ts --project=desktop-shell
pnpm run test:smoke tests/smoke/shortcuts.spec.ts --project=web
```

**`shortcuts.spec.ts` is not optional here.** It drives the header by keyboard and opens popovers
through cycling chords, so it is the suite most likely to notice a focus change — and the one most
likely to have been relying on focus staying put.

**Run the browser suites before opening the PR, not just `check:fast`.** `check:fast` runs no browser
suite at all, and every assertion in this bead is a browser assertion. `ah-dwk6`'s retrospective
records a default-on change that passed `check:fast` and broke nine specs across two smoke files
precisely because of that gap; this change touches eleven popovers and is in the same class.

## User-facing decisions

Taken by the navigator on 2026-08-22. Mockup: `docs/ui/ah-pdly-popover-focus.html`.

**The panel itself takes focus.** Offered as (A) the panel, (B) the close button, (C) the first
focusable element inside. **A chosen.**
*B rejected* for two reasons: it announces the way *out* before saying what you are in — a
screen-reader user's first word would be "close" — and **`ExportMenu`, `BadgeMenu` and `TurnPicker`
have no close button**, so it would need a fallback and stop being one rule.
*C rejected* because it never says what opened, which is the actual complaint; because in
`GamePicker` the first focusable element is a rename **text field**, so the next thing typed would
be a rename; and because "the first thing" differs per panel, giving eleven behaviours instead of
one.

**Focus returns to the chip in every case** — Escape, the ✕, a press outside, and after choosing
something in the panel. Offered against exempting the choose-something case. **No exceptions
chosen**: that is precisely the case where a keyboard user most needs to know where they now are,
and the chip is what now shows the choice they made.

**No focus trap and no `aria-modal`.** Not offered as a choice — recorded here because it is the
thing a reader will most reasonably assume was included. See *Files to change* for why.

**No visible change for a mouse user, and no new string.** Nothing is added to the interface; a focus
ring appears where a keyboard user already expected one.

## Out of scope

- **Every panel file.** The change is in `PopoverFrame` and `ChipPopover` only.
- **`ImportSummaryDialog`, `OrdersImportSummaryDialog`, `SettingsDialog`** and any other true modal.
  They are not `PopoverFrame` users; `ImportSummaryDialog` already autofocuses its close button
  (`ImportSummaryDialog.tsx:79`) and is the pattern this bead is catching up with, not a target.
- **A focus trap, `aria-modal`, or making these dialogs modal in any sense.**
- **The `dismissLayer.ts` capture-phase stack.** `usePopoverDismiss` deliberately listens in the
  bubble phase so a text field inside a popover gets Escape first (`popover.tsx:12-16`); nothing here
  changes that ordering.
- **Any change to what the popovers contain, their chips, their labels or their dismissal rules.**
- **`aria-expanded` / `aria-haspopup` on the chips.** Already correct.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
pnpm run test:smoke tests/smoke/workspace.spec.ts --project=web
pnpm run test:smoke tests/smoke/workspace.spec.ts --project=desktop-shell
pnpm run test:smoke tests/smoke/shortcuts.spec.ts --project=web
```

Acceptance, each checkable by running or looking:

1. `git diff` touches `packages/shared/src/workspace/popover.tsx` and test files, **and nothing
   else** — no panel file, no `AppHeader.tsx`, no `AppShell.tsx`.
2. Opening any header chip by keyboard puts the focus ring on the panel; Escape puts it back on the
   chip.
3. Opening one chip while another is open leaves focus in the newly opened panel.
4. Tab from an open panel still reaches the rest of the header — nothing is trapped.

**Only a human can check** the thing this bead is actually for: drive the header with the keyboard
alone, and with a screen reader if one is to hand, and confirm that opening a chip now announces the
panel rather than silence. Psylocke's pass; say in the bead which was done.

## Known traps

- **`packages/shared` has no jsdom, by decision (ah-nass).** Its component tests render with
  `renderToStaticMarkup`, which runs **no effects**, attaches no refs and fires no timers —
  silently. A `popover.test.tsx` case that opens a popover and asserts `document.activeElement` is a
  test the harness cannot run, and four beads have each paid about half an hour discovering that.
  Everything in this bead except the `tabindex` attribute is a smoke test.
- **`preventScroll` on both `focus()` calls.** Without it the browser scrolls the focused node into
  view; a panel anchored under a header chip can shove the whole workspace, and it will look like a
  layout bug rather than a focus bug.
- **The containment test in the close effect.** Header chips dismiss one another in a single render,
  so a restore without it fights the newly opened panel for focus. Increment 3 exists for this and
  should be written first.
- **`frameRef` is an existing prop with a real caller** (ah-mwqa, a popover that measures itself).
  Do not reuse it for the focus ref, or every panel that does not pass one loses the fix — that is
  nine of eleven, and every test in increment 1 would still pass.
- **`check:fast` runs no browser suite**, and every behaviour in this bead is browser behaviour.
  See *The test plan*.
- **WebKit's driver answers `""` for text it considers clipped**, so a Chromium smoke assertion can
  pass while the native shell shows nothing. The `native` CI job is what tells you. Focus assertions
  are less exposed to this than text ones, but the `desktop-shell` project is in the commands above
  for a reason.
- **The smoke suite rebuilds the web bundle with the service worker disabled**, so a PWA run straight
  afterwards fails with timeouts that look like a broken worker.
notes: Navigator, 2026-08-23 (asked by Wolverine during implementation): the plan's 'focus returns to the chip in every case' is narrowed to Escape and the close button. A press outside leaves focus where the pointer put it - the dismiss fires on pointerdown and the browser's own mousedown default then moves focus to whatever was pressed, so restoring would mean yanking focus off a control the user just clicked. Keyboard users, who the bead is for, are unaffected.

title: A unit with no men left is warned for having no month-long order it could not give
description:
The navigator's words, 2026-08-22:

  "It'd be nice not to get the 'no month-long order' warning for units that have
  no men left in them."

The warning is the one ah-dwk6 shipped in v0.10.0, reading exactly "has no order
that spends the month". A unit with no men cannot spend a month on anything, so
the advice is not actionable: there is no order the player could add that would
satisfy it.

## This asks to amend a decision, not to fix an oversight

ah-dwk6's acceptance criteria are explicit on the point:

  "There are no exemptions: an empty block warns and a unit on GUARD warns."

So exemption-free was a deliberate choice in that bead's planning, not something
missed. This bead asks for the first exemption. A planner should treat it as the
navigator revising that decision with a case in hand, and should NOT read the
"no exemptions" line as still binding.

Worth noting this is the second false-positive filed against a warning in this
family: ah-vw63 (v0.10.0) removed the spare-teacher warning from units that were
not teaching at all. Same shape -- a check firing where its advice cannot apply.

## What needs deciding

"No men left" needs a definition. A unit's men come from its man-type items, so
a unit at zero men may still hold silver, equipment or a mount, and may still be
a real thing the player cares about rather than a husk. Whether the exemption
keys on the men count alone, or on the unit being empty of everything, is a
user-facing judgement for the navigator.

Also worth settling: whether such a unit is silently skipped, or flagged
differently -- a unit that has lost all its men may itself be news, and
suppressing the only line that mentions it could hide something the player would
want to know.

## Test impact, already known

ah-dwk6's acceptance pins the committed turn-71 template at ten expected
findings, "the two additions being this code against units 14451 and 13432 and
nothing else". An exemption changes that expectation if either unit has no men,
and needs a fixture that exercises the exemption if neither does. Whoever plans
this should check the corpus for a men-less unit before assuming one exists.

The check's toggle is Settings -> Warnings -> Orders, "Units that do nothing",
on by default.
design:
## Context

The navigator, 2026-08-22:

> *"It'd be nice not to get the 'no month-long order' warning for units that have no men left in
> them."*

The warning is `unit-does-nothing`, shipped by `ah-dwk6` in v0.10.0, reading exactly
**"has no order that spends the month"**. A unit with no men cannot spend a month on anything, so
the advice is not actionable: there is no order the player could add that would satisfy it.

**This amends a decision; it does not fix an oversight.** `ah-dwk6`'s acceptance criteria say:

> *"There are no exemptions: an empty block warns and a unit on GUARD warns."*

Exemption-free was a deliberate choice in that bead's planning. This bead is the navigator revising
it with a case in hand, and **that line is superseded, not still binding.** An implementer who reads
`ah-dwk6` and concludes this bead contradicts it has read correctly and should carry on regardless.

It is the second false positive filed against a warning in this family: `ah-vw63` (v0.10.0) removed
the spare-teacher warning from units that were not teaching at all. Same shape — a check firing where
its advice cannot apply.

### Three things established by reading, before any code is written

**1. The corpus has no men-less unit, so a fixture is needed.** `ah-dwk6`'s acceptance pins the
committed turn-71 template at ten findings, *"the two additions being this code against units 14451
and 13432 and nothing else"*. Both of those units **have men**:

```
* Drones (14451) … 50 lizardmen [LIZA], 7500 silver [SILV]. Weight: 500.
* Drone  (13432) … hill dwarf [HDWA], horse [HORS], 22 silver [SILV].
```

So **the ten-finding expectation is unchanged by this bead** and must stay at ten. The exemption is
exercised by a new unit-level test, not by the template.

**2. `men == 0` alone is not safe, and the model says why.** `report/model.rs:141-152` carries two
fields: `men`, and `men_estimated` — *"Whether `men` is a guess rather than a count."* The count is a
guess when the ruleset does not recognise every item the unit holds
(`report/composition.rs:55-73` returns early without counting). And `Unit::default()` is
**`men: 0, men_estimated: true`**.

So an exemption on the count alone would silently hide a real unit whose only fault was carrying an
item the ruleset has not been taught — turning a false positive into a false negative, which is
worse: a missing warning cannot be noticed.

**3. The guard is already idiomatic in this file.** `semantics.rs:863` does exactly this for the
study-cost check:

```rust
// A headcount that is a guess cannot price a study …
let cost = ruleset
    .filter(|_| !actor.unit.men_estimated)
```

and `:2370` does it again. This bead follows the house pattern rather than inventing one.

## Files to change and what to reuse

- **`crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs`** — `check_idle_units` (around line 1968) gains one guard;
  its test module gains cases; `with_men` may need extending (see *Known traps*).
- **Nothing else.** No TypeScript, no UI, no settings, no new code, no new finding type.

Reuse:

- **`ReportUnit::men` and `::men_estimated`** — already on the model, already populated.
- **`semantics.rs:863`'s idiom** — read it before writing the guard.
- **`with_men(unit, men)`** (test helper, `semantics.rs:2756`) — and read *Known traps* about it
  before using it.
- **`check_idle_units`'s existing early-`continue` style** — the new guard is a third `continue`
  beside `ordered.unread` and `spends_the_month`, in the same shape.

## Increments

### 1 — The exemption

`check_idle_units`, after the `unread` guard and before or after the intents guard — **order does not
matter for correctness, so put it beside `unread`**, because both are "this unit is not judged at
all" rather than "this unit is fine":

```rust
for ordered in &hex.units {
    // A line we could not read may well be a month's work - `ASSASSINATE 4021` is - so a unit
    // holding one is not judged at all. Silence here is the price of never being wrong.
    if ordered.unread {
        continue;
    }
    // A unit with no men cannot spend a month on anything, so there is no order the player could
    // add that would satisfy this - the advice would be unfollowable rather than merely unwelcome
    // (ah-udff, revising ah-dwk6's "no exemptions"). Only when the count is a count: `men` is 0 on
    // a unit whose items the ruleset could not read, and exempting that one would hide a real unit
    // instead of a husk.
    if ordered.unit.men == 0 && !ordered.unit.men_estimated {
        continue;
    }
    if ordered.intents().any(spends_the_month) {
        continue;
    }
    …
}
```

**Write the comment.** Every guard in this function has one saying why silence is correct there, and
the reason for this one — that it revises an explicit earlier decision — is exactly the kind of thing
that gets undone by a later reader who finds `ah-dwk6` first.

**No other check changes.** A men-less unit still gets every other finding it earns; this exempts
`unit-does-nothing` and nothing else.

### 2 — The tests

In `semantics.rs`'s test module, following the shape of the existing `unit-does-nothing` cases:

| case | expectation |
|---|---|
| A unit with **0 men, count known**, and no month-long order | **no** `unit-does-nothing` |
| A unit with **0 men, count known**, holding 7500 silver and a horse, and no month-long order | **no** `unit-does-nothing` — the navigator's decision **A**: the exemption keys on men alone, whatever else it holds |
| A unit with **0 men but `men_estimated: true`** | **warns**, as today. This is finding 2 above and the one most likely to be dropped |
| A unit with **1 man** and no month-long order | warns, unchanged |
| A men-less unit with an **unreadable line** | still not judged — the `unread` guard already covered it and still does |
| A men-less unit that **does** have a month-long order | no finding, for the ordinary reason |

**Write the third case first.** The other five would all pass a naive `men == 0` implementation; that
one is the only test that distinguishes a correct fix from a plausible one.

And, unchanged and asserted:

- **The committed turn-71 template still produces exactly ten findings**, with the same two
  `unit-does-nothing` entries against 14451 and 13432. Both units have men; if this number moves,
  the exemption is firing where it should not.

### 3 — Nothing in the UI

Stated as an increment so it is not discovered as an omission.

The navigator chose **i, silently skipped**: the check does not fire, the unit appears nowhere in the
warnings, and the count drops by one. So:

- **No new finding kind**, no observation-that-is-not-a-problem, no new severity.
- **The Settings → Warnings → Orders toggle "Units that do nothing" is unchanged** and still turns
  the whole check off.
- **No change to the problems chip, the diagnostics list, or the walk.** They count what the core
  emits, and the core simply emits one fewer.

## The test plan

Rust, `cargo test -p atlantis-core` (and whatever `pnpm run check:fast` runs for the crate —
`cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy` are in it). The tests are unit tests in `semantics.rs`'s own
module, beside the existing `unit-does-nothing` cases.

`pnpm run check:fast` before the PR. **The browser suites are not affected** — no UI changes — so
`test:smoke` is not needed locally; CI runs it anyway.

The turn-71 template assertion is the regression guard for the whole bead and already exists. Do not
change its expected count to make anything pass: if it moves, the change is wrong.

## User-facing decisions

Settled with the navigator on 2026-08-22 (`docs/ui/no-men-warning.html`). **Decided; raise
disagreements through the `human` queue rather than choosing differently.**

| # | Question | Chosen |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | What does "no men left" mean? | **A — no men, whatever else it holds.** The exemption keys on the men count alone: a unit with 7500 silver and no men is exempt, because it still cannot spend a month. Matches the reason exactly, and it is one number already on the model |
| 2 | Does the unit vanish, or say something else? | **i — silently skipped.** The check does not fire and the unit appears nowhere in the warnings |

**Option B (empty of everything) was declined**: it does not answer the ask, since a unit with silver
and no men still cannot spend a month.

**Option C (a threshold on what it holds) was declined**: a threshold is a number nobody can defend,
and it is two rules where one will do.

**Option ii (an observation line instead of a warning) was declined**, and the reason constrains
increment 3: it would add a kind of finding nothing else has, and every unit ever emptied would say
it for ever rather than only in the turn it happened. **Do not add a replacement line of any kind.**

The navigator accepted the stated cost of A and i together: a unit holding 7500 silver and no men now
says nothing at all.

## Out of scope

- **Every other check.** A men-less unit still earns every other finding it qualifies for.
- **`ah-dwk6`'s other behaviour** — what counts as spending the month, the `unread` rule, the
  finding's wording, the toggle.
- **A second exemption of any kind.** This bead adds one, for one stated reason.
- **Anything about how men are counted**, `men_estimated`, or `composition.rs`. Both fields are read
  as they are.
- **Any UI, settings or TypeScript change.** See increment 3.
- **Making the turn-71 template contain a men-less unit.** The fixture is committed and other beads
  pin counts against it; the new coverage is a unit-level test.

## Validation

1. `pnpm run check:fast` passes, including `cargo clippy` and `cargo fmt --check`.
2. A unit with no men and no month-long order produces **no** `unit-does-nothing` finding.
3. A unit with no men **holding silver and a horse** likewise produces none — decision A.
4. A unit whose men count is a **guess** (`men_estimated: true`) still warns. **Reverting only the
   `!men_estimated` half of the guard must make a test fail.**
5. The committed turn-71 template still produces **exactly ten** findings, with `unit-does-nothing`
   against 14451 and 13432 and nothing else.
6. A unit with one man and no month-long order still warns.
7. Settings → Warnings → Orders → "Units that do nothing" still turns the whole check off, and is
   still on by default.
8. No new finding code, no new severity, and no new line anywhere in the UI.

## Known traps

- **`with_men` does not touch `men_estimated`, and the default is `true`.** `Unit::default()` is
  `men: 0, men_estimated: true` (`report/model.rs:184-186`), and the helper at `semantics.rs:2756`
  sets only `men`. So a test written as `with_men(unit, 0)` has an **estimated** count, the exemption
  correctly does not fire, and the test fails for a reason that looks like the implementation is
  broken. Set `men_estimated = false` explicitly, or extend the helper — **and if you extend it,
  check its existing callers still mean what they said.**
- **`men == 0` alone is the wrong fix**, and it passes five of the six tests. Validation item 4 is
  the guard; write that test first.
- **`ah-dwk6` says there are no exemptions.** That is superseded by this bead. Do not "discover" the
  contradiction and hand the bead back — the *Context* section is the answer.
- **Do not change the turn-71 expected count.** It is ten, both pinned units have men, and a moved
  number means the exemption is firing where it should not.
- **Do not add a replacement line.** Option ii was declined by name; a "helpful" observation that the
  unit has no men is exactly what was rejected.
- **A false negative is worse than the false positive being fixed.** A warning that appears wrongly
  is noticed and complained about; one that fails to appear is not. That asymmetry is the whole
  reason for the `men_estimated` half of the guard.
- **Disk space.** Eleven of this repository's retrospectives name `scripts/diskPreflight.ts` refusing
  to start a bead below its 8 GB floor, and it can trip mid-`check:fast` as a failing *tooling* test
  that reads like a defect in the diff. This bead compiles Rust, which is the heaviest consumer.
  Safe offline reclaims: `~/.cargo/registry/src`, `target/debug/incremental`,
  `~/Library/Caches/Mozilla.sccache`.
acceptance_criteria:
- `pnpm run check:fast` passes, including `cargo clippy` and `cargo fmt --check`.
- A unit with no men and no month-long order produces NO `unit-does-nothing` finding.
- A unit with no men holding silver and a horse likewise produces none (decision A: the exemption keys on men alone).
- A unit whose men count is a GUESS (`men_estimated: true`) still warns. Reverting only the `!men_estimated` half of the guard MUST make a test fail.
- The committed turn-71 template still produces EXACTLY TEN findings, with `unit-does-nothing` against 14451 and 13432 and nothing else.
- A unit with one man and no month-long order still warns.
- Settings > Warnings > Orders > "Units that do nothing" still turns the whole check off and is still on by default.
- No new finding code, no new severity, and no new line anywhere in the UI.

title: Two units a month apart in study both read MINI 2
description:
The navigator's words, 2026-08-22:

  "it would be great to see the details of a skill in a unit's skill list as
  well as in the unit in hex. currently you only have e.g. 'mini 2', but there
  is a big differnce between mini2 (90) and mini2 (150). so I would add the
  (xxx)."

The point is progress. Two units both reading "MINI 2" can be a month apart in
study, and the level alone cannot say which is which.

## The two surfaces are NOT in the same state

Worth knowing before planning, because the bead is smaller than it reads:

UNITS IN HEX -- genuinely missing the number.
  packages/shared/src/workspace/UnitTableDock.tsx:687
    const skills = unit.skills.map((skill) => `${skill.tag} ${skill.level}`).join(", ");
  This is the "mini 2" the navigator describes.

THE UNIT PANE -- already shows the points, in a different format.
  packages/shared/src/workspace/UnitPanel.tsx:137
    value={`${skill.level} · ${skill.points}`}
  So the unit pane renders "2 · 90", not "2". Either the navigator did not
  notice it, or the middot form does not read as the same fact as the "(90)"
  the report itself uses -- which is itself worth asking about.

## The data is already there

No parser work. crates/core/src/report/model.rs:103 documents the model as "A
skill with its level and accumulated study points, as in `stealth [STEA] 5
(450)`", and packages/shared/src/turnDiff.ts:99 already formats skills as
`${skill.name} ${skill.level} (${skill.points})`.

So there are now three renderings of one fact in the app: "TAG level" (units in
hex), "level · points" (unit pane), and "name level (points)" (turn diff). The
game's own reports use "name [TAG] level (points)".

## For the planner

The navigator asked for "(xxx)", which matches the report's own notation and the
turn-diff's. Worth settling with them:

  - whether the unit pane's middot moves to parentheses so all three agree, or
    stays as it is because the pane is a label/value layout where a bracket
    reads oddly;
  - whether the units-in-hex column has room for the number on every skill, or
    whether that cell gets long enough to need a different treatment -- it is a
    comma-joined list of every skill the unit has, inside a table column the
    player can already resize and reorder (ah-1owr.1/.2/.3).
design:
## Context

The navigator's words, 2026-08-22:

> *"it would be great to see the details of a skill in a unit's skill list as well as in the unit in
> hex. currently you only have e.g. 'mini 2', but there is a big difference between mini2 (90) and
> mini2 (150). So I would add the (xxx)."*

**The point is progress.** Two units both reading `MINI 2` can be a month apart in study, and the
level alone cannot say which is which.

**No parser work.** `crates/core/src/report/model.rs:103` documents the model as *"A skill with its
level and accumulated study points, as in `stealth [STEA] 5 (450)`"*. The data is already there.

### One fact, five spellings — all verified on `origin/main`

| Where | Renders | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Units in hex** | `MINI 2` | `UnitTableDock.tsx:687` |
| **Unit pane** | `2 · 90` | `UnitPanel.tsx:137` |
| **Unit tooltip** | `2` | `unitTooltip.ts:50` — `String(skill.level)` |
| Turn diff | `mining 2 (90)` | `turnDiff.ts:99` — **already right** |
| The game's own report | `observation [OBSE] 2 (90)` | the `.rep` file |

**The bead counted three. There are four in-app**, and the one it missed is the one that matters
most — see below.

### 🔴 The tooltip is not optional, and this is the finding that shapes the bead

`UnitTableDock.tsx` says of the skills cell:

> *"The cell truncates, so the whole label belongs in the tooltip whether or not it also changed"*

**The cell truncates, and the tooltip is the designed fallback — and the tooltip shows the level with
no points at all.** So adding `(90)` to the cell without adding it to the tooltip makes a unit with
several skills **more** likely to have the number truncated away, and **still** unable to recover it
on hover. **That is worse than today for exactly the units a player is comparing.**

Branch from `origin/main`.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### 1. Units in hex — `UnitTableDock.tsx:687`

```ts
const skills = unit.skills.map((skill) => `${skill.tag} ${skill.level} (${skill.points})`).join(", ");
```

The navigator's choice, and it matches both the report's own notation and `turnDiff.ts:99`.

### 2. 🔴 The tooltip gains the points — `unitTooltip.ts:50`

```ts
value: `${skill.level} (${skill.points})`
```

**Forced by §1**, not a nicety: the cell truncates *into* this tooltip by design, so the fallback must
carry at least what the cell does.

### 3. The unit pane — `UnitPanel.tsx:137`

```ts
value={`${skill.level} (${skill.points})`}
```

The navigator chose to make them agree. **They confirmed the middot was not reading as the same
fact** — the pane already showed `2 · 90` and did not answer the question they were asking — which is
evidence about the notation rather than the data, and is why this is a consistency fix rather than a
one-line one.

### 4. The column width does **not** change

`unitTable.ts:312` gives skills `220 / 1344`, and its comment is explicit:

> *"A player who never drags must see no difference at all, so these are a restatement of the Tailwind
> width classes they replace rather than a new choice."*

**Widening the default would break that promise for every column**, since the shares are relative.
The content is longer and will truncate sooner — **and that is what §2 is for.** The column is
user-resizable (ah-1owr.2) and reorderable (ah-1owr.3), so a player who wants it wider has it.

**Do not bump `DEFAULT_COLUMN_SHARES`.**

### 5. Consider one formatter, but do not force it

Four sites now format a skill, and three will agree. **If a shared helper falls out naturally, take
it** — but `turnDiff.ts` uses `skill.name` where the others use `skill.tag`, and the tooltip splits
label from value, so a helper that serves all four may take more parameters than it saves.
**The implementer's call**, and either way is acceptable if the four agree on `(points)`.

### 6. Unchanged

`turnDiff.ts:99` is already correct. The parser, the model, the column order and every other cell.

## Increments

1. **The hex list shows progress.**
   RED: `unitTable` / `UnitTableDock` tests — a unit with `MINI 2 (90)` renders that; two units at the
   same level and different points **render differently**. That second assertion is the bead.
   GREEN: `:687`.
2. **The tooltip does not lose it.**
   RED: `unitTooltip` tests — the value carries level and points.
   GREEN: `:50`.
3. **The pane agrees.**
   RED: `UnitPanel` tests — `2 (90)`, not `2 · 90`.
   GREEN: `:137`.
4. **Nothing else moved.**
   RED: `turnDiff`'s existing tests, and the column-share tests.
   GREEN: nothing — **if a column-share test fails, the width was changed and it must not be.**

## The test plan

| Test | Where | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| **two units at the same level, different points, render differently** | `UnitTableDock` tests | the bead |
| the hex list renders `TAG level (points)` | same | §1 |
| **the tooltip carries level and points** | `unitTooltip` tests | 🔴 §2 |
| the unit pane renders `level (points)` | `UnitPanel` tests | §3 |
| `turnDiff` still renders `name level (points)` | existing | **unchanged** |
| **`DEFAULT_COLUMN_SHARES` is unchanged** | `unitTable` tests | §4 |
| a unit with no skills renders nothing odd | all three | the empty case |
| a skill with 0 points renders `(0)`, not blank | all three | zero is a real value |

**Suites:** `pnpm run check:fast`. **No Rust change** — the model already carries points.

## User-facing decisions

Interviewed with the navigator on 2026-08-22 over `.cerebro/scratch/ah-ded4-skill-points.html`. The
mockup is committed to `docs/ui/`.

**Q1 — units in hex.** Chosen: **`MINI 2 (90)`**, matching the report's own notation and the turn
diff. Accepted cost: the content is longer in a fixed-width, truncating column. Rejected: **points on
hover only**, which leaves two units reading `MINI 2` looking identical until each is hovered — the
problem as reported.

**Q2 — the unit pane's middot.** Chosen: **make all of them agree on `(points)`.** The pane already
showed `2 · 90`; the navigator confirmed that had not told them what `(90)` would have, so the
notation was the problem rather than the data. Accepted cost: a surface they did not complain about
changes. Rejected: **leaving the middot**, which would keep three spellings of one fact and leave the
pane on the one the game does not use.

**Not asked** (architecture, forced by the code): **the tooltip must gain points too**, because the
cell truncates into it by design; and **the column width must not change**, because
`DEFAULT_COLUMN_SHARES` promises a player who never drags sees no difference.

## Out of scope

- **Widening the skills column** or any `DEFAULT_COLUMN_SHARES` value.
- **`turnDiff.ts`**, already correct.
- **The parser and the model** — the data is there.
- **Showing the skill's *name* in the hex list.** The report writes `name [TAG] level (points)`; this
  keeps the tag, which is what the column has room for.
- **ah-udff**, the other bead filed today.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
```

Then by hand, with a real report:

1. Open the units-in-hex table and find **two units with the same skill at the same level**. They must
   now read differently — `MINI 2 (90)` and `MINI 2 (150)`. **This is the acceptance**, and it is the
   thing that was impossible before.
2. **Hover a unit whose skills cell is truncated** and confirm the tooltip shows the points. This is
   the case that would otherwise be worse than today.
3. Open the unit pane for the same unit: `2 (90)`, not `2 · 90`.
4. Open the turn diff and confirm it is unchanged.
5. Confirm the **skills column is exactly as wide as it was** — a player who never drags must see the
   same layout. Then drag it wider and confirm the full text appears.
6. Find a unit with **many skills** and confirm the cell truncates gracefully and the tooltip carries
   the whole list.
7. Find a skill at **0 points**, if the report has one: it must read `(0)`, not blank.

## Known traps

- **🔴 The tooltip must gain the points.** The skills cell truncates *into* it by design
  (`UnitTableDock.tsx`'s own comment), and it currently shows the bare level. Adding points to the
  cell alone makes a many-skilled unit **worse** than today: more truncation, and the number still
  unreachable.
- **🔴 Do not widen the skills column.** `DEFAULT_COLUMN_SHARES` is documented as a restatement of the
  shipped widths so *"a player who never drags must see no difference at all"*, and the shares are
  relative — widening one narrows the rest.
- **There are four in-app renderings, not the three the bead names.** `unitTooltip.ts:50` is the
  fourth and the easiest to miss.
- **`turnDiff.ts` is already right.** Changing it to match would be churn and would break its tests.
- **Zero is a real value.** `(0)` must render; a falsy check would blank it and lose exactly the
  distinction this bead is about.
- **The pane changed for a reason.** The navigator confirmed `2 · 90` did not read as the same fact.
  Do not "restore" the middot on the grounds that it already showed the number.
acceptance_criteria:
- The units-in-hex list renders `TAG level (points)` - "MINI 2 (90)" - matching the report's own notation and turnDiff's. Two units at the same level with different points RENDER DIFFERENTLY; that assertion is the bead.
- THE TOOLTIP GAINS THE POINTS (unitTooltip.ts:50, currently `String(skill.level)`). This is forced, not optional: UnitTableDock's own comment says "the cell truncates, so the whole label belongs in the tooltip", so adding points to the cell alone makes a many-skilled unit WORSE than today - more truncation and the number still unreachable.
- The unit pane (UnitPanel.tsx:137) renders `level (points)`, not `level · points`. The navigator confirmed the middot had not told them what "(90)" would have, so the notation was the problem rather than the data.
- DEFAULT_COLUMN_SHARES IS UNCHANGED. Its comment promises "a player who never drags must see no difference at all", and the shares are relative so widening one narrows the rest. The column is already user-resizable and reorderable.
- turnDiff.ts:99 is already correct and is NOT changed.
- A skill at 0 points renders "(0)", not blank - a falsy check would lose exactly the distinction this bead is about.
- A unit with no skills renders nothing odd on any of the three surfaces.
- No parser or model change - crates/core/src/report/model.rs:103 already carries points.
- `pnpm run check:fast` passes.

title: A dry run of prepare-worktree resets and cleans the verifier's working tree
description:
Noticed while writing ah-qled.11's consumer fixture, which needed a dry run to assert the no-install branch.

scripts/prepare-worktree's header says --dry-run will 'print the commands that would run, run none of them, and still print the path and sha'. In the body, dry_run is only consulted around the install and prewarm commands: the git worktree add (or the fetch/reset/clean of the reusable detached tree), the submodule update and the rev-parse all run unconditionally. So a --dry-run creates a real branch and a real worktree on disk.

That is the opposite of what a caller reading the header expects, and it is the one mode an agent is told to use to 'say what it is about to do in a tree it does not own'.

## Acceptance
- Either --dry-run creates nothing and prints what it would have run, or the header stops promising that it creates nothing - decided deliberately, not by whichever is easier.
- tests/prepare-worktree.sh asserts whichever was chosen.
design:
## Context

`scripts/prepare-worktree`'s header promises `--dry-run` will *"print the commands that would run,
**run none of them**, and still print the path and sha"*.

**`dry_run` is consulted in exactly two places** — `:155` and `:166`, around the install and prewarm
commands. **Everything else runs unconditionally:**

```
:123  git -C "$consumer" worktree add -b "$branch" "$abs_path" "$from_ref"   creates a branch AND a tree
:126  git -C "$consumer" worktree add --detach "$abs_path" "$from_ref"       creates a tree
:134  git -C "$abs_path" reset --hard "$from_ref"                            🔴 DESTRUCTIVE
:135  git -C "$abs_path" clean -fd                                           🔴 DESTRUCTIVE
:139  git -C "$abs_path" submodule update --init --recursive
:176  git -C "$abs_path" rev-parse --short HEAD                              reads a tree that must exist
```

### 🔴 It is worse than the bead says: a dry run does not merely create, it destroys

The bead reports that `--dry-run` *"creates a real branch and a real worktree"*. **On the reuse path
it also `reset --hard`s and `clean -fd`s an existing tree** (`:134-135`) — and the tree that path
exists for is **Psylocke's**. So `prepare-worktree --path .cerebro/worktrees/psylocke --dry-run`
**wipes the verifier's working tree**, having promised to run nothing.

**This is the one mode an agent is told to use *"when an agent says what it is about to do in a tree
it does not own"*.**

**A secondary cost**: the branch and worktree a dry run leaves behind make a later *real* run refuse —
`:98`, *"already exists — refusing to reuse it for a new branch"* — so a dry run can block the bead it
was describing.

### The choice the bead asks for, decided

> *"Either `--dry-run` creates nothing and prints what it would have run, or the header stops
> promising that it creates nothing — decided deliberately, not by whichever is easier."*

**`--dry-run` creates nothing.** Weakening the header would leave a mode whose name says one thing
and whose behaviour does another, in a script that resets working trees — and every caller reaching
for it is reaching for safety. **The header is right; the body is wrong.**

Cerebro change, so **two PRs**.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### 1. Every mutation goes behind the flag

`:123`, `:126`, `:134`, `:135`, `:139` — each printed rather than run when `dry_run` is set, in the
same shape `:155` and `:166` already use, so there is one idiom in the file rather than two.

### 2. The path and sha are still printed — from the ref, not from a tree

`:176` reads `HEAD` of a tree that, under a correct dry run, does not exist. **The answer is
available without one:**

```bash
git -C "$consumer" rev-parse --short "$from_ref"
```

That is **the sha the tree *would* be at** — which is what a caller planning work wants, and for the
reuse path it is also what the tree would hold *after* the reset it is being told about. **Say that in
a comment**, because "the sha" quietly changing meaning between modes is the kind of thing that reads
as a bug later.

**The path-and-sha line on stdout is the contract every caller parses**, and it must survive.

### 3. The checks still run — they are the point

A dry run must still **validate and refuse**:

- the `--path` outside `.cerebro/worktrees/` refusal;
- `:98`, *"already exists — refusing to reuse it for a new branch"*;
- `:107-108`, *"is on branch X, not detached — refusing to reset a tree that may hold work"*.

**These are reads, not writes**, and reporting them is most of a dry run's value. **A dry run that
skips the refusals is as useless as one that mutates.**

### 4. What must not change

Real runs. `--branch`, `--from`, the detached-tree reuse, the exit-2 messages, and the stdout
contract are all unchanged when `dry_run` is unset.

## Increments

1. **A dry run creates nothing.**
   RED: `tests/` — `--dry-run --branch` on a fresh path: **no worktree, no branch**, and
   `git worktree list` is unchanged.
   GREEN: guard `:123`, `:126`, `:139`.
2. **🔴 A dry run destroys nothing.**
   RED: `--dry-run` against an existing detached tree **with a scratch file in it**: the file
   survives, the tree's HEAD is unmoved. **This is the one that matters** — it is the verifier's tree
   in real life.
   GREEN: guard `:134`, `:135`.
3. **The contract survives.**
   RED: a dry run still prints **one line: path and sha**, and the sha is `from_ref`'s.
   GREEN: the `rev-parse` change.
4. **The refusals still fire.**
   RED: dry runs of each refusal case exit 2 with the same message as a real run.
   GREEN: nothing — these are reads and should already pass. **If any does not, a check was guarded
   as though it were a mutation.**
5. **Real runs are untouched.**
   RED: the existing tests.
   GREEN: nothing.

**In `atlantis-hud` (PR two):** the submodule pin bump. **PR one merges first.**

## The test plan

| Test | Where | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| **`--dry-run --branch` creates no worktree and no branch** | `tests/prepare-worktree*.sh` | the bead |
| **🔴 `--dry-run` on a detached tree preserves an untracked file and HEAD** | same | the destructive half |
| a dry run prints path and sha, sha from `from_ref` | same | the contract |
| **each refusal still fires under `--dry-run`** | same | a dry run must still check |
| the commands it would run are printed to stderr | same | the header's promise |
| real `--branch`, `--from` and reuse runs are unchanged | same | **no regression** |
| every existing test | `tests/*.sh` | **unchanged** |

**Suites:** `for t in tests/*.sh`.

## User-facing decisions

**None to ask for**, but one is recorded because the bead demanded it be deliberate:
**`--dry-run` is made honest rather than the header weakened.** A mode named for describing that
instead resets working trees is a footgun, and the callers reaching for it are reaching for safety —
including three planned beads whose validation steps say *"`--dry-run` first, every time"*.

**Decided here** (architecture): taking the sha from `from_ref` rather than dropping it from the
output, so the stdout contract survives; and **keeping every refusal live under `--dry-run`**, since
they are reads and are most of what a dry run is for.

## Out of scope

- **`prune-worktrees.sh`'s `--dry-run`**, which I checked while planning this: every `rm -rf` and
  `worktree remove` is behind its flag (`:278`, `:332`, `:383`), and the one unguarded call
  (`git worktree prune`, `:341`) only clears registrations whose directory is already gone, which its
  header states deliberately. **It is honest; this bug is one script, not a pattern.**
- **What `prepare-worktree` does on a real run.**
- **ah-qled.2**, which added `--dry-run`'s install and prewarm handling — **rebase if both are in
  flight**.

## Validation

In `.claude/cerebro`:

```bash
for t in tests/*.sh; do bash "$t" || echo "FAILED: $t"; done
```

Then by hand — **and step 2 before anything else, because today's behaviour is destructive**:

1. `git worktree list` and note it.
2. **In a scratch clone, not this one**: make a detached tree, drop an untracked file in it, run
   `prepare-worktree --path … --dry-run`, and confirm **the file is still there and HEAD has not
   moved.** On today's code it is gone. Do **not** rehearse this against
   `.cerebro/worktrees/psylocke`.
3. `prepare-worktree --path .cerebro/worktrees/scratch --branch scratch-test --dry-run` in this
   repo — then `git worktree list` and `git branch --list scratch-test`: **neither must exist.**
4. Confirm the same command printed **one line on stdout**: a path and a short sha, and that the sha
   matches `git rev-parse --short origin/<default branch>`.
5. Confirm the commands it would have run appear on **stderr**, so a caller capturing stdout gets the
   contract line alone.
6. Run each refusal under `--dry-run` — a path outside `.cerebro/worktrees/`, an existing path with
   `--branch`, a tree on a branch — and confirm each **still exits 2 with its usual message**.
7. Do a **real** run and confirm it behaves exactly as before.

## Known traps

- **🔴 `:134-135` are the dangerous ones.** `reset --hard` and `clean -fd` mean today's `--dry-run`
  **destroys** on the reuse path — and that path exists for the verifier's tree. Guarding only the
  `worktree add` calls fixes the bead's headline and leaves the worst of it.
- **Never rehearse this against `.cerebro/worktrees/psylocke`.** Use a scratch clone; the current
  behaviour is exactly what you are testing for.
- **The refusals are reads and must keep firing.** Guarding them as though they were mutations makes a
  dry run agree with everything, which is worse than one that mutates because it looks fine.
- **The stdout line is a contract.** Callers parse the path and sha; dropping it under `--dry-run`
  breaks them as surely as the mutation does.
- **The sha means something slightly different in dry-run** — the ref's, not an existing tree's.
  Comment it, or it reads as a bug later.
- **Commands go to stderr**, like everything else this script narrates, so stdout stays the contract.
- **ah-qled.2 touches the same flag.** Rebase.
acceptance_criteria:
- `--dry-run` creates nothing and DESTROYS NOTHING. The header is kept and the body made honest, deliberately: a mode named for describing that instead resets working trees is a footgun, and three planned beads tell implementers to dry-run first.
- Every mutation is guarded, not just the two the bead names: :123 and :126 (worktree add), :139 (submodule update), and CRITICALLY :134 (reset --hard) and :135 (clean -fd). The reset/clean path exists for Psylocke's tree, so today `--dry-run --path .cerebro/worktrees/psylocke` WIPES THE VERIFIER'S TREE.
- A dry run against an existing detached tree preserves an untracked file in it and leaves HEAD unmoved.
- The stdout contract survives: one line, path and short sha. The sha comes from `git rev-parse --short "$from_ref"` - the sha the tree WOULD be at - with a comment saying so, since its meaning differs slightly between modes.
- Every refusal STILL FIRES under --dry-run and exits 2 with its usual message: --path outside .cerebro/worktrees/, "already exists - refusing to reuse it for a new branch", "is on branch X, not detached". These are reads, and reporting them is most of a dry run's value. A dry run that agrees with everything is worse than one that mutates, because it looks fine.
- The commands that would have run are printed to STDERR, so a caller capturing stdout gets the contract line alone.
- Real runs are unchanged: --branch, --from, detached-tree reuse, exit-2 messages and the stdout contract.
- Testing is done in a SCRATCH CLONE, never against .cerebro/worktrees/psylocke - the current behaviour is exactly what is being tested for.
- prune-worktrees.sh's own --dry-run was checked while planning and is honest (every rm -rf and worktree remove is behind its flag); this bug is one script, not a pattern.
- ah-qled.2 touches the same flag; rebase if both are in flight.

title: A bead list can silently answer about the wrong repository and read as a quiet day
description:
Found by Forge while reading for ah-qled.9, and split out of it: this is a defect, not a customisation.

`scripts/work-beads:67` invokes `bd` with no `-C`:

    argv=(bd list --status "$status" --exclude-type "$excluded_csv" --json)
