`needs mining 3 to build a Mine`; (C) two different messages for a shortfall and for no skill at all.
**Chosen: A.** It carries everything needed to act on it in one line and reads the same whether the unit is
one level short or has none of the skill. Rejected B because a level-2 unit and a level-0 unit would look
identical; rejected C because two shapes in one problem list read as two different warnings, for two strings
and two branches that say the same thing.

**Helpers.** Offered: warn on a helper lacking the skill; do not; or establish the rule first.
**Chosen: warn on helpers too.** A helper contributes its month, and a helper that cannot contribute has
wasted one. The existing `build-help-not-building` check covers the other helper mistake and this sits beside
it.

**The settings entry.** Approved as proposed: group `Building`, title **`Building without the skill`**,
description **`A BUILD order for a structure the unit has not the skill or level to build.`**, defaulting on.

### Strings, verbatim

| Where | String |
|---|---|
| Message, unit has some of the skill | `cannot build <article> <Kind>: needs <skill> <n>, has <skill> <m>` |
| Message, unit has none | `cannot build <article> <Kind>: needs <skill> <n>, has no <skill>` |
| Message, helper | the same, with `cannot help build` in place of `cannot build` |
| Settings title | `Building without the skill` |
| Settings description | `A BUILD order for a structure the unit has not the skill or level to build.` |
| Code | `build-without-skill` |

`<skill>` is the ruleset's own lower-case name — `mining`, `building`, `horse training` — not the tag.

## Out of scope

- **Ships.** `shipbuilding [SHIP] 1: Longships [LONG] from 10 wood` states a requirement in the same sentence,
  but ships are items, not buildings, and `ah-bwly.1` deliberately does not carry a requirement for them.
  A `BUILD` of a ship is therefore not judged. Say so in the commit rather than leaving it looking accidental.
- **Whether the unit has the materials**, or enough men, or is in the right terrain. Different checks, and
  `not-enough-items` already exists for the first.
- **Roads.** They are buildings and do carry a requirement (`building` 2), so they come along for free.
  Nothing special is needed.
- **Any change to `check_building`, `check_building_outside` or `check_build_help`.** This is a fourth check
  beside them, not a branch of any of them — the same reasoning `check_building_outside`'s own doc gives for
  not living inside `check_building`: *"hosting this there would silently switch it off with a different
  toggle."*
- **Teaching the check about study**: a unit studying the skill this month still cannot build this month.
  No lookahead.

## Validation

```bash
cargo test -p atlantis-hud-core
pnpm run check:fast
pnpm run test:smoke
```

All green. Then look at it:

1. Load the fixture report, find or write a unit with `mining` below 3 and give it `BUILD` inside a Mine.
   Confirm the warning appears in the region pane's problem list and in the map-wide problems popover, reading
   exactly `cannot build a Mine: needs mining 3, has mining 1`.
2. Raise that unit's skill in the report fixture, or pick a unit that has it, and confirm the warning goes.
3. Give a unit `BUILD HELP <n>` where the target builds something the helper lacks the skill for; confirm the
   helper is warned with `cannot help build …`.
4. Settings → Warnings → Building: confirm the fourth toggle appears, is on, and that turning it off clears
   the warning without touching the other three.
5. Confirm an `Inn` reads `an Inn`, not `a Inn`.

## Known traps

- **`ah-vkut`'s retrospective is required reading.** A default-on check that fires on a common order shape
  breaks unrelated fixtures that used that shape as scenery. Fix them with a `check_ignoring_*` helper, never
  by weakening the check.
- **`codes::ALL` must be appended to and its length bumped**, and the generated TypeScript regenerated. The
  `generated_ts` test fails until you do, which is the intended reminder.
- **`structure_after_orders`, never `unit.structure_id`.** `ENTER` then `BUILD` is the correct way to write
  the order, and reading the report's structure would warn about the correct thing.
- **`Some(None)` from the structure lookup means the report does not describe that structure** — stay silent.
  `check_magic_study` (semantics.rs:1764-1782) has the exact `match` to copy.
- **`skill_level` returns 0 for a skill the unit lacks**, which makes the comparison uniform — but the
  *message* must still distinguish the two cases, since `has building 0` reads wrong.
- **The map is keyed upper-cased.** A report says `Mine`; the catalogue holds `MINE`. `mage_capacity`
  (rules.rs:673) is the precedent for the accessor and for the `to_ascii_uppercase()`.
- **22 of 58 buildings have no requirement.** Silence for those is correct behaviour, not a gap — including
  everything the page says cannot be built by players.
- **Do not let `unit <n>` appear in the message.** `ProblemMessage` turns that pattern into a link.
- **`crates/core/src/movement/fleet.rs` has a second copy of the structure-after-orders logic**
  (`OrderedUnits::structure_of`), which `structure_after_orders`' own doc warns must be kept in step. This
  bead does not change either, but do not "tidy" one into the other while passing.
- **Work in a worktree under `.cerebro/worktrees/`**, never the main checkout, per `CLAUDE.md`.

title: Scrape the skill and level each structure needs to be built
description:
Establishing groundwork for ah-bwly.2, which cannot be built without it.

The buildings catalogue says what a structure costs and what it is made of, but not what skill builds it or at what level. That is the whole of this bead.

**The rules page is not needed.** Planning established that the DATA page already carries both facts, in a place the parser is already standing. `parseBuildingReference`'s pass two reads `A unit with this skill may BUILD <structures>` out of each SKILL's entry, and uses it for cost and materials only - but the sentence lives inside an entry of the form `mining [MINI] 3: ...`, so the skill tag and the minimum level are both in hand at that moment and are simply dropped.

What the page states, verbatim, from the committed fixture:

  mining [MINI] 3        a Mine, an Arcane Mine
  mining [MINI] 5        an Alchemist Lab
  lumberjack [LUMB] 3    a Timber Yard, a Forest Preserve
  lumberjack [LUMB] 5    a Sacred Grove
  quarrying [QUAR] 3     a Quarry, a Mystic Quarry
  hunting [HUNT] 3       a Trapping Hut
  hunting [HUNT] 5       a Trapping Lodge
  herb lore [HERB] 3     a Faerie Ring
  horse training [HORS] 3  a Stables, an Oasis
  horse training [HORS] 5  a Mythic Stables
  farming [FARM] 3       a Farm, a Ranch
  building [BUIL] 1      a Tower, a Fort, a Stockade
  building [BUIL] 2      a Castle, the roads
  building [BUIL] 3      a Citadel, a Magical Tower, a Magical Fortress, an Inn, a Temple
  building [BUIL] 4      a Magical Castle
  building [BUIL] 5      a Magical Citadel, a Black Keep

This is strictly more than the rules page's two tables, which between them name only Tower, Fort, Castle, Citadel, Stockade and the ten plain trade structures - no Arcane Mine, no Sacred Grove, no Black Keep, no roads.

A structure named in neither place carries no requirement, and that must read as 'the catalogue does not say' rather than 'no skill needed' - the same absence-is-not-a-claim rule the rest of BuildingEntry already follows.
design:
## Context

`ah-bwly.2` wants to warn a player whose unit is told to BUILD something it has not the skill for. It cannot,
because the buildings catalogue says what a structure costs and what it is made of but not **what skill builds
it, or at what level**. Putting those two fields in the ruleset is the whole of this bead. Nothing a player
sees changes.

**The rules page is not needed, and this is the finding that shapes the bead.** The parent bead suspected the
requirement was stated only on the rules page and asked that it be established before anything was promised.
It was, and the answer is better than feared: **the data page already carries both facts, in a place the
parser is already standing.**

`parseBuildingReference`'s pass two (`packages/ruleset/src/data.ts`) walks every entry paragraph looking for
`A unit with this skill may BUILD <structures>.` and uses it to fill `cost` and `materials`. That sentence
lives inside a **skill's** entry, which opens `mining [MINI] 3: …` — so the skill tag and the minimum level are
already in the string the loop is holding, and are simply thrown away.

What the committed fixture states, measured during planning:

```
mining [MINI] 3          a Mine, an Arcane Mine
mining [MINI] 5          an Alchemist Lab
lumberjack [LUMB] 3      a Timber Yard, a Forest Preserve
lumberjack [LUMB] 5      a Sacred Grove
quarrying [QUAR] 3       a Quarry, a Mystic Quarry
hunting [HUNT] 3         a Trapping Hut
hunting [HUNT] 5         a Trapping Lodge
herb lore [HERB] 3       a Faerie Ring
horse training [HORS] 3  a Stables, an Oasis
horse training [HORS] 5  a Mythic Stables
farming [FARM] 3         a Farm, a Ranch
building [BUIL] 1        a Tower, a Fort, a Stockade
building [BUIL] 2        a Castle, the roads
building [BUIL] 3        a Citadel, a Magical Tower, a Magical Fortress, an Inn, a Temple
building [BUIL] 4        a Magical Castle
building [BUIL] 5        a Magical Citadel, a Black Keep
```

**36 of the 58 buildings carry a requirement, and no structure is named by more than one skill** — both
measured against the fixture, and both worth a test.

This is strictly more than the rules page offers. Its two tables between them name only Tower, Fort, Castle,
Citadel, Stockade and ten plain trade structures — no Arcane Mine, no Sacred Grove, no Black Keep, no roads.
So parsing the rules page would be more work for less data.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### Changed — `packages/ruleset/src/data.ts`

**`BuildingEntry` gains two optional fields**, following the absence-is-not-a-claim discipline every other
field in that type already documents:

```ts
export type BuildingEntry = {
  description: string;
  produces?: string;
  size?: number;
  cost?: number;
  materials?: string[];
  mages: number;

  /**
   * The tag of the skill that builds it - `BUIL`, `MINI`. Absent for a structure no skill's entry
   * names, which is 22 of the 58: a lair, a ruin, the two Lairs, and everything the page says
   * "cannot be built by players". Absent means the catalogue does not say, never that no skill is
   * needed.
   */
  buildSkill?: string;
  /** The lowest level of `buildSkill` that can build it. Absent exactly when `buildSkill` is. */
  buildLevel?: number;
};
```

**The two fields are written together or not at all.** A `buildSkill` without a `buildLevel` is not a state
the page can produce and must not be one the type can hold in practice; assert it in a test rather than
encoding it in the type, which would cost a discriminated union for no gain.

**`parseBuildingReference` pass two** is where they are filled. It currently iterates `paragraphs` and, for
each `A unit with this skill may BUILD …` statement, splits the clause list and writes `cost` and `materials`
onto the existing entry. Add, before the statement loop, a read of the paragraph's own opening:

```ts
const opening = paragraph.match(/^[^.:[\]]{1,40} \[([A-Z0-9]{2,6})\] (\d+): /);
```

That is `SKILL_OPENING`'s shape (`data.ts:335`) — **reuse the existing constant rather than writing a second
one**, exporting it if it is not already exported. Then, where `cost` and `materials` are written:

```ts
existing.cost = Number.parseInt(built[2], 10);
existing.materials = built[3]…;
if (opening) {
  existing.buildSkill = opening[1];
  existing.buildLevel = Number.parseInt(opening[2], 10);
}
```

**Do not restructure pass two.** It carries a hard-won comment about why the clause splitter splits only
before `a`/`an` plus a capital — *"the trailing `or stone [STON]` is another material for the Inn, not another
structure"* — and about ships carrying no article and so never matching. Both still hold and both are load
bearing.

### Changed — `crates/core/src/movement/rules.rs`

The Rust `BuildingEntry` mirrors the TypeScript one and gains the same two fields:

```rust
/// The tag of the skill that builds it. `None` for a structure no skill's entry names, and for a
/// ruleset cached before ah-bwly.1 - the catalogue not saying, never "no skill needed".
#[serde(default)]
pub build_skill: Option<String>,
/// The lowest level of `build_skill` that can build it.
#[serde(default)]
pub build_level: Option<i64>,
```

`#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]` on the struct maps these to `buildSkill` / `buildLevel` automatically.

**`BuildingEntry` deliberately does not `deny_unknown_fields`** — its own doc comment at
`crates/core/src/movement/rules.rs:337-339` says why: *"a ruleset cached before ah-9js carries a `name` and a
single `material` string, and refusing those would turn an old cache into a failed load."* So the JSON could
carry these fields before Rust knew them. Add them anyway and in the same bead: `ah-bwly.2` reads them from
Rust, and a field only one side knows about is exactly the drift this catalogue has had before.

**`Ruleset` itself does `deny_unknown_fields`** (`rules.rs:356`), so nothing may be added at the *top* level
without the struct changing in the same commit. Not an issue here — the change is inside `BuildingEntry` — but
worth knowing before reaching for a different shape.

Both fields are `Option` with `#[serde(default)]`, so every cached ruleset in the wild keeps loading.

### Regenerated — `config/public/ruleset.json`

```bash
pnpm --filter @atlantis/ruleset scrape -- \
  --rules tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-rules.html --data tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-data.html
```

The diff must be **additive only**: 36 buildings each gain `buildSkill` and `buildLevel`, and nothing else
changes. Any other difference means pass two was disturbed.

### Not changed

- `packages/ruleset/src/rules.ts`. The rules page is not parsed for this, for the reason in *Context*.
- `parseBuildingReference` pass one, which decides what a building is.
- Anything in `packages/shared` or the app. No player-visible surface; the consumer is `ah-bwly.2`.

### Where state lives

Nothing stateful. A scraper and a generated file.

## Increments

Each opens with the named failing test.

1. **The two fields are read.** `packages/ruleset/src/data.test.ts` →
   `"says which skill builds a structure, and at what level"`. Assert against a small hand-built page
   fragment: a `mining [MINI] 3:` entry naming a Mine yields `buildSkill: "MINI"`, `buildLevel: 3`.
2. **Absence stays absence.** Same file → `"leaves the requirement absent for a structure no skill builds"`.
   A structure present in pass one and named by no skill has neither field — not `null`, not `""`, not `0`.
3. **The catalogue as a whole.** `packages/ruleset/src/committed.test.ts` →
   `"names the skill and level for every structure a skill can build"`. Assert against the real committed
   file: exactly **36** buildings carry `buildSkill`, every one of them also carries `buildLevel`, every
   `buildSkill` is a key of `skills`, and every `buildLevel` is between 1 and that skill's `maxLevel`.
   Name three explicitly — `MINE` → `MINI` 3, `TOWER` → `BUIL` 1, `CITADEL` → `BUIL` 3.
4. **Rust reads it.** `crates/core/src/movement/rules.rs` tests → `"a building's build requirement survives a
   round trip"`, plus one asserting a ruleset **without** the fields still loads, which is the cached-ruleset
   case the `Option` exists for.
5. **Regenerate**, and confirm the diff is additive only.

## The test plan

| File | Pins |
|---|---|
| `packages/ruleset/src/data.test.ts` | increments 1, 2 |
| `packages/ruleset/src/committed.test.ts` | increment 3 |
| `crates/core/src/movement/rules.rs` (its `#[cfg(test)]` module) | increment 4 |

Increment 3 belongs in `committed.test.ts` deliberately: that file already carries two independent assertions
of exactly this kind — the twenty-six mundane skills, and the mage-seating buildings — and this is a third of
the same species. **Note that `ah-bet5` is planned against that file's tautology**; it adds a new
`pageGrammar.test.ts` and leaves `committed.test.ts` alone, so the two beads do not collide. If `ah-bet5`
merges first, consider whether increment 3 sits better in the new file — the rule it asserts is a page-derived
one — but do not block on that.

**Every existing test must still pass untouched.** 102 tests across five files pass in the ruleset package
today.

**Suites to run:** `pnpm run check:fast`, which covers the vitest suites, `cargo check --workspace` and
clippy. Nothing renders, so the browser suites are irrelevant.

## User-facing decisions

**None.** A player sees nothing: this adds two fields to a generated data file. Every decision about the
warning itself — its wording, its settings entry, when it fires — belongs to `ah-bwly.2` and is the
navigator's, as for every other advisory check.

## Out of scope

- **The warning.** `ah-bwly.2`, blocked on this bead.
- **Ships.** `shipbuilding [SHIP] 1: Longships [LONG] from 10 wood [WOOD]` states a requirement in the same
  sentence form, but ships are **items, not buildings**, and pass two's clause splitter deliberately never
  matches them — they carry no `a`/`an` article. Putting a build requirement on an `ItemEntry` is a different
  shape in a different type, and BUILD-a-ship is a case `ah-bwly.2` can decide it does not cover. **Say so in
  the commit** rather than leaving it looking accidental.
- **Roads.** They *are* buildings and do carry a requirement (`building [BUIL] 2`), so they come along for
  free. Nothing special is needed and nothing should be added for them.
- **The rules page tables.** Not parsed, for the reason in *Context*. If a future bead wants the material and
  cost figures cross-checked between the two pages, that is its own work and its own evidence.
- **Anything about what a structure produces**, which `ah-3cj4.1` already delivered.
- **Widening `deny_unknown_fields` or restructuring `Ruleset`.**

## Validation

```bash
pnpm --filter @atlantis/ruleset run test
pnpm run check:fast
```

Both green, with the 102 existing ruleset tests still passing.

Then confirm the regenerated file by hand:

```bash
git diff --stat config/public/ruleset.json
python3 -c "
import json;d=json.load(open('config/public/ruleset.json'))
b=d['buildings']
have=[k for k,v in b.items() if 'buildSkill' in v]
print(len(b),'buildings,',len(have),'with a build requirement')
print('MINE',b['MINE'].get('buildSkill'),b['MINE'].get('buildLevel'))
print('TOWER',b['TOWER'].get('buildSkill'),b['TOWER'].get('buildLevel'))
print('half-filled:',[k for k,v in b.items() if ('buildSkill' in v)!=('buildLevel' in v)])
"
```

It must print `58 buildings, 36 with a build requirement`, `MINE MINI 3`, `TOWER BUIL 1`, and an empty
half-filled list. Anything else and the parse is wrong.

**No person needs to look at a screen for this bead.** There is nothing to see.

## Known traps

- **The skill and the level come from the paragraph's own opening, not from the BUILD sentence.** The sentence
  says *what* is built; the entry header says *who by* and *at what level*. Reading only the sentence gets the
  structures and no requirement at all, which is the shape the parser has today.
- **Reuse `SKILL_OPENING`.** A second regex for the same thing is how the two drift apart, and the name bound
  is `[^.:[\]]{1,40}` for a documented reason — letting it wander across a full stop matches the tail of the
  previous sentence.
- **Absence must stay absent.** 22 of the 58 buildings have no requirement, including everything the page says
  *cannot be built by players*. Writing `null`, `0` or `""` turns "the catalogue does not say" into "no skill
  needed", which is exactly the claim `ah-3cj4.1` spent a bead removing from `size` and `cost`.
- **Never write one field without the other.** A `buildSkill` with no `buildLevel` would let a consumer read a
  requirement of level `undefined` and compare it against a unit's level as `NaN`, which is false for
  everything — a warning that silently never fires.
- **`Ruleset` in Rust has `deny_unknown_fields`; `BuildingEntry` deliberately does not.** Adding a field
  inside `BuildingEntry` is safe for old caches; adding one at the top level is not.
- **The regenerated JSON diff must be additive.** Pass two also writes `cost` and `materials`; a refactor that
  reorders or re-splits the clause list will move those too, and a large diff means the change was not the one
  intended.
- **No structure is named by two skills** on the current page — verified during planning. Do not add
  merge-or-keep-lowest logic for a case that does not exist; if the page ever grows one, the test in increment
  3 is what will say so.
- **Work in a worktree under `.cerebro/worktrees/`**, never the main checkout, per `CLAUDE.md`.

title: Every PR still runs apt to install browser libraries, on hit and miss alike
description:
Split out of ah-3c80, which bounds this exposure rather than removing it. File and rank together with it.

ah-3c80 gives the browser jobs a timeout-minutes, so a stalled apt step becomes a 15-minute failure instead of a 55-minute held runner. It does not stop apt running. Every browser job still installs Playwright's system libraries at run time - on a cache hit as well as a miss, because the browser caches and the libraries do not - so 100% of CI runs still touch the failure surface that stalled four times in five days.

Running the browser jobs in the official image instead bakes the libraries in and deletes both install steps:

    container: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v<version>-<distro>

Two things that need deciding rather than assuming, which is why this is its own bead:

- The image tag must track the pinned @playwright/test version, or the browser in the image and the client driving it drift apart. That wants a rule - a comment naming the pairing, a check that they match, or renovate config - not just a tag typed once.
- Running in a container changes the environment for every browser test: the user, the filesystem layout, the availability of anything the workflow currently assumes from ubuntu-latest. The desktop-shell smoke project and the pwa job both need looking at, and the native job - which uses xvfb and a webview and is NOT one of these jobs - must be left alone.

Do after ah-3c80's composite action lands: with the cache/install/install-deps trio in one place, this becomes a change to one file rather than three.
design:
## Context

`ah-3c80` bounded this exposure; it did not remove it. Its `timeout-minutes: 15` turns a stalled apt
step into a fifteen-minute failure instead of a fifty-five-minute held runner — but **apt still runs
on every browser job, on a cache hit as well as a miss**, because the browser caches and the system
libraries it links against do not. So 100% of CI runs still touch the step that stalled four times in
five days.

The official image bakes those libraries in and deletes both install steps.

**`ah-3c80` landed exactly as planned**, which makes this bead small: `.github/actions/playwright-browser/action.yml`
now holds the cache/install/install-deps trio once, and four workflows call it —
`ci.yml:327` (smoke), `ci.yml:383` (pwa), `deploy.yml:119`, `release.yml:311`.

### Two facts that decide this bead, both measured

**1. The version is not pinned, and has already drifted seven minors.** `package.json` declares
`"@playwright/test": "^1.55.0"`; `pnpm-lock.yaml` resolves **1.62.1**, and the locally installed
binary reports `Version 1.62.1`. A container tagged from the declared range would ship browsers seven
minor versions behind the client driving them. **So the image tag must track the *lockfile*, not
`package.json`** — and something must enforce that, or the next `pnpm update` desynchronises them
silently and the failure appears as a browser that will not launch.

**2. Only two of the four callers are browser jobs.** `deploy.yml` and `release.yml` install a Rust
toolchain (`dtolnay/rust-toolchain`), `wasm-pack` (`taiki-e/install-action`) and run
`pnpm run build:web` around their Playwright step. Containerising those means the Playwright image
must also carry Rust and wasm-pack, or those steps must install into the container — a much larger
change, on the **release path**, for a workflow that runs on a tag rather than on every PR.

**So this bead containerises `ci.yml`'s `smoke` and `pwa` only, and the composite action stays** for
the two callers that still need it. That is narrower than the bead's title promises, and the title
should change with it: apt stops running **on the PR path**, which is 4 of the 5 jobs per PR and the
whole of the measured cost, and continues to run on deploy and release.

Branch from `origin/main`; every line number here is that tree.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### 1. The two PR browser jobs run in the image — `.github/workflows/ci.yml`

On `smoke` (`:280`) and `pwa` (`:358`), beside the `timeout-minutes: 15` `ah-3c80` added:

```yaml
    # The libraries Playwright links against are baked into this image, so no apt runs here at all -
    # which is the failure `timeout-minutes` above exists to bound (ah-3c80, four stalls in five
    # days). The tag must match the version in pnpm-lock.yaml; `scripts/playwrightImage.test.ts`
    # fails the gate if they drift (ah-f9q9).
    container: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.62.1-noble
```

and **delete `- uses: ./.github/actions/playwright-browser`** from both (`:327`, `:383`) — the cache
step goes with it, since there is nothing left to cache.

**`timeout-minutes: 15` stays on both.** It now guards nothing known, which is the point: it costs
nothing and the next hang will not be the one anybody predicted.

**Verify the tag exists before relying on it.** `v1.62.1-noble` is the expected shape (Ubuntu 24.04);
if Playwright has moved to another distro suffix for this version, use whatever
`mcr.microsoft.com/playwright` actually publishes for 1.62.1 and put *that* in the test below.

### 2. Drift is caught at the gate, not in CI — `scripts/playwrightImage.test.ts` (new)

This is the durable half of the bead, and it runs in `check:fast` — no CI round trip:

```ts
/**
 * The container tag and the installed Playwright must be the same version.
 *
 * `package.json` declares a caret range (`^1.55.0`) and the lockfile resolves something quite
 * different (1.62.1 when this was written) - so the tag cannot be derived from the manifest, and a
 * `pnpm update` that moves the lockfile would otherwise leave CI running a browser the client
 * cannot drive. The failure that produces is "executable doesn't exist", in CI, on a change that
 * looks unrelated - which is exactly the shape ah-f9q9 was filed to stop (ah-3c80's four stalls).
 */
```

It reads the resolved `playwright` version out of `pnpm-lock.yaml`, reads every
`mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v<version>` out of `.github/workflows/`, and asserts **every tag equals
that version**. Two cases:

| Test | Pins |
|---|---|
| `every workflow's Playwright image matches the lockfile` | the coupling |
| `there is at least one image tag to check` | the test cannot pass by finding nothing — the failure mode a grep-based test always has |

The second case matters more than it looks: a regex that stops matching (a moved workflow, a renamed
image) would otherwise make this test pass forever while checking nothing.

### 3. What must **not** change

- **`deploy.yml` and `release.yml` keep the composite action.** They need Rust and wasm-pack; see
  *Context*. Leaving them is deliberate, not an oversight, and the action's doc comment should say so.
- **`native` is not containerised.** It runs xvfb and a native webview and has its own
  `timeout-minutes: 30` for a different hang surface (`ci.yml:438`).
- **The composite action itself is unchanged**, and stays. Its description says the trio was
  *"written out four times"*; that becomes two, so update the count.

## Increments

1. **The drift check exists first.**
   RED: `scripts/playwrightImage.test.ts` — it fails immediately, because no workflow yet names an
   image. That is the `there is at least one image tag to check` case earning its place before the
   feature exists.
   GREEN: after increment 2. Write the test first anyway: it is what makes the tag a decision rather
   than a literal.

2. **The two jobs move into the image.**
   RED: none expressible locally — CI configuration has no local suite.
   GREEN: `container:` on `smoke` and `pwa`, the two `uses:` lines deleted, and the drift test green.

3. **It actually works, which only CI can say.**
   RED: none. **This increment is the PR run**, and it is the whole risk of the bead. Watch for:
   - **Node.** The image ships its own; `actions/setup-node` with `node-version-file: .nvmrc` (22)
     may be redundant or may conflict. If it fails, drop the step for these two jobs and confirm the
     image's Node satisfies `.nvmrc`. **Say which in the PR.**
   - **pnpm.** `packageManager: pnpm@9.12.0` needs corepack enabled in the container.
   - **Permissions.** The image runs as root; a step that assumed the runner user may need adjusting.
   - **Caches.** `actions/cache` paths that were relative to the runner's home now resolve inside the
     container.
   Each of these is a normal container-migration snag; none is a reason to abandon the bead, and all
   of them are why `deploy.yml` and `release.yml` are out of scope.

4. **The exposure is gone from the PR path.**
   RED: none — the check. `git grep -n "playwright install" .github/workflows/ci.yml` must return
   **nothing**, and the composite action must have exactly two callers.

## The test plan

| Check | How |
|---|---|
| **the tag matches the lockfile** | `scripts/playwrightImage.test.ts`, in `check:fast` |
| the check cannot pass vacuously | its second case |
| no apt on the PR path | `git grep -n "playwright install" .github/workflows/ci.yml` returns nothing |
| the composite action still has two callers | `git grep -n playwright-browser .github` returns `deploy.yml` and `release.yml` |
| **the browser jobs pass** | all four `smoke` shards and `pwa` green on the PR, in both projects |
| they are not slower | compare durations against the baseline in `ah-3c80`'s plan: smoke 1–4 min, pwa under 1 |

**Suites:** `pnpm run check:fast` covers the drift test. Everything else is the PR's own CI run, and
this bead cannot be validated any other way.

## User-facing decisions

**None** — nothing reaches a player, and CI configuration has no interface, so no mockup.

**Decided by the planner, as tooling**, and each narrows the bead as filed:

- **Only `ci.yml`'s `smoke` and `pwa`.** `deploy.yml` and `release.yml` build Rust and wasm around
  their Playwright step, and containerising the release path speculatively is not worth it. The bead
  as filed says "apt never runs in CI"; after this it never runs **on the PR path**, which is where
  every measured stall happened.
- **The tag tracks `pnpm-lock.yaml`, not `package.json`.** The manifest's caret has already drifted
  seven minors from what is installed, so it cannot be the source of truth.
- **A gate-time test rather than a comment.** Forge's note asks for "a rule — a comment naming the
  pairing, a check that they match, or renovate config". A comment does not survive `pnpm update`; a
  test does, and it costs a millisecond.
- **`timeout-minutes` stays.** Defence in depth against the hang nobody has predicted yet.

## Out of scope

- **`deploy.yml` and `release.yml`.** Explained above. If someone later wants them containerised, it
  needs an image carrying Rust and wasm-pack, or those tools installed into the container — its own
  bead, with the release path's risk properly weighed.
- **The `native` job**, which is a different runtime entirely.
- **Pinning `@playwright/test` to an exact version in `package.json`.** Tempting, and unnecessary
  once the lockfile is the source of truth; it would also make routine upgrades noisier.
- **Renovate or any dependency-bot configuration.** The drift test is the mechanism this bead adds.
- **Removing `timeout-minutes`** now that the apt step is gone from these jobs.
- **Deleting the composite action.** Two callers still need it.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast                                              # the drift test
git grep -n "playwright install" .github/workflows/ci.yml        # must return nothing
git grep -n "playwright-browser" .github                         # deploy.yml and release.yml only
```

Then the PR run, read deliberately:

1. All four `smoke` shards and `pwa` green, in **both** projects.
2. **Their durations within a minute or two of the baseline** — smoke 1–4 minutes, pwa under one
   (measured in `ah-3c80`'s plan). A materially slower job means the image is doing work the runner
   was not, and is worth understanding before merging.
3. **No apt in the logs** of either job. That is the acceptance, and it is one search.
4. Break the coupling deliberately: change the tag to `v1.61.0-noble` and confirm
   `pnpm run check:fast` **fails naming the mismatch**. Restore it. A drift check nobody has watched
   reject anything is decoration.
5. Confirm `deploy.yml`'s and `release.yml`'s jobs are untouched in the diff.

## Known traps

- **The tag must match the *lockfile*, not `package.json`.** `^1.55.0` versus an installed 1.62.1 is
  the trap in one line, and it is already true today.
- **A grep-based test can pass by matching nothing.** The `at least one image tag` case is not
  padding; without it, a renamed image or moved workflow makes this test silently vacuous.
- **The image runs as root and ships its own Node.** `actions/setup-node` may be redundant or may
  fight it. Expect to adjust, and record what was needed — the next person containerising a job will
  read this bead.
- **`actions/cache` paths resolve inside the container.** Any cache keyed on a host path will quietly
  stop hitting, showing up as a slower job rather than a failure.
- **`deploy.yml` and `release.yml` are deliberately left alone**, and their Playwright step still runs
  apt. Anyone "finishing the job" by containerising them must first solve Rust and wasm-pack inside
  the image.
- **`native` must not be containerised.** xvfb, a native webview and a fixed port; a different hang
  surface with its own ceiling.
- **This bead can only be proven on CI.** There is no local equivalent, so the PR is the experiment —
  which is exactly why it is scoped to the two jobs whose failure costs a re-run rather than a
  release.
acceptance_criteria: ci.yml's smoke and pwa jobs run in the official Playwright container, tagged to match the Playwright version pnpm-lock.yaml resolves rather than the caret range package.json declares, and neither job uses the playwright-browser composite action any more - so git grep 'playwright install' over ci.yml returns nothing and no apt appears in either job's logs. Both keep timeout-minutes: 15. A new scripts/playwrightImage.test.ts runs in check:fast and fails when any workflow's image tag differs from the lockfile's resolved version, with a second case asserting it found at least one tag so it cannot pass vacuously; changing a tag deliberately makes check:fast fail naming the mismatch. deploy.yml and release.yml are untouched and keep the composite action, which stays with its caller count corrected - they install a Rust toolchain and wasm-pack around their Playwright step, so containerising them is a separate bead. The native job is not containerised. All four smoke shards and pwa pass on the PR in both projects with durations within a minute or two of the measured baseline of 1-4 minutes for smoke and under one for pwa, and whatever the container needed for Node, pnpm, permissions or caches is recorded in the PR.

title: Three readers answer where a unit stands after its orders
description:
## The cost being paid

"Where does this unit stand, and who is aboard, once this month's ENTER/LEAVE/SAIL have run" is
implemented three times over three different inputs — parsed intents, the raw orders document, and
the preview walker's working state. Each reader has been corrected separately, as it was discovered,
across a chain of five beads. The codebase says so itself and defers the decision to a bead that has
since closed without making it.

`crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs`, on `structure_after_orders`:

> The movement layer, which is handed a report rather than parsed intents, answers the same question
> through `crate::movement::fleet::OrderedUnits::structure_of` and must keep the same rule. **Two
> models of it exist on purpose until something decides where a shared one would live (ah-ssd); a
> change here belongs in both.**

ah-ssd is closed (PR #419). Nothing decided. This bead is that decision.

The cost is not hypothetical: the divergence has already burned a navigator verification, shipped a
regression the whole core suite was green on, and led a planner to copy the rule from the one reader
still stating it wrongly.

## Evidence

**A defect fixed twice in the same function, costing a Psylocke verification.**
- 43d1b73 (ah-mjy, PR #415) added `structure_after_orders` — "one model of where a unit stands after its ENTER/LEAVE orders".
- 0d94cf2 (ah-mjy, PR #418) rewrote it. Its commit body: "**Verification of ah-mjy failed on case A4**: a mage given ENTER 5 / LEAVE was warned, though the engine runs every LEAVE before any ENTER... `a_mage_that_leaves_and_re_enters_is_judged_on_the_last_order` asserted the old rule and passed, **which is how this reached the navigator**."

**One concept whose change had to touch several files.**
- ad4f457 (ah-ssd, PR #419): 11 files, 543 insertions for one rule — `movement/fleet.rs`, `movement/mode.rs`, `movement/plan.rs`, `movement/request.rs`, `movement/trace.rs`, `orders/effects.rs`, `orders/forms.rs`, `orders/semantics.rs`, plus tests.
- 5d6b30f (ah-048, PR #396): 14 files, 476 insertions across Rust, wasm, Tauri and TS for the passenger half of the same question.

**A chain of beads each fixing one more reader.**
- ah-p1p (closed, already labelled `refactoring`) consolidated the movement words; its delivery "did not touch `crates/core/src/orders/effects.rs`".
- ah-l2i's description: "the consolidation left the same concept in two places... **Cost paid: the ah-p1p bead itself**".
- ah-048's description: "the same defect ah-l2i was filed for, **one reader further on**".
- ah-ssd's description: "Two more readers ask the same question the same way, one layer down", naming `movement/mode.rs:286` and `movement/fleet.rs:89`, and "`check_sailing` already does the intent-aware thing for weight... **so the two disagree about who is on the same boat**".

**A module a planner and an implementer misread the same way.**
- docs/retrospectives/ah-ssd.md §"The plan specified a rule the codebase had already settled differently" — the plan quoted `orders/effects.rs:570-575` as "the authoritative version" of the rule, "and that file was the one reader ah-mjy did *not* correct — **so the plan copied the rule from the only place still stating it wrongly**." ~25 min of REFACTOR-phase rewrite.
- docs/retrospectives/ah-ssd.md §"The adversarial review found a regression the whole suite was green on" — `steps_followed_by`'s two `structure_id` comparisons "look identical and answer different questions"; **all 803 core tests were green** on it.

## Where

- `crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs` — `is_aboard`, `structure_after_orders`, `could_captain` (over parsed `Intent`s).
- `crates/core/src/movement/fleet.rs` — `OrderedUnits`/`aboard_by_unit`, `structure_of`, `could_captain`, `steps_followed_by` (over the raw orders document via `orders::walk`).
- `crates/core/src/orders/effects.rs` — `WorkingUnit.entered` and the ENTER/LEAVE arms of `visit` (over the preview walker's working state; this is the reader that applied the two orders in plain document order).
- Consumers reaching the rule through one of the three: `crates/core/src/movement/mode.rs` (`aboard_structure`, `crew_sailing_levels`), `movement/trace.rs`, `movement/plan.rs`.

## What a refactoring would change

One module owns the after-orders standing — `structure_of(unit)` and `could_captain(unit, structure)`
— and nothing else computes it. The seam is the input, since the three layers genuinely hold
different things: the rule takes an iterator of `Enter(id) | Leave` events and each caller supplies a
small adapter. `effects::Working::visit` stops carrying its own `entered` flag and asks the shared
reader at the end of the block. `could_captain` moves alongside it, being the deliberately-different
second predicate that only makes sense read as a pair. Deleting the "two models exist on purpose"
paragraph in `semantics.rs` is the acceptance signal.

Note for triage: the three models exist for a real reason, so an adapter per caller may buy less than
it costs, and the doc comments now cross-reference each other. The counter-argument is that
cross-references are what failed — ah-ssd's plan read one and trusted it.

Filed by Forge, daily sweep of 2026-08-19, range a19f579..cec1dd0.
design:
## Context

*"Where does this unit stand once this month's ENTER/LEAVE have run"* is implemented **three times**,
over three different inputs, and each has been corrected separately across a chain of five beads. The
codebase says so itself and defers the decision to a bead that has since closed without making it —
`semantics.rs`'s `structure_after_orders`:

> The movement layer, which is handed a report rather than parsed intents, answers the same question
> through `crate::movement::fleet::OrderedUnits::structure_of` and must keep the same rule. **Two
> models of it exist on purpose until something decides where a shared one would live (ah-ssd); a
> change here belongs in both.**

`ah-ssd` is closed (PR #419). Nothing was decided. **This bead is that decision.**

The cost is measured, not hypothetical:

- **A defect fixed twice in one function, costing a navigator verification.** `ah-mjy` added
  `structure_after_orders` (43d1b73), then rewrote it (0d94cf2) because *"verification of ah-mjy
  failed on case A4 … `a_mage_that_leaves_and_re_enters_is_judged_on_the_last_order` asserted the old
  rule and passed, which is how this reached the navigator."*
- **One rule, changes touching everything.** `ah-ssd` was 11 files and 543 insertions; `ah-048` 14
  files across Rust, wasm, Tauri and TypeScript, for the passenger half of the same question.
- **A planner misled by the cross-references.** `ah-ssd`'s retrospective: the plan quoted
  `orders/effects.rs` as *"the authoritative version"*, *"and that file was the one reader ah-mjy did
  not correct — so the plan copied the rule from the only place still stating it wrongly."* ~25
  minutes of REFACTOR-phase rewrite.
- **A regression 803 green tests missed.** `steps_followed_by`'s two `structure_id` comparisons
  *"look identical and answer different questions"*; the adversarial review caught it, the suite did
  not.

Forge's own triage note offers the counter-argument and then demolishes it: *"the doc comments now
cross-reference each other. The counter-argument is that cross-references are what failed — ah-ssd's
plan read one and trusted it."* **That is exactly right, and it nearly happened again in this
session:** `ah-vkut` and `ah-dwk6` were both planned by reading `structure_after_orders`'s doc comment
and trusting it. Reading `effects.rs` instead would have produced the same mistake `ah-ssd` made.

### What this bead is, precisely — because it is not what the title suggests

**The three readers appear to agree today.** Worked through case by case, `effects.rs` reaches the
settled rule by a *different mechanism* rather than a different answer. It applies ENTER and LEAVE in
document order with a flag (`effects.rs:582-588`):

```rust
} else if command.is("enter") {
    if let Some(structure) = super::forms::read_only_number(arguments) {
        self.units[active].unit.structure_id = Some(structure.to_string());
        self.units[active].entered = true;
    }
} else if command.is("leave") && arguments.is_empty() && !self.units[active].entered {
    self.units[active].unit.structure_id = None;
}
```

against `semantics.rs`'s *"every LEAVE runs before any ENTER"*. Enumerating the blocks that matter:

| Block | Settled rule | `effects.rs` |
|---|---|---|
| `ENTER 5` then `LEAVE` | in 5 | enters 5, LEAVE skipped → **5** |
| `LEAVE` then `ENTER 5` | in 5 | leaves, then enters → **5** |
| `LEAVE` alone | nothing | **nothing** |
| `ENTER 4` then `ENTER 5` | 5 (last wins) | 4 then 5 → **5** |
| `LEAVE`, `ENTER 4`, `LEAVE` | 4 | leaves, enters 4, LEAVE skipped → **4** |
| `ENTER <unreadable>` then `LEAVE` | no ENTER parsed → nothing | flag unset, LEAVE applies → **nothing** |

**So this bead is not fixing a live divergence. It is removing the ability to diverge** — and the
history says that ability gets used about once per bead that touches the area. That reframing matters
for how it is built: increment 1 is a differential test proving the three agree *before* anything
moves, so the consolidation has a baseline. **If that test finds a disagreement, stop: that is a live
defect, a much larger finding, and it wants the navigator.**

Branch from `origin/main`; every line number here is that tree.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### 1. The one owner — a new `crates/core/src/orders/standing.rs`

The three layers genuinely hold different things — parsed `Intent`s, the raw orders document, and the
preview walker's working state — so **the seam is the input**, exactly as Forge proposes: the rule
takes a sequence of events and each caller supplies a small adapter.

```rust
//! Where a unit stands once this month's ENTER and LEAVE orders have run.
//!
//! One reader, because there used to be three and they were corrected one at a time over five beads
//! (ah-f03z): ah-mjy fixed this rule twice in one function - the second time only because a
//! navigator verification failed on it - and ah-ssd's own plan copied the rule out of the one file
//! still describing it wrongly. Cross-referencing doc comments was the previous answer, and
//! cross-references are what failed.

/// A unit's ENTER and LEAVE orders, in the order they were written.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum Boarding<'a> {
    Enter(&'a str),
    Leave,
}

/// Where the unit ends the month's boarding orders, given where the report found it.
///
/// **Every LEAVE runs before any ENTER**, whatever order the lines were typed in - the engine's own
/// order, confirmed by the navigator on 2026-08-18 after a verification failed on exactly this. So a
/// block holding any ENTER ends inside the last one entered, a block holding only LEAVEs ends in
/// nothing, and a block holding neither stays where the report found it. Document order matters only
/// among ENTERs.
pub fn standing_after<'a>(
    reported: Option<&'a str>,
    boardings: impl IntoIterator<Item = Boarding<'a>>,
) -> Option<&'a str>;

/// Whether this unit could be the one giving `structure_id` its SAIL order: standing in it per the
/// report, or boarding it this month.
///
/// Deliberately *not* `standing_after(..) == Some(id)`, and it lives here so the difference is read
/// as a pair rather than discovered. A unit that also LEAVEs is not excluded: the server would still
/// read its SAIL line before running the LEAVE.
pub fn could_captain<'a>(
    reported: Option<&'a str>,
    structure_id: &str,
    boardings: impl IntoIterator<Item = Boarding<'a>>,
) -> bool;
```

**`could_captain` moving alongside is the point, not a bonus.** It is the deliberately-different
second predicate, and `ah-ssd` found `steps_followed_by`'s two `structure_id` comparisons *"look
identical and answer different questions"*. Two functions in one module, whose doc comments name each
other, is how that stops being a trap.

### 2. Three adapters, each a few lines

- **`semantics.rs`** — `structure_after_orders` (`:1656-1672`) becomes a call:
  `standing_after(ordered.unit.structure_id.as_deref(), ordered.intents.iter().filter_map(boarding_of))`
  where `boarding_of` maps `Intent::Enter { structure } → Boarding::Enter(structure)` and
  `Intent::Leave → Boarding::Leave`. `could_captain` (`:1680`) likewise.
  **Delete the "Two models of it exist on purpose" paragraph.** That deletion is the acceptance
  signal.
- **`movement/fleet.rs`** — `OrderedUnits::read` builds `aboard_by_unit` inline (`:42-51`). It keeps
  the map (it is a per-unit cache the movement layer wants) but fills it by calling
  `standing_after` over the boardings it walks out of the document. `structure_of` (`:103-108`) and
  `could_captain` (`:120-123`) then read the cache rather than restating the rule.
- **`orders/effects.rs`** — the harder one. `Working::visit` mutates `structure_id` as it goes and
  carries its own `entered` flag (`:329`, `:585-587`). Collect the block's boardings and **apply the
  shared answer once at the end of the block**, dropping `entered` entirely.

  **This is where the risk is**, because `visit` is a mutating walk and other arms may read
  `structure_id` mid-block. **Check that before moving it**: if anything between the ENTER and the
  end of the block depends on the intermediate value, the end-of-block application changes behaviour
  and this adapter needs a different shape. Say which, in the PR, either way.

### 3. Nothing else

`movement/mode.rs` (`aboard_structure`, `crew_sailing_levels`), `movement/trace.rs` and
`movement/plan.rs` reach the rule *through* `OrderedUnits`, so they change not at all. Confirm that
by reading rather than assuming — a fourth reader hiding in one of them is precisely the shape of
this bead's history.

## Increments

1. **Prove the three agree, before touching anything.**
   RED: a new test that runs the same blocks through all three readers and asserts one answer — the
   six rows in *Context*, plus `no boarding orders at all` and `ENTER a structure the report does not
   list`. Put it where it can see all three; a Rust integration test under `crates/core/tests/` is
   the natural home.
   GREEN: it should pass **as written, before any refactor**. **If it does not, stop and take the
   disagreement to the navigator** — that is a live defect and a bigger bead than this one.
   This test is the baseline the whole refactor is measured against and it must survive to the end.

2. **The rule has one home.**
   RED: `standing.rs`'s own unit tests — the same table, over `standing_after` directly, plus
   `could_captain` differing from `standing_after` for `ENTER 4` + `LEAVE` asked about 4.
   GREEN: the module.

3. **The intent reader delegates.**
   RED: none — `semantics.rs`'s existing tests are the check, in particular
   `a_mage_that_leaves_and_re_enters_is_judged_on_the_last_order` and `ah-vkut`'s and `ah-dwk6`'s
   ENTER/LEAVE cases.
   GREEN: the adapter, and **the deleted paragraph**.

4. **The document reader delegates.**
   RED: none — `movement/fleet.rs`'s existing tests, and increment 1's differential test.
   GREEN: `OrderedUnits::read` filling its cache through `standing_after`.

5. **The preview walker delegates.**
   RED: none — `effects.rs`'s existing tests, including `preview("unit 900\nENTER 4\n")` (`:1152`).
   GREEN: boardings collected and applied at end of block; `entered` deleted.
   **Run increment 1's differential test after this one specifically.** It is the adapter most likely
   to change behaviour.

6. **Nothing else computes it.**
   RED: none — this is the check. `git grep -n 'structure_id' crates/core/src` and read every hit:
   none outside `standing.rs` may implement the ENTER/LEAVE rule. Comparisons against a *known*
   structure id are fine; re-deriving where a unit stands is not.

## The test plan

| Test | Where | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| **`the three readers agree about where a unit stands`** | `crates/core/tests/` (new) | the baseline, written first and kept |
| the six blocks in *Context*, each through all three | same | the rule, from every input |
| `no boarding orders leaves the report's answer` | same | the untouched case |
| `standing_after` unit cases | `standing.rs` | the rule itself |
| **`could_captain differs from standing_after for ENTER then LEAVE`** | `standing.rs` | the pair, read as a pair |
| `a_mage_that_leaves_and_re_enters_is_judged_on_the_last_order` | `semantics.rs` | ah-mjy's verification failure, unchanged |
| `ah-vkut`'s ENTER/LEAVE cases | `semantics.rs` | unchanged |
| `preview("unit 900\nENTER 4\n")` (`effects.rs:1152`) | `effects.rs` | unchanged |
| `movement/fleet.rs`'s own tests | there | unchanged |

**Suites:** `cargo test --workspace` — all 803-plus of them — and `pnpm run check:fast`. The browser
suites are not needed: nothing rendered changes, and if a smoke test moves, this bead changed
behaviour and should not have.

## User-facing decisions

**None.** No behaviour changes, nothing reaches a player, no mockup — the artefact is a Rust module.

**Decided by the planner, as architecture:** that the seam is the *input* (an iterator of boardings)
rather than a shared trait or a common data structure, since the three layers genuinely hold
different things and Forge's reading of that is right; that `could_captain` moves with it, because
`ah-ssd` proved the pair is only safe read together; and that **increment 1 comes first**, so a
disagreement is discovered as a finding rather than as a refactor that silently changes an answer.

**A judgement worth flagging to the navigator:** Forge notes the three models exist for a real reason
and that an adapter per caller may buy less than it costs. This plan does the consolidation anyway,
on the strength of the evidence — a defect fixed twice, a failed verification, a regression 803 green
tests missed, and a planner misled by the very cross-references that were supposed to prevent it.
**If it turns out the adapters are larger than the readers they replace, that is a real result and
worth saying so in the PR rather than pressing on.**

## Out of scope

- **Any change of behaviour.** If `cargo test --workspace` needs an existing assertion changed, stop
  and work out why: this is a consolidation, and the differential test exists to prove it.
- **`ah-048`'s passenger question** — who is aboard a fleet — beyond what `could_captain` already
  answers.
- **`steps_followed_by`'s two comparisons.** `ah-ssd` already fixed the regression; this bead removes
  the conditions that made it possible, and does not revisit the function.
- **The TypeScript, wasm and Tauri layers** that `ah-048` touched. They consume answers; they do not
  compute this rule.
- **`movement/mode.rs`, `trace.rs`, `plan.rs`** — they reach it through `OrderedUnits` and should not
  change. If one of them turns out to compute it itself, that is a **fourth** reader: fold it in, and
  say so, because it changes the bead's size.

## Validation

```bash
cargo test --workspace
pnpm run check:fast
git grep -n "entered" crates/core/src/orders/effects.rs     # must find nothing
git grep -n "Two models of it exist" crates/core/src        # must find nothing
```

Those last two greps are the acceptance in one line each: the preview walker's private flag is gone,
and the paragraph admitting the duplication is gone because the duplication is.

Then, by hand:

1. **Run increment 1's differential test at each step**, not only at the end. It is cheap, and it is
   the only thing that will tell you *which* adapter changed an answer.
2. In the running app, preview a unit with `ENTER 5` then `LEAVE` and confirm the unit pane shows it
   inside structure 5 — the preview walker is the reader with no browser test of its own, and this is
   the case that failed `ah-mjy`'s verification.
3. Then `LEAVE` then `ENTER 5`: also inside 5. Then `LEAVE` alone: outside.
4. Load a turn with a fleet and confirm sailing still works — `could_captain` decides who is taken to
   be giving the SAIL order, and it is the predicate most easily broken by "simplifying" it into
   `standing_after(..) == Some(id)`.

## Known traps

- **The readers agree today.** This bead removes the *ability* to diverge, so the first sign of
  trouble is a test that used to pass. Increment 1 exists to make that unmistakable.
- **`could_captain` is deliberately not `standing_after(..) == Some(id)`.** A unit that boards *and*
  leaves can still be the captain, because the server reads the SAIL line before running the LEAVE.
  Collapsing the two is the single most likely wrong "simplification" here, and `ah-ssd` already
  found a regression of exactly that shape that 803 green tests missed.
- **`effects.rs`'s `visit` is a mutating walk.** Moving from "apply as you go" to "apply at the end of
  the block" is only safe if nothing in between reads `structure_id`. **Check, and say what you
  found.**
- **`ENTER` with an unreadable argument sets no flag today** (`effects.rs:583`), so a following LEAVE
  applies. The shared rule must keep that: an ENTER that did not parse is not an ENTER.
- **`OrderedUnits`'s `aboard_by_unit` distinguishes three states** — absent (no boarding orders, use
  the report), `Some(None)` (left into nothing), `Some(Some(id))`. Flattening it to
  `Option<String>` loses the first, and the report's own answer with it.
- **Deleting the "Two models" paragraph is the acceptance signal**, and it is also the thing most
  likely to be left behind. The grep is the check.
- **Look for a fourth reader.** Five beads each found one more. `git grep` for `structure_id` across
  `crates/core/src` and read every hit before declaring this done.
acceptance_criteria: One module - crates/core/src/orders/standing.rs - owns where a unit stands once its ENTER and LEAVE orders have run, taking an iterator of boarding events plus where the report found it, and could_captain lives beside it as the deliberately-different second predicate with each doc comment naming the other. The three existing readers become adapters over it: semantics.rs's structure_after_orders and could_captain, movement/fleet.rs's OrderedUnits::read filling aboard_by_unit, and orders/effects.rs's Working::visit, which drops its private entered flag and applies the shared answer at end of block - having first checked and reported whether anything between an ENTER and the end of the block reads structure_id. Nothing else computes the rule: git grep over crates/core/src finds no other implementation, and any fourth reader found is folded in and named. A differential test asserting all three readers give one answer for the same block is written FIRST and passes before any refactor, covering ENTER-then-LEAVE, LEAVE-then-ENTER, LEAVE alone, two ENTERs, LEAVE-ENTER-LEAVE, an unparseable ENTER followed by LEAVE, and no boarding orders at all; if it fails before the refactor, that is a live defect and goes to the navigator rather than being refactored past. No behaviour changes: cargo test --workspace passes with no existing assertion altered, and the browser suites are untouched. The 'Two models of it exist on purpose' paragraph in semantics.rs is deleted, and git grep finds neither it nor effects.rs's entered flag.

title: A taller header breaks smoke tests that name a different feature
description:
## The cost being paid

The workspace's vertical budget at the smoke suite's viewport is an unowned shared resource. Nothing
bounds the header/chip strip, `panelLayout.ts` takes `railRem` as a given, and ~35 of 210 smoke tests
spend from the leftover slack without declaring it. So a change to one feature's height surfaces as
failures in tests that name a different feature — four times in five days, across two implementers,
costing roughly a working day.

ah-v09e names the pattern itself: "This is the third sighting of *workspace geometry is a shared
global that smoke tests pin from many angles*."

It is already load-bearing as scar tissue in committed test code: two tests in `workspace.spec.ts`
raise the viewport to 1280x900 with comments naming the cause, and `shortcuts.spec.ts` waits on
`problems-chip` before capturing a corner coordinate, citing ah-1uj.

## Evidence

- docs/retrospectives/ah-2r3.md — "A bigger default units pane pushed the map's initial fit out a zoom tier, breaking two unrelated smoke tests": ~2 hours.
- docs/retrospectives/ah-1uj.md — "Several beads landing header chips in quick succession broke pixel-exact smoke tests that had never failed before": four CI round trips (~40 min) plus several hours of local diagnosis. - docs/retrospectives/ah-etb0.2.md — "One extra button in the header broke two unrelated smoke tests, in the desktop project only": two CI cycles, ~40 min, two full 13-minute local smoke runs. Commit a9b6c8f. Its Seen before names ah-1uj: "the header strip is shared ground, and a change to it surfaces somewhere unrelated."
- docs/retrospectives/ah-v09e.md §Seen before — "A one-step type increase cascaded into fourteen smoke failures across four unrelated mechanisms": ~4 hours wall clock, six browser-suite runs. Commit 5151f26, 13 files.
- Scar tissue: tests/smoke/workspace.spec.ts:1455-1460 and :1600-1605 (viewport raised to 1280x900, comment names advisory-check chips); tests/smoke/shortcuts.spec.ts:192-197 (waits on problems-chip, cites ah-1uj).
- ah-1uj §Prevent by item 1 proposed a header height budget on 2026-08-17. Two more incidents landed after it was written; no bead was ever filed for it.

## Where

- `playwright.config.ts` — no `viewport` key; both projects inherit `devices["Desktop Chrome"]`. The effective 1280x683 is an inherited default, not a decided policy.
- `packages/shared/src/workspace/AppHeader.tsx` — 13 controls in one wrapping flex row; 3 commits added to it in this range alone (7f120e8 Trade chip, fb1b2a1 type scale, a9b6c8f Send button).
- `packages/shared/src/workspace/panelLayout.ts` — `dragOrdersHeight` derives its ceiling from `railRem` and never asks what set it.
- `packages/shared/src/workspace/useOverlayInsets.ts`, `mapOverlayInsets.ts`, `AppShell.tsx`.
- No upper bound on header height exists anywhere; `workspace.spec.ts:3452` asserts only a *lower* bound. The jsdom unit tests have no layout, so this is only ever catchable by a browser round trip.

## What a refactoring would change

Pin the smoke viewport explicitly in `playwright.config.ts` so the size stops being an inherited
accident, and assert the header's height against a stated maximum once — turning N mysterious
failures into one that names the header. Give the vertical budget a testable seam: a pure function
beside `panelLayout.ts` taking viewport height and header height and returning the rail's height, so
"does anything still fit?" gets a fast unit test instead of a 13-minute browser round trip. Then let
the slack-dependent tests declare the room they need rather than inherit it, replacing the two
hand-rolled `setViewportSize` workarounds.

Note for triage: a header-height budget alone would have caught ah-1uj and probably ah-etb0.2, but
ah-v09e and ah-2r3 entered through row height and pane default height — the seam is the part that

Filed by Forge, daily sweep of 2026-08-19, range a19f579..cec1dd0.
design:
## Context

The workspace's vertical budget at the smoke suite's viewport is an **unowned shared resource**.
Nothing bounds the header/chip strip, `panelLayout.ts` takes `railRem` as a given, and ~35 of 210
smoke tests spend from the leftover slack without declaring it. So a change to one feature's height
surfaces as failures in tests that name a **different** feature.

Forge measured four incidents in five days — roughly **seven hours**, the largest single cost in the
sweep:

- `ah-2r3` — a bigger default units pane pushed the map's initial fit out a zoom tier, breaking two
  unrelated smoke tests: **~2 hours**.
- `ah-1uj` — header chips landing in quick succession broke pixel-exact tests that had never failed:
  **four CI round trips (~40 min)** plus hours of local diagnosis. A bead about STUDY validation in
  `semantics.rs` had to touch `MapCanvas.tsx`, `shortcuts.spec.ts` and `workspace.spec.ts` — **3 of
  its 7 files were layout collateral.**
- `ah-etb0.2` — **one extra button in the header** broke two unrelated tests, desktop project only:
  two CI cycles, ~40 min, two full 13-minute local smoke runs.
- `ah-v09e` — a one-step type increase cascaded into **fourteen** failures across four unrelated
  mechanisms: **~4 hours**, six browser-suite runs.

**`ah-1uj` proposed a header height budget on 2026-08-17. Two more incidents landed after that was
written, and no bead was ever filed.** This is that bead.

**The mechanism is written down in the test suite's own scar tissue**, and it is worth quoting
because the fix follows from it (`workspace.spec.ts:1455-1460`):

> The default window (1280x683) leaves the orders editor's pin already at its own ceiling **once
> enough advisory-check chips share the header with it** (ah-1uj is one of several) — dragging it
> taller would then have nowhere to go, whatever the gesture.

So the chain is: **header grows → the rail shrinks → `dragOrdersHeight`'s ceiling
(`railRem - UNIT_MIN_REM - RAIL_GAP_REM`, `panelLayout.ts:85`) reaches zero → a *drag* test fails,
naming the drag.** Nothing anywhere connects the two ends, and the jsdom unit tests have no layout,
so it is only ever catchable by a 13-minute browser round trip.

Two more facts that shape the fix:

- **The viewport is an inherited accident, not a policy.** `playwright.config.ts` has no `viewport`
  key; both projects take `devices["Desktop Chrome"]` (`:86`, `:90`).
- **`dragOrdersHeight` is already pure and already takes `railRem`** (`:83-85`). What is missing is
  the function that *computes* `railRem` from the viewport and the header — the one thing nobody can
  unit-test.

**Forge's triage note names the right target:** a header budget alone would have caught `ah-1uj` and
probably `ah-etb0.2`, but `ah-v09e` and `ah-2r3` entered through row height and pane default height —
*"the seam is the part that covers all four."*

Branch from `origin/main`; every line number here is that tree.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### 1. The seam — `packages/shared/src/workspace/panelLayout.ts`

A pure function from what the window and the header actually are, to what the rail gets:

```ts
/**
 * How much vertical room the rail has once the header has taken its share, in rem.
 *
 * The missing half of `dragOrdersHeight`, which takes `railRem` as a given and never asks what set
 * it (ah-csni). Because nothing computed it in one place, a taller header surfaced as a *drag* test
 * failing - four incidents in five days, ~7 hours, each naming a feature that had not changed.
 */
export function railRemFor(viewportPx: number, headerPx: number, rootFontPx: number): number;

/**
 * Whether the rail still has room for the orders editor to be dragged at all.
 *
 * `dragOrdersHeight`'s own ceiling, asked as a question instead of discovered as a stuck gesture:
 * false means the pin is already at its limit and any drag test is about to fail for a reason that
 * has nothing to do with dragging.
 */
export function railHasRoomToDrag(railRem: number): boolean;
```

`railHasRoomToDrag` must be **`railRem - UNIT_MIN_REM - RAIL_GAP_REM > 0`**, reusing the very
constants `dragOrdersHeight` uses at `:85` — not a re-derivation. If the two ever disagree, this
seam is worthless.

Whatever else feeds the budget — the units pane's default height (`ah-2r3`), the type scale
(`ah-v09e`) — enters through `headerPx` and `rootFontPx`, which is why this covers all four incidents
and a header-only budget would not.

### 2. The viewport becomes a decision — `playwright.config.ts`

Pin it explicitly in the shared `use:` block (`:78`), so the size stops being inherited:

```ts
  use: {
    // Pinned rather than inherited from `devices["Desktop Chrome"]`: ~35 smoke tests spend from
    // this window's leftover vertical slack, so it is a decided policy, not a default that can
    // move under them when Playwright updates its device list (ah-csni).
    viewport: { width: 1280, height: 720 },
```

**Read the current effective size first and pin *that*, whatever it is.** The number above is the
Desktop Chrome default and is written here as the expected answer, not as an instruction: if the
suite's behaviour changes at all when it is pinned, the value is wrong and the real one must be
measured rather than asserted. **Nothing about how the suite behaves may change in this step.**

### 3. One test that names the header — `tests/smoke/workspace.spec.ts`

```ts
test("the header fits its budget, so a taller one fails here and not somewhere else", async ({ page }) => {
```

Measure `app-header`'s `boundingBox().height`, assert it is at or below a stated maximum, and — the
part that earns its keep — assert `railHasRoomToDrag(railRemFor(viewportHeight, headerHeight, root))`
so the failure says *the header has grown past what the rail can spare*, not *a drag went nowhere*.

**Choosing the number is the implementer's, and it is a measurement, not a guess.** Run the suite,
read the header's real height in both projects, and set the budget at roughly **125% of the larger**
— enough that a normal change does not trip it, tight enough to catch a chip or a type step. Write
the measured figures into the comment, so the next person raising it knows what it was.

Raising the budget must stay possible and deliberate: the test names the constant, and a bead that
genuinely needs a taller header changes it **in the same commit as the header change**, which is the
whole point — the cost lands on the change that caused it.

### 4. The scar tissue declares itself — `workspace.spec.ts:1460`, `:1605`

Two tests raise the window to `1280x900` by hand, each with a paragraph explaining why. Replace the
literal with a named helper beside the other smoke helpers:

```ts
/**
 * A window with room for the orders/unit split to actually move.
 *
 * At the pinned viewport the editor's pin can already sit at its own ceiling once the header is
 * full (ah-1uj, ah-csni), so a test *about the drag mechanism* needs headroom the default does not
 * promise. Declaring it here is the point: these tests were the only ones that noticed, and they
 * noticed by failing.
 */
async function withRoomToDrag(page: Page): Promise<void>;
```

Both call sites become `await withRoomToDrag(page);` and keep their existing comments. **Do not go
hunting for the other ~33 slack-dependent tests** — see *Out of scope*.

## Increments

1. **The viewport stops being an accident.**
   RED: none. Pin it, run the full smoke suite, and confirm **nothing changes**. If anything does,
   the pinned value is not what was inherited.
2. **The budget has a seam.**
   RED: `panelLayout.test.ts` — `railRemFor` over a table (a tall header leaves less), and
   `railHasRoomToDrag is false when the header eats the rail`, with the numbers taken from the real
   viewport and a header at and past the budget.
   GREEN: the two functions.
3. **A taller header fails by name.**
   RED: the new smoke test. To see it fail for the right reason, temporarily add a tall element to
   `AppHeader.tsx` and confirm **this** test goes red and says so. Remove it.
   GREEN: the assertion and the measured constant.
4. **The workarounds say what they need.**
   RED: none. Replace the two literals with `withRoomToDrag`; both tests must still pass unchanged.

## The test plan

| Test | Where | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| `railRemFor` over a table | `panelLayout.test.ts` | the seam, in milliseconds |
| **`railHasRoomToDrag is false when the header eats the rail`** | same | the failure, catchable without a browser |
| it agrees with `dragOrdersHeight`'s own ceiling | same | the two must not drift |
| **`the header fits its budget…`** | `workspace.spec.ts` | one named failure instead of N mysterious ones |
| the two drag tests | `workspace.spec.ts` | unchanged, via `withRoomToDrag` |
| every other smoke test | both projects | **unchanged** — this bead moves no pixels |

**Suites:** `pnpm run check:fast` for the unit tests, and **the full smoke suite in both projects** —
`ah-etb0.2` failed in the desktop project only, so a web-only run proves nothing here.

## User-facing decisions

**Nothing reaches a player**, and there is no mockup — the artefact is a budget and a test.

**But there is a consequence the navigator should know about, and it is the point of the bead:**
after this, a change that makes the header taller — another chip, a bigger type scale, a control
moved *into* the header — **fails CI with a test that names the header**. That is deliberate: today
the same change fails two unrelated tests and costs an afternoon. Raising the budget stays possible
and is a one-line, deliberate act in the same commit as the change that needs it.

**Decided by the planner, as tooling:** the seam's shape and that it must reuse `dragOrdersHeight`'s
own constants; pinning the viewport to whatever is currently inherited rather than choosing a new
size; and 125%-of-measured as the rule for the budget rather than a number invented here.

**Ordering worth noting:** `ah-l9mp` (P2, unplanned) moves the staleness/movement/badge controls out
of the workspace and **the level indicator into the top bar** — that is a header change, and it will
consume budget. It should be built after this, and its own PR is where the budget is re-measured if
it needs to be.

## Out of scope

- **The other ~33 slack-dependent smoke tests.** Only the two that already hand-rolled a taller
  window are converted. Auditing thirty-three tests for undeclared assumptions is a much larger bead
  and would bury this one; the seam is what makes them cheap to fix *when* they next fail.
- **Reducing the header's height**, moving controls out of it, or redesigning it. `ah-l9mp` is the
  bead that changes what is in the header.
- **The units pane's default height** (`ah-2r3`) and **the type scale** (`ah-v09e`). Both feed the
  budget through `railRemFor`'s arguments; neither is changed.
- **Making the smoke suite faster**, or reducing the 13-minute local run. Real, and different.
- **A lower bound on the header.** The existing assertion that it is visible stays; this bead adds a
  ceiling, not a floor.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
pnpm exec playwright test --project=web
pnpm exec playwright test --project=desktop-shell
```

Both projects, because `ah-etb0.2` failed in one only.

Then the experiment that proves the bead, which takes two minutes:

1. Add a tall element to `AppHeader.tsx` — a `<div className="h-16" />` will do.
2. Run the smoke suite. **The new header-budget test must fail, and it must be the one that names the
   problem.** Note whether anything *else* also fails: some collateral is expected, and the point is
   that a developer now has one failure that says "the header grew" among them.
3. Remove the element and confirm everything is green again.
4. Confirm the two drag tests still pass through `withRoomToDrag`, and that `git diff` shows the
   `1280x900` literals gone.

## Known traps

- **`railHasRoomToDrag` must use `dragOrdersHeight`'s own constants** (`UNIT_MIN_REM`, `RAIL_GAP_REM`,
  `panelLayout.ts:85`), not copies. A seam that can disagree with the thing it describes is worse than
  no seam, because it will be believed.
- **Pinning the viewport must change nothing.** If the suite behaves differently once it is explicit,
  the pinned number is not what was inherited — find the real one rather than adjusting tests to it.
- **Measure the budget, do not invent it**, and in **both projects**: `ah-etb0.2` broke in
  desktop-shell only, so the larger of the two is the one that matters.
- **The new test must be able to fail.** Step 1 of *Validation* is not optional; a budget nobody has
  seen reject anything is decoration.
- **Do not convert the other slack-dependent tests.** It is tempting, it is a much bigger bead, and
  it would make this one impossible to review.
- **`ah-l9mp` will change the header.** If it lands first, the budget measured here is against the
  old header — re-measure rather than assuming.
- **The failure this fixes is a *drag* test failing when the *header* grew.** If the new test passes
  while a drag test fails, the seam is not wired to the same numbers the drag uses.
acceptance_criteria: panelLayout.ts gains railRemFor(viewportPx, headerPx, rootFontPx) and railHasRoomToDrag(railRem) as pure functions, the second computed from dragOrdersHeight's own UNIT_MIN_REM and RAIL_GAP_REM rather than copies of them, and unit-tested including a case where a header at and past the budget leaves no room to drag - so the failure is catchable in milliseconds instead of a 13-minute browser round trip. playwright.config.ts pins the viewport explicitly in its shared use block, set to whatever is currently inherited from devices Desktop Chrome, with the full smoke suite behaving identically before and after. One smoke test asserts the app-header's height against a stated maximum and asserts railHasRoomToDrag holds at it, so a taller header fails with a test that names the header; the maximum is measured in BOTH projects and set at roughly 125% of the larger, with the measured figures in the comment. That test is proven able to fail by temporarily adding a tall element to AppHeader.tsx. The two hand-rolled setViewportSize 1280x900 workarounds in workspace.spec.ts become a named withRoomToDrag helper that says what room it needs and why, with both tests still passing. No pixels move: every other smoke test passes unchanged in both the web and desktop-shell projects. The other roughly 33 slack-dependent tests are deliberately not audited.

title: Warn when a BUILD names a structure the unit cannot build
description:
Filed at the navigator's request while planning ah-3cj4 (2026-08-19), which makes the data this needs available for the first time.

The rules page states, for each structure a player can build, the skill and minimum level it requires - "Mine: 10 wood or stone, mining (3), iron", and the fortification table's "Skill (min level)" column. Once ah-3cj4.1 has the buildings in the ruleset, a BUILD order naming a structure type can be checked against the ordering unit's skills.

So: a unit ordered to BUILD a Mine without mining at level 3 spends its month for nothing, and the app could say so before the turn goes in - the same class of wasted month as ah-vkut and ah-dwk6.

Blocked by ah-3cj4.1: without the buildings in the ruleset there is nothing to check against. Note also that ah-3cj4.1 as scoped captures each building's description and product from the DATA page; the skill and level requirement is stated on the RULES page, so this bead may need that scraped too - establish which before promising the check.

Every warning's wording and its settings entry are the navigator's, as for every other advisory check.

title: Click a skill, item or structure named in a pane to read its game data
description:
The second half of ah-5jkt: the skills and items named in the unit pane, and the products, market goods and structures named in the region pane, become clickable and open the reference dialog from ah-5jkt.1.

Blocked on ah-5jkt.1, which builds the dialog and the lookup.
design:
## Context

The second half of `ah-5jkt`. A skill or item named in the unit pane, and a product, market good or structure
kind named in the region pane, becomes clickable and opens the game-data dictionary **already on that entry**.

**Blocked on `ah-5jkt.1`**, which builds the dictionary and the lookup. **Read its plan before starting**
