(`bd show ah-5jkt.1 --json`): it is the interface this bead consumes, and at the time of writing it is
in progress rather than merged, so treat the signatures below as the contract it commits to rather than code
you can already read.

What `ah-5jkt.1` provides, and this bead uses:

```ts
// packages/shared/src/gameData.ts
export type GameDataIndex = { … };
export function skillEntryId(tag: string): string;
export function itemEntryId(index: GameDataIndex, tag: string): string | null;
export function buildingEntryId(kind: string): string;
```

and, in `AppShell`, a memoised `gameData: GameDataIndex | null` plus the state that opens
`GameDataDialog` on a given entry id. `null` means the ruleset has not loaded — which `ah-5jkt.1` settled as
*offer nothing at all* rather than offer a control that fails.

**The panes already hold everything the lookup needs.** No parsing, no plumbing from the core:

- `SkillInfo` is `{ name, tag, level, points }` — `skill.tag` is `"LUMB"`, a direct key.
- `ItemAmount` is `{ amount, name, tag }`, and `MarketItem` adds `price`. Products, wanted and for-sale lists
  all carry tags.
- `StructureInfo.kind` is `"Fort"`, `"Longship"`, `"Mine"` — upper-cased, a key into the buildings map.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### Changed — `packages/shared/src/workspace/primitives.tsx`

`Row` currently types its label as a string (`primitives.tsx:92`):

```ts
export function Row({ label, value }: { label: string; value: ReactNode })
```

**Widen `label` to `ReactNode`.** `value` already is. Four call sites read `Row` — `UnitPanel`, `RegionPanel`,
`UnitTooltip` and `PlannerPanel` — and all four keep compiling unchanged, since a string is a `ReactNode`.
`Field` (`primitives.tsx`) needs the same widening only if a linked label lands in one; check before changing
it, and do not widen it speculatively.

**New in the same file**, because all four panes need it and a second copy is how two affordances drift apart:

```ts
/**
 * A name that opens its game-data entry. Dotted underline at rest, blue under the pointer - the
 * pane reads as prose until you look for the link (ah-5jkt.2).
 */
export function GameDataLink({
  entryId,
  onOpen,
  children
}: {
  entryId: string;
  onOpen: (entryId: string) => void;
  children: ReactNode;
}): JSX.Element;
```

A `<button type="button">` — not a `<span>` with a click handler — so it is tab-reachable and announces
itself. Classes: `border-b border-dotted border-ink-dim hover:text-select hover:border-select` plus the
focus ring the rest of the application uses,
`focus-visible:outline focus-visible:outline-1 focus-visible:outline-select`. **The focus ring is not
optional**: the chosen affordance is hover-led, and without a focus state the feature is invisible to anyone
on a keyboard.

### Changed — `packages/shared/src/workspace/UnitPanel.tsx`

Signature gains one optional prop:

```ts
export function UnitPanel({
  unit, hex, preview = null, onOpenGameData
}: {
  unit: ReportUnit | null;
  hex: HexNode | null;
  preview?: UnitPreview | null;
  /** Absent while the ruleset has not loaded; nothing is then linked. */
  onOpenGameData?: (entryId: string) => void;
})
```

- **Skills** (`UnitPanel.tsx:97-111`): the `Row`'s label becomes
  `<GameDataLink entryId={skillEntryId(skill.tag)} …>{skill.name}</GameDataLink>` followed by the plain
  `{skill.tag}` as today. **Only the name is the link**, not the tag — the tag is an identifier the reader
  scans past, and underlining both doubles the dotted rules for nothing.
- **Items** (`UnitPanel.tsx:113-129`): the same, with `itemEntryId(index, item.tag)`. That returns
  `string | null`, because an item's category is not knowable from its tag alone; **when it is `null`, render
  the plain text with no link** rather than a link that opens nothing.
- The `+ N more` line, `unit.structureId` (`UnitPanel.tsx:79`, a structure *id*, not a kind) and everything
  else are untouched.

### Changed — `packages/shared/src/workspace/RegionPanel.tsx`

Same prop, and four places:

- **Products** (`RegionPanel.tsx:130-135`) — prose, `${item.amount} ${item.name}` joined by ` · `. The item's
  **name** becomes the link; the amount and the separators stay plain. This is the fiddliest of the four
  because it is a sentence rather than a list of rows: build it as an array of fragments rather than a joined
  string.
- **Wanted** (`:139-149`) and **For sale** (`:152-163`) — both already `Row`s keyed by tag, so the change is
  the label only, exactly as the unit pane's items.
- **Structures** (`:181-192`, as `ah-kdgc` left it) — **the `kind` alone becomes the link**, never
  `structure.name` (this region's own name for it, not a catalogue entry) and never the bracketed id. So
  `Odds and Ends [12] · ` stays plain and `Fort` is the link, via `buildingEntryId(structure.kind)`.
  The `, needs …` clause stays plain.

### Changed — `packages/shared/src/workspace/AppShell.tsx`

Pass the callback to both panes, from the state `ah-5jkt.1` already added:

```tsx
onOpenGameData={gameData === null ? undefined : (id) => setGameDataOpen({ entryId: id })}
```

at the `<UnitPanel>` site (`AppShell.tsx:2877`) and the `<RegionPanel>` site (`:2851-2859`).
**`undefined` when `gameData` is `null`** is what makes the panes render plain text before the ruleset loads,
which is `ah-5jkt.1`'s decision applied here rather than a second one.

### Not changed

- **`UnitTooltip.tsx`.** It renders skills and items as `Row`s from precomputed `{label, value}` pairs
  (`unitTooltip.ts:48`), but it is a transient hover surface — a link inside something that disappears when
  the pointer leaves is a trap, not a feature. Out of scope, deliberately.
- **`UnitTableDock.tsx`.** Its Skills cell is a comma-joined summary string (`UnitTableDock.tsx:484`) in a
  windowed table of up to three hundred rows. Linking there is a different bead with a different performance
  question.
- **`PlannerPanel`**, which reads `Row` but names nothing from the catalogue.
- **The dictionary itself**, which is `ah-5jkt.1`.

### Where state lives

Nothing new. The panes take a callback; the dialog's open state stays in `AppShell` where `ah-5jkt.1` put it.

## Increments

Each opens with the named failing test.

1. **The link itself.** New `primitives.test.tsx` → `"a game data link is a button carrying its entry id"`.
   Widen `Row`'s label and write `GameDataLink`.
2. **Skills.** `UnitPanel.test.tsx` (new — there is none today) →
   `"a skill's name opens its game data entry"`, and `"nothing is linked while the ruleset has not loaded"`.
3. **Items, including the unresolvable one.** Same file →
   `"an item whose category cannot be resolved is left as plain text"`.
4. **Market rows.** `RegionPanel.test.tsx` → `"a market good's name opens its game data entry"`.
5. **Products prose.** Same file → `"links each product's name inside the products line"`. Assert the amounts
   and separators are still plain text.
6. **Structure kinds.** Same file → `"links a structure's kind, and not its name or number"`. Assert
   explicitly that `Odds and Ends` is **not** a link — that is the mistake this increment exists to prevent.
7. **Wiring.** `AppShell` passes the callback, and omits it when `gameData` is `null`.

## The test plan

Unit, vitest, co-located. Component tests render with `renderToStaticMarkup` from `react-dom/server` —
**not Testing Library.** `RegionPanel.test.tsx` exists and has a `draw()` helper at its lines 89-92;
**`UnitPanel.test.tsx` does not exist and this bead creates it.**

| File | Pins |
|---|---|
| `packages/shared/src/workspace/primitives.test.tsx` (new) | increment 1 |
| `packages/shared/src/workspace/UnitPanel.test.tsx` (new) | increments 2, 3 |
| `packages/shared/src/workspace/RegionPanel.test.tsx` | increments 4, 5, 6 |

**One assertion worth stating as a rule:** every linked element must be a `<button>` with a `type="button"`.
Assert it structurally in `primitives.test.tsx`, so a later "simplification" to a `<span>` fails a test rather
than silently removing the feature from keyboard users.

**Smoke:** add one case to `tests/smoke/workspace.spec.ts` — select a hex, click a skill name in the unit pane,
assert the game-data dialog opens showing that skill. It is the only test that proves the whole path, and the
panes are already exercised there.

**Suites to run:** `pnpm run check:fast` and `pnpm run test:smoke`.

## User-facing decisions

Mockups: `docs/ui/ah-5jkt-pane-links.html` (this bead) and `docs/ui/ah-5jkt-dictionary.html` (the dialog it
opens, from `ah-5jkt.1`).

**How visible a clickable name is.** Offered: (A) always coloured in the select blue already used for unit
ids; (B) **a dotted underline at rest, colouring blue under the pointer**; (C) nothing until hover.
**Chosen: B.** It is discoverable without shouting, the panes still read as prose, and blue keeps meaning
"a unit" rather than meaning everything. Rejected A because nearly every line in these panes would go blue and
the distinction would be lost; rejected C because nobody hovers a noun to find out whether it does something,
and it would be useless on a keyboard.
**The accepted cost:** a lot of dotted rules on a dense pane.

**What becomes clickable.** All four offered, all four chosen:

- **Unit pane: skills and items.**
- **Region pane: wanted and for sale.**
- **Region pane: products**, despite being prose rather than rows.
- **Region pane: structure kinds** — the kind only.

**Following from `ah-5jkt.1` rather than decided again here:** while the ruleset has not loaded, nothing is
linked at all; and a structure the catalogue does not describe still opens the dialog, which says so.

### Strings

**No new visible strings.** Every link's text is the name the pane already shows.

## Out of scope

- **The dictionary dialog**, its tabs, its filter, its cross-references — all `ah-5jkt.1`.
- **The unit tooltip and the units table**, for the reasons given above.
- **Linking a unit id, a faction or a region** from these panes. `ah-bu2c` covers factions and `ah-87he`
  covers unit numbers in problem lists; do not anticipate either.
- **Widening the scrape.** A Mine's thin entry is `ah-3cj4`'s business, and that epic has already closed
  once.
- **Any change to what the panes say.** This bead makes existing words clickable and adds none.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
pnpm run test:smoke
```

Both green. Then look at it, because the whole decision was a visual one:

1. Select a hex with a crowded unit — `1:7,53` (Inholm). Confirm the unit pane's skills and items carry a
   dotted underline and colour blue under the pointer, and that the panes still read comfortably. **If they
   look busy, say so rather than shipping it** — that was the accepted risk of this option.
2. Click a skill; the dictionary opens on the Skills tab with that skill selected.
3. Click an item; it opens on the right one of the five item tabs.
4. In the region pane, click a product inside the products sentence, a market good, and a structure's kind.
5. Confirm `Odds and Ends` in `Odds and Ends [12] · Fort` is **not** clickable and shows no underline.
6. Click a `Mine`; it opens and says the catalogue describes it thinly rather than erroring.
7. Tab through the unit pane and confirm each link takes focus with a visible ring, and Enter opens it.
8. Break the ruleset fetch and confirm no underlines appear anywhere and nothing is clickable.

## Known traps

- **`Row`'s label is typed `string` today** (`primitives.tsx:92`) and must be widened to `ReactNode`. Four
  call sites read it; all keep compiling.
- **Only the name is the link, never the tag.** `lumberjack LUMB` links `lumberjack`. Linking both doubles the
  dotted rules for no gain.
- **A structure's `kind` is the catalogue entry; its `name` is this region's own.** Linking `Odds and Ends`
  would look right and open nothing sensible. There is a test for exactly this.
- **`itemEntryId` returns `string | null`.** A `null` must render plain text, never a link that opens an empty
  dialog.
- **Products are prose, not rows.** Building the line as a joined string and then trying to inject links into
  it is how the amounts end up linked too. Build fragments.
- **Use a `<button type="button">`.** A clickable `<span>` is invisible to the keyboard and to a screen
  reader, and the affordance chosen here is hover-led, which makes that worse rather than better.
- **`ah-5jkt.1` may still be in flight.** If its exported names differ from those quoted in *Context*, its
  merged code is the truth and this plan is the stale one — follow the code, and say so in the commit.
- **Work in a worktree under `.cerebro/worktrees/`**, never the main checkout, per `CLAUDE.md`.

title: Look up any skill, item or building in the game data from the palette
description:
The first half of ah-5jkt: make the scraped ruleset readable. Parse the ruleset JSON the app already holds, add skills, items and buildings to the command palette as searchable entries, and open a reference dialog showing what was scraped about the chosen thing.

Does not touch the panes; ah-5jkt.2 makes named things there clickable onto the same dialog.
design:
## Context

The application scrapes the game server's rules and data pages into `ruleset.json` and ships it, but no part
of the interface ever shows it to a player. This bead makes it readable: a **game data dictionary** dialog,
reachable from the command palette. `ah-5jkt.2`, blocked on this one, makes skills, items and structures named
in the panes clickable onto the same dialog.

**Two facts established during planning that shape everything below.**

1. **The ruleset is held only as raw JSON text and is never parsed in TypeScript.** `AppShell.tsx:287` holds
   `useState<RulesetState>`, `AppShell.tsx:297` exposes `rulesetText`, and every consumer hands that string to
   the Rust core (`client.orderVocabulary(rulesetText)` and friends, `packages/core-client/src/index.ts:522-741`).
   There is no `JSON.parse` of it anywhere in `packages/shared` or `packages/browser-core`. This bead
   introduces the first one.
2. **The scraped data contains no prose at all** — not one description, rules note or flavour line, in any
   category. The dialog is a stat block, and that is the ceiling. The gap is filed separately as **`ah-3cj4`**
   (the scraper takes only fortifications and no prose); it is not this bead's work.

The real shape, read from the shipped `config/public/ruleset.json`:

| Key | Count | Keyed by |
|---|---|---|
| `skills` | 96 (70 magic) | tag, e.g. `MINI` |
| `items` | 171 — 86 equipment, 58 monster, 14 man, 9 ship, 4 mount | tag, e.g. `LONG` |
| `buildings` | 10, all fortifications | **upper-cased name**, e.g. `TOWER`, `MAGICAL CASTLE` |

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### New — `packages/shared/src/gameData.ts`

The parse, the index and the lookups. Pure, no React, fully unit-testable.

```ts
/** The seven lists the dictionary shows, in tab order. */
export type GameDataCategory =
  | "skill" | "man" | "mount" | "ship" | "monster" | "equipment" | "building";

/** One thing in the dictionary, whatever kind it is. */
export type GameDataEntry = {
  /** Unique across every category: `skill:MINI`, `equipment:MITH`, `building:FORT`. */
  id: string;
  category: GameDataCategory;
  /** The display name, e.g. `mining`, `Longship`, `Fort`. */
  name: string;
  /** The four-letter tag, or null for a building, which has none. */
  tag: string | null;
};

export type GameDataIndex = {
  entries: readonly GameDataEntry[];
  byId: ReadonlyMap<string, GameDataEntry>;
  /** Raw scraped record for an entry, for the detail pane to read. */
  detailOf: (id: string) => GameDataDetail | null;
};

/** What the detail pane renders. One variant per shape the scrape actually has. */
export type GameDataDetail =
  | { kind: "skill"; entry: GameDataEntry; cost: number | null; maxLevel: number; magic: boolean;
      produces: readonly { id: string; name: string; level: number }[];
      requires: readonly { id: string; name: string; level: number }[] }
  | { kind: "item"; entry: GameDataEntry; weight: number; moves: number;
      capacity: { walk: number; ride: number; fly: number; swim: number };
      selfMobile: { walk: boolean; ride: boolean; fly: boolean; swim: boolean };
      combat: { skill: number; attacksPerRound: number; hitsToKill: number; damagePerAttack: number } | null;
      cargoCapacity: number | null; sailingSkill: number | null; capacityCondition: string | null;
      /** Derived: the skills that produce this item, and at what level. */
      producedBy: readonly { id: string; name: string; level: number }[] }
  | { kind: "building"; entry: GameDataEntry; size: number; cost: number;
      materials: readonly string[]; mages: number }
  | { kind: "absent"; entry: GameDataEntry };

/** Parses the ruleset text. Returns null when the text is not a ruleset at all. */
export function parseGameData(rulesetText: string): GameDataIndex | null;

/** The entry a report's tag names, or null. `skillTag` and `itemTag` are what the panes hold. */
export function skillEntryId(tag: string): string;
export function itemEntryId(index: GameDataIndex, tag: string): string | null;
export function buildingEntryId(kind: string): string;
```

Behaviour that matters:

- **`parseGameData` is called once per ruleset text and its result memoised** — see *Where state lives*. It
  `JSON.parse`s, walks `skills`, `items` and `buildings`, and builds `entries` sorted **alphabetically by
  `name`, case-insensitively, within each category** (the navigator's choice; see *User-facing decisions*).
- **An item's category is its `kind` field**, which is already one of `man | mount | monster | ship | equipment`
  (`packages/ruleset/src/data.ts:16`). No classification logic is needed or wanted.
- **`producedBy` is derived**, since the scrape stores only the forward direction. Build it in one pass over
  `skills`: for each skill, for each `produces` entry, append `{ id: skillEntryId(skill.tag), name, level }` to
  that item's list. Do it while indexing, not per render.
- **`buildingEntryId(kind)` upper-cases**, because `buildings` is keyed by the upper-cased name
  (`"MAGICAL CASTLE"`), while a report says `Fort` or `Road N`. A kind with no matching key yields an id whose
  `detailOf` returns `{ kind: "absent" }` — that is the state `ah-5jkt.2` will meet constantly and this bead
  must already handle.
- **`itemEntryId` needs the index** because an item's category is not knowable from its tag alone; the others
  do not.

**Do not import from `@atlantis/ruleset`.** It is not a dependency of `@atlantis/shared`, its index does not
export `SkillEntry`, `SkillReference`, `BuildingEntry` or `BuildingReference` (only the item and movement
types), and its `Ruleset` type name collides with the unrelated `Ruleset` in
`packages/shared/src/rulesets.ts`. Declare the handful of shapes this module reads locally, in this file, and
say in a comment that they mirror `packages/ruleset/src/data.ts`. Adding the dependency to reuse three type
aliases would couple the app to the scraper's build.

### New — `packages/shared/src/workspace/GameDataDialog.tsx`

The dictionary. `ShortcutHelp.tsx:18` is the closest existing analogue — a read-only, scrollable reference
overlay with a close button and the summoned-from focus-return ref (lines 26-42) — and `BattlesDialog.tsx:19`
is the model for the controlled list-and-detail layout (`selectedIndex` + `onSelect`, `grid` sizing, its
`battles-backdrop` / `battles-dialog` / `battles-close` test ids). Follow both.

```ts
export function GameDataDialog({
  index,
  initialEntryId,
  onDismiss
}: {
  index: GameDataIndex;
  /** Where to land. null opens on the first tab's first entry. */
  initialEntryId: string | null;
  onDismiss: () => void;
}): JSX.Element;
```

Structure: house backdrop (`fixed inset-0 z-40 flex items-start justify-center bg-black/50 pt-[10vh]`,
`data-testid="game-data-backdrop"`, `onPointerDown` self-target dismiss), inner
`role="dialog" aria-modal="true" aria-label="Game data"`, `w-[56rem] max-h-[85vh]`, then a tab strip, then a
`grid grid-cols-[15rem_1fr]` of list column and detail pane. `useEscapeToDismiss(onDismiss)`
(`workspace/dismissLayer.ts:12`).

All internal state is the dialog's own: the selected category, the filter text, the selected entry id, and a
**back stack** of entry ids for cross-reference navigation. Nothing is lifted and nothing persists — reopening
starts fresh.

Reuse `paletteKeyReduce` (`commandPalette.ts:106`,
`(state: { index: number; count: number }, key: string) => number | null`) for Up/Down/Home/End in the list.
It is exactly this behaviour and it is already tested; do not write a second one.

### Changed — `packages/shared/src/commandPalette.ts`

Game data joins the flat list, labelled with the tab it lives on.

```ts
export type PaletteEntryKind =
  | "unit" | "region" | "action" | "order-help"
  | "skill" | "man" | "mount" | "ship" | "monster" | "equipment" | "building";

export type PaletteInput = {
  ownUnits: Array<{ unitId: string; name: string; run: () => void }>;
  regions: Array<{ regionId: string; label: string; run: () => void }>;
  actions: Array<{ id: string; label: string; binding?: string; run: () => void }>;
  orderCommands: readonly string[];
  insertOrder: (command: string) => void;
  /** Every dictionary entry, or [] when the ruleset has not loaded. */
  gameData: readonly GameDataEntry[];
  openGameData: (entryId: string) => void;
};
```

`buildPaletteEntries` appends them **last**, after order help, so units and regions keep their position at the
top of an empty query. Each becomes
`{ id: \`data-${entry.id}\`, kind: entry.category, label: entry.tag === null ? entry.name : \`${entry.name} ${entry.tag}\`, run: () => input.openGameData(entry.id) }`.

Including the tag in `label` is deliberate: `filterPalette`'s `score` runs on `label`, so typing `MITH` finds
mithril. The label format matches what the panes already show (`UnitPanel.tsx:97-111` renders
`` `${skill.name} ${skill.tag}` ``), so the palette and the panes read the same.

`CommandPalette.tsx:118` currently renders `{entry.kind === "order-help" ? "order" : entry.kind}`. The new
kinds are already the words to show, so that expression needs no change beyond staying correct — verify it,
do not rewrite it.

### Changed — `packages/shared/src/workspace/AppShell.tsx`

- **The parsed index, memoised on the text:**
  ```ts
  const gameData = useMemo(() => (rulesetText === null ? null : parseGameData(rulesetText)), [rulesetText]);
  ```
  `rulesetText` is already there at line 297 and is `null` while loading and when unavailable, which is exactly
  the gate the navigator asked for. One parse per ruleset load, not per render, not per keystroke.
- **`const [gameDataEntryId, setGameDataEntryId] = useState<string | null>(null)`**, plus a boolean or a
  sentinel for "open on nothing in particular". Simplest: `useState<{ entryId: string | null } | null>(null)`
  — `null` means closed. Only `AppShell` holds this; `ah-5jkt.2` will set it from the panes.
- **Feed the palette:** in the `paletteEntries` memo (`AppShell.tsx:781-863`), pass
  `gameData: gameData?.entries ?? []` and `openGameData: (id) => setGameDataOpen({ entryId: id })`. Add
  `gameData` to the dependency array at lines 852-863.
- **Render it** beside the other dialogs, near `CommandPalette` at lines 2559-2561:
  ```tsx
  {gameDataOpen !== null && gameData !== null ? (
    <GameDataDialog index={gameData} initialEntryId={gameDataOpen.entryId} onDismiss={() => setGameDataOpen(null)} />
  ) : null}
  ```

**No new shortcut and no new palette action entry.** The way in is the data entries themselves; the navigator
chose the palette route and did not ask for a separate control. `shortcuts.ts` is not touched.

### Where state lives

The parsed index is a `useMemo` in `AppShell` keyed on `rulesetText`; the open/closed state and the landing
entry are `AppShell` state; everything inside the dialog — tab, filter, selection, back stack — belongs to the
dialog and dies with it. **No store, nothing persisted.** A parsed 277-entry index is small and cheap to
rebuild, and persisting a reference dialog's scroll position is not worth a store.

## Increments

Each opens with the named failing test.

1. **Parse and categorise.** New `packages/shared/src/gameData.test.ts` →
   `"sorts every category alphabetically and puts each item under its own kind"`. Write `parseGameData` for
   skills, items and buildings, and the `entries` list. Assert the five item kinds land in five categories and
   that a building has `tag: null`.
2. **Rubbish in.** Same file → `"returns null for text that is not a ruleset"`. Cases: `""`, `"{}"`,
   `"not json"`, and a JSON object with no `skills` key.
3. **The lookups.** Same file → `"finds a building by its report kind, whatever its case"` and
   `"reports an absent entry rather than throwing"`. Write `skillEntryId`, `itemEntryId`, `buildingEntryId`
   and `detailOf`, including the `{ kind: "absent" }` branch for `Mine` and `Road N`.
4. **The derived reverse link.** Same file → `"says which skill produces an item, and at what level"`.
   Assert `MITH` reports `mining` at level 3 — the real values from the shipped file.
5. **The dialog's list and tabs.** New `GameDataDialog.test.tsx` →
   `"lists every ship on the Ships tab and details the chosen one"`. Render with a small hand-built index.
6. **Landing on an entry.** Same file → `"opens on the entry it was given, with that entry's tab selected"`.
   Pass `initialEntryId: "ship:LONG"` and assert both the tab and the selected row.
7. **Following a cross-reference.** Same file → `"following a produced item switches tab and offers a way
   back"`. The back stack, and the trail control.
8. **The absent state.** Same file → `"says the game data does not describe a structure it never scraped"`.
   Assert the exact sentence from *User-facing decisions*.
9. **Palette entries.** `commandPalette.test.ts` →
   `"lists game data after order help, labelled with the tab it opens"` and
   `"offers no game data when the ruleset has not loaded"` (pass `gameData: []`). Then widen
   `PaletteEntryKind` and `PaletteInput`, and wire `AppShell`.

Increments 1-4 are pure and need no rendering; do them first and the rest is layout against a proven index.

## The test plan

Unit, vitest, co-located. Component tests render with `renderToStaticMarkup` from `react-dom/server` —
**not Testing Library, which this repository does not use.** Follow `commandPalette.test.ts`'s `entries()`
helper (lines 11-28) for building a fixed `PaletteInput`.

| File | Pins |
|---|---|
| `packages/shared/src/gameData.test.ts` (new) | increments 1-4 |
| `packages/shared/src/workspace/GameDataDialog.test.tsx` (new) | increments 5-8 |
| `packages/shared/src/commandPalette.test.ts` | increment 9, added to the existing file |

**Build the test index by hand, in the test file.** Do not read `config/public/ruleset.json` from a unit test:
it is 277 entries of shipping data that will change under the suite the next time the scraper runs, and a test
that breaks when the game changes its prices is a test nobody trusts. Use four or five entries chosen to cover
the branches — a skill that produces things, a skill that requires things, a ship, a monster with a combat
block, a building.

**One test that must read the real file**, and only one: a smoke-level guard in `gameData.test.ts` asserting
`parseGameData(readFileSync("config/public/ruleset.json", "utf8")) !== null` and that its `entries.length` is
greater than 200. That pins the parser against the actual shipped shape without pinning any value in it.

**Browser:** add one case to `tests/smoke/shortcuts.spec.ts`, beside the existing palette tests at lines 52-66
— open the palette, type a skill name, press Enter, and assert the game data dialog appears showing it. That
file already has the `"Escape closes only the palette, not the dialog under it"` pattern at lines 89-100, which
is the one to extend if dialog stacking needs pinning.

**Suites to run:** `pnpm run check:fast` and `pnpm run test:smoke`.

## User-facing decisions

Mockups: `docs/ui/ah-5jkt-dictionary.html` is the design that was chosen; `docs/ui/ah-5jkt-game-data.html` is
the first round, kept because its rejected options are recorded here and a later reader may want to see them.

**The shape of the thing.** The first round offered (A) a small one-thing-at-a-time dialog and (B) a
list-beside-detail browser. The navigator rejected both as posed and specified a third: **a full dictionary
with a type selector, the list showing every entry of the selected type, the detail on the right, and — when
opened by clicking a specific skill or item — landing straight on that entry.** That is what is built. Do not
reduce it to a single-entry lookup.

**How the types divide.** Offered: (A) three tabs matching the data's own keys — Skills, Items, Buildings;
(B) **seven tabs** splitting items by their `kind` — Skills, Men, Mounts, Ships, Monsters, Equipment,
Buildings; (C) a dropdown instead of tabs. **Chosen: B.** Every list is then short enough to read down — nine
ships, four mounts, fourteen men — so "what ships are there?" is answerable by looking, and the split costs
nothing because `kind` is already on every item. Rejected A because 171 items in one list makes browsing by
category impossible; rejected the dropdown because it hides what is available behind a click.
**Tab order is exactly: Skills, Men, Mounts, Ships, Monsters, Equipment, Buildings.** Each tab shows its count.

**Reverse links.** Offered: derive "Produced by" and "Built by", or show only what the data states directly.
**Chosen: derive them.** "How do I get mithril?" is the question a player actually has, and without it they
would browse 96 skills to answer it.

**Cross-references are clickable.** A skill's `produces` and `requires`, and an item's derived `producedBy`,
open that entry — switching tab if needed and pushing a back step.

**Escape.** Offered: close the whole dialog, or retrace the trail first. **Chosen: close the whole dialog**,
because Escape means the same thing in every other dialog in this application and the Back control already
handles stepping back.

**A filter box on the list.** Offered: yes, scoped to the selected type; or no, since the palette searches.
**Chosen: yes.** Equipment has 86 entries and Monsters 58; scrolling those to find one is poor, and the box
keeps you inside the dialog once you are browsing.

**The palette label.** Offered: match the tabs (`skill`, `ship`, `monster`, …); one label reading `game data`;
or three matching the data's keys. **Chosen: match the tabs**, so what the palette says is where you land, and
a Longship is told from a longbow at a glance. This is why `PaletteEntryKind` gains six members rather than one.

**Palette placement.** Game data entries join the same flat list as everything else, rather than sitting behind
a `?` prefix — one box and one habit. They are appended **last** so an empty query still shows your own units
first.

**When the ruleset has not loaded.** Offered: offer nothing until loaded and explain a failure where it is
met; always offer and let the dialog explain; or offer nothing silently. **Chosen: the first.** No game-data
entries appear in the palette while `rulesetText` is `null`, and if `ah-5jkt.2`'s pane links somehow reach the
dialog without an index, it says so rather than rendering an empty dictionary.

**List order.** Offered: alphabetical by name, or ordered by the numbers that matter per type. **Chosen:
alphabetical**, case-insensitively, matching how anyone looks something up in a reference.

**Keyboard and focus**, approved as proposed:

- Focus opens in the **filter box**.
- **Up/Down** move the selected entry, **Home/End** jump to the ends — via `paletteKeyReduce`.
- **Left/Right** switch tabs.
- **Enter** follows a focused cross-reference; otherwise it does nothing.
- **Escape** closes the dialog.
- **Tab** reaches, in order: the tab strip, the filter box, the list, the Close button.
- Focus returns to whatever summoned the dialog when it closes — the same `summonedFrom` ref
  `CommandPalette.tsx:35-49` and `ShortcutHelp.tsx:26-42` already use.

### Strings, verbatim

| Where | String |
|---|---|
| Dialog title and `aria-label` | `Game data` |
| Tabs | `Skills` `Men` `Mounts` `Ships` `Monsters` `Equipment` `Buildings`, each followed by its count |
| Filter placeholder | `Filter <tab name lower-cased>…` — e.g. `Filter ships…` |
| Skill fields | `Study cost` → `<n> silver per man per month`; `Highest level`; `Magic` → `yes` / `no` |
| Skill, no cost | `not priced` |
| Skill group headings | `Produces`, `Requires` |
| Skill produces/requires row | name on the left, `at level <n>` on the right |
| `Requires` when empty | `nothing — it can be studied from the start` |
| `Produces` when empty | `nothing` |
| Item fields | `Weight`; `Moves` → `<n> hexes a month`; `Carries` → `<n> walking · <n> riding · <n> flying`; `Moves itself` → the true modes joined by `, ` |
| Ship fields | `Cargo capacity`; `Sailing skill needed` → the linked skill name and level |
| Monster group | `Combat`, with `Skill`, `Attacks a round`, `Hits to kill`, `Damage an attack` |
| Item reverse link group | `Produced by` |
| Building fields | `Protects` → `<n> men`; `Building cost`; `Materials`; `Mages needed` |
| Absent entry | `The game data does not describe this. Only fortifications were scraped from the rules page.` |
| Back control | `← Back`, followed by the name of the entry it returns to |
| Close button | `Close` |

## Out of scope

- **Clicking anything in a pane.** Every pane change is `ah-5jkt.2`, which is blocked on this bead. Do not
  touch `UnitPanel.tsx`, `RegionPanel.tsx` or `primitives.tsx` here — in particular, do **not** widen
  `Row`'s `label` prop from `string` to `ReactNode`; that is `.2`'s change and it touches four call sites.
- **Widening the scrape.** Mines, Shafts, roads, terrain, races and any prose at all are missing, and that is
  **`ah-3cj4`**, filed and unranked. This bead only has to say so gracefully.
- **A shortcut of its own** for the dialog. The palette is the way in.
- **Searching game data from anywhere but the palette.**
- **Anything from `movement`, `risk` or `gaps`** in the ruleset. They are rules constants rather than a
  dictionary of things, and they want a different presentation. Not asked for.
- **`ah-wkwk`** (the palette finding a specific structure by name or id) is a different bead about the
  player's own structures, not the game data catalogue. Do not conflate them.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
pnpm run test:smoke
```

Both green. Then look at it, because a dictionary is judged by reading it:

1. Open the palette, type `mining`, and confirm the skill appears labelled `skill` and opens the dialog on it.
2. Walk all seven tabs. Confirm the counts read 96 / 14 / 4 / 9 / 58 / 86 / 10 and that each list is
   alphabetical.
3. On `mithril`, confirm `Produced by` names `mining` at level 3, and that clicking it moves to the Skills tab
   with a back control naming `mithril`.
4. Filter within Equipment and confirm it narrows only that tab.
5. Confirm Escape closes from a deep trail, and that focus returns to where you opened it from.
6. Break the ruleset fetch (rename `config/public/ruleset.json` in the dev server, or block the request) and
   confirm the palette simply offers no game data rather than erroring.

## Known traps

- **`buildings` is keyed by the upper-cased name, not a tag** — `"MAGICAL CASTLE"`, not `"MCAS"`. A report
  says `Fort`. Upper-case before looking up, and expect misses: only ten fortifications exist, so `Mine`,
  `Shaft`, `Road N` and every ship-as-structure will fall to the absent branch. That is correct behaviour here,
  not a bug to work around.
- **Ships are items, not buildings.** A `Longship` in a report's structure list is `items["LONG"]`. Anyone
  reaching for `buildings` to resolve a structure kind will find nothing and conclude the data is broken.
- **Do not add `@atlantis/ruleset` as a dependency of `@atlantis/shared`.** Its index does not export the skill
  or building types anyway, and its `Ruleset` type collides by name with `packages/shared/src/rulesets.ts`'s.
  Mirror the shapes locally.
- **Parse once.** `parseGameData` on every render, or per palette keystroke, re-parses a 277-entry document
  behind a filter that runs on every character. Memoise on `rulesetText` and nothing else.
- **`rulesetText` is `null` both while loading and on failure** (`AppShell.tsx:192-195, 297`). One `null` check
  covers both, which is why the navigator's "offer nothing" decision is cheap.
- **`COLUMNS`-style constants do not apply here, but `SHOWN_LIMIT` does**: `CommandPalette.tsx:6` caps the
  palette at 12 rows. Adding 277 entries does not change that cap, but it does mean an empty query now has 277
  more candidates behind it — which is exactly why they are appended last.
- **WebKit's driver returns `""` for text it considers clipped**, so a truncated entry name can read as empty
  in the native suite while Chromium passes. Assert on the rendered markup in unit tests rather than on visible
  text.
- **Work in a worktree under `.cerebro/worktrees/`**, never the main checkout, per `CLAUDE.md`.

title: The map's top band is spent on controls that could live in settings
description:
The staleness, movement and badges controls sit alongside the map and take room the map could use. They belong in settings: put them there and give the space back to the map.

The selected level is different — it is something the player changes often and wants to see at a glance, so it moves up into the top bar, next to the faction name, rather than into settings.

Raised by the navigator 2026-08-19.
design:
## Context

The staleness, movement and badge controls sit in a strip floating over the map's top-left corner —
the part of the canvas the map most wants — and take room it could use. The bead asks for them to
move into settings, and for the **selected level** to move up into the top bar instead, because it is
changed often and wants to be seen at a glance.

**Reading `LayerChips.tsx` turned up a distinction the bead does not make, and the navigator acted on
it.** The strip holds four things, and they are not the same kind of thing:

| Control | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Staleness** | one switch, set once |
| **Movement** | one switch, set once |
| **Badges** | a popover menu of ~10 marks — ships, shafts, lairs, roads — flicked **while reading the map**, whose chip already lights when any is off *"so a hex missing a mark is never a mystery"* |
| **Level** | a `<select>` when the game has several levels, plain text when it has one |

So **staleness and movement move; badges stays.** Hiding a badge to read a crowded hex behind a
settings dialog would be open-dialog, find-tab, toggle, close, look — with the dialog covering the
very hex being read. The map gains most of the band, and a one-chip strip survives.

Branch from `origin/main`; every line number here is that tree.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### 1. Two toggles leave the strip — `workspace/LayerChips.tsx`

The `LAYERS` array (`:21-24`) and the block that renders it (`:41-57`) go. What remains is the
`ChipPopover` for Badges (`:59-83`), and the strip shrinks to one chip.

**Its doc comment must be updated rather than left**, because it currently explains a composition
that will no longer exist. It already records why badges moved *into* a popover — *"ten of them will
not fit in a strip that shares the map's top band with the zoom cluster"* — and that reasoning is
exactly why badges stays on the map now:

```tsx
/**
 * The badge menu, above the map.
 *
 * Staleness and movement used to sit here too. They are set once and then forgotten, so they moved
 * into Settings → Global beside the other display preferences and gave the band back to the map
 * (ah-l9mp). Badges did not: it is ten marks flicked *while reading* a crowded hex, and its chip
 * lights when any of them is off, so a hex missing a mark is never a mystery. Behind a dialog that
 * gesture becomes four, with the dialog over the hex being read.
 *
 * The level selector left too, for the opposite reason - it is changed often enough to want to be
 * visible without looking at the map's corner, so it is in the top bar.
 */
```

**Keep `data-testid="layer-chips"`** on the container. Smoke tests use it, and the strip still exists.

### 2. The level moves to the top bar — `workspace/AppHeader.tsx`

The level block (`LayerChips.tsx:85-104`) moves as-is, keeping **today's rule exactly**: a `<select>`
with `aria-label="Map level"` when `levels.length > 1`, and a plain `<span>` when it is one. The
navigator chose that continuity — it costs the header nothing in the common single-level case.

`AppHeader` gains `levels: MapLevel[]`, and reads `level`/`setLevel` from the store as `LayerChips`
does today (`:31-32`) — the store is already the shared home for both, so nothing is threaded through
`AppShell` that need not be.

**Place it beside the faction name**, which is what the bead asks for and what makes it glanceable.

**It costs header height, and `ah-csni` is being built right now to bound exactly that.** A `<select>`
is taller than a text chip. If `ah-csni` has landed, its budget test will say so immediately; if the
budget is exceeded, **raise it in this bead's own commit** — that is the mechanism working, not a
problem, and `ah-csni`'s plan says so.

### 3. Two entries in Settings → Global — `workspace/SettingsDialog.tsx`

Into the **Global** tab (`:179` onward), which already holds App theme, Map theme, Biome textures,
the getting-around guide, pane transparency and interface size — every other *"how the map and panes
look"* control. Place them after **Biome textures**, since all three are about what the map draws:

```tsx
        <SettingToggle
          label="Staleness"
          hint="Shade hexes by how long ago you last saw them."
          …
        />
        <SettingToggle
          label="Movement"
          hint="Draw the routes units are ordered to travel."
          …
        />
```

Both strings are the navigator's, chosen to keep the names players already know from the chips.
**Match `SettingToggle`'s actual prop names** (`workspace/SettingToggle.tsx`) rather than the sketch
above, and give each a `data-testid` in the house form the Warnings tab uses
(`settings-warning-${code}` → `settings-layer-staleness`, `settings-layer-movement`).

### 4. Nothing about the state changes

`layers`, `toggleLayer`, `level` and `setLevel` all live in `workspaceStore` already
(`LayerChips.tsx:27-32`), and `layers` is already persisted. **No store change, no migration, and a
player's existing choices survive** — the same switches, driven from a different place. If this bead
touches `workspaceStore.ts`, something has been rebuilt that already worked.

## Increments

1. **The toggles appear in settings.**
   RED: `SettingsDialog.test.tsx` — `the Global tab offers the map layer toggles`, asserting both
   labels, both hints and both `data-testid`s in the static markup. Its first case hard-codes a
   `titles` array for the Warnings tab; check whether the Global tab has a similar list that also
   needs both names.
   GREEN: the two `SettingToggle`s.

2. **They leave the strip.**
   RED: `LayerChips.test.tsx:20` asserts `Staleness` is in the markup — it must **fail**, then be
   rewritten to assert the strip holds **only** Badges.
   GREEN: `LAYERS` and its render block deleted, the doc comment rewritten.

3. **The level moves up.**
   RED: `AppHeader`'s render test — `the header names the level`, and `a single level is plain text,
   not a select`. Both from static markup.
   GREEN: the block moved, `levels` threaded in.

4. **The map got the band back, and nothing else moved.**
   RED: none — the check. Smoke suite in **both** projects: the layer toggles are reachable through
   Settings, the level through the header, badges still on the map, and a player's persisted choices
   still honoured.

## The test plan

| Test | Where | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| `the Global tab offers the map layer toggles` | `SettingsDialog.test.tsx` | labels, hints, testids |
| **the existing `Staleness` assertion** (`LayerChips.test.tsx:20`) | rewritten | the strip now holds only Badges |
| `the badge chip is still there and still lights when a badge is off` | `LayerChips.test.tsx` | the thing that stayed |
| `the header names the level` | `AppHeader` test | the move |
| `a single level is plain text, not a select` | same | today's rule, kept |
| **toggling staleness in Settings changes the map** | smoke | the wiring, end to end |
| **the level selector in the header changes level** | smoke | the wiring, end to end |
| the badge menu still opens from the map | smoke | unchanged |

**Suites:** `pnpm run check:fast`, and the smoke suite in **both** projects — this moves controls
between two panes and the header, and `ah-etb0.2` broke desktop-shell only for less.

**Watch `ah-csni`'s header budget** if it has landed; see §2.

## User-facing decisions

Interviewed with the navigator on 2026-08-19 over `.cerebro/scratch/ah-l9mp-strip.html`. The chosen
mockup is committed to `docs/ui/ah-l9mp-strip.html`.

**Q1 — does Badges belong in settings?** Chosen: **no — staleness and movement move, badges stays on
the map.** It is the only one of the three used *while reading* rather than set once, and its chip
carries the "something is hidden" signal. Rejected: **all three into settings** (the bead as written —
simplest rule and the whole band back, but hiding one badge becomes four gestures with a dialog over
the hex being read, and the signal needs a new home) and **all three out, with Badges as a header
chip** (one click, nothing over the map — but it spends from the budget `ah-csni` is being built to
protect).

**Q2 — the level in the top bar.** Chosen: **keep today's rule** — a control when there is a choice,
plain text when there is not. Costs the header nothing in the common single-level case and preserves
behaviour exactly. Rejected: a chip that opens a list (matches the other header controls, but a new
popover for something a `<select>` already did) and moving the select unchanged into a row of chips.

**Q3 — the settings wording.** Chosen: **"Staleness"** — *"Shade hexes by how long ago you last saw
them."* — and **"Movement"** — *"Draw the routes units are ordered to travel."* Keeps the names
players already know from the chips. Rejected: fuller names (`Shade stale hexes`, `Show movement
routes`), which say more without the description but break continuity with the labels in use.

**Not asked:** placing the two entries after Biome textures (all three are about what the map draws),
and keeping `data-testid="layer-chips"` on the surviving strip.

## Out of scope

- **The Badges menu itself** — its contents, its chip, its popover. It stays exactly as it is.
- **The zoom cluster**, which shares the map's top band and is not part of this.
- **Any change to `workspaceStore`.** The state and its persistence are already right.
- **Reclaiming the space the strip leaves.** The map fills its canvas; nothing needs to be told the
  band is free. If something does, that is a finding worth reporting rather than a change to make
  here.
- **A settings entry for the badges**, which would duplicate a control that is staying.
- **The header budget itself**, which is `ah-csni`. This bead may raise the number; it does not build
  the mechanism.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
pnpm exec playwright test --project=web
pnpm exec playwright test --project=desktop-shell
```

Then by eye:

1. **The map has the band back.** Only the Badges chip floats in the top-left; staleness and movement
   are gone from it. Confirm the map draws under where they were.
2. **Settings → Global** shows Staleness and Movement after Biome textures, with the agreed hints.
   Toggle each and watch the map change **while the dialog is open** if it is non-modal, or
   immediately on close if not — either is fine, but note which, because it is the thing that makes a
   settings-based toggle feel worse than a chip.
3. **The level is in the top bar**, beside the faction name, and changes level. Then load a game with
   **one** level and confirm it reads as plain text rather than a dead select.
4. **A player's existing choices survive.** With staleness previously off, reload: it must still be
   off, and Settings must show it off. This is the one thing a store change would silently break.
5. **Badges still opens from the map**, and its chip still lights when a badge is off.
6. **Header height.** If `ah-csni` has landed, its budget test is the answer. If it has not, measure
   by eye that the header has not wrapped to a second row at the smoke viewport.

## Known traps

- **`LayerChips.test.tsx:20` asserts `Staleness` is in the strip.** It is *supposed* to fail;
  rewriting it to assert the strip holds only Badges is part of the work, not collateral.
- **Keep `data-testid="layer-chips"`.** The strip survives with one chip in it, and smoke tests
  address it by that id.
- **The level's two shapes are today's behaviour**, not a simplification to make: `levels.length > 1`
  gives a `<select>` with `aria-label="Map level"`, one level gives a `<span>`. Collapsing them to a
  select leaves a dead control in every single-level game.
- **A `<select>` is taller than a text chip**, so this bead spends header height — the exact resource
  `ah-csni` bounds. Raising the budget in this bead's own commit is the intended path.
- **Do not touch `workspaceStore`.** `layers` is already persisted and already correct; a "tidy-up"
  there is how a player's saved preferences get lost.
- **`SettingToggle`'s real prop names** are in `workspace/SettingToggle.tsx`; the sketch in §3 is
  intent, not a quotation.
- **Both smoke projects.** Controls moving between panes is precisely the change that broke
  desktop-shell alone in `ah-etb0.2`.
acceptance_criteria: The staleness and movement toggles are gone from the strip over the map and appear in Settings > Global after Biome textures, labelled Staleness and Movement with the hints 'Shade hexes by how long ago you last saw them.' and 'Draw the routes units are ordered to travel.', each with a data-testid in the house form. The Badges chip stays on the map with its popover and its lit-when-something-is-hidden behaviour unchanged, and the strip keeps its layer-chips testid. The selected level moves to the top bar beside the faction name, keeping today's rule exactly: a select with aria-label 'Map level' when the game has more than one level, plain text when it has one. LayerChips's doc comment is rewritten to describe what remains and why badges did not move. No change to workspaceStore, so a player's persisted layer choices survive a reload and show correctly in Settings - verified by hand with staleness previously off. Toggling either setting changes the map, and the header selector changes level, both covered by smoke tests in the web and desktop-shell projects. If ah-csni's header budget has landed and the level control exceeds it, the budget is raised in this bead's own commit.

title: Walk a turn's problems one at a time, by mouse as well as by key
description:
Working through a turn's problems means finding each one in a list and clicking to the unit that has it. There should be a way to walk them in order instead — next problem, previous problem — reachable both by mouse and by keyboard, so a player can remedy them one at a time without leaving the keyboard.

Stepping to a problem selects the unit it belongs to (following the hex if it is elsewhere, as in ah-87he). When a new unit is selected this way the order editor takes focus with the cursor at the end of the existing orders, so the player can type the fix straight away.

Raised by the navigator 2026-08-19.
design:
## Context

Working through a turn's problems means finding each one in a list and clicking to the unit that has
it. The bead asks for **next problem / previous problem**, reachable by mouse and by keyboard, so a
player can remedy them one at a time without leaving the keyboard.

**Most of the engine already exists**, which is the most useful thing to know before starting:

- **`walkProblems` (`AppShell.tsx:737-753`)** steps `problemTargets`, and when the target is a
  different unit calls `goToUnit(target.unitId)` and sets `pendingProblem`, which lands the selection
  once that unit's block has loaded (`:731-735`). It is already wired to `nextDiagnostic` /
  `prevDiagnostic` — **F8 and Shift-F8** (`shortcuts.ts:58`, `:112`).
- **`stepDiagnostic` (`diagnosticNav.ts:80-92`) already wraps**: `(last + direction + count) % count`,
  with `count === 0 → null`. The navigator chose wrapping, so **this is already the behaviour** and
  needs documenting rather than changing.
- **`goToUnit`** follows a unit into another hex and switches level — `ah-87he` uses it too.

So the new work is **a mouse route**, and one behaviour the bead asks for that would change what F8
does today.

### Where the bead and the code disagree, and why the code is only half right

The bead asks that the editor take focus *"with the cursor at the end of the existing orders, so the
player can type the fix straight away"*. What `selectProblem` does now
(`OrdersEditor.tsx:422-437`) is **select the offending token**, so you can type straight over the
wrong order.

Which is right depends on the finding, and there are now three shapes — the second of which this
session's own beads created:

| Finding | Carries | `toEditorDiagnostics` gives | Right landing |
|---|---|---|---|
| `spends 250 silver it has not got` | line **and** columns | the token | **select it** — you are editing that order |
| `has no order that spends the month` (`ah-dwk6`) | a line, **no columns** | `from = 0, to = line.length` — **the whole `unit 4117` line** | **end of the orders** — the fix is a new order, and typing over the block header is the worst outcome available |
| `nobody is guarding this hex` | **no line** | skipped entirely (`orderLint.ts:31-33`) | nothing in this unit's orders helps |

The middle row is measured, not assumed: `orderLint.ts:41-48` widens a collapsed span to its whole
line, so today's `selectProblem` on an `ah-dwk6` finding selects `unit 4117` and the next keystroke
replaces it.

Branch from `origin/main`; every line number here is that tree.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### 1. The landing depends on what the finding carries — `OrdersEditor.tsx:422-437`

`selectProblem` gains one branch:

```ts
    selectProblem(problem) {
      const editor = view.current;
      if (!editor) {
        return;
      }
      // A finding with no columns has no token to put the cursor on - and `toEditorDiagnostics`
      // widens a collapsed span to its whole line, so selecting it would select `unit 4117` and
      // the next keystroke would replace the block header. Those findings are about an order that
      // is *missing* (ah-dwk6, ah-vkut), so the useful place to be is the end of the block, ready
      // to type the order that is not there (ah-dlao).
      if (problem.columnStart === null || problem.columnEnd === null) {
        const end = editor.state.doc.length;
        editor.dispatch({ selection: { anchor: end, head: end }, scrollIntoView: true });
        editor.focus();
        return;
      }
      … today's body, unchanged …
    },
```

**`doc.length` is the end of the orders, not the end of the file**, because the editor holds one
unit's block: `OrdersPanel.tsx:98` sets it from `readUnitOrders(document, unitId)`. Verify that still
holds before relying on it — if the editor is ever given the whole document, this must become the end
of the unit's block instead.

A finding with **no line at all** never reaches here: `toEditorDiagnostics` skips it
(`orderLint.ts:31-33`) and `selectProblem` already returns early on `!placed`. Confirm hex-level
findings are also absent from `problemTargets` — if they are targets, the walk stops on something it
cannot land on, and they should be filtered there.

### 2. The mouse route — `OrdersPanel.tsx`

Two stepper buttons in the orders pane's header row, beside the per-unit problem list that is already
there. The navigator chose this over the header (which would spend from the budget `ah-csni` exists
to protect) and over the problems panel (which `ah-87he` just made close on a jump, so it is not open
while you work).

`OrdersPanel` takes one new prop, and `AppShell` passes the function it already has:

```ts
  /** Step to the next or previous problem in the whole turn - the same walk F8 and Shift-F8 make. */
  onWalkProblems?: (direction: 1 | -1) => void;
```

`AppShell` passes `onWalkProblems={walkProblems}` where it renders `OrdersPanel` (`:3012-3026`).
**Nothing about `walkProblems` changes.** That is the point: one engine, two ways in, so the mouse
and the keyboard cannot drift apart.

The buttons, following the house pattern for a clickable thing in a pane —
`type="button"`, the `focus-visible:outline focus-visible:outline-1 focus-visible:outline-brass` pair
used by `CollapsiblePanel.tsx:75`, and `aria-label`s, since a bare chevron announces nothing:

```tsx
<button type="button" aria-label="Previous problem" data-testid="walk-problem-prev" …>‹</button>
<button type="button" aria-label="Next problem" data-testid="walk-problem-next" …>›</button>
```

**Never disabled, and never hidden.** The walk wraps, so there is no end to be at; and a stepper that
greys out reads as broken where a key that does nothing does not. When the turn has **no** problems
at all, `stepDiagnostic` returns `null` and the click is a no-op — which is right, and is why the
buttons need no state of their own.

Their tooltip names the keys, so the mouse route teaches the keyboard one: `title="Next problem (F8)"`
and `title="Previous problem (Shift-F8)"`.

### 3. Nothing else

`walkProblems`, `stepDiagnostic`, `goToUnit`, `pendingProblem` and the shortcut registry are all
unchanged. If this bead's diff touches `diagnosticNav.ts`, something has been reimplemented that
already worked.

## Increments

1. **The landing suits the finding.**
   RED: `OrdersEditor`'s tests (or new ones beside them) — `a finding with columns selects its token`
   (unchanged behaviour, written first so the change is visibly scoped) and
   **`a finding with no columns puts the cursor at the end of the orders`**, asserting the selection
   is collapsed at `doc.length` rather than covering the `unit` line.
   GREEN: the branch in §1.
   **There is no jsdom** (`UnitTableDock.test.tsx:8-14`), so if these need a live CodeMirror they
   belong in the smoke suite instead — check which before writing, and put them where they can
   actually run.

2. **The pane offers the walk.**
   RED: `OrdersPanel`'s render test — `the walk buttons are present and labelled`, asserting both
   `data-testid`s and both `aria-label`s in the static markup.
   GREEN: the two buttons and the prop.

3. **Clicking walks.**
   RED: `tests/smoke/workspace.spec.ts` — `the next-problem button steps to the next problem`,
   modelled on the existing F8 coverage: load a turn with several problems, click
   `walk-problem-next`, and assert the unit pane now describes a different unit. Then
   `walk-problem-prev` returns to the first.
   GREEN: `onWalkProblems={walkProblems}` in `AppShell`.

4. **It wraps, and the buttons never die.**
   RED: `the walk wraps at the end` — click next as many times as there are problems plus one, and
   assert it is back at the first; and `the buttons stay enabled with no problems at all`, on a turn
   with none.
   GREEN: nothing — `stepDiagnostic` already wraps. **If this needs a code change, something was
   reimplemented.**

## The test plan

| Test | Where | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| `a finding with columns selects its token` | `OrdersEditor` tests / smoke | today's behaviour, unchanged |
| **`a finding with no columns puts the cursor at the end of the orders`** | same | the bead's actual request, where it applies |
| `the walk buttons are present and labelled` | `OrdersPanel` render test | markup and accessible names |
| `the next-problem button steps to the next problem` | `workspace.spec.ts` | the mouse route |
| `the previous-problem button steps back` | same | both directions |
| **`the walk wraps at the end`** | same | the existing behaviour, now documented |
| `the buttons stay enabled with no problems at all` | same | never-disabled |
| the existing F8 / Shift-F8 coverage | `shortcuts.spec.ts` | **unchanged** — one engine, two ways in |

**Suites:** `pnpm run check:fast`, plus the smoke suite in **both** projects — this bead adds a
control to a pane, and `ah-etb0.2` is the precedent for a control that broke desktop-shell only.

**Watch the header budget.** If `ah-csni` has landed, its test will tell you at once whether these
buttons cost anything; they are in the orders pane rather than the header precisely so they should
not.

## User-facing decisions

Interviewed with the navigator on 2026-08-19 over `.cerebro/scratch/ah-dlao-walk.html`. The chosen
mockup is committed to `docs/ui/ah-dlao-walk.html`.

**Q1 — where the cursor lands.** Chosen: **select the token where there is one, end of the orders
where there is not.** So `spends 250 silver it has not got` selects the `GIVE`, and
`has no order that spends the month` leaves you ready to type a new order. Rejected: **always the end
of the orders**, which is the bead as written — one rule, easy to describe, but it loses the token
selection F8 has today, so for a wrong order you have to go and find it, which is the thing the bead
exists to stop; and **always select**, unchanged, which for the new missing-order warnings selects
`unit 4117` and lets the next keystroke replace the block header.

**Q2 — where the mouse control lives.** Chosen: **the orders pane, above the editor** — where the
fixing happens, and visible while you type. Accepted cost: the pane is per-unit, so a control that
walks the whole turn sitting in it reads slightly oddly. Rejected: **the problems panel's title bar**
(costs the header nothing and could highlight the current row, but `ah-87he` just made that panel
close on a jump, so it is not open while you work) and **beside the problems chip in the header**
(next to the count it walks, but it spends from exactly the budget `ah-csni` was planned to protect).
Also rejected: keyboard only, which declines the bead's request.

**Q3 — the ends of the list.** Chosen: **wrap around, and say so.** A turn's problems are a set to
work through rather than a sequence with an end, and the buttons never look dead. **This is already
what `stepDiagnostic` does**, so it is a documentation and never-disable decision rather than a
behaviour change. Rejected: stopping at the ends with a disabled button.

**Not asked:** the `aria-label`s and the `title`s naming the keys; that `walkProblems` is passed down
rather than reimplemented.

## Out of scope

- **`walkProblems`, `stepDiagnostic`, `goToUnit` and `pendingProblem`.** All already correct; this
  bead adds a caller.
- **The F8 / Shift-F8 bindings** and the shortcut registry.
- **Hex-level findings becoming walkable.** They have no line and nothing in a unit's orders to land
  on. If they turn out to be in `problemTargets`, filter them there and say so — but giving them a
  landing place is a different bead.
- **A position indicator** — "problem 3 of 7". Genuinely useful, and it wants its own thought about
  where it lives; not filed.
- **The problems panel** and the header chip, both considered and rejected under Q2.
- **`ah-87he`'s clickable unit numbers**, which are the other way into the same journey and already
  merged.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
pnpm exec playwright test --project=web
pnpm exec playwright test --project=desktop-shell
```

Then by hand, in the running app, and **the point is to actually fix a turn with it**:

1. Load a turn with several problems across different hexes. Click **next problem** repeatedly and
   confirm each press selects the right unit, moves the hex when it needs to, and switches level when
   the unit is on another one.
2. **Land on a finding with a token** — `spends … silver it has not got` — and confirm the offending
   order is **selected**, so typing replaces it.
3. **Land on `has no order that spends the month`** and confirm the cursor sits at the **end of the
   block**, with nothing selected, ready for a new order. Type `WORK` and confirm it lands sensibly.
4. Click **next** past the last problem and confirm it **wraps** to the first.
5. Load a turn with **no** problems. The buttons are present, enabled, and do nothing.
6. **F8 and Shift-F8 still do exactly what they did** — walk the same list, in the same order, from
   the same starting point. Alternate between the keys and the buttons and confirm they share one
   position rather than keeping two.
7. Keyboard: tab to the buttons, confirm the brass focus ring and that Enter and Space both work.

## Known traps

- **`toEditorDiagnostics` widens a collapsed span to the whole line** (`orderLint.ts:41-48`). That is
  why a no-columns finding must be branched on *before* it reaches that mapping, not after — the
  mapping will happily give you a selection, and it will be the `unit` line.
- **The editor's document is one unit's block** (`OrdersPanel.tsx:98`), so `doc.length` is the end of
  the orders. Confirm before relying on it; if that ever changes, this lands at the end of the wrong
  thing and nothing will fail loudly.
- **`stepDiagnostic` already wraps.** Reimplementing the wrap in the button handler gives two
  positions that drift apart — and the drift only shows when a player alternates mouse and keyboard.
- **One engine, two ways in.** The buttons must call `walkProblems`, not a copy of it. `ah-f03z` is a
  whole bead about what happens when one rule gets two implementations.
- **Never disable the buttons.** With no problems the click is already a no-op via
  `stepDiagnostic`'s `count === 0 → null`; a disabled state would be a second source of truth about
  whether there is anything to walk.
- **There is no jsdom**, so anything that needs a live editor is a smoke test. Decide where each test
  goes before writing it, not after it fails oddly.
- **Both smoke projects.** A control added to a pane broke desktop-shell only once already
  (`ah-etb0.2`).
acceptance_criteria: The orders pane carries previous-problem and next-problem buttons above the editor, labelled for a screen reader, tooltipped with F8 and Shift-F8, carrying the house focus-visible brass ring, reachable by Tab and activating on Enter and Space. They call AppShell's existing walkProblems rather than any copy of it, so mouse and keyboard share one position - alternating between them continues the same walk. The walk wraps at both ends, which stepDiagnostic already does, and the buttons are never disabled or hidden: with no problems at all they are present, enabled, and do nothing. Landing on a finding that carries columns still selects the offending token exactly as today; landing on one with a line but no columns puts a collapsed cursor at the end of the unit's block instead, so typing adds an order rather than replacing the unit header - which is what toEditorDiagnostics' widening of a collapsed span to its whole line would otherwise cause. A finding with no line reaches the editor not at all. walkProblems, stepDiagnostic, goToUnit, pendingProblem and the shortcut registry are unchanged, and the existing F8 and Shift-F8 coverage passes untouched. The smoke suite passes in both the web and desktop-shell projects.

title: Reach the scraped game data from the palette and from any named thing in a pane
description:
The application scrapes the game data — skills, structure types, items and so on — but there is no way for a player to read it. Two ways in, both landing on the same modal dialog showing what was scraped about the thing:

1. From the palette: searching finds skills, structure types, items, etc. by name; choosing one opens the dialog.
2. From the panes: a skill, item or structure type named in the region or unit pane is clickable and opens the same dialog.

Raised by the navigator 2026-08-19.
close_reason: All children closed; last was ah-5jkt.2, delivered in PR #474

title: Faction password sits in cleartext in the saved orders on disk
description:
A player's orders document opens with '#atlantis <id> "<password>"', and the whole document is stored in the game's SQLite order_drafts table (see saveDraft, packages/shared/src/orderDraft.ts:53). So the faction password is on disk in cleartext, in a file a backup or a shared machine can reach.

This predates any feature that sends orders: the line arrives inside the server's own orders template, and the editor preserves the document byte for byte on purpose (packages/shared/src/ordersDocument.ts:3-13). Nothing reads the password out - it is never parsed, logged or surfaced - but it is stored.

Raised while planning ah-etb0 (sending orders to the game server). The navigator's decision there was to leave it alone rather than smuggle a fix into that bead, because stripping the password would change the byte-for-byte rule that import, export and the editor all depend on, and would need its own design: where the password is held instead when a send needs it, what happens to existing drafts, and whether an exported file should still carry it.

Unranked. Argue it up or down at triage - it is an exposure of a secret the player already has on their own machine, not a remote hole.
close_reason:
Invalid - the navigator's decision. The password must stay in the stored orders, because it is what lets an exported orders file be uploaded to the game server without being hand-edited first.

Investigated while planning. Three findings that make this a won't-fix rather than a deferral:

1. The password is on disk by two routes, not one. imported_turns.raw_report stores every imported report byte-for-byte and the orders template is a section inside it (migrations/0002_imported_turns.sql:5). Scrubbing order_drafts.order_text alone would have removed one copy of two.

2. Export is contractually required to carry it. docs/ui/README.md:141 - 'That line carries the faction password, so export must round-trip it and it must never be logged' - and ordersDocument.test.ts:88 and :204 assert the preservation.

3. Nothing here crosses a trust boundary. The password is the player's own secret, on the player's own machine, and it arrived in the .rep file the server emailed them, which is already in their downloads folder. The database copy is a copy, not a new exposure.

The narrowed version - redacting only the exported backup JSON, which is the one artefact that travels between people - was considered and also rejected, for the same reason as the whole: a restored game would carry '#atlantis <id> "<password>"' and its orders could not be uploaded until the player edited them by hand.

The existing guarantees stand and are not weakened: the password is never logged, never quoted back in a diagnostic, and never extracted into a field of its own (parser.rs:96, ordersImport.ts:41, with tests at parser.rs:664 and :672).

title: Units in hex names the structure a unit is standing in
description:
The structure column in the "Units in hex" table shows only the structure number in brackets, while
the region pane's structure list shows the name, the number and the type. The same structure reads
very differently in the two places, and the number alone does not say what the unit is standing in.

- `packages/shared/src/workspace/UnitTableDock.tsx:596`:
  `{unit.structureId ? `[${unit.structureId}]` : ""}`
- `packages/shared/src/workspace/RegionPanel.tsx:187`:
  `{structure.name} [{structure.structureId}] · {structure.kind}`

The column should read like the region pane's line.

Two things the planner has to settle:

- **The lookup.** The unit carries only `structureId`; the name and the kind live on the region's
  structures. The table does not do that join today, so it needs the region's structures in hand
  (or a lookup built once per hex rather than per row - the file's own header note says a hex can
  hold three hundred units across two dozen structures).
- **The width.** "Name [12] · Mine" is far wider than "[12]", in a table that is already dense and
  has had column width complained about before. Whether the column truncates, wraps, carries the
  full text in a tooltip, or whether the table's column sizing needs revisiting.
design: ## Context The Structure column of the "Units in hex" table shows only a bracketed number — `UnitTableDock.tsx:596`, `{unit.structureId ? \`[${unit.structureId}]\` : ""}`. Two panes away, the region pane writes the same structure as `{structure.name} [{structure.structureId}] · {structure.kind}` (`RegionPanel.tsx:187`). The same object reads completely differently in the two places, and a bare number does not say whether a unit is standing in a fort or sitting aboard a ship. After this bead the column reads like the region pane's line, and "who is in a ship" is answerable by scanning the table instead of by cross-referencing two panes. **The join needs no plumbing.** `UnitTableDock` already has the region: its prop is `hex: HexNode | null`, and `HexNode.region` is a `ReportRegion` carrying `structures: Array`. The component reads it transitively today at `UnitTableDock.tsx:77` (`unitsForHex(hex)`, which is `hex?.region ? sortUnitsForDisplay(hex.region.units) : []`, `hexMapModel.ts:224-226`). So `hex.region.structures` is in hand with **no prop change and no change to `AppShell.tsx:2960`**. **The constraint that shapes the whole bead:** every row is pinned to `rowHeightAt(interfaceSize)` so the pane can window three hundred units, and the table is `table-fixed` (`UnitTableDock.tsx:311-322`). The text therefore **cannot wrap**. Whatever does not fit is truncated, and the tooltip is the only way to read the rest. This is why the width question was put to the navigator rather than decided here. ## Files to change, and what to reuse ### New — `packages/shared/src/structureLabel.ts` There is no shared helper for this today; the format is written by hand in three places that do not agree (`RegionPanel.tsx:187` uses brackets, the private `formatStructures` at `turnDiff.ts:110-118` uses parentheses). This bead adds one and uses it in two of them. ```ts import type { StructureInfo } from "@atlantis/core-client"; /** * How a structure is named wherever it is written out in full: `Odds and Ends [12] · Fort`. * * One helper because the units table and the region pane must agree - the same structure read two * different ways in two panes is the defect this was extracted for (ah-kdgc). */ export function structureLabel(structure: StructureInfo): string; /** * The label for the structure a unit names, or the bare `[id]` when the region never described it. * * `null` when the unit is in no structure at all. A unit can name a structure the report did not * carry - a stale hex, or one seen from outside - and that is not the same as being outdoors. */ export function unitStructureLabel( structureId: string | null, structures: readonly StructureInfo[] ): string | null; ``` Behaviour: - `structureLabel` returns `` `${structure.name} [${structure.structureId}] · ${structure.kind}` ``. All three fields are non-nullable `string` on `StructureInfo` (`packages/core-client/src/generated/StructureInfo.ts`), so there is no absent case to handle. - `unitStructureLabel` returns `null` when `structureId` is `null`; `structureLabel(match)` when a structure with that `structureId` is in `structures`; and `` `[${structureId}]` `` when it is not. **Look the structure up through a `Map` built once per render of the table, not by scanning the array per row.** The module's own header note says a hex can hold three hundred units across two dozen structures, and the table re-renders on scroll. So `UnitTableDock` builds `useMemo(() => new Map(hex?.region?.structures.map((s) => [s.structureId, s]) ?? []), [hex])` and passes the resolved label down. Keep `unitStructureLabel`'s array signature anyway — it is what makes it testable — and have the memo feed it, or add a `Map` overload; that choice is the implementer's, but the per-row scan is not acceptable. ### Changed — `packages/shared/src/workspace/UnitTableDock.tsx` **The column width.** In the `` at lines 323-332, the eighth `` becomes `` (13rem). The two unsized `` entries — Skills and Items, columns 6 and 7 — absorb the loss; both already carry `truncate`, so this widens an existing behaviour rather than introducing one. **`const COLUMNS = 8` at line 35 does not change** — no column is added or removed, so `Spacer`'s `colSpan` stays correct. **The cell**, replacing lines 595-597: ```tsx {structureLabel ?? ""} ``` Note the added `truncate` — the cell has none today because `w-20` and a bare `[12]` never overflowed. The `` already carries `whitespace-nowrap` (line 526), so `truncate` is what turns an overflow into an ellipsis rather than a clipped word. `structureTitle` combines the two things that want the tooltip: - the full label, always, since the cell may be truncated; - and, when `structureChange` is non-null, `originalTooltip(structureChange)` on a second line beneath it. So: `[structureLabel, originalTooltip(structureChange)].filter(Boolean).join("\n")`, and `undefined` when that is empty — `Td`'s `title` prop is `string | undefined` (`UnitTableDock.tsx:602-617`). `originalTooltip` and `changeFor` are already imported at line 24; `structureChange = changeFor(unit, "structureId")` already exists at line 492 and is unchanged. `UnitRow` (lines 461-483) takes one new prop, `structureLabel: string | null`, supplied by the caller at lines 372-387 from the memoised map. Passing the resolved string rather than the map keeps `UnitRow` free of the lookup and keeps the test for it trivial. ### Changed — `packages/shared/src/workspace/RegionPanel.tsx` Line 187 becomes `{structureLabel(structure)}`, so the two panes cannot drift apart again. The `needs` clause that follows it on line 188 stays exactly as it is — `needs` is region-pane detail and does not belong in a table cell. **`turnDiff.ts:110-118` is deliberately not touched.** Its `formatStructures` uses parentheses, joins a whole list, and is pinned by snapshot-shaped assertions at `turnDiff.test.ts:250`; folding it in would change recorded diffs for a cosmetic gain. Say so in the commit rather than leaving the divergence looking accidental. ### Changed — `packages/shared/src/unitTable.ts` Two changes, both following from navigator decisions. **Sorting.** The `"structure"` sort currently orders by `structureId`. It becomes **name first, then id as the tie-break**, so units in one structure still group together: ```ts // sort key for the "structure" column (unit) => { const label = unitStructureLabel(unit.structureId, structures); return label === null ? "" : label; } ``` Sorting on the label string gives name-then-id ordering for free, because the label begins with the name and continues with the bracketed id. Units in no structure sort to one end, as they do today with an absent id — keep whichever end they currently land on and pin it with a test, rather than changing it silently. This means `sortUnits` needs the structures. Thread them through as a parameter from `UnitTableDock.tsx:78` (`sortUnits(filterUnits(units, filter), sort)`); do not reach for a module-level cache. **Filtering.** `filterUnits` at `unitTable.ts:74` matches structure id.
