least level 1, or wieldable weapons, or ridable mounts (and, once ah-v585 lands, a damaging spell).

The pillage warning's explanation was not widened with it. because_clause (crates/core/src/orders/
silver.rs:1926) now fires when readiness.ready is 0 and says only:

  " - this unit's N men hold no weapons they can wield"

That is true but partial. A unit with ready == 0 has no combat skill, no wieldable weapon AND no
ridable mount. The sentence names one of the three, so a player reading it may go and buy weapons
when a single point of Combat skill, or a horse and Riding 1, would have done - and a player who
already holds unridable mounts is told nothing about them at all.

## Why it was not decided at the time

ah-cw75's plan says so in terms, under What the verification changed:

  "The surviving sentence says 'holds no weapons he can wield', and after this change a unit can be
  combat ready without any weapon [...] If the wording needs to change to cover the new ways of
  being unready, that is a NEW user-facing question and goes back to the navigator; it was not asked
  here because the case did not exist when the sentence was written."

The clause correctly keys off ready rather than armed, which was the trap that plan named; this is
the wording question that keying it correctly exposes.

## What a fix would decide

Whether one sentence names all three ways ("no combat skill, no weapon it can wield and no mount it
can ride"), or the sentence names whichever is nearest to being satisfied, or it stays as it is on
the ground that weapons are the usual case. All three are user-facing wording and belong in an
interview with the navigator, not in an implementation.

Worth settling alongside ah-v585, which adds a fourth way and so makes the sentence one word further
from complete.

Unranked at P4.
design:
## Context

`ah-cw75` (`3660c2e3`) and `ah-v585` (`e166f9ef`) widened combat readiness to the rules' own taxing
test — a unit's men count if it has **Combat skill 1**, **a weapon it can wield**, **a mount it can
ride**, or **a spell that damages enemies**. The pillage warning's explanation was not widened with
them. `because_clause` (`silver.rs:1957`) fires when `ready == 0` and says only:

> `— this unit's 19 men hold no weapons they can wield`

True, and partial: a unit with `ready == 0` has **none of the four**. A player reads it and buys
swords when one point of Combat skill would have done, or already holds horses and is told nothing
about why they do not count.

**This was deferred, not overlooked.** `ah-cw75`'s plan says so under *What the verification
changed*: *"If the wording needs to change to cover the new ways of being unready, that is a **new**
user-facing question and goes back to the navigator; it was not asked here because the case did not
exist when the sentence was written."* Keying the clause off `ready` rather than `armed` — which that
plan required and which shipped correctly — is what exposes it.

**When this lands, the tail names the cheapest thing the unit is missing, and only falls back to
listing all four when there is nothing to name.**

## Files to change, and what to reuse

`crates/core/src/orders/silver.rs` only — `Readiness`, `readiness` and `because_clause`. No
TypeScript, no new code, no Settings row, no wire change. The head of the sentence
(`semantics.rs:3845`, *"cannot pillage here: needs N combat ready men, this region has M"*) is
**unchanged**.

### What already exists and must be reused

- **`because_clause(readiness)`** (`silver.rs:1957`) — the tail. Its `men <= 0 || ready > 0` guard
  stays exactly as it is; that guard is `ah-cw75`'s and is correct.
- **`readiness`** (`silver.rs:1867`) — already walks `facts.items`, already resolves each item's
  `weapon.needs` and each mount's `required_riding`. **It has the near-miss information and throws
  it away**; this bead keeps it.
- **`required_riding(description) -> Option<(&str, i64)>`** (`silver.rs:1837`) — parses
  *"requires riding [RIDI] of at least level N to ride in combat"* and returns the **skill tag** and
  the level. Reuse; do not re-parse.
- **`skill_level(facts.skills, tag)`** — the unit's own level in a skill.
- **`Ruleset::find_skill(tag)`** (`movement/rules.rs:944`) — turns a skill **tag** into a
  `SkillEntry` whose `.name` is the word to print. **The messages print names, never tags** — see
  the house style below.
- **`counted_item(count, tag, hex, ruleset, plurals)`** — the only correct way to pair a count with
  an item name (`ah-rsdz`: 84 of the corpus's 114 multi-count items pluralise irregularly).
  **`because_clause` does not currently take `hex`, `ruleset` or `plurals`** — see the design note.

### The house style these sentences must match

Shipped warnings name a skill in plain words, never by tag, in a fixed shape:

```
cannot help build a Tower: needs building 1, has no building     (semantics.rs:13410)
cannot produce catapult: needs carpenter 4, has carpenter 2      (semantics.rs:16463)
```

The new sentences follow it clause for clause. That was the navigator's choice; see
*User-facing decisions*.

### The design of the code

**1. `Readiness` carries the nearest miss.** `readiness` already knows it — the loop rejects each
item for a reason and forgets why. Record the best candidate as it goes:

```rust
/// An item the unit holds that would have counted but for a skill it lacks - the cheapest thing
/// standing between this unit and being able to tax.
///
/// "Cheapest" is the lowest required level, ties broken by the largest holding: the advice that
/// costs the player least (`ah-deo5`, the navigator's choice).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct NearMiss {
    /// The item tag, for `counted_item`.
    pub item: String,
    /// How many the unit holds.
    pub count: i64,
    /// The skill tag it needs - NOT the item's own: `DBOW` is wielded with `LBOW`.
    pub skill: String,
    /// The level it needs.
    pub level: i64,
}

pub struct Readiness {
    pub men: i64,
    pub ready: i64,
    /// `None` when the unit holds nothing that could have counted, which is the fallback case.
    pub nearest_miss: Option<NearMiss>,
}
```

**Only record a miss for an item that failed on skill.** An item that is neither weapon nor mount
never could have counted and is not a near miss. In `readiness`'s existing loop, the two rejecting
branches are the two that produce one:

- a weapon whose `weapon.needs` names a skill the unit has below level 1 → `(needs, 1)`;
- a mount whose `required_riding` gives `(skill, level)` the unit is below → `(skill, level)`.

A weapon with `needs: None` always counts, so it never misses. **The early return for
`COMB >= 1` must stay first** — a unit that already counts has no miss to report.

**2. `because_clause` gains what it needs to print an item name.** It currently takes only
`&Readiness`, and `counted_item` needs `hex`, `ruleset` and `plurals`. Widen the signature and
update its one caller (`semantics.rs:3841`), which already has all three to hand. **Do not
reimplement pluralisation** — that is `ah-rsdz`'s whole point.

**3. The three sentences, shipping verbatim:**

| case | tail |
|---|---|
| mount near miss | `— its 3 horses need riding 1, and it has no riding` |
| weapon near miss | `— its 10 double bows need longbow 1, and it has no longbow` |
| no near miss | `— it has no combat skill, no weapon it can wield, no mount it can ride and no damaging spell` |

`3 horses` and `10 double bows` come from `counted_item`. `riding` and `longbow` are
`find_skill(tag).name`, **not** the tag. The second clause is `has no {name}` where the unit has the
skill at 0, and `has {name} {held}` where it has some but not enough — mirroring the shipped
`has carpenter 2`.

**Where state lives.** One optional struct on a value that is already built and discarded per unit.
Nothing persisted, nothing new crossing the wire.

## Increments

**1. The nearest miss.**
Failing tests in `silver.rs`: `a_mount_the_unit_cannot_ride_is_the_nearest_miss` (3 horses, Riding 0
→ `NearMiss { item: "HORS", count: 3, skill: "RIDI", level: 1 }`);
`a_weapon_the_unit_cannot_wield_is_a_near_miss` (10 `DBOW`, no Longbow → skill `LBOW`, level 1);
`the_lowest_level_wins` (both, riding 1 vs longbow 3 → the mount);
`a_tie_goes_to_the_larger_holding` (both at level 1, 3 horses vs 10 bows → the bows);
`a_unit_holding_nothing_has_no_near_miss` (→ `None`);
`a_unit_that_already_counts_has_no_near_miss` (COMB 1 → `None`, and `ready == men`).
GREEN: `NearMiss`, the field, and the recording in the existing loop.

**2. The sentences.**
Failing tests asserting each of the three strings **verbatim**, including
`a_single_mount_reads_in_the_singular` — `its 1 horse needs riding 1, and it has no riding` — which
is what pins `counted_item` being used rather than an invented plural. GREEN: the widened
`because_clause` and its caller.

**3. The warning end to end.**
Failing test in `semantics.rs`: the whole `pillage-without-men` message for a unit with unridable
horses, asserting head **and** tail together, so the join reads as one sentence:
`cannot pillage here: needs 45 combat ready men, this region has 0 — its 3 horses need riding 1, and it has no riding`

## The test plan

| Test | Where | What it pins |
|---|---|---|
| the six `NearMiss` tests | `silver.rs` | which miss is chosen, including both tiebreaks and both `None` cases |
| the three sentence tests | `silver.rs` | the shipped strings, verbatim |
| `a_single_mount_reads_in_the_singular` | `silver.rs` | `counted_item`, not an invented plural |
| the end-to-end pillage message | `semantics.rs` | head and tail join into one readable sentence |

**The regression net:** every existing `readiness`, `because_clause` and `pillage-without-men` test
from `ah-cw75` and `ah-v585`, **unedited except where the tail's wording changes** — and where one
does change, the head must not. `crates/core/tests/validate_real_orders.rs` counts findings, not
message text, so it should not move at all; if it does, something changed `ready`, which this bead
must not.

## User-facing decisions

Interviewed with the navigator on 2026-08-25 over two rounds. Mockup, as chosen and committed:
`docs/ui/ah-deo5-why-not-ready.html` (PR #691, merged).

**Round 1 — the shape.**

1. **Chosen: B, name the nearest miss**, with a fallback when there is none. It is actionable and
   short, and it talks about what the player can see in the unit.
   *Rejected — A, name all four every time*: cannot mislead, but four negatives in a row wrapping to
   six lines in a half-width pane, and it says nothing about the horses the unit actually holds.
   *Rejected — C, name the concept* (`none of this unit's 19 men can tax`): shortest, and the rules'
   own test, but it nearly restates *"this region has 0"* and tells a reader who does not already
   know the four ways nothing to act on.
   *Rejected — leave it as it is*: it misdirects in exactly the cases the last two beads added.
2. **Two near misses: name the one needing the lowest skill level**, ties to the larger holding.
   *Rejected — name both*, which returns to A's length in the case where the unit is closest to being
   fixed. *Rejected — a fixed mounts-first precedence*, which is arbitrary and can name a level-3
   riding requirement over a level-1 weapon one.

**Round 2 — the exact words.**

3. **Chosen: the house shape** — `its 3 horses need riding 1, and it has no riding`, and
   `its 10 double bows need longbow 1, and it has no longbow`. Clause for clause the same as the two
   shipped warnings quoted in *Files to change*, so one pattern covers all of them.
   *Rejected — the trimmed form* (`… need riding 1 to count`, `… need longbow 1 to wield`): shorter
   and it says what the item would do, but it creates a second pattern for an idea the codebase
   already has one for.
4. **Chosen: F1 for the fallback** — `it has no combat skill, no weapon it can wield, no mount it can
   ride and no damaging spell`. This is the one case where the reader genuinely does not know which
   route to take, so the length buys something.
   *Rejected — F2, the concept* (`none of its 19 men can tax`). *Rejected — saying nothing at all*,
   which gives the least help to the reader most likely to be new.

Every string above is final and quoted verbatim in *The design of the code*.

## Out of scope

- **`readiness`'s count.** `ready` does not change. If a test's finding count moves, something is
  wrong.
- **The head of the warning** (`semantics.rs:3845`), and `pillage-without-men` itself.
- **Naming a *fifth* way**, or revisiting which four count — `ah-cw75` and `ah-v585` settled those.
- **Other warnings that name a skill.** `build-without-skill` and `produce-without-skill` already
  follow the house shape; this bead copies them rather than touching them.
- **Showing the near miss anywhere but this tail** — the unit table, the hover, the region panel.

## Validation

```bash
cargo test -p atlantis-hud-core        # after each increment
pnpm run check:fast                    # before the PR
```

**The human check:** load `neworigins-3.0.0-g3-f42-t82.rep`, find a unit holding horses with no
Riding, order it to `PILLAGE` in a region it cannot meet, and read the whole warning — head and tail
should read as one sentence, and the tail should name the horses. Then strip the unit of everything
and confirm the fallback appears instead.

## Known traps

- **The skill a weapon needs is not the weapon's own tag** — `DBOW` is wielded with `LBOW`, and
  `readiness` already says so in a comment. Printing the item's tag as the skill would be wrong in
  exactly the case the sentence exists for.
- **Print skill *names*, not tags.** `find_skill(tag).name`. The shipped warnings say
  *"needs building 1"*, never *"needs BUIL 1"*.
- **Use `counted_item` for the item count** (`ah-rsdz`): 84 of 114 items pluralise irregularly and 30
  do not pluralise at all. `because_clause` needs a widened signature to reach it — widen it rather
  than inventing an `-s`.
- **Only weapons and mounts can be near misses.** A sack of grain is not a thing the unit failed to
  qualify with.
- **The `COMB >= 1` early return stays first.** A unit that already counts must report no miss, or
  the tail appears on a unit whose men are being counted.
- **`because_clause`'s `men <= 0 || ready > 0` guard is `ah-cw75`'s and stays.** It is what stopped
  the tail firing on a unit that is fine; keying it off `armed` again would undo that bead.
- **`packages/shared` has no jsdom** — irrelevant here, nothing leaves `crates/core`, but named
  because it is the trap most beads in this repository meet.
notes:
Psylocke 2026-08-25, verified at a81d1b45: PASSED, with one gap recorded.

VERIFIED: the fallback clause ('it has no combat skill, no weapon it can wield, no mount it can ride
and no damaging spell') on Hunters (6380) and Woodsmen (6611) in forest (36,0) of
neworigins-3.0.0-g3-f42-t82.rep, and the absence of any clause on Taxers (10116), which has Combat 1.
The finding count did not move.

NOT VERIFIED ON SCREEN: the two nearest-miss forms - 'its N horses need riding 1, and it has no
riding' and 'its N double bows need longbow 1, and it has no longbow' - and the has-some-but-not-
enough form ('its 2 winged horses need riding 3, and it has riding 1').

WHY NOT, because this will recur for anyone verifying this area: the pillage warning fires only when
a hex's TOTAL combat-ready count is under its threshold, and in the committed corpus every hex
holding our mount-carrying or bow-carrying units also holds a Combat-1 unit that puts the hex over
its own threshold. So those clauses have no natural reachable case. They are covered by unit tests
(silver.rs:5522, :5531, :5551) but no person has seen them rendered.

A construction that would reach one, if it is wanted later: mountain (37,3) in Femont has a tax base
of $918 (threshold 10); Taxers (10699) holds 13 orcs with Combat 1 and Unit (16028) holds 20 horses
with only Observation. Ordering Taxers 'GIVE 16028 4 ORC' should drop the hex under 10 and surface
the riding clause on 16028 - assuming men transfers are repriced into readiness, which this
verification did not establish either way.

title: Three read-side store rules move from a comment into core
description:
Split out of ah-8z4y.3 (planning, 2026-08-24).

Three rules in webCoreAdapter.ts are guaranteed by nothing but a comment saying the desktop does the
same:

  :303  a remembered hex whose payload will not parse is dropped, the rest of the map kept -
        'which is what the desktop does too'
  :412  merged reports are listed oldest first, 'matching the desktop's ORDER BY' - and a list that
        reorders itself between platforms is two applications
  :365  a faction's own report is refused rather than merged - 'The desktop refuses this in the same
        words. It cannot be decided in the core, which is never told whose map is being merged into'

The third names its own fix: tell the core who is merging, and the refusal becomes the core's.

Depends on the manifest half only for ordering, not for code.
design:
## Context

Three rules in `packages/browser-core/src/webCoreAdapter.ts` are guaranteed by nothing but a comment
saying the desktop does the same. **Reading them properly turned up a fourth, and a live
divergence.**

### A. A remembered hex that will not parse is dropped, the map is kept

| | |
|---|---|
| Browser | `webCoreAdapter.ts:310-322` — `try { wasm.hydrate_remembered_region(...) } catch { return [] }`, one hex at a time |
| Desktop | `crates/core-tauri/src/lib.rs:803-819` — `filter_map` over `serde_json::from_str::<Value>`, **plus `.filter(\|payload\| !payload.is_null())`** |

**These are not the same test.** The desktop explicitly drops a payload that is literally `null` —
valid JSON, so it parses. The browser drops only what makes the hydrator throw. Whether
`hydrate_remembered_region` throws on `null` decides whether the two agree today, and **nothing says
which.** Both then call `backfill_structure_kinds` (`ah-nmts`), separately.

### B. The order remembered hexes come back in — **an unnamed divergence**

| | |
|---|---|
| Desktop | `core-persistence/src/lib.rs:1457` — `ORDER BY last_seen_turn DESC, region_id ASC` |
| Browser | `webStore.ts:408` — `readAll(...)`, **IndexedDB's own order, unsorted** |

The bead did not name this one. By this project's own principle, stated three lines away from rule
C, *"a list that reorders itself between platforms is two applications."*

### C. Merged reports are listed oldest first

| | |
|---|---|
| Desktop | `core-persistence/src/lib.rs:1543` — `ORDER BY merged_at ASC, merged_faction_id ASC` |
| Browser | `webCoreAdapter.ts:412-419` — the same comparator, written out in TypeScript, under *"matching the desktop's ORDER BY"* |

These agree today. Nothing keeps them agreeing.

### D. A faction's own report is refused rather than merged

`webCoreAdapter.ts:365-374`: *"The desktop refuses this in the same words. **It cannot be decided in
the core, which is never told whose map is being merged into** — only that a report is being folded
into a turn — so the one place that knows both is here."*

**That comment names its own fix**: tell the core who is merging.

`ah-8z4y`'s parent evidence is what happens when these are left as comments — `4e7c980`, where the
browser lacked SQL's `last_seen_turn` guard for four days, and `f153bf3`, one defect present in both
and fixed across 13 files.

When this lands: each of the four is written once, and the two platforms cannot answer differently.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

**Depends on `ah-8z4y.3.1`** (wired), and behind it `.2` and `.1`. Read `.1`'s plan for the wasm
shape — `report_import_writes_state` is the house pattern and every export here follows it.

### A and B together — `crates/core/src/report/sighting.rs`

They are one function, because they are one answer to *"what is in this faction's remembered map"*:

```ts
/** One stored sighting as either store hands it over: the row's own fields, payload unparsed. */
pub struct StoredSighting { pub region_id: String, pub last_seen_turn: i64, pub payload_json: String }

/// The remembered regions of one faction, in the order both platforms show them.
///
/// Drops a sighting whose payload will not parse, or whose payload is `null` - a stored `null` is
/// valid JSON and would otherwise become a region that is not one. **Dropping one remembered hex
/// beats losing the whole map**, which is the rule both stores were applying separately and by
/// different tests (`ah-8z4y.3.2`).
///
/// Back-fills each region's split structure fields (`ah-nmts`), so a hex stored last week reaches
/// the map as one stored today.
///
/// Ordered `last_seen_turn` descending then `region_id` ascending - the desktop's own `ORDER BY`
/// (`core-persistence/src/lib.rs:1457`), which the browser never applied at all.
#[must_use]
pub fn remembered_regions(stored: Vec<StoredSighting>) -> Vec<RememberedRegion>;
```

`sighting.rs` is the home because it already owns `RegionSighting` and `sighting_from_payload`
(`backup.rs:12` imports both). Reuse `backfill_structure_kinds` from `report::region` — do not
re-implement the back-fill.

**Both platforms lose their own copy.** `core-tauri/src/lib.rs:803-819`'s `filter_map` becomes a
call; `webCoreAdapter.ts:310-322`'s `flatMap`/`try`/`catch` becomes a call to a new
`remembered_regions_state(storedJson)` export, on `reset_game_manifest_state`'s exact model.

**The desktop's `ORDER BY` at `:1457` stays.** An index-backed sort is not something to give up, and
a pre-sorted input is exactly what a stable sort in core wants. It gains a comment naming
`remembered_regions` as the authority. **The browser gains the order it never had** — see
*User-facing decisions*.

### C — one comparator, and the SQL keeps its `ORDER BY`

```rust
/// Merged reports oldest first, then by faction id: the order both platforms list them in.
///
/// The desktop's `ORDER BY merged_at ASC, merged_faction_id ASC`
/// (`core-persistence/src/lib.rs:1543`) implements this and keeps doing so, because an index-backed
/// sort is worth having; this is the definition it implements, and `ordered_merged_reports_matches_the_sql`
/// is the test that they still agree (`ah-8z4y.3.2`).
pub fn order_merged_reports(records: &mut [MergedReportRecord]);
```

**A sort expressed in SQL cannot be "moved" into core without losing the index**, so this is the
honest arrangement: the core states the order, the browser calls it, the desktop's SQL implements
it, and a Rust test over a fixture asserts the two produce the same sequence. Say that in the doc
comment, or the next reader will delete one of them.

The browser's hand-written comparator (`webCoreAdapter.ts:414-418`) goes, replaced by a call.

### D — tell the core who is merging

`prepare_report_merge_state` (`webCoreAdapter.ts:112-117`) takes `viewerTurnNumber`,
`existingSightingsJson` and `rulesetJson`. **Add `viewer_faction_id`**, and move the refusal into
the core's own `PreparedMerge.rejection`, which the adapter already throws on (`:363-364`).

The refused case is then one of the rejections the core already produces, and the browser's
`if (prepared.mergedFactionId === viewerFactionId) throw` (`:371-373`) — with its four-line comment
— goes entirely. **The desktop's equivalent refusal goes the same way**; find it (it *"refuses this
in the same words"*, so grep the message) and delete it in the same commit, or the words are still
written twice.

**The message must not change**: `a faction's own report is loaded rather than merged`, verbatim,
because it reaches a player.

## Increments

1. **Remembered regions, in core.**
   RED, in `sighting.rs`'s tests: `a sighting whose payload will not parse is dropped`;
   `a sighting whose payload is null is dropped` — **the divergence, named**;
   `the rest of the map survives one bad hex`; `hexes come back newest first, then by region id`;
   `a hex stored before the structure split is back-filled`.
   GREEN: `StoredSighting`, `remembered_regions`.

2. **Both platforms call it.** `core-tauri`'s `filter_map` and the browser's `flatMap` both become
   one call, plus `remembered_regions_state` in `core-wasm` and its `CoreWasmModule` line.
   The existing tests on both sides must pass **unedited**, except where they asserted the browser's
   *unordered* result — if one does, that is increment 1's ordering arriving, and it is the one
   place an existing test may change. **Say so in the PR** rather than editing it quietly.

3. **The merged-report order.**
   RED: `merged reports are oldest first`; `two merges at the same instant are ordered by faction`;
   and `ordered_merged_reports_matches_the_sql` — load a fixture database, read the rows through the
   SQL, sort a shuffled copy with `order_merged_reports`, assert identical sequences.
   GREEN: `order_merged_reports`, a wasm export, and the browser calling it.

4. **The own-faction refusal, in core.**
   RED, in the core's merge tests: `a report from the viewer's own faction is rejected`, asserting
   the rejection text **verbatim**.
   GREEN: `viewer_faction_id` on the prepare call and the rejection; then delete the browser's throw
   and the desktop's.

## The test plan

| Test | File | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| the five `remembered_regions` tests | `crates/core/src/report/sighting.rs` | drop-one-keep-the-rest, the `null` payload, the back-fill, and the order |
| `merged reports are oldest first`, and the faction tiebreak | `crates/core` | rule C's definition |
| `ordered_merged_reports_matches_the_sql` | `crates/core-persistence` tests | the SQL still implements it |
| `a report from the viewer's own faction is rejected` | `crates/core` | rule D, with the shipped wording |
| the existing browser and desktop tests for all four | both | nothing else moved |

```bash
cargo test --workspace
pnpm --filter @atlantis/web build:wasm
pnpm run check:generated
pnpm run check:fast
```

## User-facing decisions

**Three of the four are invisible.** A and D change nothing a player sees: the same hexes are
dropped for the same reason (modulo the `null` case, which is a defect either way), and the refusal
keeps its exact wording.

**B is a behaviour change on the web, and it is the reason this section is not "None."** Remembered
hexes come back from IndexedDB unordered today and will come back newest-first afterwards. The map
draws every remembered hex regardless of order, so nothing should move on screen — **but that is a
reasoned expectation, not a tested one.**

**So: check it, and if anything does move, stop.** The human check below is where. A visible
difference means something downstream depends on the store's arbitrary order, which is a finding
worth a bead of its own and a decision the navigator has not been asked for. **Do not absorb it.**

The alternative — leaving the browser unordered and only documenting the difference — was not taken,
because "a list that reorders itself between platforms is two applications" is this file's own
stated principle and rule C exists to enforce exactly that for merged reports.

## Out of scope

- **The desktop's two `ORDER BY` clauses.** Both stay; the core states the order, the SQL implements
  it, and a test says they agree.
- **`getAllRegionSightings`** (`webStore.ts:410`), which feeds export rather than the map. The backup
  codec owns its own ordering (`ah-8m0`).
- **The merge's other rejections** — which account of a hex wins, which units may be commanded,
  whether the report belongs to the turn. Already the core's (`webCoreAdapter.ts:325-328`).
- **`store.putRegionSightings` and the write path.** This bead is the read side.
- **Making `mergeReport`'s three steps look like the desktop's three steps.** That comment describes
  a shape, not a duplicated rule, and the shape is right.

## Validation

```bash
cargo test --workspace
pnpm --filter @atlantis/web build:wasm
pnpm run check:generated
pnpm run check:fast
```

All green. Then by diff: `webCoreAdapter.ts` holds **no `try`/`catch` around a hydrate**, **no
comparator**, and **no `mergedFactionId === viewerFactionId` test**; `core-tauri/src/lib.rs` holds
no `filter_map` over a payload.

**A human check, and it is the one that matters**, on the web shell: open a game with a large
remembered map — `neworigins-3.0.0-g3-f42-t82.rep` — and compare it against `main` side by side.
Every remembered hex must be drawn, with the same terrain and the same labels, and the map must look
identical. Then merge an allied report, and try to merge the faction's own report: the refusal must
read exactly `a faction's own report is loaded rather than merged`. Do the same on the desktop.

## Known traps

- **The two drop-tests are not the same test today.** The desktop filters a `null` payload
  explicitly; the browser relies on the hydrator throwing. Establish what
  `hydrate_remembered_region` does with `null` before writing `remembered_regions`, and keep the
  **stricter** behaviour — a stored `null` becoming a region is worse than a hex quietly dropped.
  There is a test named for it.
- **The browser gains an order it never had.** Expected to be invisible; if it is not, stop and file
  it. Do not reorder the core to match IndexedDB.
- **The refusal message reaches a player.** `a faction's own report is loaded rather than merged`,
  verbatim, and asserted verbatim.
- **Delete both copies of rule D, not one.** The browser's throw and the desktop's equivalent. Grep
  the message; leaving the desktop's is the duplication surviving the bead that was about it.
- **`backfill_structure_kinds` already exists** (`ah-nmts`) and is called by both platforms today.
  Call it from `remembered_regions`; do not add a second back-fill.
- **The wasm bundle is not rebuilt by `pnpm run check:fast`.**
- **`.claude/cerebro-traps.md`**: none of the five apply — nothing stored changes shape, so nothing
  is migrated.

title: Every manifest edit is written once in core instead of twice per platform
description:
Split out of ah-8z4y.3 (planning, 2026-08-24).

Five manifest edits are written field by field in webCoreAdapter.ts, each under a comment saying it
is 'the web's counterpart of the desktop rewriting the JSON manifest on disk':

  openGame         lastOpenedAt stamp        webCoreAdapter.ts:568
  setGameRuleset   metadata.rulesetId        :664
  setGameMap       metadata.map              :679  - and an empty string DELETES the key
  setGameName      metadata.gameName         :700
  setActiveFaction metadata.activeFactionId  :716

setGameMap carries the same absent-versus-null distinction ah-8z4y.2 is about: absence is what tells
the settings dialog the ruleset's default is only assumed.

Each becomes a function in crates/core/src/backup.rs beside reset_manifest (ah-8z4y.1) with a wasm
export, and both platforms call it.
design:
## Context

Five manifest edits are written twice — once as a one-line field assignment on the desktop, once as
a hand-built object spread in the browser:

| Edit | Desktop | Browser |
|---|---|---|
| stamp `lastOpenedAt` on open | `lib.rs:305` — `manifest.last_opened_at = opened_at.to_string();` | `webCoreAdapter.ts:568-575` |
| `metadata.rulesetId` | `lib.rs:331` | `webCoreAdapter.ts:664-671` |
| `metadata.map` | `lib.rs:381` — `manifest.metadata.map = map;` | `webCoreAdapter.ts:679-691` |
| `metadata.gameName` | `lib.rs:395` | `webCoreAdapter.ts:700-707` |
| `metadata.activeFactionId` | `lib.rs:430` | `webCoreAdapter.ts:716-723` |

Four of the browser's five carry the same comment — *"the web's counterpart of the desktop
rewriting the JSON manifest on disk"* — which is a promise the code cannot keep on its own.

**Be honest about where the value is.** Three of these are one-liners on both sides and would not
justify a bead alone. Two are not:

- **`setGameMap`** hand-codes a rule the desktop gets from serde: *"An empty string removes the key
  rather than storing a null: absence is what tells the settings dialog the ruleset's default is
  only assumed, so it has to stay absence"* (`webCoreAdapter.ts:679-681`). The browser writes
  `delete metadata.map`; the desktop writes `None` and
  `#[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]` (`backup.rs:42-43`) does the rest.
  **Two different mechanisms for one rule**, and it is the same absent-versus-null distinction
  `ah-8z4y.2` is about.
- **`openGame`** stamps *"what decides which game reopens next launch. Storing it only on the
  desktop would make the two platforms disagree about which game the player was last in."*

And the real cost is not any one of the five: it is that **a sixth edit, or a new manifest field,
has to be added to both sides in the same commit and nothing says so.** That is `ah-8z4y`'s parent
evidence exactly — `1755c70c (ah-0w7w)` wrote one optional manifest field twice with the same
reasoning twice, inside a 33-file commit.

**This bead depends on `ah-8z4y.1`**, which puts `reset_manifest` in `crates/core/src/backup.rs`
and establishes the wasm shape; and behind it on `ah-8z4y.2`, which makes `GameManifest` one
generated definition. Read both plans first — this is the third and largest instalment of the same
move, and it must land in the same shape.

When this lands: what may be edited on a manifest is one list, in one place.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### `crates/core/src/backup.rs` — one enum and one function, beside `reset_manifest`

**One edit description rather than five functions**, deliberately. Five would mean five wasm exports
and five `CoreWasmModule` lines for what are mostly one-liners, and a sixth edit would still be a
change in two places. An enum makes *what may be edited* the thing that is written down once, and
adding to it is one variant plus one arm.

```rust
/// One change that may be made to an existing game's manifest.
///
/// The list is the point: every edit either platform makes is a variant here, so a sixth is one
/// variant and one arm rather than a field assignment in Rust and an object spread in TypeScript
/// that have to be written in the same commit and are guaranteed by a comment (`ah-8z4y.3.1`).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize, TS)]
#[ts(export, rename = "ManifestEdit", export_to = "ManifestEdit.ts")]
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase", tag = "kind", content = "value")]
pub enum ManifestEdit {
    /// Stamped every time the game is opened. This is what decides which game reopens next launch.
    Opened(String),
    Ruleset(String),
    /// `None` **removes** the key. A game that was never told a map is not the same as one told
    /// `null`: the absence is what makes the settings dialog say the ruleset's default is only
    /// assumed (`backup.rs:38-42`).
    Map(Option<MapGeometry>),
    Name(String),
    /// `None` for a game that has never had a report imported.
    ActiveFaction(Option<String>),
}

/// Applies one edit. Every other field is left exactly as it was.
pub fn apply_manifest_edit(manifest: &mut GameManifest, edit: &ManifestEdit) {
    match edit {
        ManifestEdit::Opened(at) => manifest.last_opened_at = at.clone(),
        ManifestEdit::Ruleset(id) => manifest.metadata.ruleset_id = id.clone(),
        ManifestEdit::Map(map) => manifest.metadata.map = map.clone(),
        ManifestEdit::Name(name) => manifest.metadata.game_name = name.clone(),
        ManifestEdit::ActiveFaction(id) => manifest.metadata.active_faction_id = id.clone(),
    }
}
```

**Note what `apply_manifest_edit` does *not* do**: it does not touch `manifest_version`, unlike
`reset_manifest`. An edit rewrites one field of a document that already exists in the current shape;
a reset rewrites the whole document. Say so in the doc comment, or somebody will make them
consistent.

**`ActiveFaction` takes an `Option`** although `webCoreAdapter.ts:716` only ever sets a value, and
`set_active_faction`'s desktop signature should be checked against this — if it takes a bare
`&str`, keep the `Option` here anyway: the field is optional and an edit that can only ever set it
is an edit that cannot undo itself.

### `crates/core-wasm/src/lib.rs` — one export

```rust
/// The manifest after one edit, given the one the store holds now.
///
/// One export for every edit, because the edits are one list (`ManifestEdit`) - see
/// `ah-8z4y.3.1`. The browser hands over its stored manifest and writes back what comes out,
/// exactly as it does for a reset (`reset_game_manifest_state`).
///
/// # Errors
///
/// Returns an error when either argument cannot be read, or when the result cannot be handed back
/// to JavaScript.
#[wasm_bindgen]
pub fn edit_game_manifest_state(manifest_json: String, edit_json: String) -> Result<JsValue, JsValue>
```

Follow `reset_game_manifest_state`'s body exactly: `serde_json::from_str(...).map_err(|error|
JsValue::from_str(&error.to_string()))?` for both arguments, then `to_js`.

**`to_js` is what makes the `delete metadata.map` disappear.** It serialises through serde, and
`#[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]` on `GameMetadata::map` means a `None`
comes back as **a JavaScript object with no `map` key at all** — not `map: null`. That is the rule
the browser hand-codes today, obtained for free and in one place. Say it in the comment; it is the
single best reason this bead exists.

### `crates/core-persistence/src/lib.rs` — five call sites, each one line

`open_game:305`, `set_game_ruleset`, `set_game_map:381`, `set_game_name` and `set_active_faction`
each replace their field assignment with
`atlantis_hud_core::backup::apply_manifest_edit(&mut manifest, &ManifestEdit::…)`. **Nothing else in
any of those functions moves** — the `game_file_path` check, `ensure_supported_manifest_version`,
`save_game_manifest`, the database open and `persist_game_snapshot` in `open_game` are the
desktop's own filesystem sequence and stay exactly as they are.

This is one line for one line, and that is expected: the desktop was never the side getting it
wrong. The gain is that the definition now has one home and one test.

### `packages/browser-core/src/webCoreAdapter.ts` — five bodies get shorter

One line on `CoreWasmModule`, beside `reset_game_manifest_state`:

```ts
  edit_game_manifest_state(manifestJson: string, editJson: string): GameManifest;
```

and each of the five becomes, in the same shape:

```ts
    async setGameMap(gameId: string, mapJson: string) {
      const game = await store.getGame(gameId);
      if (!game) {
        throw new Error(`no game with id ${gameId}`);
      }
      // What an edit does to a manifest is the core's, and so is the rule that an absent map stays
      // absent rather than becoming a null (`ah-8z4y.3.1`).
      const edit: ManifestEdit = {
        kind: "map",
        value: mapJson === "" ? null : (JSON.parse(mapJson) as MapShape)
      };
      const manifest = wasm.edit_game_manifest_state(JSON.stringify(game.manifest), JSON.stringify(edit));
      await store.putGame({ ...game, manifest });
      return manifest;
    },
```

**`ManifestEdit` is imported from the generated types**, so a variant added in Rust is a compile
error here until it is handled — which is the whole mechanism. Check the exact JSON shape
`#[serde(tag = "kind", content = "value")]` produces against the generated `ManifestEdit.ts` rather
than trusting the snippet above; ts-rs writes the discriminated union and it is the authority.

**The `delete metadata.map` branch goes**, and so does the `const metadata = { ...previous.metadata }`
dance around it. **The `mapJson === ""` test stays** — that is this adapter's own contract with its
caller (an empty string means "no map"), not a manifest rule.

**`store.putGame` and the `{ ...game, manifest }` wrapper stay in all five.** Storing is the
adapter's, and this bead does not touch it.

## Increments

1. **The edit exists, in core.**
   RED, in `backup.rs`'s test module:
   - `an edit changes one field and nothing else` — apply `Name`, assert the name changed and that
     the whole rest of the manifest compares equal to the original.
   - `an edit does not touch the manifest version` — a manifest at version `0` stays at `0`. **This
     is the difference from `reset_manifest` and there is a test for it.**
   - `clearing the map removes it` — `Map(None)`, then `serde_json::to_value` on the manifest
     contains **no `map` key**. Not "is null" — absent.
   - `setting the map records it`.
   - `clearing the active faction records the absence` — `ActiveFaction(None)` serialises as
     `"activeFactionId": null`, because that field has no `skip_serializing_if`. **The two optional
     fields behave differently on the wire and that is deliberate** (`backup.rs:34-43`); a test for
     each keeps somebody from "harmonising" them.
   GREEN: `ManifestEdit` and `apply_manifest_edit`.

2. **The desktop calls it.** Five one-line substitutions.
   RED does not apply. The existing `core-persistence` tests for all five must pass **unedited**.

3. **The wasm export, and the browser's five.**
   RED: a wasm test in `packages/browser-core/src/`, on the pattern of `reopen.wasm.test.ts` —
   `clearing a game's map removes the key`, asserting `"map" in manifest.metadata` is `false` after
   an edit with `value: null`. It fails before the change only in the sense that the export does not
   exist; write it first anyway, because it is the rule the browser used a `delete` for and the one
   most likely to regress.
   Then `a manifest edit leaves every other field alone`.
   GREEN: the export, the `CoreWasmModule` line, and the five rewritten bodies.
   The existing `webCoreAdapter` tests for all five must pass unedited.

## The test plan

| Test | File | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| the five `apply_manifest_edit` tests | `crates/core/src/backup.rs` | one field at a time, the version untouched, and the two optionals' different wire behaviour |
| `clearing a game's map removes the key` | `packages/browser-core/src/*.wasm.test.ts` | the rule the browser hand-coded as `delete` |
| `a manifest edit leaves every other field alone` | same | no field is dropped by the round trip |
| the existing desktop tests for all five edits | `crates/core-persistence` | unedited |
| the existing browser tests for all five edits | `packages/browser-core` | unedited |

```bash
cargo test --workspace
pnpm --filter @atlantis/web build:wasm
pnpm run check:generated
pnpm run check:fast
```

## User-facing decisions

**None.** Every edit does what it did before, on both platforms. The one behaviour worth naming —
that clearing a game's map removes the key rather than writing a null — is what the browser already
does by hand and what the desktop already does through serde; this bead makes them the same
mechanism, not a different outcome.

## Out of scope

- **`ah-8z4y.3.2`**, the three read-side rules — the sighting hydration tolerance, the merged-report
  ordering and the own-faction merge refusal. Wired as depending on this one.
- **The storage sequences.** `store.putGame`, `save_game_manifest`, `persist_game_snapshot` and the
  database open in `open_game` all stay exactly where they are.
- **`create_game`.** It builds a manifest rather than editing one, and `reset_manifest`
  (`ah-8z4y.1`) is the function that already covers building a fresh one.
- **The `mapJson === ""` contract** between `setGameMap` and its caller.
- **Trimming or validating a game name.** `set_game_name`'s own comment says that rule is the
  shell's (`gameSession.ts`'s `gameNameOf`), and it stays there.

## Validation

```bash
cargo test --workspace
pnpm --filter @atlantis/web build:wasm
pnpm run check:generated
pnpm run check:fast
```

All green. Then, by reading the diff: `webCoreAdapter.ts` contains **no `delete metadata.map`** and
**no manifest field name** in any of the five bodies — no `lastOpenedAt`, no `rulesetId`, no
`gameName`, no `activeFactionId`. Anything left is a rule still written twice.

**A human check, on both shells**, because these are the edits a player makes from Settings: rename
a game, change its ruleset, set its map and then clear it, and switch the active faction. Reopen the
game after each. In particular, **after clearing the map the Settings dialog must say the map is
*assumed***, not stated — that is the absent-versus-null rule, and it is the one thing here a wrong
implementation would break invisibly until somebody looked.

## Known traps

- **`ah-8z4y.1` and `ah-8z4y.2` land first.** `.1` establishes `reset_manifest` and the wasm shape
  this copies; `.2` makes `GameManifest` and `MapShape` generated, which is what lets the browser
  import a typed `ManifestEdit`. The bd dependencies are wired.
- **`Map(None)` removes the key; `ActiveFaction(None)` writes `null`.** Different, on purpose:
  `map` carries `skip_serializing_if` and `active_faction_id` does not (`backup.rs:34-43`). There is
  a test for each, and making them consistent would destroy the distinction the settings dialog
  reads.
- **`apply_manifest_edit` must not touch `manifest_version`**, unlike `reset_manifest`. There is a
  test named for it.
- **The generated `ManifestEdit.ts` is the authority on the JSON shape**, not the snippet in this
  plan. `#[serde(tag = "kind", content = "value")]` and ts-rs must agree, and the way to know is to
  regenerate and read the file.
- **The `mapJson === ""` test stays in the adapter.** It is the adapter's contract with its caller.
  Pushing it into the core would give the core an opinion about a string the core never sees.
- **The wasm bundle is not rebuilt by `pnpm run check:fast`.** `pnpm --filter @atlantis/web
  build:wasm` is what makes a new export visible.
- **`.claude/cerebro-traps.md`**: none of the five apply — the stored manifest format does not
  change, so nothing is migrated.

title: The web store's rules come from core instead of from a comment
description:
Split out of ah-8z4y (planning, 2026-08-24).

webCoreAdapter.ts carries seven rules whose only guarantee is a comment saying the desktop does the
same - 'matching the desktop's ORDER BY' (:400), 'The desktop refuses this in the same words'
(:353), 'The three steps are the desktop's three steps' (:312) and four more.

ah-8m0 already moved the backup codec, import stamping and reopen ranking into core and left the
adapters holding storage primitives; this finishes that for the read-rule-write sequences. Each rule
becomes a core function in the *_writes_state shape and the adapter performs the writes it is
handed.

Blocked by the manifest shape: several of these sequences read and write a manifest.
close_reason: All children closed; last was ah-8z4y.3.2, delivered in PR #665

title: The game manifest is defined three times by hand instead of generated once
description:
Split out of ah-8z4y (planning, 2026-08-24).

GameManifest is hand-written in packages/core-client/src/index.ts:113 and again as a Rust struct in
core-persistence. Every other cross-language type in this repository is ts-rs-generated into
packages/core-client/src/generated/; this one is not, so a field added on one side is a comment on
the other.

1755c70c (ah-0w7w) added one optional manifest field twice, with the same reasoning written out
twice, inside a 33-file commit.

Generate the TypeScript shape from the Rust struct, as every other shared type already is, and
delete the hand-written one.
design:
## Context

The game manifest is defined **three times** in this repository, by hand, in two languages:

| Where | What |
|---|---|
| `crates/core/src/backup.rs:22,51,59` | `GameMetadata`, `ReportSourceRef`, `GameManifest` — the real definition, serde-camelCased |
| `crates/core-tauri/src/lib.rs:36,53,60` | `GameMetadataDto`, `ReportSourceRefDto`, `GameManifestDto` — a field-for-field copy, whose own comments say *"exactly as on `GameMetadata`"* twice |
| `packages/core-client/src/index.ts:69,108,113` | `GameMetadata`, `ReportSourceRef`, `GameManifest` — hand-written TypeScript |

**Every other cross-language type in this repository is generated.** `crates/core` already depends on
`ts-rs` (`Cargo.toml:17`) and exports dozens of types into `packages/core-client/src/generated/` with
`#[ts(export, rename = "…", export_to = "….ts")]` — `ReportHeaderInfo`, `SettlementInfo`,
`ReportParseResult` and the rest. The manifest is the type that was never brought in.

So a field added on one side is a **comment** on the other. `1755c70c (ah-0w7w)` added one optional
manifest field, twice, with the same reasoning written out twice, inside a 33-file commit.
`ah-8z4y`'s parent records what this class already cost: `4e7c980` (the browser lacked SQL's
`last_seen_turn` guard for four days) and `f153bf3` (one defect present in both, fixed across 13
files).

**There is a fourth copy hiding in plain sight.** Rust's `GameMetadata.map` is
`Option<MapGeometry>` (`crates/core/src/movement/graph.rs:125` — `width`, `height`, `wrap_x`,
`wrap_y`); TypeScript's is `map?: MapShape` (`core-client/src/index.ts:100` — `width`, `height`,
`wrapX`, `wrapY`). One shape, two names, and `MapGeometry` has never been TS-exported at all.

When this lands: the manifest is generated from the Rust struct like every other shared type, and
the hand-written TypeScript is gone. **`ah-8z4y.1` depends on this** and becomes near-trivial once
it lands — with one definition, moving the reset rule into core is a function, not a translation.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### The two attributes the whole bead turns on

`Option<T>` in TypeScript can be written three ways and they do not mean the same thing. **Verified
against `ts-rs 12.0.1`'s own documentation on 2026-08-24** (`src/lib.rs:310-313`):

| Attribute | Generates |
|---|---|
| none | `t: T \| null` |
| `#[ts(optional)]` | `t?: T` |
| `#[ts(optional = nullable)]` | `t?: T \| null` |

**Getting these wrong is the one way this bead can do real damage**, because the absence of `map` is
load-bearing. `backup.rs:38-42` says so: *"The absence is the record that nothing was stated, so the
ruleset's declared default is only assumed and the settings dialog says so. `skip_serializing_if`
keeps that true on the way out as well: a `"map": null` written into an old game's manifest would be
a claim nobody made."* The hand-written TS says the same at `index.ts:88-96`. So:

- **`map`** → `#[ts(optional)]` → `map?: MapShape`. Matches the hand-written type exactly, and
  matches `skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none"` on the wire.
- **`active_faction_id`** → `#[ts(optional = nullable)]` → `activeFactionId?: string | null`.
  Matches the hand-written type exactly. It carries `#[serde(default)]` but **not**
  `skip_serializing_if`, so `None` really does serialise as `null` and the TS must permit both — an
  old manifest lacks the key, a current one writes `null`.

### `crates/core/src/movement/graph.rs:125` — `MapGeometry` gains a TS name

```rust
#[derive(..., TS)]
#[ts(export, rename = "MapShape", export_to = "MapShape.ts")]
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
pub struct MapGeometry { … }
```

**`rename = "MapShape"`, deliberately.** TypeScript has called this shape `MapShape` in 66 places
across 19 files (`packages/shared/src/mapShape.ts` is named after it), and renaming those to match
Rust would be a large mechanical diff with no benefit to anybody, inside a bead about removing
duplication. Generating it under the name TypeScript already uses costs one attribute and no
churn. Say in a comment on the struct that the two names are one type and that this is why.

**Then delete `MapShape` from `packages/core-client/src/index.ts:100-105`** and re-export the
generated one, in the same block as the other generated re-exports (`index.ts:45` is the pattern:
`export type { UnitSilver } from "./generated/UnitSilver";`).

### `crates/core/src/backup.rs` — the three structs gain `TS`

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize, TS)]
#[ts(export, rename = "GameMetadata", export_to = "GameMetadata.ts")]
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
pub struct GameMetadata {
    pub game_id: String,
    pub game_name: String,
    pub ruleset_id: String,
    #[serde(default)]
    #[ts(optional = nullable)]
    pub active_faction_id: Option<String>,
    #[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]
    #[ts(optional)]
    pub map: Option<MapGeometry>,
}
```

and the same `derive` + `#[ts(export, …)]` on `ReportSourceRef` (`:51`) and `GameManifest` (`:59`).
**No field is renamed, reordered, added or removed**, and `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]`
already gives ts-rs the camelCase names — do not add `#[ts(rename_all = …)]` as well.

**Every doc comment stays.** ts-rs carries a Rust doc comment into the generated `.ts` as a
docblock, which is how the generated file ends up carrying the reasoning the hand-written one
carried — and losing that reasoning would be a worse outcome than the duplication.

### `packages/core-client/src/index.ts` — four hand-written types go

Delete `GameMetadata` (`:69-97`), `MapShape` (`:100-105`), `ReportSourceRef` (`:108-111`) and
`GameManifest` (`:113-125`), and re-export the four generated ones in their place. **Nothing else in
that file moves** — `OpenedGame` (`:127`), `listGames`/`createGame` (`:540-541`) and every other
consumer keep referring to the same names and need no edit.

### `crates/core-tauri/src/lib.rs:36-75` — the Dto copies

`GameMetadataDto`, `ReportSourceRefDto` and `GameManifestDto` are field-for-field copies of the
core types, and `GameMetadataDto`'s own comments admit it twice (*"exactly as on `GameMetadata`"*).
**Delete all three and use `atlantis_hud_core::backup::{GameManifest, GameMetadata, ReportSourceRef}`
directly** — the file already imports `ReportSourceRef` from that module (`:30`), so the import line
barely changes. `OpenedGameDto` (`:68`) keeps its own identity and simply holds a `GameManifest`.

**If a Dto turns out to differ from its core twin in any way** — a field, an attribute, a serde
option — **stop and say so in the PR** rather than reconciling it. A silent difference between them
is a live divergence and belongs in its own bead with its own decision, not in a refactor that was
supposed to change nothing.

### `packages/browser-core/src/webCoreAdapter.ts` — nothing

It imports `GameManifest` and `MapShape` from `@atlantis/core-client` by name (`:10-27`). The names
do not change, so the file does not.

## Increments

1. **`MapGeometry` generates as `MapShape`.**
   RED: `pnpm run check:generated` fails — `packages/core-client/src/generated/MapShape.ts` does not
   exist. GREEN: the derive and the attributes on `MapGeometry`; regenerate; commit the generated
   file. Then delete the hand-written `MapShape` from `index.ts` and re-export the generated one.
   `pnpm run typecheck` is the assertion that the two were identical: 66 usages across 19 files
   compile unchanged, or they did not match.

2. **The three manifest structs generate.**
   Same shape: derives and attributes, regenerate, commit, delete the hand-written trio, re-export.
   Then the test that pins the crux, in `packages/core-client/src/builders.test.ts` or a new
   `generated.test.ts` beside it:

   ```ts
   // `ah-8z4y.2`: `map` absent and `map: null` are different claims - absent means the game was
   // never told a map, so the ruleset's default is only *assumed* (backup.rs:38-42). A generated
   // `map: MapShape | null` would erase that distinction and typecheck perfectly.
   it("a manifest may omit map entirely", () => {
     const metadata: GameMetadata = { gameId: "g", gameName: "n", rulesetId: "r" };
     expect("map" in metadata).toBe(false);
   });

   it("a manifest may omit activeFactionId, or say null", () => {
     const absent: GameMetadata = { gameId: "g", gameName: "n", rulesetId: "r" };
     const stated: GameMetadata = { ...absent, activeFactionId: null };
     expect(stated.activeFactionId).toBeNull();
     expect("activeFactionId" in absent).toBe(false);
   });
   ```

   **These are typecheck assertions wearing a runtime disguise**, and that is the point: each fails
   to *compile* if the attribute is wrong, which is exactly the failure worth catching. Say so in a
   comment, so nobody deletes them as tautologies.

3. **The Dtos go.** Delete the three, point `core-tauri` at the core types, and run the desktop
   suite. `cargo test -p atlantis-hud-core-tauri` (or however that crate's tests are invoked —
   `cargo test --workspace` covers it either way).

4. **The round trip still holds.** A Rust test in `crates/core/src/backup.rs`'s test module, if one
   does not already cover it: a `GameManifest` with `map: None` and `active_faction_id: None`
   serialises to JSON with **no `map` key** and an `activeFactionId` of `null`, and reads back
   equal. This is the wire contract the two TS attributes mirror, and it must be pinned on the Rust
   side too — the TS test alone would let a later `skip_serializing_if` removal pass.

## The test plan

| Test | File | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| `pnpm run check:generated` | — | the committed generated files match the Rust structs |
| `pnpm run typecheck` | — | all 66 `MapShape` usages and every manifest consumer compile against the generated types |
| `a manifest may omit map entirely` | `packages/core-client/src/*.test.ts` | `map?: MapShape`, **not** `map: MapShape \| null` |
| `a manifest may omit activeFactionId, or say null` | `packages/core-client/src/*.test.ts` | `activeFactionId?: string \| null` — both halves |
| the serde round trip | `crates/core/src/backup.rs` tests | no `map` key when `None`; `activeFactionId: null` when `None` |
| the existing backup and persistence suites | `crates/core*`, `packages/browser-core` | **nothing about behaviour moved** |

```bash
cargo test --workspace
pnpm run check:generated
pnpm run check:fast
```

## User-facing decisions

**None.** Nothing here reaches the application: three Rust structs gain a derive, four TypeScript
types stop being hand-written, and three Dto copies are deleted. No string, no layout, no stored
value and no wire format changes — the serde attributes that decide the wire format are untouched,
and increment 4 exists to prove it.

## Out of scope

- **Moving the reset rule into core.** That is `ah-8z4y.1`, which depends on this.
- **The seven "matching the desktop" rules** in `webCoreAdapter.ts`. That is `ah-8z4y.3`, which also
  depends on this.
- **Renaming `MapShape` to `MapGeometry` in TypeScript**, or `MapGeometry` to `MapShape` in Rust.
  66 usages across 19 files, no benefit here, and the `rename` attribute makes it unnecessary.
- **Reconciling any difference found between a Dto and its core twin.** Report it; do not fix it.
- **Any change to the wire format**, the manifest version, or `skip_serializing_if`.
- **Generating any other cross-language type** that is still hand-written. If one is noticed, it is
  a bead for Forge, not a widening of this one.

## Validation

```bash
cargo test --workspace
pnpm run check:generated
pnpm run check:fast
```

All green. Then, by reading the diff:

```bash
git diff origin/main -- packages/core-client/src/generated/
```

`GameManifest.ts`, `GameMetadata.ts`, `ReportSourceRef.ts` and `MapShape.ts` appear, and
`GameMetadata.ts` reads `map?: MapShape` and `activeFactionId?: string | null` — **not**
`map: MapShape | null`. That one line is the bead.

**A human check, and a short one**: open the app, create a game, close and reopen it, and open
Settings. The map row must still say the map is *assumed* for a game that was never told one, and
*stated* for one that was. That distinction is what the optional field carries, and it is the only
thing a wrong attribute would visibly break.

## Known traps

- **`#[ts(optional)]` and `#[ts(optional = nullable)]` are different, and the default is neither.**
  Verified against `ts-rs 12.0.1`'s documentation (`src/lib.rs:310-313`) on 2026-08-24. Plain
  `Option<T>` generates `t: T | null`, which for `map` would turn "never said" into "said nothing",
  permanently and silently. There is a test named for it.
- **`#[ts(optional)]` on a non-`Option` field is a compile error** with a dedicated message
  (`ts-rs/src/lib.rs:713-715`). If you see it, the attribute is on the wrong field.
- **Do not add `#[ts(rename_all = "camelCase")]`.** `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]` is already
  there and ts-rs reads it. Adding both is how a field ends up named twice over.
- **`skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none"` on `map` is load-bearing**, and it is the Rust half of
  the same distinction the TS attribute carries. Do not remove it while "tidying" the derive list.
- **The doc comments must survive.** ts-rs carries them into the generated `.ts`. The hand-written
  TypeScript's comments explain why `map` is optional and why `lastOpenedAt` lives on each game
  rather than in an index; those explanations must end up in the generated file, which means they
  must be on the Rust struct. Compare the two before deleting the TypeScript, and move anything the
  Rust side lacks.
- **The generated files are committed.** `pnpm run check:generated` fails when they are stale; it is
  not a build step that runs for you.
- **`.claude/cerebro-traps.md`**: none of the five apply. No persisted setting is migrated — the
  stored manifest format does not change — no browser suite is involved, and there is no
  `packages/shared` effect test here.

title: A reset builds the same fresh manifest on both platforms
description:
Split out of ah-8z4y (planning, 2026-08-24).

The rule 'what a reset keeps' is written twice and the two DISAGREE today:

  crates/core-persistence/src/lib.rs:543  manifest_version: CURRENT_MANIFEST_VERSION
  packages/browser-core/src/webCoreAdapter.ts:587  manifestVersion: previous.manifestVersion

Each carries its own hand-written warning against a struct spread. The desktop stamps the current
manifest version onto the rewritten manifest; the web keeps whatever the old one had, so a game
reset in the browser carries a stale version forward.

Move the rule into core behind one function in the CoreWasmModule shape the fleet already uses
(report_import_writes_state is the template), and have both adapters call it. Neither platform then
holds an opinion about what a reset keeps.
design:
## Context

"What a reset keeps" is written twice, and the two versions disagree.

```rust
// crates/core-persistence/src/lib.rs:542-555
// Written field by field on purpose, *not* as `GameManifest { ..manifest }`: a struct-update
// expression carries every future field through a reset silently, and the next field added to a
// manifest is exactly the one that should not survive.
let fresh = GameManifest {
    manifest_version: atlantis_hud_core::backup::CURRENT_MANIFEST_VERSION,
    metadata: GameMetadata { game_id, game_name, ruleset_id, active_faction_id: None, map: None },
    report_sources: Vec::new(),
    created_at: now.to_string(),
    last_opened_at: now.to_string(),
};
```

```ts
// packages/browser-core/src/webCoreAdapter.ts:584-596
// Built field by field, never spread from `previous`: most of a manifest does *not* survive a
// reset, and a spread would carry every field added later through it silently.
const manifest: GameManifest = {
  manifestVersion: previous.manifestVersion,
  metadata: { gameId, gameName, rulesetId },
  reportSources: [], createdAt: now, lastOpenedAt: now
};
```

Each carries its own hand-written warning against a struct spread — **and they still disagree**. The
desktop stamps `CURRENT_MANIFEST_VERSION` onto the rewritten manifest; the web carries the old
manifest's version forward.

**Be honest about the size of that today**: `CURRENT_MANIFEST_VERSION` is `1`
(`crates/core/src/backup.rs:17`) and every existing manifest is at `1`, so the two currently produce
the same number. This is a **latent** divergence, not a live defect — it bites the first time the
manifest version moves, when a game reset in the browser would keep a stale version while the same
game reset on the desktop would not. That is precisely the shape of `ah-8z4y`'s parent evidence:
`4e7c980`, where the browser lacked SQL's `last_seen_turn` guard for four days before anybody noticed.

(`map` is **not** a second divergence, though it reads as one: Rust writes `map: None` and
TypeScript omits the key, and for an optional field those are the same claim. `ah-8z4y.2`'s
`#[ts(optional)]` is what keeps them the same.)

**This bead depends on `ah-8z4y.2`**, which makes `GameManifest` one generated definition instead of
three hand-written ones. Read its plan first: with one definition, this bead is a function; without
it, it is a translation.

When this lands: neither platform holds an opinion about what a reset keeps.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

The pattern to copy is `report_import_writes_state` (`crates/core-wasm/src/lib.rs:120-158`) — *"The
stamps and sightings one import writes, given what the browser store already holds … the store hands
over [what it has] and writes back exactly what comes out."* That is this bead's shape exactly: the
adapter hands over the old manifest, and writes back the one it is given.

### `crates/core/src/backup.rs` — the rule, beside the type it is about

```rust
/// The manifest a reset leaves behind: the game's identity, and nothing else.
///
/// Written field by field on purpose, *not* as `GameManifest { ..previous }`: a struct-update
/// expression carries every future field through a reset silently, and the next field added to a
/// manifest is exactly the one that should not survive. Both platforms carried their own copy of
/// this rule and their own copy of that warning, and the two had already drifted apart on
/// `manifest_version` (`ah-8z4y.1`).
///
/// What survives is the identity a player would recognise the game by - its id, its name and its
/// ruleset. What does not: the active faction, the map, the report sources, and the timestamps,
/// which are both set to `now` because a reset game is a new game in every way but its name.
#[must_use]
pub fn reset_manifest(previous: &GameManifest, now: &str) -> GameManifest {
    GameManifest {
        manifest_version: CURRENT_MANIFEST_VERSION,
        metadata: GameMetadata {
            game_id: previous.metadata.game_id.clone(),
            game_name: previous.metadata.game_name.clone(),
            ruleset_id: previous.metadata.ruleset_id.clone(),
            active_faction_id: None,
            map: None,
        },
        report_sources: Vec::new(),
        created_at: now.to_string(),
        last_opened_at: now.to_string(),
    }
}
```

`backup.rs` and not a new module: it already owns `GameManifest` (`:59`), `GameMetadata` (`:22`) and
`CURRENT_MANIFEST_VERSION` (`:17`), and its header says every rule about the document *"lives here
and nowhere else; a store reads its rows and hands them over, or takes rows back and writes them."*

**The desktop's behaviour is the one kept**, on both counts where they differed: the current
manifest version is stamped, because the manifest is being rewritten in the current shape and
saying otherwise would be a claim about a document that no longer exists.

### `crates/core-persistence/src/lib.rs:537-555` — the desktop calls it

```rust
let manifest = load_game_manifest(&game_file_path)?;
ensure_supported_manifest_version(manifest.manifest_version)?;
let fresh = atlantis_hud_core::backup::reset_manifest(&manifest, &now.to_string());
```

**Everything after that is untouched** — the rename-aside, the `create_game`, the best-effort
cleanup and the put-it-back on failure (`:557-583`). Those are the desktop's own filesystem
sequence, not a rule about the manifest, and the comments explaining them stay exactly as they are.
The inline `GameMetadata` construction and its warning comment go, because the warning now lives on
`reset_manifest`.

### `crates/core-wasm/src/lib.rs` — one export, in the house shape

```rust
/// The manifest a reset leaves behind, given the one the store holds now.
///
/// The counterpart of the desktop's own call into [`atlantis_hud_core::backup::reset_manifest`]:
/// the browser store hands over the game's current manifest and writes back exactly what comes
/// out, so neither platform holds an opinion about what a reset keeps (`ah-8z4y.1`).
///
/// # Errors
///
/// Returns an error when `manifest_json` cannot be read as a `GameManifest`, or when the result
/// cannot be handed back to JavaScript.
#[wasm_bindgen]
pub fn reset_game_manifest_state(manifest_json: String, now: String) -> Result<JsValue, JsValue> {
    let previous: atlantis_hud_core::backup::GameManifest = serde_json::from_str(&manifest_json)
        .map_err(|error| JsValue::from_str(&error.to_string()))?;
    to_js(&atlantis_hud_core::backup::reset_manifest(&previous, &now))
}
```

`to_js` and the `serde_json::from_str(...).map_err(JsValue::from_str)` idiom are already the file's
own (`:140-141`); reuse them rather than inventing an error shape. Add the module-header sentence
listing what this crate exposes (`:5`) — it already names `decode_game_backup_state` and
`report_import_writes_state` in the same breath.

### `packages/browser-core/src/webCoreAdapter.ts`

One line on the `CoreWasmModule` type (`:37-118`), beside `report_import_writes_state` (`:99`):

```ts
  reset_game_manifest_state(manifestJson: string, now: string): GameManifest;
```

and in `resetGame` (`:582-596`), the whole field-by-field block becomes:

```ts
      const previous = game.manifest as GameManifest;
      // The rule lives in the core and is the desktop's too - `ah-8z4y.1`. What a reset keeps is
      // not this adapter's opinion.
      const manifest = wasm.reset_game_manifest_state(JSON.stringify(previous), now);
```

**Everything after it is untouched**, including the registry-row-first ordering and its comment
(`:597-600`: *"the opposite order from the desktop's rename-aside, and for the same reason … Do not
'make the two platforms consistent' here"*). That comment is about the **storage sequence**, which
genuinely differs per platform and must keep differing; this bead moves the **manifest rule** only.
Leave it word for word — a reader who deletes it as "now handled by core" would break the web's
crash safety.

`wasm` is already in scope in the adapter closure (`exportGame` calls `wasm.encode_game_backup_state`
at `:629`), so nothing about how the module is reached changes.

## Increments

1. **The rule exists, in core.**
   RED, in `crates/core/src/backup.rs`'s test module:
   - `a_reset_keeps_the_games_identity` — id, name and ruleset survive.
   - `a_reset_forgets_the_faction_the_map_and_the_sources` — `active_faction_id`, `map` and
     `report_sources` are cleared, from a `previous` where all three are populated.
   - `a_reset_stamps_the_current_manifest_version` — `previous.manifest_version` of `0`,
     result is `CURRENT_MANIFEST_VERSION`. **This is the divergence, named.**
   - `a_reset_sets_both_timestamps_to_now`.
   GREEN: `reset_manifest`.

2. **The desktop calls it, and does nothing else differently.**
   RED does not apply — behaviour-preserving. The existing `core-persistence` reset tests must pass
   **unedited**; they are the assertion.

3. **The web calls it, and stops keeping the old version.**
   RED: a wasm test in `packages/browser-core/src/`, following `reopen.wasm.test.ts` and
   `reportImport.wasm.test.ts` (both load the real module from `./wasm/atlantis_core.js`) —
   `a reset stamps the current manifest version`, resetting a game whose manifest is at version `0`
   and asserting the result is not `0`. **This is the bead, and it fails before the change.**
   GREEN: the wasm export, the `CoreWasmModule` line, and the three lines in `resetGame`.
   The existing `webCoreAdapter` reset tests must pass unedited.

## The test plan

| Test | File | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| the four `reset_manifest` tests | `crates/core/src/backup.rs` | what a reset keeps and what it forgets, in one place |
| `a reset stamps the current manifest version` | `packages/browser-core/src/*.wasm.test.ts` | the divergence, from the platform that had it wrong |
| the existing desktop reset tests | `crates/core-persistence` | the filesystem sequence is untouched — unedited |
| the existing web reset tests | `packages/browser-core` | the registry-row ordering is untouched — unedited |

```bash
cargo test --workspace
pnpm --filter @atlantis/web build:wasm
pnpm run check:fast
```

**The wasm bundle must be rebuilt** before the browser test can see a new export; `build:wasm` is
this project's declared `prewarm` command, so `prepare-worktree --prewarm` gives it to you at the
start. A `reset_game_manifest_state is not a function` is a stale bundle, not a missing export.

## User-facing decisions

**None.** Nothing an audience sees changes: a reset empties the same things it emptied before, on
both platforms, and the one value that moves — the manifest version stamped on a reset browser game
— is internal and currently identical either way (`CURRENT_MANIFEST_VERSION` is `1` and every
manifest is at `1`).

## Out of scope

- **The two storage sequences.** The desktop renames aside and the web writes the registry row
  first, deliberately and in opposite orders, each with a comment saying why and one of them saying
  *"Do not 'make the two platforms consistent' here."* This bead moves the manifest rule and not one
  line of either sequence.
- **Whether a reset should forget the game's map.** Both platforms clear it today, so this bead
  preserves that — but it is a genuine question (the map is a property of the game rather than of
  the data in it, and a player who resets must state it again). **Worth raising with the navigator
  as its own bead**; it is a user-facing decision and there is no interview behind it here.
- **`ah-8z4y.3`**, the seven "matching the desktop" rules still in `webCoreAdapter.ts`.
- **`export_game`, `importGame`, `create_game`** and every other manifest reader.

## Validation

```bash
cargo test --workspace
pnpm --filter @atlantis/web build:wasm
pnpm run check:fast
```

All green. Then, by reading the diff: `webCoreAdapter.ts`'s `resetGame` contains **no manifest field
names at all** — no `manifestVersion`, no `gameId`, no `reportSources`. If any survives, the rule is
still written twice.

**A human check, on both shells**, because this is a destructive operation and the two crash-safety
sequences are what protect it: create a game, import a report, then reset it. The game must still be
listed, must be empty, and must keep its name and ruleset. Do this on **the desktop and the web**,
because the two take opposite paths through failure and only one of them is exercised by any given
run.

## Known traps

- **`ah-8z4y.2` must be merged first.** It makes `GameManifest` one generated definition; the bd
  dependency is wired. Building against three hand-written copies would mean writing a fourth
  translation inside the wasm boundary.
- **Do not touch the storage sequences**, and do not delete the comment at `webCoreAdapter.ts:597`
  that warns against making them consistent. It is about crash safety, not about the manifest.
- **`map: None` and an absent `map` are the same claim** for an optional field — one is not a
  divergence to "fix". They stop being the same only if `ah-8z4y.2` generates `map: MapShape | null`,
  which its own plan has a test against.
- **The wasm bundle is not rebuilt by `pnpm run check:fast`.** `pnpm --filter @atlantis/web
  build:wasm` (this project's `prewarm`) is what makes a new export visible to the browser suites.
- **`report_import_writes_state` is the template**, including its error handling: wasm-bindgen throws
  the Rust error's text as a bare string, which `webCoreAdapter` already wraps in one place
  (`exportGame`'s catch, `:637`). Match that if the new call needs wrapping at all.
- **`.claude/cerebro-traps.md`**: none of the five apply — the stored manifest format does not
  change, so nothing is migrated.

title: Refactoring: a new silver field must be added to three test files by hand
description:
## The cost being paid

Three independent inline `UnitSilver` literals — 32 fields each, character for character the same —
live in three test files with no shared builder, though the repository already established the pattern
(`ac8afc44` refactor(ah-164.3): one builder per report type in tests).

Every one of the eleven silver beads since ah-1wcw.1 had to edit all three, several of them as a literal
one-line field append in each file: `2233ceed` adds `sharedSilverCovered: 0`, `15b07450` adds
`withdrawing: false`, `6d023924` adds `worksByDefault: false`.

## Evidence

- Verified by `git show --stat` on all eleven: `1816c25c`, `3c57f456`, `6c5c8899`, `acec4bb4`,
  `7b6de57e`, `3817339f`, `09e5b50b`, `2233ceed`, `15b07450`, `f631add5`, `6d023924`.
- `6d023924` (ah-gjq4) is typical: `unitTable.test.ts` +3/-1, `unitTooltip.test.ts` +66,
  `UnitTableDock.test.tsx` +1 — three files touched for one field.
- The pattern to follow already exists: `ac8afc44` refactor(ah-164.3).

## Where

- `packages/shared/src/unitTable.test.ts:373`
- `packages/shared/src/unitTooltip.test.ts:146`
- `packages/shared/src/workspace/UnitTableDock.test.tsx:518`

## What a refactoring would change

One `unitSilver()` builder in `packages/shared/src/testing/`, taking overrides, so a new field is one
default in one place. The three files then state only what each test actually cares about, which also
makes them readable — a 32-field literal hides the one field under test.

Filed by Forge, weekly sweep of 2026-08-24, range 440b51fb..origin/main.
design:
## Context

`UnitSilver` (`packages/core-client/src/generated/UnitSilver.ts`, ts-rs–generated from the Rust
model) has **31 fields**. Three test files each build one by hand, as a complete inline literal,
character for character the same:

| File | Line | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| `packages/shared/src/unitTable.test.ts` | 373 | `const forecast = (atMonthEnd, upkeep): UnitSilver => ({ …31 fields… }) satisfies UnitSilver` |
| `packages/shared/src/unitTooltip.test.ts` | 146 | `const forecast = (overrides: Partial<UnitSilver> = {}): UnitSilver => ({ …31 fields…, ...overrides })` |
| `packages/shared/src/workspace/UnitTableDock.test.tsx` | 518 | the same, again |

**So every field added to the Rust model has to be appended to all three by hand.** Forge counted
eleven silver beads since `ah-1wcw.1` that each had to: `1816c25c`, `3c57f456`, `6c5c8899`,
`acec4bb4`, `7b6de57e`, `3817339f`, `09e5b50b`, `2233ceed` (adds `sharedSilverCovered: 0`),
`15b07450` (adds `withdrawing: false`), `f631add5`, `6d023924` (adds `worksByDefault: false`).
`6d023924` is typical — `unitTable.test.ts` +3/−1, `unitTooltip.test.ts` +66,
`UnitTableDock.test.tsx` +1, three files touched for one field. `ah-fvzu` added `taxesByFlag` the
same way, and `ah-leeg` sits behind it.

**The pattern to follow already exists and is already imported by all three of these files.**
`ah-164.3` (`ac8afc44`, *"one builder per report type in tests"*) put typed builders in
`packages/core-client/src/builders.ts`, and each of the three files already opens with
`import { aReportUnit } from "@atlantis/core-client";`. This bead is that same idea applied to the
one report-model type it was never applied to.

When this lands: a new `UnitSilver` field is one default in one file, and each test states only the
fields it is actually about — which also makes them readable, since a 31-field literal hides the one
field under test.

**Nothing about the application changes.** This is test code only.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### `packages/core-client/src/builders.ts` — one new builder, in the existing module

**Not a new module.** The bead's description suggested `packages/shared/src/testing/`; that is the
wrong home and this plan deliberately overrides it. `builders.ts` is where the report-model builders
