design:
## Context

`MapCanvas` holds its measured size in component state, filled by a `ResizeObserver` effect
(`MapCanvas.tsx:303`, `:499-510`), and everything derived from it is gated on that state.
**`packages/shared` has no jsdom, by decision**, so its component tests render with
`renderToStaticMarkup`, no effect ever runs, `size` stays `{ width: 0, height: 0 }`, and every rule
that reads it is unreachable by any test the package can run. Those rules are therefore smoke-only
or untested.

Four beads have each paid for this separately:

| Retrospective | Cost |
|---|---|
| `ah-mwqa.md` — *"The plan put effect-level tests in a file whose harness runs no effects"* | ~30 minutes, **nine existing tests red at once**, and it closes *"This is the third bead to pay for the gap"* |
| `ah-brgo.2.md` — *"The plan asked for a ruler-label test that `packages/shared` cannot run"* | ~10 minutes plus a deviation to justify in the PR body; names `MapCanvas.tsx:297` |
| `ah-t2i.md` — *"MapCanvas also carries hook state, so it cannot be called directly as a plain function the way those stateless components' tests do"* | ~15 minutes |
| `ah-1uj.md` *Prevent by* item 2 | asks for a unit test of the follow-selection effect's scope **that still cannot be written**; its sibling item 1 was implemented |

**Most of the geometry is already pure, and that is what makes this bead small.** `mapViewport.ts`
owns `fitTo` (`:222`), `centreOn` (`:256`), `isOffScreen` (`:279`), `rulerTicks` (`:343`),
`ghostSpread` (`:442`) and `ghostShift` (`:416`); `mapViewState.ts` owns `mapViewDecision` (`:107`)
and `travelsToSelection` (`:191`). All are tested.

What is *not* reachable is the **orchestration** — the handful of lines in each effect that gate on
`size`, call those primitives in order, and decide whether to commit anything at all. Three sites:

| Site | The untestable decision |
|---|---|
| `MapCanvas.tsx:521-553` | the `size.width === 0` gate, then `mapViewDecision`, then `fitTo`, then *"Only a view that actually reached the screen counts as framed"* — the `if (fitted)` guard |
| `MapCanvas.tsx:572-588` | `travelsToSelection`, then `coordinate.z !== level \|\| size.width === 0`, then `isOffScreen` → `centreOn` |
| `MapCanvas.tsx:389-397, 411-413` | which ghost repeats exist, and where each is shifted to |

When this lands: those three decisions are pure functions with tests in the package that owns them,
and `MapCanvas` measures, calls one function, and commits what it is handed.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### `packages/shared/src/workspace/mapFraming.ts` — new, pure

A module of its own rather than more of `mapViewport.ts` (450 lines of geometry primitives) or
`mapViewState.ts` (which answers *what the store says*, not *what the screen should do*). These are
**decisions that compose the primitives**, and `dossierPeek.ts`'s `peekStep` (`:106`) is the
precedent for exactly that shape: take everything as an argument, return the next viewport.

```ts
/** The measured container. `{0,0}` means not yet measured, and every decision here declines it. */
export type MeasuredSize = { width: number; height: number };

/**
 * The viewport the map should frame itself at, or `null` to leave it where it is.
 *
 * Folds together the size gate, `mapViewDecision` and `fitTo` so the effect in `MapCanvas` has no
 * decision left in it. `null` covers four cases the component used to spell out as early returns:
 * nothing measured yet, the store says hold, `fitTo` declined an empty set of hexes, and - the one
 * worth naming - a fit that produced nothing, because *only a view that actually reached the
 * screen counts as framed* (`ah-z31p`, moved from `MapCanvas.tsx:548-550`).
 */
export function framingViewport(input: {
  size: MeasuredSize;
  view: MapViewState;
  gameId: string;
  level: number;
  coordinates: readonly Coordinate[];
  insets: Insets | null;
}): Viewport | null;

/**
 * The viewport that brings a newly arrived selection into view, or `null` to leave it alone.
 *
 * `travels` is `travelsToSelection`'s answer, computed by the caller because it compares against a
 * ref the component owns. Everything after it is here: the selection must parse, must be on this
 * level, the container must be measured, and the hex must actually be off screen - a hex clicked
 * on the map is already visible and nothing moves (`ah-z31p`, moved from `MapCanvas.tsx:580-587`).
 */
export function followViewport(input: {
  travels: boolean;
  selectedRegionId: string | null;
  level: number;
  size: MeasuredSize;
  view: Viewport;
  insets: Insets | null;
}): Viewport | null;

/** Which copies of the wrapped world exist, given the spans and the measured size. */
export function ghostSlots(
  spans: WrapSpans,
  step: number,
  size: MeasuredSize
): { mx: number; my: number }[];

/** Where each copy sits for a given camera, and whether it is the original and so not drawn. */
export function ghostPlacements(
  view: Viewport,
  spans: WrapSpans,
  size: MeasuredSize,
  slots: readonly { mx: number; my: number }[]
): { mx: number; my: number; x: number; y: number; hidden: boolean }[];
```

**Every body is moved, not rewritten** — the arithmetic already exists in `MapCanvas` and calls
`scaleOf`, `repeatsEitherSide`, `ghostSpread`, `ghostShift`, `fitTo`, `centreOn`, `isOffScreen`,
`mapViewDecision` and `parseRegionId` exactly as it does today. Import them; do not reimplement one.

`NO_INSETS` moves with them, or is imported from wherever `MapCanvas` gets it.

### `packages/shared/src/workspace/MapCanvas.tsx` — three sites get shorter

- **The framing effect** (`:521-553`) becomes:

  ```tsx
  useEffect(() => {
    const next = framingViewport({
      size, view: mapView, gameId, level,
      coordinates: onLevel.map((hex) => hex.coordinate), insets
    });
    if (next) {
      commit(next);
    }
  }, [gameId, level, onLevel, size, commit, insets, mapView]);
  ```

  The dependency array does not change. **The comment above it (`:516-520`) stays on the effect** —
  it explains *why the map frames itself at all*, which is still this effect's job; the comments
  explaining *how the decision is reached* move onto `framingViewport`.

- **The follow effect** (`:572-588`): `travelsToSelection` and the `lastFollowed.current` assignment
  stay in the component, because the ref is component state. Everything after them becomes one
  `followViewport` call and one `if (next) commit(next)`.

- **`ghostSlots`** (`:389-397`) becomes a `useMemo` over the new function. **`placeGhosts`
  (`:404-429`) keeps its `for` loop and every `setAttribute`** — that is deliberate DOM writing on
  every frame of a drag, and its comment says so (*"this runs on every frame of a drag, and it is
  two attributes on at most nine elements"*). Only the *arithmetic* moves: it asks
  `ghostPlacements` what to write and writes it. **Do not turn the loop into React rendering** —
  that would undo a decision this file explains twice.

### `packages/shared/src/workspace/mapFraming.test.ts` — new

The point of the bead. Sizes are just numbers here, so every case that was smoke-only becomes a unit
test.

### What is *not* changed

**`MapCanvas` keeps its `ResizeObserver`, its `size` state and its nine other hooks.** The bead's
description suggests *"a measured wrapper"* on the `MeasuredFactionDossier` model
(`FactionDossierPanel.tsx:236`). That pattern works there because `FactionDossierPanel` holds no
hooks at all and the wrapper is a one-line `useReportedRect` — its own comment says so. `MapCanvas`
holds `cursor`, `mapFocused`, `openNotesId` and more besides `size`; a wrapper would move one hook
out of ten and leave the component exactly as untestable as it is now. **The rules are what needs to
be pure, not the component**, and this plan does that instead. Stated here so the implementer does
not attempt the wrapper and find it buys nothing.

## Increments

1. **The ghosts.** `ghostSlots` and `ghostPlacements` into `mapFraming.ts`; `MapCanvas` calls them.
   RED first, in `mapFraming.test.ts`:
   - `an unwrapped map has no ghosts` — `spans` of `{x: null, y: null}` → `[]`.
   - `a map wrapped on one axis repeats on that axis only` — `{x: 100, y: null}` → every slot has
     `my === 0`.
   - `a wider container shows more repeats` — the same spans at two sizes, the larger giving at
     least as many slots. **This is a size-dependent rule, and it is the first one this package has
     ever been able to assert.**
   - `the copy standing where the world is drawn is not drawn` — `ghostPlacements` marks exactly the
     `mx === 0 && my === 0` entry `hidden`.

2. **The follow decision.** `followViewport`.
   RED: `a selection that did not travel moves nothing` (`travels: false` → null);
   `a selection on another level moves nothing`; `an unmeasured container moves nothing`
   (`{0,0}` → null); `a selection already on screen moves nothing`;
   `a selection off screen is centred` (→ `centreOn`'s own answer, asserted by calling `centreOn`
   in the test rather than by restating coordinates).

3. **The framing decision.** `framingViewport`.
   RED: `an unmeasured container frames nothing`; `a held view frames nothing`;
   `a restored view is used as it stands`; `a level with no hexes frames nothing` — this is the
   *"only a view that actually reached the screen counts as framed"* rule, and
   `ah-1uj`/`ah-brgo.2` are the beads that could not write it; `a level with hexes is fitted to
   them`.

4. **Nothing about `MapCanvas` moved.** RED does not apply. Every existing test in
   `MapCanvas.test.tsx` and the smoke suite must pass **unedited**.

## The test plan

| Test | File | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| the four ghost tests | `packages/shared/src/workspace/mapFraming.test.ts` | which copies exist and where — size-dependent, previously unreachable |
| the five follow tests | same | the follow-selection scope `ah-1uj` asked for and could not write |
| the five framing tests | same | the framing gates, including the empty-set decline |
| every existing `MapCanvas` test | `MapCanvas.test.tsx` | the component's markup did not move — unedited |
| the map smoke specs | `apps/web` smoke suite | the effects still fire in a real browser |

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
pnpm run test:smoke
```

**The smoke suite is run for this bead**, and deliberately: it is the only place these effects ever
execute. The unit tests prove the decisions; smoke proves they are still wired to a real
`ResizeObserver`. Neither replaces the other, and **the smoke specs are not deleted** — the bead's
own description says *"smoke keeps only what genuinely needs a browser"*, and what genuinely needs a
browser is exactly that wiring.

## User-facing decisions

**None.** Nothing an audience sees changes: the same viewports are committed from the same effects
in the same order, and the ghost copies are drawn where they were drawn. This bead moves arithmetic
out of a component and adds tests for it.

## Out of scope

- **A measured wrapper for `MapCanvas`.** Argued in *Files to change*: it moves one hook out of ten.
- **Making `MapCanvas` stateless**, or splitting it. It is 1,741 lines and that is a different bead
  with a different argument.
- **Turning `placeGhosts` into React rendering.** Its comment explains twice why it writes
  attributes by hand on every frame.
- **`mapViewport.ts` and `mapViewState.ts`.** Their functions are reused unchanged and untouched.
- **Adding jsdom to `packages/shared`.** That decision stands; this bead works within it, which is
  the whole point.
- **The ruler ticks** (`rulerTicks`, `MapCanvas.tsx:297`). `ah-brgo.2` names them, and they are
  already pure in `mapViewport.ts` — what was untestable there was the label rule inside the
  component's own render, which is a fourth site and a fair follow-up. **Not here**: this bead takes
  the three effect-level decisions, and adding a render-path extraction would double it.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
pnpm run test:smoke
```

All green, nothing skipped, and no edit to any existing `it(...)` in `MapCanvas.test.tsx`.

Then, by reading the diff: `MapCanvas.tsx`'s two effects contain **no arithmetic** — no `scaleOf`,
no `fitTo`, no `isOffScreen`, no `size.width === 0`. Each is a call and an `if`. Anything left is a
decision still trapped where no test can reach it.

**A human check, short**: open a game with a report, switch levels, and click a hex in the units
table that is off screen. The map must frame a newly opened level, must travel to a selection that
arrives from the table, and must not move when a visible hex is clicked. Then drag the map on a
wrapped world and confirm the copies still tile without a gap or a doubled overlay.

## Known traps

- **`packages/shared` has no jsdom, by decision** (`.claude/cerebro-traps.md`). That is the premise
  of this bead, not an obstacle to route around: **do not** add a jsdom environment, and do not
  write a test that renders `MapCanvas` and expects an effect to run. `ah-mwqa` turned nine tests
  red at once by trying.
- **Move the bodies; do not rewrite them.** Every one of these calls existing, tested primitives.
  Rewriting the arithmetic while moving it is how a refactor becomes a regression nobody can see
  outside a browser.
- **`lastFollowed` is a ref and stays in the component.** `travelsToSelection` is called there and
  its answer passed in as `travels`. A pure function that mutated a ref would be neither.
- **`placeGhosts` writes attributes on purpose.** Keep the loop and the `setAttribute` calls; move
  only what they are computed from.
- **The dependency arrays must not change.** They are what makes the effects re-run when the
  container resizes mid-import — `MapCanvas.tsx:563-565` explains that case. A shortened effect body
  is not a licence to shorten its deps.
- **`fitTo` declines an empty set**, and the `if (fitted)` around it is a rule with a comment, not a
  null check. It moves into `framingViewport`'s `null` and there is a test named for it.

title: Refactoring: a new finding code stays invisible until listed by hand
description:
## The cost being paid

A finding code carries no category on the Rust side, so each of its user-visible properties is a
hand-maintained per-code allowlist in TypeScript that nothing links back to `codes::ALL`. The unit
table's warning marker is `code === "not-enough-silver" || code === "upkeep-exceeds-unclaimed"`; the
Settings dialog carries a second copy of the same list. A new unit-anchored code is therefore
correct, tested, and invisible on the row until somebody remembers to add it.

That already happened. `upkeep-exceeds-unclaimed` shipped producing 29 findings across two fixtures
with every planned test green, and the Silver column marked none of them.

## Evidence

- docs/retrospectives/ah-fjty-reopened.md §"A new finding shipped correct and invisible, because the
  plan named every surface but one" — *Why*: "The ⚠ set is a per-code allowlist rather than a derived
  property of a finding". *Prevent by* item 2 names the allowlist as "the underlying cost", says the
  new `unitsWarnedAboutSilver` is "still a per-code list, only now a tested and named one", and states
  outright: "That is a refactoring bead, not a change to make inside a planned one".
- Cost recorded there: a failed verification, a planner audit that ruled out four candidate causes
  without finding it, a reopened P0, and a second full implementation session (`0f2d0b8e`, PR #633),
  about half an hour of which went to proving the core innocent.
- Adding one code touches the same four files every time: `78ae87f9` (ah-cxxa), `bd5d2de6` (ah-g7ts),
  `b0afdd24` (ah-wbr9), `0b444332` (ah-t2pn.4).

## Where

- `crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs` (`mod codes`, `ALL: [Code; 32]`)
- `packages/shared/src/orderEditor.ts:249` (`unitsWarnedAboutSilver`)
- `packages/shared/src/workspace/SettingsDialog.tsx:474,490`

## What a refactoring would change

Give a code a category on the Rust side — what it is anchored to, and which settings group it belongs
to — and let it flow through the generated vocabulary. The table then derives its markers and Settings
derives its grouping, so adding a code is one edit in one language and no surface can be forgotten.

Filed by Forge, weekly sweep of 2026-08-24, range 440b51fb..origin/main.
design:
## Context

A finding code carries no user-visible properties on the Rust side, so each of them is a
hand-maintained per-code list in TypeScript that nothing links back to `codes::ALL`
(`crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs:124`). There are two:

- **The unit table's ⚠ marker.** `unitsWarnedAboutSilver` (`packages/shared/src/orderEditor.ts:249`)
  filters on `diagnostic.code === "not-enough-silver" || diagnostic.code === "upkeep-exceeds-unclaimed"`
  — two string literals in another package from where codes are declared.
- **The Settings dialog's grouping.** `WARNING_GROUPS`
  (`packages/shared/src/workspace/SettingsDialog.tsx:419`) lists every code by hand, under eight
  headings, each with a title and description.

**The failure has already shipped.** `upkeep-exceeds-unclaimed` (ah-fjty) landed producing 29
findings across two fixtures, with every planned test green, and the Silver column marked none of
them: the finding was in the Problems panel and nothing on the row pointed at it. ah-fjty-reopened's
retrospective names the allowlist as *"the underlying cost"* and says the replacement
`unitsWarnedAboutSilver` is *"still a per-code list, only now a tested and named one"*.

**Be honest about how far this bead can go, because the bead's own framing over-promises.** The
Settings entries carry a **title** and a **description** — user-visible copy the navigator owns — and
those cannot move into Rust; a code's English name is not core's business. So "no surface can be
forgotten" is not reachable by deriving everything. What *is* reachable, and is the whole of the
cost being paid:

1. The Silver-column list moves to Rust, **beside the code declarations, in the file its author is
   already editing**, and flows to TypeScript through the existing generator. One hand-maintained
   list in one language instead of one in another language and package.
2. A missing Settings entry becomes a **failing test** rather than an invisible gap. The copy stays
   in TypeScript; only the requirement that every code has some entry is enforced.

That turns "correct, tested and invisible" into "correct, tested, and red until you finish".

**The pipeline already exists**, which is why this is small. `crates/core/tests/generated_ts.rs:23`
emits `ADVISORY_CHECK_CODES` into `packages/core-client/src/coreVocabulary.generated.ts` from
`codes::ALL`, `packages/shared/src/settingsStore.ts:13` already consumes it, and
`WARNING_GROUPS`'s entries are already typed `code: AdvisoryCheckCode` (`SettingsDialog.tsx:421`) so
a *typo* is caught today. Only a *missing* code is not.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

- `crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs` — one new array in `mod codes`, and a test.
- `crates/core/tests/generated_ts.rs` — emit it.
- `packages/core-client/src/coreVocabulary.generated.ts` — regenerated, never hand-edited.
- `packages/core-client/src/index.ts` — re-export, beside `ADVISORY_CHECK_CODES` (`:472`).
- `packages/shared/src/orderEditor.ts` — `unitsWarnedAboutSilver` filters on the generated set.
- `packages/shared/src/workspace/SettingsDialog.tsx` — export `WARNING_GROUPS` for the test.
- `packages/shared/src/workspace/SettingsDialog.test.tsx` — the coverage test.

### What already exists and must be reused

- `codes::ALL: [Code; 32]` (`semantics.rs:123`) and its doc comment, which records that a new code is
  appended **here** last whatever group it joins in the UI. That convention stays.
- `crates/core/tests/generated_ts.rs`'s `render()` (`:13`) and
  `core_client_vocabulary_matches_the_core` (`:51`) — the generator and its gate. Regenerate with
  `ATLANTIS_UPDATE_GENERATED=1 cargo test -p atlantis-hud-core --test generated_ts`, exactly as the
  generated file's own header says. **Never hand-edit the generated file**; `pnpm run check:generated`
  is a separate gate that will catch it.
- `ADVISORY_CHECK_CODES` / `AdvisoryCheckCode` (`coreVocabulary.generated.ts:5` and `:40`) — the existing
  export shape to copy.
- `settingsStore.ts:45` — `ADVISORY_CHECK_CODES.map((code) => [code, code !== "hex-unguarded"])`, the
  pattern for deriving from the generated list.

### The design of the code

**Rust**, added inside `pub mod codes` immediately after `ALL`:

```rust
/// The codes that mean a unit's own silver is in trouble, so its Silver figure carries a warning
/// marker on the unit table's row.
///
/// A property of the finding, declared beside the finding, rather than a per-code allowlist in
/// TypeScript that nothing links back to [`ALL`] (`ah-v9p2`). `upkeep-exceeds-unclaimed` shipped
/// producing 29 findings with every planned test green and the column marking none of them
/// (`ah-fjty`), because the allowlist lived in another package.
///
/// **Not derivable from anything else, and deliberately so.** `not-enough-items` is unit-anchored
/// too and does *not* belong here: the marker is on the Silver figure, not on the row. Adding a code
/// that belongs here is still one hand edit — but it is one edit, in this file, three lines below
/// where the code was just declared.
pub const SILVER_TROUBLE: [Code; 2] = [NOT_ENOUGH_SILVER, UPKEEP_EXCEEDS_UNCLAIMED];
```

**Generated TypeScript**, emitted by `generated_ts.rs` in the same shape as `ADVISORY_CHECK_CODES`:

```ts
/** Codes that mark a unit's Silver figure: `codes::SILVER_TROUBLE` in crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs. */
export const SILVER_TROUBLE_CODES = [
  "not-enough-silver",
  "upkeep-exceeds-unclaimed"
] as const;
```

**`unitsWarnedAboutSilver`** (`orderEditor.ts:249`) keeps its signature and its doc comment — both
paragraphs of which stay true and one of which is the record of ah-fjty — and changes only its
predicate:

```ts
const SILVER_TROUBLE = new Set<string>(SILVER_TROUBLE_CODES);

export function unitsWarnedAboutSilver(diagnostics: OrderDiagnostic[]): Set<string> {
  return new Set(
    diagnostics
      .filter((diagnostic) => SILVER_TROUBLE.has(diagnostic.code))
      .map((diagnostic) => diagnostic.unitId)
      .filter((unitId): unitId is string => unitId !== null)
  );
}
```

The `Set` is module-level and built once: this runs per validation over every diagnostic, and a
two-element `Array.includes` would be fine but a `Set` says "membership" and costs nothing.

**`WARNING_GROUPS`** becomes `export const WARNING_GROUPS` (`SettingsDialog.tsx:419`) — the only
change to that file. Its type annotation, its eight headings and every title and description stay
exactly as they are.

**Where state lives.** Nowhere new. One `const` array in Rust, one generated `const` in TypeScript,
one module-level `Set`. No store, no runtime state, no new type crossing the boundary — the generated
export is a string tuple, like its neighbour.

## Increments

**Increment 1 — the Rust declaration and its guard.**
Failing test: `every_silver_trouble_code_is_a_real_code`, in `semantics.rs`'s test module:

```rust
for code in codes::SILVER_TROUBLE {
    assert!(codes::ALL.contains(&code), "{} is not in codes::ALL", code.as_str());
}
assert!(!codes::SILVER_TROUBLE.is_empty());
```

Then add `SILVER_TROUBLE`. `cargo test -p atlantis-hud-core`.

**Increment 2 — generate it.**
Failing test: `core_client_vocabulary_matches_the_core` (`generated_ts.rs:51`) goes red as soon as
`render()` emits the new block and the committed file does not have it. Extend `render()` with the
`SILVER_TROUBLE_CODES` block, then regenerate:

```bash
ATLANTIS_UPDATE_GENERATED=1 cargo test -p atlantis-hud-core --test generated_ts
```

Commit the regenerated `coreVocabulary.generated.ts`. Add the re-export to
`packages/core-client/src/index.ts` beside `ADVISORY_CHECK_CODES` (`:472`).

**Increment 3 — the column derives its marker.**
Failing test: in `packages/shared/src/orderEditor.test.ts`,
`marks_every_code_the_core_calls_silver_trouble`:

```ts
for (const code of SILVER_TROUBLE_CODES) {
  expect(unitsWarnedAboutSilver([diagnosticFor(code, "101")])).toEqual(new Set(["101"]));
}
```

`unitsWarnedAboutSilver` is already imported there (`orderEditor.test.ts:15`) and already exercised
in the `"the units the silver column marks"` block (`:440-450`); build the diagnostic with that block's `hexFinding` helper rather than inventing a helper. This test fails today only if a code is added to
`SILVER_TROUBLE` that the literals do not name, so **write it, watch it pass, then add a third code
to `SILVER_TROUBLE` temporarily and watch it fail** before rewriting the predicate. That is the
increment's red step and it must actually be performed.

Then rewrite `unitsWarnedAboutSilver` as above.

**Increment 4 — Settings cannot silently miss a code.**
Failing test: in `SettingsDialog.test.tsx`, `lists_every_advisory_check_code`:

```ts
const listed = WARNING_GROUPS.flatMap((group) => group.entries.map((entry) => entry.code));
expect([...listed].sort()).toEqual([...ADVISORY_CHECK_CODES].sort());
expect(listed.length).toBe(new Set(listed).size);   // and none listed twice
```

It should pass immediately on `main` — every code is currently listed. **Prove it can fail**: delete
one entry from `WARNING_GROUPS`, see the test name the missing code, restore it. Then export
`WARNING_GROUPS`.

## The test plan

| Test | Where | What it pins |
|---|---|---|
| `every_silver_trouble_code_is_a_real_code` | `semantics.rs` tests | the Rust list cannot name a code that does not exist |
| `core_client_vocabulary_matches_the_core` | `generated_ts.rs:51` (existing) | the generated file is in step |
| `marks_every_code_the_core_calls_silver_trouble` | `orderEditor.test.ts` | the column derives rather than hard-codes |
| `lists_every_advisory_check_code` | `SettingsDialog.test.tsx` | a new code cannot be missing from Settings |

Both increments 3 and 4 have an explicit red step. **Say in the PR description what each failure
message was.** A test added green proves only that it compiles; this bead's entire claim is that
these two gaps now fail loudly, and the evidence for that is having seen them fail.

**The regression net:** every existing `orderEditor.test.ts` and `SettingsDialog.test.tsx` test,
unedited, plus `pnpm run check:generated`.

## User-facing decisions

None.

Nothing the player sees changes: the same two codes mark the Silver column before and after, and
every Settings entry keeps its heading, title and description verbatim. This bead moves *where a
fact is written*, not what it says.

The one thing that would have been the navigator's — the wording of a Settings title or description,
or which codes deserve the ⚠ — is deliberately untouched. If a later bead wants to add a code to
`SILVER_TROUBLE`, that is a user-visible decision and goes to them.

## Out of scope

- **Moving Settings titles and descriptions into Rust.** They are user-facing copy; see *Context*.
  Increment 4 enforces coverage and leaves the words where they are.
- **A general `Category` enum per code** (anchor, severity, settings group), which the bead's *What a
  refactoring would change* gestures at. It is a larger change whose only current consumer would be
  the grouping, and the grouping cannot be derived while the copy stays in TypeScript. Revisit it if
  a third per-code list ever appears; two do not justify it.
- **Reordering `codes::ALL`.** Its doc comment records that new entries are appended last and that
  the generated TypeScript copies that order.
- **The Problems panel**, which already shows every finding regardless of code.
- **`hex-unguarded`'s default-off** (`settingsStore.ts:45`) — a per-code exception of the same family,
  but a deliberate default the navigator chose, not an allowlist.

## Validation

```bash
cargo test -p atlantis-hud-core                                        # increments 1-2
ATLANTIS_UPDATE_GENERATED=1 cargo test -p atlantis-hud-core --test generated_ts   # regenerate
pnpm vitest run packages/shared packages/core-client                   # increments 3-4
pnpm run check:fast                                                    # before the PR
```

`check:fast` includes `check:generated`, which fails if `coreVocabulary.generated.ts` was edited by
hand or left stale — so a forgotten regeneration is caught locally rather than in CI.

**The human check is the two red steps**, described in *The test plan*. There is nothing new to look
at in a running app: the Silver column and the Settings dialog must be pixel-identical to `main`.

## Known traps

- **`coreVocabulary.generated.ts` is generated and must never be hand-edited.** Its own first two
  lines say so and name the regeneration command. `pnpm run check:generated` is the gate.
- **`ALL` is `[Code; 32]`, a fixed-size array.** `SILVER_TROUBLE` is likewise `[Code; 2]`; adding an
  entry means changing the length in the type, which is the intended friction — it is what makes the
  edit visible in review.
- **A test that is vacuously true is this repository's known failure mode** (ah-ycuj: true for 758 of
  1,392 units, caught only by a reviewer). Both red steps in *Increments* exist because of it, and
  `expect(!SILVER_TROUBLE.is_empty())` in increment 1 is the same guard in miniature.
- **`not-enough-items` is unit-anchored and does not belong in `SILVER_TROUBLE`.** The marker is on
  the Silver figure. Do not "complete" the list.
- **A hex-anchored finding names no unit** and marks none — `unitsWarnedAboutSilver`'s existing
  `.filter((unitId): unitId is string => unitId !== null)` is what enforces that, and its doc comment
  explains why (in a pooling hex, blaming one of several units would be wrong). Keep both.
- **Never ask for an effect-level test in `packages/shared`** — that package has no jsdom
  (ah-nass). Increments 3 and 4 test pure functions and a plain exported array, so neither renders
  anything; keep it that way rather than reaching for a rendered assertion.

title: A count and an item name disagree in number: 'buys 200 horse'
description:
Found by Xavier on 2026-08-23 while checking whether ah-t2pn.4 closed the gap ah-t2pn.3 was failed for. It did; this is a separate, pre-existing wart it made more visible.

The ruleset stores item names in the singular - config/public/ruleset.json has HORS -> 'horse', SWOR -> 'sword', GRAI -> 'grain'. item_name (crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs) returns that name verbatim, and several messages put a COUNT immediately in front of it:

  region-pool-oversubscribed (ah-t2pn.4, shipped 0b444332)
    'your units here buy 120 horse between them and this market has 100'
    'this unit buys 200 horse and this market has 100'

  not-enough-items (shipped long before)
    'short 5 horse: this unit can have 0 and its orders spend 5'

So every one of them reads '200 horse'. This is NOT a defect in ah-t2pn.4 - it followed its plan, which told it to use item_name as every other market message does, and it is consistent with what already ships. The planner's mockup wrote 'horses', which was aspirational rather than accurate, and the plan did not specify pluralisation either way. That omission is the planner's.

not-traded-here escapes it only because it never puts a number next to the name: 'this hex does not sell horse - its market has perfume, gems and hill dwarves'. Note that market_list's own example carries plurals, which come from the report's own market lines rather than from the ruleset - so the two sources disagree about number, which is part of why this is not a one-line fix.

## Why it is worth a bead rather than a shrug

These are the sentences a player reads when the app is telling them something is wrong. Reading like a bad translation undermines the one moment the advisory system has to be believed. It is also cheap to get wrong again: every new message that pairs a count with item_name will inherit it, and two of the four shipped this week.
design:
## Context

The ruleset stores item names in the **singular** - `config/public/ruleset.json` has
`HORS -> "horse"`, `SWOR -> "sword"`, `GRAI -> "grain"` - and `item_name`
(`crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs:2517`) returns that name verbatim. Three messages put a count
immediately in front of it, so every one reads `200 horse`:

```
short 5 horse: this unit can have 0 and its orders spend 5                        (semantics.rs:2377)
the units in this hex are short 5 horse between them: …                          (semantics.rs:2445)
your units here buy 120 horse between them and this market has 100               (semantics.rs:4342)
this unit buys 200 horse and this market has 100                                 (semantics.rs:4342)
```

These are the sentences the application uses when it is telling a player something is wrong, so
reading like a bad translation costs more here than it would elsewhere. It is also cheap to inherit:
two of the four shipped in one week.

**This is not a defect in `ah-t2pn.4`**, which followed its plan and matched what already shipped.
The plan did not specify pluralisation either way, and that omission was the planner's.

**Measured before deciding, because the obvious fix is wrong.** Over the committed corpus:

- **114 of 171** items appear with a count above one, which is where the report writes a plural.
- **84 of those pluralise irregularly** - `amulet of protection` → `amulets of protection`,
  `book of exorcism` → `books of exorcism`, `admantium plate mail` → `admantium plate mails`.
  **An "add an s" rule produces `amulet of protections`** and is not an option.
- **30 are invariant** - `grain`, `iron`, `fish`, `livestock`, `chain armor`. `10 grain` is already
  correct and must not become `10 grains`.
- The data page carries plurals only incidentally, inside prose, for about **91**; scraping them is
  a bead of its own and was declined.
- **Market and product lines add nothing.** Every item named on a `For Sale`, `Wanted` or
  `Products` line is also held by somebody, so widening the search to them buys **0** extra tags.
  Measured; do not spend time on it.

There is already a precedent for reading names from the report: `not-traded-here`
(`semantics.rs:1470`) takes its market names from the report's own lines and so already prints
plurals - *"its market has perfume, gems and hill dwarves"*.

When this lands: a count and an item name agree in number wherever they appear, and the next
message that pairs them inherits the rule instead of the bug.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

All of it in `crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs`. No TypeScript, no ruleset, no scraping.

### The plural table, built once per report

```rust
/// Every item's plural, as the report itself writes it.
///
/// Keyed by upper-case tag. Built from every unit line in the report that shows **more than one**
/// of something: `5 horses [HORS]` is the engine's own plural, which is why this beats any rule -
/// `amulets of protection` and `books of exorcism` are not what adding an `s` produces, and
/// `10 grain` is what an invariant noun looks like rather than a missing plural.
///
/// A tag is absent when nobody in the report holds more than one of it.
type Plurals = BTreeMap<String, String>;

/// Reads the plural of every item any unit in the report holds more than one of.
///
/// **The whole report, not one hex**, and deliberately: the unit a message is about is often the
/// one that has *too few* of the thing - `short 5 horses` is said of a unit holding none - so the
/// hex it stands in is exactly where the evidence tends not to be. Built once in `review_turn`
/// and passed down, rather than scanned per message.
fn plurals_in(report: &ParsedReport) -> Plurals;
```

It walks `report.regions`' units' `items` (`ItemAmount { amount, name, tag }`,
`report/model.rs:35`) and records `name` for every entry with `amount > 1`, upper-casing the tag.
**Every unit the report shows, ours and foreign alike** - a foreign unit's inventory is as good a
dictionary as ours, and this reads nothing from it but a noun.

Where two units disagree about a tag's plural, keep the first by document order and say so in a
comment; it does not arise on the committed corpus and a stable answer matters more than which.

### The helper every message uses

```rust
/// A count and an item's name, agreeing in number: `1 horse`, `5 horses`, `10 grain`.
///
/// The acceptance criterion `ah-rsdz` was filed for: the rule lives here and nowhere else, so a
/// message added later inherits it by using this instead of `item_name`.
fn counted_item(
    count: i64,
    tag: &str,
    hex: &Hex<'_>,
    ruleset: Option<&Ruleset>,
    plurals: &Plurals,
) -> String;
```

exactly:

```
if count == 1 { format!("1 {}", item_name(tag, hex, ruleset)) }        // the ruleset's singular
else {
    let name = plurals.get(&tag.to_ascii_uppercase())
        .cloned()
        .unwrap_or_else(|| item_name(tag, hex, ruleset));             // the settled fallback
    format!("{count} {name}")
}
```

- **`count == 1` takes the singular from the ruleset**, not from the report: a report line for one
  item shows the singular too, but the ruleset is the catalogue and is always present.
- **Any other count takes the plural branch, including 0.** `0 horses` is what English does. It is
  not expected to arise - a shortfall of nothing is not reported - and costs nothing to be right
  about.
- **The fallback is the singular**, the navigator's choice: wrong, but wrong only for the residue
  rather than everywhere, and never *invented*. Do not add an `-s` here.

### The three call sites

**Exactly three**, and they produce six sentences between them. Every other `item_name` call names
an item with no count beside it and **must not change**:

| Line | Code | Change |
|---|---|---|
| `2377` | `not-enough-items`, per unit | `short {short} {name}` → `short {}`, `counted_item(short, tag, …)` |
| `2445` | `not-enough-items`, hex level | `are short {short} {name} between them` likewise |
| `4342` | `region-pool-oversubscribed` | all four sentences; the noun agrees with `{wanted}`, never with `{available}` |

**Leave `704` and `1470` alone.** `PurchaseAnswer::NotSold`'s name and `not-traded-here` both name
an item with no number against it, which is exactly why the bead says `not-traded-here` escaped the
defect.

**Do not change case anywhere.** `4342` lowercases its goods and `2377`/`2445` do not; that
inconsistency is pre-existing and out of scope. At `4342`, **apply `.to_lowercase()` to the whole
`counted_item` result** - a leading digit is unaffected by it, so `"2 Longships".to_lowercase()`
is `"2 longships"` and behaviour is identical to today's. Nine ruleset names are capitalised and
**all nine are ships** (`AIRS BALL CLOU COG CORS GALL GLLY LONG RAFT`); **no ship appears with a
count anywhere in the corpus**, so this decides nothing visible today.

### Threading it

`plurals_in(report)` is called once in `review_turn`, beside the other once-per-report values, and
`&Plurals` is threaded down the same path `ruleset` already takes, to:

- `check_resources` (`semantics.rs:1418`) → `report_shortfalls` (`2272`) - sites `2377` and `2445`;
- `check_region_pools` (`4298`) - site `4342`.

One extra parameter on each, in the same position relative to `ruleset` throughout, so the call
sites read alike.

## Increments

1. **`plurals_in`.** Opening test in `semantics.rs`:
   `reads a plural from a unit that holds more than one` - a report whose unit holds
   `5 horses [HORS]` gives `HORS -> "horses"`.
   `ignores a unit that holds exactly one` - `1 horse [HORS]` contributes nothing.
   `reads an irregular plural as the report writes it` - `3 amulets of protection [AMPR]` gives
   `amulets of protection`, **not** `amulet of protections`. This is the test the whole bead exists
   for.
   `reads an invariant noun unchanged` - `10 grain [GRAI]` gives `grain`.
   `reads a foreign unit's inventory too`.

2. **`counted_item`.** `one_reads_singular` - `counted_item(1, "HORS", …)` is `1 horse` even when
   the table has a plural. `many_reads_plural` - `5 horses`. `an_unknown_plural_falls_back` - a tag
   absent from the table gives `5 horse`, today's behaviour, for the residue only.
   `an_invariant_noun_does_not_gain_an_s` - `10 grain`.

3. **`not-enough-items`.** Thread the table into `report_shortfalls` and move both sites.
   `a_shortfall_of_several_reads_plural` - `short 5 horses: this unit can have 0 and its orders
   spend 5`. `a_shortfall_of_one_reads_singular` - `short 1 horse: …`. The hex-level sentence
   likewise.

4. **`region-pool-oversubscribed`.** Thread it into `check_region_pools` and move all four
   sentences. `the_market_sentences_agree_in_number` - the plural agrees with `{wanted}`, asserted
   for a case where `{wanted}` and `{available}` differ in number: `this unit buys 2 horses and
   this market has 1`.

5. **Nothing else moved.** `a_message_with_no_count_is_unchanged` - `not-traded-here` still reads
   `this hex does not sell horse - its market has …`, singular and untouched.

6. **The corpus.** `crates/core/tests/validate_real_orders.rs`'s `EXPECTED` table (line ~62) counts
   findings by code and does not read their text, so it should not move. Run it. Any change means a
   finding appeared or vanished, which this bead does not do.

## The test plan

| Test | Pins |
|---|---|
| the five `plurals_in` tests | the table: >1 only, irregulars verbatim, invariants unchanged, foreign units included |
| the four `counted_item` tests | 1 → singular, many → plural, unknown → singular fallback, invariant unchanged |
| the three `not-enough-items` tests | both sentences, and the count-of-one case |
| `the_market_sentences_agree_in_number` | all four, and that the noun follows `wanted` not `available` |
| `a_message_with_no_count_is_unchanged` | `not-traded-here` and the hover name are untouched |

All in `crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs`, over small hand-built reports in the style of the
existing message tests. No TypeScript suite is involved: every string here is built in Rust.

Suites: `cargo test -p atlantis-core`, `pnpm run check:fast`.

## User-facing decisions

Interviewed with the navigator on 2026-08-23. Mockup: `docs/ui/ah-rsdz-plurals.html`, which carries
the measurements above.

**Where the plural comes from.**
Chosen: **the report's own item lines** - the engine's own words, so irregulars come out right
without a rule, and no scraping. `not-traded-here` already reads names this way.
Rejected: **scraping plurals into the ruleset**, the shape `ah-19l2.1` and `ah-1ad6.1` used - one
catalogue available whether or not anyone holds the item, but the page states plurals only
incidentally inside prose, for about 91 of 171, and extracting them is a bead of its own.
Rejected: **both sources**, best coverage and two things to keep in step.
Rejected: **rewording so a count never abuts a name**, which needs no data and is right for all 171
items - and changes sentences that are otherwise fine, moving the awkwardness rather than removing
it.

**When no plural is known.**
Chosen: **fall back to the singular** - today's behaviour, for the residue only. Wrong, and never
invented.
Rejected: **falling back to "+s"**, right far more often than not and confidently wrong on
`amulet of protections` - trading a rare oddity for a rarer, worse one.
Rejected: **naming it once without a count**, which reads well and drops the numbers, the useful
part of the sentence.

**How wide.**
Chosen: **every message that pairs a count with a name**, through one helper - the acceptance
criterion's own words, so the next message inherits the rule.
Rejected: **only the two named**, a smaller diff that leaves the next message free to repeat the
mistake.

**Decided here, not asked**, each following from the above rather than opening anything new: the
table is built from the **whole report** rather than the current hex, because the unit a message is
about is often the one that has too few of the thing; **foreign units' inventories count**, since
nothing is read from them but a noun; **case is not touched**, because the only capitalised names
are the nine ships and no ship appears with a count anywhere in the corpus; and **a count of 0
takes the plural**, which is what English does and which is not expected to arise.

## Out of scope

- **Scraping plurals into the ruleset.** Declined above. If the residue turns out to matter in
  play, that is the follow-up, and this bead's helper is where it would plug in.
- **The capitalisation inconsistency** between `4342` and `2377`/`2445`. Pre-existing, invisible
  today, and not this bead's.
- **`not-traded-here` and the `NotSold` hover name.** Neither puts a number against a name; the
  bead names this as the reason they escaped.
- **Any message outside `semantics.rs`.** The tooltip's strings are built in TypeScript from
  figures, not from item names with counts; `ah-eacd`'s food sentences already handle their own
  number.
- **Plurals of anything but items** - men, races, structures. None of them is printed with a count
  through `item_name`.

## Validation

```bash
cargo test -p atlantis-core
pnpm run check:fast
```

All green, no `#[ignore]`. Then, by eye, over a real report:

- a unit short of several of something reads `short 5 horses: …`, and one short of exactly one
  reads `short 1 horse: …`.
- a hex where units between them buy more than the market offers reads
  `your units here buy 120 horses between them and this market has 100`.
- an invariant noun still reads `short 10 grain`, **not** `10 grains`.
- `not-traded-here` is unchanged.

**A human must confirm the invariant-noun case**, because it is the one where a plausible
implementation is confidently wrong and every assertion over hand-built fixtures would still pass
if the table were bypassed.

## Known traps

- **Never derive a plural.** 84 of the 114 items the corpus shows with a count above one pluralise
  irregularly, and 30 do not pluralise at all. Any rule - `+s`, `+es`, head-noun detection - is
  wrong on real items this application prints today. The report's own word is the only correct
  source, and where there is none the singular stands.
- **Build the table from the whole report, not the hex.** A unit short of horses may hold none, and
  so may everything else in its hex; the evidence is usually somewhere else in the report. Using
  `hex` here would make the fallback the common case rather than the residue.
- **`count == 1` must take the ruleset's singular**, not the table. The table only ever holds
  plurals, so a lookup at 1 would either miss or return a plural.
- **Only three call sites take a count.** `semantics.rs:704` and `:1470` name an item with no
  number and must not change - `not-traded-here` is the message the bead names as having escaped
  the defect, and "fixing" it would introduce one.
- **At `4342` the noun agrees with `{wanted}`, not `{available}`.** `this unit buys 2 horses and
  this market has 1` is correct; agreeing with the wrong number is invisible until the two differ.
- **Market and product lines add no coverage.** Measured: every tag they name is also held by some
  unit. Widening the scan to them is work for nothing.
- **`.claude/cerebro-traps.md`** has nothing that bites here - no rendering, no persisted default,
  no scraping, and every string is built in Rust.
acceptance_criteria: A count and an item name read correctly together wherever the two appear - at minimum region-pool-oversubscribed and not-enough-items. A count of 1 reads singular. The rule lives in one place that every message uses, rather than at each call site, so the next message to pair the two inherits it.

title: Warn when a unit cannot produce what it is ordered to
description: ah-19l2.1 puts each recipe's required skill and level into the ruleset, and SkillEntry.produces has carried the level since before it. A unit ordered to PRODUCE a catapult without carpenter 4 makes nothing and wastes the month, and the client says nothing. Split out of ah-19l2.2 by the navigator on 2026-08-23, which settled that such a unit simply shows expense 0: catching the wasted month is a new advisory code, with its own wording interview and its own row in validate_real_orders' EXPECTED table, so it earns its own bead. Sits beside study-at-maximum and unit-does-nothing in kind.
design:
## Context

A `PRODUCE` order wastes the whole month in two ways the client says nothing about:

- **the unit has not the skill.** Catapults need carpenter 4; a unit with carpenter 2 ordered to
  make one makes nothing.
- **the region has not the resource.** `@produce iron` in a hex whose `Products` line names grain,
  wood and furs makes nothing.

`ah-19l2.2` settled that such a unit shows **expense 0** - right about the silver, silent about the
month - and the navigator split this bead out of it on 2026-08-23 to say the rest, then grew it on
2026-08-23 to cover the region case as well as the skill one.

**There is an exact precedent for the skill half.** `build-without-skill` (`semantics.rs:107`,
checked by `check_build_skill` at line ~2589) already says this about `BUILD`:

> `cannot build a Mine: needs building 1, has no building`

This bead is that check, twice, for `PRODUCE`. Read `check_build_skill` end to end before starting;
its structure - gate on the ruleset, gate on the option, one finding per unit on the first matching
order, the catalogue's lower-case skill name, the `has no X` / `has X n` split - is the structure to
copy rather than reinvent.

**`ah-19l2.2` blocks this and must land first.** Until it does, `PRODUCE` is
`Intent::MonthLong("PRODUCE")` (`intents.rs:384`) and carries no item, so there is nothing to check.
`ah-19l2.2` introduces `Intent::Produce { item }` and `recipe_for`, and both are used here. The
dependency is wired in the bead graph.

One fact settles which orders the region check touches, and it is worth stating because it looks
like a judgement and is not: **only a recipe with no material inputs comes from the region.** Iron,
wood, grain, furs and the rest are produced from the hex itself and appear on its `Products` line;
a sword is made *from* iron and can be made anywhere there is iron to hand. So the region check runs
on exactly the recipes `ah-19l2.1` records with `inputs: []`, and `@produce sword` by a unit with no
iron is already covered by `not-enough-items` from `ah-19l2.2`. No gap, no overlap.

When this lands: the two commonest ways to waste a month on a `PRODUCE` are marked on the line that
causes them.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### `crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs` - two codes and one check

Two new codes in `mod codes` (line 81), appended to `ALL` **in that array's own order**, which the
generated TypeScript copies - the array's doc comment (line ~128) says so explicitly and says that
new-here-last holds regardless of where they land in the settings UI:

```rust
pub const PRODUCE_WITHOUT_SKILL: Code = Code("produce-without-skill");
pub const PRODUCE_NOT_HERE: Code = Code("produce-not-here");
```

`ALL` becomes `[Code; 28]` - **the length is in the type** (`pub const ALL: [Code; 26]`), so it must
be bumped or it will not compile. That is the compiler catching the one thing easy to forget here.

One new check function, beside `check_build_skill` (line 2637), dispatched from **`semantics.rs:330`**,
immediately after `check_build_skill(hex, ruleset, &options, &mut findings);`:

```rust
/// Both ways a `PRODUCE` order makes nothing: the unit cannot make it anywhere, or not here.
///
/// Two codes rather than one because they are separately toggleable and separately true, and a
/// unit that fails both gets both marks - the navigator's choice, 2026-08-23: suppressing one must
/// never silently hide the other, and a player who fixes only the region would move a unit that
/// still cannot do the job.
fn check_production(
    hex: &Hex<'_>,
    ruleset: Option<&Ruleset>,
    options: &CheckOptions,
    findings: &mut Vec<Finding>,
);
```

Its shape, mirroring `check_build_skill`:

1. `let Some(ruleset) = ruleset else { return };` - with no ruleset nothing can be said. Unlike
   `check_build_skill` there is no `knows_buildings`-style whole-catalogue gate to add: a ruleset
   with no recipes answers `None` from `recipe_for` for every item, which the loop already reads as
   silence. Say that in a comment, because its absence beside a copied function reads as an
   omission.
2. For each unit, the **first** `Intent::Produce` in its block - one warning per unit, as the three
   `BUILD` checks already do. A `PRODUCE` is a month-long order, so a unit has at most one that
   matters anyway.
3. `recipe_for(item, hex, ordered, ruleset)` - `ah-19l2.2`'s lookup, reused. `None` means the item
   resolves to nothing, or nothing produces it; that is the second sentence below, not silence.
4. **The skill check.** Find the skill whose `produces` names the tag and the level it needs.
5. **The region check**, only when `recipe.inputs.is_empty()`.

**Which skill, when more than one produces the same tag.** Take the skill the unit already has, if
any produces it; otherwise the one needing the lowest level; ties broken by tag, alphabetically, so
the message is stable across runs. Document it - a message that changes between runs on a
`BTreeMap` iteration order is the kind of thing nobody notices until a test flakes.

**The messages**, verbatim, all four:

```
cannot produce catapults: needs carpenter 4, has carpenter 2
cannot produce catapults: needs carpenter 4, has no carpenter
cannot produce quicksilver: no skill produces it
cannot produce iron here: this region produces grain, wood and furs
```

and, for the 5-in-350 hexes whose line reads `Products: none.`:

```
cannot produce iron here: this region produces nothing
```

The item is the **catalogue's name**, as `build-without-skill` uses the catalogue's structure kind -
`catapults`, not the `catapult` the player typed and not `CATP`. Plural where the ruleset's own
`produces` clause is plural; use the item's `name` and pluralise nowhere in Rust - see
*Known traps*.

**A list joiner is needed and does not exist in Rust.** `semantics.rs:1222` uses a bare
`.join(", ")`. Add a small private helper mirroring `unitTooltip.ts:171`'s `namesInAList` exactly,
so the two surfaces read alike:

```rust
/// `a`, `a and b`, `a, b and c` - the shape `namesInAList` already uses in the interface.
fn in_a_list(names: &[String]) -> String;
```

**No truncation.** Measured over the corpus: 350 `Products` lines, the longest naming **6** items,
177 of them naming 3. The sentence stays short without a cap, and a cap would be a rule to maintain
for a case that does not occur.

### `packages/shared/src/workspace/SettingsDialog.tsx` - a new group

A new group **after `Building`** (line 558) and before `Sailing` (line 584), in the same shape as
its neighbours:

```tsx
{
  heading: "Producing",
  entries: [
    {
      code: "produce-without-skill",
      title: "Producing without the skill",
      description:
        "A PRODUCE order for an item the unit has not the skill or level to make."

```

`SettingsDialog.test.tsx:100` asserts the groups by name - "renders one toggle per advisory code,
grouped Studying/Teaching / Resources / Guarding / Orders / Building / Sailing". **That test name
and its assertions both move**; rename it to include Producing rather than adding an assertion
beside a name that has stopped being true.

## Increments

1. **The two codes.** Add them to `mod codes`, bump `ALL` to `[Code; 28]`, and add two `Case`
   fixtures to the table that ends at **`semantics.rs:9604`** - its assertion at line 9606 is
   `cases.len() == codes::ALL.len()`, *"every code in codes::ALL needs a fixture here, or a silenced

   Then `a_unit_with_no_such_skill_at_all_is_told_so` - the `has no carpenter` wording.

4. **Both at once.** `a_unit_failing_both_checks_gets_both_marks` - no mining skill, `@produce iron`,

Suites: `cargo test -p atlantis-core`, `pnpm run check:generated`, `pnpm run check:fast`.

## User-facing decisions

Interviewed with the navigator on 2026-08-23, in two rounds. Mockups:
`docs/ui/ah-wbr9-skill.html`, `docs/ui/ah-wbr9-region.html`.

**Round 1 - the skill message.**
Chosen: **mirror `build-without-skill`**, quoted verbatim above. The reader already meets that
sentence for `BUILD`, so there is nothing new to learn, and it uses the catalogue's name.
Rejected: *leading with the waste* ("this month is wasted: producing catapults needs carpenter 4,
this unit has 2") - says the consequence first, which is what the player cares about, and diverges
from the shape every other advisory uses. Rejected: *echoing the order's own word*
("cannot produce catapult"), which reads oddly beside the `BUILD` message.

**Round 1 - an item nothing in the game produces.**
Chosen: **its own sentence under the same code** - `cannot produce quicksilver: no skill produces
it`. Catches a mistyped or imagined item, which wastes a month just the same.
Rejected: *silence*, on the grounds that `ah-19l2.2` already shows `?` in the Silver column - a
question mark in a column with no sentence anywhere saying why.

**Round 1 - how far the bead reaches.**
Chosen: **skill and region together**, two codes in one bead. The navigator overrode the
recommendation to keep it to the skill alone and file the region case separately; the region case
is arguably the commoner mistake, and both are the same shape of check on the same order.

**Round 2 - the region message.**
Chosen: **say what the hex has** - `cannot produce iron here: this region produces grain, wood and
furs`, and `... produces nothing` for a hex whose line reads `Products: none.` It tells the player
what they *can* order, which is the next thing they will want.
Rejected: *mirroring the skill sentence* ("this region produces none"), which reads as one family
with the skill message but says nothing about what would work. Rejected: *saying only what is
missing* ("this region has none"), the shortest, which sends the reader back to the Products line.

**Round 2 - a unit failing both checks.**
Chosen: **both marks.** Each is independently true and separately toggleable, so suppressing one
must not silently hide the other.
Rejected: *skill only* - the more fundamental problem, and it would send a player to move a unit
that still cannot do the job when it arrives. Rejected: *region only* - fixable by moving, and
wrong on arrival.

**Round 2 - where the toggles live.**
Chosen: **a new `Producing` group**, after `Building` and before `Sailing`, holding
"Producing without the skill" and "Producing what the region has not".
Rejected: *into `Resources`*, which would mix "you cannot afford it" with "you cannot do it".
Rejected: *into `Orders`*, the catch-all, where nobody would look for them.

**Decided here, not asked**, because each follows from the above rather than opening anything new:
one finding per unit on its first `PRODUCE` (what the three `BUILD` checks already do, and a
`PRODUCE` is month-long so a unit has at most one that matters); both codes **on** by default, as
`build-without-skill` is and as every code but `hex-unguarded` is; and no truncation of the
Products list, measured at 6 items worst case across the whole corpus.

## Out of scope

- **Whether the region has *enough*** of the resource for every unit ordered to take it. That is
  the same shape of question as `ah-t2pn`'s tax pool and belongs with it, not here.
- **`BUILD` recipes**, which `build-without-skill` already covers.
- **Anything about silver or materials.** `ah-19l2.2` prices the order and warns when it cannot be
  afforded; this bead is only about the order making nothing at all.
- **A unit whose men are too few to make even one.** That is `made == 0` with no error - the order
  is legal and produces nothing this month, which is a different thing from being unable to.
- **Regions the report never described.** A hex holding one of our units is always fully described,
  so this does not arise - see *Known traps* for the check that proves it.
- **Pluralising item names in Rust.** See *Known traps*.

## Validation

```bash
cargo test -p atlantis-core
pnpm run check:generated
pnpm run check:fast
```

All green, no `#[ignore]`. Then, by eye, with the app open on a real report:

- the settings tab shows a **Producing** group between **Building** and **Sailing**, with two
  toggles, and turning each off removes only its own marks.
- a unit ordered `@produce iron` in a hex whose Products line lacks iron carries a mark on that
  line reading `cannot produce iron here: this region produces …`, listing what the line does name.
- a unit producing something its region has and its skill allows carries **no** mark - the false
  positive is the failure mode that matters, since this check runs on the commonest order in the
  corpus.

**A human must confirm the last of those.** `PRODUCE LIVE`, `PRODUCE HORS` and their kind are among
the most frequent orders in the committed turns; a check that marks them wrongly would put a mark on
half the map, and no assertion over hand-built fixtures proves it does not.

## Known traps

- **`ah-19l2.2` must land first**, and `ah-19l2.1` before it. Without `Intent::Produce { item }`
  there is no item to check. If `PRODUCE` still matches `MonthLong`, stop and check the bead graph.
- **A new code is three edits, not one.** `mod codes` (line 81); the `ALL` array, whose length is
  in its type (`[Code; 26]` - adding two without bumping to 28 does not compile, which is the good
  case); and a `Case` fixture in the table ending at line 9604, whose assertion holds
  `cases.len() == codes::ALL.len()`. The third is 9,000 lines from the first and is the one that
  gets missed.
- **`inputs.is_empty()` is what separates a region question from a materials question.** A recipe
  with inputs is made from goods the unit carries and can be made anywhere; running the region check
  on it would mark every `@produce sword` in the game. There is a test for exactly this.
- **A hex whose `Products` line is absent parses to the same empty `Vec<ItemAmount>` as
  `Products: none.`** (`report/model.rs:212` carries a plain `Vec`, with no "was it stated"
  distinction). The check treats empty as "produces nothing" and warns. That is safe **because a
  region holding one of our own units is always fully described** - a hex we only glimpse from
  next door has no unit of ours to carry a `PRODUCE` order. Verify that on the corpus before
  relying on it: if any region carrying an own unit has an empty products list *and* no
  `Products: none.` line, this assumption is wrong and the check must go silent for it instead.
- **Do not pluralise in Rust.** The messages above read `catapults` because the catalogue's
  `produces` clause names them that way and the item's own `name` is what to print; inventing an
  `-s` in the core would be the core having an opinion about English, which this module explicitly
  does not (`silver.rs:118`, "how it is said is the interface's business").
- **Message stability when two skills make the same item.** Pick deterministically - the unit's own
  skill first, then lowest level, then tag alphabetically - or the sentence changes with map
  iteration order and a test flakes months later.
- **`SettingsDialog.test.tsx:100`'s test *name* lists the groups.** Rename it; leaving a test called
  "grouped Studying/Teaching / Resources / Guarding / Orders / Building / Sailing" while asserting
  eight groups is a lie that passes.
- **Nothing makes the settings tab fail when a toggle is missing.** That test's title list is
  hardcoded and never compared against `codes::ALL`, so a code added in Rust with no entry in
  `SettingsDialog.tsx` ships as an advisory the player cannot turn off. Add both entries
  deliberately; the compiler will not help here as it does on the Rust side.
- **`.claude/cerebro-traps.md`: no effect-level test in `packages/shared`.** `SettingsDialog.test.tsx`
  is an existing `renderToStaticMarkup` test; extend it in that style and do not reach for effects.

title: PRODUCE spends silver in the Silver column and the shortfall check
description: Once the ruleset carries production recipes (ah-19l2.1), a PRODUCE order that costs silver can be forecast. Today PRODUCE is Intent::MonthLong and both forecast_unit and the ledger drop it on the floor, so a real committed turn (g3-f42-t82, unit 12881 Carpenters, '@produce catapult') hides a 3000-silver-per-catapult expenditure from both the Silver column and the not-enough-silver check.
design:
## Context

`PRODUCE` never becomes a first-class intent. `intents.rs:384` maps it to
`Intent::MonthLong("PRODUCE")` - "Nothing here reads them further; what matters is that the unit's
month is spoken for" - and both `forecast_unit` and the ledger drop `MonthLong` on the floor
(`semantics.rs:~1071`, `Intent::Work | Intent::Entertain => {}` and the `MonthLong`/`Build` arm
beside it).

For most recipes that is harmless: the rules pay for production in materials and man-months, not
silver. **Two of the ruleset's 53 recipes are not like that** - catapults and steel defenders, both
3000 silver, both 1 per 4 man-months, both carpenter 4.

The case is real. `tests/fixtures/reports/neworigins-3.0.0-g3-f42-t82.rep` line 7137 carries
`@produce catapult`, ordered by unit **12881 `Carpenters`** - our faction, 10 wood elves, carpenter
[CARP] 5. Ten men at 1 per 4 man-months is 2 catapults: **6000 silver**, plus 500 wood, 60 ironwood
and 160 furs, none of it visible in the Silver column or to `not-enough-silver`.

**`ah-19l2.1` blocks this and must land first**: it puts each recipe's inputs, silver and
man-months into `SkillEntry.produces`, which is where every number below comes from. Read its plan
before starting - it defines `Production`, `ProductionInput`, `inputsAreAlternatives`, `manMonths`
and `outputs`, and this bead is the only consumer of any of them. **`ah-19l2.1` also declares
`gaps.production`; closing that gap is this bead's job**, so delete `PRODUCTION_GAP` from
`packages/ruleset/src/build.ts`, drop `production` from the Rust `Gaps` (`rules.rs:243`), and
regenerate `config/public/ruleset.json`.

When this lands: a producing unit's Silver column shows what its production costs, the shortfall
check warns when it cannot afford it, `not-enough-items` warns when it lacks the materials, and the
last invisible expenditure in the corpus becomes visible.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### `crates/core/src/orders/intents.rs` - PRODUCE grows an argument

Replace the `MonthLong("PRODUCE")` arm (line 384) with a variant carrying what is produced, in the
shape `Withdraw` already uses (lines 372-379) - an item as the order wrote it, resolved later by
`semantics`, because resolving a name is that module's business:

```rust
/// `PRODUCE <item>`. Still a full month order; unlike the other month-long ones, what it makes
/// can cost silver and materials, so the item is carried rather than discarded (`ah-19l2.2`).
Produce { item: String },
```

`PRODUCE` with no argument, or with more than one token, keeps `Intent::MonthLong("PRODUCE")`: the
month is still spoken for and nothing can be priced. Match on `[item] if item.kind !=
TokenKind::Number` exactly as `Withdraw` does at line 376.

**Every `match` on `Intent` must gain an arm.** They are exhaustive, so the compiler names them all;
`moves_silver_per_man` (`silver.rs:~1030`) is the one that needs thought - `Produce` **is** priced
per man, so it belongs in that list, which makes a guessed headcount doubt a production exactly as
it already doubts a `TAX`.

### `crates/core/src/orders/silver.rs` - the arithmetic, shared by both surfaces

One new public function, and it is the only place the "how many" question is answered. Both the
column and the ledger call it, which is what stops the two drifting - the failure `ah-ycuj`'s corpus
test exists to catch:

```rust
/// Which limit decided how many a unit produces, when it is not its men.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[cfg_attr(test, derive(ts_rs::TS), ts(export))]
#[serde(rename_all = "kebab-case")]
pub enum ProductionCap {
    /// The unit holds less silver than the recipe wants for that many.
    Silver,
    /// The unit holds too little of at least one material input.
    Materials,
}

/// What one `PRODUCE` order makes, and what it takes to make it.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Default)]
pub struct ProductionPlan {
    /// How many the unit will actually make.
    pub made: i64,
    /// How many its men alone would make - `men / man_months`, rounded down. Equal to `made`
    /// unless something capped it.
    pub wanted: i64,
    /// Silver the whole run costs: `made * <the recipe's SILV input>`. `0` for the great majority
    /// of recipes, which take no silver.
    pub silver: i64,
    /// Every material the whole run consumes, silver excluded, in the recipe's own order.
    pub materials: Vec<ItemAmount>,
    /// What stopped it making `wanted`, or `None` when nothing did.
    pub capped_by: Option<ProductionCap>,
}

/// What a unit's `PRODUCE` order makes this month, from the recipe and what the unit holds.
///
/// `held` is the unit's inventory as the report shows it, and the cap is taken against **that**
/// rather than against a running balance - see the note below, which is a decision and not an
/// oversight.
///
/// `None` when the recipe cannot be applied at all: an unknown item, an item no skill produces, a
/// ruleset with no recipes, a guessed headcount, or a recipe whose inputs are alternatives. Each
/// of those is a `?` in the column rather than an invented number.
#[must_use]
pub fn plan_production(recipe: &Production, men: i64, held: &[ItemAmount]) -> Option<ProductionPlan>;
```

The arithmetic, exactly:

```
if recipe.man_months is None or 0, or recipe.outputs is None, or recipe.inputs_are_alternatives:
    return None                            // see *Known traps* for each
wanted = men / man_months                  // integer, floored; 0 when the unit is too small
if wanted <= 0: return Some(everything zero, capped_by: None)

silver_each    = the SILV input's amount, or 0
materials_each = every other input

by_silver    = if silver_each > 0 { held(SILV) / silver_each } else { i64::MAX }
by_materials = min over materials_each of ( held(tag) / amount )   // i64::MAX when there are none
made = min(wanted, by_silver, by_materials)

capped_by = if made == wanted        { None }
            else if by_silver <= by_materials { Some(Silver) }     // silver named first when both
            else                     { Some(Materials) }
```

**The cap is taken against what the unit *holds*, not against a running balance**, and both
surfaces therefore read the same number. That is the whole point: the ledger has a running balance
and `forecast_unit` does not, so capping against one would give the two surfaces different answers
for the same order and `ah-ycuj`'s corpus test would go red - correctly. Capping against holdings
is imprecise in both directions (a unit that BUYs wood first makes more than this says; one that
spends its silver elsewhere makes fewer), it is the figure the player can see in the report, and it
needs no assumption about the order orders resolve in. Say all of this in the doc comment.

Four new fields on `UnitSilver` (`silver.rs:85`), after `given_to_nobody` (line ~160):

```rust
/// How many of the item its `PRODUCE` order names this unit will make. `0` for a unit with no
/// such order, and for one whose men cannot make even one.
pub produced: i64,
/// The item's name, as the ruleset or the report calls it, for the hover to say. `None` when
/// the unit produces nothing.
///
/// A name and not a tag, unlike every other `*_tag` field here, and deliberately: the unit does
/// not hold the thing yet, so the interface cannot look its name up in the unit's own items the
/// way `ah-eacd`'s `nameOfHeldItem` does - it would render `CATP`. `semantics` fills this with
/// `item_name` (`semantics.rs:1801`), which is the same function the `not-enough-items` message
/// already uses.
pub produced_name: Option<String>,
/// How many its men alone would have made. Equal to `produced` unless `production_capped_by`
/// says something stopped it.
pub production_wanted: i64,
/// What stopped it making `production_wanted`, or `None` when nothing did. Drives the hover's
/// note and nothing else - the figures above are already the capped ones (`ah-19l2.2`).
pub production_capped_by: Option<ProductionCap>,
```

The silver the run costs is **inside `expense`** like every other spending order, not carried
separately - it is spending, and a reader looking for it looks at Expense.

One new `SilverDoubt` variant (`silver.rs:~212`), beside `UnpricedSkill` which it is exactly
analogous to:

```rust
/// `PRODUCE` of something the ruleset prices nowhere - an unknown item, an item no skill makes,
/// a recipe stating alternatives rather than requirements, or no ruleset at all.
UnpricedProduction,
```

`doubt_subject` carries the item as the order wrote it, the way `UnknownGoods` already does.

### `crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs` - both surfaces

**Resolving the item and finding its recipe** is one lookup, needed by the column and the ledger,
so it is one function beside `resolve_item` (`semantics.rs:~1580`):

```rust
/// The recipe for what a `PRODUCE` order names: the item it resolves to, and the skill entry that
/// makes it. `None` when the item cannot be resolved, no skill produces it, or there is no
/// ruleset - all of which are `UnpricedProduction`.
fn recipe_for<'a>(
    item: &str, hex: &Hex<'_>, actor: &Ordered<'_>, ruleset: Option<&'a Ruleset>,
) -> Option<&'a Production>;
```

It resolves the name with `resolve_item`, then scans `ruleset.skills` for a `SkillEntry` whose
`produces` names that tag, returning that `Production`. **The unit's own skill is not consulted** -
a unit that cannot make the thing is settled below.

In `forecast_unit`'s intent loop: a `Produce` arm calling `recipe_for` and `plan_production`, adding
`plan.silver` to `expense`, and filling the four new fields. `None` from either sets
`doubt = UnpricedProduction` and `doubt_subject = Some(item.clone())`, leaving `expense` `None` on
the same rule every other unpriced term follows.

In `apply` (`semantics.rs:~1035`), a `Produce` arm beside `buy` (line 1305):

```rust
Intent::Produce { item } => produce(ledger, hex, actor, placed, item, ruleset),
```

and `produce` charges the silver with `charge` (so `charged_at` points a finding at the line) and
debits each material with `charge` on its own tag. **It does not `credit` the output**, which is
where it differs from `buy` (line 1333) - see *User-facing decisions*. An unresolvable recipe puts
the unit in `ledger.doubted`, exactly as `buy` does at line 1316.

### `packages/shared/src/unitTooltip.ts` - one note

One new branch, placed **immediately before** the `shortForOrders` branch (line ~212). Both are
about an order the game will not carry out as written, and the shortfall is the more urgent of the
two, so it keeps its position above the upkeep notes and this sits directly under it:

```ts
if (silver.productionCappedBy !== null && silver.producedName !== null) {
  const has = silver.productionCappedBy === "silver" ? "silver" : "materials";
  return `This unit has ${has} for ${silver.produced} ${silver.producedName}, not the ${silver.productionWanted} its men could make.`;
}
```

**Do not reach for `nameOfHeldItem`** (`unitTooltip.ts:104`, added by `ah-eacd`). It looks a tag up
in `unit.items` and falls back to `tag.toLowerCase()`, and a unit about to *make* a catapult does
not hold one - so it would render `catp`. That is why `producedName` is a name rather than a tag;
the core fills it with `item_name`, which is what the `not-enough-items` message already uses.

The name is the item's singular as the catalogue writes it (`catapult`), so the sentence reads
`silver for 1 catapult` and `silver for 3 catapult`. **Pluralise in the interface**, where English
belongs: `${n} ${name}${n === 1 ? "" : "s"}` - the same shape the step-6 sentence `ah-eacd` shipped
already uses for `faction food item(s)`.

## The test plan

Unit, `crates/core/src/orders/intents.rs`: increment 1, beside the existing per-order parse tests.

Unit, `crates/core/src/orders/silver.rs`: increments 2 and 3, pure over a hand-built `Production`
and an `ItemAmount` slice - no report, no hex, matching how `faction_food_tests` and

style of the `ah-fjty`/`ah-eacd` tests near lines 4700-4900.
