Neither is edited to make it pass without reading what it says first.

Suites: `cargo test -p atlantis-core`, `pnpm --filter @atlantis/ruleset test`,
`pnpm run check:generated`, `pnpm run check:fast`.

## User-facing decisions

Interviewed with the navigator on 2026-08-23, in two rounds. Mockups:
`docs/ui/ah-19l2.2-produce.html`, `docs/ui/ah-19l2.2-edges.html`.

**Round 1 - how many does the unit make?** This *is* the number in the column, since the silver is
3000 times it.
Chosen: **its men, capped by the silver and materials it holds.** Carpenters shows **3000**, not
6000: materials allow 2 catapults, its 3000 silver pays for 1.
Rejected: *men alone* (6000) - what the order asks for and simplest, but it overstates whenever
silver or materials fall short, and overstating expense shows red where the truth may be black,
which this module's header names as the dangerous direction. Rejected: *decline to price it* -
never wrong, never useful, and this is the one order in the corpus where the figure mattered.

**Round 1 - do the materials move too?**
Chosen: **yes, silver and materials.** The ledger already tracks every item tag and already emits
`not-enough-items`; the inputs are captured by `ah-19l2.1` regardless.
Rejected: *silver only* - a smaller bead matching the parent's title, which would leave a second
false silence of exactly the kind this family exists to remove.

**Round 1 and 2 - what the hover says.**
Chosen: **speak only when the cap bites, and name which constraint bit.** Silent at full rate.
Otherwise, exactly:
> `This unit has silver for 1 catapult, not the 2 its men could make.`
> `This unit has materials for 1 catapult, not the 2 its men could make.`

and when both bind, **the silver sentence**, because silver is what the column is about.
Rejected: *always saying the count*, which shows the working every time at the cost of another line
in a hover that already has several. Rejected: *saying nothing*, the most consistent with every
other priced order, which leaves the reader to divide men by man-months to check a figure whose
basis they cannot see. Rejected: *naming the item that ran out* ("This unit is 250 wood short…"),
the most actionable wording, which duplicates the `not-enough-items` mark now firing on the same
unit.

**Round 2 - a unit ordered to produce something its skill cannot make.**
Chosen: **expense 0 and no mark.** The column correctly shows it spending nothing, and this bead
stays about costing.
Rejected: *a new advisory now*. It is a real wasted month worth catching, and it is a new code with
its own wording interview and its own row in `validate_real_orders`'s table - so **it was filed as
its own unranked bead**, `ah-wbr9`, "Warn when a unit is ordered to PRODUCE something its skill
cannot make", at the navigator's direction.

**Round 2 - do the produced goods arrive in time to be spent?**
Chosen: **no - debit the inputs, do not credit the output.** Production resolves in the month's
last phase, so goods made this month cannot be given away this month. This matches how the ledger
already treats wages and takings from entertaining (`semantics.rs:~1071`, `ah-uwa3`).
Rejected: *crediting the output*. Truthful about where the month ends, and it looks like the
obvious answer - but it would **silence** a `not-enough-items` warning that should fire, because
the engine will refuse a `GIVE` of goods that do not exist yet. This is the one place `produce`
deliberately differs from `buy`, which does credit what it buys (line 1333) because a purchase
resolves during the month.

## Out of scope

- **Warning that a unit lacks the skill or level to produce what it ordered.** `ah-wbr9`, filed
  unranked. `recipe_for` deliberately does not consult the unit's own skills.
- **`BUILD` recipes.** The building skill states its costs in the same grammar; `Intent::Build` is
  a separate arm and `ah-19l2.1` did not scrape them.
- **Crediting produced goods to next month.** Nothing in this tree models a following turn.
- **`PRODUCE` with no argument.** Stays `MonthLong`; the month is spoken for and nothing is priced.
- **Cooking, and any recipe of alternatives.** `plan_production` returns `None` and the column
  shows `?` - see *Known traps*.
- **Capping against a running balance** rather than holdings, and the imprecision that leaves.
  Deliberate; see *Files to change*.

## Validation

```bash
cargo test -p atlantis-core
pnpm --filter @atlantis/ruleset test
pnpm run check:generated
pnpm run check:fast
```

All green, with no `#[ignore]`. `crates/core/tests/silver_agrees_with_the_warning.rs` in particular,
since it is the guard over exactly the two surfaces this bead adds an order to.

Then, by eye, loading `neworigins-3.0.0-g3-f42-t82.rep` with its own committed orders template:

- unit **12881 `Carpenters`** shows a non-zero **Expense** where it showed none, and its hover
  reads `This unit has silver for N catapults, not the 2 its men could make.` if its silver caps it.
- no unit that is *not* producing changed at all.
- `gaps.production` is gone from `config/public/ruleset.json`.

**A human must confirm the first of those**, because it is the whole point of the family and no
assertion proves that the figure a player sees is the one that was meant.

## Known traps

- **`ah-19l2.1` must land first.** Every number here comes from `SkillEntry.produces`' new fields.
  If `inputs` is empty on every recipe, the ruleset predates it: regenerate before diagnosing
  anything else.
- **`ah-ycuj`'s corpus test is why both surfaces share `plan_production`.** Pricing a `PRODUCE`
  twice - once in `forecast_unit`, once in `apply` - is exactly how the column and the warning
  drifted apart over `PILLAGE`, which is the drift that bead exists to catch. One function, two
  callers.
- **Do not cap against a running balance.** The ledger has one and `forecast_unit` does not, so the
  two would answer differently for the same order. Holdings are the number both can read.
- **`inputs_are_alternatives` must be honoured, not ignored.** Cooking's "any of grain, livestock
  and fish" consumes *one* of the three; reading it as three requirements would say a meal costs a
  grain **and** a livestock **and** a fish, and debit all three. `plan_production` returns `None`
  for such a recipe, which shows `?` and charges nothing - the module's posture, since which input
  the engine takes cannot be told.
- **`outputs` is `None` for cooking** (the page states a formula), and `man_months` is
  `Option<u32>` for a ruleset scraped before `ah-19l2.1`. Both are `None`-checked into
  `UnpricedProduction` rather than defaulted - a `1` there would invent a rate.
- **`produce` must not `credit` its output**, unlike `buy`. The comment saying why belongs in the
  code, because the asymmetry with the function directly above it looks like an omission.
- **`EXPECTED_SPENDING`'s comment in `validate_real_orders.rs` says the committed turn's spending is
  "all of it on `STUDY`".** That may stop being true. Check it, and update the sentence rather than
  only the number.
- **`.claude/cerebro-traps.md`: no effect-level test in `packages/shared`.** The hover work is pure
  and belongs in `unitTooltip.test.ts`; do not add a `.test.tsx`.

title: Scrape what each PRODUCE recipe consumes into the ruleset
description: The data page states every production recipe in the skills section, not the items section - which is why ItemEntry has no production field and the scraper never saw the inputs. The scraper already reads WHICH items a skill produces and at what level (data.ts readProduction, the Production type); it discards everything after ' from ', which is exactly where the inputs are. This bead captures them: material inputs and quantities, silver, and man-months per output, for all 53 production segments the page states. No forecasting - that is ah-19l2.2.
design:
## Context

The data page states every production recipe, and the client cannot read any of it.

**The recipes are in the skills section, not the items section** - which is why `ItemEntry`
(`packages/ruleset/src/data.ts:40`) has no production field and the parent bead concluded the data
"does not exist". It does; it is shaped as skills:

> `carpenter [CARP] 4: A unit with this skill may PRODUCE catapults [CATP] from 250 wood [WOOD],
> 30 ironwood [IRWD], 80 furs [FUR] and 3000 silver [SILV] at a rate of 1 per 4 man-months and
> steel defenders [STED] from 30 rootstone [ROOT], 250 iron [IRON], 50 furs [FUR] and 3000 silver
> [SILV] at a rate of 1 per 4 man-months.`

**And the scraper already reads half of it.** `readProduction` (`data.ts:534`) matches
`may PRODUCE ([^.]*)\.`, splits the clause on the rate phrase, and takes the tag before ` from ` -
producing `Production { tag, level }` (`data.ts:123`). Everything after ` from `, and the rate
itself, is thrown away. **This bead captures what that function already walks past**; it is an
extension of a working parser, not a new one.

Why it matters, measured rather than assumed:

- The page states **53 production segments** across 31 `may PRODUCE` clauses.
- Exactly **one clause costs silver**: carpenter 4, covering catapults and steel defenders, both
  3000 silver, both 1 per 4 man-months.
- That sounds negligible, and it is not: `tests/fixtures/reports/neworigins-3.0.0-g3-f42-t82.rep`
  line 7137 carries **`@produce catapult`**, ordered by unit 12881 `Carpenters` - our own faction,
  10 wood elves, carpenter [CARP] 5, so qualified. At 1 per 4 man-months that is 2 catapults and
  **6000 silver**, invisible to the Silver column and to `not-enough-silver` alike.

`ruleset.json`'s `gaps` map declares only `weather`. This gap is undeclared, and an undeclared
missing capability is one somebody re-discovers - which is what the parent bead was filed about.

**This bead is the data half only.** Spending it - PRODUCE as a first-class intent, silver charged
in the column and the ledger - is `ah-19l2.2`, which this blocks. The navigator chose that split on
2026-08-23. Because the forecast is not here yet, this bead **also declares the gap**, so the
interim state is recorded rather than silent.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### `packages/ruleset/src/data.ts` - the parse

Reuse, and extend rather than replace: `PRODUCTION` (line 519), `PRODUCTION_RATE` (line 521),
`PRODUCED_TAG` (line 523), `readProduction` (line 534) and `mergeProduction` (line 555). The
existing structure - cut the clause into one segment per production, the rate phrase being what
ends each - is right and stays. Two changes to it: keep the rate text instead of discarding it as a
split separator, and read the ` from ` tail instead of dropping it.

`Production` (line 123) grows. It is exported and mirrored in Rust (below), so both move in the
same commit:

```ts
/** One thing a production recipe consumes: an item tag and how many, silver being `SILV`. */
export type ProductionInput = { tag: string; amount: number };

/** One thing a skill can make, the level at which it can first be made, and what it takes. */
export type Production = {
  tag: string;
  level: number;
  /**
   * What one output consumes, in the order the page lists it. Empty for a recipe that takes
   * nothing but labour - which is most of them: iron, wood, herbs and every other raw resource
   * are produced from the region itself.
   *
   * An input the page writes without a number is one: `swords [SWOR] from iron [IRON]`.
   */
  inputs: ProductionInput[];
  /**
   * Whether `inputs` are alternatives rather than requirements - the page's `from any of grain
   * [GRAI], livestock [LIVE] and fish [FISH]`, which consumes one of the three and not all three.
   *
   * True for cooking alone today. Carried as a flag rather than a different shape because one
   * irregular recipe does not earn a union type, and a consumer that ignores it over-states what a
   * recipe costs - the safe direction for a warning, and the wrong one silently for a forecast,
   * which is why `ah-19l2.2` must read it.
   */
  inputsAreAlternatives: boolean;
  /** Man-months per `outputs`. 1 for `at a rate of 1 per man-month`, 4 for `1 per 4 man-months`. */
  manMonths: number;
  /**
   * How many the recipe makes per `manMonths`. Every recipe on the page today makes exactly one.
   *
   * `null` for cooking, whose output the page states as a formula rather than a number - "a number
   * of meals [MEAL] equal to skill level divided by 2, rounded up". Null rather than a guess: this
   * type does not model formulae, and a 1 there would be wrong at every level above 2.
   */
  outputs: number | null;
};
```

**The input grammar, from the page as it stands.** Enumerated over the committed fixture, so this
is a description and not a guess. The ` from ` tail is a list of terms separated by `, ` and ` and `
(with and without the Oxford comma), each term `[<amount> ]<name> [TAG]`, the amount defaulting to
1. The whole list may be prefixed `any of`. Real examples, one per shape:

| Tail | Reads as |
|---|---|
| *(absent)* | `inputs: []` - iron, wood, herbs, horses, fish, grain, livestock, … |
| `iron [IRON]` | `[{ tag: "IRON", amount: 1 }]` |
| `3 iron [IRON]` | `[{ tag: "IRON", amount: 3 }]` |
| `herb [HERB] and mushroom [MUSH]` | two inputs, one each |
| `250 wood [WOOD], 30 ironwood [IRWD], 80 furs [FUR] and 3000 silver [SILV]` | four inputs, silver among them as `SILV` |
| `any of grain [GRAI], livestock [LIVE] and fish [FISH]` | three inputs, `inputsAreAlternatives: true` |

**Silver is an input like any other**, carried as `{ tag: "SILV", amount: 3000 }`. Do not give it a
field of its own: the page writes it in the same list with the same grammar, and a special case
would have to be kept in step with a grammar that already handles it.

**The rate grammar** is closed and small - the page states exactly four phrasings:
`at a rate of 1 per man-month`, `… 1 per 2 man-months`, `… 1 per 3 man-months`, `… 1 per 4
man-months`. So `outputs` is always 1 and only `manMonths` varies. **Parse both numbers anyway**
and throw `RulesetScrapeError` on a shape that is neither - a page that starts saying `2 per
man-month` must stop the scrape, not be silently read as 1. That is the posture `readProduction`
already takes when a clause yields no tag (line 549).

**Cooking is the one recipe that needs saying twice**, because it breaks two rules at once and both
of its breakages are quiet:

- its output is a formula, so `outputs: null`;
- its ` from ` is preceded by the words `rounded up`, so the segment reads
  `a number of meals [MEAL] equal to skill level divided by 2, rounded up from any of grain
  [GRAI], …`. Splitting on the **first** ` from ` happens to give the right answer on both sides
  here - the head still contains `[MEAL]`, the tail is the `any of` list - and that is luck, not
  design. Pin it with a test named for the luck, so a later "tidy-up" of the split cannot break it
  unnoticed.

### `crates/core/src/movement/rules.rs` - the mirror

`Production` (line 295) carries `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase", deny_unknown_fields)]`. **So
adding fields to the JSON breaks Rust deserialisation of every ruleset until this struct matches** -
the two are one change, in one commit, and the Rust side is not optional follow-up work.

```rust
/// One thing a production recipe consumes: an item tag and how many, silver being `SILV`.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase", deny_unknown_fields)]
pub struct ProductionInput {
    pub tag: String,
    pub amount: i64,
}
```

and on `Production`, four new fields, every one `#[serde(default)]` in the style the struct's
neighbours already use for "absent in a ruleset generated before this was scraped" (`cast` and
`produces` at lines 322-330 are the precedent to copy):

```rust
/// What one output consumes. Empty for a recipe that takes nothing but labour, and for a
/// ruleset generated before inputs were scraped.
#[serde(default)]
pub inputs: Vec<ProductionInput>,
/// Whether `inputs` are alternatives rather than requirements - cooking's "any of" alone today.
#[serde(default)]
pub inputs_are_alternatives: bool,
/// Man-months per `outputs`. Absent for a ruleset generated before the rate was scraped;
/// `None`, never 1, so a consumer can tell "not scraped" from "one a month".
#[serde(default)]
pub man_months: Option<u32>,
/// How many the recipe makes per `man_months`. `None` both for a ruleset generated before this
/// was scraped and for cooking, whose output the page states as a formula.
#[serde(default)]
pub outputs: Option<u32>,
```

`man_months` is `Option<u32>` and **not** a bare `u32` with `#[serde(default)]`, deliberately: the
default would be 0, which is not a rate but a division by zero waiting in `ah-19l2.2`.

### `packages/ruleset/src/build.ts` - the gap

The forecast does not exist yet, so the capability is still missing and is still worth declaring.
Add a second `Gap` beside `WEATHER_GAP` (line 89), and widen `gaps` (line 57, line 153):

```ts
const PRODUCTION_GAP: Gap = {
  modelled: false,
  note:
    "The ruleset now carries what each PRODUCE recipe consumes, but nothing spends it: PRODUCE " +
    "is parsed as a month-long order and neither the Silver column nor the shortfall check " +
    "charges it. Two recipes cost silver - catapults and steel defenders, 3000 each.",
  consequence:
    "A unit ordered to produce a catapult or a steel defender is shown spending nothing, and is " +
    "not warned when it cannot afford one. Treat a producing unit's silver as an upper bound.",
  evidence:
    "may PRODUCE catapults [CATP] from 250 wood [WOOD], 30 ironwood [IRWD], 80 furs [FUR] and " +
    "3000 silver [SILV] at a rate of 1 per 4 man-months"
};
```

`gaps` becomes `{ weather: Gap; production: Gap }` at line 57 and `{ weather: WEATHER_GAP,
production: PRODUCTION_GAP }` at line 153.

**The Rust `Gaps` is a named struct with `deny_unknown_fields`** (`rules.rs:240-246`), not a map -
so it moves in this commit too, exactly as `Production` does, and for the same reason. Add:

```rust
/// PRODUCE recipes are carried but nothing spends them - see `ah-19l2.2`. `None` for a ruleset
/// generated before this gap was declared, and `None` again once `ah-19l2.2` removes it.
#[serde(default)]
pub production: Option<Gap>,
```

`Option<Gap>` with `#[serde(default)]`, because a `Gap` has no meaningful default value and an
older ruleset genuinely does not have this key. `Ruleset::weather_modelled` (`rules.rs:652`) reads
`self.gaps.weather.modelled` and is untouched.

**`ah-19l2.2` deletes `PRODUCTION_GAP`** as part of closing the gap. Say so in its doc comment.

### `config/public/ruleset.json` - regenerated, never edited

```
pnpm --filter @atlantis/ruleset scrape -- \
  --rules tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-rules.html \
  --data tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-data.html
```

`committed.test.ts:24` holds the file exactly equal to what the scraper produces from the committed
pages, so a hand edit fails there. That test is the guard working, not an obstacle.

## Increments

1. **The rate.** Change `readProduction` to keep the rate phrase rather than split it away, parse
   `outputs` and `manMonths` from it, and throw on any other shape. `inputs` stays `[]` and
   `inputsAreAlternatives` `false` for now.
   Opening test in `packages/ruleset/src/data.test.ts`:
   `reads how long each production takes` - carpenter's catapult is `manMonths: 4`, an armorer's
   chain armor is `1`, admantium swords are `2`, plate armor is `3`.
   Then `refuses a production rate it does not recognise` - feed a doctored paragraph saying
   `at a rate of 2 per man-month` and expect `RulesetScrapeError`.

2. **The inputs.** Parse the ` from ` tail.
   Opening test: `reads what each production consumes` - `SWOR` from one `IRON`; `PARM` from three
   `IRON`; `HPOT` from one `HERB` and one `MUSH`; `GLID` from two `FLOA`; and `IRON` itself from
   nothing (`inputs: []`).
   Then `reads silver as an input like any other` - `CATP` is
   `[WOOD 250, IRWD 30, FUR 80, SILV 3000]` and `STED` is `[ROOT 30, IRON 250, FUR 50, SILV 3000]`,
   in the page's order.

3. **Cooking, the irregular one.** `reads cooking's alternative inputs` -
   `inputsAreAlternatives: true`, inputs `GRAI`, `LIVE`, `FISH` one each. Then
   `reads cooking's formula output as unknown rather than one` - `outputs: null`, `manMonths: 1`.
   Then the luck-pinning test: `reads cooking's product from a sentence that says "from" twice` -
   the product is `MEAL`, asserting the head/tail split survives `rounded up from`.

4. **The Rust mirror.** Add `ProductionInput` and the four fields. Opening test in
   `crates/core/src/movement/rules.rs`'s test module:
   `a_ruleset_without_production_inputs_still_loads` - deserialise a `Production` JSON object
   carrying only `tag` and `level`, and assert the four new fields take their defaults. This is
   what `#[serde(default)]` is for and it is the assertion that proves `deny_unknown_fields` was
   handled the right way round.

5. **Regenerate, and pin the two that matter.** Run the scrape. Add to
   `packages/ruleset/src/committed.test.ts`'s existing `describe` block:
   `prices the two productions that cost silver` - from the **committed** `ruleset.json`, not from
   a re-parse: carpenter's `produces` contains `CATP` at level 4 with 3000 `SILV` among its inputs
   and `manMonths: 4`, and `STED` likewise. This is the acceptance criterion's own test, and
   reading the committed file is what makes it one.

6. **The gap.** Add `PRODUCTION_GAP`, widen `gaps`, regenerate, and extend
   `build.test.ts`'s gap assertions (line 91) with the production gap in the same style.

## The test plan

| Test | File | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| `reads how long each production takes` | `data.test.ts` | the four rate phrasings map to 1/2/3/4 man-months |
| `refuses a production rate it does not recognise` | `data.test.ts` | the scrape stops rather than guessing when the page changes shape |
| `reads what each production consumes` | `data.test.ts` | the input grammar, including the no-number-means-one rule and the empty case |
| `reads silver as an input like any other` | `data.test.ts` | `SILV` is not special-cased, and both silver recipes are read whole |
| `reads cooking's alternative inputs` | `data.test.ts` | `any of` is not read as a conjunction |
| `reads cooking's formula output as unknown rather than one` | `data.test.ts` | `outputs: null` rather than a wrong number |
| `reads cooking's product from a sentence that says "from" twice` | `data.test.ts` | the head/tail split survives `rounded up from` |
| `a_ruleset_without_production_inputs_still_loads` | `rules.rs` | `deny_unknown_fields` plus `#[serde(default)]` keeps older rulesets loading |
| `prices the two productions that cost silver` | `committed.test.ts` | the acceptance criterion, from the committed file |
| the widened gap assertions | `build.test.ts` | the gap is declared and says what it prevents |

Suites: `pnpm --filter @atlantis/ruleset test`, `cargo test -p atlantis-core`, `pnpm run check:fast`
(which carries `check:generated`).

## User-facing decisions

**None.** This bead changes no interface: it adds fields to a scraped data file and to the Rust
struct that mirrors it. Nothing new is shown, no message changes, no setting is added. The
declared gap is data in `ruleset.json`, not a sentence anybody reads on screen.

The two decisions the parent bead put to the navigator on 2026-08-23 were **scope**, and they are
what produced this bead rather than choices inside it:

- **Scrape the data now and forecast in a follow-up**, rather than declaring the gap and stopping,
  or doing both in one bead. Decided on the measurement in *Context*: one silver-costing clause in
  the whole ruleset, and a real committed turn that hits it for 6000 silver.
  Rejected: *declare the gap and stop* - cheap and honest, but it would record a defect instead of
  retiring one, now that the 6000-silver order is known about. Rejected: *scrape and forecast
  together* - large enough to want splitting anyway, and it would land in economy code three other
  beads moved through this week.
- **Capture the whole recipe** - skill, level, every input and quantity, silver, and man-months -
  for all 53 segments, not only the two that cost silver.
  Rejected: *only what costs silver*, which parses the same sentences for less, and would need a
  second pass over them for anything else. Rejected: *recipe minus man-months*, which cannot say
  how many a unit makes in a month - and that is exactly what turns 3000 silver into 6000.

## Out of scope

- **Spending the data.** PRODUCE stays `Intent::MonthLong("PRODUCE")` (`intents.rs:384`), and both
  `forecast_unit` and the ledger go on dropping it. That is `ah-19l2.2`, which this blocks.
- **Material shortfalls.** The inputs are captured; nothing checks whether a unit holds 250 wood.
  It is what the captured data makes possible, and it is not this bead nor `ah-19l2.2` - file it
  when somebody wants it.
- **`BUILD` recipes.** The building skill states its own costs in the same section
  (`may BUILD a Tower from 10 stone [STON]`), in a grammar close enough to be tempting. Out: the
  parent bead is about PRODUCE, `Intent::Build` is a separate arm, and one grammar at a time.
- **Whether a unit is skilled enough to produce what it ordered.** `produces` has carried the level
  since before this bead and nothing reads it; that remains true after it.
- **Modelling cooking's output formula.** `outputs: null` records that the page states one, and
  meals cost no silver, so nothing downstream needs the number.
- **Re-fetching the pages.** The committed fixtures are the input; `source.fetchedAt` does not move.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm --filter @atlantis/ruleset test
pnpm --filter @atlantis/ruleset scrape -- \
  --rules tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-rules.html \
  --data tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-data.html
cargo test -p atlantis-core
pnpm run check:fast
```

All green. Then, by eye against the regenerated `config/public/ruleset.json`:

- `skills.CARP.produces` contains `CATP` with `inputs` `[WOOD 250, IRWD 30, FUR 80, SILV 3000]`,
  `manMonths: 4`, `outputs: 1`, `level: 4` - and `STED` beside it.
- `skills.COOK.produces[0]` has `outputs: null` and `inputsAreAlternatives: true`.
- `skills.MINI.produces` entries have `inputs: []` - raw resources take labour and nothing else.
- `gaps.production` is present and its `evidence` is the page's own sentence.

**A human need confirm nothing on screen**, and that is worth stating: nothing in this bead is
visible to a player. The check is the diff and the regenerated file.

## Known traps

- **`deny_unknown_fields` on the Rust `Production` (`rules.rs:293`) makes this one change, not
  two.** Regenerating `ruleset.json` with new keys and leaving the Rust struct alone fails
  deserialisation of *every* ruleset, not just the changed part - and the failure surfaces far from
  the edit. Move both in the same commit; increment 4 exists to force it.
- **`#[serde(default)]` on `man_months: u32` would default to 0**, which is a rate of nothing and a
  division by zero in `ah-19l2.2`. `Option<u32>`, so "not scraped" is distinguishable from "one a
  month". Same reasoning as `cost: Option<i64>` two fields above it.
- **`config/public/ruleset.json` is generated.** `committed.test.ts:24` holds it exactly equal to
  the scraper's output from the committed pages. Hand-editing it to add the new fields fails there;
  run the scrape.
- **Cooking says ` from ` twice.** `rounded up from any of grain [GRAI]` - splitting on the first
  occurrence gives the right answer on both sides by luck. Increment 3 pins it; do not "simplify"
  that split without re-reading the sentence.
- **`any of` is an alternative, not a conjunction.** Reading cooking's three foods as three
  requirements says a meal costs a grain *and* a livestock *and* a fish. Nothing downstream is hurt
  today because meals cost no silver, which is exactly why it would go unnoticed until it did.
- **The scraper throws rather than guesses**, and that is the established posture here
  (`RulesetScrapeError` at `data.test.ts`'s existing refusal tests and at `data.ts:549`). A new
  page shape must stop the scrape; a scraper that quietly reads `2 per man-month` as 1 is worse
  than one that fails.
- **`.claude/cerebro-traps.md`** has nothing that bites here: no rendering, no persisted default,
  no smoke suite. `packages/ruleset`'s tests read files and assert on JSON.

title: Record why a food item pays 50 silver of upkeep, not the data page's 30
description:
The code uses 50: SILVER_PER_FOOD = 50 in crates/core/src/orders/silver.rs, with own_food_pass computing 'needed = ceil(owed / 50)'.

The rules agree: 'Units may substitute one unit of grain, livestock, fish or meals for each 50 silver (or fraction thereof) of maintenance owed. Food value for a fractional maintenance cost still consumes the entire unit of food.'

The data page does not. Every food item's entry at https://atlantis-pbem.com/data reads that it 'can be eaten to provide 30 silver towards a unit's maintenance cost'. The rules changelog offers a possible explanation - 'Meals are now 50 silver each (was 30 silver)' - which suggests the data page text is stale, but that changelog line is about a meal's market value, not its maintenance value, so it does not actually settle it.

The code is probably right. But nothing in the repository records that this was looked at, so the next person to read the data page will file it as a bug. Whichever number is correct, the reasoning should be written down where the constant is.
design:
## Context

The application charges maintenance and lets food pay it, at **50 silver a food item**:
`SILVER_PER_FOOD = 50` (`crates/core/src/orders/silver.rs:66`), with `own_food_pass:779` computing
`needed = ceil(owed / 50)` and `feed_from_faction_food:875` and `feed_after_silver` doing the same.

**The rules page and the data page disagree, and both are committed to this repository**
(`tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-rules.html`, `neworigins-data.html`) - so this is checkable,
not remembered.

The question was **settled with the navigator on 2026-08-23: the value is 50, and the data page is
stale.** This bead does not change any behaviour. It writes down the reasoning where the constant
is, so the next person to read the data page does not file it as a bug - which is the whole of why
the bead exists.

**The evidence, in full, because the point of the bead is that it be recorded:**

1. The rules page, in its own *Maintenance Costs* section - the section that describes the
   mechanic: *"Units may substitute one unit of grain, livestock, fish or meals for each **50**
   silver (or fraction thereof) of maintenance owed. Food value for a fractional maintenance cost
   still consumes the entire unit of food."*
2. The data page says **30**, in an identical generated sentence on **all four** food items:
   *"This item can be eaten to provide 30 silver towards a unit's maintenance cost."* It is
   reproduced verbatim into the scraped ruleset's `items.GRAI.description` and its three siblings.
3. The rules changelog: *"Changes from New Origins v7 - Meals are now 50 silver each (was 30
   silver)."*

The bead's own description set (3) aside as being about a meal's market value. **The fact that
changes the reading is (2)'s "all four".** A generated per-item string carrying exactly the old
number, on every food item at once, beside a changelog recording exactly a 30 → 50 move for a food
item and a rules section carrying exactly the new one, is a page that was not regenerated - not a
second opinion.

**The report corpus does not settle it, and that was checked rather than assumed.** The bead's
`design` field suggested a fixture might carry a unit whose food fell between turns. It does not.
All nine consecutive-turn pairs in `tests/fixtures/reports/` were walked, computing for every unit
present in both turns with an unchanged headcount what each hypothesis predicts it would eat
(`ceil(owed/50)` against `ceil(owed/30)`, capped by what it held):

| pair | unit | men | owes | food | ate | @50 | @30 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| g5 t23→t24 | 5026 | 1 leader | 50 | 160→147 | 13 | 1 | 2 |
| g5 t23→t24 | 8333 | 1 leader | 50 | 273→258 | 15 | 1 | 2 |
| g5 t23→t24 | 10835 | 1 leader | 50 | 177→52 | 125 | 1 | 2 |
| g5 t24→t25 | 5026 | 1 leader | 50 | 147→130 | 17 | 1 | 2 |
| g7 t71→t72 | 326 | 1 goblin | 10 | 1→0 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| g7 t71→t72 | 2120 | 1 leader | 50 | 1→0 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| g7 t71→t72 | 5049 | 30 gnolls | 300 | 2→0 | 2 | 2 | 2 |
| g7 t71→t72 | 7955 | 380 high elves | 3800 | 134→0 | 134 | 76 | 127 |

Every row is either a supply unit visibly trading food (13, 15, 17, 125 items eaten by a single
leader that owes 50) or a unit whose holding is too small to tell the two apart. **No row
discriminates.** Do not spend time re-deriving this; if you want the decisive evidence it is a
turn played on purpose - a `CONSUME` unit with one leader and several food items, which eats 1 at
50 and 2 at 30 - and that is the navigator's to produce, not this bead's.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### `crates/core/src/orders/silver.rs` - the comment

`SILVER_PER_FOOD` (line 66) today carries the rules quotation and nothing else. Replace its doc
comment with one that also records the disagreement and its settlement. Write it out; this text
**is** the deliverable:

```rust
/// "Units may substitute one unit of grain, livestock, fish or meals for each 50 silver (or
/// fraction thereof) of maintenance owed. Food value for a fractional maintenance cost still
/// consumes the entire unit of food."
///
/// **The data page says 30, and it is stale** (`ah-j00u`, settled with the navigator 2026-08-23).
/// Every food item's entry there reads "can be eaten to provide 30 silver towards a unit's
/// maintenance cost", and that sentence is scraped verbatim into
/// `config/public/ruleset.json`'s `items.GRAI.description` and its three siblings - so a reader
/// who checks the catalogue rather than the rules will find 30 and think this constant wrong.
///
/// It is not. The rules page carries 50 in the *Maintenance Costs* section, which is the section
/// that describes the mechanic; the changelog records "Meals are now 50 silver each (was 30
/// silver)"; and the data page's 30 appears identically on all four food items, which is what a
/// generated string that was never regenerated looks like rather than a second opinion.
///
/// The report corpus was searched for a unit whose food fell between two turns and cannot settle
/// it: every candidate is a supply unit visibly trading food, and the rest hold too little to tell
/// `ceil(owed/50)` from `ceil(owed/30)`. `ruleset.test.ts`'s
/// `still records the data page's stale food value` fails when upstream fixes the page, which is
/// the signal to delete this note.
const SILVER_PER_FOOD: i64 = 50;
```

Nothing else in the crate changes. **The constant keeps its value**, so no test of upkeep,
food coverage or the payment order moves.

### `packages/ruleset/src/committed.test.ts` - the self-retiring test

Add one `it` to the existing `describe("the committed ruleset", ...)` block (line 23), beside the
five already there and in their style - each of those asserts something about the committed
`config/public/ruleset.json` and names what regenerates it:

```ts
/**
 * The data page says a food item pays 30 silver of maintenance; the rules page says 50, and 50 is
 * what the core charges (`ah-j00u`). This holds the disagreement in place so it cannot be
 * forgotten: when upstream regenerates the data page, this test fails, and whoever sees it should
 * confirm the rules page still says 50, delete this test, and delete the note on
 * `SILVER_PER_FOOD` in `crates/core/src/orders/silver.rs`.
 *
 * A failure here is good news and is never fixed by changing the expectation.
 */
it("still records the data page's stale food value", () => {
  for (const tag of ["GRAI", "LIVE", "FISH", "MEAL"]) {
    expect(COMMITTED.items[tag]?.description, tag).toContain(
      "eaten to provide 30 silver towards a unit's maintenance cost"
    );
  }
});
```

`COMMITTED` is already in scope (line 11). The four tags are the same four as `FOOD_TAGS`
(`silver.rs:69`); a comment should say so, because the two lists must not drift.

**Nothing in `packages/ruleset/src/build.ts` changes.** Recording this as a structured `gaps` entry
was considered and rejected - see *User-facing decisions*.

## Increments

One, because the bead is one decision written down twice.

1. **The self-retiring test, then the comment.** Add the `it` above to `committed.test.ts` and watch
   it **pass** - it asserts the state of the committed ruleset today, so a red here means the tags,
   the field name or the sentence are not what this plan says, and that must be understood before
   the comment claiming them is written. Then replace `SILVER_PER_FOOD`'s doc comment.
   Run: `pnpm --filter @atlantis/ruleset test` and `cargo test -p atlantis-core`.

There is no red-to-green step here and inventing one would be dishonest: nothing changes
behaviour, and the TDD skill's loop applies to code that does. What the test pins is a *fact about
a committed fixture*, and its whole purpose is to fail later.

## The test plan

| Test | Pins |
|---|---|
| `the committed ruleset > still records the data page's stale food value` | that all four food items in `config/public/ruleset.json` still carry the data page's "30 silver" sentence. **Designed to fail one day**; that failure is the signal to retire this bead's note, not to update the expectation. |

Nothing else is added, and nothing existing should move. **If any test changes behaviourally, stop
and re-read the plan** - this bead changes a constant's comment and adds one assertion, and a
moving upkeep figure means something else was edited.

Suites: `pnpm --filter @atlantis/ruleset test`, `cargo test -p atlantis-core`, `pnpm run check:fast`.

## User-facing decisions

Settled with the navigator on 2026-08-23. No mockup: nothing here is a layout, a wording or a
control - the question is a matter of fact about the game, and what was put to the navigator was
the evidence above.

**Is a food item worth 50 silver of maintenance, or 30?**
Chosen: **50; the data page is stale.** `SILVER_PER_FOOD` keeps its value, the reasoning is
recorded where the constant is, and no behaviour changes.
Rejected: **30**, which would raise every Upkeep figure in the application by up to 40% and change
`ah-eacd`'s forced-feeding item counts with it - not supported by the *Maintenance Costs* section,
which is the one that describes the mechanic.
Also offered and declined: **parking the bead** while the navigator plays a turn with a `CONSUME`
unit holding food, which is the only authority that outranks both pages (a leader owing 50 eats 1
item at 50 and 2 at 30). The navigator chose to settle it on the documentary evidence rather than
hold the bead. **If a turn later contradicts this, the bead is reopened** - it is a settlement, not
a proof, and the comment says so by naming its evidence rather than asserting the answer.

**How should the record behave when the data page is corrected upstream?**
Chosen: **a self-retiring test** - one assertion that the four food descriptions still say 30, so
the note cannot quietly outlive its reason.
Rejected: a comment on the constant alone, which is what the bead's acceptance criteria literally
ask for and which would still be there, unread, long after the disagreement is gone.
Also rejected: a structured entry beside `gaps.weather` in the scraped ruleset. It costs a type
change for no gain - `Gap` is declared `modelled: false` (`packages/ruleset/src/build.ts:38-46`)
and this rule *is* modelled, so it would need a sibling `conflicts` block, and `gaps` is written by
the scraper (`build.ts:153`) whose own note says to re-run rather than hand-edit.

## Out of scope

- **Changing `SILVER_PER_FOOD`, or anything that reads it.** The value is confirmed, not revised.
- **Correcting the data page**, or teaching the scraper to override the description text. The
  description is what the page says; the application does not read it for arithmetic, only for the
  catalogue a player sees, and rewriting a scraped string to say something the source does not is
  worse than the disagreement.
- **Committing the corpus probe** that produced the table in *Context*. It found nothing, so as a
  test it would assert a negative that a future fixture could helpfully falsify - and a P3 bead is
  not the place to build that. The method and its result are recorded above; that is enough for the
  next person to decide whether to redo it.
- **`withdrawCost: 37` on grain**, noticed while reading the ruleset and unrelated to maintenance.
  If it looks wrong, it is its own bead.
- **The other three food tags' market values.** This bead is about the maintenance value only.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm --filter @atlantis/ruleset test
cargo test -p atlantis-core
pnpm run check:fast
```

All green. Then, by eye:

- `SILVER_PER_FOOD`'s comment names all three pieces of evidence, names the test that retires it,
  and does not assert 50 without saying why.
- `git diff` touches **exactly two files** - `crates/core/src/orders/silver.rs` and
  `packages/ruleset/src/committed.test.ts` - and changes no constant, no signature and no
  assertion's expected value.

**A human need confirm nothing here**, and that is worth saying: the bead's one judgement was made
by the navigator before the work started, and everything left is checkable by reading the diff.

## Known traps

- **A failure of the new test is good news and is never fixed by changing the expectation.** It
  means upstream regenerated the data page. The response is to check the rules page still says 50,
  then delete the test and the note it names. Say this in the test's own comment, because whoever
  meets it will meet it years from now and out of context.
- **The four food tags are duplicated** - `FOOD_TAGS` (`silver.rs:69`) and the new test's list.
  There is no way to share them across the Rust/TypeScript boundary that is cheaper than the
  duplication, so name the other list in both comments.
- **`.claude/cerebro-traps.md`'s `packages/shared` jsdom rule does not apply**: the new test is in
  `packages/ruleset`, which reads files and asserts on JSON, with no rendering at all.
- **Do not "fix" the scraped description** to say 50. `committed.test.ts`'s first assertion
  (line 24) holds `config/public/ruleset.json` exactly equal to what the scraper produces from the
  committed pages, so any hand edit to that file fails there - which is the guard working, not an
  obstacle to route around.
- **The bead's own description argues the changelog line "does not actually settle it".** That was
  written before anyone noticed the 30 appears on *all four* items. The plan's reading supersedes
  the bead's; do not restore the bead's conclusion from its description.
acceptance_criteria: The question is settled - ideally against a real turn report where a unit's food was eaten for upkeep, which is the only authority that outranks both pages. SILVER_PER_FOOD carries a comment naming the source that settles it and noting the data page's disagreement. If 30 turns out to be right, the constant and its tests change with it.

title: Cost a PRODUCE order that spends silver
description:
PRODUCE never becomes a first-class intent - intents.rs:384 maps it to Intent::MonthLong("PRODUCE"), and both forecast_unit and the ledger drop MonthLong and Build on the floor (semantics.rs ~1071-1078).

For most items that is harmless, because the rules pay for production in materials and man-months rather than silver. But not all: the data page prices a catapult at 250 wood + 30 ironwood + 80 fur + 3000 silver, and a steel defender at 30 rootstone + 250 iron + 50 fur + 3000 silver. Those are silver expenditures the client cannot see.

The deeper problem is that the data to see them does not exist. ItemEntry (movement/rules.rs:178-203) has no production field, and across all 171 items in config/public/ruleset.json the only keys are tag, name, kind, weight, capacity, selfMobile, moves, description, combat, withdrawCost, cargoCapacity, sailingSkill, capacityCondition. There is no CATA or MSTD entry at all. The scraper in packages/ruleset picks up study costs, withdraw costs and cast costs, and nothing about what an item is made from.

Note that ruleset.json's own 'gaps' map declares only 'weather'. This gap is undeclared, which is the part worth fixing first: a missing capability that nothing records is one somebody re-discovers.
design: The scraper work and the forecast work are separable and probably want to be separate beads - this one should be planned as the data question first, since without inputs in the ruleset there is nothing to forecast from. Worth asking the navigator whether silver-costing production is common enough in real play to be worth the scraping; catapults and steel defenders are late-game and rare, and the honest answer may be to declare the gap and stop.
acceptance_criteria: Either the ruleset scraper captures production inputs (skill, level, material inputs and quantities, man-months, output count) and ItemEntry carries them, so a silver-costing PRODUCE can be forecast; or the gap is recorded in ruleset.json's gaps map with a note on what it prevents. If the data is captured, a test pins the catapult and steel defender silver costs from the committed ruleset.
close_reason: All children closed; last was ah-19l2.2, delivered in PR #615

title: Taxing a hex your own unit is pillaging is forecast as if the money were still there
description:
The rules are unusually blunt about this: 'Note that PILLAGE comes before TAX, so a unit performing TAX will collect no money in that region that month.' Pillaging empties the region for every taxer in it, your own included.

Nothing checks. The forecast credits TAX from the region alone (silver.rs ~460, 'income.saturating_add(men.saturating_mul(TAX_PER_MAN).min(base))'), and the ledger's apply (semantics.rs:1040-1045) receives one intent at a time and reads only hex.region.tax_base - it never scans hex.units for a Pillage. Its comment frames the optimism as being about foreign units, but the same code makes it optimistic about the player's own orders sitting in the same document.

So a player who orders one unit to PILLAGE and three others to TAX in the same hex is shown four sources of income where the game will pay one. This is a mistake the client is well placed to catch, because both orders are in the file being edited.
design:
## Context

The rules are unusually blunt: *"Note that PILLAGE comes before TAX, so a unit performing TAX will
collect no money in that region that month."* Pillaging empties the region for every taxer in it,
your own included.

Nothing checks. Both surfaces credit `TAX` from the region alone and neither scans the hex for a
`PILLAGE`:

- `forecast_unit` (`crates/core/src/orders/silver.rs:504-509`) reads `region.tax_base` and the unit's
  own men.
- `apply` (`crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs:1157-1166`) reads `hex.region.tax_base` and
  `actor.unit.men`. Its comment frames the optimism as being about *foreign* units — *"and
  optimistically, none of it goes to anybody else"* — but the same code is optimistic about the
  player's own orders sitting in the same document.

So a player who orders one unit to pillage and three others to tax the same hex is shown four
sources of income where the game will pay one. **This is a mistake the client is unusually well
placed to catch, because both orders are in the file being edited.**

When this lands, a taxing unit in a hex any own unit is pillaging forecasts **zero** tax income on
both surfaces, and a new `taxed-a-pillaged-hex` finding on its `TAX` line says why.

**Not blocked, and not part of `ah-t2pn`.** `ah-t2pn`'s family models own units *contending* for a
pool; this is the pool being *emptied* before any of them reaches it, which is a different fact and
a different rule. No dependency edge is wired, and none is wanted: this bead zeroes the tax term, and
`ah-t2pn.1` splits whatever the tax term turns out to be. **If `ah-t2pn.1` has landed when you pick
this up**, the two compose without either changing: a pool of zero splits to zero for everybody. See
*Known traps* for the one line where that matters.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

`ah-abwx` is the worked precedent for this exact shape of change — one arm mirrored across the two
surfaces so they cannot disagree — and `ah-ycuj`'s corpus test is the net under it.

### Both surfaces need the same new fact: "is this hex being pillaged by an own unit?"

It is one predicate, and it must be computed **once** and read by both, or the two surfaces will
drift again — which is the whole reason `ah-abwx` and `ah-ycuj` exist.

`semantics.rs` already holds the hex, so the predicate lives there:

```rust
/// Whether any own unit in this hex is ordered to pillage it.
///
/// "PILLAGE comes before TAX, so a unit performing TAX will collect no money in that region that
/// month" - so this empties the region's tax base for every *other* own unit taxing it. Foreign
/// units are not here to begin with (`Hex::read` filters them out) and their orders are unknowable,
/// so this is only ever about the orders in the document being edited.
fn own_unit_pillages(hex: &Hex<'_>) -> bool {
    hex.units
        .iter()
        .any(|ordered| ordered.intents.iter().any(|p| matches!(p.intent, Intent::Pillage)))
}
```

### `crates/core/src/orders/silver.rs` — the column

`forecast_unit` cannot see the hex, so it is handed the fact. Add one field to `RegionWages`
(`silver.rs:312`), which is exactly what that struct is for — *"everything about the region that the
arithmetic needs, lifted out so the function takes values"*:

```rust
/// Whether an own unit in this hex is ordered to pillage it, which empties the tax base before any
/// `TAX` order reaches it (`ah-cxxa`). Not a property of the region as the report prints it - it is
/// a property of the orders being written against it - but it belongs here because it is exactly
/// what the `TAX` arm needs and nothing else in this module has a view of the hex.
pub pillaged: bool,
```

`RegionWages` derives `Default`, so every existing test construction keeps compiling with
`pillaged: false`, which is today's behaviour.

The `TAX` arm becomes:

```rust
Intent::Tax => {
    if region.pillaged {
        // Zero, and never a doubt: a pillage empties the hex whatever the base was, so this
        // collects nothing even where the base itself is unknown (`ah-cxxa`).
    } else {
        match region.tax_base {
            Some(base) => {
                income = income.saturating_add(men.saturating_mul(TAX_PER_MAN).min(base))
            }
            None => income_doubt = income_doubt.or(Some(SilverDoubt::UnknownTaxBase)),
        }
    }
}
```

**The `pillaged` branch comes first and short-circuits the `UnknownTaxBase` doubt.** That is the
navigator's decision, and it is not an oversight: the zero is certain even when the pillager's own
takings are not, and doubting it would hide a fact we actually know.

**`Intent::Pillage`'s own arm is untouched** (`silver.rs:510`, shipped by `ah-abwx`). A pillaging
unit still earns twice the base and is still doubted where the base is unknown. A unit that both
pillages and could tax is unaffected — it is not taxing.

Both `RegionWages` construction sites in `semantics.rs` set the new field:

- `forecast_hex` (`semantics.rs:354`) — `pillaged: own_unit_pillages(hex)`.
- `charge_upkeep` (`semantics.rs:982`) — the same. It reads `RegionWages` only through
  `late_income`, which prices `Work` and `Entertain` and never `Tax`, so the value changes nothing
  there today. **Set it anyway**: two literals that differ by a field are two things to keep in step,
  and this one is one edit away from mattering.

### `crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs` — the ledger

The `Tax` arm at `semantics.rs:1157-1166`:

```rust
Intent::Tax => {
    // "PILLAGE comes before TAX", so a pillage in this hex leaves every other own taxer with
    // nothing (`ah-cxxa`). Mirrors `forecast_unit`'s arm exactly - two surfaces reading one order
    // must not price it two ways.
    if !own_unit_pillages(hex) {
        let ceiling = hex.region.tax_base.unwrap_or(i64::MAX);
        credit(ledger, who, SILVER, actor.unit.men.saturating_mul(TAX_PER_MAN).min(ceiling));
    }
}
```

`apply` runs per intent and already takes `hex`, so no plumbing. Correct the arm's existing comment
about optimism, which now describes foreign units only.

**Compute it once per hex, not once per intent.** `apply` is called for every placed intent of every
unit, so calling `own_unit_pillages` inside it walks the hex quadratically on a path that runs on
every keystroke. Compute it in `ledger_for` (`semantics.rs:~800`, the function that builds the ledger
and calls `apply` in a loop) and pass it into `apply` as a `bool` parameter.

### The new check — `semantics.rs`

```rust
pub const TAXED_A_PILLAGED_HEX: Code = Code("taxed-a-pillaged-hex");
```

Appended **last** to `codes::ALL` and its length literal bumped — the array's own doc comment states
that rule and why (the generated TypeScript copies the order).

A new per-hex check, called from `review_turn`'s per-hex block beside `check_markets`:

```rust
/// Own units ordered to tax a hex one of their faction-mates is pillaging.
///
/// One finding per taxing unit, on its own `TAX` line: each is separately editable and each is
/// equally affected. The pillager itself is never named - its orders are fine, and it is the only
/// unit here that will collect anything.
fn check_pillaged_tax(hex: &Hex<'_>, pillaged: bool, options: &CheckOptions, findings: &mut Vec<Finding>);
```

It emits nothing unless `pillaged`. For each own unit with a `Tax` placement it pushes a finding
anchored on that placement's line, built with `Ordered::finding` (`semantics.rs:749`), which is the
per-hex helper the other per-unit checks use.

Message, verbatim:

```
a unit is pillaging this hex, so this TAX will collect nothing
```

### `packages/shared/src/workspace/SettingsDialog.tsx`

A new entry in the **Orders** group — not Resources. This is not about running out of money; it is an
order that will do nothing, which is what `not-traded-here` and `give-target-not-here` are about, and
they live there.

- title: `Taxing a hex you are pillaging`
- description: `TAX orders in a hex where one of your own units is ordered to PILLAGE, which collects the region's money first.`

On by default through `DEFAULT_ADVISORY_CHECKS`' existing "everything except `hex-unguarded`" rule
(`packages/shared/src/settingsStore.ts:43`), and `reconcileAdvisoryChecks` (`:51`) gives an existing
user's saved settings the new code at its default. **No migration is needed and none must be
written.**

### Generated TypeScript

`packages/core-client/src/coreVocabulary.generated.ts` moves. Regenerate, never hand-edit:

```
ATLANTIS_UPDATE_GENERATED=1 cargo test -p atlantis-hud-core --test generated_ts
```

`UnitSilver` gains no field, so `generated/UnitSilver.ts` does not move.

## Increments

1. **The column collects nothing.**
   RED: `crates/core/src/orders/silver.rs`, `fn a_taxer_in_a_pillaged_hex_collects_nothing` — a
   30-man unit ordered `TAX` with `RegionWages { tax_base: Some(2500), pillaged: true, .. }` asserts
   `income == Some(0)` and `doubt == None`. Use the module's `forecast_holding` helper
   (`silver.rs:1017`).
   Then `fn a_taxer_in_a_pillaged_hex_with_no_stated_base_still_collects_nothing` — the same with
   `tax_base: None`, asserting `income == Some(0)` and **`doubt == None`**, not `UnknownTaxBase`.
   That second test is the navigator's decision and the one an implementer is most likely to get
   backwards.
   GREEN: the `pillaged` field and the reordered `TAX` arm.

2. **The ledger agrees.**
   RED: `semantics.rs`, `fn the_ledger_credits_a_taxer_nothing_in_a_pillaged_hex` — a hex with one
   `PILLAGE` and one `TAX` asserts the taxer's silver balance is unchanged by its `TAX`.
   GREEN: `own_unit_pillages`, computed in `ledger_for` and passed into `apply`.

3. **The two surfaces agree.**
   RED: `semantics.rs`, `fn the_column_and_the_warning_agree_about_a_taxer_in_a_pillaged_hex` — the
   same hex where the taxer also spends more than it holds; asserts the column is negative **and**
   `not-enough-silver` fires. Before this bead the taxer looked solvent on both.
   GREEN: nothing further — increments 1 and 2 make it pass. If it does not, stop: a divergence here
   is the finding, not a thing to patch.

4. **The pillager keeps its own income.**
   RED: `semantics.rs`, `fn the_pillager_itself_still_earns_twice_the_base` — asserts the pillaging
   unit's forecast is `Some(5000)` against a $2,500 base, unchanged from `ah-abwx`.
   Then `fn a_unit_that_pillages_is_not_warned_about_its_own_pillage`.
   GREEN: nothing — this is the regression net under increments 1–2, and it fails loudly if the
   predicate is applied to the pillager's own arm.

5. **The finding.**
   RED: `semantics.rs`, `fn every_taxer_in_a_pillaged_hex_is_told_why` — one `PILLAGE` and two `TAX`
   units assert exactly two `taxed-a-pillaged-hex` findings, one on each `TAX` line, each reading
   `a unit is pillaging this hex, so this TAX will collect nothing`, and **none** on the pillager.
   Then `fn a_hex_nobody_pillages_says_nothing`.
   Then a case in the shipped `every_advisory_code_can_be_silenced` fixture test, which every new
   code must join.
   GREEN: `codes::TAXED_A_PILLAGED_HEX`, `codes::ALL` bumped, `check_pillaged_tax`.

6. **Regenerate the TypeScript.** `ATLANTIS_UPDATE_GENERATED=1 cargo test -p atlantis-hud-core
   --test generated_ts`, then `pnpm run check:generated`.

7. **The settings row.**
   RED: `packages/shared/src/workspace/SettingsDialog.test.tsx`, asserting the new title and
   description in the **Orders** group.
   GREEN: the entry in `SettingsDialog.tsx`.

## The test plan

**Rust, `crates/core`** — every test named in *Increments*, plus:

- `fn a_pillage_in_one_hex_does_not_empty_another` — two regions, a pillage in the first and a taxer
  in the second; asserts the second collects in full. `own_unit_pillages` takes a hex and this is
  what proves it was not hoisted to the report.
- `fn a_unit_that_pillages_and_is_also_ordered_to_tax_is_still_told` — the predicate is about the
  hex, not about other units, so a unit doing both is warned about its own `TAX` line. Stated here
  because the bead's own text says *"a unit that both could tax and does pillage is unaffected"*,
  which is true of its **pillage** and false of its **tax**; without this test the two readings are
  a coin toss.

**`crates/core/tests/validate_real_orders.rs`** audits the committed corpus and will move if any
fixture pillages a hex it also taxes. Read the diff; do not loosen the assertion.

**`ah-ycuj`'s corpus agreement test** must stay green **untouched**. It is the net under this bead:
both surfaces must move in the same PR, and changing one alone passes its own tests and fails that.

**TypeScript** — `SettingsDialog.test.tsx` only. The traps file's no-jsdom rule is respected: that is
a static render, and no effect-level test is asked for.

**Suites that must run:** `pnpm run check:fast` and `pnpm run check:generated`.

## User-facing decisions

Interviewed with the navigator on 2026-08-23 against `docs/ui/ah-cxxa-pillage.html`.

**What tells the player.** Nobody here is short of money — this is income that will not arrive — so
`not-enough-silver` is the wrong check.
**Chosen: a new finding**, `taxed-a-pillaged-hex`, on each taxing unit's own `TAX` line, shipping
verbatim:

> `a unit is pillaging this hex, so this TAX will collect nothing`

The precedent is `ah-1wcw.2`: an unsellable `SELL` earns 0 in the column and the shipped
`not-traded-here` *check* is what tells the player why. This is the same shape.
*Rejected — a hover note only*: explains the zero where it appears and costs no code or Settings
row, but nothing marks the order line in the Problems panel, which is where a player goes to fix
orders.
*Rejected — both*: two strings for one fact, and the note is redundant once the finding is on the
line.

**A region that states no tax base.**
**Chosen: the taxers show a certain `0`, not `?`.** A pillage empties the hex whatever the base was,
so they collect nothing either way; the zero is certain even when the pillager's own takings are not.
*Rejected — doubt them like the pillager*: consistent with the pillager's row and with *never a
number that might be wrong*, but the taxers' number is not in doubt at all, and doubting it would
hide a fact we know.

**The Settings row**, verbatim, in the **Orders** group:

- title: `Taxing a hex you are pillaging`
- description: `TAX orders in a hex where one of your own units is ordered to PILLAGE, which collects the region's money first.`

**Decided by the planner, and stated so the implementer does not re-open them:** the pillager itself
is never named by the finding — its orders are fine and it is the only unit here that will collect
anything; a unit ordered to both pillage and tax **is** warned about its `TAX` line; the check is on
by default through the existing rule, with no migration; and the finding is per taxing unit rather
than per hex, because each `TAX` line is separately editable and each is equally affected.

## Out of scope

- **A foreign unit pillaging the hex.** Permanently out: foreign orders are unknowable, and a report
  shows only what happened last turn.
- **The threshold on pillaging** — whether the faction has enough combat-ready men for the pillage to
  succeed at all. `ah-abwx` scoped it out and so does this; if the pillage fails, the taxers would
  have collected after all, and the client cannot tell.
- **What a pillage does to the region next turn** (ruin, population loss). Not economy, not this.
- **`ah-t2pn`'s contention.** A different rule about the same pool; see *Known traps*.
- **`WORK`, `ENTERTAIN` and the markets.** A pillage empties the *tax base*, and the rules say
  nothing about it touching the others. Do not extend the predicate to them on a guess.

## Validation

```
cargo test -p atlantis-hud-core
pnpm run check:fast
pnpm run check:generated
pnpm --filter @atlantis/shared test
```

All green, and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean.

Checkable by looking, once, before opening the PR: load a fixture, order one unit to `PILLAGE` and
another in the same hex to `TAX`, and confirm the taxer's **In** row falls to 0 and its `TAX` line
is marked — then move the pillager to another hex and confirm both come back.

## Known traps

- **Both surfaces in one PR.** `ah-ycuj`'s corpus test compares the column against the ledger over 26
  real turns; changing one arm and not the other passes that arm's own tests and fails `ah-ycuj`.
  This is exactly the divergence `ah-abwx` was filed to fix.
- **`own_unit_pillages` is per hex, computed once.** `apply` runs per placed intent, so calling it
  there walks the hex once per order — quadratic in the size of a city, on a path that runs on every
  keystroke. Compute it in `ledger_for` and pass it down.
- **The `pillaged` branch must come *before* the `tax_base` match**, or a hex with no stated base
  raises `UnknownTaxBase` and the navigator's chosen certain-zero is lost. Increment 1's second test
  is what holds that.
- **Do not apply the predicate to `Intent::Pillage`'s own arm.** The pillager collects; only taxers
  are emptied. Increment 4 is the net.
- **If `ah-t2pn.1` has already landed**, its `tax_shares_for` splits the base between taxers. The two
  compose without either changing — a hex that is pillaged yields zero to every taxer, and a split
  of zero is zero for each — but put the `pillaged` check **before** the split rather than trying to
  express it as a pool of zero, so the certain-zero is not routed through machinery that can produce
  a doubt.
- **`codes::ALL` carries its own length**, and a new code must also join the shipped
  `every_advisory_code_can_be_silenced` fixture test; the compiler catches the first, nothing catches
  the second but that test itself.
- **`packages/shared` has no jsdom** (`ah-nass`, and the traps file). `SettingsDialog.test.tsx` is a
  static render; do not add an effect-level test.
acceptance_criteria: When any own unit in a hex issues PILLAGE, other own units in that hex taxing there are forecast at zero tax income, and a finding tells the player that the pillage will leave their taxers with nothing. A unit that both could tax and does pillage is unaffected. A test covers a hex with one PILLAGE and one TAX.

title: Refactoring: plan-bead's rules are repeated, and 86 lines have no heading
description:
An adversarial read-through of the six cerebro documents during ah-ywj7 found that skills/plan-bead/SKILL.md no longer reads as one argument. The cost is being paid now, by every planner session that reads it.

Concretely, all in skills/plan-bead/SKILL.md:

- The planning/planner label distinction is explained FIVE separate times, each slightly differently, and four of those also re-explain why the matching rule is what it is. A reader who hits the fourth restatement stops believing there is one rule.
- 'Choosing what to plan' opens with the candidate query and then spends ~120 lines on family ownership, the pre-write re-check and reclaiming before returning to candidate selection.
- When it returns, it returns UNDER THE WRONG HEADING: roughly 85 lines of core candidate-selection doctrine (never claim a bead, highest priority first, a P4 is not a candidate, and the whole blocker rule) sit underneath '### A bead from an issue: go and read the issue', which ended long before. This one PREDATES ah-ywj7 and is the worst structural problem in the file; ah-ywj7 made it worse only by pushing those paragraphs further from their heading.
- The opening 'Five rules keep that honest' paragraph is a table of contents pretending to be an argument: five forward references and a warning that none of them closes the hole. A reader gets no rule from it.
- The P0 section now argues against three different things at once, including a bd tooling erratum that is stated again where it actually belongs.
- agents/planner.md restates the whole collision model twice despite promising that plan-bead has it 'at the point each applies'.

Suggested shape, not decided: give the collision machinery its own top-level section stating the two labels, the reader rule, the write order, the re-check and the reclaim ONCE; reduce 'Choosing what to plan' to a pointer plus the business of choosing; and give the orphaned block its own heading regardless of anything else.

Not done in ah-ywj7 because restructuring the most-read part of the skill is approach-level, outside a planned bead, and the plan for ah-ywj7 explicitly left the readability judgement to the navigator.

Scope note: cerebro submodule, not this application.
design:
## Context

`skills/plan-bead/SKILL.md` is 1,132 lines and is read in full by every planning session. An
adversarial read-through during `ah-ywj7` found it no longer reads as one argument, and the cost is
being paid now rather than predicted.

Every claim below was verified against the file before planning:

- **86 lines sit under the wrong heading.** `### A bead from an issue: go and read the issue` ends
  at line **672**. Lines **673-758** - *You never claim a bead*, *Highest priority first*, *A P4 is
  not a candidate at all*, *Plan beads whose blockers are unbuilt* and *never plan a bead whose
  blocker is unplanned* - sit beneath it, and none of them is about a GitHub issue. **This predates
  the collision work**; that work only pushed them further from a heading they never had.
- **The hold is explained five times**, at lines 229, 416-428, 484-525, 588 and 918-932, four of
  which also re-argue why the matching rule is what it is.
- **`## Choosing what to plan` opens at 404 with the candidate query**, then spends about 170 lines
  on family ownership, the pre-write re-check and reclaiming before returning to the business of
  choosing.
- **The opening paragraph of `## You are one of the planners` is five forward references** followed
  by a warning that none of them closes the hole. A reader gets no rule from it.
- **`agents/planner.md` restates the collision model twice**, despite promising that `plan-bead` has
  it "at the point each applies".

**Nothing about how the fleet behaves changes.** No rule is added, removed or altered. This is the
structure of a document, and the whole risk of the bead is losing a rule while moving it - which is
what *Validation* is built around.

This is a change to the **cerebro submodule**. It follows the two-repository shape: a pull request in
`rmstdope/cerebro`, then a `chore(<bead>): bump cerebro …` pull request here moving the pointer, as
`044011e4` and `7983d8f` did.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### `skills/plan-bead/SKILL.md`

**A new top-level section, `## How two planners stay off each other's work`, placed immediately
after `## You are one of the planners`** and before `## Telling the fleet view what you are doing`.
It states the coordination story **once**, in four subsections:

- `## How two planners stay off each other's work` (new, top level), containing
  - `### The two labels, and who may remove them`
  - `### One planner owns a whole family`
  - `### Check you still hold it before you write`
  - `### Reclaiming a hold nobody is holding`

Its content is moved, not rewritten: `### One planner owns a whole family` (currently 430-577),
`### Reclaiming a label nobody is holding` (578-638), the pre-write re-check, and **one** telling of
the label rule assembled from the five scattered explanations. The four surviving restatements at
229, 588, 918-932 and 1110 become pointers to it - or, where they are a single clause inside a
larger instruction (918-932 and 1110 are both mid-procedure), they keep the command and drop the
justification.

**`## Choosing what to plan` is reduced to choosing.** After the move it holds the candidate query,
one pointer to the new section for the coordination it must obey, and then:

**A new subsection `### Which bead, and in what order`**, taking lines **673-758** - the block that
has no heading today. This is the fix the bead calls the worst, and it is worth landing on its own
before anything else moves (see *Increments*).

`### A bead from an issue: go and read the issue` keeps lines 639-672 and nothing else.

**The opening paragraph of `## You are one of the planners` becomes one claim**, with the detail
left to the section that owns it. The shape agreed with the navigator:

> A planner takes a bead by naming itself on it, and never touches a bead named for anyone else.

The five forward references go. The paragraph that follows - the incident that produced the rules -
is **not** kept here; if it is worth keeping it belongs in the new section, beside the rules it
explains, and `docs/` is where the fleet records history that is not itself a rule.

### `agents/planner.md`

Remove the two restatements of the collision model the bead names, at `:16` and in the
*What you never do* list. That file already promises `plan-bead` carries this "at the point each
applies"; the change makes the promise true. **Keep every rule that is only stated there** - the role
file is read at session start and the skill is loaded after it, so a rule that exists nowhere else
must not be deleted on the assumption the skill has it. Check each against the skill before removing
it.

### What must not change

- `emacs/cerebro.el` and its ert tests. They read labels, not prose.
- `scripts/`. Nothing here is executable.
- `skills/beads-workflow/SKILL.md`, `docs/agent-workflow.md`, the submodule `CLAUDE.md`. They
  describe the same machinery correctly and at their own altitude; this bead is about one file's
  internal shape, not about re-cutting the boundaries between documents.

## Increments

Each is a commit that leaves the file coherent. `bash tests/prose-decoupling.sh` after every one.

**1. The orphaned block gets a heading.**
Insert `### Which bead, and in what order` before line 673. Nothing moves; one line is added. This
is the whole of the pre-existing defect, it is independently valuable, and it is the increment to
land first so the rest can be abandoned without losing it.

**2. The new section exists, holding the label rule once.**
Create `## How two planners stay off each other's work` with `### The two labels, and who may
remove them`, assembled from the five existing explanations. Replace those five with pointers or
bare commands.

**3. Ownership, the re-check and reclaiming move under it.**
Move `### One planner owns a whole family` and `### Reclaiming a label nobody is holding` bodily,
renaming the second to `### Reclaiming a hold nobody is holding`. Add `### Check you still hold it
before you write` from the text currently inside `## Choosing what to plan`.

**4. `## Choosing what to plan` is reduced.**
What is left is the query, the pointer, `### Which bead, and in what order`, and
`### A bead from an issue: go and read the issue`.

**5. The opening paragraph becomes a claim.**

**6. `agents/planner.md` loses its two restatements.**

**7. Read it through in one sitting**, start to finish, and fix what reads as a seam. A structural
move always leaves a sentence that referred to something now above rather than below it: search for
`below`, `above`, `earlier` and `later` and check each one still points the right way.

## The test plan

There is no test for prose, and pretending otherwise would be worse than saying so. What there is:

| Check | What it pins |
|---|---|
| `bash tests/prose-decoupling.sh` | no unresolvable bead citation was introduced while moving text |
| `for t in tests/*.sh; do bash "$t"; done` | nothing executable was disturbed |
| ERT suite | the fleet view is untouched |
| **The rule inventory below** | no rule was lost in the move |

**The rule inventory is the real test.** `plan-bead` carries **58** bolded normative openers today
and `agents/planner.md` **22**. Before starting:

```bash
cd .claude/cerebro
grep -o '^\*\*[^*]*\*\*' skills/plan-bead/SKILL.md | sort > /tmp/rules-before
grep -o '\*\*[^*]*\*\*' agents/planner.md | sort > /tmp/planner-before
```

and at the end, `comm -23` the before against the after. **Every line that disappears must be
accounted for out loud in the PR body** - moved into the new section, merged with a duplicate, or
deliberately dropped as a restatement. A rule that vanishes silently is the one failure this bead
can actually cause. The counts will not match exactly and are not meant to: consolidating five
tellings into one removes four.

## User-facing decisions

The audience is planner sessions and the navigator, who reads this file too. Taken 2026-08-23;
outlines at `.cerebro/scratchpad/beast/ah-wltt-shape.html`.

**The collision machinery gets its own top-level section, early, and `agents/planner.md` is tidied
too.** Chosen over restructuring the skill alone (the role file would keep telling the story a third
time), over fixing only the orphaned heading (leaves five explanations of one rule), and over placing
the new section later, after `## You keep a buffer sized to the fleet`.

**The opening paragraph becomes one claim**, with the detail left to the section that owns it -
*"A planner takes a bead by naming itself on it, and never touches a bead named for anyone else."*
Chosen over keeping the incident alongside it, and over leaving the paragraph alone.

**Nothing else about the skill's content is the navigator's to re-decide here**, and this bead must
not become the occasion to revisit a rule. If the restructure makes a rule look wrong, say so and
file it; do not fix it in this diff.

## Out of scope

- **Any change to what the rules say.** Moving and merging tellings only.
- **The other four cerebro documents.** They are correct at their own altitude.
- **`emacs/`, `scripts/`, and every test suite** except keeping them green.
- **Splitting `plan-bead` into several files.** Considered and not proposed: the skill is loaded as
  one unit, and a reader who has to follow a link mid-procedure is worse off than one reading a long
  section.
- **The length of the file.** This bead makes it shorter by removing duplication, but shortening is
  not the goal and no target is set.
- **Revisiting the collision rules themselves**, which shipped in `ah-ywj7` and have not yet been
  run against for long enough to judge.

## Validation

```
cd .claude/cerebro
bash tests/prose-decoupling.sh
for t in tests/*.sh; do bash "$t"; done
emacs -Q --batch -l ert -l emacs/cerebro.el -l emacs/cerebro-test.el -f ert-run-tests-batch-and-exit
```

Acceptance, each checkable by running or looking:

1. `grep -n '^#\{2,3\} ' skills/plan-bead/SKILL.md` shows `## How two planners stay off each other's
   work` with its four subsections, and `### Which bead, and in what order` inside
   `## Choosing what to plan`.
2. No line between `### A bead from an issue: go and read the issue` and the next heading mentions
   claiming, priority order or blockers.
3. The rule inventory diff is accounted for line by line in the PR body.
4. `grep -c '^\*\*' skills/plan-bead/SKILL.md` is **lower** than 58 and no rule is missing from the
   accounted diff.
5. Every `above`, `below`, `earlier` and `later` in the file points somewhere that is still in that
   direction.
6. `agents/planner.md` no longer explains the label matching rule, and still states every rule that
   exists nowhere else.

**Only a human can judge whether it now reads as one argument.** That is the entire point of the
bead, no command can answer it, and it is the navigator's call - read it start to finish before
merging.

## Known traps

- **`tests/prose-decoupling.sh` forbids bead citations a consumer cannot resolve** in skills and
  agent prompts. Moving text cannot introduce one, but *writing* the new section's opening can - the
  temptation is to explain the rules by naming the incident that produced them. Do not.
- **A rule that exists only in `agents/planner.md`** must survive. The role file is read at session
  start, before the skill is loaded; deleting a rule there because the skill "probably" has it is how
  a rule is lost for good. Check each one.
- **The skill is symlinked into consumers** by `scripts/sync-symlinks.sh`, so a consumer sees the
  change the moment the submodule pointer moves. There is no staging.
- **Land increment 1 first and separately.** It is the whole of the pre-existing defect and one line
  of diff; if the rest of the restructure stalls or is abandoned, that fix should still be in.
- **Directional words break silently.** `above`, `below`, `earlier`, `later` and "see the section
  after this" are correct today and a move makes some of them lies that no test will catch.
- **Do not fix a rule you disagree with while moving it.** A refactor whose diff also changes
  behaviour cannot be reviewed as either one.
- **`bd show <id> --json` returns an array**, so the design field is `.[0].design`.
acceptance_criteria:
- The two labels and the rule for reading them are stated in exactly one place, and everywhere else points at it.
- No block of the skill sits under a heading that does not describe it.
