title: The map's view controls are split between two corners
description:
Move the badges selector dropdown next to the map zoom buttons.

Raised by the navigator 2026-08-21.

CONTEXT. ah-l9mp (v0.10.0) moved the staleness and movement toggles into
Settings > Global and lifted the level selector into the top bar, but its
acceptance explicitly kept badges where it was: "The Badges chip stays on the
map with its popover and its lit-when-something-is-hidden behaviour unchanged,
and the strip keeps its layer-chips testid."

So this is not a reversal of that decision. Badges stayed on the map on purpose
because it is a thing the player changes while looking at the map; this bead is
about where on the map it sits. Grouping it with the zoom buttons puts every
control that acts on the map view in one place.

The popover and the lit-when-something-is-hidden behaviour are not in question
here -- only the position.
design:
## Context

Move the badges selector next to the map zoom buttons, so every control that acts on the map view is
in one place. The navigator's request, 2026-08-21.

**This is not a reversal of ah-l9mp.** That bead moved staleness and movement into Settings > Global
and lifted the level selector into the top bar, but deliberately kept Badges on the map — *"it is ten
marks flicked while reading a crowded hex, and its chip lights when any of them is off"*
(`LayerChips.tsx:9-13`). Badges stays on the map; this bead is about **where on the map**.

**The popover and the lit-when-something-is-hidden behaviour are not in question. Position only.**

Today the two live in different files and different positions:

| | Where | Which file |
|---|---|---|
| Badges chip | top-**centre** | `AppShell.tsx:3103-3107` renders `LayerChips` |
| Zoom cluster | top-**right** | `MapCanvas.tsx:1531-1541` |

**It looks like a CSS move and it is not**, which is the whole reason this plan is long for a P3.
Three things protect the current arrangement, all recorded in comments, and one of them records a
regression that already happened:

1. **`data-map-overlay="top"` (`AppShell.tsx:3104`) is what zoom-to-fit reads** to know which edge is
   covered, so `frameAll` frames the world into the strip the player can actually see.
   `BadgeMenu.tsx:20` warns that a panel which grew that box would make zoom-to-fit fit the map into
   a smaller one.
2. **The strip is `z-20` and lifts to `z-30` only while a menu is open.** `AppShell.tsx:3091-3101`
   records what happened without it (**ah-v09e**): *"the Badges menu's lower rows landed on the units
   dock's title bar and stopped taking clicks"* — and why it must stay conditional: lifting it always
   *"swallows clicks meant for whatever sits under it — twelve smoke tests' worth"*.
3. **Only the top 48px of the map takes clicks.** `MapCanvas.tsx:1527-1529`: the inspector panels
   cover the rest with a full-bleed overlay clearing only the first forty-eight pixels, so
   *"controls anywhere else are unreachable however visible they look"*.

**The zoom cluster has none of the first two.** So moving the chip *into* it would drop both.

Branch from `origin/main`; every line number here is that tree.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### The decision: bring the zoom buttons to the strip, not the chip to the cluster

`zoomBy` and `frameAll` (`MapCanvas.tsx:654-672`) close over MapCanvas-local state — `viewRef`,
`size`, `commit`, `onLevel`, `insets`, `clearPeekRestore` — so **neither control can simply be moved
as JSX.** One of them has to reach across.

**Chosen: expose the two actions from `MapCanvas` through a ref handle, and render both controls in
AppShell's existing strip.** The repository already has exactly this pattern and says why:

```ts
/** What the shell may do to the editor from outside: the shortcut layer lands here. */
export type OrdersEditorHandle = { focus(): void; select(from: number, to?: number): void; … }
```

So:

```ts
/** What the shell may do to the map from outside: the view controls land here. */
export type MapCanvasHandle = {
  zoomBy(steps: number): void;
  frameAll(): void;
};
```

via `useImperativeHandle`, and the three `ZoomButton`s move out of `MapCanvas.tsx:1531-1541` into
`LayerChips` beside the Badges chip.

**Why this way round.** Every protection above already lives on AppShell's strip, and this keeps them
there **without touching any of them**: one `data-map-overlay="top"` element, one `z-20`/`z-30` rule,
one place inside the 48px band. Nothing about the inset mechanism or the stacking order changes,
which is exactly what you want in a bead about position.

**Rejected: moving the chip into MapCanvas's cluster.** Smaller diff, but it would have to carry the
overlay marker and the z-handling with it — and the marker would then sit **inside the map host**,
where `useOverlayInsets` measures (`useOverlayInsets.ts:22-29` walks `host.parentElement`). `frameAll`
reads `insets`, so an overlay marked inside the host is a change in kind to a mechanism whose own
comment says a wrong box makes zoom-to-fit fit the map into a smaller one. Not worth it for a
position change.

**Rejected: right-aligning the strip and leaving the cluster in MapCanvas.** It needs a hard offset
equal to the zoom cluster's width, which is wrong the moment a fourth button appears.

### The arrangement — `LayerChips.tsx`

The navigator chose **the chip left of the zoom buttons, keeping its own pill**:

```
[ Badges ▾ ]  [+] [−] [⤢]
```

The chip **keeps its bordered pill** (`rounded-md border border-edge bg-panel/95 … backdrop-blur`) so
its lit state still reads as a distinct thing rather than a fourth button; the `ZoomButton`s keep
their own `h-7 w-7 rounded border` styling. **Two container styles side by side is the accepted
cost** — a single shared pill was rejected as a restyle beyond what was asked.

The strip's own wrapper (`AppShell.tsx:3103`) changes from `justify-center` to right-aligned, so the
cluster sits where the zoom buttons are today and the player's hand finds them unchanged.

**`LayerChips`'s doc comment must be updated.** It currently explains why Badges stayed on the map
while staleness, movement and the level selector left; it now also has to say why the zoom buttons
joined it, or the next reader will wonder what map controls are doing in a file called `LayerChips`.
**Consider renaming the component** to something that describes what it now is — the implementer's
call, but a file named for chips holding the zoom cluster is a small lie.

### What must not change

The popover, the `data-badges-all` lit rule, `toggleBadge`, `setAllBadges`, the `layer-chips` testid,
and every zoom behaviour including wheel and keyboard. **If `BadgeMenu.tsx` appears in the diff,
scope has slipped.**

## Increments

1. **The map can be driven from outside.**
   RED: a test that `zoomBy` and `frameAll` on the handle change the view — mirroring however
   `OrdersEditorHandle` is tested.
   GREEN: `MapCanvasHandle` and `useImperativeHandle`.
2. **The controls sit together.**
   RED: `layer-chips` contains the Badges chip **and** the three zoom buttons, in that order.
   GREEN: move the `ZoomButton`s, right-align the strip.
3. **Nothing that protected the old position was lost.**
   RED: the three checks below — one marked overlay element, the conditional z-lift, and the 48px
   band. **This is the increment the bead exists to survive**; see *Known traps*.
   GREEN: nothing, if increment 2 kept the strip intact. If anything here fails, the controls were
   moved out of the strip rather than into it.

## The test plan

| Test | Where | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| `the map handle zooms and frames` | `MapCanvas` tests | the new surface |
| **`the badges chip and the zoom buttons share one strip`** | `LayerChips` tests | the bead |
| `the chip keeps its own pill` | same | the chosen arrangement |
| **`the strip is still the only element marked data-map-overlay="top"`** | `AppShell` tests | hazard 1 |
| **`the strip lifts to z-30 only while a menu is open`** | same | hazard 2 — the ah-v09e regression |
| **`zoom to fit does not frame the world under the controls`** | smoke | hazard 1, the behaviour |
| **`the Badges menu's lower rows still take clicks over the units dock`** | smoke | ah-v09e, by hand and in CI |
| `zoom in, zoom out and zoom to fit still work from their new home` | smoke | the move |
| `wheel and keyboard zoom` | existing | **unchanged** |
| the existing badge tests | `LayerChips`/`BadgeMenu` | **unchanged** |

**Suites:** `pnpm run check:fast`, plus the smoke suite — the z-order and inset behaviours are
layout, and there is **no jsdom in this repository**, so they cannot be unit-tested.

## User-facing decisions

Interviewed with the navigator on 2026-08-21 over `.cerebro/scratch/ah-ljil-badges-position.html`,
committed to `docs/ui/`.

**Q1 — the arrangement.** Chosen: **the chip left of the zoom buttons, keeping its own pill.** Reading
order matches use, the lit state stays legible as its own thing, and the menu drops where there is
room below it. Accepted cost: two container styles side by side. Rejected: **one pill around all
four** (says most clearly that they belong together, but the zoom buttons would lose their outlines —
a restyle beyond the request — and the lit chip reads less loudly inside a shared box) and **the chip
right of the zoom buttons** (zoom keeps the exact position the hand knows, but the widest control
ends furthest right so the cluster's edge shifts as the chip lights, and the menu opens hard against
the window edge).

**Q2 — the overlay marker.** Chosen: **keep one marked `data-map-overlay="top"` element and test
zoom-to-fit explicitly**, rather than marking the zoom cluster as a second top overlay (which would
make `useOverlayInsets` union two elements on one edge — something nothing does today) or dropping
the marking (which would let zoom-to-fit frame the world under the controls).

**Not asked** (architecture, decided here): exposing `MapCanvasHandle` and moving the zoom buttons to
the strip rather than the chip to the cluster; and whether to rename `LayerChips`.

## Out of scope

- **The badge popover, its contents, and the lit-when-something-is-hidden rule** — explicitly not in
  question.
- **Which badges exist**, and anything in `BadgeMenu.tsx`.
- **Wheel, keyboard and pinch zoom**, and the view model behind them.
- **Re-opening ah-l9mp.** Badges stays on the map; only its position moves.
- **The level selector**, which is in the top bar by ah-l9mp's decision.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
pnpm exec playwright test --project=web
```

Then by hand — and **the last three are the point of this bead, not the first**:

1. Look at the map: **Badges sits immediately left of `+ − ⤢`**, top-right, and nothing remains
   top-centre.
2. Zoom in, zoom out and zoom to fit all still work from their new home; wheel zoom still works.
3. Turn a badge off: the chip **lights** exactly as before, and the map drops that mark.
4. **Press zoom-to-fit with the panels open.** The world must frame into the *visible* strip, not
   under the region or unit panel. **This is hazard 1** — if the world is framed too small or slides
   under a panel, the overlay marker was lost in the move.
5. **Open the Badges menu with the units dock expanded, and click a row in the lower half of the
   menu.** It must respond. **This is ah-v09e happening again** if it does not.
6. **Close the menu and click where its lower rows were.** The click must reach whatever is under it
   — the units dock — not be swallowed by the strip. That is the other half of the same rule, and it
   is worth twelve smoke tests by the comment's own account.
7. Shrink the window until the panels crowd the top: both controls stay inside the clickable 48px
   band and stay usable.

## Known traps

- **The strip's `z-20` / `has-[[aria-expanded='true']]:z-30` must survive.** The zoom cluster has no
  z-handling of its own; if the controls end up in MapCanvas's div instead of the strip, the open
  Badges menu goes back under the panels — **that exact bug already shipped once (ah-v09e)** and its
  comment is still in the file.
- **Conditional, never unconditional.** A permanently-lifted strip swallows clicks meant for the
  panels beneath it.
- **Exactly one element keeps `data-map-overlay="top"`.** Two marked elements on one edge is
  something `useOverlayInsets` has never done; none, and zoom-to-fit frames under the controls.
- **Do not mark anything inside the map host.** `useOverlayInsets` measures from `host.parentElement`,
  and `frameAll` reads the result — marking inside the host changes what a mechanism its own comment
  calls delicate is measuring.
- **`zoomBy` and `frameAll` cannot be moved as JSX.** They close over MapCanvas's `viewRef`, `size`,
  `commit`, `onLevel` and `insets`. Moving the buttons means exposing the actions, not the state.
- **The 48px band.** Controls below it are invisible to the pointer however visible they look.
- **`BadgeMenu.tsx` should not appear in the diff.**
- **Update `LayerChips`'s doc comment**, which currently explains a layout this bead changes.
acceptance_criteria:
- The Badges chip sits immediately left of the zoom buttons, top-right, and nothing remains top-centre. The chip keeps its own bordered pill; the ZoomButtons keep their own styling.
- Zoom in, zoom out and zoom to fit all work from their new home; wheel and keyboard zoom are unchanged.
- MapCanvas exposes zoomBy and frameAll through a ref handle (MapCanvasHandle), mirroring OrdersEditorHandle - the buttons move to the strip, the actions stay with the map. The chip is NOT moved into MapCanvas.
- Exactly one element still carries data-map-overlay="top", and zoom-to-fit still frames the world into the visible strip rather than under the region or unit panel.
- The strip keeps `z-20` with a conditional lift to `z-30` while a menu is expanded. With the units dock expanded, the Badges menu's lower rows still take clicks; with the menu closed, clicks in that area still reach the units dock underneath. (This is the ah-v09e regression, and both halves must hold.)
- Both controls stay inside the clickable top 48px band, including on a short window.
- The popover, the data-badges-all lit rule, toggleBadge, setAllBadges and the layer-chips testid are unchanged. BadgeMenu.tsx does not appear in the diff.
- LayerChips's doc comment is updated to explain the new arrangement.
- `pnpm run check:fast` and the smoke suite pass.

title: Every push can start a second, duplicate CI run competing for the same runners
description:
.github/workflows/ci.yml declares no concurrency group, so two events on the
same sha produce two independent, complete CI runs.

ah-87he's retrospective caught it precisely: runs at 2026-08-19T08:52:19Z and
08:52:34Z on the same sha f723340, plus 09:10:46Z on 28cd4c4 -- three runs for
two commits.

MEASURED RATE. Across the 40 non-outage beads closed in the 72 hours to
2026-08-20: 126 CI runs, of which 10 were a duplicate trigger within 60 seconds
of another. Eight per cent.

WHAT IT COSTS. CI wall-clock is 34% of everything the implementer fleet spends
(7.9 hours of 23.3 in that window; the median bead sits through 18 minutes of
CI against a 33-minute total). Removing 8% of runs takes roughly 2.7% off the
typical bead -- under a minute. Small, and worth saying plainly.

The better argument is contention. On 2026-08-19 the Actions queue starved with
8-9 runs in flight and five jobs sitting ~50 minutes before any started, while
githubstatus.com reported Actions fully operational. Duplicate runs cost most
exactly when the fleet is busiest and the runners are already the bottleneck.

CARE NEEDED ON MAIN. cancel-in-progress on a pull_request branch is safe. On
main it is not: cancelling an in-flight run could kill the one gating a release.
design:
## Context

`.github/workflows/ci.yml` declares **no concurrency group**, so two events on the same sha produce
two independent, complete CI runs.

ah-87he's retrospective caught it precisely: runs at `2026-08-19T08:52:19Z` and `08:52:34Z` on the
same sha `f723340`, plus `09:10:46Z` on `28cd4c4` — **three runs for two commits**.

**Measured rate.** Across the 40 non-outage beads closed in the 72 hours to 2026-08-20: **126 CI
runs, of which 10 were a duplicate trigger within 60 seconds of another. Eight per cent.**

**What it costs, honestly.** CI wall-clock is 34% of everything the implementer fleet spends (7.9
hours of 23.3 in that window; the median bead sits through 18 minutes of CI against a 33-minute
total). Removing 8% of runs takes roughly **2.7% off the typical bead — under a minute.** Small, and
worth saying plainly rather than dressing up.

**The better argument is contention.** On 2026-08-19 the Actions queue starved with 8–9 runs in
flight and five jobs sitting ~50 minutes before any started, while githubstatus.com reported Actions
fully operational. **Duplicate runs cost most exactly when the fleet is busiest** and the runners are
already the bottleneck.

Branch from `origin/main`.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### The whole change — one block in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`

There is **no `concurrency:` key anywhere in the file today** (checked). Add one at the top level,
after `permissions:` (`ci.yml:9-12`) and before `jobs:`:

```yaml
# One run per ref (ah-pg3j). Two events on the same sha used to produce two complete, independent
# runs - 10 of 126 runs in the 72 hours to 2026-08-20 were a duplicate inside 60 seconds. The
# direct saving is small (~2.7% of a typical bead); the real one is contention, since duplicates
# cost most on exactly the days the Actions queue is already starving.
#
# `cancel-in-progress` is deliberately conditional. On a pull request, superseding an older run is
# what we want: only the newest head matters. On `main` it is not - cancelling an in-flight run
# there could kill the one gating a release, so pushes to main queue behind each other instead.
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}
```

**Why `github.ref` is the right key.** On a `pull_request` event it is `refs/pull/<n>/merge` — unique
per pull request, so two PRs never cancel each other. On `push` to main it is `refs/heads/main`. The
two can never collide, which is what lets one group serve both triggers safely.

**`cancel-in-progress` accepts an expression**, which is what makes the navigator's chosen split — PR
branches only, main left alone — a single line rather than two workflows.

**Nothing else changes.** No job, no gate, no trigger. `on:` keeps its deliberate absence of
`paths`/`paths-ignore` (`ci.yml:28-31`): a workflow skipped by path filtering never reports its
checks at all and blocks the merge instead of speeding it up.

**Scope is `ci.yml` alone.** `deploy.yml` and `release.yml` also have no concurrency group, and they
are **out of scope** — cancelling a deploy or a release is a different risk with a different answer,
and the bead is about the duplicate CI runs that were measured.

### One consequence to expect, not to fix

The `changes` gate counts **any `.github/workflows/` touch as code** (`ci.yml:73`, confirmed at
`:60`), so **this PR will itself run the full suite**. That is correct and is the point — a change to
how CI is triggered should be proved by a full run — but it means the PR is not the fast docs-shaped
one its size suggests. Do not "fix" that by exempting the file.

## Increments

One increment; this is a four-line change and splitting it would be theatre.

1. **One run per pull-request ref.**
   RED: there is no unit test for a workflow file — the check is the behaviour, so it is proved in
   *Validation* below, on the PR itself.
   GREEN: the `concurrency:` block.
   Then **`yamllint`/`actionlint` if either is available** (`pnpm run check:fast` does not cover
   workflow YAML), or at minimum confirm the file parses by GitHub accepting the run at all — a
   malformed `concurrency:` key fails the workflow outright, which is loud and immediate.

## The test plan

There is no suite that can assert this; **the evidence is the PR's own run history**, and the
implementer must go and look at it rather than assuming:

| Check | How | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| **Two pushes in quick succession leave one run** | push twice inside a minute, then `gh run list --branch <branch>` | the bead |
| The superseded run reports **cancelled**, not failed | the same listing | that a cancel is not a red check |
| The newest run completes and gates the PR | the PR's checks | no self-inflicted breakage |
| **A push to main is never cancelled** | `gh run list --branch main` after the merge | the release-gating guard |
| `gh run rerun` still works | run it once on the merged run | the acceptance criterion |

**Suites:** `pnpm run check:fast` is unaffected — it does not read workflow YAML. The full CI suite
runs on this PR anyway, per the gate note above.

## User-facing decisions

**None to ask for.** Nothing here reaches a player, and the one judgement this bead contained —
whether to cancel in-flight runs on `main` as well as on pull requests — **was already taken by the
navigator on 2026-08-20: PR branches only, leaving main alone.** It is recorded in the bead's design
and is not reopened.

**Decided here** (architecture): `${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}` as the group key rather
than `github.head_ref` (which is empty on a `push` event, collapsing every main push into one group);
and leaving `deploy.yml` and `release.yml` alone.

## Out of scope

- **`deploy.yml` and `release.yml`.** Same missing key, different risk; not measured, not asked for.
- **Path filtering on the `on:` trigger.** Deliberately absent, and `ci.yml:28-31` explains why.
- **The `changes` gate**, including that it treats `.github/workflows/` as code.
- **Shortening CI itself.** This bead removes duplicate runs; it does not make a run faster.
- **A merge queue.**

## Validation

```bash
# The file must at least parse; GitHub rejects a malformed concurrency key outright.
actionlint .github/workflows/ci.yml   # if available
```

Then, on the PR itself — **this is the whole verification and it cannot be skipped**:

1. Open the PR. Push a second commit **within a minute** of the first.
2. `gh run list --branch <branch>` — the first run is **`cancelled`**, exactly one run is in flight,
   and it is the one for the newer sha.
3. Confirm the PR's required checks go green off that newer run, and that **the cancelled run does
   not show as a failing required check**.
4. Merge, then `gh run list --branch main`: the push-to-main run **completes**. Push another commit
   to main soon after if you can, and confirm the first is **not** cancelled — this is the guard that
   protects a release, and it is the one thing here that could do real damage.
5. `gh run rerun <run-id>` on a completed run and confirm it runs.
6. Open a **second** PR while the first is running and confirm the two do not cancel each other —
   proof the group key is per-ref and not global.

## Known traps

- **`cancel-in-progress` must stay conditional.** A bare `true` cancels runs on `main`, and the run
  it cancels may be the one gating a release. This is the single dangerous mistake available in this
  bead, and it looks tidier than the correct version.
- **Use `github.ref`, not `github.head_ref`.** `head_ref` is empty on a `push` event, so every push
  to main would share one group and — with a bare `true` — cancel each other.
- **A cancelled run is not a failure.** Expect `cancelled` in the run list; if it surfaces as a red
  required check on the PR, the group key is wrong and PRs are cancelling one another.
- **This PR runs the full suite**, because the gate counts `.github/workflows/` as code. That is
  intended. Do not exempt the path to make the PR faster.
- **`deploy.yml` and `release.yml` are not in this bead.** A helpful sweep across all three
  workflows is a scope change with a release-shaped risk attached.
- **There is no test that proves this.** The verification is the run history on the PR; an
  implementer that ships this without looking at `gh run list` has not checked anything.
acceptance_criteria:
- Two CI runs are never in flight for the same pull-request head at once; the older is cancelled when a newer push supersedes it.
- Runs on main are unaffected - a release-gating run is never cancelled by this change. `cancel-in-progress` is conditional on `github.event_name == 'pull_request'`, never a bare true.
- The concurrency group keys on `${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}`, so two different pull requests never cancel each other and every push to main does not collapse into one group.
- A rerun requested by hand (`gh run rerun`) still works.
- A superseded run reports as `cancelled` and does not surface as a failing required check on the PR.
- Only .github/workflows/ci.yml changes. deploy.yml and release.yml are untouched.
- The `on:` trigger keeps its deliberate absence of paths/paths-ignore.
- Verified on the PR's own run history with `gh run list`, not assumed - there is no suite that can prove this.

title: A faction's name tells you nothing about the faction
description:
A faction's name appears in several places — the faction info drop-down, the units-in-hex list — but naming it is all it does. Make it clickable: choosing a faction opens a dialog gathering everything known about it.

The dialog lists the attitude towards that faction, the hexes it has been seen in, and its known units. Hovering a hex or a unit in those lists highlights the hex on the map — for a unit, the hex it stands in.

Raised by the navigator 2026-08-19.
design:
## Context

A faction's name appears in the attitudes list and in the units-in-hex table, and naming it is all it
does. The bead asks for it to be clickable, opening a view of the attitude toward it, the hexes it has
been seen in and its known units — with **hovering a hex or a unit highlighting that hex on the map**.

**The bead asks for two things that cannot both be true, and settling that is most of the design.**
It says *dialog*. Every dialog in this workspace is modal — `fixed inset-0 … bg-black/50` with
`aria-modal="true"` (`BattlesDialog.tsx:49-54`, `ChangesDialog.tsx:53-58`) — so it dims the whole
screen, map included. A highlight drawn while the map is dimmed behind a box is work nobody can see.

**`TradePanel` already solves this exact shape**, and it is a *popover*: anchored, map visible, with
`onHoverRoute(route | null)` and a doc comment that is worth inheriting wholesale:

> The row the reader is on, so the map can draw it - and `null` the moment they look away. **Called
> on focus as well as on hover: every row is a button, so this list is tabbed through, and a
> hover-only feature would show a keyboard reader nothing at all.**

It also carries two scars this bead must not re-earn — see *Known traps*.

Branch from `origin/main`; every line number here is that tree.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### 1. What the data can answer — a new `packages/shared/src/factionDossier.ts`

Pure, testable without a browser, and the place the three caveats live:

```ts
/** Everything this turn's report knows about one faction. */
export type FactionDossier = {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  /** As declared toward them, or `null` when the attitudes block does not name them. */
  attitude: string | null;
  /** Hexes holding at least one of their units, in report order. */
  hexes: { regionId: string; unitCount: number }[];
  units: { unitId: string; name: string; regionId: string }[];
};

/**
 * What is known, and only what is known.
 *
 * Two limits the panel states out loud (ah-bu2c), because an empty-looking faction otherwise reads
 * as "they have nothing" rather than "we cannot see anything":
 *
 * - "Seen in" means "has a unit in *this turn's* report". There is no memory of earlier turns.
 * - A foreign unit that conceals its faction has `factionId: null` (`ReportUnit.ts:13`), so it
 *   belongs to no dossier at all - not even the right one.
 */
export function dossierFor(parsed: ParsedReport, attitudes: DeclaredAttitudes | null, factionId: string): FactionDossier;
```

`attitude` comes from `DeclaredAttitudes.levels` → `FactionRef {name, id}`
(`generated/DeclaredAttitudes.ts`, `generated/FactionRef.ts`), falling back to
`defaultAttitude` where the block does not name the faction — and to `null` when there is no
attitudes block at all. `hexes` and `units` are `parsed.regions[].units` filtered on `factionId`,
which is the same walk `AppShell`'s `unitRegions` memo already makes (`:640-648`).

### 2. The panel — `packages/shared/src/workspace/FactionDossierPanel.tsx` (new)

Built on **`PopoverFrame`** (`popover.tsx:61-84`), the frame `TradePanel` uses, so it is anchored and
the map stays visible. Props follow `TradePanel`'s shape deliberately:

```tsx
  dossier: FactionDossier;
  labelFor: (regionId: string) => string;
  /**
   * The row the reader is on, so the map can ring it - and `null` the moment they look away.
   * Called on focus as well as on hover, for the reason TradePanel's own comment gives: every row
   * is a button, this list is tabbed through, and a hover-only feature shows a keyboard reader
   * nothing.
   */
  onHoverHex: (regionId: string | null) => void;
  onSelectHex: (regionId: string) => void;
  onSelectUnit: (unitId: string) => void;
  onDismiss: () => void;
```

Three sections — **Attitude**, **Seen in**, **Known units** — and **two lines of plain text stating
the limits**, which the navigator chose:

- under *Seen in*: `Where their units are this turn. Earlier turns are not remembered.`
- under *Known units*: `A unit hiding its faction is not counted here.`

Every hex and unit row is a `<button>`, so clicking navigates as well as hovering highlighting —
`onSelectHex` / `onSelectUnit` route to `selectHex` and `goToUnit`, which is what `ah-87he` just made
the convention for a unit id.

### 3. Anchored where it was opened from

The navigator chose this over a header chip, so **no header room is spent** — which matters because
`ah-csni` exists to bound exactly that.

Two entry points, each rendering the popover beside the name that was clicked:

- **`FactionPanel.tsx:107`** already renders each attitude name with
  `data-testid={`faction-attitude-name-${faction.id}`}`. It becomes a button that opens the dossier
  beside itself. **This is a popover inside a popover** — check that `PopoverFrame`'s positioning and
  dismissal behave when nested, and if they do not, render the dossier *in place of* the attitudes
  list with a way back rather than fighting it. **Say which was needed.**
- **`UnitTableDock.tsx`**, wherever it prints `factionName` for a foreign unit: the same button,
  opening beside that row.

### 4. The ring — `MapCanvas.tsx`

A **brass ring**, the navigator's choice: brass is the app's pointing colour, and it must not be
mistaken for the white selection ring (`--color-selection-ring: #f5f8fc`, `theme.css:62`).

`MapCanvas` gains `highlightedRegionId: string | null` and draws a ring on that hex. **Reuse the
selection ring's geometry** and change only its colour, so the two marks are the same shape and
differ in exactly the way a reader can name.

`AppShell` holds the state, memoised, and **gated on the popover being open** — the pattern
`tradeArrow` already uses (`:1988-1994`):

```ts
const [hoveredFactionHex, setHoveredFactionHex] = useState<string | null>(null);
const factionRing = useMemo(
  () => (dossierFor !== null ? hoveredFactionHex : null),
  [dossierFor, hoveredFactionHex]
);
```

**No framing, no panning.** The trade arrow frames the map on hover; this must not — a ring that
moves the map while the reader is running down a list would throw the list out from under them.

## Increments

1. **The dossier is computable.**
   RED: `factionDossier.test.ts` — `names the hexes a faction's units are in`,
   `counts units per hex`, `reads the declared attitude`, `falls back to the default attitude`,
   `has no attitude when there is no attitudes block`, and
   **`a unit concealing its faction belongs to no dossier`**.
   GREEN: `dossierFor`.

2. **The panel renders it.**
   RED: `FactionDossierPanel.test.tsx` — the three sections, both limit lines verbatim, and every hex
   and unit row being a `<button>` with an accessible name.
   GREEN: the component.

3. **The map rings the hovered hex.**
   RED: a `MapCanvas` render test — `rings the highlighted hex in brass, distinctly from the
   selection`, asserting the two rings differ in colour and that no ring is drawn for `null`.
   GREEN: the prop and the ring.

4. **It opens from both places, and hovering works by keyboard too.**
   RED: smoke — `a faction name in the units table opens its dossier`,
   `a faction name in the attitudes list opens its dossier`, and
   **`tabbing to a hex row rings it on the map`**, which is the case a hover-only implementation
   fails and nobody notices.
   GREEN: the two buttons and the `onFocus`/`onBlur` pair beside `onPointerEnter`/`onPointerLeave`.

5. **Clicking goes there.**
   RED: smoke — `clicking a hex row selects that hex` and `clicking a unit row selects that unit`,
   each asserting the popover closed.
   GREEN: `onSelectHex` / `onSelectUnit` wired to `selectHex` and `goToUnit`.

## The test plan

| Test | Where | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| the six `dossierFor` cases | `factionDossier.test.ts` | what is known, and the two limits |
| **`a unit concealing its faction belongs to no dossier`** | same | `factionId: null` |
| the three sections and both limit lines | `FactionDossierPanel.test.tsx` | the agreed wording, verbatim |
| every row is a button with a name | same | keyboard reachability |
| `rings the highlighted hex in brass, distinctly from the selection` | `MapCanvas` test | the two marks differ |
| a faction name opens the dossier, from **both** places | smoke | the entry points |
| **`tabbing to a hex row rings it on the map`** | smoke | focus, not just hover |
| `clicking a hex row selects that hex` / a unit row | smoke | navigation, popover closed |
| **`reopening after dismissal draws no ring`** | smoke | the Copilot #398 scar, below |

**Suites:** `pnpm run check:fast`, and the smoke suite in **both** projects.

## User-facing decisions

Interviewed with the navigator on 2026-08-19 over `.cerebro/scratch/ah-bu2c-faction.html`. The chosen
mockup is committed to `docs/ui/ah-bu2c-faction.html`.

**Q1 — dialog or popover.** Chosen: **a popover, like Trade.** A modal dialog dims the map the
highlight is drawn on, so the bead's two requirements are incompatible; the popover keeps the map
visible and reuses a pattern that already works. Rejected: **a dialog with the highlight dropped**
(room for everything, hexes and units as links, consistent with `ah-87he` — but it drops something
asked for) and **a modal dialog with the highlight anyway**, which is the bead as written and is work
nobody can see.

**Q2 — what the highlight looks like.** Chosen: **a brass ring**, brass being the app's pointing
colour. Accepted cost: two rings on screen at once, so a reader learns which is the selection.
Rejected: **a tint** (unmistakably not a selection, but it hides the terrain and badges of the hex
being looked at) and **ringing every hex at once with no hover** (answers "where are they?" at a
glance and would work with a dialog — but it is not what was asked for, and twenty hexes is a lot of
rings).

**Q3 — the two limits in the data.** Chosen: **say both, briefly, in the panel** — that "seen" means
this turn only, and that a unit concealing its faction is not counted — so an empty-looking faction
is not read as "they have nothing". Rejected: saying neither, and saying only the concealment one.

**Q4 — where the popover anchors.** Chosen: **beside the name that was clicked**, in both places. No
header room is spent, and it appears where the reader's eye already is. Rejected: **a faction chip in
the header** (one predictable place, matching every other popover — but it costs the header budget
`ah-csni` protects, and a chip for "whichever faction you last clicked" is an odd permanent fixture)
and **replacing the Faction popover's contents** (no new surface, but it hides the list you came from
and the units-table route still needs an anchor).

**Not asked:** that clicking a row navigates as well as hovering highlighting, which follows
`ah-87he`; and that the ring never frames or pans the map.

## Out of scope

- **Any memory of earlier turns.** The dossier is this turn's report. Saying so in the panel is the
  whole of the treatment.
- **Attributing concealed units** to a faction by inference.
- **Unit counts, concentrations or "where are they strongest"** — free once the list exists, and
  noted in the mockup, but not proposed.
- **The Faction popover's existing attitudes list**, beyond making its names clickable.
- **`ah-87he`'s clickable unit numbers**, already merged; this uses the same `goToUnit`.
- **Framing or panning the map on hover.** The trade arrow does; this deliberately does not.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
pnpm exec playwright test --project=web
pnpm exec playwright test --project=desktop-shell
```

Then by eye, with a turn that has foreign factions in several hexes:

1. Open the **units-in-hex** table, click a foreign faction's name. The dossier opens **beside that
   row**, the map stays visible, and the attitude, hexes and units are right.
2. **Hover a hex row.** A brass ring appears on that hex, and it is clearly not the white selection
   ring — look at both at once and satisfy yourself a reader could name the difference.
3. **Tab through the rows without touching the mouse.** The ring must follow focus. This is the case
   that silently does nothing if only `onPointerEnter` is wired.
4. **Look away** — move the pointer off the list — and the ring goes.
5. **Dismiss the popover and reopen it.** No ring must be drawn until you hover again. This is the
   Copilot #398 scar, below, and it is invisible until you look for it.
6. Click a hex row: the popover closes and that hex is selected. Click a unit row: the unit is
   selected, following it to another hex or level if need be.
7. Open the dossier for a faction the attitudes block does **not** name, and one with **no visible
   units**. Both limit lines should make the emptiness read as "we cannot see" rather than "there is
   nothing".

## Known traps

- **A dialog would defeat the feature.** Modal means `bg-black/50` over the map. If the popover ever
  becomes a dialog, the highlight stops meaning anything.
- **Hover must also fire on focus.** `TradePanel`'s comment says exactly why, and a hover-only
  implementation passes every test that uses a mouse.
- **A dismissed popover must forget its hovered row.** `TradePanel` has a `useEffect` for this after
  Copilot #398: the popover unmounts without the row ever firing `onPointerLeave` or `onBlur`, so
  reopening draws the last hover with the pointer nowhere near it. **Copy that effect.**
- **Memoise the highlighted id.** `tradeArrow`'s comment: a fresh object each render re-frames on
  every render, and each framing commits a viewport, which renders again. This bead does not frame,
  but the identity discipline still applies to anything the map depends on.
- **`factionId` is `null` for a concealed unit** (`ReportUnit.ts:13`). Grouping by it without
  filtering puts every concealed unit in one phantom faction.
- **Brass, not the selection white.** `--color-selection-ring` is `#f5f8fc`; a second ring in that
  colour is indistinguishable from a selection, which is the one thing this must not be.
- **A popover inside a popover** is the attitudes-list route. Verify `PopoverFrame` nests; if it does
  not, swap the panel's contents with a way back rather than forcing it, and record which was needed.
- **Do not frame or pan on hover.** Running down a list while the map jumps under you is worse than
  no highlight at all.
acceptance_criteria: Clicking a faction's name in the attitudes list or in the units-in-hex table opens a popover anchored beside that name - not a modal dialog, because a modal dims the map the highlight is drawn on - showing the attitude declared toward that faction, the hexes its units are in this turn with a count each, and its known units. The panel states both limits in plain text: that 'seen in' means this turn's report only and earlier turns are not remembered, and that a unit concealing its faction is counted nowhere. Every hex and unit row is a button: hovering OR focusing it rings that hex on the map in brass, visibly distinct from the white selection ring, and looking away clears it; clicking navigates to that hex or unit and closes the popover. The map is never framed or panned by a hover. Dismissing and reopening the popover draws no ring until something is hovered again - the Copilot #398 behaviour TradePanel already guards. A pure factionDossier module computes all of it from the parsed report and the declared attitudes, with a unit whose factionId is null belonging to no dossier at all, covered by unit tests; keyboard reachability and both entry points are covered by smoke tests in the web and desktop-shell projects. No header room is spent.

title: The palette finds structure types but not the structures on your map
description:
The palette should find individual structures in the player's world, not only types: searching by a structure's name or by its id turns it up and takes you to it.

Related to the game-data palette work (ah-…), but a distinct thing: this finds a structure that exists on the map, not a structure type in the scraped data.

Raised by the navigator 2026-08-19.
design:
## Context

The palette should find **an individual structure in the player's world** — by its name or its id —
not only a structure *type* in the scraped data.

**`ah-5jkt` has just landed and it changes what this bead has to solve.** The palette now carries a
`building` kind from the game-data dictionary (`commandPalette.ts:8-20`), holding Mine, Tower,
Stockade and the rest. So typing `mine` will match a **dictionary page** *and* **every Mine on the
map** — two different things sharing a word:

- **"Mine" the page** says it costs 10 wood or stone and increases the iron available in a region.
- **"Mine" the building** is a thing standing in a hex you can go to.

A reader typing `mine` wants one of them and the palette cannot know which, so **the list must make
the difference obvious at a glance.** That is the whole design, and it is why the entry kind is
`structure` rather than being folded into `building`.

Branch from `origin/main`; every line number here is that tree.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### 1. A new entry kind — `packages/shared/src/commandPalette.ts`

`PaletteEntryKind` (`:8-20`) gains one member. **Beside `region`, not beside `building`** — a
structure is a place you go to, and its neighbour in the list is the hex, not the dictionary page:

```ts
export type PaletteEntryKind =
  | "unit"
  | "region"
  /**
   * One structure standing in the world - `Soggy Saw Mill [1]`, not the dictionary's `Mine`.
   *
   * A separate kind from `building` on purpose (ah-wkwk): since ah-5jkt the palette holds both,
   * and typing `mine` matches a page describing what a Mine costs *and* every Mine on the map.
   * The kind label beside the row is what tells them apart.
   */
  | "structure"
  | "action"
  …
```

`PaletteInput` (`:31-41`) gains the source, in the shape the others use:

```ts
  structures: Array<{ structureId: string; label: string; run: () => void }>;
```

and `buildPaletteEntries` (`:51`) maps it **immediately after `regions`** (`:59-64`), which is the
navigator's ordering: with the places, well above the ~270-entry dictionary, so an empty query still
shows one.

The doc comment at `:44-50` explains the current order and **must be updated** — it currently reads
"units first … then places, then the app's own actions" and needs structures named among the places.

### 2. The label — `packages/shared/src/workspace/AppShell.tsx`

Built where the other palette inputs are built, from `parsed.regions[].structures`. The navigator
chose **the kind only where the name does not carry it**:

| The structure | Label |
|---|---|
| named | `Arcane Mine [12] · cavern (3,41)` |
| unnamed | `Building [4] · Mine · plain (9,22)` |

The unnamed case is the one that needs the help, and the repository already knows how to detect it:
`semantics.rs`'s `structure_label` matches `"Building"` and `"Ship"` case-insensitively as *"the
engine's own words for an unnamed structure"* (`crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs:1434-1442`).
**Use the same rule, and say in a comment that it mirrors that function** — two places deciding
"is this named?" differently is exactly the shape `ah-f03z` is a whole bead about.

The hex label comes from `hexLabel` (`AppShell.tsx:590-600`), which the problems panel and trade panel
already use, so a hex reads the same everywhere.

`run` is **`() => selectHex(regionId)`** — exactly what choosing a region does (`:554-567`), which is
the navigator's choice and needs nothing new. The structure is then visible in the region pane's
structure list.

### 3. The row shows its kind — `workspace/CommandPalette.tsx:116-119`

The kind already prints beside every row:

```tsx
{entry.kind === "order-help" ? "order" : entry.kind}
```

`structure` prints as `structure` with no special case, which is what distinguishes it from
`building`. **Check it does not overflow** — `structure` is a longer word than any kind there today,
and the column is `shrink-0`.

### 4. Nothing about the dictionary changes

`ah-5jkt`'s `building` entries, their labels and their `openGameData` behaviour are untouched. If this
bead's diff reaches the game-data path, the two have been conflated — which is the thing it exists to
keep apart.

## Increments

1. **Structures are offered.**
   RED: `commandPalette.test.ts` — `offers a structure in the world`, asserting an entry with
   `kind: "structure"`; and **`a structure and a building type both match "mine", and are told
   apart`**, asserting both appear with different kinds. That second test is the bead.
   GREEN: the kind, the input field, and the mapping after `regions`.

2. **They sit with the places.**
   RED: `structures come after regions and before actions`, over `buildPaletteEntries`' output order.
   GREEN: the position of the mapping — and the updated doc comment.

3. **The label says enough, and no more.**
   RED: `a named structure shows its name and hex` and
   **`an unnamed structure shows its kind too`** (`Building [4] · Mine · plain (9,22)`), plus
   `a ship placeholder is treated as unnamed` for the `Ship` case.
   GREEN: the label builder in `AppShell`.

4. **Choosing one goes there.**
   RED: smoke — `choosing a structure selects its hex`: open the palette, type a structure's name,
   choose it, and assert the region pane names that hex.
   GREEN: `run: () => selectHex(regionId)`.

5. **Finding one by id.**
   RED: `finding a structure by its id`, typing `12` and expecting `Arcane Mine [12]`. The id is in
   the label, so this should pass once the label is right — **if it does not, the matcher is scoring
   digits differently from words** and that is worth knowing before it is worked around.

## The test plan

| Test | Where | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| `offers a structure in the world` | `commandPalette.test.ts` | the new kind |
| **`a structure and a building type both match "mine", and are told apart`** | same | the collision, which is the bead |
| `structures come after regions and before actions` | same | the ordering |
| `a named structure shows its name and hex` | same | the label |
| **`an unnamed structure shows its kind too`** | same | `Building [4] · Mine` |
| `a ship placeholder is treated as unnamed` | same | the `Ship` half of the rule |
| `finding a structure by its id` | same | id search |
| `choosing a structure selects its hex` | smoke | the action |
| the existing palette tests | `commandPalette.test.ts` | **unchanged** — nothing above structures moves |

**Suites:** `pnpm run check:fast`, plus the smoke suite. **No Rust change**, so `cargo test` is
unaffected — but `structure_label`'s rule is being mirrored in TypeScript, so read it rather than
remembering it.

## User-facing decisions

Interviewed with the navigator on 2026-08-20 over
`.cerebro/scratch/ah-wkwk-structures.html`. The chosen mockup is committed to
`docs/ui/ah-wkwk-structures.html`.

**Q1 — how a structure row reads.** Chosen: **the kind only where the name does not carry it** — so
`Arcane Mine [12] · cavern (3,41)`, but `Building [4] · Mine · plain (9,22)`. Short where it can be,
informative where it must be. Accepted cost: two shapes of row, decided by a property the reader
cannot see. Rejected: **name, id, kind and hex always** (matches the region pane exactly, so a
structure reads the same everywhere — but long enough to wrap in a narrow palette) and **name and hex
only** (short enough to scan a dozen of, but an unnamed structure then says nothing about what it is).

**Q2 — where structures sit.** Chosen: **with the places, immediately after regions.** A structure is
somewhere you go, and it lands well above the ~270-entry dictionary so an empty query still shows one.
Rejected: above the dictionary but below actions, and last of all — which would put a structure below
270 entries and out of sight.

**Q3 — what choosing one does.** Chosen: **go to its hex**, exactly as choosing a region does; the
structure is then visible in the region pane. Rejected: **also selecting a unit inside it** (closer to
"take me to this building", but which unit — the first is arbitrary and an empty structure has none)
and **highlighting it in the region pane's structure list** (most precise, but the region pane cannot
be told what to show today and that seam is not this bead's to invent).

**Not asked:** that the kind is `structure` rather than an extension of `building`, which follows
directly from Q1's premise; and that the unnamed-structure rule mirrors `structure_label`'s.

## Out of scope

- **The game-data dictionary**, its `building` entries and `openGameData` — `ah-5jkt`'s, and
  deliberately untouched.
- **Structures in hexes the player cannot see.** The source is this turn's parsed report; there is no
  memory of earlier turns, the same limit `ah-bu2c` states out loud for factions. Not restated here
  because the palette does not claim completeness.
- **Selecting a unit inside the structure**, or telling the region pane what to show — both
  considered under Q3.
- **Deduplicating structures that share a name.** Two hexes with a Mine are two entries, told apart by
  their hex, which is exactly what the label is for.
- **Searching by what a structure produces or costs** — that is the dictionary's job, and it is
  reachable in the same palette.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
pnpm exec playwright test --project=web
```

Then by hand, with a turn that has several structures:

1. Open the palette and type **`mine`**. You should see **both** a `structure` row for each Mine on
   the map *and* a `building` row for the dictionary page, and be able to tell them apart without
   thinking about it. **This is the acceptance** — if you hesitate, the labels are wrong.
2. Type a structure's **id** (`12`) and confirm it is found.
3. Choose a structure and confirm the map goes to its hex and the region pane lists it.
4. Find a structure the player has **not named** — the turn-71 fixture has `Building [4]` and
   `Ship [218]` shapes — and confirm the row shows its kind.
5. Type nothing at all and confirm structures appear **above** the dictionary, and that units still
   come first.
6. Two structures with the same name in different hexes: both listed, told apart by the hex.

## Known traps

- **`building` and `structure` are different kinds and must stay so.** The whole bead is that typing
  `mine` should offer both and make the difference visible. Folding them together, or reusing
  `building`, deletes the feature while appearing to implement it.
- **The unnamed rule is already written down in Rust.** `structure_label`
  (`semantics.rs:1434-1442`) matches `Building` and `Ship` case-insensitively as the engine's words
  for an unnamed structure. Mirror it and say so — `ah-f03z` is a whole bead about one rule with
  several implementations.
- **The doc comment at `commandPalette.ts:44-50` describes the list's order** and will be wrong the
  moment structures are inserted. It is the only place that order is explained.
- **`structure` is a long kind label** in a `shrink-0` column. Check it at the palette's real width
  before assuming it fits.
- **Do not touch the dictionary path.** If `openGameData` or the `building` entries appear in the
  diff, the two things have been conflated.
- **Id search should work for free**, because the id is in the label. If it does not, find out why the
  matcher scores digits differently rather than special-casing it — that would be a matcher bug
  affecting unit numbers too.
acceptance_criteria: The palette offers every structure in this turn's report as its own entry kind, structure, distinct from the building kind ah-5jkt added for the game-data dictionary - so typing 'mine' offers both a dictionary page and every Mine standing on the map, each labelled with its kind so they are told apart at a glance. A structure entry is labelled with its name, id and hex, and additionally its kind when the report gives it no name of its own - detected by the same Building/Ship placeholder rule as structure_label in semantics.rs, mirrored with a comment saying so rather than reinvented. Structures are offered immediately after regions, with the places and above the dictionary, and commandPalette.ts's doc comment describing the list's order is updated to name them. Choosing a structure selects its hex, exactly as choosing a region does, and the structure is then visible in the region pane. Searching by a structure's id finds it. Nothing about the dictionary's building entries or openGameData changes, and the existing palette tests pass unchanged.

title: Order OCD: order keywords uppercase themselves as you type
description: Placeholder - planned by Beast in this session.
design:
## Context

Orders are case-insensitive to the engine, so a turn typed in lower case runs exactly as one
shouted in capitals. Some players want the keywords uppercase anyway — it separates the commands
from the names and reads like the manual — and doing it by hand is tedious and easy to miss. This
bead adds the setting, **Order OCD**, and the editor behaviour behind it.

Its blocker `ah-bn6.1` publishes the vocabulary this needs and **must be built first**. Read its
plan (`bd show ah-bn6.1 --json`) before starting: it creates
`client.orderVocabulary(rulesetJson: string | null): Promise<string[]>` — every word the rules know,
uppercase, sorted, deduplicated: the order names, the grammar's own fixed words (`ALL`, `UNIT`,
`EXCEPT`, the attitudes, the item classes, `N NE SE S SW NW IN OUT`), and, when a ruleset is passed,
every item and skill tag plus **each word** of every item and skill name. Singular words only —
matching a typed plural is this bead's job, below. **That method does not exist yet**; if
`ah-bn6.1` has not merged, stop and take another bead.

The design was settled with the navigator over two rounds and is drawn in `docs/ui/order-ocd.html`.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### New — `packages/shared/src/orderCase.ts`

There is **no order tokeniser in TypeScript**; all lexing lives in Rust
(`crates/core/src/orders/lexer.rs`), and nothing on the TS side knows how to skip a quoted string.
This module is that knowledge, and it is the whole of the risk in this bead.

```ts
/** The words the rules know, uppercase. Built once from `client.orderVocabulary`. */
export type Vocabulary = ReadonlySet<string>;

export function buildVocabulary(words: readonly string[]): Vocabulary;

/**
 * Whether a bare word is a keyword, trying the plural spellings the core's own rule allows:
 * the word as written, then without a trailing `es`, then without a trailing `s`.
 */
export function isKeyword(word: string, vocabulary: Vocabulary): boolean;

/** The bare-word spans of one line: outside quotes, before any `;` comment. */
export function bareWords(line: string): Array<{ from: number; to: number; text: string }>;

/** One line with every keyword uppercased. Returns the line unchanged when nothing matches. */
export function uppercaseLine(line: string, vocabulary: Vocabulary): string;

/** A whole orders block, line by line. Returns the text unchanged when nothing matches. */
export function uppercaseKeywords(text: string, vocabulary: Vocabulary): string;

/**
 * The word that has just been finished at `at`, when it is a keyword worth uppercasing.
 * `null` when there is none, when it is not a keyword, or when `at` is inside a quote or a comment.
 */
export function keywordJustFinished(
  line: string,
  at: number,
  vocabulary: Vocabulary
): { from: number; to: number; upper: string } | null;
```

**`bareWords` — the exact rule**, decided here so nobody has to guess:

1. Walk the line left to right. A `;` **outside quotes** ends the line: everything from it is a
   comment and is never touched.
2. A `"` opens a quoted run that ends at the next `"`. Nothing inside is a bare word. An
   **unterminated** quote swallows the rest of the line, which is what `lex_line`
   (`crates/core/src/orders/lexer.rs:94`) does with the same input — a half-typed name must not be
   shouted at while it is being typed.
3. Everything else splits on whitespace into tokens. Strip one leading `@` (the repeat prefix) and
   any trailing `,` or `.` from a token; what remains is a bare word **only if it is entirely ASCII
   letters**. A token containing a digit or any other character — `2042`, `me@example.com`,
   `nw2` — is not a word and is never touched. This is what keeps unit ids and addresses safe, and
   it is deliberately stricter than the Rust lexer.

`isKeyword` mirrors `item_spellings` (`crates/core/src/movement/rules.rs:255`): try the uppercased
word, then it without a trailing `ES`, then without a trailing `S`. That is what makes
`give 2 longbows` produce `GIVE 2 LONGBOWS` from a vocabulary that carries only `LONGBOW`. Read
that function's doc comment before implementing — it explains why the order matters.

`uppercaseLine` replaces each matching span with `text.toUpperCase()`, right to left so the earlier
offsets stay valid.

### `packages/shared/src/settingsStore.ts`

Follow `movementPlanner` exactly — it is the nearest existing boolean:

- `orderOcd: boolean;` and `setOrderOcd: (value: boolean) => void;` in `SettingsState` (`:53-105`).
- `orderOcd` added to the `Persisted` `Pick<…>` (`:107`).
- `orderOcd: false` in `DEFAULTS` (`:194-203`) — **off by default**, agreed with the navigator.
- `orderOcd: state.orderOcd` in `partialize` (`:264-278`).

Nothing else. A plain boolean needs no reconciliation in `applyPersistedSettings` (`:286`) and no
migration: rehydration merges it verbatim, and an old stored blob without the key falls back to the
default.

### `packages/shared/src/workspace/SettingsDialog.tsx`

In `GlobalSettings` (`:182`), two selectors beside the existing pair at `:193-194`, and one toggle
beside the *Movement planner* one (`:274-280`):

```tsx
<SettingToggle
  title="Order OCD"
  description="Uppercase the command keywords as you write, so MOVE, STUDY and ALL stand out from names. Text inside quotes is left alone."
  testId="settings-order-ocd"
  checked={orderOcd}
  onChange={setOrderOcd}
/>
```

That description is the bead's own sentence, which the navigator chose to ship word for word. It
names `ALL`, and under the chosen reach that is true. `SettingToggle`'s props are
`{ title, description, testId, checked, onChange }` (`SettingToggle.tsx:1-12`); it renders the
`aria-label` from `title`.

### `packages/shared/src/workspace/AppShell.tsx`

Fetch the vocabulary the way the command list is already fetched (`:287`, `:1260-1263`), but keyed
on the ruleset as well, since the item and skill half of it comes from there:

```tsx
const [orderVocabulary, setOrderVocabulary] = useState<readonly string[]>([]);
```

with an effect on `[client, rulesetText]` calling `client.orderVocabulary(rulesetText)` and setting
the result, guarded by the same `cancelled` flag the neighbouring effect uses. `rulesetText` is
already in scope at `:290` (`ruleset.status === "ready" ? ruleset.text : null`) and is what
`argumentCompletions` passes (`:1274-1277`). Pass `orderVocabulary` down to `OrdersPanel` beside
`commands`, and on to `OrdersEditor`.

### `packages/shared/src/workspace/OrdersPanel.tsx`

Thread two new props through to the editor: `orderVocabulary: readonly string[]` from the shell, and
`orderOcd` read here with `useSettingsStore((state) => state.orderOcd)` — the panel re-renders on a
settings change, which is what keeps the editor's `latest` ref current.

### `packages/shared/src/workspace/OrdersEditor.tsx` — the behaviour

Two new props on `OrdersEditorProps`, `orderOcd: boolean` and `orderVocabulary: readonly string[]`,
both added to the `latest` ref (`:102-103`). **Read them only through `latest.current`**: the editor
is built once per `unitId` in a `useLayoutEffect` (`:105`) and deliberately not rebuilt when props
change, so a captured value would freeze at whatever it was when the unit was opened.

Derive the set once per render beside the ref assignment:
`const vocabulary = useMemo(() => buildVocabulary(orderVocabulary), [orderVocabulary]);` and put
*that* in `latest` rather than the array.

**(a) Uppercase as the word ends.** A new extension in the array at `:113`:

```ts
EditorView.inputHandler.of((view, from, to, text) => { … })
```

Return `false` — meaning "not handled, insert as usual" — unless **all** of these hold:
`latest.current.orderOcd` is true; `text` is exactly `" "` or `"\n"`; `from === to` (a plain
insertion, not a replacement). Then take the line at `from`, call
`keywordJustFinished(line.text, from - line.from, latest.current.vocabulary)`, and if it returns a
span, dispatch **one** transaction that both uppercases the span and inserts `text`, and return
`true`.

One transaction is the point: `Ctrl+Z` must put back the word as typed *and* remove the space in a
single press. Do **not** annotate it `External` — the `updateListener` at `:127-137` ignores
`External` transactions, and this change must reach `onChange` and be saved. Do **not** set
`Transaction.addToHistory.of(false)` here either; this one belongs in the history.

There is no transaction filter or input handler in this file today — this is the first, and
`EditorView.inputHandler` is the narrow hook: it sees the keystroke and nothing else, so autocomplete
acceptance, paste and the external splices at `:216-230` are untouched.

**(b) Tidy a unit's orders when it is first opened.** The navigator chose E3: switching the setting
on rewrites nothing, and a block is tidied the first time its unit is opened with the setting on. The
mount effect keyed on `unitId` (`:105`) is exactly that moment. After the view is created, if
`latest.current.orderOcd`, compute
`uppercaseKeywords(latest.current.text, latest.current.vocabulary)`; when it differs, dispatch a
replacement of the whole document with `Transaction.addToHistory.of(false)` and **no `External`
annotation**, so the `updateListener` fires, `onChange` runs and the tidied block is written to the
orders document and marked dirty. The precedent for the editor rewriting text on its own is the
trailing-newline tidy at `:255-271` — read it, and note that it *does* use `External` because that
change is editor-only. This one is not: it must be saved.

If the vocabulary has not arrived yet (an empty array while the call is in flight), the pass is a
no-op and the block is tidied at the next open. Do not add a second effect to catch that — a
retry-when-loaded pass would rewrite a document the player is already typing in.

### Where state lives

`orderOcd` is a persisted global preference in `settingsStore` — there is no per-game settings store
in this repository, so global is the only option and no scope decision arises. The vocabulary is
React state in `AppShell`, derived from the client and `rulesetText`, and is not persisted: it is a
pure function of the open ruleset. The editor holds neither; it reads both through `latest`.

## Increments

**1. The scanner and the uppercasing.** New `packages/shared/src/orderCase.test.ts`, opened by
`describe("bareWords")`:
- `it("finds the words of a plain order line")` — `move n nw` gives three spans.
- `it("never looks inside a quoted name")` — `name unit "seven of eight"` gives `name` and `unit`
  only.
- `it("stops at a comment")` — `study combat ; cheaper here` gives `study` and `combat`.
- `it("treats an unterminated quote as swallowing the rest of the line")` — `name unit "seven of`
  gives `name` and `unit`.
- `it("ignores a token that is not all letters")` — `give 2042 all silv` skips `2042`.
- `it("looks past a repeat prefix")` — `@move n` finds `move`.

Then `describe("uppercaseLine")`: `it("uppercases the keywords and leaves the names alone")`
(`name unit "seven of eight"` → `NAME UNIT "seven of eight"`),
`it("uppercases a plural item")` (`give 2 longbows` → `GIVE 2 LONGBOWS` from a vocabulary of
`["GIVE", "LONGBOW"]`), `it("leaves a word the rules do not know")`, and
`it("returns the line unchanged when nothing matches")` asserting object identity is not required
but the string is equal. Then `describe("keywordJustFinished")`:
`it("finds the word just finished")`, `it("finds nothing inside a quote")`,
`it("finds nothing in a comment")`, `it("finds nothing when the word is not a keyword")`.
Implement `orderCase.ts` to green.

**2. The setting.** In `packages/shared/src/settingsStore.test.ts`, beside
`it("persists a toggled advisory check")` (`:81`), add
`it("persists the Order OCD preference")` — default `false`, set `true`, assert it is in the
persisted blob and survives a reset-and-rehydrate the way the neighbouring test does. Then add the
field, setter, `Persisted` entry, default and `partialize` line, and the `SettingToggle` in
`GlobalSettings`.

**3. Fetching the vocabulary.** `AppShell` state, effect and prop threading through `OrdersPanel` to
`OrdersEditor`. No new unit test — `AppShell` has none and one is not worth standing up; increment 5
covers it end to end. Adding the props to `OrdersEditorProps` and not passing them is a compile
error, which is the guard here.

**4. The two editor behaviours.** The input handler and the on-open tidy. `OrdersEditor` is a
CodeMirror component with no unit test file in this repository and is covered by smoke only, so this
increment is written against increment 5's tests — write those first and watch them fail.

**5. The smoke test.** In `tests/smoke/orders-editor.spec.ts`, beside the existing typing tests
(the `selectUnit(page, unitId)` helper is at `:41`), add
`test("with Order OCD on, a keyword uppercases as the word ends and a quoted name is left alone")`:
open settings, tick `settings-order-ocd` (the pattern for reaching the dialog is in
`tests/smoke/settings.spec.ts`, e.g. `:81`), close it, select a unit, type
`name unit "seven of eight"` followed by a space, and assert the editor holds
`NAME UNIT "seven of eight"`. Then, in the same test, press `Control+z` once and assert the last
word is back as typed with no trailing space — the single-undo promise. Add a second test,
`test("with Order OCD off, nothing is uppercased")`, typing the same line with the setting in its
default state.

## The test plan

| Suite | What it pins | Command |
|---|---|---|
| `packages/shared/src/orderCase.test.ts` (new) | the scanner: quotes, comments, unterminated quotes, `@`, non-letter tokens; plural matching; the uppercasing itself | `pnpm test` |
| `packages/shared/src/settingsStore.test.ts` | the preference defaults off and persists | `pnpm test` |
| `tests/smoke/orders-editor.spec.ts` | it really fires on the space, one undo puts it back, a quoted name survives, and off means off | `pnpm test:smoke` |

`pnpm run check:fast` before the PR. Run `pnpm run test:smoke` locally too for this one — the
behaviour lives in a CodeMirror extension that no unit test reaches, so the smoke suite is the only
thing that proves it works.

## User-facing decisions

Decided with the navigator on 2026-08-17 over two rounds; mockup `docs/ui/order-ocd.html`
(scratchpad iterations were `.cerebro/scratchpad/ah-bn6.html`).

**When it fires: T1, as the word ends.** The space (or newline) after a word flips it; never
mid-word. Rejected: T2, tidying the line when the caret leaves it — "the line you are looking at is
the one that looks wrong"; T3, tidying the block when the unit is put away — you never see it work;
T4, a palette command only — it stops being the setting the bead asked for.

**How far it reaches: R2, commands and argument keywords**, and within that **K3, every word the
rules know** — the grammar's fixed words, the item tags and names, and the skill tags and names, so
`study combat` becomes `STUDY COMBAT`. Rejected: R1, commands only (`all` and `silv` stay lower,
which is half the job); K1, grammar words only; K2, grammar words and item tags but not names. K3 is
why `ah-bn6.1` exists.

**Orders already written: E3, tidied when the unit is next opened.** Rejected: E1, never touching
existing text (a half-written turn stays mixed, which is what the OCD player minds most); E2,
rewriting the whole turn on the click (one click silently rewriting every unit, with no undo across
units).

**The setting's wording: the bead's own sentence, shipped as suggested** —
`Uppercase the command keywords as you write, so MOVE, STUDY and ALL stand out from names. Text
inside quotes is left alone.` Rejected: dropping `and ALL` (only needed under R1, which was not
chosen), and a shorter sentence that also mentioned comments.

**Decided in the mockup's closing banner and not contested:** nothing inside quotes is ever changed,
including a quoted name containing a keyword; nothing after a `;` comment is changed; the setting is
**off by default**; it lives in the global settings tab; and **one `Ctrl+Z` undoes both what you
typed and what the setting did to it** — never two presses to get one word back.

**Strings, exactly as they ship:** the toggle's title is `Order OCD` and its description is the
sentence quoted above. There is no other new text — no toast, no confirmation, no menu entry.

## Out of scope

- **The vocabulary itself.** `ah-bn6.1` builds and publishes it; this bead only consumes it.
- **A palette command or a keyboard shortcut** to tidy on demand. T4 was offered and rejected;
  do not add one "as well".
- **Lower-casing, or any other formatting** — no indentation, no alignment, no comment tidying.
- **The export path.** `ordersExportText` (`workspace/ordersExport.ts`) is untouched; what is
  exported is whatever the document holds.
- **Uppercasing on import.** An imported orders file is left exactly as it arrives; only typing and
  opening a unit tidy anything.
- **Plurals in the vocabulary.** Matching handles them at the point of use, by the three spellings;
  nothing is added to `ah-bn6.1`'s list.
- **A per-game version of the setting.** There is no per-game preference store, and adding one is
  not this bead.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
pnpm run test:smoke
```

By eye, with a game and a ruleset open:

1. Settings → the global tab shows **Order OCD**, off. Tick it.
2. Select a unit and type `move n nw` — `move` becomes `MOVE` the moment the space lands, then `N`,
   then `NW` when you type the space after it. Nothing changes mid-word.
3. Type `name unit "seven of eight"` and a space. `NAME UNIT` shouts; the quoted name does not.
4. Type `study combat ; cheaper here` — `STUDY COMBAT` uppercases, the comment does not.
5. Type `give 2042 all silv` — `GIVE ALL SILV` uppercase, `2042` untouched.
6. Press `Ctrl+Z` once after a word has been uppercased: the word comes back as you typed it and the
   space goes, in one press.
7. Select another unit whose orders are in lower case, with the setting on: its block is uppercased
   as it opens, and the draft is dirty (it is a real change, and it saves).
8. Turn the setting off. Typing changes nothing, and a unit opened afterwards is left alone.

## Known traps

- **`latest.current` or nothing.** The editor is built once per `unitId` (`OrdersEditor.tsx:105`)
  and is deliberately not rebuilt when props change. A setting or vocabulary captured directly in
  the extension closure freezes at mount, so toggling the setting would appear to do nothing until
  the unit is changed.
- **`External` suppresses `onChange`.** The `updateListener` at `:127-137` returns early when every
  transaction carries the `External` annotation. Both changes in this bead must be saved, so neither
  may use it — unlike the trailing-newline tidy at `:255-271`, which is editor-only and correctly
  does.
- **One transaction, or two undo presses.** Uppercasing the word and inserting the space must be a
  single dispatch. Two dispatches give the player a `Ctrl+Z` that removes the space and leaves the
  word shouting, which is exactly the "possessed editor" feeling T1 was chosen despite.
- **The unterminated quote.** A name is a half-typed quote for as long as it takes to write, so a
  scanner that only recognises *closed* quotes will shout at every word of a name as it is typed.
  `lex_line` (`crates/core/src/orders/lexer.rs:94`) treats an unterminated quote as running to the
  end of the line; do the same.
- **`item_spellings` strips, it does not generate** (`crates/core/src/movement/rules.rs:255`), and
  its doc comment insists the three spellings are tried in order. Match a typed word by trying its
  spellings against the set — never by trying to manufacture plurals into the set.
- **Only whole ASCII-letter tokens.** A token with a digit or a symbol is left alone, which is what
  keeps `2042`, `nw2` and an email address safe. Splitting tokens on punctuation instead looks
  tidier and is how `n@example.com` acquires an `N`.
- **`vite preview` without `--strictPort`** silently serves another agent's bundle; if a smoke run
  behaves as though the code is not there, check that first.
- **The smoke suite rebuilds the web bundle with the service worker disabled**, so a PWA run
  straight after a smoke run fails with timeouts that look like a broken worker. Not this bead's
  fault when it happens.
