title: A Whirlpool draws as a building, because the lair kinds are enumerated and omit it
description:
Found during verification of ah-o0d3 (2026-08-21, origin/main 19f93c3). That bead passed - `Lair` and `Ruin` in `neworigins-3.0.0-g7-f39-t17.rep` now draw lair marks, which is the first time that mark has ever appeared from a real report - and this is the follow-up filed alongside the pass.

## What the player sees

A **Whirlpool** draws as a **building**. The navigator, verifying ah-o0d3: "Lairs seems to be drawn as buildings. E.g. Whirlpool is drawn as a building" - and, once the Lair case was confirmed working, "should not Whirlpool be as well?"

## The cause

`LAIR_KINDS` (`packages/shared/src/workspace/mapThemes/hexView.ts:69`) is:

    lair, cave, ruin, ruins, barrow, crypt, tomb, pit

`whirlpool` is not in it, so it falls through to `building` in `classify()`. This is independent of ah-o0d3's comma defect: that bead made `Whirlpool, closed to player units` resolve to `whirlpool`, and the set then has nothing to match it with. One bug sat on top of the other, which is why the symptom survived the fix.

## Why it looks like the same class of thing

Every fixture line for these structures has the identical shape - a name, a kind, and the same qualifying clause:

    + Lair [1] : Lair, closed to player units.
    + Ruin [1] : Ruin, closed to player units.
    + Crypt [1] : Crypt, closed to player units.
    + Whirlpool [1] : Whirlpool, closed to player units.

A Whirlpool is closed to player units, cannot be built, and is a feature of the world rather than anyone's structure - exactly what the other members of the set are. My recommendation is that it belongs in `LAIR_KINDS`.

**But the mark is called "lair", and that is the navigator's decision, not mine.** Worth putting to them at planning:

- whether a Whirlpool should share the lair mark, or earn one of its own - it is the only sea feature among a set of caves and tombs, and a player scanning for "somewhere a monster lives" may not want it answered by a whirlpool;
- whether the **Lairs badge** should govern it, which follows from whichever mark it gets;
- **whether the set should be enumerated at all.** Every kind qualified "closed to player units" is arguably the real category, and matching on that clause would catch whatever the engine adds next. Against it: the clause is prose from the report and would couple the map to its wording, which is the same class of coupling ah-o0d3 was filed to remove.

## A second finding, about the plan rather than the code

ah-o0d3's own acceptance step 1 said: "Find a hex holding a **Lair**, a **Ruin** or a **Crypt**" in the turn-71 report. **That report contains none of the three.** Its only lair-type structures are two Whirlpools:

    $ grep -iE ': *(Lair|Crypt|Ruin|Whirlpool),' tests/fixtures/reports/neworigins-3.0.0-g7-f95-t71.rep
    + Whirlpool [1] : Whirlpool, closed to player units.
    + Whirlpool [1] : Whirlpool, closed to player units.

So the bead's headline acceptance was unperformable against the report it named, and following it exactly is what produced a "failed" first impression of a fix that works. `g7-f39-t17` (Lair and Ruin), `g3-f42-t42` (Lair) and `g5-f21-t25` (Crypt) are the fixtures that actually exercise it. Whoever plans this should name one of those, and it is worth a moment's thought about how a plan comes to cite a fixture nobody checked held the case.

## Acceptance

A Whirlpool draws whatever mark the navigator chooses for it, in all four themes, and obeys whichever badge governs that mark. The regression test uses a fixture that genuinely contains the structure it claims to.
close_reason: Covered by ah-lcyn, which Storm built as PR #502. ah-lcyn's acceptance names Whirlpool explicitly, alongside Ice Cave, Demon Pit, Bog, Empowered Altar, Giant's Castle and Magician's Tower, all caught by matching the report's own 'closed to player units' marker. Storm confirms Whirlpool is covered and tested there. The three design questions raised here - whether a Whirlpool shares the lair mark, whether the Lairs badge governs it, and whether the set should be enumerated at all - were put to the navigator on 2026-08-21 while planning ah-lcyn and answered: match the marker, everything closed to player units draws as a lair. Closed by the navigator's decision, 2026-08-21. Its second finding, that ah-o0d3's validation named turn-71 for a Lair/Ruin/Crypt that report does not contain, was correct and is my error; ah-lcyn's plan has been amended in place with a measured map of which fixture holds which case.

title: Advisory-check fixtures declare the check they are about, instead of running all 23
description:
The large half of ah-11lh, split out deliberately. ah-11lh does the cheap subset - the corpus per-code expectation table and named fields for the silencing cases; this is the ~200-fixture change it declined.

## What it would do

Make the seam opt-in instead of opt-out: a Rust fixture declares the code it is about, so the other 22 checks cannot perturb it. That retires the four opt-OUT helpers the test module has accreted, one per over-broad check - check, check_ignoring_transfer_targets, check_ignoring_empty_builds, check_idle (crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs:2686 onwards) - rather than adding a fifth each time a check turns out to be broad.

It would also address the half ah-11lh explicitly left alone: the smoke suite's ~85 exact-count assertions against the single turn-71 report in workspace.spec.ts, silenced today by clicking through the Settings dialog. That is the expensive half, because check:fast does not run the browser suites, so a break there costs a sharded CI round trip rather than a local rerun.

## Why it is P4 and not queued behind ah-11lh

Forge's own note for triage on ah-11lh argues this may cost more than it saves, and the planner agreed:

- every incident was a TRUE POSITIVE - the fixtures were under-specified and the new check was right about them. No bead was handed back; no human escalation blamed the code.
- ~200 fixtures is a mechanical rewrite of the tests that protect the checks, which is the highest-risk place in the repository for a large mechanical change and the one where a mistake is least visible.
- 11 of the 23 codes landed inside one sweep, so "every future check pays this" may extrapolate from a spike that is over.

## What would justify raising it

Evidence that the cost recurs after ah-11lh lands. ah-bwly is the next new-advisory-check bead in the backlog; if it pays the same fixture-migration cost with the corpus table already in place, that is the third sighting after the fix and the argument is made. Record it here rather than rediscovering it.

title: A split child inherits the planning label and reads as abandoned to the other planner
description:
Found by Xavier on 2026-08-17, twice in one session.

## What happens

`bd create --parent <id>` copies the parent's labels onto the child. A planner marks its candidate with `planning` before splitting it, so every child of that split is created already carrying `planning` - a label nobody chose to put there.

Two costs, both paid today:

1. **The labels have to be cleared by hand.** Xavier split ah-do8 into three children; all three came out labelled `planning`, and were excluded from every candidate query until noticed and cleared one by one.
2. **The other planner reads them as abandoned.** plan-bead's reclaim check (`SKILL.md`, 'Reclaiming a label nobody is holding') frees a `planning` label that no live planner names in its state file. A planner mid-split names only the child it is planning now - Beast's state file said `ah-bn6.1` while `ah-bn6.2` sat labelled - so the sibling looks abandoned and the rule says to free it. Xavier stopped at the 'say what you are about to free before you free it' step; the mechanical answer was wrong.

The second is the dangerous one: freeing it hands one planner's candidate to the other, which is the exact failure the label exists to prevent.

## Shape of a fix, for planning to settle

- The splitting planner removes `planning` from every child as it creates them, and plan-bead says so where it says to split. Simplest; relies on a step being remembered at the one moment a planner is busiest.
- `bd create --parent` is told not to inherit this particular label - a `--no-inherit-labels` flag or similar, if bd has one. Upstream, and not ours.
- The reclaim check treats a child whose parent a live planner is holding as held. Precise, and more logic in a check that has to stay simple enough to trust.

## Where
.claude/cerebro/skills/plan-bead/SKILL.md - the split section and the reclaim section.

## Validation
A planner splits a bead it holds; the children carry no `planning` label. The other planner's reclaim check frees nothing while the first is mid-split.
design:
## Context

`bd create --parent <id>` copies the parent's labels onto the child — "inherits parent labels", as
`bd`'s own help puts it. A planner marks its candidate with `planning` **before** it does anything
else (`plan-bead`'s *Choosing what to plan*: "Label before you think"), so by the time it splits that
bead, every child is created already carrying `planning` — a label nobody chose to put there.

Two costs, both paid on 2026-08-17:

1. **The labels have to be cleared by hand.** Xavier split `ah-do8` into three children; all three came
   out labelled `planning` and were excluded from every candidate query — `bd list --exclude-label
   planning` is how both planners choose work — until it was noticed and cleared one bead at a time.
2. **The other planner reads them as abandoned.** *Reclaiming a label nobody is holding* frees a
   `planning` label that no live planner names in its state file. A planner mid-split names only the
   child it is planning *now*: Beast's state file said `ah-bn6.1` while `ah-bn6.2` sat labelled, so the
   sibling looked abandoned and the rule said to free it.

The second is the dangerous one — freeing it hands one planner's candidate to the other, which is the
single thing the label exists to prevent. It was caught only because the same section says *"say what
you are about to free before you free it, and the navigator can stop you"*, and the mechanical answer
was wrong.

All of the work is in the **`.claude/cerebro` submodule** (`rmstdope/cerebro`), in
`skills/plan-bead/SKILL.md`. See *Known traps*.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

The navigator chose (2026-08-17): **the splitting planner clears the label as it creates the
children.** The fix goes where the labels appear.

### `skills/plan-bead/SKILL.md` — *Too big for one increment* (line 688)

After the `bd create --parent` instruction and its priority paragraph (lines 690–695), before "The
children then queue like anything else":

> **Take `planning` off every child as you create them.** `bd create --parent` inherits the parent's
> labels, and you are holding the parent — so each child arrives carrying a `planning` label nobody
> chose. That excludes it from every candidate query, including your own, and makes it look abandoned
> to the other planner, whose reclaim check names only the child you happen to be planning right now
> (ah-3ox, twice in one session).
>
> ```bash
> bd update <child> <child> ... --remove-label planning
> bd dolt push
> ```
>
> In the same breath as the `bd dep add` edges, before you plan any of them. The parent keeps its
> label until you retype it as an epic and drop it with the rest.

`bd update` takes several ids at once, as the priority-reconciliation snippet in the triage section
already shows — use that form so it is one call and cannot be half-done.

### `skills/plan-bead/SKILL.md` — *Reclaiming a label nobody is holding*

One sentence, so the check's remaining false positive is named where somebody meets it:

> **A just-split family is the one shape that fools this.** A planner mid-split names one child in its
> state file while its siblings carry the label they inherited, so a sibling reads as abandoned when
> it is not. The rule above — say what you are about to free before you free it — is what catches it,
> and the split section is what stops it arising. If you see a labelled bead whose parent another
> planner is holding, leave it alone and say so.

### `skills/plan-bead/SKILL.md` — *Finishing one, and the session*

That section already warns that the `planning` list "is not all yours". Add the family to its
examples in the same breath: a child of a bead the other planner holds is theirs, whatever the state
files say.

### Nothing else

- **No script, no elisp, no code.** This is an agent's instructions, and the agent is the runtime.
- **The reclaim check itself is unchanged.** The navigator rejected making it parent-aware: it has to
  stay simple enough to trust at a glance, and the "say before you free" guard already caught this.
- **No change to `bd`.** Whether `bd create --parent` could be told not to inherit is upstream and
  was rejected as not ours.

## Increments

One. There is no test harness for `agents/*.md` or `skills/*/SKILL.md`; the cerebro repo's CI covers
elisp and scripts, and this bead adds neither.

**What stands in for a test** is the walk-through in *Validation*: split a bead in the live backlog and
show that the children come out unlabelled. That is the same discipline ah-cg1 and ah-60w used for the
same kind of change, and the before/after belongs in the PR body.

## The test plan

No automated test.

| Check | How | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| The children come out clean | Split a held bead, then `bd list --label planning --status open` | Only the parent is listed, not the children |
| The reclaim check finds nothing | Run *Reclaiming a label nobody is holding*'s `comm -23` while mid-split | Empty, where today it names the siblings |
| Both sections agree | Read them | The split section says to clear, the reclaim section says a split family is the shape that fools it, and neither contradicts the other |

## User-facing decisions

Fleet tooling — nothing a player sees — but it changes how the two planners behave, so the navigator
chose it (2026-08-17):

> **The splitting planner clears the label as it creates the children.** One instruction at the moment
> the labels appear, no new logic anywhere.

*Rejected: making the reclaim check treat a held parent as holding its children* — precise and it
survives a planner that forgets, but it puts more reasoning into the one check that has to stay simple
enough to trust at a glance. *Rejected: both* — belt and braces for a failure that has happened twice,
at the cost of two changes to keep in step. *Rejected: stopping `bd` inheriting the label* — the
cleanest place, and upstream rather than ours.

The accepted cost, stated plainly: **this relies on a step being remembered at the moment a planner is
busiest.** The reclaim section's "say before you free" guard stays as the net under it, which is why
the second edit above is part of this bead and not a nicety.

## Out of scope

- **Any change to the reclaim check's logic.**
- **`bd`'s label inheritance.**
- **The `planning` label's role generally** — it stays the planners' only coordination, uncla imed and
  unleased, for the reasons `plan-bead` gives at length.
- **`ah-bn6.1`/`ah-bn6.2` and `ah-do8`'s children**, the beads that exposed this. Already cleared by
  hand.
- **Whether an implementer's labels inherit the same way.** They do not use `--parent` while holding a
  claim, so the shape does not arise — worth a sentence in the PR body, not a change.

## Validation

From the main checkout, with a bead you are actually splitting:

```bash
bd list --label planning --status open --json | jq -r '.[].id'   # before: the parent alone
# ... bd create --parent, bd dep add, bd update <children> --remove-label planning ...
bd list --label planning --status open --json | jq -r '.[].id'   # after: still the parent alone
```

Both outputs in the PR body. Then the check only a person can make: read the split section as a
planner who has just decided a bead is too big, and satisfy yourself that the clearing step is
impossible to miss at that moment — it is the whole of the fix, and if it reads as an aside it will be
skipped.

## Known traps

- **This bead lives in another git repository.** `.claude/cerebro` is a submodule of
  `rmstdope/cerebro`: branch, commit and open the PR **inside the submodule**, then a second small PR
  in `atlantis-hud` bumps the pointer (`chore(ah-3ox): bump cerebro to …`, precedent `d014de2`).
- **The instructions are the runtime.** Vagueness here is the defect, not a style problem: a planner
  does what the skill says, and this fix is one sentence that has to survive being read in a hurry.
- **Do not tell the planner to clear the parent's label too.** It is still holding the parent until the
  family is split and the parent is retyped as an epic; clearing it early hands the parent to the other
  planner mid-split, which is this bug with the parties reversed.
- **`plan-bead` is edited by more than one bead at a time** — ah-bqi and ah-cg1 both touched the
  cerebro repo today. Rebase before opening the PR.
close_reason: Delivered in cerebro PR #56, pointer bumped in PR #414

title: The ruleset carries what a skill requires before it can be studied
description:
Split out of ah-3ej's planning (2026-08-17), and narrowed after checking the source.

STUDY completion narrows to the skills a unit can study, but only by the two facts the ruleset carries today: a skill the data page prices nowhere cannot be studied at all, and a skill the unit has already taken to its maximum cannot be studied further. What it cannot do is drop a skill whose prerequisites the unit has not met.

**The data page states them**, in each skill's own description, 65 times in the committed fixture:

    This skill requires force [FORC] 1 to begin to study.
    This skill requires force [FORC] 1 and pattern [PATT] 1 to begin to study.

Nothing scrapes them. So this bead is: read them into SkillEntry, and add the third filter to the completion.

**Per-unit-type permissions are not in the bead any more.** ah-3ej's description asked for 'which kinds of unit may learn a skill' as well; the data page states no such rule anywhere - no 'only leaders', no 'may be studied by' - so there is no source to read and nothing to plan. If that rule exists it lives in the rules page's prose or in the engine, and finding it is a separate investigation.

Filed at P4, unranked, for the navigator to rank at triage.
design:
## Context

Split out of ah-3ej's planning (2026-08-17) and narrowed after checking the source.

ah-3ej narrows `STUDY` completion to the skills a unit can study, but only by the two facts the
ruleset carries: a skill the data page prices nowhere cannot be studied at all, and a skill the unit
has already taken to its maximum cannot be studied further. **What it cannot do is drop a skill whose
prerequisites the unit has not met** — so a fresh mage is still offered the whole magic tree, and the
turn fails on whatever was picked.

**The data page states the prerequisites**, in each skill's own description. Checked against the
committed fixture `tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-data.html` while planning:

- **66 statements**, all of one form: `This skill requires <requirements> to begin to study.`
- **32** name one requirement — `force [FORC] 1`
- **34** name two, joined by ` and ` — `force [FORC] 1 and pattern [PATT] 1`
- **No other wording**, and no three-requirement form.

So the grammar is tiny and the whole bead is: read them, carry them, filter by them.

**Per-unit-type permissions are not in this bead.** ah-3ej's description also asked for "which kinds
of unit may learn a skill". The data page states no such rule anywhere — no "only leaders", no "may be
studied by", nothing keyed to a unit's kind — so there is no source to read. If the rule exists it
lives in the rules page's prose or in the engine, and finding it is a separate investigation, not a
scrape.

**Depends on ah-3ej**, which creates the `skill_completions(ruleset, unit)` signature and the
`level_of` helper this bead's filter uses.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

### `packages/ruleset/src/data.ts`

`parseSkillReference` (line 476) walks the same `entryParagraphs` as the item parser and already reads
each skill's cost and cast cost. It gains one more field, in the same tolerant style — a skill whose
requirement sentence cannot be read keeps its other fields rather than stopping the run.

```ts
/** A skill a unit must already have before it may begin another, as the data page states it. */
export type SkillRequirement = { tag: string; level: number };
```

on the skill entry as `requires: SkillRequirement[]` — empty for the majority that state none.

The parse, from the paragraph:

```ts
  // `This skill requires force [FORC] 1 to begin to study.` and, for half of them,
  // `... force [FORC] 1 and pattern [PATT] 1 to begin to study.` Sixty-six statements in the
  // committed page and no third form, so ` and ` is the whole of the separator grammar.
  const stated = paragraph.match(/This skill requires (.+?) to begin to study\./);
  const requires = stated
    ? stated[1]
        .split(" and ")
        .flatMap((clause) => {
          const part = clause.match(/\[([A-Z0-9]{2,6})\]\s+(\d+)/);
          return part ? [{ tag: part[1], level: Number(part[2]) }] : [];
        })
    : [];
```

Matching on the **tag and the number** rather than on the skill's name keeps this independent of how
the name is spelled, and `flatMap` drops a clause that does not parse rather than inventing a level.

### `crates/core/src/movement/rules.rs`

`SkillEntry` (line 297) gains:

```rust
    /// What a unit must already have before it may begin this skill, as the data page's
    /// `This skill requires force [FORC] 1 to begin to study.` states it. Empty for a skill with no
    /// prerequisites, and for a ruleset scraped before they were read.
    #[serde(default)]
    pub requires: Vec<SkillRequirement>,
```

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
pub struct SkillRequirement {
    pub tag: String,
    pub level: u32,
}
```

`#[serde(default)]` for the reason every other field on this struct has one: a ruleset cached before
this bead must still load.

### `crates/core/src/orders/completion.rs`

`skill_completions` (as ah-3ej leaves it) gains a third filter beside the two it already has:

```rust
        .filter(|skill| meets_requirements(unit, skill))
```

```rust
/// Whether the unit already has everything the skill asks for.
///
/// True when the ruleset states no requirements, and true when there is no unit to judge - the
/// same rule the ceiling filter follows, and what keeps the answer sensible when the report cannot
/// be read (ah-3ej).
fn meets_requirements(unit: Option<&ReportUnit>, skill: &SkillEntry) -> bool {
    skill.requires.iter().all(|required| {
        level_of(unit, required).is_some_and(|level| level >= required.level)
    })
}
```

`level_of` is ah-3ej's, and takes the tag to look up — check its signature when this bead is built and
widen it to take a tag rather than a `SkillEntry` if that is what it turned out to be. Whichever, the
case-insensitive tag match must be the same one, for the same reason.

**Note the asymmetry, and keep it**: no unit means *offer* the skill (nothing is known to be missing),
while a unit that is present and lacks the prerequisite means *hide* it. That matches ah-3ej's ceiling
filter exactly.

### `config/public/ruleset.json`

Re-scraped and committed, which `committed.test.ts` enforces:

```bash
pnpm --filter @atlantis/ruleset scrape -- \
  --rules tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-rules.html \
  --data tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-data.html
```

Expect 66 skills to gain a non-empty `requires`.

## Increments

1. **The scrape.** RED: the four `parseSkillReference` tests below. GREEN: the parse and the type.
2. **The core carries it.** RED: `committed.test.ts` fails against the regenerated file. GREEN: the
   Rust field, and the committed `ruleset.json`.
3. **The completion uses it.** RED: the three `skill_completions` tests. GREEN: `meets_requirements`.

## The test plan

| Test | File | What it pins |
|---|---|---|
| `reads a single prerequisite` | `packages/ruleset/src/data.test.ts` | `force [FORC] 1` → `[{ tag: "FORC", level: 1 }]` |
| `reads two prerequisites joined by and` | same | `force [FORC] 1 and pattern [PATT] 1` → both, in order |
| `a skill with no prerequisite states none` | same | `requires: []`, not absent |
| `an unreadable clause is dropped, not guessed` | same | A malformed clause yields no requirement and does not throw — the tolerant style this parser already keeps |
| `study_hides_a_skill_whose_requirement_the_unit_lacks` | `crates/core/src/orders/completion.rs` | Unit with no `FORC` → a skill requiring `FORC 1` is not offered |
| `study_offers_a_skill_whose_requirement_the_unit_meets` | same | Unit at `FORC 2` → a skill requiring `FORC 1` is offered |
| `study_offers_a_skill_with_no_requirements` | same | Unchanged for the majority |
| `study_without_a_unit_offers_a_skill_with_requirements` | same | The asymmetry above |
| `is exactly what the scraper produces from the committed fixture pages` | `committed.test.ts` | The regenerated artefact |

Suites: `pnpm -r run test`, `cargo test --workspace`, and `pnpm run check:generated` — all inside
`pnpm run check:fast`.

## User-facing decisions

**None to ask.** The visible effect is that the `STUDY` list gets shorter in exactly the way the
navigator already chose for ah-3ej: a skill the unit cannot study is absent, with no explanation and
no greyed-out row. This bead adds a third reason for absence and no new behaviour, wording or control.

Recorded so it is not re-opened: ah-3ej settled that a row reads `COMB` with a dimmed
`combat · 45 silver · at 3`, that a skill never studied omits the level, and that unavailable skills
are simply not offered. All three still hold.

**Worth telling Psylocke**: after this bead a fresh mage is offered only the handful of magic skills
it can actually begin, rather than the whole tree. That is a large and intended change in what the
list contains.

## Out of scope

- **Per-unit-type permissions.** No source; see *Context*.
- **`cannot be studied via normal means`**, which five skills state in words and which `cost: None`
  already encodes — ah-3ej's first filter covers them.
- **Teaching.** A teacher changes how fast a unit studies, not what it may begin.
- **Warning about a prerequisite in the order checks.** `semantics.rs` says nothing about
  prerequisites today and this bead does not change that — the completion stops *offering* an
  impossible skill; typing one by hand is still unwarned. A fair follow-up, filed separately if
  wanted.
- **ah-9js**, which moves the buildings table to the data page. Same file, different entries, no
  overlap — but expect to rebase.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run check:fast
```

Then read the artefact and the application: `jq '.skills.FORC' config/public/ruleset.json` shows no
requirements, `jq '[.skills[] | select(.requires | length > 0)] | length'` is 66, and in the
application a unit with no magic skills typing `STUDY ` is offered the skills it can begin — not the
whole catalogue and not the whole magic tree.

## Known traps

- **Match the tag, not the name.** `force [FORC] 1` gives both; the tag is stable and the name's
  spelling is the page's business.
- **` and ` is the only separator**, and there is no three-requirement form in the committed page.
  Splitting on commas as well would be inventing a grammar the page does not use — if a future page
  grows one, the test that pins two-requirement parsing is what will fail first.
- **`#[serde(default)]` is not optional.** A ruleset cached before this bead has no `requires`, and
  without the default it fails to load — the same trap ah-a2k.1 and ah-a2k.3 both had to handle.
- **The no-unit case offers the skill.** Inverting it empties the list for anyone whose report cannot
  be read, which is the failure ah-3ej's plan calls out explicitly.
- **`level_of` is ah-3ej's and must be shared, not copied.** Two case-insensitive tag lookups that can
  disagree is precisely the drift this repository files refactoring beads about.

title: A fleet with enough sailors is warned it is short of them
description:
Found while planning ah-eet, on a real fixture report, not from reading the code.

The 'fleet-undercrewed' check sums each aboard unit's sailing skill *level*, once per unit
(crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs, check_sailing: '.flat_map(|ordered| ordered.unit.skills.iter())
.filter(tag == SAIL).map(level).sum()'). The engine counts a level per *man*: a unit of 2 gnolls at
sailing 1 supplies 2 sailing levels, not 1.

Evidence, tests/fixtures/reports/neworigins-3.0.0-g5-f21-t24.rep:1359-1362 --

    + Ship [235] : Raft; Load: 220/450; Sailors: 2/2; MaxSpeed: 2.
      * Drones (10575), ... 2 gnolls [GNOL], 2180 silver [SILV]. Weight: 20.
        Skills: sailing [SAIL] 1 (30).
      * Drones (10594), ... 20 gnolls [GNOL]. Weight: 200. Skills: fishing [FISH] 1 (30).

The server states Sailors: 2/2 -- two levels aboard, two needed, so this Raft sails, and it does
sail in that turn's own orders template (line 2353, 'sail se ne'). Our sum is 1, so we warn
'Raft [235] is short of sailors: 1 sailing levels aboard, it needs 2, so it will not sail'. That is
a false warning on a committed fixture, against a fleet that sailed.

The rules agree with the server: 'The sailors are the number of skill levels of the Sailing skill
that must be aboard the ship' (tests/fixtures/ruleset/neworigins-rules.html:3747-3752), and a
unit's skill level is held by each of its men.

Why it went unnoticed: every unit in the Longship fixture ah-j0e was built against holds exactly
one man (neworigins-3.0.0-g3-f42-t41.rep:2018-2025 -- one centaur at SAIL 2, one centaur at SAIL 2,
Sailors: 4/4), where per-unit and per-man agree. Every unit fixture in the semantics tests has
men: 1 for the same reason.

The fix is one multiplication -- level * unit.men -- plus a test with a multi-man crew, and the
same question should be asked of movement/mode.rs:220 crew_sailing_levels, which the route planner
uses and which sums the same way. Direction of the defect: false warnings, on every fleet crewed by
units of more than one man, which is most of them.

Not ah-eet's scope: that bead is the load half of this check, and touches nothing on the crew side.
acceptance_criteria: A fleet whose aboard units supply enough sailing levels counted per man is not warned. The Raft [235] case from neworigins-3.0.0-g5-f21-t24.rep is silent. A unit of N men at sailing level L contributes N*L. crew_sailing_levels in movement/mode.rs is checked for the same defect and fixed or explicitly excluded with a reason.
close_reason: Superseded by ah-j0e, which Psylocke reopened at P0 for the same defect (sailing levels summed per unit, not per man). ah-paj's evidence - the g5-f21-t24 fixture, the rules quote and why the Longship fixture hid it - is copied into ah-j0e's notes. Navigator's decision, 2026-08-17.

title: Warn when a DECLARE order names the unit's own faction
description:
Filed by the corpus investigation ah-v25.

## Evidence
`DECLARE: Can't declare towards your own faction.` - 2 occurrences across 2 turns of 1 game in
tests/fixtures/reports/ (docs/order-checks/corpus-errors.generated.md). A DECLARE order named the
faction's own id.

## What the check would need
From the report: the faction's own id (`ReportHeader.faction_id`). From the orders: the DECLARE
order's target faction id.

## What it must not do
Never blocking; accept on doubt (crates/core/src/orders/semantics.rs:1-17) - though this check has
no doubtful case: the faction's own id is always known once the report has been read.

## Validation
A DECLARE naming the faction's own id warns. A DECLARE naming any other faction stays silent.
close_reason: Navigator at triage 2026-08-16: not a real error worth a check — a DECLARE towards your own faction is refused harmlessly.

title: Refactoring: every harness change is two PRs and a bump; five retrospectives paid for it
description:
## The cost being paid
The harness lives in a submodule under .claude/cerebro, so every harness bead is a cerebro PR plus a consumer pointer bump, every fresh worktree has an empty .claude/cerebro until somebody remembers to init it, and every path to a script is a literal `.claude/cerebro/scripts/…` in prose. Fourteen consumer commits touch only the pointer in two days (twelve "bump cerebro to …", the move, and a repoint after cerebro's history was rewritten). Five of the twelve retrospectives on main name the submodule as the reason a run cost time — about 32 minutes plus a detached superproject HEAD and one PR closed unmerged — and three of them are the same trap paid by three implementers, whose prevention (one line in the skill) has still not landed.

## Evidence
- git log --first-parent -- .claude/cerebro: 8049f17 (the move: "between the two commits this repository had no way to start an agent at all"), 1d92e5e (repoint: the pinned sha "no longer exists on any branch there, so git submodule update --init on a fresh clone had nothing to fetch"), and 12 bump commits (be6f8fa … 150ba17)
- docs/retrospectives/ah-4ao.md §"A fresh implementer worktree does not carry an initialized submodule" (5 min); ah-axj.md (5 min, "Seen before: ah-4ao — identical symptom, identical fix, same missing step"); ah-aao.md (10 min plus a detached superproject HEAD, "the second implementer to pay for that gap")
- docs/retrospectives/ah-u3i.md §"The bump PR's diff went empty under me while it waited for CI" (10 min; #258 closed unmerged after #256 absorbed the same sha)
- docs/retrospectives/ah-3bl.md §"git -C .claude/cerebro worktree add with a relative target path nests the worktree inside the submodule" ("every implementer doing one of these bumps runs this exact command shape")
- grep 'submodule update' .claude/cerebro/skills/implement-bead/SKILL.md → no hits, after three retrospectives asked for it
- bead ah-p31 description had to weigh "a dedicated worktree … costs a full build and a submodule init, and the fleet has recorded worktree/submodule trouble twice already" as a design constraint

## Where
.claude/cerebro (gitlink); .gitmodules; .claude/cerebro/skills/implement-bead/SKILL.md (Workspace, two-PR delivery); the run-* launchers' hard-coded paths

## What a refactoring would change
Take the choreography out of every implementer's hands: one script that creates an implementer worktree (worktree add + submodule init + pnpm install) and one that delivers a cerebro change (cerebro PR, then the bump PR against the merged sha, closing cleanly if a peer's bump already carries it) — or fold the harness back in if the reuse the submodule buys is not being used. Xavier's call with the navigator; the cost is what Bishop can say.

Filed by Bishop, weekly sweep of 2026-08-15 (first sweep, whole of origin/main), range e60bbbd..150ba17.
close_reason: Navigator (2026-08-15): invalid - the harness must stay its own repository, because cerebro will be consumed by other repositories too; the submodule split is deliberate.
